Title: Welcome Speech in Conjunction with the Launch of Financial Awareness Week 2009
text: Governor's Speech at the Second Seminar on "Inflation and Its Impact on Society - The Islamic Solution" Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Ahmad Mohd Don Speech/Interview Date: 06 Jul 1996 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English I am pleased to be invited this morning to officiate this second workshop on "Inflation and its impact on society - the Islamic solution". I would like to take this opportunity to extend a warm welcome to all participants, particularly those who are visiting Malaysia for the first time. Gauging from the outcome of the first workshop which I attended in Jeddah, last December, I am confident that this workshop will prove equally interesting and enlightening. Having already deliberated on the concepts, causes and impact of inflation, this workshop will provide another forum for participants, Syariah scholars, economists and bankers from all over the world to examine additional pertinent issues related to inflation. I believe that, at the conclusion of the workshop, the wisdom of the distinguished participants will be able to put forward an Islamic solution to the macroeconomic challenge that lies before us. In the meantime, I would like to endeavour to outline my own thoughts on price stability, the role of the central bank in this process and finally, the roles of the government and private sector in achieving this objective. Inflation is an issue that has been the subject of many debates and conferences. You may ask, why has there been and is there still concern over controlling inflation? Why is it important for an economy to achieve price stability, and direct effort to maintain this stability? Inflation has been recognised as a destabilising phenomenon, based on experience in the 1970s and early 1980s, arising from the two oil shocks and virulent inflation. World inflation averaged only about 3% in the decade of the 1950s. The rate, however, rose to 10% in the 1970s and was on average 20% in the last five years. The high global rates reflected mainly the experience in the developing nations while industrial countries witnessed relatively lower inflation. In the case of the Islamic countries, the inflation rate increased fivefold to 20% between the 1950s and the first half of the 1990s. Within the group of Islamic countries, the experience is somewhat mixed. Countries like Turkey, Sudan and Nigeria experienced high inflation while others like Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Malaysia witnessed low inflation. I hardly need to stress the dangers and costs of inflation. Inflation is not only a source of uncertainty, inefficiency and distortions, but also hampers decision-making and planning, and removes the incentive to save. If inflation is not contained in the initial stages, it can become firmly entrenched and would eventually undermine economic growth. On the other hand, there are many benefits to maintaining price stability. Firstly, price stability leads to efficient resource allocation and enhances economic welfare. Secondly, price stability improves business sentiment. Thirdly, stability in prices helps to retain the purchasing power of money, thereby providing the incentive to save. Fourthly and most importantly, it is only in an environment of price stability that economic growth can be sustained. Indeed, historically, countries with price stability generally experienced higher growth. Developments in Latin America in contrast to those in Asia in the past decade is testimony to this. This is certainly true for the Malaysian experience as well. Growth has taken place in an environment of relative price stability, evidenced from the average annual rate of inflation of 3% over the past three decades. The track record in containing inflation is testimony of the commitment of the Malaysian authorities to price stability. I must say, however, that such commitment requires great patience to pursue consistent policies. The commitment must be evident, whether during the period of slack in the economy or when pressures build up in the economy. Only in this way can the authorities gain and maintain a credible long-term commitment to price stability. May I add at this juncture that the attainment and maintainance of price stability remains important regardless of the types of economic systems - whether free market economies, planned economies or Islamic economies. Inflation is a phenomenon experienced in all these economies. The central bank has an important role in achieving the objective of price stability. In fact, in recent years, a view that is gaining importance is that monetary policy should only aim at achieving price stability. Objectives of monetary policy have become clearer, focusing in the main on reducing inflation and achieving price stability. The importance given to price stability is not for its own sake but rather a means to enhance economic welfare and growth, and thereby a favourable standard of living. The basic and primary concern of a central bank is to protect and preserve both the internal and external value of the nation's currency. Money will retain its domestic value only if prices remain stable. This task of the central bank of maintaining monetary stability, has in recent years, been increasingly complicated by the globalisation of financial markets and global economic integration. An inevitable result of financial globalisation is the erosion of the autonomy in the formulation and implementation of domestic monetary policies since domestic monetary policies need to take into account external considerations. While extensive work on inflation has been done in the context of a market economy, these issues are equally relevant within the Islamic framework. However, the methodology proposed by Muslim economists is a departure from the purely secular approach as it is drawn from the rich spiritual and religious tradition of Islam. In the arena of monetary policy, the significance of establishing an Islamic framework cannot be overemphasised. This framework would be one through which Islamic monetary instruments can be utilised. There is, of course, at the outset, the need to understand fully the mechanics of these instruments. The central bank can develop monetary instruments based on Islamic principles in the same way that Islamic banks have developed based on Islamic principles. If there exists an Islamic interbank money market, the central bank has another avenue to influence the liquidity situation. Nevertheless, at this juncture, many unanswered questions still remain. This is not surprising given that Islamic banking has only been introduced in the 1970s, and emerged in some countries only in very recent years. A case in point is that related to the Islamic monetary instruments. Although there is some knowledge of the mechanism and outcome of specific Islamic instruments, empirical testing concerning operating monetary policy with these instruments is still lacking. It is hoped that further indepth work would be undertaken to enhance our knowledge on the subject. This would contribute towards the development of an Islamic financial infrastructure necessary for the efficient implementation of monetary policy in the context of an Islamic financial system. Another issue that I would also like to raise is the relationship of inflation and savings. As a matter of policy, the central bank in a developing economy not only accords priority to the effective mobilisation of savings but also ensures that funds mobilised are utilised effectively to finance productive domestic economic activity to support the expansion of productive capacity. It has been said that savings are generally encouraged when there is an attractive rate of return, a specific reason to save or a convenient mechanism for saving. In this regard, the central bank aims to ensure that savers earn a positive real rate of return on their savings. In most countries, inflation may be caused by a combination of factors, which may necessitate a comprehensive macroeconomic package to address the inflation problem. Indeed, monetary policy alone, no matter how sound and prudent, cannot do the job of short-term stabilisation and the promotion of stable long-term price development in such an environment. It would also need to be complemented with fiscal policy restraint as well as measures to alleviate supply constraints. As such, monetary and fiscal measures need to complement each other; the former could be geared principally to managing liquidity in the economy, while the latter could focus on fiscal consolidation. Other supply-side measures could be instituted to complement macroeconomic policies while other measures including the promotion of savings are important as part of the drive to control inflation in the economy. Of special importance is the proper co-ordination of these policies, as well as the commitment to price stability by all levels of the government. In addition, the private sector needs to be aware of their role to combat inflation and increase savings. The conventional causes of inflation in the form of demand-pull and cost-push factors also feature when viewed from the Islamic perspective. Basically, Islam attributes the occurrence of inflation to excesses in the behaviour of man. This contradicts the principle of moderation, which Islam stresses, should be the main guiding principle, among other principles, in the life of man. The voluntary nature of this principle of qanaa (moderation) means that it will be effective only if individuals voluntarily uphold such principles. Another concept is zuhd (abstinence). Both qanaa and zuhd have a significant role to play in curbing excess demand. On the other hand, excesses on the supply side can also lead to inflationary pressures. Speculation and hoarding to manipulate prices are strongly condemned in Islam. In this respect, Islam teaches the need to harmoniously blend the secular and spiritual aspects of existence so that Muslims would not only strive for a reward in the life hereafter but also for a pleasant, fulfilling and meaningful life in the present world. Just as conventional economics emphasises the contribution of both the public sector and private sector in arresting inflation and containing inflationary pressures, both the state and society have a role to play in an Islamic economy. The Quran and the Sunnah provide guidance with respect to their duties and responsibilities in ensuring the establishment of a just socioeconomic order. In this respect, both the state and society must understand the significance of carrying out their activities or affairs in accordance with the Quran and the Sunnah. Much has been written from the perspective of conventional economics on causes of inflation and policies to contain inflation. However, literature based on Islamic concepts are, in contrast, scarce and limited. It is hoped that this seminar with the presence of distinguished Muslim scholars, will find new approaches in the implementation of Islamic economic principles to address issues associated with inflation. Admittedly, there is certainly still a lot to be accomplished ahead of us. It is recognised that it will only be through sustained research, by unceasing original thinking and, above all, by a great deal of practical experimentation, that we may be able to discover most of the answers that we need. Nevertheless, seminars such as this provide the opportunity for adding depth to our knowledge by way of dialogue and discussion in discovering Islamic solutions. Therein lies the challenge for Muslim scholars, economists and the entire Muslim community in the future. I now have the pleasure to declare open this second workshop on "Inflation and its Impact on Society - the Islamic Solution". Bank Negara Malaysia 6 July 1996

Title: Speech at the Ceremony for the 50th Anniversary of Bank Negara Malaysia: "50 Years of Central Banking - Stability and Sustainability"
text: Assistant Governor Rafiah Salim's Speech at the Opening Ceremony of the Conference on the Documentation of Derivatives Transactions Speaker: Assistant Governors / Advisers Speech/Interview Date: 08 Jun 1996 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English It is my great pleasure and honour to welcome you to the Opening Ceremony of the Conference on Documentation of Derivative Transactions this morning. A special note of welcome to our speakers from three continents, some of whom have so graciously taken time off from their busy schedules to be here with us. I hope your stay with us will be a pleasant one and you will find some time to see some of our beautiful country. This is the first time, I believe that a conference of this nature is being jointly organised by three institutions - Bank Negara Malaysia, Bar Council Malaysia and Institute of Banks Malaysia. The Conference serves to underline the perceived importance and impact that the emergence of new financial products in the form of derivatives would have for the banking and financial system. I want to specially thank the International Swaps and Derivatives Association for their assistance and cooperation in organising this Conference. This is the second time a team of speakers from ISDA has come to Bank Negara Malaysia to speak to our lawyers and bankers. Some of you present here would recall that last year Ms. Gay Evans, the President of ISDA, and her team of specialists gave a brief overview of the ISDA documentation for derivatives at Bank Negara Malaysia. ISDA's continued support for Bank Negara Malaysia's efforts to promote better understanding and management of hedging instruments is much appreciated. The trend towards customization of financial products This gathering of lawyers and bankers in one hall augurs well for the banking and finance industry. The trend in the financial services industry at present and, probably more so in the future, is discernibly gravitating to the customization of banking and financial products. Energising this trend is the increased competition within the industry due to the globalization of financial markets. The availability of new technology which enables bankers to meet and satisfy more and more of their customers' unique or special needs no doubt contributes to this trend. Unfortunately, the existing legal framework and statutory developments do not appear to have kept pace with the trend. Modern bankers would bemoan the lack of a law like the Sale of Goods Act 1957 to provide some legal guidance for dealing in derivatives or the Bills of Exchange Act 1949 for dealing with modern electronic payment systems. Sailing in uncharted waters, bankers and lawyers have tried to improve matters for themselves by defining their obligations and rights in contractual terms. A move from status to contract The trend to customise financial products would inevitably call for the technical expertise of the banker to package a product for the exacting needs of his customer to be married with the consummate skills and expertise of the lawyer to precisely document the contractual relationship between the customer and the banker. The banker would look to the lawyer to control legal risks and to preserve the means of terminating unwanted transactions. It would appear therefore that the stage is being set for the enhancement of the partnership of bankers and lawyers on a grand scale to meet the needs of the modern banking and financial system especially in the light of various new customised financial products, the legal dimensions of which can only be defined contractually. Prudential management of derivatives business I am sure those of us gathered here are only too keenly aware of the volatile and complex nature of these new financial products. Most of them are derivatives and have been developed to meet the needs of customers to hedge against specific risks in their portfolio or cashflow. Derivatives traders are therefore a new breed of bankers who are on the cutting edge of developments in the banking and financial industry. Unfortunately recent events relating to rogue derivative traders have not advanced the professional image of derivative traders. Following the debacle in the Singapore office of Barings and the collapse of one of the oldest merchant bank group in the world, Nick Leeson has become a household name in this part of the world. In a recently published book entitled "The Law on Financial Derivatives", Alastair Hudson writes that in heaven there was a discussion between the recently deceased as to which profession had existed first. The doctor said, "Eve was made out of Adam's rib, therefore a doctor must have been needed from the beginning." Not to be out done, the Engineer retorted, "The world was manufactured out of chaos: that required an engineer." The Derivatives Trader was silent for a while and then he quietly asked, "Who do you think created the chaos?" Chaos is the right word to describe the fallout from any debacle relating to derivatives. The amounts committed to derivatives are so phenomenally huge that it could reasonably be predicted that chaos on an unprecedented level would be the only logical outcome of any future financial catastrophe involving derivatives. It has been estimated that between 1986 and the end of 1994, the total volume of exchange-traded derivatives grew from US0.6 trillion to US8.8 trillion. During the same period, the over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives markets expanded more than 10 times, to a notional value outstanding estimated at US12 trillion. With deregulation, globalization of the world financial markets, and consequently increased velocity of capital flows, the emerging markets of East Asia appear to be the next geographical spot in the globe for growth in derivatives activity. The ability of the banking community in the financial centres of the countries in this region to hedge currency and interest rate risks appears to facilitate the flow of capital into these countries. Since such hedging transactions are contractual, the ability of our lawyers to adequately document and thereby manage the attendant legal risks of these transactions could be a limit to the expansion of derivatives and other hedging activity in this country. Bank Negara Malaysia Guidelines for Derivatives As lawyers know, only the law or some form of regulation can restore a semblance of order and confidence in any matter. Similarly, as a result of a number of debacles involving derivatives, the regulators have taken steps to introduce certain minimum standards which must be observed by our banking and financial houses in relation to derivatives business. Bank Negara Malaysia issued our Guidelines on Minimum Standards on Risk Management Practices for Derivatives in July this year. As we said in the Guidelines, in general, individual risks associated with derivative transactions are not new to banks. Banks have been active for some years in basic forward and swap transactions and would have routinely addressed credit risk, market risk, liquidity risk, operational risk and legal risk in their treasury operations.. However, the longer dated nature and complexities of certain derivative transactions would require a higher degree of expertise and understanding and would warrant refinements to the earlier simplistic approaches to identify and manage these risks. I would want to reiterate the call in our Guidelines that to ensure that the solvency of our banks remain intact, a sound risk management policy is vital. Management has to ensure that derivative activities are conducted in a knowledgeable and prudent manner. They must also ensure that there are no compromises at all with regards to the control procedures and processes. I must emphasize here that the Bank Negara Guidelines prescribe only the minimum standards that banks should observe to ensure prudent conduct in the operations of derivative activities. Banks are free and are in fact encouraged to adopt more stringent standards in their risk management policies than that set out in the Guidelines. Enhancing legal services for the banking community At this point, ladies and gentlemen, I must share with you one of our deepest concerns about the services industry in this country. You would know that the Government is locked in continuing negotiations under GATS to liberalise market access by foreign service providers to the Malaysian consumer. An open economy like Malaysia, where the export sector constitutes a large percentage of the GNP, is very vulnerable and subject to the vagaries of our trading partners. There is only limited scope for manoeuvre and positioning in our international trade negotiations. If we are not careful, our negotiations or positionings can result in embarrassing retaliatory measures being taken against us by other countries. If our Malaysian service providers are not in a strong competitive position or worst still, if they are unable to provide the legitimate services needed by Malaysian consumers, Malaysia would be hard-pressed to keep out the foreign service provider from any sector. At the negotiation table, it is always being argued that competition from foreign service providers would only be beneficial for the Malaysian consumer since it would bring in the much needed expertise at a lower cost into the country. It is difficult to counter such logical arguments at the international negotiation table. It is important therefore that the Malaysian services industry be strengthened to compete on par with the foreign service provider. It important therefore that the Malaysian legal fraternity acquires the new knowledge and skills that are needed for a fast moving and growing banking and financial services industry. I fear that with the recent deregulation of derivatives business under our Guidelines, the banking community may find that the necessary legal expertise and skills are not available in Malaysia. As a last resort, the banks may have to source such legal assistance from abroad. Our lawyers have been hitherto a versatile and resilient group of professionals. It would be a sad reflection of the new breed of lawyers if they are not able to meet the challenges of the new banking and financial developments. Unless the lawyers make the effort to read, keep in touch and generally take the means to become au fait in these new developments and products, I do not think expertise or skill of the required professional standard would develop in Malaysia. Standardisation of derivative documentation Standardization of documentation, especially for complex and volatile products like derivatives helps the lawyers to get a handle on these products. Recent events and legal suits have witnessed the growing concerns pertaining to the legality of derivatives contracts, in particular, the issue of enforceability of such contracts. Apart from ambiguity on the rights and responsibility and the lack of clear authority, much of the problem can be attributed to improper and inadequate documentation on the part of the contracting parties. Banking institutions offering or trading derivatives contracts must therefore, ensure that approved policies on documentation requirements and formal procedures are in place, clearly stated and defined as well as closely monitored. In this regards, standard and well-tested legal documentation should be adopted. In many cases, because of the complex nature of derivatives transactions, execution of legal documentation may take some time. One solution is for banking institutions to use standardised legal documentation in order to reduce time taken to complete the necessary documentation as well as to achieve consistency. Where transactions involve more complex and exotic products, banking institutions must ensure that all documentation are completed and perfected within a reasonable timeframe after the deal is transacted. The Conference on Documentation of Derivative Transactions sets out to achieve exactly the above objectives. It is indeed timely that this Conference should be organized. I believe that although a number of our Malaysian banks are presently utilising the standard form ISDA documentation, with modifications to suit various situations, Malaysian lawyers are frequently not involved in such transactions and as such have not had the occasion to scrutinise these ISDA documents and advise clients on them. In this context I must congratulate our Judiciary who have taken a proactive stance on derivatives. Last year, for the Judicial Conference they had requested for Bank Negara to arrange an international banker to speak to them on derivatives transactions. This year , ILKAP has requested Bank Negara to mount a one day seminar on the same topic for the members of the Judiciary. The judges are definitely preparing themselves to face the developments in the banking and finance sector. With the fast pace at which Malaysians are taking roles in the global capital markets, there is a need for us all, bankers, lawyers, as well as businessmen, to be well acquainted with all the legal issues that arise in connection with derivatives. With that final call, ladies and gentlemen, it is my pleasure to declare open the Conference on Documentation of Derivatives Transactions. Bank Negara Malaysia 8 October 1996

Title: Keynote Address at the Financial Advisers Seminar (18 October 2008) on Reaping Opportunities as Financial Advisers
text: Governor's Speech Launching of the National-Level Saving Promotion Campaign Presenter: Tan Sri Dato' Ahmad Mohd Don / Venue: Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 16 Dec 1996 / On behalf of the Cabinet Committee on The Promotion of Savings chaired by yang Amat Berhormat, the Deputy Prime Minister would like to express my appreciation and gratitude to the Honourable Prime Minister for being willing to attend this evening to launch the National Savings Promotion Campaign. The launch of this savings encouragement campaign is a testament to the Government's determination and commitment in providing the basis for developing and stimulating economic growth to continue to be sustainable in the future. One of the factors contributing to the rapid growth of our economy is the high rate of national savings. The savings rate has increased from 21% in 1960 to 36.5% in 1995. For 1996, the country's savings rate is estimated to reach a high of 38.8%. However, this rate is not enough to finance the higher investment rate, which is estimated at 45.1% for 1996. To reduce this disparity, the national savings rate that we are achieving at the moment needs to be further enhanced. As a result of this increase in savings, it will not only help develop the country's economy, but it will also improve the quality of life and secure the future of all of us. Recognising the importance of this, the Government has set up a Cabinet Committee on the Promotion of Savings to coordinate all savings encouragement efforts throughout the country. It is the responsibility of the Committee to formulate savings encouragement strategies. In addition, it is also responsible for coordinating the implementation of programmes that raise awareness among the public on the benefits of saving. The Committee also acts as a catalyst in the development of financial infrastructure that can enhance savings among the public. The launch of the Savings Incentive Campaign today, is an important first step towards achieving this goal. It is the culmination of cooperation and discussions held over the past few months between various ministries, agencies and others including the Ministry of Finance, Education, Information, Human Resources, National Unity and Community Development, Domestic Trade and Consumer Affairs, Housing and Local Government as well as financial institutions, mass media, consumer associations, trade unions and bank Negara Malaysia. To plan and implement various action plans, five Committees were established, namely the Finance, Education, publicity, employees and women's committees. The role of the Finance Committee is to identify new financial savings products or investment schemes, promote the improvement of a more efficient financial infrastructure and to ensure that there are no obstacles or restrictions in the financial system that could affect savings activities. The role of the Education Committee is to foster the habit of saving and educating students on the importance of saving and encouraging them to be thrifty. The dissemination of all information through publications, electronic media and others is entrusted to the Publicity Committee. The dissemination of information will also be channeled through face-to-face communication, civic activities, interviews and other outdoor activities. As for the Employees Committee, it is tasked with reviewing and encouraging and nurturing savings habits among employees. Among its activities is the conduct of a joint educational program between employers and trade unions on savings. The role of the Women's Committee is to conduct educational programmes for women, encourage them to plan their expenses and to inculcate savings and thrifty habits. This savings encouragement campaign is a comprehensive effort. Participation at all levels both at the state and district levels is encouraged so that this campaign reaches all levels. Although compulsory savings such as contributions in the Employees Provident Fund have contributed to the country's high savings rate, this savings encouragement programme will emphasise on voluntary savings. This is because voluntary savings are an important factor in determining the overall savings rate of the country. Voluntary savings allow us to choose the form and amount that needs to be tabbed according to the needs and capabilities of the person. In addition, the campaign also aims to increase savings through prudent practices such as thrift, planning expenses and moderation in daily life. This prudent practice can avoid waste and produce a tabble surplus. The savings encouragement strategy to be implemented covers two aspects. First, develop a local financial infrastructure by introducing new financial products and efficient mechanisms to promote savings. Further, the quality of banking services should be further enhanced with the aim of providing appropriate services to promote savings. The second aspect of this strategy is to disseminate comprehensive and complete information and educate the public on the importance of saving. Through these two strategies, we will be able to enhance and maintain the country's high savings rate. As the dissemination of information is so important in the success of this effort, Bank Negara Malaysia in collaboration with financial institutions has published a pamphlet on "The Importance of Saving" and a booklet entitled "Financial Savings Products in Malaysia". The purpose of the brochure is to raise public awareness of the benefits of saving and its benefits. This brochure also focuses on the importance of saving through prudent practices. The booklet "Financial Savings Products in Malaysia" describes the criteria that should be taken into account when choosing financial savings products such as security and risk, rate of return, liquidity and so on. This booklet also provides information on the different types of financial savings products at the moment as well as explaining the differences between savings and investments. This information is expected to help people choose the right products to meet their financial and savings needs. To ensure that this savings encouragement campaign will be successful and have a lasting impact, a number of activities will be carried out throughout 1997 for specific target groups such as students, employees and women. Among the activities scheduled after the launch is a savings encouragement campaign among school students. The purpose of this campaign is to inculcate savings and thrift habits among school students as the future savings rate depends on their saving habits. While savings encouragement campaigns for employees are just as important as they determine the current savings rate. The purpose of the employee savings encouragement campaign will not only raise awareness and foster savings habits, but also provide new mechanisms to make it easier for them to save. Women play an important role in the management of family and household expenses. Therefore, savings encouragement activities for women will emphasise on budget planning. By planning a budget, we will get a surplus that in turn can be tabbed. In the past few months, all the Committees have worked hard and cooperated in planning and preparing the activities to be carried out throughout 1997. I on behalf of the Cabinet Committee thank all parties involved. Finally, I once again thank the Prime Minister for taking the time to launch this Savings Promotion Campaign. Bank Negara Malaysia 16 December 1996

Title: Speech at the Islamic Financial Services Board Annual Meeting and Global Islamic Finance Forum (GIFF)
text: Assistant Governor Rafiah Salim's Paper at the 50th Anniversary of the Malaysian Bar Council Commemorative Conference - "The Bar, Law and Justice - The Years Ahead" Speaker: Assistant Governors / Advisers Speech/Interview Date: 15 Aug 1997 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English It is timely that the Bar has selected the theme The Bar, Law and Justice - The Years Ahead', as the Malaysian Bar turns 50 and the country with 40 years of independence marches into the next millennium. The topic chosen reflects the importance of the role of the Bar, Law and the Judiciary in nation building and ensuring a developed nation, which is based on the rule of law. This essentially means having, first, a good legal foundation to facilitate economic transactions, which will improve transparency and predictability in legal matters. Secondly, having a judiciary, which plays its role as the third independent arm of the government, which upholds the rule of law and protects the rights of the citizen. The Bar or the legal profession has a pivotal role to play in the process. The given topic to me is International Trade and Finance - Gearing the Malaysian Legal Profession' . This paper will attempt to provide a brief perspective of the major developments in the arena of International Trade and Finance, its impact on the country and the necessary preparation that the legal profession must make, in order to face the challenges and new demands placed upon it. This is by no means an attempt to provide a comprehensive study of the foregoing. In fact, I have decided to approach this topic from the perspective of international developments in the area of finance and trade in services, its direct impact on the legal profession in this country and the action plan that the lawyers of this nation must adopt in order to sustain their business and to grow with the rest of the nation. Globalisation and Its Effects The developments taking place in the arena of International Trade and Finance cannot be appropriately discussed without first scrutinising the phenomenon called globalisation and liberalisation. Before we examine the impacts of globalisation, it is useful to first attempt a snapshot of what globalisation actually is and how it manifests itself. Globalisation is not a single phenomenon. It has become a catchall concept to describe a range of trends and forces changing the face of the world in which we live. While some are not new, for example trade liberalisation has been under way since 1945, clearly the pace of change is accelerating. As an economic phenomenon, globalisation is manifested in a shift from a world of distinct national economies to a global economy in which production is internationalised and financial capital flows, freely and instantly between countries. Multinational Enterprises wield vast economic power, while anonymous institutional investors influence currency rates, the availability and price of international capital, and interest rates. Apart from it, the framework of rules within which economic activity takes place is increasingly defined in the international framework of the WTO, the IMF, the World Bank, the OECD, and G7 summits, and is heavily influenced by regional trading blocks such as APEC, the European Union, AFTA and NAFTA. Globalisation is accelerated by information technology. In fact globalisation is both a cause and a consequence of the information revolution. It is driven by dramatic improvements in telecommunications; exponential increases in computing power coupled with lower costs, and the development of electronic communications and information networks such as the Internet. These communications technologies are helping to overcome the barriers of physical distance. Communities of various types, including international interest groups like Greenpeace or Amnesty international, as well as business and labour organisations, now function across national borders. Even the framework of social policies affecting individual citizens is becoming more sensitive to international influences, including the global news media. The impact of globalisation is rather obvious. It is even changing the context in which governments operate and the globalisation of financial market is just one aspect of this changed environment. The two main impacts of globalisation can be briefly stated as first, globalisation puts great pressure on the adaptability of national economies, by generating fierce international competition and by increasing economic dynamism worldwide. Secondly, the national capacity to attract business is becoming increasingly important, as potential investments can be made at a growing number of locations worldwide. As competition between companies increases, so does competition between countries, which requires measures to improve and ensure that the business climate of the country remains attractive. In fact the economics of globalisation focuses on the increasing power of the market and the decreasing ability of the governments or states to dictate economic policy. This does not mean that there is no place for sovereignty but countries wanting to be part of the world capitalist economy are invariably and significantly constrained by global market forces and economic practices. This inevitably leads to a nation adapting to globalisation by being a trading state, which means liberalising or opening up one's economy to foreign goods, capital, and services. In particular, globalisation of finance has resulted in increased capital flow to developing countries in the form of foreign direct investment (FDI). This has also paved the way for domestic financial reform programmes, in many developing countries. The resultant financial reform programmes consist of reform of the interest rate regime supported by the development of market-based monetary control procedures; development of money and interbank markets; reform of prudential regulations and the supervisory system; recapitalization and financial restructuring of weak financial institutions, supported by enterprise restructuring policies; measures to strengthen competition among banks; reform (including reducing the scope) of selective credit regulations; development of long-term capital markets; reform of the clearing and settlement system for payments; and development of foreign exchange markets supported by appropriate prudential regulations on foreign exchange exposure, and the liberalisation of exchange and trade restrictions. The impact of globalisation and these reforms have changed the topography of the businesses in many countries. It has changed the means and reasons for doing business and invariably, these changes have direct impact on the demands made on lawyers, including their skills and deliverables. Liberalisation The other significant phenomenon in the area of international trade and finance is the liberalisation of trade, especially trade in services. As you may be aware, Malaysia's offers under the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS) binds it to a package of market access commitments on a number of services industries or sectors. The service sectors committed under the package are both non-financial and financial services. The non-financial services encompass Business services, Communication services, Construction and Related Engineering services, Social services, Tourism services, Education services, Medical Speciality services, Computer and Related services, Research and Development services, Rental Leasing services, Other Business services like, advertising, management consulting, Operational Headquarters services, Audio Visual services, Transportation services. Financial Services sector includes insurance, reinsurance and other related financial services. Subscribing to the GATS means, subscribing and complying with some primary concept inter-alia, Most Favoured Nation, Transparency, Mutual Recognition, Progressive Liberalisation and Dispute Settlement Understanding. Briefly, the concept of Most Favoured Nation requires a government to treat all Foreign Service suppliers equally. Transparency requirement imposes a duty on the government authorities to have clear, consistent and transparent policies apart from making it available in writing. The concept, Mutual Recognition needs the various professional bodies to develop rules and criteria on the admission of Foreign Service suppliers into the country. As you may be fully aware, the term Progressive Liberalisation means further trade liberalisation based on the international agenda. Lastly, subscribing to Dispute Settlement Understanding places the nation under the jurisdiction of the dispute settlement mechanism of the international trade organisation i.e. World Trade Organisation (WTO). Specific Commitments on Legal Services The impact of trade in service liberalisation cannot be fully appreciated without examining the specific commitments of Malaysia under the GATS, especially under the legal services sector. Like most of Malaysia's commitments under the GATS, the offers on legal services reflect and embody the current policies of the nation, especially those on foreign equity participation in the services sector. In the area of legal services, advisory and consultancy services on home country law, international law and offshore corporation law can be provided by a foreign lawyer, in Malaysia. This can be done if, the services are supplied through a corporation incorporated in Federal Territory of Labuan and the services are supplied only to offshore corporations established in Federal Territory of Labuan. However, a foreign lawyer can freely provide the aforesaid services through cross-border and consumption abroad modes, in Labuan and West Malaysia. Cross-border refers to the supply of service from a country outside Malaysia to a customer in Malaysia without having any presence (a body corporate or representative) in Malaysia. Consumption abroad is the delivery of service to a Malaysian in a country outside Malaysia. In other words the consumer goes abroad to obtain the services. Given the current commitments, foreign lawyers can provide legal services to Malaysians and their companies through fax, telephone or the Internet. Alternatively, a Malaysian corporation can go abroad to obtain legal services from foreign lawyers. The foregoing commitment opens up the legal services market to foreign legal consultants. It also paves the path for foreign legal firms to set up office in Labuan and monopolise the legal business in Labuan. Consequently, our lawyers face the challenge of providing services that are at least at par with their foreign competitors, if their services are to be utilised in Labuan. ASEAN Agreement on Trade in Services Negotiations on Financial Services Another development that cannot be ignored is the development at ASEAN level, at AFTA and the negotiations that is going on under the Asean Framework Agreement on Trade in Services (AFAS). The AFAS is an agreement made within the auspices of AFTA and Article (5) of the GATS. It aims - (a) to enhance Cooperation in services amongst Member States in order to improve the efficiency and competitiveness, diversify production capacity and supply and distribution of services of their service suppliers within and outside ASEAN; (b) To eliminate substantially, restrictions to trade in services amongst Member States; and (c) To liberalise trade in services by expanding the depth and scope of liberalisation beyond those undertaken by Member States under the GATS, with the aim to realising a free trade area in services. In other words, the objective of AFAS is to accelerate the liberalisation process in the area of trade in services. This Agreement will enable the ASEAN countries to enjoy the privileges and the benefits of regional integration and market openings prior to other GATS Members. The most pertinent issue that have to be noted here is that, service sector liberalisation including legal services will not only take place under GATS but much earlier, under AFAS. This would mean that commitments to further liberalise the legal services would have to be made during the negotiations under AFAS, which is expected to be concluded by mid 1998. Invariably, the market access liberalisation cannot wait until the next round of GATS negotiation, which is 2 years down the road. Apart from the market access commitments, other provisions in the GATS and AFAS mandates concrete steps towards the establishment of mutual recognition of standards, criteria for authorisation, licensing and certification of service suppliers. Given the above, it is important to perceive the imminent globalisation and liberalisation of legal services in Asean and the world at large. Many bar associations being aware of this phenomenon are already working on mutual recognition and rules and regulations to govern foreign law consultants. The International bar association has also been making initiatives in this area. The guidelines on foreign legal consultants are one of it. Perhaps the Malaysian Bar should take the necessary steps towards this as, under the AFAS, we may have no choice but to open the doors to foreign legal service providers. Developments at the Asia-Pacific Economic Corporation (APEC) In the Joint Ministerial Statement made in Cebu, Philippines, April 5-6, 1997, the leaders of APEC nations undertook, to facilitate increased private sector participation in infrastructure, promote the development of the financial and capital markets, and support the freer flow of capital. This was to be achieved through collaborative initiatives. I mention here some of the initiatives identified. One of the important initiatives is strengthening financial market supervision of the APEC Members. It has been recognised that regulatory and supervisory capabilities have to keep up with the rapid changes in international financial markets. Regional and international expert bodies as well as national regulatory and supervisory authorities are required to provide a significant range of technical assistance and expertise, to identify important gaps in available training resources and to strengthen the financial market supervision of APEC member countries. The other initiative is in the area of strengthening clearing and settlement infrastructure. Well-developed clearing and settlement systems are perceived to be indispensable to the development of capital markets. Member economies with relevant experiences in strengthening clearing and settlement infrastructure are required to share their expertise with interested economies and provide technical support with the assistance of the appropriate international and regional multilateral institutions, towards this goal. Supporting development of rating agencies and strengthening information disclosure standards is considered another crucial area for APEC initiative. Independent rating agencies are believed to play an important role in developing the region's capital markets and attracting cross-border capital flows. Current experiences with credit rating agencies within the region relative to international best practices will be examined as a result of this initiative. The adoption of best practices, as well as full information disclosure by issuers, will be adopted eventually. Regional forum on pension fund reform and issues related to pension reform in APEC member economies, including those issues related to sustainability, the relative roles of the private and public sectors in pension fund management, implications for domestic savings and capital market development and the prudential regulation of pension fund investments are to be examined. The benefits and costs associated with alternative approaches, and their implications on national budgets and income distribution will also be examined and appropriate action plans will be developed in the long run. Another area of importance, is securitisation. Securitisation is recognised as a viable form of financing economic growth. However, some member economies may be faced with structural, regulatory, fiscal and other constraints that inhibit its development. Interested economies are to participate in a forum to be hosted by Malaysia in 1997 to assess the level of Securitisation activities within each participating economy, identify impediments to their growth and development, and identify measures to remove such impediments. The findings of the forum are to be embodied in a voluntary action plan of each member. Lastly, voluntary action plan for supporting the freer and stable flow of capital has also been identified as one of the pertinent issue. The importance of a freer and stable flow of capital to economic development in the region is well recognised and therefore, the countries are to prepare a voluntary action plan, for reducing barriers to capital flows in the region. Though what I have indicated above seems to be a tall order, and possible implications seem remote for now, the fact remains that the APEC members will have to develop concrete action plans on the above initiatives which will definitely have a great impact on the rules on trade in services of the APEC nations, including Malaysia. This will inevitably increase the impact of globalisation and liberalisation mentioned earlier. The APEC initiatives will accelerate the pace of change in the regulatory and supervisory legal regimes. As a result, there will certainly be new rules and regulations in the APEC nations. Hence, the lawyers in this region must be vigilant and keep abreast with the changes in order to provide the required legal services. Current Negotiations on Financial Services At this juncture it is also necessary to discuss the current negotiation on Financial Services, at the WTO. The financial service sector is considered one of the most important in world trade. Therefore, liberalisation of financial service regimes can have an impact in terms of monetary stability and macroeconomic policy of a country. However, there are issues involved in the current sectoral negotiations, which transcend even these considerations. These relate to the influence of developing countries in negotiating process at the WTO. Since Marrakesh, there has been an obvious tendency for the developed countries to press for liberalisation in sectors of interest to them in isolation, without a package based on "reciprocity and mutual benefit". For instance, compare the excellent results obtained in the basic telecommunications negotiation, which is favourable for developed countries with, the mediocre results on movement of natural persons favourable to developing countries. Apart from it, the developed countries undertake the negotiation of basic rules and principles outside the WTO and subsequently seek to introduce them into the WTO rules. A good example is the concept of progressive liberalisation undertaking in the telecommunications agreement, negotiated among the OECD members and later at APEC. This could be due to the perception of the major developed countries that they were somewhat "out negotiated" in the Uruguay Round, particularly in GATS and Trade Related Investment Measures (TRIMS), as they were not able to exercise a degree of intellectual leadership comparable to their economic strength in defining the rules, principles and institutional frameworks. The solution they seek is thus, to first negotiate the basic rules and principles among the major like-minded countries i.e. OECD and G10 and then present it as a basis for further negotiations in the WTO. Trade and Investment The above trend has resulted in the emergence of what is commonly referred to as "new issues" in the trade scene. One of such new issue is Trade and Investment. According to a recent report by the WTO, foreign direct investment and international trade generally are mutually supportive, and that together they are playing the central role in the ongoing integration of the world economy. Through investment and trade, firms in each country are able to specialise in producing what they can produce most efficiently. Trade facilitates this process by allowing an economy to specialise in production, then to exchange part of that output abroad in order to achieve the particular mix of goods and services its citizens want to consume. FDI facilitates this process by increasing the international mobility of capital and thus the efficient use of the world's supply of capital and technology, including organisational, managerial and marketing skills. This joint process is considered central to development strategies and more generally, to worldwide efforts to increase wealth and raise living standards. Hence, some countries had insisted on including investment policy in the Uruguay Round of the WTO negotiations and this resulted in the agreement on Trade Related Investment Measures (TRIMS). However, the TRIMS agreement confines itself solely to strict adherence to local content and trade balancing requirements. TRIMS does not cover rules to regulate flows of FDI. Thus, industrial countries are of the view that since the globalisation of business activities develop further, FDI plays a more and more prominent role in world economy and therefore there must be a more comprehensive agreement on investment. Despite resistance from the developing countries, it was agreed at the Singapore WTO Ministerial meeting that a committee will be set up to look into this issue. The other new issues include trade and labour standards and trade and environmental issues. I do not wish to delve deeper into the specifics of these new issues. What suffices is to note that the outcomes of negotiations at the international forums are not predictable anymore. Liberalisation and other changes may take place much ahead of the national time frame. The results of the negotiations may require the contents of national agenda to shift. Thus, a nation cannot take its time about preparing its domestic industries to compete with Foreign Service suppliers. The industries have to be prepared and they have to be prepared soon. The same applies to the legal profession. The lawyers must be ready to face stiff competition and challenges posed by the changes caused by trade liberalisation. Technology In addition to the foregoing developments that affect lawyers, the advent of technology has broken-down the conventional barriers to export of legal services into a country. Cross border legal services is being rendered every second via telephone, faxes and the Internet. Short of appearing in court to represent clients, a foreign lawyer can now fulfil the need of his multinational company or client in Malaysia without having to have an office or presence in Malaysia. Even if the formal doors of the market are not opened, technology will punch big holes into the legal and administrative barriers, to open markets. Technologies, with market access liberalisation are cousins who will usher in competition, new standards and inevitable changes to the legal profession. What Must Be Done What I have done so far is to map out some of the momentous developments in international trade and finance which has significant impact on the service industry of Malaysia, including the Malaysian legal profession. With the market liberalisation and technological advancements, it is crucial for the lawyers to be aware of the challenges ahead. The net effect of the foregoing developments is firstly, an increase in competition and secondly, the new demands on the legal profession. Increase Value to Customer Increasing competition on a variety of fronts will require lawyers to change the way they practice. It will also require change in what they practice. Every lawyer knows, clients ask who is the best person to do the job when they have problems to solve. When their problems are acute enough, people have uncanny ways of finding out who is the best for them. Since personal experience plays such a fundamental role in creating long term perceptions about professionals, every experience clients has, markets the practice. A recent research by the Australian Bar suggests that people do not expect a complete smooth ride from their lawyers. What they do expect is greater awareness and empathy in their lawyers, of their needs. As such, lawyers must develop a much keener understanding of how they create value to their clients, to successfully meet increasing competition. Every law firm must examine ways and means of increasing the value they provide to their clients. Upgrade Standard of Service Apart from the aforesaid, it is also necessary to upgrade the standard of service offered by the profession. Clients now are looking for objectivity, accountability, honesty and appropriateness in everything they consume. Technical knowledge diffusing through the community at an incredible rate increases the expectations of those people who use professional services. In a huge range of ways, the consumer has become more sophisticated, and meeting consumer needs has become more complex. Consumers will not simply sit by and let professionals fail to meet their expectations anymore. What they spend on and where they spend is now a critical decision. It is therefore no coincidence that many developing countries have begun writing guides to ISO 9000 standards for service sector. These guides cover hospitality industry, education, software developers, lawyers and accountants, because these occupations are considered highest value adding in developed western economics. The legal profession of Malaysia must enhance its standard of service in order to meet or exceed the international standards. This will enable it to compete on equal footing with foreign legal service providers. Use of Technology The other pertinent factor that has to be considered is the impact of technology, which is changing the face of legal service. Advanced telephone systems, facsimile transmission, legal data base and computer hardware and software technologies are all being used to shorten time frames and increase efficiency. The mere presence of these technologies has improved the quality of legal work. It has also accelerated the demand for better quality in legal service. Documents are expected to be better and sense perfect. According to a recent survey carried out by various bar associations around the world, it was discovered that lawyers are not as sophisticated or adaptive in their personal use of technology when compared to professionals in other fields. If a legal practise sufficiently focuses on servicing a tightly defined set of clients better than anyone else did, technologies in their system can build competitive barriers and prevent client from switching to other lawyers. The strategic use of technology to leverage the intellectual resources of small firms enables them to compete directly with very large partnerships. Using information captured by technology to add value to clients is the marketing challenge. What gives an additional niche to lawyers is the elegant use of new technology to anticipate and exceed clients' expectations, not the brute force of technology, which is easily matched by a competitor. Skills Lastly, human resource dynamics are driving demand for more diversity in legal service. Technology offers many ways of freeing up people to do the range of work human beings do best. In other words, the time saved by technology is expected to be used to increase the skills of lawyers. Litigation support offered by many accounting firms, is a response to client needs for accounting and valuation skills in a legal context. Growing numbers of lawyers in other countries have backgrounds in engineering, architecture, science or medicine. The ability to work in teams and yet maintain independence, familiar to corporate lawyers, is now becoming a source of competition for legal practitioners. Various law society 'specialist accreditation schemes' recognise that, in practice, there is no such thing as a pure specialist. Lawyers can redefine their roles by redefining their skills. This means repositioning them in the minds of their clients. To do this they must meet the diversity of their clients' needs more effectively. You may have noticed this trend in Wall Street lawyers and lawyers engaged in legal work relating to derivatives and corporate finance. There is greater demand for lawyers who have multi- disciplines to their credit. Just a basic degree in law may not suffice in future as the international trade and finance transactions get more sophisticated and complex. Someone even suggested jokingly that when everything else fails, what lawyers should do is to kill all the MBAs, because they carry the future with them. Opportunities in Other Markets Before I conclude, I must also stress the fact that it is time, the Malaysian Legal profession started thinking and going global. It is opportune for the legal profession to spread its wings and start utilising the vast opportunities conferred by globalisation and the market liberalisation around the region. This is the opportunity for the Malaysian legal firms to be the first few participants in a developing market, especially in the neighbouring countries. This is the moment for collaborative approach in marketing and delivery of legal skills. Malaysian legal firms can collaborate with other firms in the region to enhance the services provided and to venture into new markets. It is necessary to note that globalisation and liberalisation is like a chess game, every time the opponent makes a dent in your defence i.e. enters your domestic market, he creates an opportunity for you to mount an attack i.e. an entry into his market. To conclude, I wish to emphasis that it is not only important for the Malaysian legal profession to harness itself to meet the dynamics of the changing environment but to be prepared to change itself to successfully meet the challenges of globalisation and liberalisation and to effectively use the technological development for its own benefit. Bank Negara Malaysia 15 August 1997 This paper reflects the personal views of the author and should not be taken as representing the views of the Bank.

Title: Opening Address at the Opening Ceremony of the 10th ASEAN Insurance Regulators Meeting and 33rd ASEAN Insurance Council Meeting
text: Governor's Speech at the Opening of the Saving Promotion Seminar Presenter: Tan Sri Dato' Ahmad Mohd Don / Venue: Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 26 August 1997 / First of all, on behalf of the Cabinet Committee on The Promotion of Savings chaired by the Honourable Deputy Prime Minister/The Minister of Finance Malaysia would like to thank the attendees for being willing to attend this morning's Fundraising Incentive Seminar. As the brothers and sisters are aware, the national savings encouragement campaign was launched by the Prime Minister on 16 December 1996 and after that, several activities were held. While all attention is currently focused on the turbulence in the currency market in the region, we need to continue to work to build on the foundation that has brought success to the country so far. One element that has enabled our country to achieve economic success is the high rate of national savings. With the country's high savings rate, we have been able to achieve a high rate of investment. This development has enabled Malaysia to increase its productive capabilities by not relying heavily on foreign savings. If we rely too much on foreign loans, we will face high risks and cost of funds especially in less stable market conditions as at the moment. Therefore, we need to work to increase domestic savings rates and thus help reduce those risks. The purpose of this seminar is to enable all participants, both from government departments/agencies and the private sector to get a clear picture of the goals we are aiming to achieve, the strategies that have been formulated as well as to provide information and feedback on the progress that has been made so far. In this way, we can evaluate the activities that have been carried out as well as ways to further enhance our efforts. The seminar will also raise awareness among all relevant agencies on the activities carried out by each Committee. With this, we will be able to get a comprehensive understanding to achieve a more effective level of coordination between the committees and the relevant agencies. Finally, this will further strengthen the relationship between the Committee and the relevant agencies. I am confident that all participants who attend the Seminar today will benefit from the information presented by the speakers as well as during the discussion and question-and-answer sessions. We are aware that the country's savings rate is currently among the highest in the world (37.8% of the GNP in 1996), but it is important that we continue to improve our savings culture among Malaysians. Although the country has managed to maintain a relatively high savings rate for three decades in a row (pretending 28.6% 1970-1996), we should not be satisfied with this achievement. This high savings rate could decline as experienced by developed countries in Europe and the United States if measures are not taken to maintain the savings rate currently achieved. In addition, demographic structures can also affect savings rates. The rate of the population saving will decrease as the number of the elderly population increases. Therefore, it is important that young workers are encouraged to save and at the same time we need to inculcate the habit of saving to the younger generation who will be saving in the future. As you and sisters know, our country has Vision 2020 to achieve the status of a developed country led by the manufacturing sector. At the moment our country is still dependent on foreign investment in financing the development of the country. While government policy still encourages foreign investment to cover the lack of investment by local investors, we need to work to raise local capital so that our country can be financially independent. The increased competition to attract foreign investors as well as financial turbulence abroad demonstrates the need for us to further increase our savings so that our economic growth is not affected in the future. At the moment our country is facing a gap between investment and savings as our high investment rate exceeds the savings rate and this is reflected by the current account deficit. Since the domestic savings rate is not enough to finance domestic investments, the country is forced to rely on foreign investments or borrow from abroad. Therefore, in order to provide the foundation for the country's sustainable growth in the future, the financial structure in terms of savings encouragement strategies should emphasise on the development of financial infrastructure in developing new and attractive financial products, as well as improving the quality of banking services and providing advisory services to customers so that all efforts to inculcate savings habits among Malaysians will be successful. However, an important aspect that needs to be emphasized is the practice of saving that will increase savings instead of encouraging savers to switch from one type of savings to another. This initial savings encouragement campaign aims to spread awareness on the importance of saving and the benefits derived from it. The concept of saving recommended by the Cabinet Committee is in the form of financial and non-financial savings. In terms of financial savings, this savings encouragement campaign encourages individuals to keep money in banking or non-banking institutions. Several measures have been taken by financial institutions by providing a wide range of savings products. In the early stages of the savings encouragement campaign, two documents were published, namely the importance of saving and financial savings products with the aim of informing the public of the types of savings and investment products available in the financial markets at the moment. In addition to financial savings, this savings encouragement campaign will also emphasise on non-financial savings that have been underserved so far. This concept of non-financial savings is essential in our life practice. It encourages people to be thrifty, moderate, and not wasteful. Currently many Malaysians enjoy an increase in income, thanks to the rapid growth of the economy for nine consecutive years. The lack of thrift has spread noticeably among our society today. We need to remember that financial resources and revenue resources are limited and if wasteful attitudes are not curbed all the Government's efforts to encourage the people to save will be in vain. Through this savings encouragement campaign, three main targets, namely the working class, women and school students, will be educated on the importance of planning their finances and day-to-day budget. The ways of recording all daily income and expenses will be taught so that at the end of the month or year they can identify where the savings can be implemented. With this, any excess of income as a result of thrift can be tabbed. As the brothers and sisters are aware, the Government established a Cabinet Committee on the Promotion of Savings in August 1996. Following this, five main committees comprising the Education Committee, The Workers' Committee, the Women's Committee, the Information Committee and the Finance Committee were formed to implement the action plan of the savings activities which was drafted and agreed by the Cabinet Committee. Here I would like to call on all members of the Committee to work together in carrying out all the commitments of the action plan that have been tabled and agreed by the Chairman of the Cabinet Committee. To ensure that the savings encouragement campaign runs smoothly, the secretariat's organisational structure has been updated and the role of the Secretariat has been strengthened to enable the Secretariat to coordinate all the activities of the savings encouragement campaign implemented by each Committee. The current secretariat consists of representatives who are fully involved with the task of encouraging savings from each committee. I hope that all participants involved in carrying out the task of this savings encouragement campaign will be able to fully understand the purpose and spirit behind this savings encouragement campaign. Our current task is to be the driving force to carry out all the activities we have developed. I would like to stress that the success of this campaign is unlikely to be achieved in such a short time. What is important is that this campaign will get the expected results in the long term where the people who save will multiply, the people practice planning their finances and spending in an orderly manner and adopting a healthy lifestyle such as thrifty, not wasteful and wasteful. Therefore, the brothers and sisters involved in this campaign must work hard and work together among all committees to ensure that the success of this campaign can be traced among the three main target groups. Finally, I once again hope that the brothers and sisters will benefit from this seminar and wassalamualaikum. Bank Negara Malaysia 26 August 1997

Title: Welcoming Address for the Talk on 'Managing Risks in Mortgage Financing'
text: Governor's Speech at the 23rd Malaysian Financial Markets Association Annual Dinner Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Ahmad Mohd Don Speech/Interview Date: 07 Nov 1997 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English Terlebih dahulu, izinkan saya merakamkan ucapan terima kasih kepada Persatuan Pemasaran Kewangan Malaysia kerana menjemput saya dan isteri menghadiri majlis Makan Malam Tahunan ini dan seterusnya memberi saya peluang menyampaikan sepatah dua kata sempena meraikan majlis ini. This year has been an eventful one for all of us, and particularly for you who are managers and dealers in the foreign exchange markets. The regional currency turbulence which has affected many Asian countries and their financial markets, including Malaysia, has now spread across the world, to the New York Stock Exchange which experienced the sharpest one day point loss in its history. Regardless of the causes and origins of these developments and the rationality, or even the morality of the impact, the recent currency turbulence has shown that it respects no boundaries, and no country is immune from this malaise, once it is allowed to spread. Even more disturbing is the fact that strong economic fundamentals are no safeguard against currency volatility. There may be sound macro-economic conditions in a country, or a country may be in the process of resolving its macro-economic problems, yet, these countries are not spared from the recent currency turbulence. A closer study of the recent experience shows that developments in the currency and other financial markets tend to take on a life of their own. Once a financial market is destabilised by volatile capital flows, any weaknesses present in the system are magnified. Given the dynamics of the real world, we cannot expect to be insulated from the impact of capital flows. However, to maintain market confidence it is critical that the financial system be managed prudently with sufficient margin as buffer. These elements will become even more important in the future as institutional funds, huge as they are today, grow further in size. To a large extent, the problem of destabilising flows is also a reflection of the increasing globalisation of financial markets, supported by the rapid progress in communication and information technology. Malaysia, like most countries, is committed to financial liberalisation. But the liberalisation process has to be at a pace that we can comfortably adjust to. The financial world today is increasingly more complex and inter-related. Significant failure in one market is likely to be felt in other markets as well. Against the background that I have just outlined, there are at least three broad elements which must be dealt with in analysing and drawing lessons from the recent regional currency turbulence. First, there is the need to ensure sound macro-economic conditions. In the case of Malaysia, these include the policies needed to ensure a steady reduction in the balance of payments current account deficit, or commonly referred to as the savingsinvestment gap. A number of measures have been implemented by the Government to reduce this deficit. Efforts have also been directed to promote exports and reduce imports. These measures have already begun to yield results. More recent measures include the deferment of a number of the less urgent infrastructure projects. A national savings campaign has also been initiated since the beginning of this year to sustain a high rate of savings. Secondly, there is always a need to keep interest rates firm, the degree of which would depend on the need to curtail aggregate spending and contain inflationary pressures. While there are already signs of slower growth, the response of Bank Negara Malaysia in the given circumstances, however, is not to pursue an accommodative monetary policy. Under the current environment, the potential for rising inflationary pressures exists. This policy of continued restraint is supplemented with stringent prudential controls in the banking system. This is to ensure that the financial policies and fiscal policies reinforce each other to restrain excessive spending and that financial resources are efficiently channelled to investment in areas in productive sectors. In the context of this monetary environment, banking institutions have been asked to draw up their own credit plans. Within these plans, banks are encouraged to channel more credit to directly productive and export related activities. While restraining credit growth, it is not the intention to limit completely the access to financing. The production of goods and services and exports must continue to grow as they provide the very basis for strengthening the balance of payments as well as restoring market and investor confidence. Investors therefore need to be more selective in their investment activities, directing investment to productive activities that have high value added. And thirdly, there is the need to strengthen the banking system since the continuing operation of an economy depends on the existence of sound and well-functioning banking institutions. The position of Bank Negara Malaysia in this regard is very clear. Our banking system is strong but there is always room for improvement. While the ratio of non-performing loans, the coverage for non-performing loans, the capital adequacy ratio, the ratio of collateral value of property to credit, and other prudential indicators are currently favourable, they can come under pressure when there is excessive turbulence in any of the financial markets. In strengthening further the banking system, you would have noted that the period for classifying a loan as nonperforming has now been shortened from 6 to 3 months to comply with international standards. The minimum general provision has also been raised. Banking institutions are also required to be more transparent in publishing data on their loan exposure by sector, non-performing loans and movements in the provisions for bad and doubtful debts. With greater transparency, banks will be more discerning in their lending decisions. I also wish to reiterate my message at the recent Annual Conference with Financial Institutions that the Tier-1 status will not be accorded to a banking institution based solely on its capital strength. In evaluating whether a particular institution deserves to be granted Tier-1 status, Bank Negara will also consider other equally important aspects pertaining to that banking institution. Banking institutions should be mindful that all the elements of CAMEL are equally important. Indeed, asset quality, level of management expertise and capability, productive use of resources to generate earnings and the prudent management of the liquidity position are part and parcel of the policy to strengthen the capital base of banking institutions. Banking institutions should not regard that a larger capital base must be accompanied by growth in loans in order to maintain the level of return on capital which shareholders and the market may expect. Banking is a long haul business. Most important is the soundness of the banking institution.
