It is hoped that through this framework, both lender and borrower groups would be able to coordinate measures aimed at realising greater collective benefit and increased opportunities for tangible win-win scenarios. This multi-bank debt reconstruction approach as espoused by the CDRC aims to provide necessary conditions for financial institutions to assess properly the longer term future of the debtor. The principal objectives of the CDRC are as follows: To minimise losses to creditors, shareholders, and other stakeholders through voluntary coordinated workouts; Preserve viable businesses during the current economic conditions and hence, jobs; To implement a comprehensive framework for debt restructuring; and To implement "best practice" for debt restructuring. Under the CDRC framework, which will be announced in more detail by the chairman of the Steering Committee, Dato? C. Rajandram, the following key prerequisites should be firmly adhered to: Financial institutions should be supportive and not precipitate insolvency; The sharing of reliable information among all interested stakeholders should form the basis of decision making; Financial institutions should cooperate to reach a collective view on whether a company should be given financial support based on specified terms; Losses should be shared in the normal order of standard restructuring. The CDRC framework calls for the financial institutions to voluntarily give the debtor a reasonable period of time in order for creditors/appointed consultant to determine the debtor company?s financial health and needs before further decisions are made. The major financial creditors should act in a co-ordinated manner to facilitate short term viability and stability whilst confirmation of the present position of the debtor and relative positions of the creditors is obtained in a timely and cost effective manner, enabling the available options to be presented, assessed and a way forward agreed upon. During this "standstill" period, the financial institutions should keep credit lines in place and not precipitate insolvency actions, unless either the creditors or debtor formally terminates the debt restructuring exercise. CDRC will complement both Danaharta and Danamodal in helping to restore confidence and strengthen the banking system and hence expediting the economic recovery process of the country, as envisage by the Government.. In this respect, all three parties have been meeting regularly to ensure that their activities are properly coordinated to achieve the desired objectives. I wish to again emphasise that the role of financial institutions in spearheading economic recovery is extremely important and urgent. Therefore, the financial institutions have to play an active role in the restructuring exercises, by committing resources necessary to ensure the orderly and expeditious restructuring of the loans. It is now time for financial institutions to demonstrate that we are capable and willing to work in the broader interest of the economy. I strongly urge that this attitude should pervade the banking hierarchy and that every bank officer understand the difficult times we are facing and that we must work together to resolve the problem facing us. Bank Negara Malaysia 27 October 1998

Title: Keynote Address at the InsurTech Leaders Summit
text: Deputy Governor's Speech at the International Conference on "Managing the Asian Financial Crisis: Lessons & Challenges" Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 02 Nov 1998 First of all, I would like to thank the organisers for inviting me to speak at this international conference on "Managing the Asian Financial Crisis: Lessons and Challenges". It is a great pleasure for me to speak today before such a distinguished gathering of speakers and participants. In the first section of my presentation this afternoon, I will attempt to put into perspective the events prior to 1 September 1998 which culminated in the introduction of selective capital control measures and subsequently discuss some issues of importance related to these controls. The Need for a Comprehensive Solution Much has been discussed as to the solution to the East Asian Crisis. After more than a year into the crisis, however, no general consensus has emerged on the appropriate policy response and concrete results have yet to emerge. In the mean time, while the debate continues on the initiatives that have been taken, where the weaknesses lie and the relative merits of the more conventional versus the more interventionist approach, the financial crisis has now spread to other regions and the economic crisis in the region has deepened. The lack of progress in yielding the desired results may be on account of several factors. These include the lack of understanding and diagnosis of all the problems and issues involved, the emphasis on partial solutions as opposed to a more comprehensive approach, and the inappropriate sequencing of policies. Finally, there has been tendency to generalise the problems confronting the region, reflecting the failure to recognise the important differences in the East Asian economies, their institutions and economic structure. What is needed is a viable solution that will produce a sustainable outcome. For such a solution to be developed, there is a need to recognise and to come to terms with the whole spectrum of problems and issues associated with the crisis. The East Asian crisis is the result of an amalgamation of several elements. Any solution would therefore need to be comprehensive in its approach. While such a solution will involve addressing issues within individual national economies, of equal importance is the need to review the international financial architecture, with a view to enhance its ability to cope with the risks and challenges of globalisation. Thus, while such a move would require a concerted effort by the international community, it in no way reduces the importance for commitment and determination by individual countries to do their part in this process. It is only in this context that a more permanent solution can emerge that will allow the global economy to reap the benefits of globalisation. In the recent weeks following the IMF/World Bank annual meetings in Washington, D.C., there is an emerging consensus on the need to develop a more comprehensive solution to the crisis. In particular, there is a recognition of the need to strengthen the architecture of the international financial system to better cope with the challenges of the international financial markets. Most significant was the acceptance of the fact that the current financial crisis was a global problem, and therefore required a global solution. This is a departure from the situation last year, when the crisis was seen as a regional problem arising from internal factors in the affected countries. An important development was also the emerging consensus on the need to improve the transparency of financial market players, including additional regulatory and disclosure measures. In this connection, the IMF and relevant international financial agencies have been tasked to review and determine the appropriate disclosure requirements or regulations to ensure better assessment of the risks involved in the operations of institutional investors, including their highly leveraged operations. Another shift in thinking has also occurred on the issue of capital controls. Such controls on capital movements may be considered under specific circumstances to provide breathing space for macroeconomic and financial measures to take effect. The IMF, in particular, now acknowledges that liberalisation of capital movements need to be carried out in an orderly manner and sequenced in a manner that is in tandem with the pace of strengthening of the domestic financial system and within an effective prudential framework. And of importance was the consensus on the need to involve the private sector in both preventing and resolving financial crises. Here, the IMF is examining options to use market-based mechanisms to cope with the risk of sudden changes in investor sentiment that could lead to financial crises. Over the weekend, a move was made by the G-7 in terms of an agreement on a package of proposals to contain the crisis and prevent future crises. These include a combination of improved regulation and transparency and a new financial safety net at the IMF to assist countries in coping with liquidity crises. The measures also included proposals for closer regulation of banks to promote safe and sustainable capital flows and a review of the activities of institutional investors, including that of hedge funds. It is hoped that further concrete steps will be taken following these discussions to strengthen the architecture of the international financial system and to ensure the prospects for the restoration of stability in the global financial markets. Malaysia's Programme Malaysia has responded to the crisis with a series of policy packages during the course of the crisis. The policy response has evolved according to the changing conditions operating to achieve the objectives of monetary and financial stability in an environment of sustainable growth. Within a brief period of experiencing the turbulence in the financial markets in mid-1997, Malaysia recognised the fundamental nature of the regional financial crisis. Unlike on previous occasions when the response to bouts of speculative pressure was to sharply increase interest rates supported by intervention operations, it was recognised that this would not be a sustainable response. On July 14, the ringgit was therefore left to adjust downwards and interest rates were brought down to the levels prior to the currency attack. While this resulted in an initial 5% depreciation in the currency, this policy allowed the international reserves to remain intact and reduced the damage on the financial system and real sector arising from sharply higher interest rates. The view taken was that high interest rates was unlikely to contribute to stabilising the currency given the factors causing the shift in flows. Policy at the early part of the crisis essentially focused on addressing the key areas of vulnerabilities, in particular, to contain inflation, to maintain the standard of living and Malaysia's competitiveness. In this context, interest rates were adjusted with the expected rate of inflation to ensure that savers earn a positive rate of return. Secondly, the focus was to reduce further the current account deficit which was 10% of GNP in 1995 and which had been reduced to 5% in 1996. The deficit was seen as a potential source of instability given the uncertainty with respect to developments in the capital account. Finally, while the financial sector was strong in terms of capitalisation (risk weighted capital ratio of 11.3%) and quality of loan portfolio (nonperforming loans of 3.6%) and in terms of performance, initiatives were taken to reduce further the banking sector vulnerabilities to adverse developments following the adjustments that had occurred in the financial markets. Policies with respect to the financial sector aimed specifically to enhance the efficiency of the banking institutions, to rationalise and consolidate the banking institutions, thereby ensuring the intermediation process to provide adequate financing to support economic growth. Of importance was for the financial sector to remain resilient to further adjustments that might occur. While there were encouraging signs of stability in the financial markets over the period March to early June this year, events in Japan and then Russia triggered a further wave of adjustment during this period. At this stage of the prolonged period uncertainty, the inefficiencies that had emerged in the financial system, had its effect on the real sector. Several measures followed that aimed to minimise the implications of the financial developments on the real sector. On the fiscal front, expenditure was increased to protect the more vulnerable segments of society. Special funds were set up to enhance access to financing by specific identified sectors. With inflation having peaked in July, interest rates were adjusted downwards in early August. These measures were designed to contain the severity of the adverse implications on overall economic development. In terms of the overall macroeconomic framework, Malaysia had contained inflation, improved its external balance, maintained low external debt exposure, external reserves remained in tact and the banking sector continued to perform its intermediation function. Despite these positive trends, Malaysia continued to remain vulnerable to external developments. Malaysia Moves to Exchange Controls By mid-year, exactly one year since the outbreak of the crisis, the external environment continued to deteriorate. The risk of further waves of instability of increasing proportions still very much remained on the horizon. Despite the measures and reforms that had been put in place by the affected countries, there did not appear to be signs of stability returning to the financial markets. On its part, Malaysia had persevered to undertake adjustment policies and implemented financial reforms to reduce the risks and vulnerabilities to external developments. While the measures are ongoing, the prospects for these initiatives to yield the desired results can only be achieved in a stable environment. A source of concern that was emerging during this period was the increase in the rate of the internationalisation of the ringgit. This trend became increasingly apparent since April 1998. This trend reflected an increasing outflow of ringgit as opposed to foreign currency. This ringgit outflow was attracted by higher and higher interest rates in the region of 20 to 40% offered by offshore centres while onshore rates were in the region of 11%. The strong demand for offshore ringgit at high costs increased the vulnerability of the ringgit. The build up of offshore ringgit represented a potential source of instability to the ringgit. In view of the openness of the Malaysian economy, this trend could have fundamental damage to the real economy. This trend would affect the ability for Malaysia to conduct independent monetary policy based on domestic conditions. Following these developments, Malaysia announced the introduction of exchange control measures on September 1, 1998. Features of the Exchange Control Measures The exchange control measures adopted by Malaysia have therefore been designed and implemented to achieve specific objectives. The policies are selective and not comprehensive and restrictive as has been suggested by the critics of controls. The controls are aimed specifically at eliminating access to ringgit by speculators by reducing the offshore market in ringgit, limiting the supply of ringgit to speculators. The controls also aimed at stabilising short-term capital inflows, by requiring inflows of capital to remain in the country for a period of 12 months. While in Malaysia, however, these funds can be actively managed in the form of ringgit assets. These funds can be converted upon maturity of the twelve month holding period. Specifically, it is only the following items that are controlled: Ringgit-denominated transactions among non-residents; via non resident external account; Outflows of short-term capital by requiring such inflows to remain in the country for a minimum period of one year; Import and export of ringgit by travellers, both residents and non-residents are restricted; and Malaysian investments abroad now require approvals. There are no controls on: Current account transactions (amendment in rules only require trade transactions, both in the goods and services, to be settled in foreign currencies and no longer in domestic currency); Repatriation of interest, dividends, fees, commissions and rental income from portfolio investment and other forms of ringgit assets; and Foreign direct investment inflows and outflows, including income and capital gains are not subject to any restrictions. Malaysia's controls are therefore selective, designed to achieve the specific objective of containing speculative capital. The measures do not apply to foreign direct investment. The controls are not intended to disrupt or dislocate genuine trade-related activities or direct foreign investment flows. As part of the measures, the ringgit has been fixed against the United States dollar to provide a greater degree of certainty to the market for the conduct of trade and investment activities. Following the introduction of selected exchange control measures, the ringgit strengthened against the United States dollar by 10.5% from the end-August level of RM4.22 to an intraday high of US1.00RM3.82 on 1 September 1998. The ringgit appreciated further to US1.00RM3.80 after which the ringgit's rate was fixed at that rate, effective 11 a.m on 2 September 1998. Overall, the Government has adopted a flexible approach in the implementation of the new exchange control rules. The situation has been closely monitored. Emphasis has been placed on the efficiency of the implementation process as well as the dissemination of information on the changes to the exchange control rules to provide a greater understanding of the measures. Efforts have been directed to ensure that the administrative machinery is in place to ensure prompt response to requests so that disruptions and inefficiencies will be minimised. Preconditions for Controls The capital control measures introduced by Malaysia are not unique. Many countries including the industrial countries have resorted to capital controls. Countries such as Germany, Switzerland and the United States imposed capital controls when they faced difficulties in achieving domestic and external balance in post-war years. Capital controls played an important role in the defense of a number of European currencies arising from the aftermath of market disturbances within the exchange rate mechanism (ERM) of the European Union. Among the developing countries, the use of capital controls has been much more prevalent. The Latin American countries (Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Venezuela), the South Asian countries (India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka), the former centrally planned economies and, closer home, China and Taiwan, have all used capital controls. The experience of countries in achieving the objectives of capital controls has varied. The use of controls has been widely criticised by proponents of the free market systems on grounds that it leads to distortions and inefficiencies. Capital controls have been identified as a major cause for creating distortions in some of these economies, undermining their prospects for growth and development. A more constructive approach towards control would be to consider when and under what circumstances such capital controls can be applied, in what form they should take, the preconditions that would ensure it would yield the desired results and how it might be efficiently implemented. There are several preconditions for success and the existing conditions and circumstances in Malaysia gives us confidence that the capital control measures would achieve the desired objectives. Let me compare and contrast some of the unique characteristics of Malaysia which we believe would contribute to achieving our desired objectives. Firstly, capital controls have historically been imposed by countries facing balance of payments constraints. In view of the weak external reserves level, many of these countries imposed restrictions on almost all transactions with non-residents, including current account transactions. On the contrary, the corrective measures taken by Malaysia have strengthened our external payments position significantly. A significant improvement in the current account has already taken place. The official forecasts for current account balance of RM20.1 billion for 1998 (7.7% of GNP) and RM11 billion for 1999 (4.2% of GNP) were based on conservative assumptions. Many of the countries that imposed capital controls faced capital flight. In this regard, it must be noted that Malaysia has generally not experienced significant capital outflows of the type and magnitude experienced by other countries facing balance of payments and reserves constraints. Our capital outflows have been in the form of prepayments of external loans by both the public and private sectors, Malaysians investments in productive ventures abroad with potential to yield spin-off benefits for the domestic economy and, finally liquidation of investments by portfolio investors. Most of the outflows of portfolio investments have already occurred, while the aggressive programme of prepayment of external loans and overseas investment have been put on hold to ease strains on the reserves position. Meanwhile, our external reserves are intact, unencumbered and increasing. The build-up in external reserves to date has been significant. As at 15 October 1998, international reserves stood at US22.6 billion, an increase of US2.4 billion from endAugust level, adequate to finance 4.3 months of imports. This growth in reserves would provide greater overall confidence. In addition, the short-term debt is half the size of foreign exchange reserves, which means that Malaysia is not highly vulnerable to credit outflows over the short term, and more than 56% of Malaysia's external debt have remaining maturity that exceeds four years. Experience of countries has shown that countries with strong balance of payments position such as China and Taiwan have achieved a greater degree of success with capital controls. An important feature of countries which had failed to achieve the desired objectives via capital controls is the inflationary bias in these countries caused by an inappropriate mix of macroeconomic policies, including exchange rate and monetary policies. Most of these countries have either had trade and payments regimes which were protectionist in nature or where public expenditure had been diverted to less productive sectors such as military expenditure. This in turn resulted in supply constraints and a general rise in prices of goods and services. In comparison, such risks for Malaysia are low: Inflationary pressures both at home and abroad are subdued. On the domestic front, weak domestic demand has more than offset the effects of the depreciation of the ringgit against the currencies of major trading partners. Excess capacity in product and labour markets would contribute to lower inflation. More importantly, the fiscal stimulus is being funded by non-inflationary financing, mainly domestic savings. The inflation outlook is expected to remain subdued. Generally, the low inflation environment and strong expansion in income levels in the last decade has resulted in high savings and is expected to remain high at about 40% of GNP; Malaysia also ranks favourably in terms of overall competitiveness. Malaysia has pursued an export-oriented industrialisation (EOI) strategy since the 1970s, which has exposed the economy to international competition. Malaysia's economy is relatively open with high foreign presence in the domestic industries, including the financial services. Several policy measures have been put in place to enhance productivity improvements on an on-going basis to increase the nation's competitiveness; Overall, the ringgit is not overvalued at current levels. The level at which the ringgit is fixed against the US dollar is deemed sustainable. During the period February to mid-year, the ringgit traded at about the RM3.80 level. Thereafter, the ringgit depreciated following developments in the Japanese yen. The ringgit is also not overvalued when measured in terms of real effective exchange rate, given the low domestic inflation rate; and The measures provide some breathing space to ensure that the ongoing structural adjustment measures could continue uninhibited by external developments. The Government is in fact on course in its efforts to restructure the financial sector, in particular, the recapitalisation of the financial institutions. Mechanisms have been put in place to deal with the situation rising non-performing loans (establishment of Danaharta), recapitalisation of the banking institutions (Danamodal) and restructuring of the corporate debt (Steering Committee on Corporate Debt). These measures are also aimed at preserving the gains that have been made in terms of strengthening the balance of payments position and in terms of containing inflation to create a positive environment to support economic recovery. The selective exchange controls imposed by Malaysia have a greater chance of success because the circumstances and conditions are in our favour. As highlighted earlier, Malaysia is not substituting controls for appropriate macroeconomic policies. The controls are to provide some breathing space to allow us to take comprehensive adjustment policies in an environment of stability in the financial markets. Structural adjustments are ongoing to ensure that macroeconomic fundamentals remain strong in the medium term. Overall, the introduction of the recent capital control measures will protect our economy from the instabilities of short-term capital flows and foreign currency speculation and create an environment that is conducive for a revival in investor and consumer confidence. Conclusion In this century, the world has experimented with several international monetary systems. The role of the international monetary system is to provide a framework to facilitate cross-border trade and investment through a stable exchange rate system. Such a well functioning and efficient international monetary system is essential to the functioning of the global economy. It is only in this context that the benefits of globalisation can be realised. This is even more important for small open economies such as Malaysia where trade accounts for almost 200% of GNP. An unstable international financial system will leave such countries highly vulnerable to developments in global financial markets. The urgent attention given by the international community towards this has already contributed positively to the financial markets. The strategy for Malaysia in moving forward is to operate within this framework and become an integral part of the global system. In this context, the strategy is to place emphasise on economic recovery and the transformation of the economy to become more efficient and competitive. Importance is also given to restructuring and strengthening the banking system. As can be observed in most financial crisis, stability and recovery in financial markets generally followed the recovery of the real sector. Therefore, while efforts are being directed to ensure a stable macroeconomic framework of low inflation and a positive external balance and a financial system that is resilient to external shocks, important consideration is also given to minimise the damage of the financial turmoil on the domestic economy, in particular, to the more vulnerable segments of society. Malaysia's favourable initial macroeconomic conditions, relatively strong financial system and low external debt exposure has allowed for greater flexibility in its policy strategy. To further facilitate the continued restructuring and transformation exercise, the controls represent a means to an end. It represents a means of creating the stable environment that will allow Malaysia to prepare itself to be an integral part of the global financial system within the new international financial architecture from a position of strength and resilience. Bank Negara Malaysia 2 November 1998

Title: Speech at the 10th Anniversary Dinner of Cagamas Berhad
text: Governor Tan Sri Ali Abul Hassan's Speech at the Malaysian Insurance Industry Dinner Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 06 Nov 1998 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English In these challenging times, it is almost impossible for any gathering of the business fraternity to escape from discussing issues stemming from the current economic situation. To move forward, we need to first appreciate the effects of the economic downturn on the insurance industry. I will share with you some of my thoughts on this matter. It is heartening to note that despite the slowdown in premium growth from 20% in 1996 to 14.4% in 1997, premiums represented a higher proportion of nominal GNP that is, 4.2% compared with 4.1% a year earlier. Total assets of the industry also increased by 13% to RM35 billion as at end 1997 to account for 3.1% of the total assets of the financial system. The effect of the economic slowdown has been more severe in 1998. For the first half of 1998, the insurance industry recorded a much lower growth of 3.4% in premium income to RM5.2 billion, compared with an increase of 19.3% in the corresponding period in 1997. The industry suffered large losses on their equity investments. Arising from this, the combined assets of life and general insurance funds only managed to register a marginal growth rate of 6.5% to RM 36.4 billion in June 1998 compared with a growth of 11.1% during the first six months in 1997. The general funds grew at 7.6% while the life funds saw a lower growth of 5.9%. The impact of the economic turmoil has somewhat diverted our focus from moving towards consolidation and strategic positioning of the Malaysian insurance industry in a liberalised and globalised market environment. Instead, our immediate attention and resources are channeled to focus more on short-term measures to alleviate insurers from absorbing the full brunt of the economic downturn. Fortunately, we have implemented some long-term measures which have made the industry more resilient and enhance insurers? fundamental strength for future progress. Seen in a different perspective, the current economic setback has brought to light various weaknesses and deficiencies in the insurance industry. While the current economic condition has affected the progress of the industry, let?s not be overwhelmed by it. Instead, insurers should make use of this opportunity to review its future strategies and direction to enable it to move swiftly once the economy recovers. We should be mindful that while the world is experiencing a slowdown now, before long, the persistent call for further liberalisation will continue. Insurers ill-equipped to face global competition will find themselves increasingly being forced out of the industry. From a positive viewpoint, the present crisis offers many lessons for those who are willing to learn. The immediate task is for the industry to align its strategy with the National Economic Recovery Plan. The industry must play its role as a source of longterm funds and a tool for efficient risk management. The industry must transform and emerge stronger, ready to shoulder additional responsibility and play a bigger developmental role in promoting our social and economic well being. With this in view, Bank Negara had introduced more stringent prudential requirements in 1997 to strengthen and position the industry to compete in a liberalised environment. However, the current economic crisis has severely impacted the performance of insurers with a number of insurers unable to meet capital and solvency margin requirements. Recognising this setback, Bank Negara has recently implemented temporary measures to allow time for insurers to get back on their feet. Notwithstanding the reprieve given to insurers, I wish to remind you that the relaxation is not a long term solution to the industry. Such measures will be lifted once the economy recovers. For a long time, the Malaysian insurance industry has been made up of too many insurers, a large number of which do not have very strong prospects for long-term viability due to their small size. Such fragmentation will not augur well for an industry undergoing a period of restrained growth. The limited market size will result in a marginalisation of the smaller insurers and sooner or later will eventually lead to their demise. Therefore, I would like to urge all insurers, especially the smaller ones to answer the clarion call to merge to form larger and more viable entities. At the very least, the financial crisis has reinforced the need for Malaysian insurers to consolidate to remain viable in the long term. What is left to be decided is only the mode. On its part, Bank Negara will provide all the assistance needed to promote mergers among insurers. We will also be issuing a set of guidelines, setting out the parameters within which mergers could be carried out, together with some incentives to encourage mergers. We have to acknowledge that the past decade of high economic growth and stability which we had enjoyed may not return in the immediate future. We therefore have to work harder and should make the necessary adjustments to survive and prosper. In this regard, I like to urge insurers to take proactive steps to maintain and preserve their customers? base by enhancing policyholders value. During a period of economic uncertainty, consumers are keen to maximise their premium dollars and reduce on any unnecessary spending. The pressure will be on insurers to find more creative insurance solutions to meet the insurance needs of consumers. This should include developing a scheme to assist the customer in meeting his premium instalments over this difficult period. Past experience has shown that in times of economic difficulty, moral hazards increase and with it the escalation of claims ratios. This demands that insurers exercise greater care and prudence in their technical underwriting and risk assessment functions. My advice to insurers is not to compromise sound underwriting principles in a quest for higher turnover. I would remind you that unlike most businesses, in insurance, the cost of error in judgement does not surface until much later. Short sightedness or reckless underwriting measures will usually extract a high price, paid in the long run. Rather, insurers should strategise over a broader horizon and pay more attention to effective management of resources and productivity. This will involve a review of asset management strategy, cost cutting measures, increasing technical and operational efficiency as well as rationalising and streamlining operations. There are many areas in which the industry can improve on to capitalise on the potential within the insurance industry which remains vast despite the current economic setback. As the insuring public becomes more discerning and sophisticated, product innovation and development will become increasingly important. Product innovation in the Malaysian insurance market, however, remains limited with many homogenous products dominating the market. With the growing convergence of financial products, insurers will soon find themselves displaced if they continue to rely on traditional products. Global insurers are already aware of the large untapped market in Malaysia and are knocking hard on our doors notwithstanding the current economic setback. Another critical area which can make a difference to a financial institution?s operation is technological advancements. While technological development has swept through the business fraternity worldwide, Malaysian insurers have yet to fully realise its potential as many have yet to venture on-line. Many still focus the use of technology on accounting or record keeping functions. To maintain a competitive edge to be able to render prompt and efficient service to the insuring public, it is important for insurers to extend technological development to cover the front-end operations. Takaful business is yet another area that holds tremendous potential for insurers. Considered still a relatively new development, the Takaful market is comparatively small with its contribution income and total assets constituting 2.7% and 1.6% respectively of conventional business in 1998, but growing very rapidly at an average annual rate of 65% and 45% respectively for the past three years. Bank Negara has identified the strengths and weaknesses of the takaful industry and will be working with the takaful operators to draw up a strategic five-year plan to spearhead its development. As in the past, Bank Negara will continue to put in place measures to further spur the development of the insurance industry. As usual, we welcome suggestions from you and other proposals you wish Bank Negara to consider. Under this present economic condition, it is especially important for both the regulators and the industry to collabrate to tide over this difficult period. Towards this end, in response to LIAM?s proposal, Bank Negara had agreed to extend the period that life insurers may continue to pay an overriding commission of 20% instead of 15% in the first policy year to the year 2000. Prior to this, the higher commission rate of 20% was only applicable for new policies issued until 1998. It is hoped that this will help ease the financial burden on the agency force during this period of slow growth in new business. Tonight we are also celebrating the success of the graduates of the Malaysian Insurance Institute (MII) educational qualifications. As Chairman of MII, I would like to congratulate them for a well-earned success. I hope that this will lead them to further success in their careers. With the newly acquired knowledge and expertise, they are now better equipped to play an important role in propelling the industry forward. As continuous education is vital to enable one to keep abreast of developments, I hope that your acquisition of knowledge will not end here, but instead will continue well into the future. Learning is an operational tool for continuous improvement and a process for developing core competencies and creating values for the insurance industry. It is in this context that MII will be a strategic partner of insurers determined to excel in the future. Allow me at this juncture to highlight to you some of the initiatives taken by MII this year. MII has had a very active calendar of training and educational activities and successfully conducted close to 200 short courses involving more than 3000 participants. In 1998, MII achieved a few firsts. Among them is the inaugural batch of 11 students completing the Chartered Financial Consultants Course (ChFC). Implemented in 1996 in joint collaboration with the American College, ChFC is the highest internationally recognised professional qualification for life insurance agents and those involved in personal financial planning. MII is also the only institute in the world currently given the right by the American College to conduct the ChFC course on a continuous basis. It also commenced the first Diploma in Insurance and Risk Management International class under the sponsorship of the Asean Insurance Training Fund that was launched in May this year. The successful implementation of the Asean Insurance Training Fund marks another milestone in the history of MII and the Malaysian insurance industry. It signifies the transformation of MII from a local learning institution to a regional learning centre of insurance. Although the Asian crisis has affected the initial response to this programme, it is expected that there will be increased participation in the future. MII has also scheduled additional courses under this programme, including marine insurance and takaful insurance. Kejayaan yang dicapai oleh MII sebahagian besarnya adalah hasil daripada sumbangan, baik dari segi masa mahupun wang ringgit oleh persatuan insurans, penanggung insurans, broker insurans, ajuster dan individu yang hadir pada malam ini. Di sini, saya ingin merakamkan terima kasih dan penghargaan kami kepada tuan-tuan dan puan-puan sekalian dan bagi pihak MII, kami berharap sokongan seperti ini akan diteruskan pada masa hadapan. Akhir kata, saya berharap tuan-tuan dan puan-puan dapat sama-sama merasai kemeriahan majlis malam ini dan semoga kita semua dapat mencapai kejayaan dalam tahun 1999. Bank Negara Malaysia 6 November 1998

Title: Speech at the 23rd Malaysian Financial Markets Association Annual Dinner
text: Governor Tan Sri Ali Abul Hassan's Speech at the Malaysian Financial Markets Association Annual Dinner Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 13 Nov 1998 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English This is the first time I am in the company of such a large gathering of foreign exchange and money market dealers. I have heard a great deal about forex dealers, and one particularly story struck me as very interesting. Three chaps were discussing on what is the oldest profession in the world. The first, an engineer said that the world is created according to engineering principles, and therefore, God was an engineer. He, therefore, claimed that engineering was the oldest profession in the world. The second chap, an architect quoted the bible which says that God created order out of chaos. This, he said, was what architects always do and therefore God must be an architect. Therefore, his profession must be the oldest profession. The third chap, a forex dealer asked: "You say God created order out of chaos ? who do you think created chaos in the first place?". I am sure that members of Persatuan Pasaran Kewangan Malaysia did not contribute to the financial chaos that has shaken the world since July 1997. However, given the severity of the situation created by some foreign hedge funds and other currency manipulators, Malaysia had to impose exchange controls to stop further manipulation of the Ringgit exchange rate. These measures may have adversely affected the members of your Association, and we regret this. However, the exchange control has enabled Bank Negara Malaysia to pursue appropriate policies and measures to put Malaysia on a firmer path towards economic recovery. The measures, which have given a breathing space for us to halt the free-fall of the economy, have shown positive results. The economy is already showing signs of turning around, with the country?s reserves rising and inflation falling. The trade surplus has improved, resulting in an increase in the foreign currency reserves by US3.26 billion, from US20.23 billion as at the end of August 1998 to US23.49 billion as at the end of October 1998. Aside from the exchange control measures, the Government had also implemented other measures to create a conducive environment for economic recovery and cushion the economic shocks. The establishment of Danaharta and Danamodal are meant to alleviate the loans problem faced by the banks and to recapitalise the banks so as to create a healthy environment to reinvigorate lending in productive sectors. Bank Negara Malaysia had imposed a minimum annual loan growth of 8% to be met by all banking institutions by the end of this year to enable the country to achieve an expected 1% GDP growth next year. Since the total outstanding loan in the banking system as at 22nd October this year was RM418.3 billion, the financial institutions need to increase its lending by RM36.7 billion in order the meet the total outstanding loan target of RM454.9 billion by the end of the year. The government has set in place the infrastructures for economic recovery. Interest rates have been reduced, greater liquidity has been injected into the banking system and the intermediation process has been enhanced. It is now up to the private sector and business community to generate the momentum of growth. I would also like to stress the point that financial institutions have to play their roles in this crucial time and I expect them to live up to the expectations. Let me now turn to the capital market. I envisage that there is a tremendous room for us to develop our capital market to meet the funding requirement of both the public and private sectors. As the issuance of debt securities increases and a more realistic benchmark yield curve starts to exist, we expect to see a commensurate improvement in the volume of interbank dealings, market making activities and pricing of capital market instruments. We should be able to achieve a more vibrant secondary market with the existence of the Bond Information and Dissemination System, and the implementation of the Real Time Electronic Transfer of Funds and Securities in May 1999 to provide an efficient mechanism for clearing and settlement of debt securities. As the world is grappling with the challenge of reforming the global financial architectures, redefining the roles of the International Monetary Fund and The World Bank, and enhancing the regulation of hedge funds, we have to prepare ourselves for other major developments affecting the industry. The advent of the Euro as the official currency of the European Monetary Union on 1st January next year calls for a need to ensure that the payment system linking Malaysian financial institutions and other foreign banks continue to function efficiently to facilitate corporate needs and commercial transactions. Malaysia?s bilateral trade with the European Union in 1997 constituted 14.3% of Malaysia?s global trade. Between January and August this year, Malaysia?s trade with the European Union totalled RM47.6 billion. With the large volume of trade between the European Union and Malaysia currently, it is important for Malaysian banks to be ready for the Euro. The banks should be able to adjust to the competition and financial products that come along with the Euro. Attention should also be drawn to the legal aspects of the Euro pertaining to outstanding trades and agreements. Another important issue is the millennium bug or Y2K problem. To ensure no disruption to retail and wholesale banking activities and loss in productivity, all financial institutions should have been making substantial and adequate preparations to upgrade their current systems to be Y2K compliant. The central bank has formed an Industry Y2K Steering Committee to ensure a planned and coordinated approach to address the Y2K problem. Based on the Y2K implementation timeline, most of the financial institutions have completed the assessment and renovation stage and have entered the testing stage as at the end of September 1998. The financial institutions are expected to complete the testing stage by the end of this year. Persatuan Pasaran Kewangan Malaysia has come a long way since its inception in 1973. I was informed that the number of association?s active members has grown from 400 in the early years to 1,320 currently. The association, which has been accommodating the growing needs of the dealers community, should continue to be the focal point for forums and discussions of various issues relating to the industry along with associations of bankers and Bank Negara Malaysia. It should also constantly review the techniques and practices in the forex and money markets so as to develop and maintain high standards which are comparable to international practices. Let us all not be intimidated by the current economic turmoil. Instead, we should all garner our resources and strength to rise to the occasion and deal with the challenges to reignite our economy. With the support of all, we should be able to weather the storm and return to economic tranquillity, putting us in a more resilient position to withstand new challenges in the years ahead. I do not want to burden you with a long speech. I know you are here to have good time, and you want to enjoy yourselves and want to let your hair down ? that is those of you who still have hair! I thank you for your attention and wish you an enjoyable dinner and a pleasant evening. Bank Negara Malaysia 13 November 1998

Title: Keynote Address at the National Credit Management Conference
text: Assistant Governor Dr. Awang Adek Hussin's Speech at the MCA Seminar - "Currency Stabilisation: An Assessment After Six Months" Speaker: Assistant Governors / Advisers Speech/Interview Date: 04 Feb 1999 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English I am honoured to be given the opportunity to speak at this seminar on "Currency Stabilization: An Assessment After Six Months". The organisation of this Seminar is both timely and appropriate, given the unique experience of Malaysia in recent months. The Government too is constantly monitoring the various measures and their consequences to ensure they yield the intended results. I will focus my presentation on the salient points of the recent exchange control measures and provide some of my own personal thoughts and assessment of the exchange control policy in place. As we all know, the selective exchange control measures implemented by Malaysia on 1 September 1998 were both unexpected and unprecedented. These extreme measures are necessary to address the fallout from the regional financial crisis, which are equally unprecedented in terms of the rapidity, magnitude and far reaching implications. The affected currencies in the region were unable to stabilise quickly as originally expected. Instead, we saw what had begun as an Asian financial crisis threatened to turn itself into a world financial meltdown, spreading its influences to Russia, South Africa and Latin America. Even the United States and Europe are likely to feel some of the effects as well. Consequently, the growth forecast for the world economy has been repeatedly revised downwards. Closer to home, the crisis first hit Thailand in May 1997 and then spread to Indonesia and South Korea, with the adverse effects spilling over to other countries in the region. The Malaysian economy, although fundamentally sound, was not spared. Malaysia, too, had to undergo a difficult period over the last 20 months to cope with the effects of the regional financial crisis. Of course, Malaysia is not the worst affected, but the pains of adjustments have been just as real. The Malaysian ringgit went from about RM2.50 to a US dollar to RM4.20, before stabilising at around RM3.80, achieved largely by the new exchange control policy. Salient Features of Exchange Control Like many other countries, Malaysia has always had some form of exchange control in place. Exchange control was first introduced in Malaysia in 1953 and has been in place ever since. The main objectives of exchange control have been to ensure that the foreign currency earning of the country is brought back and the limited financial resources of the country is used for productive purposes. Over time, many relaxations were introduced, especially when the economy experienced broad macro stability and rapid economic growth. The new exchange control policy adopted by Malaysia on 1 September 1998 is selective and highly focused on achieving certain objectives. And the most important objective is to eliminate the trading of the ringgit in the offshore market in order to cut off the activities of currency speculators from destablising the ringgit exchange rate. There are actually 3 major components underlying the present exchange control policy. One is to control the transfer of funds in the external accounts, so that no ringgit can be borrowed by foreigners for speculative activities in the currency markets overseas. Secondly, the policy to fix the exchange rate between the ringgit and the US dollar, so that there is stability and certainty of key parameters in the economy to support international trade and investment decisions. Thirdly, the introduction of the 12-month rule to prevent excessive short-term capital flows which can be highly destabilising. The previous liberal exchange control policy has served the country well and was appropriate for the kind of environment which prevailed until the Asian financial crisis emerged. The increasing relaxation of exchange control was in consonance with global financial reform and economic liberalisation undertaken in the country and elsewhere. Interest rate and exchange rate were allowed to be more market determined, while the public sector has been restructured to allow for a more vigorous private sector participation in the economy. Market forces were able to function smoothly as the players were generally small and not able to exert undue influence on the outcome. The Malaysian economy performed exceptionally well, with sustained rapid economic growth and remarkable distribution of income and wealth among all Malaysians, irrespective of their race and colour. A similar sense of optimism and strong economic performance was recorded in virtually all countries in the region. It was so pervasive in the East Asian region that it was known as a miracle. Many countries gained greater confidence and went on to remove virtually all remaining restrictions with respect to exchange and capital control. We in Asia had tremendous faith and believe in the market economy that we continued to open up and liberalise. Malaysia too was tempted to remove the remaining restrictions and control in place with respect to capital flows. Nonetheless, we decided to retain control on private sector borrowing overseas. This, on hindsight, turned out to be a critical factor in separating Malaysia from other countries in the region. While affected by the regional crisis, Malaysia has been fortunate enough to be spared of much worse consequences, due partly to Malaysia's low foreign currency borrowing compared to other countries. Nonetheless, the damage was still brutal. The country experienced a contraction in the real GDP by 4.8% in the first half of 1998 and 8.6% in the third quarter. The ringgit depreciated by 40.2% against the US dollar from July 1997 to August 1998. The Kuala Lumpur Composite Index declined by 72% from end-June 1997 to end-August 1998. At the same time, the banking and corporate sectors had come under tremendous pressures. The annual loan growth rate had moderated sharply to virtual stagnation at end-June 1998, from a growth of over 26.5% at end-1997. Lending rates climbed up to as high as 16% and in some cases even beyond 20%, and the net non-performing loans of the banking system rose to about 11.4% at end-August, compared with 4.1% at end-1997. What initially started as exchange rate instability arising from largely speculative activities, had set in motion a vicious downward spiral. If the spiral was not broken, the Malaysian economy would have been irreparably damaged through corporate bankruptcy and bank failures. It was against this background that radical measures were required to put a floor to rapid economic deterioration as well as to regain the badly needed monetary independence. What was required was for Malaysia to be able to conduct its monetary policy and increase money supply without having to worry about depreciation in the exchange rate. To us, the need to maintain this monetary independence is imperative. Before the new exchange control regime was introduced, our interest rate and exchange rate were closely related and interlinked. Any attempt to lower the interest rate would be viewed negatively by currency manipulators who would sell ringgit further in the offshore market which would in turn cause the exchange rate to depreciate sharply. Consequently, the prices of goods will rise, especially imported goods, resulting in inflationary tendencies which feed onto the cost of production and affect adversely the competitiveness of companies. At the same time, sharp depreciation of the local currency would increase the debt of companies obtained abroad and reduce substantially the capacity for the servicing of such debt. It appeared, therefore, that we were caught in a terrible bind: interest rate could not be lowered to revive the economy without causing exchange rate instability; yet the maintenance of the high interest rate regime would only push the country deeper into recession. Therein lies the fallacy of the conventional economic policy response to the current crisis as advocated by some including the International Monetary Fund or IMF. By insisting on high interest rate, the IMF hopes to stabilise the exchange rate and reduce the pressure on the currency. What happens to the companies and corporations and the real sector of the country in the process of adjustment is completely ignored, and social ramifications considered irrelevant. And even if these occur, they are conveniently considered as mere economic costs which must be sacrificed for future prosperity. This sort of argument has several weaknesses. Firstly, it believes in the principle that the end justifies the means. Secondly, in many developing economies, the social consequences of such adjustment may be too high and not sustainable, especially when confronted with social unrest and uprising. This dimension may not be well appreciated in a large developed economy, but highly relevant in the context of developing countries. In addition, it is doubtful how much interest rate hikes can stabilise the exchange rate in an environment where confidence quickly dissipates. In such an environment, some form of exchange control is necessary to contain the damage and rebuild confidence. This is why I believe the normal IMF policy prescription has not been successful in addressing the present crisis. The Impact In Malaysia, the desirable impact of the exchange control policy is increasingly clear. Firstly, it made possible the fixing of exchange rate which renders stability to the foreign exchange market. While it can be said that since the Asian currencies in general have gained greater stability, perhaps there was no real need for the control to be introduced in the first place. Yes, some stability appears to have prevailed, but there is no certainty that the Asian currencies will not be hit again in the face of the on-going crisis in Brazil, and the fear of possible devaluation of the Chinese yuan to regain international competitiveness. The advantage of the Malaysian situation now is to "lock in" this stability as the ringgit is no longer traded internationally. There is no worry of international events affecting the ringgit, and the Government effort can focus almost exclusively on strengthening the process of economic recovery in the country. Secondly, the stability in ringgit exchange rate is so crucial to support. Malaysia's trade with the rest of the world. Being an extremely open economy which benefits greatly from international trade and direct foreign investments, instability in exchange rates can be highly detrimental. In the case of large developed countries, the percentage of their international trade (export and import combined) to the entire GDP is relatively small. The ratio for US is 20% and Japan 18%. Even Germany and UK, their ratios are 45% and 46% respectively. To these countries, exchange rate may not be a critical price for resource allocation. But to Malaysia, with international trade representing more than 160% of GDP, the importance attached to the exchange rate and its stability is paramount. Another reason for the divergence in view is the advantage of resources available to the developed countries in handling the exchange rate volatility, which are generally not available to the developing countries. In the case of G7 countries, for instance, coordinated intervention has often been used to stabilise the exchange rate. As for the Asian countries, many were left on their own to fend for themselves in trying to protect their currencies -- of course with little success given the limited resources of these small countries. Despite pressing domestic concerns to revive the economy, the Malaysian economy continues to remain open and engaged. International trade and foreign investment remain important pillars supporting the domestic economy. That is why Malaysia is active in promoting greater stability in the world financial market, and for the necessary reform to be implemented towards this stability. This is not only important to the well-being of Malaysia, but rather critical to the development and prosperity of many developing countries struggling to survive the current crisis. Thirdly, the broad financial stability which has been gained arising from exchange rate stability has been extremely conducive and stimulative to the process of economic recovery. There are strong signals that the worst is over and recovery is under way in Malaysia. There is no doubt in my mind that the exchange control has been instrumental in putting a floor to economic deterioration, and in bringing back confidence that the economy is capable of growing again. Lest we take things for granted, let us be reminded by a recent report that while the progress in the financial restructuring in Malaysia has been commendable, the experience in Thailand could continue to be a drag on its economy. It has also been reported by another source that the crisis in Thailand has worsened with the economy contracting by 15.4% in 1998 and by as much as 10.1% in 1999. Given the situation in Thailand, and the continuing uncertainty facing Indonesia, it is difficult not to attribute our relative success in handling financial crisis to the fact that Malaysia has done it differently, that is through the exchange control policy. Fourthly, if there is any issue at all which has been raised with respect to the exchange control policy, perhaps it is only with respect to the 12-month rule. Many portfolio investors and fund managers have requested the Government to consider other approaches which may yield the same result in discouraging speculative capital flows. The Government has indicated its willingness to review the issue and is expected to come out with the decisions very soon. Once this is done, I am sure it will further enhance the efficacy of the exchange control policy in "locking in" financial stability and promoting real economic activity. It should also be mentioned that in complementing the measures on capital control, other policy initiatives have been implemented to improve the liquidity flows in the banking system, enhance the intermediation process, generate lending activities and ensure that viable businesses continue to receive financing. An important objective of these measures is to reduce the overall intermediation cost by reducing interest rate and releasing liquidity into the banking system. At the same time, the setting up of Danamodal to recapitalise banking institutions and Danaharta to purchase non-performing loans, together with CDRC on corporate restructuring, have all contributed greatly towards speedy economic recovery. The Results The effects of all the recent measures will necessary take some time to materialise. Nevertheless, it is encouraging to observe positive signs that things are getting better in Malaysia. The exchange rate of the ringgit is fixed against the US dollar with clear absence of pressure on the currency to depreciate, unlike in the earlier months. The interest rate has declined significantly. The 3-month intervention rate was reduced from 11% to 6.5%. This enables the business sector to operate at reasonable cost and improve their ability to service their existing borrowing. The trade balance of the balance of payments recorded a large surplus of RM51.5 billion for the first eleven months of 1998, surpassing the RM35 billion estimated for 1998 as a whole. Inflation has moderated to 5.3% in December as against 6.2% in June. In fact, the immediate effects have been the increase in the international reserves of the Central Bank from US20.5 billion at end-June to US27.4 billion at 15 January this year. The non-performing loans ratio of the banking system has also declined. Total loans approved by the banking system picked up from RM2.7 billion in May to RM7.6 billion in November 1998. We have also seen greater stability prevailing in the finanical market. The Kuala Lumpur Composite Index has strengthened by 93.5% since end August to reach 586.13 points at the close of 1998. Market capitalisation of the KLSE has recovered by RM174.4 billion to RM374.52 billion. Consumption and investment indicators have also turned positive. Sales of motor vehicles, for example, increased to 19,081 units in November 1998, compared with a monthly average of 12,517 units sold in the last ten months. The value of manufacturing investment approved by MITI increased to RM6.6 billion in the third quarter of 1998 compared with RM4 billion in the second quarter. Latest statistics have also shown that the unemployment situation has begun to stabilise, with the retrenchment of workers moderating further in recent months. The number of retrenchments declined to 5,137 workers in December, from a peak of 12,335 persons in July. Perhaps the most positive indicator is inflation, which moderated to 5.6% in November from a peak of 6.2% in June 1998. This provides greater flexibility for a relatively expansionary macroeconomic policy to be put in place to revive depressed domestic demand. As I see it, the next 6 months will be critical in determining the momentum and pace of our economic recovery. During this time, the Government will continue to persevere with its recovery programme to bring the Malaysian economy into a safe zone, irrespective of the views of those in economic orthodoxy. This sense of optimism is widely supported by improved sentiments that things are definitely getting better. Some market analysts and private sector groups have even revised upward their growth forecast for Malaysia in 1999 to between 2-3%, higher than the Government earlier forecast of 1%. It is highly possible that the actual outcome this year will surpass the forecast, when we are in the period of recession, just as the outcome tends to fall short of expectations during the high growth period. This is the famous pitfall in economic forecasting, when the forecast almost always fail to pick up turning points in economic cycles. Perhaps it is human nature to expect nothing much can go wrong during the good times, and similarly we cannot easily see how things can really improve during the bad times. My own bet is that the economic performance this year will be much better than many have expected. This optimism is also based on a more favourable performance of the financial sector as evident by the strong recovery in the stock market. It is well known in economic theory that adjustments in financial sector are faster than in the real sector. That is to say the performance of the financial sector is likely to lead that of the real sector. When the financial crisis began in July 1997, the impact on the Malaysian economy began to be felt only in early 1998. Similarly, as the recovery in the financial sector becomes stronger and more entrenched in 1999, the favourable impact of the real sector recovery will certainly be more visible and become stronger with a likely lag of 3 - 6 months. Conclusion In conclusion, let me state that exchange control is not new in Malaysia as it was in existence since 1953. Requirements of the Act were increasingly liberalised over time to keep pace with the changing time to suit the economic environment prevailing in the domestic as well as at the global level. The Government is committed to constantly review and modify the present exchange control regime as we have done successfully in the past. The country has benefited immensely from exchange control liberalisation and will not hesitate to return to the more liberal regime when the environment permits. But the situation at present dictates that Malaysia takes a series of bold actions to insulate itself from destabilising external influences. We need to regain our monetary policy independence to keep the domestic economy afloat and the real sector functioning. More importantly we need to protect the very foundations of our economy and maintain intact the social fabrics of our nation. There is no other choice for us, as we cannot continue to wait forever, hoping for the international community to set the framework for regulating short-term capital flows and controlling currency trading. Of course, over time, the Malaysian experience has gained increasing support among the international community. With the release of a recent report by the Bank of International Settlement (BIS) on the role of highly leveraged hedge funds and their interactions with banks, it has become clear that some form of regulaton is desirable and necessary. Many international efforts are directed in this direction, although the exact form of regulation to be agreed to is still far from clear. In any case, the requirement for greater disclosure is likely to be the minimum standard to be set to instill greater discipline on the part of currency traders. Moreover, borrowing by currency traders including hedge funds must be captured in the capital adequacy framework to limit the loans by financial institutions to these hedge funds. All in all, it is most likely that the decisions taken to control currency trading will fall short of our own expectations in Malaysia. Nonetheless, it would be a desirable start towards re-establishing financial stability which is so lacking and wanting in the region today. For it is only in an environment of stability that economic recovery has the best chance to succeed, and real economic growth sustained in the long term. The investors have nothing to fear even in the environment of selective control. Those who seek quick gains at the expense of long-term stability and benefits will be easily discouraged, but those long-term players with the tenacity and vision to see beyond fleeting windfalls will eventually prosper. Bank Negara Malaysia 3 February 1999

Title: Speech at the Opening of the Saving Promotion Seminar
text: Governor Tan Sri Ali Abul Hassan's Speech at the MalaysiaJapan Economic Association 21st Joint Conference - "Asian Financial Turmoil and Its Implications - The Malaysian Experience So Far" Venue: Palace of the Golden Horses, Kuala Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Lumpur Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 09 Mar 1999 First of all, I would like to thank the organisers for inviting me to speak at this conference on "Asian Financial Turmoil and Its Implications ? The Malaysian Experience So Far". It is already nearly two years since the outbreak of the Asian financial crisis in mid-1997. While we are seeing signs of recovery in crisis countries, the global financial market remains unstable with continuing exchange rate volatility which makes business decisions difficult. Most countries in the region have basically adopted the IMF-type policy approach or its variants in managing the adverse effects. Malaysia did the same initially, but subsequently, chose a different route. Malaysia?s approach was undoubtedly unorthodox and is still subject to much debate by the international community. In responding to the crisis, Malaysia did not follow conventional wisdom. We decided to change our policy direction very early in the crisis, but never losing sight of our ultimate objective of ensuring sustainable growth with price stability. The exchange controls were a necessary part of our efforts to stabilise domestic financial markets to ensure that the prospect for an economic recovery would not be jeopardised by external developments, which still posed a risk, and erode the gains made from macroeconomic adjustment policies. Today, I would like to take this opportunity to present the Malaysian case in coping with the adverse effects of the financial crisis, and to provide a broad perspective of policy issues and responses to the financial crisis. In the latter part of my address, I would like to share some policy lessons from the Malaysian experience. I would also like to touch on the role of Japan in restoring recovery in the Asian region, and the need for reform of the international financial architecture. The Effects of the Financial Crisis and Policy Responses Let me first begin with a quick flashback on the state of the Malaysian economy and the financial system prior to the financial turmoil in the region. The economic fundamentals of the Malaysian economy were strong. At the end of 1996, real GDP was growing at about 8%. The Government was enjoying a fiscal surplus. The external debt was generally low, at about 40% of GNP. The current account of the balance of payments had narrowed from a deficit of 10% to 5% of GNP, and was expected to improve further. Inflation was at its lowest, at 2.1%. On the financial front, the banking system was also strong and sound as reflected in the strong capitalisation and the high asset quality. The average risk-weighted capital ratio (RWCR) of the banking system was more than 10%. Non-performing loans, using the three month classification rule, were only 3.6% of total loans outstanding, and the ratio of loan provisions to non-performing loans was close to 100%. The banking system was already subject to strict international prudential standards. Almost all the 25 Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision recommended by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) have been adopted. When the crisis hit Thailand, these strong economic fundamentals were ignored by market participants. Indeed, it was the failure on their part to recognise the important differences that existed among the regional economies, that caused the contagion to spread rapidly. The "herd" instinct was strong. No economy, no matter how strong its economic fundamentals had a fighting chance in the face of such sudden and widespread change in market sentiments. Despite stronger fundamentals, the waves of speculation on the ringgit exchange rate caused it to depreciate to as low as RM4.88 per USD in January 1998. Consequently, the capital outflows prompted stock market prices to fall by as much as 70%. As the regional crisis deepened and spread, the international debate continued on the causes and the appropriate policy responses. To date, there is no consensus on the remedy to the East Asian problem or ways to avoid a recurrence of the crisis. One view laid the blame entirely on inapt governments and their policies, coupled with cronyism and corruption! Standard prescriptions were dispensed by the IMF involving a combination of tight monetary and fiscal policies: raising interest rates to defend exchange rates, strengthening the banking system through stricter prudential standards, and cutting down public expenditure to improve the current account balance. The rationale for these IMF policy packages are well appreciated. The problem lay in the administration of the policies. It was not dynamic enough. Policy changes to the prescriptions were not made as circumstances in Asia changed during the course of the crisis. I wish to digress a bit here to state that Malaysia was not under an IMF programme. Contrary to perception, we did not refuse to adopt a programme because we were unprepared to take the pain. Malaysia simply did not qualify for IMF assistance. Throughout the crisis, the external reserves level remained well above 3 months of retained imports. Of course, the reserves level is now sufficient to finance more than 6 months of retained imports. Although not under the Stand-by Programme, we did listen initially to the advice of IMF on how to handle the external shocks on an economy. In the initial stage of the crisis, we adopted an approach containing elements of the IMF prescription for other regional economies. When the ringgit was first attacked in early July, inter-bank interest rates were raised significantly. However, the high level of interest rates together with heavy intervention by Bank Negara Malaysia in the foreign exchange market failed to stave off the speculative pressure. This brief experience taught us that this policy approach could not be sustainable. Under normal circumstances of isolated and limited currency pressure, raising interest rates would be an effective measure to defend a currency. However, when the pressure emanates from large and incessant speculative activities, it would be naive and imprudent for a Central Bank to utilise its limited foreign exchange reserves to defend a country?s currency against such attacks. Thus, Malaysia allowed the ringgit to adjust downwards and interest rates were brought down to the level prior to the currency attack. Malaysia had greater flexibility to do this, because our external debt was low and short-term debt was less than half of external reserves. The success of an IMF policy programme requires the existence of stable market conditions and demands rational behaviour of market participants. The policy package is formulated based on the assumption that free flows of funds under a perfect market system would lead to an efficient allocation of resources. The system is assumed to be self-equilibrating, that the economy and the financial system would respond to shocks in a predictable manner and would soon reach a new stable equilibrium. The fact of the matter, however, was that these pre-conditions were not present in the region nor the global economy. It was apparent that the financial markets during the period were very unstable and market participants were behaving irrationally. The market mechanism was not functioning as it should. Portfolio decisions were not based on economic fundamentals, but were based on herd-instinct, acting more on rumours rather than facts. It is, therefore, not surprising that the IMF policy package did not succeed in restoring financial stability in the East Asian economies. Markets became more stable only after the LTCM failure, as banks reduced their lending exposure to such large institutional players, thereby curtailing their leverage activities. Even now, we believe that financial markets under the current framework are inherently unstable. Under these circumstances, in managing the economy, amidst the financial turmoil, the Malaysian Government adopted a comprehensive and forward-looking policy approach. As in the past, policies were formulated, taking into account the likely developments, and the upside and downside risks. The approach was one of pragmatism. As the crisis became more severe and prolonged, policy direction in Malaysia was changed to adjust to the changing circumstances. The objectives, however, remained unchanged, to achieve domestic and external stability. The initial policy of monetary and fiscal restraint, while contributing to restoring external balance and moderating inflation, also aggravated the decline in aggregate demand. Consequently, the downside risk that emerged was the prospect of a sharp deterioration in economic activities with ensuing implications on the soundness of the banking system. In particular, a worsening of economic conditions would translate quickly into widespread cash flow difficulties in the business sector that could lead to rising non-performing loans, that in turn could lead to an erosion in bank capital. Steps were, therefore, taken to deal with potential banking sector problems to contain its severity and ensure market confidence. Fiscal policy was relaxed in early 1998 to avoid further contraction of the economy. External conditions did not allow an easing of monetary policy. However, aggressive measures through lowering the statutory reserve requirement (SRR) were taken to reduce the cost of funds to bring lending rates down. Measures were also taken to remove distortions in loan intermediation so that the banking system continue to function and play its role in the economy, and does not suffer a breakdown that could jeopardise the prospects for economic recovery.
