This comprised the revision to the framework for the computation of the base lending rate, announcement of information on BNM?s daily operations in the money market and the implementation of the new liquidity framework. Subsequently, when inflation moderated, interest rates were eased. Following greater monetary independence accorded by the selective exchange controls, BNM reduced interest rates and the statutory reserve requirement in several rapid steps. The average base lending rate of the commercial banks now averages only 7.25% which is 225 basis points below the pre-crisis level. As the demand for credit is a direct function of economic activity, it is imperative that the corporate sector responds positively to the recovery promoting measures initiated by the Government. The Government is using a combination of measures, including expansionary fiscal and monetary policies to promote economic growth, coupled with structural reform in the financial sector, and selective exchange controls and fixing of the exchange rate to provide an environment of stability to foster business activities. Increasingly, convincing signs are emerging that both consumer and investor confidence is returning - stock prices are strongly on an upward trend, while economic activities are on the upward trend. This has been translated into an increasing demand for loans, as reflected by the increase in total loans approved by the banking system. If the current trend continues, there should be no problem at all in achieving a positive real GDP growth for 1999. In view of the importance of credit in supporting economic activities, Bank Negara will ensure the availability of adequate funds to investors at reasonable cost to promote private sector activity. Monetary policy has been accommodative. As inflation moderates, interest rates can be reduced further. I would like to note here that, in the case of Malaysia, the Government does not rely solely on lowering interest rates and providing liquidity in its efforts to stimulate the economy. Consumer and investor confidence are equally important. However, low interest rates and sufficient liquidity are necessary ingredients, as it would be impossible to stage an economic recovery in an environment of high interest rates and unavailability of credit. It is for this reason that we are encouraging banking institutions with capacity to increase lending activities to achieve a minimum loan growth of 8% for the banking system as a whole. A loan growth of at least 8% is vital for real GDP to grow by one percent. In fact, should the private sector including the banking institutions respond more favourably to Government policy measures and prospects for the international environment improve, GDP growth could be higher than projected. Thus, Bank Negara is now closely monitoring the banking institutions to ensure that those with capacity will play a more positive role in promoting economic recovery. Despite the strong emphasis on credit growth, Bank Negara will continue to be pragmatic in its approach. Banking institutions have been repeatedly reminded to continue exercising financial discipline at all times without compromising prudential standards. Proper credit evaluation procedures must be used in approving credit. This will ensure that the balance sheets of the banking institutions do not deteriorate further. Nonetheless, banking institutions have also been reminded not to unnecessarily complicate the credit process, making it difficult for borrowers to obtain credit. Any improvement in transparency and good governance by the corporate sector, which I will elaborate on later, will help banks in making their decision on the approval of loans by providing them with greater information on the borrowers, including their credit profile. While it is important to ensure that credit is made readily available to support the economic recovery process, it is equally important to ensure that the extension of credit be made on sound principles. Banks are in the business of lending but while they do this, they are also obliged to provide an optimum return to depositors as well as their shareholders. This is why it is of utmost importance that banks practise good credit management and adopt a good credit culture. What lessons can be drawn from the experiences of the 1990s? On its part, Bank Negara has stepped up efforts to promote a sound credit culture in the banking system. Several measures are being introduced to ensure that banks would have in place effective credit risk management systems. Firstly, Bank Negara will be issuing guidelines on minimum standards for credit risk management for the banking institutions. Secondly, Bank Negara is working with the industry in examining the feasibility of an agreed curriculum of training and a credit proficiency assessment in order to ensure that the industry would have a coherent set of programmes to upgrade the credit management skills of lending officers. This skill gap among the lending officers will need to be addressed. Thirdly, regulation on lending to connected parties will be tightened in order to disallow lending to controlling shareholders, who are not directors or officers of the banking institutions, from influencing the credit decisions of the banking institutions. Fourthly, in order to strengthen the corporate governance of banking institutions, Bank Negara will be periodically reviewing the appointment of directors and chief executive officers to ensure that they continue to be "fit and proper" well after their date of appointment. The Bank would like to ensure that the chief executive officers continue to steer the banking institutions to contribute meaningfully to the strengthening of the financial sector and hence, the development of the Malaysian economy. To complement these efforts, banking institutions, on their part, should ensure that they have in place well-defined credit policies, encompassing areas including the loan portfolio mix, pricing and credit quality standards. Banks must revert to the fundamentals of creditworthiness and apply conventional lending standards. Good credit administration is also essential to ensure enforcement of the policy and the presence of and adherence to proper procedures. Equally important is robust credit risk management and good corporate governance. Underlying all this, banking institutions must be equipped by skilled staff with a high level of professionalism and training. Banking institutions have also realized the importance of a thorough knowledge of their customers? business and of their real funding needs. Banks, however, are naturally disadvantaged compared to borrowers, who would have more information on the probability of the success of their projects. Consequently, bankers, who become more concerned with their credit risk, will inevitably reject loan applications if they are not sure of the degree of the viability of projects. Hence, in a situation where there is a lack of transparent information and disclosure, good borrowers will be denied credit simply because bankers have difficulty in distinguishing good borrowers from bad borrowers. Furthermore, in a situation where good and bad borrowers are seemingly similar, there will also exist cases where bad borrowers with projects which are not viable obtain credit at the expense of good borrowers. The overall quality of capital of the economy for future economic growth will also be affected. This imperfection in the credit market can, however, be minimized by reducing the problem of asymmetric information. While banks need to undertake the proper financial review of their clients including the cash flow and ability to service debt in both normal and stress situations, corporations can play a vital role in helping banking institutions base their lending decision on the viability of projects by disclosing the necessary information. While there have been quite a few key lessons for credit management from the perspective of the lenders, there are equally important lessons for the borrowers. The recent crisis has highlighted weaknesses in the debt management practices of some borrowers. Some corporations had overborrowed, and in the process, leveraged themselves to levels that were difficult to sustain. As a result, they became extremely vulnerable to increases in interest rates and the depreciation of the exchange rate. In addition to the high leverage, some of these borrowings had also been channelled into investments in the commercial real estate and stock markets. At the same time, bank credit was being used to finance long-term projects, investments that would generate income only after a long period, i.e. long after the need for the cash flow to service the borrowings. This created the problem of maturity mismatches in the funding structure. I need not elaborate on the consequences of these weaknesses, as you are well familiar with their adverse effects on the income statements and balance sheets of companies. Good corporate behaviour cannot be legislated. Corporate players need to be pro-active and not view the rules and practices as onerous. Instead, they should view good corporate governance as a weapon to achieve greater competitiveness in an increasingly liberalised and global environment. The recent crisis has shown that creditors are increasingly viewing good corporate governance as an essential element in their lending decisions and I foresee this trend continuing in the future. As such, companies that exhibit good corporate governance will find it relatively easier to obtain financing at competitive rates, compared to their competitors that do not accord priority to good corporate governance. I have already highlighted the role of information disclosure to enhance the ability of creditors to differentiate between sound and unsound companies. Information such as projected cash flows and the ability of borrowers to service their debts will allow banking institutions to move away from the excessive dependence on collateral and names to evaluate viability. It is absolutely essential that the corporate sector should make such information readily available on a timely basis. The need for the information to be reliable and comprehensive cannot be over-emphasised given that in this economic environment, corporations may be reluctant to reveal unfavourable information regarding their business performance. As information will not only facilitate lending decisions but also investor decisions, measures have been taken to improve disclosure requirements. In this regard, public listed companies are now required to submit quarterly reports within two months from the end of every quarter and audited annual accounts within four months from the end of the financial year. One of the main objectives of these measures is to increase the amount and frequency of information to all the key stakeholders, so as to increase market discipline on corporate managers. In managing their debt policies, companies should also strive to avoid the maturity mismatch problem by financing longterm projects with long-term borrowings. Corporations may also wish to consider, funding projects on a fixed-rate basis, to enable them to have more certainty in their planning as well as to avoid being caught with debt-servicing problems if interest rates rise sharply as a result of external shocks. In this respect, companies intending to undertake long-term capital investments should diversify their funding sources by tapping the ringgit bond market. Bank Negara, on its part, is committed towards the development of the ringgit bond market this year. Among others, efforts will focus on introducing a shelf registration scheme for private debt securities, deepening the repo market and broadening the investor base. It is hoped that the further development of the domestic bond market will increase the menu of debt instruments available for companies to enhance the management of their liabilities. In our efforts to enhance practices to strengthen the financial system, accountants have an important role in improving the debt management practices of companies. Malaysia does have a high standard in accounting practices that are consistent with international norms. The challenge, therefore, is to maintain these standards and ensure close adherence to these standards, even in difficult times. While regulatory authorities ensure compliance with existing standards through effective surveillance and enforcement of regulations, accountants also can play a key role in encouraging the ethic of full disclosure and accountability. You can do this in your capacity either as members of management or boards of directors or as auditors. On a more serious note, accountants have an instrumental role in promoting good corporate governance. The Malaysian Institute of Accountants and the Malaysian Association of Certified Public Accountants can be commended for their efforts in this respect, in particular their involvement in the Institute of Corporate Governance set up in March 1998 together with three other professional bodies. I hope the two Associations will continue to contribute towards the work of the Institute. As individual accountants, particularly in your role as auditors, you complement the board of directors by playing the instrumental role of enhancing the effectiveness of corporate governance through effective checks on how financial statements are prepared and presented. Latest indications are that the economic recovery process has picked up momentum. Our trade account remains in surplus, amounting to RM15.7 billion in the first quarter of 1999. This has contributed to the build-up in our international reserves, which totalled RM108.7 billion at the end of April 1999, equivalent to 6.2 months of retained imports. In the meantime, manufacturing production continued to increase on an annual basis in March 1999. The inflation rate continues on its moderating trend, to 2.9% in April 1999. At the same time, since the end of August 1998, stock prices and the market capitalisation of the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange have increased substantially. The Composite Index which was at 262 points on 1 September 1998 is now above 760 points. The market capitalisation which was RM181 billion on 1 September 1998 is now RM474 billion. We are now in a bull market. And the bull is still young!. The economy has turned around and we are now once again on the path of recovery and prosperity. We must ensure, this time around, that we do not repeat the mistakes of the past. Dengan ini, saya dengan sukacitanya merasmikan Persidangan Pengurusan Kredit Kebangsaan Malaysia 1999. Bank Negara Malaysia 18 May 1999

Title: Luncheon Address at the ADB Institute-BNM Conference on Macroeconomic and Financial Stability in Asian Emerging Markets: "Stability Policy in Asia - Quo Vadis?"
text: Adviser Dato' Nor Mohamed Yakcop's Speech at NAMLIA's 21st Annual Awards Night Speaker: Assistant Governors / Advisers Speech/Interview Date: 24 May 1999 Venue: Legend Hotel, Kuala Lumpur Language: English I would like to congratulate NAMLIA for the efforts in organising such a big convention to upgrade the standard of professionalism in the agency force. This effort of NAMLIA in advancing the agency force through propagating ethical and professional approach in marketing, technical competence and quality service to policyholders is indeed commendable. With a line up of excellent speakers who will share with you their experience and formula for success, I am confident that you would have a most fruitful and rewarding convention. These conventions provide an excellent platform for the agency force to learn from one another through group interaction and collective learning, so that you can collectively provide the highest level of service expected of every member of the agency force. We are indeed happy to gather here tonight to honour the professionals in the fraternity who have reached out and successfully brought the benefits of life insurance coverage to thousands of Malaysians and their families. It is indeed an honour for me to be with you this evening to celebrate this social role that you have played in ensuring that the Malaysian life insurance industry extends its reach, far and wide to provide protection for every Malaysian in time of need. Given the low penetration rate of life insurance in Malaysia?s population and your sense of commitment towards continuous improvement in quality of service to policyholders, I?m confident that the industry will continue to record good performance as it crosses into the new millennium. Given the challenging economic environment since 1997, the insurance industry has not been spared its ravages. Although measures put in place with the implementation of the Insurance Act 1996, in the form of enhanced solvency requirements and assets diversification have put the industry in a relatively better footing than other sectors, the industry nonetheless suffered a significant setback. After almost a decade of strong growth, insurers were confronted with dissipating profit margins and a general contraction in demand. In the life sector this was further exaberated by the combined effects of deteriorating forfeiture and surrenders as well as sluggish demand for credit related policies. New business premiums decreased by 10.2% to RM1.4 billion, compared with the increase of 11.1% in 1997. Forfeitures also deteriorated to 40.2% in 1998 from 31.2% in 1997, coupled with also increases in policy loans and surrenders which depleted the policies in force. As the impact of the crisis began to emerge policy adjustment by BNM became necessary. Financial solvency and strength were the focus of Bank Negara?s concern. This was reflected in the package of measures announced in October 1998, in revised solvency margins and some relaxation of investment regulations to offer insurers more flexibility in implementing asset management strategies to cope with the crisis. Resources continue to be dedicated to financial surveillance to ensure insurers? continuing ability to meet obligations to policyholders. Stress testing and closer scrutiny of insurers? financial position had helped to contain the adverse effect of the financial crisis on the industry. The year also saw increasing attention to the role of the insurance industry in the economic recovery process of the nation, focusing on structural reform, market penetration, domestic retention and human resources development. I am glad to say that the insurance industry as a whole remains fundamentally sound. While the life industry remains fundamentally sound, market penetration in terms of policies in force to the population, continued to make slow progress increasing only marginally from 25.3% in 1996 to 27.3% at end 1997, still a long way from the targeted 50% by year 2000. There is also heavy strain on in force business through increasing cash out by policyholders and forfeitures. However, it is difficult times that bring out the best in us as it tests our resilience and solidity. In such challenging environment the agency force need to improve its service and refocus its strategy and goodwill to provide the best to its customers. I believe the agents can also do well in bad times too. When times are bad, people feel the added need for security and purchase insurance too. For the agency force the ability to stay on through these booms and bust of the economic cycle will be rewarded through enduring relationships with policyholders. Those who have the tenacity to challenge this adversity will see the windfall in the long term. With positive signs of economic recovery already in the horizon, the prospects for the industry remain promising. To capitalise on this momentum the industry can no longer be confined to selling traditional protection policies. Life insurers must venture into more innovative financial planning products like investment-linked and annuities for the public. The agents would need to play an important role as financial planners who would attend to a whole spectrum of financial needs of the policyholder including tax and estate planning. With the advent of information technology, usage of technology has evolved from backroom operations to forefront functions such as marketing and customer servicing. The internet has now become the medium of transaction. E-commerce will be widespread as more and more people use the internet. Nonetheless while some insurance products will be available through the internet, not all can be sold through this medium. The more complicated products would require face-to face solicitation and personal service by the agency force as agents are required and will continue to be a dominant and the more influential channel. There is this story about a life insurance agent who went to see a barber. As he sat down and the barber was about to cut his hair, he told the barber that he wanted the barber?s wife to cut his hair. Stunned and furious, the barber almost lost his temper. The agent explained that if death or permanent disablement were to happen to him, the wife may have to turn barber if he has no insurance. Such is the role of the life insurance agents. I urge you to go out there and sell more policies, protect more families and help build a more robust and healthy industry. As you are aware in October 1998, BNM had announced that the overriding commissions for new business transacted will be maintained at 20% instead of 15%, plus 5% for production bonus until year 2000. Tonight I would like to take this opportunity to announce further relaxation of the cost guidelines as a measure to assist the agency force to tide over in the current environment of high forfeitures and difficult business conditions. I am glad to announce that consideration is being given to allow some relief in the benchmark qualification for persistency bonus in the costs guidelines. The minimum first year persistency requirement to qualify for persistency bonus will be reduced from the benchmark rate 90% to 80% of premiums. Similarly the minimum second year persistency requirement will be reduced from the rate of 80% to 70%. It is hoped that the reduction will not lead to more lapses but instead encourage all of you to put in more effort to maintain business in force by providing value added service and advise to policyholders. The capacity of the industry as a whole to effectively manage the business to be in force cannot be achieved without the role of each and everyone of you. I would urge all of you to do your best to enhance the level of insurance penetration in the country. In conclusion, I would like to congratulate the top producers who will be conferred the awards tonight. May I wish all of you every success in your future endeavours. May the achievements of the past inspire you to greater heights. Bank Negara Malaysia 24 May 1999

Title: Keynote Address at the Fourteenth Conference with Financial Institutions - "Towards a More Efficient, Effective and Stable Financial System"
text: Governor Tan Sri Ali Abul Hassan's Speech at the International Conference on Takaful Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 31 May 1999 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English I am pleased to be here this morning to officiate the opening of the International Conference on Takaful. Let me first of all extend a very warm welcome to all distinguished speakers and delegates, many of whom have come from afar to share with us their expertise and knowledge at this Conference. I also wish to extend a very warm welcome to all of you - Selamat Datang. I wish to congratulate the Malaysian Insurance Institute (MII) and BIMB Institute of Research and Training Sdn. Bhd. (BIRT) for jointly organising this important Conference. The takaful, or Islamic insurance industry, is a relatively new industry, and as with most pioneering work, the opportunity to learn and develop from the mutual exchange of ideas is always extremely valuable. The organisers' choice of the theme for this Conference, "Approaching New Frontiers" is particularly fitting and timely for the takaful industry as it stands poised at the threshold of a new millennium, bringing with it new developments, challenges and opportunities. The challenge ahead will be to anticipate, and make the most of the changes and opportunities. Despite the recent Asian financial crisis which had adversely affected the financial sector including the conventional insurance sector, the takaful industry has remained remarkably resilient and continues to grow from strength to strength. With increasing liberalisation and globalisation of world trade, there is a new horizon of opportunity for takaful operators. In what some have dubbed the "new age" of competition, creativity and innovation will become critical ingredients for success. Those who rise to this challenge will reap the rewards. Those who do not will fall and be forgotten! To stay relevant, the takaful industry must position itself within the hub of the mainstream financial system. It must be able to compete and offer products and services that are on par, if not better than conventional insurance products. To achieve this, several conditions must be in place. Among them are a higher degree of concensus on the interpretation of Syariah principles in the context of takaful operations, a cohesive regulatory and legal framework which emphasises transparency, consumer protection and corporate governance, as well as uniform accounting standards to lay the foundation for further growth and expansion. As the industry progresses, the capacity of Islamic reinsurance or retakaful and a pool of expertise within the Islamic business circle will also be needed to support its ongoing development. The takaful industry needs to develop new strategies to achieve these requirements and take full advantage of the opportunities. I take this opportunity to share with you some of the strategies being pursued in the Malaysian market. As we stride forward, it is often useful to take a moment to ponder on past achievements and failures and lessons learnt along the way. As one of the pioneers in the development of the takaful market in this region, Malaysia's experiences may prove useful in providing some direction and focus to our future endeavours. Permit me to briefly share with you about the history of takaful development in Malaysia. The wish of Muslims to enjoy the benefits of a modern banking and insurance system but on a basis which is not forbidden by Islam was the impetus to the development of Islamic banking and insurance in Malaysia. The Malaysian Government established a special task force back in 1982 to study the possibility of introducing Islamic insurance to complement the services of Islamic banking. Following the recommendations of the task force, the Malaysian Parliament passed the Takaful Act in 1984, making Malaysia probably the only country in the world to have a specific legislation governing takaful business. The first takaful operator was hatched in 1984 and another, about a decade later. Over the past three years, with the admission of the second takaful operator, the Malaysian takaful industry proceeded to record commendable growth, with assets and contribution income expanding at average rates of 45% and 49% respectively. The onset of the unprecedented regional financial crisis in mid-1997 has not stifled the growth momentum of the Malaysian takaful industry. While the conventional insurance sector wrestled to regain eroded market positions, the takaful sub-sector in Malaysia continued to maintain strong double digit growth. The total assets of the takaful funds continued to expand at 26% in 1998. The combined contribution income of both family and general takaful business also increased by 40%, higher than the growth rate of 34.9% recorded in 1997. Efforts to promote takaful business saw takaful operators embarking on measures to diversify their distribution channels, launch new products and organise customised training programmes for their staff and agents. In addition to the normal lines of takaful products, new products recently introduced in Malaysia include a special product for women and health takaful. The wider range of products and distribution channels available helped to spur the growth of takaful in Malaysia. Interestingly, as the insuring public in Malaysia became more discerning, efforts made by the takaful operators to increase public awareness of takaful products also attracted the non-Muslim community. The Al-Mudharabah or profit sharing principle, one of the unique features inherent in takaful products, makes takaful an attractive alternative to conventional insurance. This is attributed in no small measure to the high level of religious tolerance among Malaysians which enabled takaful to gain acceptance among the non-Muslim population. Throughout the development of the takaful industry in Malaysia, the Government and regulatory authorities have been careful to preserve the fundamental Islamic principles on which takaful business is founded. The availability of expertise in both Islamic insurance and Syariah matters has, and will continue, to remain a priority in order to safeguard the integrity of takaful practices. With the commitment of regulators and support of practitioners, Malaysia is progressively building up a pool of technical knowledge and expertise to support the development of takaful both domestically as well as abroad. In 1997, Malaysia established a Syariah Advisory Council at the Central Bank to act as an authoritative reference point on issues relating to Islamic banking and takaful. I understand that the takaful industry has also recently taken steps to draw up a code of conduct for takaful operators, which will promote good market conduct and practices, and instill professionalism among practitioners. The code will promote healthy competition by creating a more level-playing field for both conventional insurers and takaful operators through common market practices. I wish to take this opportunity to commend the takaful operators for this positive step towards greater market discipline. Although the takaful industry has made its mark and the growth has been significant so far, the industry remains small relative to conventional insurance. At the end of 1998, takaful contribution in Malaysia represented only 2% of conventional insurance premium, while takaful assets stood at only 1.6% of conventional insurance assets. The potential for the Malaysian takaful industry to grow is tremendous. I would attribute this to two major factors namely, the low level of life insurance penetration among the majority Muslim population and the overall low penetration rate of 27% in Malaysia. Outside Malaysia, there is also an enormous growth potential for the takaful industry given that there are nearly 1.7 billion Muslims worldwide, more than a quarter of the world?s population. With Islam being the second largest religion in the world, this number is expected to grow, and at a rapid pace. These factors, coupled with an increasing Islamic consciousness among Muslims, will not only sustain the present momentum but has the capacity to propel the takaful industry to a new phase of development and achievement. Our home-grown takaful operator had taken cognizance of this opportunity and has already ventured abroad by participating in equity interests in a takaful company outside Malaysia. Through its presence abroad, the operator is also able to provide technical assistance and at the same time propagate the development of takaful outside the country. There is a ready market for takaful. The secret in tapping that market lies in creating value. This value can be realised if the right combination of success factors can be created. For takaful to be successful, Government support, cooperation at the international level, and the development of human capital are essential. I am impressed by the foresight shown by Islamic countries under the Developing Eight to take the lead in fostering closer cooperation and coordination, promoting greater exchange of business and developing technical know-how to develop the takaful industry. Active Government support within the domestic market is equally important. Recognising the potential of takaful business to grow into one of the key components of the Malaysian financial system, the Malaysian Government has given its unwavering commitment and support to the development of a viable and resilient takaful sector. The result has been the development of a dynamic and competitive takaful industry in Malaysia. As the regulator of both the conventional insurance and takaful industries, the Central Bank of Malaysia plays an active role in spearheading takaful development in Malaysia. To tap the tremendous potential in the takaful industry, the Bank has drawn up a five-year strategic plan in consultation with the statutory associations, conventional insurers and takaful operators. The strategic plan focuses on a number of areas of development, each with defined objectives and strategic action plans. Let me take this opportunity to share some of the salient features of the five-year plan. Central to the plan are specific targets set for the takaful industry to achieve over the next five years. The targets include market penetration of family business of 7% of the Malaysian population, and total contribution income of both the general and family takaful business to reach 7% of the total premium income of the conventional insurance sector. These targets are supported by strategies to enhance the market penetration of takaful business by allowing more players into the market, promoting the diversification of marketing channels, encouraging product innovation and instilling a greater public awareness of the benefits of takaful. The plan also sets out strategies to strengthen the financial soundness of takaful operators and the regulatory framework governing the takaful industry. These strategies are rooted in specific action plans to achieve the ultimate objectives under the strategic five-year plan. They include:- a comprehensive review of the Takaful Act by the Central Bank to replace the existing regulatory framework with a more comprehensive legislation that incorporates the experience thus far gained from administering both the existing takaful and conventional insurance legislation; the introduction of model accounts and new statistical statements to ensure minimum reporting standards, greater disclosure of financial information and transparency of operations; measures to promote regional expansion and international cooperation in takaful; and measures to develop Malaysia into a centre for takaful training and education. The progressive implementation of the strategies outlined in the five-year plan should see the takaful sector evolve into a significant sub-sector of the Malaysian insurance industry in the coming years. Over the next five years, a few additional takaful licences will be issued to eligible parties. Preference will be given to strong financial institutions with a well established Islamic banking or conventional insurance set-up. Strong non-financial institutions with a good financial track-record will also be considered. We also welcome foreign investors with expertise in takaful to establish joint-ventures with Malaysian partners. We are willing to consider eligible foreign investors a stake of up to 49% in a joint-venture. We will issue takaful licences as an incentive to encourage mergers and acquisitions among conventional insurers. Human capital represents the third and possibly most important dimension to the successful development of a takaful industry. Without a doubt, the most valuable assets for any business in the 21st century will be knowledge and information-based. A knowledgeable and skilled workforce is the key to sustaining a competitive advantage. As a strategy, takaful operators should be capable of developing a motivated, innovative and adaptive workforce that is capable of creating and adding value for its customer. It is imperative that they are also well-versed in Syariah matters. Only then, can the Islamic principles be integrated with the dynamics of the business world. Syariah scholars play a fundamental role in guiding takaful operations. For them to effectively fulfill this role, they have to be conversant with the practical aspects of takaful business. Through appropriate rulings and recommendations on specific matters, Syariah scholars can expand the breadth and depth of takaful business, but within the bounds of Syariah. Training institutes have an important role to play in enhancing and developing world-class training programmes suited to the needs of the takaful industry. In this respect, the Malaysian Insurance Institute, the leading insurance training institute in Malaysia, has already developed several programs to increase the level of expertise in the takaful industry. The Certificate in Takaful Practice, conducted by the Institute, has been well received by both the insurance and takaful industries. As Chairman of the Institute, I am pleased to inform that the Malaysian Insurance Institute will be introducing a diploma course in takaful next year. This diploma will be modeled along the lines of diplomas currently available at the Institute. It will qualify as an entrance requirement to the prestigious Associate of the Malaysian Insurance Institute (AMII) program. At the international level, the Institute is taking steps to collaborate with other training institutions in other Muslim nations to mutually recognise the courses. The takaful industry is set to change insurance markets in a significant way. As with any change, new frontiers can be both exciting and daunting. Takaful operators, Syariah scholars and regulators have not only an interest, but also a joint responsibility, to ensure the orderly and progressive development of the takaful industry. This Conference presents an excellent opportunity for participants to crystallise a common vision for the future of the international takaful market. I would urge all of you here today to make the most of this Conference to learn more about takaful, share your experiences and take valuable lessons home with you. With your active participation, I have no doubt that you will benefit tremendously over the next two days from the rich ensemble of expertise and experience at this Conference. This Conference is also a good opportunity for you to establish new friendship and business links with takaful academicians and practitioners worldwide. You may also wish to take a bit of time out to enjoy the interesting sights that Kuala Lumpur and other parts of Malaysia have to offer, as well as the warm Malaysian hospitality. On that note, it is my great pleasure to officiate the commencement of the International Conference on Takaful. Bank Negara Malaysia 31 May 1999

Title: Opening Remarks at the Sustainability Leadership Programme for Financial Institutions
text: Deputy Governor's Keynote Address at the Hewlett-Packard Sales (M) Sdn. Bhd. Bond Issuance Signing Ceremony Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 17 Jun 1999 I am pleased to be here today to witness the signing ceremony of the Hewlett-Packard Sales (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd?s RM160 million 5-year bond issue. This Ringgit bond issue by the corporate sector is indeed a positive development. It is an indicator of increased demand for funds by the private sector in an environment of the improved economic conditions and favourable financial market conditions of ample liquidity and low interest rates. With the economy having clearly entered the recovery phase, corporate financing requirements can be expected to increase. With the stable and favourable financial market conditions expected to continue, we can expect more bond issues to come on-stream as more companies turn to the bond market for their financing needs. Bank Negara will continue to improve the financial infrastructure to deepen and broaden the bond market to the advantage of investors and borrowers. The development of an efficient corporate bond market is vital to the overall development of the financial infrastructure of the nation. This becomes even more urgent in the face of the current up turn of the economy, with significant financing needs for infrastructure, industrial and social development as well as investment in technology ? the latter being an essential element in Malaysia?s next stage of development. A developed bond market would offer companies with alternative source of funding and provide the flexibility for long term projects to be funded at a fixed rate. From the investors' viewpoint, bonds issues will be an alternative form of investment and help to mobilise savings towards more efficient allocation of resources. In addition, a well-developed bond market would reduce the heavy reliance on the banking system for financing requirements. By facilitating a more appropriate allocation of risks away from depositors to investors, the bond market will contribute towards overall financial stability. Towards this end, Bank Negara has over the decade of the 1990s systematically put in place several initiatives to set the pace for the orderly development of the private bond market. As part of this process, the first credit rating agency, Rating Agency Malaysia Berhad was established in November 1990 and the second rating agency, Malaysian Rating Corporation Berhad was set up in September 1996. In May 1992, BNM made it mandatory for all domestic bonds to be rated. With increasing number of PDS issues, efforts were also directed towards developing trading, clearing and settlement system for PDS. With the implementation of the electronic inter-bank funds transfer and scripless book-entry system, confirmation of trades and settlement of cash and securities transfers have become fully automated. This system was further upgraded in January 1996 to serve as the central depository and paying agent for all unlisted bonds. The lack of market-based benchmark for efficient and competitive pricing of bonds was addressed in 1997. Khazanah Nasional Berhad, a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Government and an investment holding arm of the Government, was given the mandate to issue the benchmark bonds on a regular basis. Since its first issue on September 1997, 6 issues have been raised with a total amount of RM5.8 billion. Rating agencies, benchmark bonds, efficient settlement and clearing systems are some of the prerequisites for a liquid secondary bond market. But these by themselves are not sufficient. For this to happen, the market needs to have up to-date information. The lack of information in the market has been often cited as a reason for the slow development of the secondary market. To address this, the Bond Information and Dissemination System (BIDS) was launched in October 1997 to provide a comprehensive database on the debt securities market. The information in BIDS, in particular, the indicative buy-sell quotes and last done price information, has added to market transparency and efficiency thereby enhancing liquidity to the market. It has been recognised that a deep and liquid bond market is important to finance the next phase of economic development. While emphasis has been placed on the development of the infrastructure and institutional building for the bond market, the future plans aim to further deepen and broaden the bond market. As the issuance of debt securities increases and an increasingly more realistic benchmark yield curve evolves, we can expect to see a significant improvement in the volume of interbank dealings, market making activities and pricing of bond issues. We should also be able to achieve a more active secondary market with the existence of the Bond Information and Dissemination System and the implementation of the Real Time Electronic Transfer of Funds and Securities in July 1999 to provide an efficient mechanism for clearing and settlement of debt securities. On the part of BNM, efforts will continue to be focussed on accelerating the development of the bond market. A revised set of Guidelines on the Issuance of Private Debt Securities and the Code of Conduct and Market Practices for the Bond Market, will be launched in the near future. This will streamline PDS trading practices and procedures and facilitate the orderly development of the market . BNM will also be introducing Guidelines on Asset Backed Securities which, apart from diversifying risks from the banking system, will increase the types of instruments in the market and widen the spectrum of papers available for investment. As the Government?s comprehensive economic recovery programme is beginning to yield positive results and as the pace of economy recovery gathers momentum, the demand for financing will also increase. Indeed, more private corporations should take advantage of the current low interest rates and issue debt securities to finance their business expansion, particularly longer-term investments. Bank Negara looks forward to working closely with the industry in the months ahead to further strengthen the development of the domestic bond market. Bank Negara Malaysia 17 June 1999

Title: Opening Address at the Malaysian Insurance Institute Seminar on Human Resource and Management
text: Governor Tan Sri Ali Abul Hassan's Keynote Address at the IBBM Chief Internal Auditors Networking Group's (CIANG) Third Annual Conference on "Risk Management and the Internal Auditor" Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 07 Jul 1999 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English I am delighted to be here this morning to deliver the keynote address in conjunction with the Third Annual Conference organised by the Chief Internal Auditors Networking Group of Institut Bank-Bank Malaysia. Allow me, first of all, to congratulate the organisers for choosing an appropriate and meaningful theme. Risk management has indeed become a corporate buzzword these days particularly in the light of the recent painful financial crisis. The economic turbulence and the unprecedented regional financial crisis, which began in mid-1997, was more protracted and more severe than anyone ever expected. Admittedly, Malaysia was not the worst affected in the region but was nevertheless subjected to sharp economic contraction in real economic activity as a result of the instability in the financial markets. The volatility seen in the Ringgit exchange rates and the sharp downturn of the Malaysian stock market at the height of the crisis clearly exerted tremendous strain on the financial system and the corporate sector. With rising interest rates and strained earnings of businesses, the country's financial institutions had to contend with the problems of rising non-performing loans and declining capital. In reacting to and managing the impact of the economic crisis, the Malaysian Government has been highly focused in adopting strategies and measures to steer the country back on the road to economic recovery. Several of these measures, including the imposition of selective exchange controls and the fixing of the exchange rate, are not standard "text book measures" and viewed by some as unconventional. The important point to note is that the financial market stability gained from the selective exchange controls and the fixed exchange rate has undoubtedly provided the necessary impetus for economic recovery. Latest indicators show that the Government's economic recovery measures continue to yield positive results. Whilst the economy contracted by 6.7% in 1998 and 1.3% in the first quarter of 1999, even the most pessimistic of economists are beginning to forecast positive growth in 1999. Based on the performance of the Malaysian economy in the first quarter of 1999, the trade balance continued to be in substantial surplus at RM15.8 billion whilst inflation moderated to 4%. Moreover, Malaysia's trade balance registered a record surplus of RM58.4 billion in 1998 which is well in excess of earlier estimates of RM35 billion. In fact, the most dramatic impact has been seen in the international reserves of the Central Bank which has seen a surge from US 20.5 billion as at end June 1998 to US 31.3 billion as at 15 June 1999. This represents an increase of about US 10.8 billion or RM41 billion over a period of just one year. In addition, the Malaysian banking system has weathered the worst of the crisis and remains strong with an RWCR of about 12.2% as at 31 May 1999, well in excess of the minimum international standard of 8%. Ladies and Gentlemen, Whilst the scenario has improved considerably since the peak of the crisis, we do not intend to be complacent with our recent accomplishments. At the 13 th Conference with financial institutions held about two months ago, BNM highlighted several lessons to be learnt from the crisis. Among these, the importance of prudent lending and sound risk management. During the crisis, a common feature noted in some banking institutions was the glaring mismatch between risk management ability and risk appetite. When the economy was growing rapidly at 8% annually, many banking institutions were enticed by larger interest margins and paid little attention to risks involved. Often, banking institutions' risk management capability did not match the increasing risks assumed. As a consequence, large amounts of funds were channelled to high-risk loans. Poor credit culture among some banking institutions had also contributed to the poor asset portfolio. Many banking institutions either relied heavily on name lending or collateral values, rather than business viability. Macroeconomic trend analysis, future cash flow analysis and sensitivity analysis were not given the importance they deserve. Companies with low capital were able to obtain excessive financing, which was beyond their debt-servicing capacity. Another major weakness of the banking system is in the area of asset and liability management. During the good times, some banking institutions adopted aggressive loan growth without giving due consideration to their liability profile. Long term assets were funded by short-term interbank borrowings, which were cheaper and more easily available. This reliance on shortterm interbank borrowings to fund long term assets, which was particularly prevalent among finance companies created large maturity mismatches between banking institutions' assets and liabilities. When the liquidity turned tight and the interest rates moved higher, these institutions suffered from negative margin. The moral of the story is that aggressive loan expansion must not be recklessly pursued without due concern to sources of funding. On the issue of aggressive loan expansion, I should also mention that the pendulum appears to have swung to the other side now. The same bank officers who lent money as if there was no tomorrow are so shell-shocked now that some of them are turning away from lending even to viable projects. The pendulum should return to the middle. While it was wrong to lend imprudently during the good years, it is equally wrong to reject viable loans requests during difficult times. One way to solve this matter may be to transfer some of the shell-shocked officers from the credit department to the recovery department and replace them with new officers who are willing to look at loan proposals with a fresh mind without being obsessed with the problems of the past. However, it may not be possible to make such a massive transfer at all times. What is important is to ensure that a situation does not arise where credit officers of banks in order to avoid making mistakes make no credit decisions at all. The senior management of the financial institutions should ensure that the officers manning the credit departments have the right attitude towards credit management. As lending activity continues to be the core business activity of banking institutions, the most significant risks are naturally credit risks. Since a robust risk management system is critical for the continued safety and soundness of individual banking institutions, Bank Negara Malaysia is currently working on measures to improve credit risk management and will issue minimum standards to be observed by all banking institutions. Some people seem to believe that the word 'risk' is a bad word not to be mentioned in public. Others associate risk with negative events such as losses. Risk is not a bad word. While it can be associated with losses, risk can also be associated with profits; hence the phrase "No risk, no gain". What is risk management? I prefer the following definition: " Risk Management is taking on prudent risks in line with a given Risk Appetite in order to maximize profit" It stands to reason, therefore, that banking institutions should not attempt to avoid risks but should take steps to exploit opportunities and manage risks for competitive advantage. At the end of the day: "Banking institutions make money by taking risks ? and lose money by not managing risks effectively" Allow me now to share my thoughts on the role of the internal auditor. The internal auditing profession, in my view, is arguably one of the most misunderstood professions. Traditionally, and perhaps for good reason, internal auditors have been "regarded as fault finders" particularly given that the traditional emphasis of internal auditing has been on compliance auditing. Despite their assurances that they are there to help, internal auditors are often looked upon as being INTRUSIVE, HARDHEADED AND THREATENING! Indeed, on a lighter vein, I am often reminded of the saying, which goes as follows: "Hungry sharks never an attach an internal auditor ... because of professional courtesy!" I believe internal auditors are a misunderstood lot. Most of them strive to be customer oriented and want to add value across the board to the organisation they serve. An auditor should be viewed as someone who not only focuses on control and the downside aspects of risk management but also as someone who fully understands the upside of risk management, that is, in terms of enhancing profitability and working for the benefit of all stakeholders. This brings me to the subject of how internal auditing should relate to corporate risk management. Indeed, the internal auditor should be seen as a "partner" to senior management in this regard. Traditionally, internal auditors have focused mainly on compliance with established policies and procedures and depended largely on substantive tests to evaluate the adequacy of control systems. However, this approach is insufficient and internal auditors who concentrate solely on compliance auditing will become irrelevant in the new millennium. Apart from looking at controls, internal auditors should increasingly adopt a risk-management focus. There is a clear need for a wider scope of audit that would include performance and management audits and the evaluation of risk management practices. The trend today is to review management performance not only by its performance record but also in terms of the adequacy and effectiveness of risk management activities. I now wish to touch briefly on how internal auditors can play a more effective role in the assessment of risk management activities. Firstly, internal auditors need to adopt strategic thinking to envisage the future and its implications. Internal auditing can play a key role in ensuring that an organisation is geared up to fully meet the challenges of the present and future. There needs to be good insight on the direction of the business enterprise and the changing environment in which it operates. Therefore, a crucial step within the risk management framework should be the establishment of a strategic business plan. Since an organisation's risk management appetite and posture is established during strategic planning, the internal auditor should be a key observer of the process. Through their observance, internal auditors are able to provide valuable input that can mitigate business risks and identify potential control issues before or at the onset of strategic initiatives. If auditing is only concerned with controls, this creates a bias for the present and the past. What this means is that you are looking at control activities designed at some previous time to deal with issues that have long been forgotten and may not be relevant to current risks. A business enterprise however, operates in the present and future and therefore, what transpired six months ago may no longer be relevant. If I may use an analogy that is often used to describe the traditional form of internal auditing, it would be this: "The old guard of internal auditors are like heavily armoured warriors who arrive at the field of battle ... long after the battle has ended ... wounded" Indeed, instead of focusing on history, audit reports should address the present and the organisation's level of preparedness to deal with the future. Secondly, in discharging their responsibilities, internal auditors must be able to set audit priorities. A sound risk assessment process should ensure that all auditable activities are first identified. These activities should then be ranked based on key considerations, such as, value at risk, materiality and regulatory implications. Audit resources are then assigned such that focus is given to high-risk components. Thirdly, in order to add value to the risk management function, internal auditors have to continually update and share the results of their risk assessments. Given the frequent pace of change in the world today, annual risk assessments can become obsolete during the year. If an organisation is having problems in coping with business and market risks, it is imperative that internal auditors swiftly draw the attention of management to the detected weaknesses. They should not allow "herd mentality" to dictate the pace or be intimidated by senior management. Indeed where applicable, internal auditors should exert a sobering influence on management, particularly in good times, when the temptation to increase the bottom line is just too great and the attendant risks are often glossed over. Fourthly, in order to be effective in enhancing risk management, internal auditors need, at all times, to preserve their independence and objectivity. Internal auditors should ensure that they are not subjected to bias and pressure from management and should vigorously defend their independence. The organisation, and more specifically the Audit Committee, must reinforce such independence. On their part, the Board and Audit Committee members must make themselves more accessible to the internal auditor and provide support to him whenever required. They should view the internal audit function as a vital part of the entire risk management framework of the organisation and not just as "one of those things that we are forced to have". Clearly, if the Board does not have high regard for the internal auditing function, such adverse views will definitely permeate into the culture of the organisation and undermine the credibility of the internal audit function. Risk management becomes even more critical in complex or large organisations where management often lacks the skills and competencies needed to effectively monitor the operations of the organisation, including the system of internal and business controls. Therefore, by being able to furnish objective and timely appraisals on the quality of an organisation's internal control and systems for managing business risks, the internal auditor will be providing an invaluable service to management. Finally, for internal auditors to play an effective role in risk management, they need to constantly upgrade their technical skills and competencies. Internal auditors should be fully conversant with the complexities of evolving forms of business risks and have the ability to fully evaluate these risks. To maintain a consistent level of effectiveness and competency, internal auditors must keep up with the latest product innovations and risk management techniques and fully embrace skills in the area of information technology. Given that we are now in an "Information or Knowledge Age" it is essential that auditors keep up with the times so that their services are not rendered obsolete. I should perhaps add here that the internal audit department should not be viewed as a "dumping ground" for non-performing staff. This would indeed be a very shortsighted view with potentially severe consequences. Instead, audit departments should hire staff with the right credentials, develop expertise either from within through rigorous on-the-job training or through external courses. In conclusion, I would like to reiterate that as the new millennium draws closer, internal auditors must undergo a paradigm shift from a "control focus" to a "risk management focus". It would also be useful to remember that: "Internal Auditors have to increasingly focus on WHERE A BUSINESS IS GOING ? AND NOT WHERE IT HAS BEEN!" I wish to take this opportunity to once more congratulate IBBM and the Chief Internal Auditors Networking Group for having successfully organised this Conference. I hope that all of you who are here today will have a rewarding and stimulating learning experience. And with that, I declare open, the Third Conference of the IBBM-Networking Group of Chief Internal Auditors on "Risk Management and the Internal Auditor". Bank Negara Malaysia 7 July 1999

Title: Opening Speech at the Bankers National Conference 1999
text: Governor Tan Sri Ali Abul Hassan's Speech on the Release of a Joint BNM-Securities Commission Publication on Y2K Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 15 Jul 1999 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English Selamat petang dan selamat datang ke majlis taklimat dan sidang akhbar bersempena dengan pengeluaran buku "Y2K ? Malaysian Financial Sector Status Update and Continuity Planning" yang diterbitkan bersama oleh Bank Negara Malaysia dan Suruhanjaya Sekuriti. Buku ini, yang akan diagihkan kepada industri perbankan dan pasaran modal, adalah bertujuan memberi jaminan kepada orang ramai serta pelabur pelabur mengenai langkah langkah konstruktif dan kemajuan dalam menangani isu isu Y2K. Regulators of financial markets around the world have been preoccupied with the Y2K issue although often very little is discussed in public forums. Today Bank Negara Malaysia and Securities Commission as the regulators of the Malaysian financial markets will share with you the many tasks that we have undertaken to ensure that the soundness of the Malaysian financial system is guaranteed. In defining the Y2K remedial activities of the financial institutions, we have adopted the 5 phase framework, namely awareness, assessment, renovation, testing and implementation as recommended by the Bank for International Settlement. The awareness phase is to spread a general understanding of the Y2K problem. The assessment phase largely involves the creation of comprehensive inventories of all software, hardware and devices that may be prone to the Y2K problem. The renovation phase is primarily technical in nature, involving the repair, replacement and retirement of systems in order to become Y2K compliant. The testing phase is the most time consuming phase to confirm the Y2K ready status of the system. The Malaysian banking and insurance industries completed the first two phases, namely awareness and assessment, by the middle of 1998. The renovation phase has been completed since the end of the first quarter of 1999. The testing phase is almost over at 97% and the Implementation phase is expected to complete in August for the remaining few financial institutions. Contingency plans for possible systems or operational disruptions have also been completed. Over the next few months, the financial institutions will continue to engage in a variety of testing activities so as to be prepared for any unforeseen Y2K event that threatens to disrupt banking and insurance services. As of 30 June 1999, 95% of the Malaysian banking and insurance industries have collectively achieved a Y2K Ready status. The remaining 5% will be ready by the end of August this year. Details of the industry's Y2K status is given in this booklet. We have provided information that is useful and illustrative of the complexity of the Y2K problem. This booklet will also explain contingency planning issues and scenarios, along with examples of how such scenarios can successfully be managed to prevent or avert any disruption in banking services. All Malaysians and investors in Malaysia can rest assured that their money is safe, and will remain safe despite any Y2K event. Let me explain why we have this confidence. Firstly, Bank Negara Malaysia has adopted internationally recognised standards for managing Y2K risks in the financial sector. These standards were provided by the Bank for international Settlement as well as organisations such as the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council of the United States of America and Global 2000, a confederation of private financial institutions, that has made available the results of their collaborative efforts. Secondly, Bank Negara Malaysia deployed its information systems examiners to perform on-site examinations to validate work done, review documentation and engage in discussions with members of the industry. Thirdly, the Y2K testing process has been rigorous, well documented and in many cases repeated, to ensure that no stone is left unturned. Draft contingency plans of individual institutions were completed and submitted to Bank Negara Malaysia by the 30th of April 1999. The various Associations, such as the Association of Banks in Malaysia, Association of Merchant Banks in Malaysia, Association of Finance Companies of Malaysia, Life Insurance Association of Malaysia and Persatuan Insurans Am Malaysia, have participated in joint discussions to help identify and provide solutions for a wide range of contingent events. The Y2K Industry Steering Committee, chaired by Bank Negara Malaysia, has also met many times to discuss issues at every critical phase of the Y2K remedial programme. Independent verification of the Y2K remediation program is crucial to ensure the integrity of this very complex project is never in doubt. In addition to the on-site examinations conducted by Bank Negara Malaysia, the internal auditors of all financial institutions have been required to conduct reviews of the Y2K remediation program, and these institutions have forwarded the reports to Bank Negara Malaysia. The monthly Y2K status update reports submitted by all financial institutions to Bank Negara Malaysia include a formal statement by the respective chief executive officers accepting responsibility for the accuracy of the Y2K status reports. As a culmination of our supervisory efforts, Bank Negara Malaysia has instructed all banks and insurance companies to conduct an independent Business Risk Self-Assessment based on the set of questions made available by Global 2000 Co-ordinating Group, and a report to be submitted to Bank Negara Malaysia by 15 August 1999. On our own part, Bank Negara Malaysia has achieved a 100% Y2K Ready status and all inter-bank payment and settlement systems have been tested successfully. Additional tests for contingency planning will be undertaken over the next few months. It has been said many times that Y2K is a business problem, and not merely an IT problem. Bank Negara Malaysia's Y2K Business Risk and Continuity Committee, which comprises the heads of all departments in Bank Negara Malaysia, has deliberated on the various business risks, such as credit, market, legal, operational and liquidity. The most critical question for banking is of course the question of 'What will happen to my money?'. All financial institutions will print statements of balances of all customer accounts as at 15 December 1999 so that even if there was a problem with the computer system, the customers' money can be fully accounted for. ATM machines will be available on the 1st of January 2000. Bank Negara Malaysia will also ensure there is adequate currency and liquidity to cater for the possibility of excessive demand for currency during the year end festive seasons. Bank Negara Malaysia has worked with the industry to define the minimum service level regardless of any Y2K event, including loss of power or telecommunication services. These service levels will include cash withdrawal and deposit. As part of its contingency planning, Bank Negara Malaysia will have a Y2K communication centre adequately equipped to handle Y2K events, including event management, communication management and disaster recovery management. Further, the communication centre will keep in touch with other central banks, Securities Commission of Malaysia and other critical agencies in Malaysia. Needless to state, members of the press will be among the critical agencies since the media will have a crucial role to play in managing the uncertainties associated with Y2K. The other critical party is the National Y2K Project Team, which has provided the framework for the financial sector Y2K contingency plan. The sectorial contingency plan will be amalgamated with the national contingency plan in September 1999. I have briefly explained the Y2K methodology used by Bank Negara Malaysia and the contingency measures to mitigate any of business risks associated with the Y2K problem. It is important to remember that the state of computerisation of the Malaysian financial system has advanced significantly only in the past few years. Many of our systems were already Y2K compliant since the 4-digit standard has been in vogue for some years amongst the newer application platforms. Financial institutions have been granting long-term loans, extended fixed deposit maturities, invested in long-term bonds and issued long-term insurance policies where the dates often cross well into the 21st century. None of these transactions have failed. While we should never make the mistake of underestimating a problem, often it may be equally disastrous if we over-exaggerate the possible impact of a problem. As part of business risk and continuity planning, we need to always thread this fine line, and collaborate closely with all parties we come into contact with to ensure that we behave in a rational and constructive manner. The Y2K Malaysian Financial Sector Status Update and Continuity Planning booklet is aimed at reassuring members of the banking and insurance industries, the investors and members of the public on the constructive measures and progress made in handling the Y2K issue. The publication will be distributed to central banks, the banking and insurance industries, institutions in the capital market, the media and Malaysian missions abroad and foreign missions in Kuala Lumpur. Allow me to stop at this point and pass the floor to Encik Ali Abdul Kadir, Chairman of the Securities Commission. We will jointly take your questions after his address. Thank you. Bank Negara Malaysia 15 July 1999

Title: Speech at the Japan-Malaysia Assosiation Symposium - "Towards Revitalising the Asian Economy"
text: Governor's Speech at the International Conference for Emerging Markets - "Globalising Economy: Strategic Challenges, Options & Operational Issues" Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 19 Jul 1999 Venue: Nikko Hotel, Kuala Lumpur Language: English It gives me great pleasure to be here with you this afternoon at this International Conference for Emerging Markets in a Globalising Economy, focussing on the strategic challenges, options and operational issues. Malaysia is indeed very honoured to host this Conference in Kuala Lumpur. On behalf of the Malaysian Insurance Institute, I wish to thank Mr. Nigel Easton and Mr. Patrick Goergen for giving us the opportunity to collaborate with UNCTAD in organising this Conference. Let me also welcome our distinguished speakers and delegates from abroad. I hope that you will have the time to see some parts of the country while you are here, and experience the unique hospitality of the Malaysian people. I believe the Conference focuses on the two most significant catalysts driving global financial market developments today firstly, emerging markets and secondly, globalisation. Never before have emerging markets attracted as much global attention than in the last few years. The reasons are as follows: with emerging markets commanding half the world population and increasing wealth, the global corporate sector acknowledges the tremendous potential for business expansion in emerging markets and is looking to establish a significant presence in these markets; there is a growing realisation that emerging market economies can substantially impact global financial markets; in pursuit of development and progress, emerging markets are undergoing phenomenal changes in terms of market conditions, the regulatory environment and the structural landscape; and emerging markets will continue to feature prominently in future initiatives towards liberalisation, and the WTO negotiations in particular. The wave of globalisation is also taking the corporate world by storm. Globalisation is rapidly and irreversibly changing the way business is conducted. This is due in no small measure to technological advances, especially in the field of communication. Today, massive amounts of funds can be moved across borders with the simple click of a key. Physical borders are no longer a barrier. E-commerce, for example, has now penetrated many markets and poses many challenges and issues that countries are still grappling with. The possibility of instantaneous communication through the internet, cell-phones and satellite technology has given the concept of home shopping, or remote commerce, new meaning and dimensions. It is said that what is not allowed in through Government doors will come in through Microsoft's "Windows". In such a dynamic and ever-changing environment, insurance markets in emerging economies are coming under enormous pressure to measure up to increasingly demanding global expectations. But for emerging economies, globalisation can be a double-edged sword. While we acknowledge the significant progress that globalisation can bring to our markets in terms of greater access to technology, capital and expertise, we are equally conscious of its potential to devastate and destabilise entire regions. We experienced these effects in the recent financial crisis. Nations were plundered and reduced to states of poverty, instability and riot. If we are to mutually share in the benefits of globalisation, we must first agree that a global economy cannot be exclusively about growth rates and private capital flows. The crisis drove home an important point, that is, growth and development, to be sustainable, must be regulated. The responsibility for a global economy is a shared one. Certainly, there is an urgent need for reforms in emerging economies. At the same time however, the global financial system must not diminish or disrupt the efforts of emerging economies. It must instead support their efforts by preserving an environment that operates on the basic principles of economic, human and social equity. While emerging markets work to rebuild and strengthen their economies, there is an equally, if not an even more, pressing need for reforms to the international financial architecture. While larger forces play out the intricacies of global financial reforms, emerging markets must not neglect to do their part. I believe that over the course of this morning's presentations, you would have explored the various issues, trends and challenges facing emerging markets and some of the options available for Governments and insurers in responding to the changes taking place around them. This afternoon, I would like to address the implications of globalisation on institutional and regulatory reforms in emerging economies. In its Guidance Paper on Insurance Regulation and Supervision of Emerging Market Economies, the International Association of Insurance Supervisors identified the common problems facing insurance markets in emerging economies as:- lax management within insurance companies; weaknesses in the legislative framework; weak corporate governance; ineffective market discipline; and inadequate information flows due to a lack of transparency or undeveloped accounting systems. Perhaps, on a lighter note, I should add that one problem that they did not identify is the over-aggressive sales pitch of insurance agents. I am told the story of how 3 insurance agents attempted to sell an insurance policy to a man. The first agent told the man: "Look at that 40-storey building. If by accident, you were to slip from the 40th floor and fall to death, the cheque for your policy will be handed to your wife 3 days after your funeral." The second agent said, "In the case of my company, the cheque will be handed to your wife even before the funeral." The third agent looked contemptuously at his two competitors and looking at the man straight in the eyes told him "In the case of my company, if you were to fall from the 40th floor, by the time you pass the 20th floor, the cheque will be on the way to your wife". While the severity of these problems may vary in degree between different markets, we must realise that where they exist, globalisation will push these problems to the fore. Intense competition can potentially turn lax management into reckless management; legislative weaknesses into gaping loopholes; weak corporate governance into highly risky ventures; ineffective market discipline into market instability; and inadequate information flows into distorted and misleading disclosures. If we are to avoid falling victim to such woes, there is a need for regulation in emerging insurance markets to bring about the necessary reforms required to support a stable and progressive market. In the wake of the recent crisis, banking and corporate reform is being shouted from every rooftop, almost as if it is a new phenomenon. But surely this has always been at the heart of regulation. The need for ongoing reform has always been high on the regulator?s agenda. I believe what really emerged from the crisis and the anticipation of a global economy was not the realisation that we needed structural reforms, but that we needed to approach reforms differently. First, let us consider institutional reforms. In many emerging markets, institutional reforms have, until now, not adequately addressed the problems of the industry at a deeper level. Formal regulation is often introduced in these economies at a time when the industry is at its lowest ebb. Under such circumstances, regulation tends to be reactive with regulators usually resorting to drastic measures that can produce immediate results. So, where operating costs were rocketing sky high, cost controls were imposed. Where professionalism was lacking, minimum training requirements were introduced. Where productivity was low, productivity targets were set for companies to achieve. In most cases, these measures produced the desired results for the moment, but they were not sufficient to yield any substantial progress in the form of real structural reform.
