There is still a need for emerging markets to improve standards of corporate governance, management accountability and transparency, accounting and disclosure, and financial resilience at both the institutional and industry levels. Today, we find that more regulators are focussing their attention at tackling the underlying problems. In recent times, we have seen substantial progress being made in Corporate Asia in a number of critical areas:- there is a notable improvement in the quality of information flowing from emerging markets; visible progress is being made towards the adoption of international financial reporting standards and best market practices; and good corporate governance which embraces high levels of management quality and accountability, as well as internal controls, is being enforced at various levels in many emerging markets. While the broad objectives are the same, the strategies adopted to address institutional reforms will differ between emerging markets, and rightly so, since each must take into consideration its individual market structures, stage of development of the industry, and national priorities and aspirations. The crisis clearly showed us that there is no one panacea that cures all. Reforms merely for its own sake will do no good to countries, if at the end of the day, the domestic industry as a whole suffers. In Malaysia, our approach to institutional reform is built on the belief that sustainable growth is only possible in an environment which values and promotes financial strength and stability, management capability and public accountability. I believe this is what is needed for domestic insurers in emerging economies to compete effectively and sustain growth in a global economy. We recognised in Malaysia that effective legislation is a necessary foundation for any meaningful reform. Therefore, in 1997, the governing legal framework was significantly strengthened with the enactment of a new Insurance Act. This was followed by measures to establish the pillars of financial strength, which include a strong capital base, sound risk management techniques and operational efficiency. To achieve this, the Central Bank has been actively pursuing an agenda to consolidate the fragmented Malaysian insurance industry. While I am pleased to note that 12 insurers of the Malaysian industry are at various stages of implementing their merger and acquisition plans, many of the financially weaker and smaller insurers remain resistant. These insurers continue to wait in the shadows, confident that they will get by somehow. Let me take this opportunity to re-emphasise that Bank Negara has not waned in its resolve to build a core of financially strong, resilient and responsible insurers despite the temporary setback suffered as a result of the financial crisis. To this end, I wish to announce several measures which will come into force shortly under the institutional reform package being progressively implemented by the Bank:- first, since there are now clear signals of recovery in the Malaysian economy, the Bank will enforce the original capital and solvency requirements which were temporarily deferred at the height of the crisis. Insurers have been given ample breathing space to weather out the crisis. Those which have not given any serious thought to consolidating their financial positions are well-advised to do so. You are forewarned to make it soon, because I assure you, the Bank is determined to bring about major structural reforms to the insurance industry. This means that the Bank will not hesitate to take tough measures against insurers that are not able to meet the new requirements when they come into effect; second, to promote mergers and acquisitions among insurers, the Bank has approved an incentive package comprising some of the proposals put forward by the industry. The incentives will afford new business opportunities for merging insurers and substantially more flexibility to rationalise their operations and costs. Among other things, eligible merging insurers will be considered for new takaful licences, allowed a grace period to align the investment portfolio of the merged entity to meet the required level of admitted assets, given freedom to rationalise their branch network, and exempted from the cost control limits in respect of certain expenses associated with the merger exercise; third, the Bank has also revised the branching policy for insurers. The revised policy will allow financially stronger and wellmanaged domestic insurers to expand their branch network for greater market access. This will enable them to consolidate their market positions and establish a strong presence in the domestic market. In addition, both local and foreign-owned insurers will be freely allowed to place electronic terminals at the premises of their intermediaries to improve operational efficiency and effectiveness. fourth, to further enhance the financial flexibility and risk management ability of insurers, the Central Bank has recently issued guidelines on derivatives as an exposure draft for comment by the industry. When implemented, the guidelines will enable insurers in Malaysia to use financial derivatives to hedge, and hence better manage, their investment portfolios. We believe that as financial complexity and contagion exposure increases with globalisation, access to such risk management tools will become increasingly critical to insurers in maintaining stability in their operations; and fifth, the Central Bank will also be releasing guidelines on related-party transactions to ensure management integrity and public accountability in the conduct of insurance business. The guidelines will reinforce the fiduciary duty owed by insurers to properly manage insurance funds in an independent and transparent manner for the interest of policy owners at all times. Let us now turn for a moment to regulatory reforms. The numerous debates surrounding the Asian financial crisis conclude that in a global economy, emerging markets have become more susceptible to external contagion effects. This certainly complicates the regulatory task. With the rate at which businesses evolve, rules and regulations become obsolete almost as soon as they are implemented. Regulators in emerging markets are struggling to keep up with the burst of product innovations, alternative distribution channels, electronically-linked payment systems, e-commerce, investment avenues and alternative risk transfers, just to mention a few. These developments create intricate links in the commercial chain which are potentially fragile in the sense that if one link snaps, the whole chain comes apart. As the recent financial crisis clearly illustrated, no member of the chain will be spared from the domino effects of a crisis anywhere along the chain. With such complex and unique interdependencies, it would be virtually impossible to prescribe regulations that deal with every possible contingency. Firstly, regulators may not even be aware of the potential risk factors emerging every day. Secondly, regulators may be faced with constraints of jurisdiction. The answer to this dilemma is not deregulation but finding the right regulatory structure. The economist, Henry Kaufman, pointed out that the fundamental flaw with the current system of supervision and regulation of financial institutions and markets is that they fail to accommodate profound structural changes in the marketplace. In such an environment, formal regulations that tend towards micro-management of individual institutions may not be appropriate. What is needed is effective, high-level supervision. That is, a regulatory framework that is more broadly geared towards:- effective risk management; creating an environment that promotes corporate responsibility and accountability; and promoting market efficiency. Instead of being watchdogs, regulators should act more like pace-setters and navigators. This approach recognises that the industry is often best placed to make decisions concerning the rapid changes revolutionising insurance markets. In an environment where time is of the essence, greater reliance should be placed on the inherent knowledge and capabilities of the industry to adapt to these changes. Market discipline will also become a more prominent feature in the regulatory infrastructure of emerging economies. However, the keys to effective market discipline lie in public disclosure and consumer education. I believe that these will become important aspects of the regulator?s role in a globalising economy. Informed and educated consumers are often the most effective means of commercial discipline as they can exert significant influence over an institution?s business decisions and practices, as well as pricing policies. In other aspects of regulatory reform: globalisation will also see a greater alignment of the regulatory framework in emerging economies with international supervisory standards; increasing cross-border exposures will require regulators to cooperate more closely with their foreign counterparts. ASEAN insurance regulators have already taken a positive step in this direction by convening annual meetings and technical group discussions to deliberate and resolve common issues; and finally, the convergence of financial products will also create the need for domestic regulators to re-examine financial sector regulation at a macro level. One option would be to create fire walls within financial group structures to contain the spread of intra-group exposures. Institutional and regulatory reforms are already well underway in Malaysia and in other emerging markets . Even so, we must realise that changes do not take place overnight. The institutional and regulatory reforms which we have just discussed take time to accomplish. While this is the ultimate direction which reforms in emerging markets should take, the pace of reforms is guided by individual market capacities. At the same time, progress towards regulating the global economy has been slow. Until structural reforms and regulation of the international financial system achieve a satisfactory level, domestic policymakers have to delicately balance the benefits of globalisation with the need to preserve the stability of the domestic market. To put it simply, it must be a win-win situation. Despite the significant presence of foreign participation in the Malaysian insurance sector, Malaysia continues to come under criticism for failing to open up its market faster. We appreciate that financial liberalisation promises many advantages, including better risk management, product innovation, wider customer choice and greater access to foreign markets. However, if implemented prematurely, financial liberalisation can create a winner-take-all society and generate unprecedented inequalities with destabilising effects on domestic markets. The effects of globalisation should be such that it benefits the larger many and not the select few. Our primary concern is that given the present state of development of the Malaysian insurance industry, more will be lost than gained by a complete opening up of the market. As domestic policymakers, we have a responsibility to our people to ensure that wealth is distributed equitably. To achieve this, it is imperative that domestic institutions are given a fair chance to equip themselves to face global competition. This is why we have chosen to approach liberalisation in a sustainable and progressive manner. It is a question of time, not intention. Our commitment to liberalisation is clear from the already high level of foreign representation in the domestic insurance industry, and the substantially improved offers which Malaysia made at the 1997 WTO negotiations. You may be aware that Malaysia increased the limit on foreign shareholding in insurance companies and offered to issue an additional six new licences for life reinsurance business. Since the offer was made, a number of major global reinsurers have expressed keen interest in obtaining a life reinsurance licence. In this connection, I wish to announce that Bank Negara has decided to begin issuing the first batch of life reinsurance licences. Parties interested to establish life reinsurance operations in Malaysia either as a branch or in joint venture with a Malaysian partner, may now submit their applications to Bank Negara. There is no doubt now the selective exchange control measures adopted by Malaysia have provided the much needed stable environment required to turn around the Malaysian economy. The sharp volatility in the exchange rate has during the period July 1997 to August 1998 undermined severely Malaysia?s economic stability. The sudden drop in the purchasing power of the ringgit on account of speculative activities of hedge funds had almost paralysed domestic companies with borrowing overseas, as well as those with heavy import contents. Financial difficulties faced by some of these companies got transmitted to other parts of the economy, exerting pressures and stress to the financial system. The Government was confronted with the difficult task of stabilising the currency market and introducing measures to stimulate economic recovery. The consequences would have been much worse if not for the timely introduction of selective exchange control. It is no exaggeration to say that it was the selective exchange controls that saved the nation. The improved economic condition is clearly evident from the positive growth of 1.4% in real GDP for the two months of February and March this year. Many private analysts and forecasters have even projected growth for 1999 to be in the range of 3 to 4.9%. The trade balance continued to register substantial surplus of RM28.2 billion in the first five months of this year. At the same time, net inflows of foreign fund since the imposition of the levy system on February 15 amounted to RM4.7 billion. The increase in the international reserves of Bank Negara Malaysia has been phenomenal to reach USD31.5 billion, enough to finance 7 months of retained imports. Inflation too moderated to 2.9% in April and May, and dropped further to 2.1% in June. At the same time, the capital adequacy ratio of the banking system has improved considerably to about 12%, and the level of nonperforming loans of the banks stabilised at about 8% on a 6-month basis. It is almost certain that we are now out of the recession and well on the way to recovery. While economies in Asia can look forward to good prospects for a hard-earned recovery from the recent financial crisis, it is critical that insurers, Governments and regulators do not waver in their commitment to effective reforms. I believe emerging markets face their biggest challenge yet ? that of managing the effects of globalisation. We should not be lulled into complacency by the encouraging economic rebound. Instead, we should accelerate the pace of reform efforts to prepare for the challenges of globalisation. When emerging markets succeed in bringing their domestic industries on par with international standards, and when we are able to seek comfort and confidence in positive global financial reforms, only then can we look forward to embracing a truly global economy that is mutually beneficial to all. This is the legacy that we should strive to leave behind us. On that note, ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to declare this Conference open and wish you fruitful discussions over the next few days. Bank Negara Malaysia 19 July 1999

Title: Speech at the Malaysian Capital Market Summit 1999 - "Strengthening the Banking System for the Next Millennium"
text: Governor Tan Sri Ali Abul Hassan's Speech at the Malaysian Capital Market Summit 1999 - "Strengthening the Banking System for the Next Millennium" Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 11 Aug 1999 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English It gives me great pleasure to be here today to share with you Malaysia?s experience in managing the banking system during the financial crisis and the way forward. With the new millennium on the horizon and the financial crisis behind us, it is timely to discuss some of the critical issues and lessons which have emerged from the financial crisis and our priorities in strengthening the banking sector to cope with challenges in the next millennium. It has been two years now since the financial crisis started in July 1997. While we do not wish to celebrate the anniversary of a crisis, we do feel relieved and grateful that the crisis is now in its tail end and the worst appears to have been over. Nevertheless, the imbalances and structural distortions as a result of the crisis have taken a heavy toll on virtually all sectors of the economy and all segments of society. Over the last two years, the Government has instituted major reforms, including introducing the selective exchange control measures, to minimise the adverse impact of the volatile external developments and to restore stability in the Malaysian economy as well as the banking sector. Much has been said on the impact of the financial crisis on the Malaysian economy. Therefore, I shall not dwell further on this matter. Given the scale and speed of the financial crisis, the Malaysian banking sector was not spared of the adverse effects of the crisis. Consequently, the banking sector, being the backbone of the economy, was the main focus of the reforms undertaken by the Government. The Government accelerated the pace of reforms in the banking sector during the crisis to ensure that the banking sector continues to remain sound and well-positioned to support early economic recovery. The broad thrust of the restructuring plan undertaken by the Government was to:- i. Create a core of strong, well-managed and adequately capitalised banking institutions to spearhead the development of the financial sector; ii. Broaden and deepen the financial markets to enable the sector to contribute as a sector of economic growth and be able to meet the changing needs of the domestic economy; iii. Improve the overall efficiency and competitiveness of the banking sector; and iv. Accelerate the development of the bond market to reduce the concentration of risks in the banking sector. Efforts undertaken by the Government mainly through the establishment of Danaharta, Danamodal and the Corporate Debt Restructuring Committee have begun to show positive results. A few months ago, it was difficult to convince a great deal of sceptic investors that Malaysia was serious in its restructuring efforts. Many waited to see if the reforms undertaken by the Government, particularly following the introduction of the selective exchange control measures, will be pursued in earnest by the Government. I have always maintained that Malaysia will be judged by the results of the various reforms undertaken by the Government. I can now say that many positive signs of recovery have emerged in our economy and the banking sector, as a result of the various measures introduced by the Government. We can see that loan approvals and disbursements in the banking sector have improved substantially in 1999. The weekly average loan approvals from January 1999 to 15 June 1999 have increased by 42% as compared to that in 1998, whilst the weekly average loan disbursements have risen by 22%. The net NPL ratio of the banking system had moderated to 7.9% on 6month classification as at end-June 1999 after peaking at 9.0% as at end-November 1998. In addition, the average monthly rate of increase in non-performing loans has moderated to 1.9% for the first 5 months of 1999 from an average monthly increase of 10.1% in 1998. The improved economic condition was also reflected in the recovery of real GDP from negative 10.3% in the last quarter of 1998 to negative 1.3% in the first quarter of 1999. For February and March 1999, real GDP growth was already positive 1.4%, and preliminary data indicates that the second quarter will record a positive GDP growth as well. The trade balance position continued to register substantial surplus of RM33.7 billion in the first half of 1999 with the improvement in export growth by 7%. The international reserves of Bank Negara Malaysia have also continued to increase to reach USD31.6 billion, sufficient to finance 6.9 months of retained imports. Nevertheless, we should not remain complacent despite these positive indicators. Instead, this past decade of rapid changes have shown that much can still be done to ensure that our banking sector would continue to remain resilient and be able to withstand future shocks. The long-term development of the banking sector is our primary concern over the next millennium. Many may question our intention of being somewhat dramatic in our recent move to consolidate and rationalise the banking sector into 6 large and strong financial groups. However, I wish to emphasise that plans to rationalise and consolidate the banking sector is not something new to our country. The banking crisis in the mid-1980s propelled a number of weak commercial banks and finance companies into insolvency and financial distress. These institutions were badly hit by the 1985-1986 recession as they were saddled with huge levels of NPLs, the aftermath of over-lending to the property sector and imprudent exposure to share-based lending during the earlier boom years. In addition, the finance company industry, in particular, was highly fragmented, comprising 47 finance companies. Given the severity of the losses and to maintain integrity of public savings and the stability of the financial system, Bank Negara Malaysia had to implement a rescue scheme. The rescue scheme involved Bank Negara Malaysia acquiring shares in some of the ailing commercial banks and the absorption of the assets and liabilities of the insolvent finance companies by stronger finance companies. As a result of the rescue scheme, the number of finance companies was reduced from 47 to 40. The merger of one commercial bank and the consolidation of the finance company industry were thus driven by the rescue scheme in order to restore stability in the banking sector. The design and implementation of the rescue scheme had been a very costly experience to the nation as a whole. We learnt from this crisis the crucial need for banking institutions to maintain high levels of capital in order to be able to withstand shocks. Therefore, banking institutions were strongly encouraged to build up their capital strength through mergers and acquisitions to attain critical mass. Nevertheless, we have seen from the past that our call for rationalisation and consolidation has always fallen on deaf ears. The only market-oriented mergers in the banking sector was between Kwong Yik Bank Berhad and DCB Bank Berhad and between Chung Khiaw Bank Berhad and UOB Bank Berhad. In fact, after the strong economic recovery in the late 1980s and early 1990s, banking institutions seemed to have forgotten the costly experience of the past and pursued reckless and aggressive lending strategies. There was no urgency for banking institutions to consolidate as the shareholders were comfortable with the returns that they received. Plans to grow bigger and stronger were of minimal concern. The market-driven approach did not seem to have much success. The last financial crisis has again clearly highlighted the vulnerabilities of a fragmented domestic banking sector. Many of these banking institutions were small and survived mainly as niche players. We saw the rapid deterioration in the performance of the finance company industry during the financial crisis. The need to arrest this rapid deterioration prompted the Government to initiate a merger programme whereby these small finance companies were to be absorbed by larger institutions. Although the merger programme for the finance company industry managed to reduce the number of finance companies from 39 to 17, the initial target was to consolidate the industry into 8 anchor finance companies. This was not achieved as a number of smaller finance companies could not agree on the pricing of their shares. Growing competition and strong pressures emerging from the external front to further liberalise the banking sector has also clearly shown that our domestic banking sector can no longer remain protected. The financial liberalisation envisaged under the GATS framework to gradually remove barriers to entry and access among the ASEAN countries and the world at large, brings home the point that Malaysia can no longer exist in isolation. In fact, it is critical that our domestic banking sector gear itself and be able to meet the challenges and competition arising from the increasing globalisation and technological advancements in the areas of banking services. It is necessary for the Malaysian banking sector to be able to compete effectively and efficiently in its turf before the domestic banking institutions can venture into regional and global markets. Furthermore, we can see that the current trend in the global markets is the rapid consolidation of banking institutions especially in the United States of America and Europe to take advantage of economies of scale and tap potential synergies, in order to compete more effectively and efficiently in the global environment. Malaysia too would need to follow this trend if we are to survive the challenges of the new millennium. In the new millennium, the banking business will experience greater and more dramatic structural changes as a result of technological advancements, financial innovation and new competition. The changes in the financial markets would also bring about higher risks and rewards to the players in the markets. The smaller banking institutions will face tremendous pressures not only from the domestic but also from the external front. If consolidation of the banking sector is not accelerated, history will only repeat itself and our banking institutions will not be able to remain relevant in the long run. Any Government intervention in the future would be at a much higher cost. The consolidation and rationalisation of the domestic banking sector is, in any case, inevitable given the rising challenges and the increasingly competitive environment. Recognising this and as the market-driven approach failed to encourage merger, Bank Negara Malaysia has to accelerate the consolidation process to ensure that the banking system is well-positioned to meet the growing and changing demands of the economy. The rationale for doing it now is that the sooner the consolidation takes place, the better it is for the Malaysian banking system. While many quarters have acknowledged the need for Malaysia to rationalise the domestic banking sector and supported the move, they have questioned the timing of this exercise. Our response is if this consolidation exercise is good, why do we need to procrastinate? Why not seize this window of opportunity that is available to us now? If we wait too long and the market is liberalised, the smaller institutions will end up being swallowed by the larger institutions. Is this what we wish to see in the future? If this happens, the intrinsic value of these smaller institutions will vanish completely. In this merger process, we are at least able to retain some of the intrinsic value of these smaller institutions in the larger institutions. The current merger exercise will rationalise the domestic banking sector into 6 strong financial groups namely the Maybank Group, Multi-Purpose Group, Bumiputra-Commerce Group, Perwira Affin Group, Public Bank Group and Southern Bank Group. These financial groups were selected on the basis of synergies in their business activities, branch distribution and other market-oriented factors. These financial groups also demonstrated their resilience during the crisis. These 6 financial groups would be supported by very strong capital, which is necessary given that in a more globalised environment, where there is greater dependence on information technology, banking institutions require large amount of capital investments to remain competitive and be able to assume higher risks. Banking institutions can no longer be owned by individuals or families who will not have the capacity to build up the capital of the institutions to support the capital needs of the institutions. The creation of these 6 strong financial groups would form the new financial architecture in Malaysia to ensure that the domestic banking sector is able to support economic transformation that will be undertaken to promote sustainable economic growth. Being bigger and stronger banking institutions, these 6 financial groups will be able to withstand pressures arising from disintermediation, increasing demands from customers and competition from regional and global players. Rationalisation of resources is necessary given the excess capacity in the banking sector. To facilitate the merger process, Bank Negara Malaysia will formulate broad principles on valuation which had in the past been the most contentious issue that can prevent the successful conclusion of merger negotiations. The broad principles, which will be fair to all parties, will minimise any disputes in the pricing of the shares. The merger parties are also required to submit weekly reports to BNM on their progress in the merger negotiations. A Steering Committee has been formed and we have assigned a number of staff to work on these mergers on a full time basis. On a working level, various committees have also be set up to oversee certain issues arising from the merger, one of which is on human resource. There have also been concerns that the interest of certain shareholders would be disregarded in the merger exercise. Minority shareholders are also fearful that their interest may not be adequately addressed in the merger process. Let me assure you that the merger exercise would be transparent and based on market-driven terms. This merger exercise is not an expropriation exercise. Instead, the shareholders of the acquired banking institutions will have the option of receiving cash or shares in the merged entity. Being a small shareholder in a giant institution is definitely more meaningful than being a controlling shareholder in a small institution. The nation?s interest has to take precedent over the interest of any one party. We are committed to ensure that the merger process is successfully implemented with minimal problems. Towards the new millennium, Bank Negara Malaysia would continue to pursue its long term agenda which is to build a resilient, competitive an dynamic banking sector which is able to meet the changing needs of the domestic environment and provide a catalytic role in the transformation of the economy. The banking sector should basically become an engine of growth in its own right whist supporting economic development. In responding to the changing economic structure, domestic banking institutions must equip themselves with strong capabilities and be more innovative and competitive. An efficient and effective banking sector will not only support efficient conduct of monetary policy but also enhances the payment infrastructure system and market surveillance mechanism to monitor capital flows and other sources of risk. The increasingly globalised financial markets would also require the Government and regulators to address the risks of the economy at a national level. Optimal policies must be put in place and there must be a co-ordinator to synchronise risk management approaches of different sectors in the economy. In moving forward, one area that needs to be addressed urgently is the problem of moral hazard in the banking sector. The blanket guarantee by the Government on all bank deposits has created a perception among the public that the regulators will continue to protect the public?s interest at all cost. However, one must realise that excessive protection would only end up promoting market inefficiencies and increase the financial burden on the Government. As such, we are actively studying the implications of introducing a Deposit Insurance Scheme for our banking sector and we expect to announce our findings of the study in due course. Such study would include assessing the effectiveness of Deposit Insurance Schemes in other countries and the suitability of the scheme for our Malaysian banking sector. We have also recognised that excessive regulation and protectionism will only stifle innovation and productivity improvements. In a growing complex environment, one should not rely solely on the Government and regulators to protect the domestic market participants and the general public. I believe that we must start to consider optimal regulatory approaches for our banking sector as well as the general economy as a whole. Financial stability is a key requisite of strong and healthy economic growth. Another critical aspect to ensure the development of a sound and efficient banking system is to have a conducive and appropriate regulatory framework in place. There is of course a wide spectrum of regulatory framework used by different countries. At one extreme is the framework adopted by a few countries like New Zealand. Let me highlight to you the case of the regulatory and supervisory approach undertaken by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, perhaps just as an example. Following the failure of the government owned bank in New Zealand in the late 1980s, the Reserve Bank intensified its supervisory efforts and imposed many rules and regulations on the banking institutions. As a result of the close monitoring by the Reserve Bank, the general public became overly reliant on the Reserve Bank to supervise the banking institutions, resulting in the problem of moral hazard. It was in the early nineties that the Reserve Bank decided to rethink their supervisory and regulatory approach. They concluded that close banking supervision cannot prevent banking failures. In the case of Barings and BCCI for example, although they are supervised, their failure arose from fraudulent activities. Recognising this, the Reserve Bank decided to move towards a disclosure-based regime where depositors themselves should make the judgement on the financial health of the banking institutions rather than relying solely on the supervision of the Reserve Bank. The Reserve Bank then placed the sole responsibility of managing the banking institutions on the directors themselves and all banking institutions were required to publish detailed financial statements to the public on a quarterly basis. The directors themselves have to sign the quarterly financial statements, attesting to the fact that, to their best knowledge and belief that information disclosed is reliable. They were also required to declare that the internal controls are appropriate to their banking businesses. This disclosure-based approach has given strong incentives for the directors to operate the banking institutions in a prudent manner. Since the change in the supervisory and regulatory approach undertaken by the Reserve Bank, much has been accomplished. There had been no bank failure in New Zealand despite some difficulties faced by a small number of banking institutions. This regime has made a dramatic difference to the soundness of the banking system in New Zealand. We can see from the New Zealand approach that a disclosure-based supervisory regime has its merits. However, for Malaysia, a more balanced approach will be adopted taking into account the stage of development of our economy and banking sector. Although Bank Negara Malaysia will be placing more emphasis on market discipline and self-regulation in the future, we will continue to complement the system with regular on-site examination on banking institutions. Indeed, Bank Negara Malaysia has been strengthening its supervisory functions through more regular on-site examination and the adoption of consolidated supervision in response to the crisis. Continued focus would be given towards developing the Malaysian bond market. One of our fundamental weaknesses lied in the slow development of our bond market. In the absence of a well-developed bond market, a significant portion of the credit risks were borned primarily by the banking sector. Large requirement for funding following big privatisation projects, were funded using short-term borrowings. This was clearly evident with the rapid increase in the bank lending activities over the last decade. Bank loans grew rapidly on an average of 25% and much of the lending were channelled towards the lucrative broad property sectors. Recognising the importance to develop the bond market, Bank Negara Malaysia has charted a long term strategic plan to promote an active bond market with a large pool of issuers, investors, traders and financial intermediaries who are able to continue to sizeable and fluid activities. As a start, I am pleased to announce that a financial guarantee insurer (FGI) will be established for the bond market. The FGI will help to provide the issuer of private debt securities an alternative to enhance its proposed debt issue?s stand-alone rating. The FGI would act like an insurer to the bond issues and provide a form of credit enhancement mechanism to help diversify some of the credit risk away from the banking system. Unlike a bank guarantee, a FGI ensures timely payment of principal and/or interest in accordance with the obligation?s payment schedule. In a normal transaction, the FGI would underwrite the timing risk arising from temporary cashflow problems facing the debt issuer. The FGI would encourage potential funds issuers to issue long-term PDS to finance projects which have long gestation periods. Further details of the FGI would be announced soon. In conclusion, I wish to re-emphasise that the existence of a sound and resilient banking sector is crucial to support economic development and serve as an engine of growth in its own right. Experience has shown that a banking crisis would translate rapidly into a downturn in the economic well-being of the country. The importance of sound macroeconomic management in line with credible, consistent and transparent policies is a right ingredient for developing economies like Malaysia. Therefore, we must strive towards strengthening the resilience of the banking sector in order to be able to undertake further risk and challenges in the future. The great challenges posed in the next millennium must not be undermined. The consolidation process is timely and must be done to safeguard our domestic banking sector. We must be prepared to bite the bullet and progress from here for the long term development of the banking sector. Our destiny is left in our own hands and we must not be complacent with our achievements thus far. The financial stability of the banking sector must remain our utmost priority. Bank Negara Malaysia 11 August 1999

Title: Speech at the Malaysia-Japan Economic Association 21st Joint Conference - "Asian Financial Turmoil and Its Implications - The Malaysian Experience So Far"
text: Assistant Governor Dr. Awang Adek's Paper at the International Conference on Islamic Economics in the 21st Century Speaker: Assistant Governors / Advisers Speech/Interview Date: 12 Aug 1999 Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English This paper consists of three parts. Firstly, it provides an overview of the Islamic financial landscape in Malaysia. Secondly, it discusses the various approaches undertaken by the Malaysian Authorities in the development of an Islamic banking system in Malaysia. And finally, some issues and future directions in the implementation of Islamic banking in Malaysia. PART 1 Overview The Islamic financial system in Malaysia may be broadly classified into three categories, namely the Islamic banking system, the non-bank Islamic financial intermediaries and the Islamic financial markets. The system may also be characterised in three different forms as follows:- 1. Full-fledged Islamic financial institutions; 2. Conventional financial institutions with Islamic windows; and 3. Conventional financial institutions with Islamic windows and full-fledged Islamic banking branches. Islamic Banking System The Islamic banking system comprises Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) as the central bank vested with powers under the Islamic Banking Act 1983 and the Banking and Financial Institutions Act 1989 (BAFIA) to regulate and supervise Islamic banking operations in Malaysia; the Islamic bank; and the commercial banks, finance companies, merchant banks and discount house participating in the Skim Perbankan Islam (SPI) (Note: the English translation is the Islamic Banking Scheme). The Islamic bank and the commercial banks are the only institutions allowed to offer Islamic current accounts. Islamic banks There is currently one Islamic bank operating in Malaysia, namely Bank Islam Malaysia Berhad (BIMB), established in 1983 under the Islamic Banking Act 1983. The Act provides BNM with powers to supervise and regulate Islamic banks, similar to the case of other licensed banks. BIMB operates a total of 80 branches with staff strength of 1,600 people. A second Islamic bank, to be known as Bank Bumi-Muamalat Malaysia Berhad (BBMMB) will be established following the merger of Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Berhad (BBMB) and Bank of Commerce (M) Berhad (BOCB). Under the arrangement, all conventional banking assets and liabilities of BBMB will be transferred to BOCB while the Islamic banking assets and liabilities of BOCB and BBMB Kewangan Berhad will be migrated to BBMB. BBMMB is expected to commence operations by the fourth quarter of 1999. Commercial banks The commercial banks participating in the SPI (SPI commercial banks) form the largest group of financial institutions in the Islamic banking system. The number of SPI commercial banks as at end-June 1999 was 24, of which four are foreign-owned locally incorporated banks. Total assets of the SPI commercial banks as at end-May 1999 was RM18.7 billion, while deposits and financing totalled RM14.5 billion and RM5.3 billion respectively. Islamic banking facilities are available in 1,663 branches of the SPI commercial banks, including 7 full-fledged Islamic banking branches. Finance companies The second largest group of banking institutions in the Islamic banking system are the finance companies. There are 18 finance companies participating in the SPI (SPI finance companies) as at end-May 1999. Total assets of SPI finance companies as at end-May 1999 was RM5.1 billion while deposits and financing each amounted to RM4.1 billion and RM2.3 billion respectively. Islamic banking facilities are available in 820 branches of the SPI finance companies, including 3 full-fledged Islamic banking branches. Merchant banks Merchant banks as a group are relatively small in the Islamic banking system. Although there are only 5 SPI merchant banks, most of the Islamic banking activities are dominated by two large merchant banks, which represent 93% of the SPI merchant bank's assets. As at end-May 1999, total assets of the SPI merchant banks amounted to RM733 million while deposits and financing totalled RM238 million and RM438 million respectively. Discount houses The discount houses are the new entrants in the Islamic banking system, when they are allowed to participate in the SPI since December 1998. All the seven discount houses are participating in SPI and they focus on short-term Islamic money market operations and underwriting/ arranging of Islamic debt securities. Non-Bank Islamic Financial Intermediaries The non-bank Islamic financial intermediaries may be broadly divided into four groups of institutions, as follows: 1. the takaful companies; 2. the savings institutions; 3. the development financial institutions; and 4. other financial intermediaries which offer Islamic banking services such as Islamic leasing companies and National Mortgage Corporation. Takaful companies (Islamic insurance) Takaful operations are regulated and supervised by BNM since 1988 with the appointment of the BNM Governor as the Director-General of Insurance and Takaful. There are presently two takaful operators, namely Syarikat Takaful Malaysia Berhad (STMB) and Takaful Nasional Sendirian Berhad (TNSB) operating a total of 113 takaful offices throughout the country. As at end-March 1999, total assets of the family takaful funds and the general takaful funds amounted to RM572 million and RM205 million respectively. Savings institutions The most prominent Islamic savings institution is the Pilgrims and Management Fund Board or popularly known as Tabung Haji. Tabung Haji is considered the first Islamic financial institution in Malaysia, established by statute in August 1969. The objective of Tabung Haji is to promote and mobilise savings of Muslims intending to go on pilgrimage, and co-ordinate activities connected with Muslims going on pilgrimage. Tabung Haji manages a fund derived mainly from the accumulation of savings of intended pilgrims. The total assets of Tabung Haji as at end-June 1999 were RM7.66 billion. The growth of Tabung Haji was derived mainly from its expanded savings base due mainly to the increase in the number of depositors, totalling 3.6 million as at end-June 1999. Bank Rakyat is the leading co-operative credit institution and has committed to establishing itself as a full-fledged Islamic cooperative bank. The bank introduced Islamic banking in 1993 and since then, the banking operations of Bank Rakyat have been geared towards Islamic banking through its 74 branches nationwide. All new branches of Bank Rakyat now offer solely Islamic banking products while the existing branches are gradually being converted to Islamic banking branches. Bank Rakyat is the fore-front institution in the provision of Islamic pawn-broking services or popularly known as Ar-Rahnu, as a joint-venture exercise with Yayasan Pembangunan Ekonomi Islam Malaysia. The National Savings Bank (NSB) offers Islamic banking services on a small scale via the Islamic window. Development finance institutions The development finance institutions (DFIs) are basically enterprises owned by the public sector. The DFIs which offer Islamic banking services are the Industrial Bank of Malaysia, the Development and Infrastructure Bank of Malaysia, and the Agriculture Bank of Malaysia, all of which provide the facilities on a window basis. The Development and Infrastructure Bank of Malaysia (DIBM) provides Islamic banking facilities in the provision of medium and long-term funds to promote industrial, investment and growth while the Agriculture Bank has developed a similar scheme to that of DIBM. In addition, the Industrial Bank of Malaysia and the Development and Infrastructure Bank of Malaysia (DIBM) are also the national agencies for the Islamic Development Bank's (IDB) financing facilities in Malaysia, in which IDB extends credit lines to both banks for direct financing and trade financing facilities. As at end-June 1999, the combined Islamic financing extended by the three institutions amounted to RM164 million. Islamic Financial Markets The Islamic financial markets in Malaysia comprise the Islamic money market and the Islamic capital market. The Islamic money market, introduced in 1994 may be regarded among the most structured Islamic money market in the world. It comprises the trading of Islamic papers, the Mudharabah inter-bank investment, and the Islamic clearing and settlement system. The participants in the Islamic money market are the Islamic bank, SPI commercial banks, SPI merchant banks, approved SPI finance companies and SPI discount houses. Among the instruments available in the Islamic money market are the Government Investment Issues, Islamic Accepted Bills, green Bankers Acceptances, Islamic debt securities (bonds and commercial papers) and Islamic Negotiable Instruments. The Islamic capital market in Malaysia comprises a primary securities market, in which new issues of Islamic Government papers and Islamic corporate securities are offered to the public as well as institutions; a secondary market, in which existing Islamic Government papers and Islamic corporate securities are transacted; and the equity market and unit trusts. Islamic Government papers refer to Government Investment Issues, introduced in 1983 under the Government Investment Act 1983. Under the Act, the Government is allowed to issue non-interest bearing government papers to the public based on Islamic principles. Since the GII is defined as liquid assets, the Islamic bank and SPI banks purchase the GII to meet the liquidity requirements as well as to park their temporary idle funds. As at end-May 1999, total outstanding issues of GII were RM2 billion. Islamic debt securities (IDS) made its debut in 1990 when a multinational company issued a RM125 million Bai' Bithaman Ajil facility for a distillation plant. Since then, IDS has become increasingly popular with various Islamic concepts such as Musyarakah, Ijarah, and Qardhul Hassan being applied. Islamic debt securities comprise the medium term Islamic bonds and the short-term Islamic commercial papers. The Islamic equity market is reflected by the stock-broking activities, Islamic unit trusts, Islamic index and the list of the Syariah-approved counters. In terms of the stock-broking activities, the country now has a full-fledged Islamic stock-broking firm and three conventional stock-broking firms offering Islamic stock-broking services. In April 1999, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange (KLSE) introduced an Islamic equity benchmark index for those who wish to invest according to Syariah. The KLSE Islamic Index tracks Syariah-compliant stocks in the KLSE, constructed from the list of Syariah-approved counters issued by the Securities Commission (SC). Unit trusts The unit trusts are a group of specialised financial intermediaries in the capital market which offer small investors the opportunity to pool their resources in a diversified portfolio of securities which are managed and selected by professional portfolio managers. The inception of Islamic unit trust began in 1993 when Tabung Ittikal was introduced by Arab-Malaysian Unit Trust. The success of the fund paved the way for the introduction of more Islamic unit trusts and as at end-May 1999, there were 13 Islamic unit trusts in the country with total fund size of RM3.55 billion. PART 2 Approaches Having painted broadly the Islamic financial landscape in Malaysia, it is useful to discuss the approaches undertaken by Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) in the development of the Islamic banking system in Malaysia. The Central Bank has adopted several principles and approaches in developing Islamic banking in Malaysia as follows: 1. Dual banking system; 2. Gradual implementation; 3. Providing adequate infrastructure; 4. Optimising available opportunities; and 5. Openness. Dual banking system The first approach is to present a dual banking system to Malaysians ? Islamic banking system operating side-by-side with the conventional banking system. Perhaps Malaysia is the only country in the world that develops a dual banking system. Other countries, particularly Muslim countries, would either have a full-fledged Islamic banking system; or conventional system with a few Islamic banks; or a totally conventional banking system. Why this approach? First of all, through a dual banking system, Malaysian Muslims have a choice to bank in a system that is in line with their religious belief. It provided an alternative to Muslims who have restrained from using the banking system which, prior to 1983, was totally conventional. SecondIy, a dual banking system provides a complete and comprehensive banking alternative to Malaysians. This means that a wider range of Islamic banking products and services will be made available in banking institutions which offer Islamic banking. In the dual banking system, there is not only an Islamic bank, but also other supporting banking institutions such as commercial banks, finance companies, merchant banks, takaful companies, securities firms, savings institutions, and rural co-operative bank. Islamic financial services are also available in the financial markets such as Islamic money market and the Islamic capital market. In short, all Malaysians would have no problem with the diversity and availability of Islamic products and services in the country. Thirdly, the menu of Islamic financial products in a dual banking system tends to be more comprehensive and wider. In a competitive environment, where conventional banking tends to be a competitor, Islamic banking operators have to be innovative and creative to ensure that their products are superior to, or at least at par with the conventional products. Therefore, the elements of efficiency and innovation are vital to ensure Islamic banking will remain relevant, and able to capture a fair share of the banking system. The operators certainly cannot afford to remain complacent. Finally, the level of sophistication in terms of Islamic banking products is prevalent in a dual banking system. It is a fact that the conventional banking system is in a sophisticated and advanced environment. Hence, Islamic banking has no choice but to keep up with the sophistication and advancement of the banking system. This element has been the plus factor on why Islamic banking products available in Malaysia are seen to be at a relatively advanced stage. As the country moves forward towards greater IT environment, Islamic banking is fortunate for being able to capitalise on the changes in the banking system. Innovation will always be an important element to motivate Islamic banking operators to be dynamic and pro-active in their pursuit to position Islamic banking in the mainstream banking. Gradual implementation Basically, the establishment of an Islamic financial system in Malaysia has undergone radical transformation in the last five years, although the first Islamic bank was established in 1983. Fundamentally, the timeline of the Islamic financial landscape may be characterised by three stages of development as follows: 1. 1983 ? 1990: Monopolistic years 2. 1990 ? 1994: Developing years 3. 1994 ? 2000: Take-off years The first stage of Islamic banking may be dubbed as monopolistic years, but with a cause. The rationale to confine Islamic banking within the structure of a single Islamic bank was to allow the Islamic bank to operate in a smooth manner without undue competition which may hinders the progress of Islamic banking. There was an understanding that the Islamic bank would be given a grace period of 10 years before the Government decides to establish another Islamic bank. The second stage was the developing years beginning 1990 when the Governor of BNM expressed his desire to create a comprehensive Islamic financial system operating in parallel with the conventional banking system in Malaysia. BNM embarked on the project to disseminate Islamic banking on a nation-wide basis, with as many players as possible and able to reach all Malaysians. Towards this end, BNM considered three options with regard to creating the nucleus of an Islamic banking system, namely: 1. allow the setting up of new Islamic banks, 2. allow the existing financial institutions to set up subsidiaries to offer Islamic banking services; and 3. allow existing financial institutions to offer Islamic banking services using their existing infrastructure and branches. After a careful consideration of various factors, BNM decided on the third option as the best approach to disseminate Islamic banking throughout the country and as a medium for the development of an Islamic banking system. The third option was seen as the most effective and efficient mode of increasing the number of institutions offering Islamic banking services at the lowest cost and within the shortest time frame. It also allowed the existing infrastructure of the banking system, including the existing branches and staff to be tapped in offering Islamic banking services. BNM consulted a number of prominent Islamic jurists whether such approach is in line with the Syariah. The feedback received was overwhelming. We received full support from the jurists who applauded the move as a positive step. The reasoning "if you cannot implement it all together, do not ignore it all together" was the strongest point to back-up the policy. This reasoning implies that if we cannot develop the Islamic banking system in total, we should not totally abandon the effort but to do it as per our efforts and capability. Following the above, in March 1993 BNM introduced the Skim Perbankan Islam or SPI (previously known as Skim Perbankan Tanpa Faedah). The scheme allows conventional financial institutions to offer Islamic banking services alongside their conventional banking services. Three commercial banks were selected for the pilot test and by the end of 1993, 18 banking institutions participated in the scheme. The number of products, about 22, were considered adequate, while the infrastructure of the Islamic money market was already in place by end-1993. The third stage was the take-off period where various measures were implemented to strengthen the Islamic banking system. This includes the introduction of the Islamic money market in January 1994, separate disclosure for SPI banking operations in October 1996, opening of full-fledged SPI banking branches beginning 1996 and the harmonisation of Syariah issues via the formation of the central Syariah advisory council at BNM in May 1997. At present, we are riding on the take-off stage, and the growth of Islamic banking is being monitored closely to make it more resilient and robust. The assets of Islamic banking have grown from only RM2.4 billion in 1993 to RM29.9 billion as at end-May 1999. Deposits increased significantly from only RM2.3 billion in 1993 to RM22.9 billion while financing increased from only RM1 billion in 1993 to RM11.7 billion during the same period. The number of institutions participating in the SPI has also increased from only three players at launching stage to 54 players, comprising 24 commercial banks, 18 finance companies, 5 merchant banks and 7 discount houses. Islamic money market also recorded a sharp increase, from only a humble RM2.1 billion in 1994 to RM118.3 billion as at end-1998. Islamic debt securities, which has become a popular feature in the domestic private debt securities market has managed to capture 20.4% of the total PDS market, with an outstanding amount of RM17.1 billion as at end-April 1999. The gradual implementation of Islamic banking has been instrumental in bringing Islamic banking to where it is today. It has not been the intention to call for a total replacement of the conventional banking system since the move may not only be unwise, but also will not meet the requirements of the economy. Thus, Malaysia will continue with the current approach to develop Islamic banking, as it has been tested to be successful. Providing adequate infrastructure One of the basic functions that determine the robustness of an Islamic banking system is adequate institutions and market infrastructure. The more complex a system, the more complicated the infrastructure will be. Similar rule also applies to Islamic banking. It must possess adequate infrastructure to enable the system to operate and function smoothly. The genesis of the present Islamic financial structure began with the institutional building undertaken since 1983. However, since there is only one Islamic bank, the structure is not complete as a banking system must have a large number of players, a broad variety of instruments and an inter-bank market to provide the matching mechanism between the deficit and surplus units in the Islamic banking system. Some of the infrastructure of the Islamic banking system may be summarised as follows: (i) Legal set-up and legal provisions This is carried out through the Islamic Banking Act 1983 for the Islamic bank and the Banking and Financial Institutions 1989 for the SPI banking institutions. (ii) Regulatory framework BNM provided the necessary framework such as the statutory requirements, liquidity requirements, prudential guidelines (such as the Guidelines on SPI and Guidelines on the Islamic Money Market) and constant monitoring of the Islamic bank and SPI banks operations through off site and on-site supervision. BNM has also established a special unit in the Bank to carry out strategic planning and formulate policies for Islamic banking. (iii) Financial disclosure This is carried out via the GP8, a model financial statement which requires SPI banks to disclose their Islamic banking operations as part of the principal financial statements of the SPI banks. The disclosure, as part of the Notes to the Accounts entails the balance sheet and the P & L of the Islamic banking operations during the financial year. BNM is also working closely with the Malaysian Accounting Standard Board to study the various accounting standards developed by the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Insitutions based on Bahrain. (iv) Payment systems The country has already a sound and reliable payment, clearing and settlement systems to ensure the process of settling monetary transactions are completed in a timely manner. The crucial issue in Islamic banking is the segregation of funds to avoid co-mingling between Islamic and conventional funds. To facilitate such arrangement, BNM has required the SPI banks to open and maintain separate current and clearing accounts with the central bank. This has resulted in each SPI banks maintaining two account numbers with the central bank, i. e. conventional account and Islamic account. In addition, the SPI banks are also required to maintain separate member accounts for funds transfer and payments. The separate payment system devised for Islamic banking has avoided possible abuse in terms of wrongful accounting entries by the SPI banks with respect to Islamic banking operations. (v) Central Syariah board BNM realised that differences in interpretations in Syariah may not be healthy for a relatively young Islamic banking system. To reduce such possibilities, BNM established the National Syariah Advisory Council in 1997, empowered as the sole authority to issue opinions and decisions in Islamic banking and takaful. Although the Islamic bank and the SPI banks also appointed Syariah advisers to advise them on day-to-day operations, they are required to refer to BNM on policy-related Syariah issues. Optimising available opportunities We are of the view that the most appropriate strategy would be to optimise opportunities, particularly on the wide array of instruments already available in the market. Firstly, we have the pure Islamic instruments. This is relatively easy since it has been accepted and recognised. Examples of such products are the Mudharabah investment account and Musyarakah financing. Next, we have the conventional financial instruments which we feel could be Islamised. What we have done is to first identify the Islamic and un-Islamic elements in the instrument. Then we eliminate all the un-Islamic features in the instrument and replaced it with Islamic elements. Islamic Accepted Bills and Islamic Negotiable Instruments are such examples. Through this approach, we have managed to increase the number of instruments in the shortest time possible without the need to reinvent the wheel. Given the abundance of banking products available in the market, it is only realistic if we capitalise and optimise the opportunities. Notwithstanding that, we still encourage innovations, because innovations are still the key factor to differentiate Islamic banking products from conventional products. Openness We are fortunate that the various schools of thoughts in Islam have adopted an open approach with regard to differences in interpretations in the field of Islamic banking. Our stance is quite simple. We respect all the recognized schools of thoughts ("mazhab") on differences in opinions. The rule of thumb is to treat all products, minus the riba, as permissible ( "harus"). As long as even only one mazhab recognise a concept as acceptable from the Syariah point of view, the product will be classified as permissible. If we cannot find any source from the Quran, Sunnah, ijma' and qias, our central Syariah board may carry out an ijtihad. So far, the process has been smooth although the Malaysian interpretations on some Syariah issues have raised questions by others. It is important to learn to respect differences in opinion and interpretation, given that the process of ijtihad has allowed us to do so within the boundary and realm of the Syariah. If we keep on insisting that our approach in Islamic banking is better and purer, degrading the efforts of others, but yet at the same time do nothing constructive to implement Islamic banking, I cannot foresee Islamic banking making much headway. The bottom line by the end of the day is whether there is growth and development in Islamic banking. Performance is measured by achievements. If we are to offer a solution to the ills of the present financial system architecture, we have no choice but to adopt an open attitude. PART 3 Issues and Future Directions The final part will discuss some issues and the way forward in the implementation of an Islamic banking. At the outset, we are witnessing radical transformation in the world economy in the last two decades. Geographical and cultural boundaries have increasingly been broken down with the advent of efficient communication, Internet and satellite. The world is within reach with a flick of a button. Rapid economic and financial changes around us can easily render yesterday's winning business strategies obsolete. Even successful companies like IBM and General Motors have discovered that they can lose significant market share if they do not respond to fast changing business environment. Progress in telecommunication has been the driving force in creating a huge global business landscape. Bankers, particularly Islamic bankers should take cognisance of this important development to strategise and position themselves. The notion that banks merely act as financial intermediaries between the ultimate savers, the households, the ultimate investors, the firms may no longer holds ground. Today, institutions that acquire telecommunication technology are able to encroach into the banking sector by their ability to offer products similar to banking products. It is only the state of readiness to manage the forces of competition that can ensure relevance of each individual institutions; whereby in the long run, the regulatory environment which has long protected the encroachment of competition, both globally and domestically, may have to be prudently dismantled. On the other hand, technology-driven domestic banks can tap the vast opportunities in the huge global banking landscape. To cope with increased competition, Islamic financial institutions should take advantage of the advancement of high technology in the conduct of their business. Notwithstanding the desire to be high-tech driven, they should not, however ignore the other important aspect of banking i. e. the "high-touch" aspect. This refers to the importance of being customer-oriented and customer-driven in all their operations. Too many Islamic banks still design their products without customer input, only to find them rejected in the marketplace. And too many Islamic banks did not focus on consumer services, only to lose them to those who are consumer-driven. Islamic financial institutions cannot be a passive spectator of these profound changes. Islamic financial institutions have to prepare themselves to play a meaningful role and contribute significantly to enhance the economic wealth. Establishing an Islamic financial institution is already a no mean feat. But to sustain its commercial role in a competitive financial landscape is more challenging and daunting. We cannot afford to remain complacent. Islamic financial institutions are lagging far behind the level necessary to enable it to thrive and compete effectively in a freely competitive global environment. There is hardly an Islamic bank in the top 500 banks in the world. This is not an enviable record. We can certainly do better than this. Financial services, particularly banking are by nature long-haul business. Islamic financial services is not only long-haul business, it transcends beyond this world and the hereafter. There is no other way to generate active competition and the desire to seek out expansion than the need to justify returns on investments. Which is why there is a need for Islamic financial institutions to be adequately capitalised. An Islamic financial institution with a sound capital is able to assume greater risk and is, therefore, likely to be more willing to expand its operations and venture into new business. In view of the changing nature of financial services and the fast evolving financial landscape, size is increasingly important to compete in today's financial world. In my view, only large and strong Islamic financial institutions will have the capacity and ability to avail themselves of the opportunities. The future success of Islamic banking rests on the ability of this emerging sector to position itself strategically to overcome future challenges. The increasing globalisation of the financial system and the prospects of further liberalisation of the banking system in the time to come, both domestically and regionally, would pose challenges not only to conventional banking institutions, but also to Islamic banking. Although size is important, we should not ignore another important aspect of banking, i. e. the need for an abundance of intellectual capital. Islamic banking lagged behind conventional banking and therefore has a lot of catching up to do. Indeed, the future of Islamic banking depends a lot on the capacity and ability of Islamic bankers to generate creative ideas and innovative products in order to convince the banking public that Islamic banking is at par if not better than the traditional banking. There is no substitute to this. We all know that at the international level, Islamic syndications based on Ijarah usually used the LIBOR as the benchmark to price the product. It would be more meaningful if Islamic banks could come up and design their own reference rate rather than LIBOR, so that Islamic banks can have their own benchmark in the pricing of its products. Relying on LIBOR as the one and only reference rate without exploring into other Islamically-acceptable benchmarks would only prove our lack of creativity and will power. We are of the view that creating an international benchmark for pricing of Islamic products is an urgent tasks and thus, it is timely for Islamic bankers to explore this proposition and give it the necessary attention. In Malaysia, we are embarking on this project to establish a domestic Islamic reference rate which would serve as an indicator for investors to manage and plan their investments, and for Islamic financial institutions to price their products. Unlike conventional benchmarks which are costdriven, the derivation of the reference rate would be sourced from the profitability trends of the SPI banks. It is time for Islamic banks to generate practical and implementable action plan which can elevate the standards of Islamic banking in the international market place. There is a need for greater efforts and more effective means of networking to strengthen the relationship among Islamic banks. Strategic alliance arrangement and smart partnerships are some the approaches that Islamic banks should seriously explore into. Malaysia is always ready to share its experiences with other Islamic countries. It has done in the past with some countries in the region, and committed itself to the training programme in Islamic banking and takaful as one of the D-8 projects. Islamic banking has a bigger agenda than just providing an alternative banking system to the Muslim community. It has to show that it has the dynamism and sophistication to strive for the betterment of the society, address to the ills of the nation, and overcome economic imbalances. Co-operation among Islamic banks should not rest merely on operational and product developments issues, but Islamic bankers should devise long-term strategies on ways and approaches to elevate the position of Islamic banking to greater heights. Finally, the international Islamic financial system must be properly planned from now. The players must be identifed, the products must be made available and the international Islamic money market must be in place. The institutions that shape up the financial system must be made aware of their role in the establishment of an international Islamic financial system. The next stage then is to capitalise and maximise on each other's strengths so that Islamic banking and finance will not only prosper to benefit the Muslims but also contribute to the world as a whole. Perhaps the IDB and some of the international Islamic financial institutions should begin to explore the need to have at least a more structured although informal international Islamic financial system. The idea must be transformed into reality. Otherwise Islamic banking will continue to lag behind. Bank Negara Malaysia 12 August 1999

Title: Speech at the International Conference for Emerging Markets - "Globalising Economy: Strategic Challenges, Options & Operational Issues"
text: Governor Tan Sri Ali Abul Hassan's Speech at the JapanMalaysia Assosiation Symposium - "Towards Revitalising the Asian Economy" Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 07 Sep 1999 Venue: Tokyo, Japan Language: English It is indeed a great honour for me to be here today to address this symposium on "Revitalising the Asian Economy". As the regional economies recover from the recent crisis, this is certainly an important issue that will preoccupy us all as we approach the new millennium. I would like to express my appreciation to Mr. Shiokawa for inviting me to share my thoughts on this subject and for the kind hospitality and excellent arrangements made for my stay in Tokyo. It is my sincere hope that my participation in this symposium will help to further strengthen the already close friendship and economic cooperation between Japan and Malaysia in particular, and between Japan and Asia more generally. Asia has for more than a decade been a dynamic growth centre in the world economy. If Asia is to regain this status, it needs to recognise that the global environment in which we operate is rapidly changing. Unless Asia adapts and prepares itself for these changes, we will not be able to take advantage of the opportunities these changes accord to us. In fact, it could threaten our very economic survival. These efforts to strengthen our resilience however cannot be achieved within a short period. What is important is that the initiatives are taken now to build the necessary foundations. Efforts to revitalise Asia will also require a reassessment of the approaches to address the new developments and challenges that have been highlighted by the crisis. Certainly, we need to think about how we can work together more effectively to address the risks and challenges of a more globalised and integrated world. Causes of the Asian financial crisis and the present economic situation in Asia The worst of the Asian crisis appears to have subsided and a major preoccupation of many analysts these days is to revise upwards the growth forecasts for Asian economies. Now that we have entered a period of relative calm, it is timely that we look back and reflect on the lessons from the crisis, so that pitfalls can be avoided in the future and thereby ensure the current revitalisation of the Asian economies will be sustainable. There is a growing literature on the causes of the Asian crisis. Much of the debate had tended to focus on two perspectives. At the outset of the crisis, the predominant view was that the crisis was due to domestic factors, namely, macroeconomic policy slippages and weak financial systems in the affected countries. As the crisis became more prolonged, however, a growing consensus emerged of the global nature of the crisis. According to this former, the financial systems in the affected countries were not adequately prepared to deal with the risks and challenges of rapid financial liberalisation, which rendered the countries vulnerable to external shocks. However, in the recent year, there has been a recognition that while it is important to address the weakness in the national economies, of equal importance was to address the weaknesses in the international financial system. In particular, it is acknowledged that the activities of currency speculators and hedge funds also contributed to the crisis. The activities of such highly leveraged institutions have exploited the unstable market conditions and weaknesses in small financial markets, with destabilising consequences in terms of sudden and massive reversals in capital flows and excessive financial volatility that have overwhelmed the relatively small financial markets in emerging economies. The crisis which started out as a currency crisis quickly turned into a financial and economic crisis because of the inappropriate initial policy responses. The initial use of reserves in a number of countries to support unsustainable exchange rates resulted in a significant loss of reserves. The early depletion of reserves weakened the capacity of the Asian countries to handle the crisis. Speculators also had access to the stock market as a source of funding, so that declines in stock market prices and exchange rates reinforced each other. Depending on their relative exposures of individual countries, the fall in the currency and stock market prices in turn had severe implications on the banking system. Arising from the depletion of reserves, some crisis-affected countries had to resort to IMF assistance, in particular, where they were vulnerable to further external shocks, because of their significant foreign debt exposure. Unfortunately, such financial assistance required following IMF policy prescriptions. What was more damaging was that the IMF policy prescription worsened the crisis. Now that the crisis is over, many have claimed that the IMF policies of tight monetary and fiscal policies have yielded good results in the long-term. It should not be forgotten that the tight monetary and fiscal policies when external demand was falling worsened domestic conditions and caused a deeper recessions than warranted. These policies reinforced by drastic policies on the financial sector caused significant financial and social dislocation. The IMF in its wisdom tended to apply the principle of "one size fits all". Adjustment policies applied in the Latin American crisis was mistakenly applied to Asia. The standard IMF demand-management prescription of tight monetary and fiscal policies was designed to deal with excesses in the public sector, whereas the Asian crisis was caused by excesses of the private sector. Hence, measures to raise interest rates to defend the exchange rate, tighten bank prudential standards and reduce public expenditure had aggravated the economic contraction and deepened banking sector problems. Consequently, consumer and investor confidence fell, resulting in a vicious circle of weaker economic activity.
