With every fall in currency values, the liquidity problems of both the financial systems and the corporate sectors cascaded towards solvency problems because the depreciated currencies translated themselves into ever higher debt in terms of domestic currencies. The IMF policy prescription did not give importance to socio-economic considerations. The impact of the measures on the poor and on employment was not on the agenda. The IMF guideline has been "no pain; no gain". Hence, blanket measures were taken to close troubled banks and eliminate subsidies without the appropriate social safety net. This not only undermined confidence but led to widespread social unrest in some cases. While the IMF did recognise these adverse effects and relaxed some of its policy prescriptions after mid-1998, the damage was already done. The most serious flaw of the IMF intervention was the failure to address the liquidity problems in Asia. Unlike in the Mexican crisis, for example, there was no front-loading of IMF financial assistance for the countries affected by the Asian crisis. Efforts by Japan to extend quick financial assistance to the affected countries were also dismissed. Furthermore, debt restructuring came later in the programme in Asia. Coupled with the tight fiscal and monetary policies, the impact of adjustment was more severe in Asia compared to Mexico. With the nascent recovery in the region, the IMF policy advice to crisis-affected countries appears to be working. However, these policies resulted in an over-adjustment. It should be remembered that the "adjustment" came with a heavy price in terms of an over-correction in domestic activity, high unemployment, and severe social dislocation and a breakdown in the banking system in some cases. The costs of the conventional IMF policy approach has been extremely high in Asia. Asia paid for the policy mistakes by the IMF. The Malaysian approach to the crisis In the Malaysian context, it was recognised that the IMF prescription of tight monetary and fiscal policies was not sustainable. Efforts to stave off the persistent waves of speculative attacks on the ringgit failed, as the speculators knew that interest rates could not be maintained at an excessively high level for a prolonged period without causing serious damage to the corporate and banking system. Higher interest rates had led to higher NPLs (non-performing loans) and affected the health of the corporate and banking system. Furthermore, significantly higher interest rates aggravated the weak domestic demand conditions. It is important to recognise that policies need to take into account local conditions, as no one solution fits all countries. On 1 September 1998, with potential risks of further instabilities looming on the horizon, the Malaysian authorities took the action to insulate the domestic economy from the financial crisis with the implementation of exchange controls. The controls were important to neutralise a major source of instability, namely the development of a large off-shore ringgit market which speculators could tap to attack the ringgit exchange rate. This issue was raised with the IMF in the context of its surveillance process. Had the IMF acknowledged the problem and undertaken appropriate action, Malaysia's exchange controls would not have been necessary. At its height, currency speculators were able to access funding for their activities. This was reflected by the very high returns of 30 - 40% earned on offshore ringgit deposits. The only solution it seemed was to raise on-shore rates to match these off-shore rates. This however would be disastrous in an economy already in recession. The exchange controls were therefore essential to restore stability and to regain monetary policy independence to lower domestic interest rates to promote economic recovery without having to worry about the exchange rate front. In fact, Malaysia's exchange control measures are not capital controls in the strict sense of the word. The controls are more prudential in nature, aimed specifically at eliminating the internationalisation of the ringgit. The other "restriction" was the requirement for portfolio investors to maintain their Malaysian portfolio holdings in the country for a period of 12 months. The aim was to encourage portfolio investors to take a longer-term view of their investments in Malaysia and avoid destabilising flows. Since February this year, this control has been replaced by a repatriation levy. There were no controls on trade and investment flows, which continue to be freely permitted. As part of the exchange control measures, the ringgit has been fixed against the US dollar to provide a greater degree of certainty to the business community for trade and investment decisions. The rate was fixed at 3.80 to the US dollar, which was the prevailing rate on 2 September 1998. The use of exchange controls has been widely criticised by proponents of the free market system on the grounds that it leads to distortion and inefficiencies. Following the social ramifications of the Asian crisis, however, there has been greater acceptability of this policy option. It has been argued that free capital mobility has not solved problems in many countries, while creating new ones; the benefits from free capital flows have not been "persuasive". In short, the arguments in favour of free capital movement have been weak in comparison to that of free trade. Market failures in the global financial markets can lead to severe consequences because of the herding behaviour of financial markets, which has a tendency to over-react to developments. Opponents to capital controls on the other hand have suggested that controls are inefficient as they lead to distortions and circumvention. They pointed to the failure of controls in the past because of capital flight, and weaknesses in the balance of payments and reserves position. I should hasten to add that Malaysia is not advocating exchange controls for other countries. In Malaysia's case, we believe that the economy had the necessary preconditions to ensure the success of the controls. Traditionally, controls have been imposed by countries facing acute balance of payments problems. In Malaysia's case, the external payments position was strong. The decision to introduce the selective exchange controls was not taken lightly. We acted only 14 months into the crisis, when developments in Russia and elsewhere, which threatened to precipitate a global financial collapse. The basic objective of the exchange controls was to insulate the Malaysian economy from such external shocks and to provide an environment of stability to facilitate the ongoing economic and financial reforms. Just before the controls were imposed, the current account surplus had risen to an estimated RM25 billion or 9.3% of GNP for the first three quarters of 1998. The national external debt had remained low, at US39.6 billion as at September 1998 or 59% of GNP. Short-term debt accounted for only 18% of total external debt or 25.3% of total reserves. On the monetary front, prudential regulations had been taken to ensure that the intermediation process remained intact. At the same time, inflation remained low. This position of strength provided a foundation for ensuring the success of the selective exchange controls. It is important to note that Malaysia did not implement exchange controls as a substitute for policy reforms. The controls were a complement to the macroeconomic measures. They were an additional tool to fine-tune and to ensure that earlier measures have the best chances of working. This was because the controls provided stability to domestic financial markets, in a way traditional macroeconomic policies could not under the difficult circumstances. The world reverberated at Malaysia because they viewed that we would hide behind controls and do nothing. Contrary to these expectations, Malaysia accelerated the financial restructuring and the economic recovery process. The results of early resolution of banking problems has also turned around the initial adverse opinions about Malaysia's exchange control measures. In the area of financial reforms, Malaysia adopted a four-pronged strategy to deal with potential banking sector problems before they reached crisis levels. First, the initial merger programmes for finance companies aimed at rationalising their operations to increase their resilience in coping with the implications of a slowdown in economic activities. To date, the number of finance companies has been reduced from 39 to 25. Two commercial banks were merged into one. Unlike other countries in the region, Malaysia did not find it necessary to increase foreign equities in the financial sector. Malaysian shareholders could recapitalise their stakes. Where they could not, a special purpose vehicle (Danamodal) was established to do so using domestic resources. Second, Malaysia in July 1998 set up an asset management company, Danaharta to acquire and manage nonperforming loans of banking institutions. This is to ensure that the level of NPLs of banking institutions remained manageable at all times so that banking institutions would be able to concentrate on their lending activities rather than focus on measures to protect the quality of their assets. Third, the recapitalisation of a few financial institutions was effected through Danamodal. Fourth, a Corporate Debt Restructuring Committee (CDRC) was set up to provide avenues for voluntary debt restructuring for viable businesses that faced temporary cash flow problems. The results of the financial restructuring programme have been quite encouraging and has contributed to market acceptance of Malaysia's exchange controls. The risk-weighted capital ratio of the banking system has now strengthened to 13% at the end of July 1999, well above the minimum level of 8%. Net non-performing loans ratio at the end of June remained at 7.9% under the six-month classification. Total NPLs removed by Danaharta from the banking system amounted to about RM30 billion at 20 August 1999 or 35% of NPLs in the banking system. A notable difference in Danaharta's approach is that there is no cheap (fire) sale. Financing of Danaharta's operations was also not a major issue, thanks to several years of fiscal surpluses. Financing was through seed capital from the Government and the issue of Government-guaranteed bonds in the domestic market. Instead of resorting to auctions, because of available domestic financing, Danaharta did not need to resort to fire sales of assets acquired. In fact, the set-up of Danaharta was aimed at effectively managing these NPLs to maximise recovery value and dispose of its assets at the appropriate time. Similarly, the approach taken by Danamodal in bank recapitalisation was also different. The recapitalisation was pre-emptive in nature. Banks were recapitalised not because of insolvency but to maintain their capitalisation at healthy levels. There were no bank closures. Such an approach has avoided any breakdown in the financial system and mitigated its social consequences. Since its inception, Danamodal has injected RM6.4 billion into 10 banking institutions. As at 20 August 1999, this amount had decreased to RM 5.9 billion with the repayments of the ESCL (Exchangeable Subordinated Capital Loans) by some institutions. As at 20 August 1999, CDRC is dealing with 47 applications with debts totalling RM31 billion, of which 10 cases with debt amounting to RM10.2 billion have been completed and are at various stages of implementation. As these policies have strengthened the banking system, efforts are now directed at consolidating the banking system further so as to prepare for greater liberalisation in the future. As part of this policy, all domestic financial institutions are required to merge to develop a core of 6 strong and well-capitalised domestic banking groups, with each group having a commercial bank, merchant bank and finance company. At the same time, the Malaysian economic recovery is now gaining momentum. The fixed exchange rate has accorded the stability necessary to facilitate production and trade. Inflation continues to moderate while the substantial surplus in the balance of payments is increasingly emanating from export growth rather than lower imports. As a result, Malaysia's international reserves has increased significantly to US31.7 billion in July 1999, providing 6.9 months of import cover. Initially, Malaysia forecast was for a growth of 1% for 1999 based entirely on the fiscal stimulus package. Now that the export sector has strengthened significantly, GDP growth can be expected to be much higher. The second quarter has registered a growth rate of 4.1% bringing growth in the first half of 1999 to a credible 1.4%. The financial markets have recovered and activity is sustained at comfortable levels. Market capitalisation has increased to RM514 billion on 30 August 1999, compared with RM182 billion on 1 September 1998. The risk of the development of an asset bubble is not a concern since the improvement in the financial market is being matched by higher activity in the real sector. The 12-month rule on portfolio investment has now lapsed without any large outflows. External reserves therefore remain at almost seven months of import cover. The improvement in equity prices (192% since 1 September 1998), has also not led to higher lending for the purchase of stock and shares (7% of total loans). More new loans are being directed at manufacturing production, which augurs well for the banking system and the Malaysian economy. On the macroeconomic policy front, public sector expenditure is being accelerated to ensure a sustained recovery based on both domestic and export-led growth. Monetary policy in 1999 will continue to be accommodative to support the expansionary fiscal stance. Lending rates have been reduced to below levels prevailing prior to the crisis. Efforts to increase bank lending in support of the economic recovery continues to be the main focus of policy. Efforts are also being taken to ensure that the current bank merger exercise would not affect the availability of adequate funds to investors at reasonable cost. As far as the exchange controls are concerned, Malaysia will continue to implement them in a pragmatic and flexible manner. As conditions stabilised we have replaced the 12-month rule with a repatriation levy in February 1999, aimed at attracting genuine investors while discouraging short-term flows. We envisage that the controls will remain for some time until there is a discernible normalisation of the currency and financial markets domestically and globally, and concrete measures are in place to reform the international financial system. In sum, I would highlight three lessons from the Malaysian experience. The first lesson is that in formulating policy measures to deal with financial crisis, it is important to make an assessment on whether conditions are present to ensure success of policies. The policy response in Asia should have been tailor-made to suit each country?s economic structure and circumstance. Most importantly, the response should have aimed at ensuring that the underlying strength of the real economy can be preserved, so that it can return to the path of recovery. The second and related lesson is that policy prescriptions that work for one problem cannot be replicated as a recipe for success in other situations. Our experience is that policy prescriptions cannot be rigid and inflexible. They have to adapt with changing dynamics, as long as the longer-term objectives are not undermined. The IMF policy prescriptions that may have worked in other countries, such as Mexico, did not work in Malaysia. Exchange controls should always remain one of the policy options, but it should not be a substitute for sound macroeconomic policies. The Malaysian experience has shown that selective and carefully crafted exchange controls, when used to complement conventional macroeconomic policies, can contribute to economic stability. The controls do not imply that Malaysia has disengaged itself from the market system. The third lesson is that countries must take into account the social dimension of any policy response. Malaysia relaxed its fiscal and monetary policy stance and complemented these with selective capital controls to restore stability and mitigate the impact of the crisis on the poorer segments of society. The Malaysian approach to the financial crisis did not include unrelated measures. For example, our policy package did not include measures to remove subsidies on oil and other essential goods, as this would have an adverse impact on the poor. In a crisis, the policy response must be sequenced properly to ensure that it can be absorbed by the market. Overall, our pragmatism in formulating short-term strategies, while remaining focused with single-mindedness on our long-term objectives, and looking beyond textbook economic prescriptions, have served us well in managing the crisis. Towards a new era of regional co-operation in Asia With the benefit of hindsight, it is important to reflect on how Asia could have done things better in crisis prevention and resolution. I certainly believe that there is much that the Asian economies -- individually and as a region -- can do to revitalise Asian economic growth and development. Individually, the pace of economic recovery will depend on the continued pursuit of appropriate macroeconomic policies and structural reforms in each crisis affected country. As a group, I believe that closer Asian economic and financial cooperation is essential to expedite and revitalise the recovery process currently underway. A strong Asia is important as a counter-balance to global developments characterised by the emergence of trading blocs in Europe as well as North America. A global economy based on three growth "poles", like a 3-legged stool, has a better chance of ensuring stability. However, a strong Asia would require a strong lead economy to serve as an "anchor". In Europe, for example, Germany acts as the anchor, while in North America, the lead is taken by the United States. Similarly, a strong and united Asia will need a strong leader. A tri-polar world economy would also imply the emergence of a tripolar exchange rate system. In Europe, we have the Euro; NAFTA has the US dollar. In Asia, unfortunately, we do not have a common currency. To a large extent, Asia's continued reliance on the US dollar for trade and investment arises because the use of the Japanese yen in world trade and payments is not reflective of the relative role of Japan as the second largest economy in the world. Japan's efforts to promote the internationalisation of the yen would likely take time to materialise. To a large extent, the problem arises because the value of the yen is often a fallout of the value of the US dollar. When the US wants a strong dollar, they will insist on a weak yen; conversely, when it is in the US interest to have a weak dollar, the yen will appreciate, often with serious consequences for Japan and Asia. In the past, "soft" yen loans have suddenly become "hard" when the yen appreciated significantly. The development of the yen as an anchor currency for a truly Asian currency will require a break in the US dollar-yen dependency relationship. During the Asian crisis, the region had looked toward Japan to assume a lead role in crisis management and resolution. In this connection, it is encouraging to note that Japan had risen to the occasion. Discussions on the IMF rescue package for Thailand, for example, were first held in Tokyo in August 1997. It was unfortunate that Japan abandoned the Asian Monetary Fund (AMF) proposal. However, subsequently, Japan played its role by providing substantial bilateral support through the Miyazawa Initiative. In many respects, the Miyazawa Initiative bears many similarities to Japan's earlier initiative on the Asian Monetary Fund. Both are quick-disbursing funds to support the Asian recovery process. The size of the Miyazawa Initiative (US30 billion) is similar to Japan's proposed contribution to the AMF (US50 billion). In retrospect, it is interesting to speculate on the likely turn of events in Asia, had the AMF been established in September 1997. Given that the crisis was initially a currency crisis and countries faced liquidity problems, up-front large financial support could have stopped the contagion. The damage caused by the crisis may have been contained. Where the IMF programmes failed, pre-authorised loan commitments under the AMF could have bolstered market confidence and expedited the recovery in Asia. On this score, therefore, it is sad that Japan was not able to withstand pressure from the United States and the IMF, and abandoned the AMF proposal. This underscores the need for a common Asian "voice" in international affairs. The AMF could have become a reality if Asia had been more united in its views. Such a consensus could also have been forged if the proposal the East Asia Economic Caucus (EAEC) had been realised. In the light of the Asian crisis, I believe it is timely to strengthen further closer Asian economic and financial cooperation, based on some combination of the EAEC and the AMF. This will ensure an effective forum for Asian countries to exchange views and resolve issues of common interest. The establishment of an AMF-type financing facility would enhance the effectiveness of such a regional forum, and ensure that it does not become another "talk shop". Such a forum would go a long way towards taking into account Asia's interests and developing self-reliance in managing Asia's economic future. Asia is a vast powerhouse with vast natural resources. It is also home to 3 countries with the highest reserves in the world. The fact that countries in the Asian region are at different levels of development should not be seen as an impediment to closer regional cooperation. We should maximise the synergies that can be tapped by exploiting such differences to complement each other in our drive towards a higher level of economic development. The recent Langkawi International Dialogue spoke of the need for smart partnerships to expedite economic recovery. I believe that through smart partnerships, we can harness the comparative advantages of each country -- be it natural resources, labour, capital or technology. By working together, we can realise a stronger and more resilient Asia in the new millennium. In this connection, it is enlightening to note that the Asian recovery in comparison to the Mexican recovery in 1995. In the case of the Mexican crisis, the recovery was more rapid and "V-shaped". This was because of the strong linkages between Mexico and the U.S. economy, where a booming US economy provided scope to absorb more imports from Mexico and expedited the recovery process. Similarly, a strong Japanese economy is also essential to ensure a rapid recovery in Asia. However, a strong Japanese economy is not enough. More important is for Japan to open up its markets to Asian exports. Here, I believe it is important to bear in mind that we live in an interdependent world. What affects Japan will also affect Asia and vice-versa. In pursuing individual country objectives, it is important that we do not lose sight of the wider implications of our policy actions on our Asian neighbours. Reforms of the international financial architecture Japan, as the only Asian economy in the Group of 7, can play an important role in raising Asia's concerns in terms of efforts to reform the international financial architecture. The need to maintain the momentum for reform is particularly urgent, given the risk of complacency setting in as the recovery gets underway. Given the diverse interests and priorities of different countries, any reform effort must take into consideration the views and concerns of all countries, both big and small. This reform is important as the present international financial system is ill-equipped to cope with the challenges of globalisation. The regulatory framework has not been changed since the 1970s, and has not kept pace with financial innovations and the advances made in IT development. Such innovations have led to quantum leaps in the speed and magnitude of cross-border capital flows, whereby contagion effects of problems in one country quickly spread to others, including those with sound economic fundamentals. This is due to the herding behaviour of market players, where markets tend to over-react to events, with no regard for the underlying economic fundamentals. A major problem with the international financial system is the lack of transparency of the market players. While increased demands are made for governments to be more transparent, it is puzzling that the private sector is not subject to greater transparency requirements, especially since the Asian crisis was caused by private sector excesses. Here, I see a larger role for Japan in ensuring that the International community, notably the G-7 countries adopt a more balanced approach to the issue of transparency. Disclosure by both the public and private sector is equally important. The transparency of the Government needs to be complemented by a mechanism to strengthen surveillance and transparency of private sector market participants. In particular, greater disclosure by offshore financial centres and other large market players is important to ensure that large market players, notably, highly leveraged institutions, do not "corner the market" in small emerging market economies and create destabilising consequences. In addition to extending disclosure requirements to the private sector, we need a global mechanism to supervise the international financial markets as mere disclosure of information cannot guarantee that the destructive volatility of international capital flows would not happen again. Such a global regulator would act in a similar capacity as that of domestic regulatory bodies. Its function should be directed at ensuring an orderly functioning of the international financial markets and at monitoring movements of short-term capital flows. Recent experience had clearly shown that currency manipulators, with their huge leverage funds, were easily able to manipulate and corner financial markets in Asian countries. Thus, measures to inhibit cross-border manipulative activities in financial markets, rules against the cornering of financial markets and appropriate international standards for financial institutions with respect to exposure to hedge funds and other leveraged financial institutions need to be considered and formulated. There should also be a mechanism to make rating agencies more accountable for their actions, particularly when their ratings have a significant adverse impact on a country, more than had been warranted by economic fundamentals. Perhaps, there is merit in reviving an earlier Japanese proposal for a system to rate the rating agencies. Recent experience suggest that rating agencies have failed to make objective assessments, despite being provided with comprehensive and timely information. Although they have access to much information, their analysis remains largely based on perceptions. There should be a more comprehensive framework for the orderly liberalisation of the capital account, with appropriate criteria to serve as guideposts for countries, particularly, emerging market countries. In particular, due consideration should be given to the state of development of the domestic economic and financial sector in relation to the openness and size of the economy before embarking on such liberalisation. The IMF's technical expertise could be directed at helping countries to develop and deepen their own domestic financial markets, as well as criteria and safeguards for capital account liberalisation. The approach should focus on creating incentives for countries to liberalise the domestic financial market rather than using legal powers to promote financial liberalisation. The recent return of stability in regional financial markets and growing signs of economic recovery have raised concern about the risk of complacency, which could derail ongoing efforts to reform the international financial system. In the unlikely event that such concerns are realised and the reform process is delayed or even aborted, Asia in general and Japan in particular would need to respond to protect its national and regional interests. Such a response could take several forms. One possibility would be to strengthen efforts to accelerate regional economic and financial cooperation. As mentioned earlier, the establishment of an Asian Monetary Fund could provide a useful vehicle to strengthen Asian cooperation to deal more effectively with future crises. Japan would of course need to take the lead in such an initiative. The lack of a deep and broad Asian capital market has often been cited as one of the contributory factors in the Asian crisis. Part of the problem lies in the lack of buying interest. Here again, Japan could play a lead role to develop an dynamic Asian bond market so that we can recycle Asian savings for investment within Asia. This would lead to a corresponding reduction in Asia's reliance on and vulnerability to capital flows from outside the region. Conclusion I believe Malaysia's experience in managing the recent crisis holds important lessons not only to policy makers, but also for writers of economic history. There are many dimensions and permutations to traditional macroeconomic management beyond the standard fiscal, monetary and structural policies. The most important lesson, in my mind, is that we should not be afraid to change and try new approaches when the old ways prove to be ineffective. Our approach was unconventional but comprehensive and forward-looking. Despite the initial criticisms, there have been encouraging results in Malaysia, and even the IMF has acknowledged that exchange controls can be useful in specific circumstances. This is Malaysia's contribution towards revitalising the Asian economy. What is most important, however, is the need for stronger support from Japan. Japan needs to assert a stronger leadership role. I believe this would be Japan's most important contribution to a new Asia. A strong Japanese role is essential to a more dynamic and higher level of regional co-operation in Asia. Japan needs to take the next step and stand up for Asia. In particular, Japan must act on the issue to reform of the international financial architecture and ensure that Asia's voice is heard. Through closer economic and financial cooperation, we can revitalise and build a new Asia that can take its rightful place in the global economy. In closing, I would like to share with you an old Malay proverb that says: "Bersatu Teguh; Bercerai Roboh." Loosely translated, it means that when we are united we will be strong; when we are divided, we will fall apart. Bank Negara Malaysia 7 September 1999

Title: Speech at the Malaysian Financial Markets Association Annual Dinner
text: Assistant Governor Dr. Awang Adek's Speech at the Seminar on the Use of the National Language in the Financial Services Industry Presenter: Assistant Governors / Advisers / Venue: Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 09 Sep 1999 / First of all, I would like to thank the organizers who invited me to give a speech at the event today. I would also like to take the opportunity here, on behalf of Bank Negara Malaysia, to congratulate the co-organisers, namely Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka and the Malaysian Insurance Institute, for their efforts in organising a seminar on the use of the National Language in the Financial Industry, within the framework of the National Language Movement of the Private Sector 1996-2000 organised by Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka. As we all know, the sovereignty of the national language has long been enshrined in the National Constitution. But, truly meaningful sovereignty is born only when the National Language is widely used by all walks of life in all sorts of activities in the country. This is a challenge that must be addressed by all parties, necessarily by the Government, and hopefully supported by the private sector. Validity to this exclamation or challenge will only be successful if the acknowledgment and commitment is followed by a stratified plan that can be translated into reality. The culmination was to achieve the basic goal of the National Language as the main language used in Malaysia, in all respects, and to be able to steer Malaysia towards a developed country in the new millennium, which has its own identity. While Bahasa Melayu is ruled as the National Language, the Government has also supported the idea of the use of bilingual, which is Malay with English, as English plays an important role in the economic and political relations of the world. This is a pragmatic strategy to expand and improve the quality of the use of the National Language, without compromising the ability to use English in certain matters, as provided in the National Language Act 1963/67. In connection with the idea of bilingual usage, Bank Negara Malaysia deeply appreciates the close cooperation that exists between Dewan Bahasa and the financial industry to further enhance the use of the National Language in the financial industry. Several important projects have been and are underway. I understand that a total of 29,000 financial terms, covering the areas of investment, insurance, banking and capital markets, are being adjusted and are expected to be fully completed by mid-next year. At the same time, efforts are also underway to translate forms and financial documents into the national language. In total there are 90 forms and documents of use of banks, 84 for financial companies and 34 for insurance companies. The forms and documents for the insurance company have been completed and the insurance policy in Bahasa Kebangsaan has also been completed and launched today. I am confident that with the translation projects undertaken together with the policy and deep commitment to see the wider adoption of the National Language in the financial sector, the success will be more evident to put the financial sector on a par with other sectors of the country in the use of the National Language. Bank Negara Malaysia remains concerned about the goals of the National Language Policy, and will continue to work with the financial industry to ensure that the use of the National Language continues to grow in the future. We do not want to see a group of Malaysians who are unable to obtain adequate and affordable financial services, simply because of the problem of the medium of instruction. After more than 40 years of our country's independence, the question of language as an obstacle in daily affairs should not arise at all. In other words, every client who deals with a financial institution should feel comfortable doing business in the national language if it chooses to do so, and the same comfort should also be felt by the staff of the financial institution involved. This should be our common goal and vision in the financial industry, in particular the banking system. Admittedly, today, there is still much room for us to enhance the use of the National Language in the financial sector. The shortage in the past is certainly due to various factors including historical factors, where the involvement of the Malays and The Bumiputeras in the financial sector in the past is somewhat lacking. As we all know, banking institutions began to exist in the homeland when the country was under colonization. It began with the establishment of Chartered Mercantile Bank in 1859. Since banks in the pre-independence era were dominated by foreign-owned banks, then the main language used was English. The development of local banks began with the establishment of Kwong Yik (Selangor) Banking Corporation in 1913 by Chinese traders. After that, several more banks were successfully established by local Chinese traders to meet the needs of the merchant community at that time. In such an atmosphere, Bahasa Melayu is certainly not used as a language of communication in local banking institutions. When the country declared independence in 1957 and Bank Negara Malaya was established in 1959, it was not until the locally owned banks boomed and the use of the Malay language began to gain attention. However, the Malay language still faces stiff competition from English which is the language of finance and world trade to this day. In any case, the twists and turns of history should not be used as an excuse for us to underestimate the efforts to expand the use of the National Language in the financial sector. Since 1959, Bank Negara Malaysia has issued its Annual Report and Quarterly Report in Malay (other than in English) for reference to those who are more likely to read in Malay. When Bank Negara Malaysia took over the regulation of the insurance sector in 1988, the Insurance Annual Report was issued in bilingual and the practice continues to this day. Apart from the Malay language, indirectly, this effort has refuted the opinion of some who doubt the ability of the Malay language as a trading and financial language, and the opinion that the Malay terms in economics and finance are less complete and diminished. Bank Negara's efforts are in support of the efforts of Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka which has published many books and dictionaries in the field of trade and finance for general reference. Since 1996, various efforts have been stepped up towards the use of the National Language. Since that year, Bank Negara Malaysia began to use the National language widely in its correspondence, except in dealings with foreigners abroad. In fact, letters received in English are often also replied to in Malay. This has had a positive effect when most banking institutions and other parties also use the national language more widely in correspondence with Bank Negara Malaysia. Indeed, Bank Negara Malaysia is committed to seeing the adoption of the national language grow rapidly in all banking institutions, and has issued a circular to financial institutions in 1996 to encourage the use of the National language by the financial industry. Bank Negara Malaysia is proud to see that most financial institutions have successfully improved the use of the national language, as well as other languages, in the aspect of documentation involving customers, such as forms and financial documents. The Central Bank has also asked financial institutions including insurance, to communicate in writing with customers who use the national language, in the same language. Bank Negara Malaysia would like to congratulate the insurance industry on the seriousness of the insurance industry, the Malaysian Insurance Institute, which has successfully carried out several important activities towards improving the use of the national language. Among them are as follows:- Organize a Web page for the Indonesian Instalment Directory (in collaboration with the Indonesian authorities), as well as provide Interactive Motor Insurance Guide and Insurance Glossary. Conduct courses and seminars in the national language, such as (i) Life Insurance Marketing Course and (ii) Private Insurance Certificate and insurance Marketing diploma. In addition, since October 1997 until now, no fewer than 16 seminars related to insurance matters and two specialized seminars on the use of the national language have been held. The Insurance Institute of Malaysia has also issued 4 textbooks for insurance exams in the national language. At the same time, the insurance industry as a whole has been able to use the national language in correspondence with the public. Correspondence received in the national language is certainly reciprocated in the national language. Certificates, insurance policies, proposal and claim forms, as well as other frequently used documents have been completed in the National language, and this version has already been given priority. The use of national language on non-standard documents and complex policy contracts, in turn, can be made based on the customer's wishes and preferences whether to use the National Language or English. Therefore, I would like to once again express my deepest appreciation for the efforts of the insurance industry. It is hoped that such efforts will continue and increase over time, and will encourage other institutions in the financial sector to achieve similar success. In conjunction with the emergence of the new millennium, efforts towards promoting the use of the National Language in local financial institutions should be intensified. The Association of Banks in Malaysia (ABM), the Association of Financial Companies Malaysia (AFCM), the General Insurance Association of Malaysia (PIAM) and the Life Insurance Association of Malaysia (LIAM), as well as other relevant bodies, are urged to play a more active role in encouraging their members to prioritise the use of the national language. The management of all banking institutions and financial companies should be an example to their subordinates, as well as to provide appropriate encouragement to ensure that the national language is used more widely in their respective institutions. Strictly speaking, all parties need to appreciate the objective of the implementation of the national language in a deeper manner, to ensure that the desire to expand the use of the National language in financial institutions can be realized faster and more effectively. Bank Negara Malaysia will continue to review and monitor the developments and achievements of banking institutions and insurance companies in the use of the National Language in the future. I would like to thank the parties involved including Dewan Bahasa for successfully conducting a comprehensive survey on the status of the use of the national language in the financial sector in 1995, which has provided a lot of useful feedback to Bank Negara. I hope that this noble endeavour can be continued in the future so that the progress of the financial sector in the use of the national language can be evaluated and enhanced from time to time. Hopefully, with the efforts and cooperation of all parties, the implementation of the use of the national language in the daily affairs of banking institutions will become more meaningful, thus meeting the tastes of consumers and meeting the goals of the National Policy. Finally, I once again congratulate the organizers for successfully organising the National Language Usage Seminar in the Financial Services Industry today. Bank Negara Malaysia 9 September 1999

Title: Closing Speech at Sarawak Financial Carnival
text: Assistant Governor Datuk Zamani Abdul Ghani's Speech at the Launch of the "Premium-Link" Website for the Insurance Industry Speaker: Assistant Governors / Advisers Speech/Interview Date: 19 Oct 1999 Venue: Hotel Istana, Kuala Lumpur Language: English I am honoured to have been invited to share in this historic moment for the Malaysian insurance industry. Today, we witness yet another milestone in the industry ? the official launch of Premium-Link?, the industry?s first step towards cyber-insurance. This event is significant because it paves the way for the development of electronic commerce or e-commerce using internet technology in the insurance sector. Let me first of all take this opportunity to extend my heartiest congratulations to Berjaya General Insurance Berhad, Capital Insurance Berhad, MBf Insurance Berhad, PanGlobal Insurance Berhad, RHB Insurance Berhad and Syarikat Takaful Malaysia Berhad for successfully pioneering the implementation of the Premium-Link Website?. I understand that Premium-Link? will enable policy owners to retrieve information on their motor insurance policies and renew their policies through an interactive internet website. We in Bank Negara Malaysia are happy to note that the participating insurers have obtained access to the MEPS payment gateway, which will enable policy owners to pay their motor insurance premiums electronically over the internet using their credit cards. This is quite a revolutionary development and certainly one to be commended considering the relative infancy of e-commerce activity in Malaysia?s financial services sector. When man first ventured into space, the small step taken by man proved to be a giant step for mankind. In the same way, there is no doubt in my mind that this small but, important step taken by the industry into cyberspace will have enormous implications for the future of the insurance industry. It is a given certainty that e-commerce will radically transform the way business is done in the 21 st century. A U.S. study estimates that over USD200 billion worth of business will be transacted over the internet by the end of next year. There are now more than 8,000 insurance-related websites, and the number is growing exponentially. However, in insurance markets, fully interactive e-commerce remains largely untapped with only 4% of insurers worldwide actually closing direct sales over the internet. In Malaysia, only about half of the licensed insurers have set up information with non-interactive websites on the internet. As it is, we still have a long way to go. As we enter the 21 st century, the insurance industry in Malaysia must prepare itself for the transition into a new business era. History tells us that irrespective of how unprepared or resistant we may be, it is not possible to hold back innovation. To try would only be to our own detriment. Significant technological advances have enabled us to leverage our limited resources into creating greater value-added output. This is true for all industries. The technological revolution will redefine how an organisation is structured, how transactions are executed, and how products are designed, made and distributed. If we do not move with the wheels of progress, we risk fading into obsolescence. At the heart of the technological revolution and e-commerce is the internet. The internet is now as commonplace as the television. An increasing proportion of households are now linked to the net. So, ladies and gentlemen, therein lies its greatest attraction to competitive business. The internet enables insurers to expand their marketing potential in ways previously not possible or economically feasible. Studies in the United States show that marketing through the internet can bring distribution costs down from as high as 139% incurred using traditional distribution channels such as the agency force, to as low as 15% using the internet. It has also made more focussed marketing strategies possible through applications like web-farming. Operationally, internet technology offers tremendous possibilities for insurers to improve their productivity and efficiency. For the policy owner, this translates into lower premiums, better returns and policy benefits and a higher level of customer service. Internet technology also offers the customers the convenience to conduct business transactions through the internet during all the 24 hours of a day and 7 days a week, and all from the comfort of their homes. The growth of electronic communication will also spawn new business opportunities for insurers, including the offer of insurance protection for IT-related risks. Our efforts should be directed at adapting our businesses to technological advancements, not avoiding them. In this spirit, the Government has given its full support to promoting e-commerce in Malaysia. At the National level, the Government had established in 1998, the National Electronic Commerce Committee chaired by the Chief Secretary of the Government to provide strategic governance of e-commerce and set the direction for the development of e-commerce in Malaysia. Two subcommittees, namely the Infrastructure Committee headed by the Ministry of Energy, Communications and Multimedia, and the Trade and Finance Committee led by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry have also been set-up under the main committee to address more specific issues to foster an orderly development of e-commerce in the country. One of the outputs of the NECC is the formulation of a Electronic Commerce Masterplan for Malaysia, which is currently being finalised. The objective of the Masterplan is to provide a comprehensive and strategic framework for action to accelerate the development of e-commerce in Malaysia. The Masterplan will identify key initiatives aimed at spurring e-commerce activity in Malaysian business. Eight pillars of competitiveness have been identified to drive e-commerce activities. These are innovation, content, intellectual property protection, distribution, market access, brand identity, trusted service interfaces and quality products and services. Given that the credit card is presently the most common payment mechanism for Internet purchases, MEPS has been entrusted to develop a payment gateway to undertake domestic e-commerce payment transactions based on the SET (Secured Electronic Transactions) protocol. SET protocol provides a more promising solution in terms of security, as the information pertaining to the credit cards will not be transmitted over the network. Instead, through SET, the identity of the cardholder is identified based on the digital certificate. Nevertheless, SET technology is still new and not many of the Internet subscribers have SET certificates. Hence, to support the development of e-commerce, we have at present allowed the usage of the SSL (Security Socket Layer) protocol to co-exist with SET. This will provide the market with a ready pool of potential users and at the same time enable the users to benefit from the availability of both protocols. Since its nationwide implementation on 22 March 1999, to date, there are 170 merchants acquired by the four participating banks in the payment gateway. In addition, a total of 3,500 e-wallets (digital certificates) were issued free to cardholders. In terms of value, a total of RM8.25 million in payments have been effected. On its part, Bank Negara Malaysia is also committed in encouraging the development of e-commerce in the financial services sector. Insurers are already freely allowed to establish electronic terminals at the premises of their intermediaries to facilitate business transactions and information flows over the internet. The Premium-Link website brings us another step closer to the creation of a full range of on-line financial services. At the moment, the system accommodates only payments made using credit cards. This will only be a temporary limitation. The Malaysian Electronic Payment System is already in the course of developing alternative payment mechanisms for internet transactions. For example, the MEPS Cash electronic purse and direct debit facilities are expected to be ready for implementation as early as next year. The extension of payment modes for internet transactions will no doubt further advance the usage of Premium-Link and other electronic applications in the insurance industry. Today?s launching of Premium-Link is also timely as I understand that the insurance industry and MEPS are fully Y2K ready. As such, transactions through this interactive internet website can be expected to take place without any Y2K glitches. Bank Negara will continue to support e-commerce developments in the insurance sector. However, as the industry progresses in this direction, I would caution you to keep sight of the crucial importance of security. Public acceptance of, and confidence in, e-commerce depend on it. Security should be a priority in any e-commerce initiative. It cannot be less in insurance, which is a business built on trust. It is imperative that the confidentiality of personal policy owner information and the authenticity of internet transactions are safeguarded vigilantly through adequate security features. The Premium-Link system presents a foretaste of the new business era that awaits us. A system like this must now permeate and spread throughout the insurance industry. We must now ensure a general availability of such a system in the general insurance sector. In addition, such a system should form the lifeblood of the life insurance sector. We must continue to move forward towards these targets. While the Premium-Link shows us how far the industry has come, the endless possibilities and potential of e-commerce show us how far more we can advance. So let this be just a beginning as we continue, with the aid of technology, to strive towards building an industry that is truly dynamic and always relevant. On that note, it gives me great pleasure to launch the Premium-Link Website. Bank Negara Malaysia 19 October 1999

Title: Speech on the Release of a Joint BNM-Securities Commission Publication on Y2K
text: Governor Tan Sri Ali Abul Hassan's Opening Speech at the Bankers National Conference 1999 Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 23 Nov 1999 Venue: Universiti Teknologi MARA, Shah Alam Language: English It gives me great pleasure to be here this afternoon to share my thoughts with you on current issues on banking and the economy and to declare open the Bankers National Conference 1999. Although I can't recall the number of times I have been asked to speak on the subject since the outbreak of the Asian financial crisis, I could not resist this opportunity to address this issue once again. Much has been said about the Asian financial crisis that has changed the life of many Malaysians in the past couple of years. The Asian Financial Crisis The onset of the Asian financial crisis in July 1997 was both unexpected and unprecedented. It caught many countries unprepared and tested severely the effectiveness of some multilateral institutions entrusted with the role to preserve global financial stability. The crisis exposed the new forces of instability in the world economy which no individual countries can withstand alone, pushing each country deeper into the crisis and some into rapid impoverishment. The devastating consequences of the crisis on the socio-economic structure of many Asian countries are now quite clear, and many are still grappling with the aftermath. While Malaysia was not the worst affected, the country still experienced the most difficult period in its history of macroeconomic management. The extreme economic conditions, which persisted following the crisis, had caused the country to ultimately adopt unconventional policy measures to keep the economy afloat and its social fabrics intact. What Caused the Crisis? I presume some of you have had the opportunity to attend forums or seminars of this nature recently, or read the recent literature, and have been well exposed to this subject, specifically with regard to the underlying reasons that sparked the financial crisis. For the benefit of those who have not been adequately informed on this matter, let me summarise some of the views. Innitially, two schools of thought dominate the debate. The first school states that Asia's economic miracle was built on poor economic fundamentals. Proponents of this school argued that Asia's healthy macroeconomic indicators ? low level of non-performing loans, low inflation, fiscal balance, low stock of government debt, high rates of domestic saving and investments ? painted a misleading picture. They pointed out that warning signals existed, but went unheeded. They quoted that weak financial regulation, lax and inexperienced supervision, low capital adequacy ratios and sometimes outright corruption all rendered the region's financial systems weaker than they appeared. The second school of thought views the self-fulfilling pessimism of international lenders as the root cause of the crisis. It argues that Asia fell victim to a financial panic similar to a classic bank run. While the central bank normally intervenes in the case of a classic bank run by acting as a lender of last resort and providing liquidity to the market, there was no such mechanism to stem the panic in the Asian financial crisis. The result is a massive outflow of capital that triggered an economic crisis bigger than any previous setback in the history of Southeast Asian development since World War II. My own feel is that the truth lies somewhere in between and somewhat closer to the second view. While the ruthless currency speculators were at work to devalue the currencies of the affected Asian countries, there were some structural weaknesses in the banking sector in the affected countries that need to be rectified. The Malaysian banking sector remains fragmented and extremely vulnerable to external shocks. As the Asian financial crisis unfolded, the failure to consolidate and rationalize the domestic banking sector came back to haunt us. In moving forward, concrete steps should be taken to remove this source of weakness in the banking sector. Consolidation of the Banking Sector The Malaysian banking system has always been characterised by a large number of small financial institutions. As small financial institutions are allowed to compete with the big ones, the former are often driven by instincts to survive in the short term by undercutting competitors in an unsustainable way, which can ultimately weaken presently sound financial institutions. Excess capacity (too many banking institutions chasing too few good business opportunities) leads to inadequate returns, encouraging banking institutions to take greater risks in order to generate income and revenue. Indeed, some of the smaller financial institutions were barely profitable. A financial institution with insufficient earnings may have to use deposits to cover its operating expenses, thereby distorting its role as an intermediary and decreasing its networth. If something is not done to rectify these weaknesses, problems are simply postponed, and an even larger crisis is likely to occur in the future. The above helps explain why we are much more focused this time in pursuing the merger program for the banking sector. With these factors, coupled with increased globalization of the financial system and threat of increased competition from the much bigger and sophisticated foreign players in the near future, time is simply not on our side. With the long term survival and prosperity of the domestic financial institutions at stake, we believe that there has been a general consensus for us to develop a more resilient and sophisticated banking sector in Malaysia. The envisaged banking sector must be one that can withstand future external shocks and challenges. Globalisation of the Financial System In the past two decades, we have witnessed the transformation of the world's financial markets from relatively isolated and regulated national markets into a more global integrated market. This was brought about by a mutually reinforcing process of advances in communication, computer-based technologies, and information and financial instruments; and by progressive internal and external deregulation of financial markets. The new technologies and the emergence of more diversified financial instruments have strengthened the interdependence between markets both within and beyond national boundaries. Malaysia too will be under pressure has to open its doors to global competition. Integrated global financial markets transmit financial contagion almost instantaneously around the world. Long distance trading relationships make the impact of devaluation in one part of the world quickly felt elsewhere. In other words, with integration of financial markets globally, the incidence of currency crisis will probably increase in the future. Unfortunately, hitherto, there is yet no mechanism to thwart a similar currency crisis. The establishment of an Asian Monetary Fund has been suggested to play the role of an international lender of last resort, but there have only been mute attempt to regulate the hedge funds and currency speculators, the scourge of our current predicament. With regard to this issue, Malaysia has done its best, and will continue to do so, to promote the introduction of some form of controls against the hedge funds and currency speculators and are awaiting further development on this issue on the international front with keen interest. Globalisation also means capital mobility that transcends national boundaries. Theoretically at least, this may lead to greater dynamic efficiency as the domestic financial sector is forced to become more efficient and innovative in response to import competition from foreign capital. As the financial services industry and financial markets became more globally integrated, the most efficient and organised banking institution will prevail. Again, it drives home the point that the domestic banking institutions in Malaysia must gear themselves to operate in a much more competitive environment in the new millennium. Role of Bankers Banking institutions in Malaysia may have learnt valuable lessons from the recent crisis. Some of them saw, at first hand, how their capital and earnings had suffered due to maturity mismatches when interest rates move in the wrong direction. Others had to bear the brunt of anger from certain quarters due to their inability to satisfy the business community's desire for credit accommodation at the time when they need it most at the height of the crisis. Some had pursued, before the crisis, a strategy of over reliance on inter-bank borrowings to fund a rapid expansion in loans that only worsened their problems during the crisis, in an already tight liquidity situation. The easy availability of credit fuelled investment in increasingly risky assets. In any case, I hope everybody has learnt well from his own past mistakes, as well as the mistakes of others, so that we can all be better bankers in the new millennium. We have to as we can expect bigger challenges ahead. If all goes well, at the end of the on-going consolidation exercise, the domestic banking institutions in Malaysia, though smaller in number, are expected to be much bigger and better capitalised. Large capital provides a buffer for temporary losses. It absorbs these losses until profitability is restored. But capital adequacy alone is a poor test of the banking institution's resilience as one big loss can erode capital quickly. My view is that, capital, at best, is no substitute for improving overall risk management capabilities as well as operational efficiency. Today's bankers need to acquire all the refined skills of a top class banker in order to survive and prosper in the long run. For the younger audience out there, including the students sitting in this hall, who harbour some thoughts of making an entry into the banking sector as new players, I hope the traumatic experience faced by the industry during the recent crisis does not deter them. The industry certainly needs to attract the brightest brains in the country who are honest and prepared to work hard to propel the industry to greater heights in the future. However, I wish to remind the prospective young bankers that there is no short cut to success. The learning process has to be a long one. In fact, the best education comes not from the classroom or by reading textbooks on finance but from adversity. No lending officer is fully trained until he has been through a full business cycle and seen what happens to perfectly fine balance sheets as the economic environment deteriorates. Lending is a risky business. It should be. As the saying goes, it only takes five minutes to train a lending officer. But it takes a couple of years to train him so the bank can get the money back. The loan officer who makes no loans that turn sour is probably not doing his job adequately. Conversely, a loan officer who makes too many bad loans is in an even worse problem. The banker's goal is to achieve the proper balance ? to manage the risks, to serve the banking institution's community of customers and to contribute to a healthy bottom line. With increased globalisation of financial markets and the expected greater competition in the new millennium, banking institutions will have to step up efforts in preserving their safety and soundness. Topping their agenda has to be the need to develop an adequate regime of in-house surveillance and a proper system of risk management and internal controls. It is often the case that, by conscious or unconscious awareness, bank management tends to overlook activities of traders who seem to bring big profits to the bank. If any lesson is clear in the business failures seen in recent years, it is that one person can make or break an organization. The lack of internal control lies at the root of financial disasters such as the collapse of Barings (where the same trader had control over both trading and settlement activities) or the Daiwa affair. Strict supervisory regulation is, therefore, vital to ensure that all risks are managed prudently. Role of Supervisors Now I wish to turn my attention to the role played by BNM over the years and in the new millennium. BNM has also learnt a great deal from the rapid turns of events over the last two decades. With the painful, yet beneficial, experience of coping with the crises of the mid-80s and 1997-98, we will leave no stones unturned in ensuring that the banking institutions in Malaysia remain financially sound regardless of the phase of the business cycle. An important lesson to remember is that in the event of a financial crisis, there is a need to ensure minimal disruption in the intermediation function. There is a growing realisation that the purpose of bank supervision is not only to protect public savings, but also to safeguard the stability of the banking system and to help prevent disruptions in the access of credit by economic agents. Nevertheless, BNM will continue to be guided by the principle that the reputation of an international financial market place will largely rest on the quality and adequacy of its regulation and supervision. Banking institutions can expect increasingly tougher and more frequent inspections over the next decade. Although the specific purposes of BNM's regulatory role are to ensure the safety and soundness of the financial system, the ultimate goal is to safeguard confidence in the banking system. The ultimate foundation of the banking system is confidence and when that confidence is eroded for whatever reason, banks face financial difficulty. BNM's role as the lender of last resort will help to avert systemic risk. This role is critical. In a worst case scenario, a financially solvent bank faced with a run will realise assets to raise cash to honour its liability obligations. The danger is that once the bank has sold its liquid assets, it will start selling its illiquid assets at a loss value or "fire-sale" price. In this scenario, a situation of tight liquidity can quickly turn into insolvency. Apart from the potential systemic risk, the huge difference between the "going concern" value and the liquidation value helps to explain why bank runs are costly and BNM's intervention is deemed necessary. Nevertheless, we are currently conducting a study on the viability of a deposit insurance scheme in the country. Such a scheme would discourage runs on banking institutions although it gives rise to the moral hazard of encouraging institutions to take on more risk. We will weigh the benefits of this proposal carefully against its weaknesses before arriving at a decision. Capital Controls Let me now turn to the issue of capital controls. Prior to the Asian financial crisis, Malaysia has been one of the most open economies in the region. This policy has enabled the country to reap the benefits of free capital movements. Notably, the steady flows of foreign direct investments into the country had brought immense benefits in terms of additional source of capital, imported managerial skills and technology transfers. However, it also brings in short-term capital flows. Following the crisis, the flood of short-term capital, seen as a sign of Asian success when it flowed into these economies in abundance, has been reversed. As evident in the recent crisis, capital flight can wreak havoc, and revolutionary changes in information technology mean that capital can exit at lightning speed. Defending the currency required maintaining relatively high interest rates, but that worsened the financial condition of banks and firms. Against this backdrop, Malaysia introduced the selective exchange controls approximately 14 months ago in September 1998. When Malaysia introduced selective controls in September 1998, it was viewed as a step back into the dark ages. Not surprisingly, the world reverberated at Malaysia. They pointed out that capital controls are undesirable from a global perspective because they create market fragmentation, thereby frustrating the integration of the global trading and financial systems. They added that capital controls are also undesirable from an individual country perspective because they create new distortions in the economic system, which may reduce growth. However, they also admitted the fact that capital controls have created a stable and conducive environment for economic recovery in the country. Above all, the country has not lost its independence, unlike a few countries that resorted to the International Monetary Fund's financial assistance program. We envisage that the capital controls will remain for some time until there is a discernible normalisation of the currency and financial markets domestically and globally, and concrete measures are in place to reform the international financial system. In conclusion, I wish to thank all the players, including the banking institutions, who have directly or indirectly contributed towards the country's economic recovery process. Although the economic downturn has bottomed out and attention has shifted from immediate crisis management to accelerating recovery, much remains to be done. Basically, what I meant to say is that the first few years in the new millennium would be one of the most critical periods in the history of the development of the country's banking system. What we do or fail to do in the aftermath of the crisis may determine the manner in which the current and future generations would judge us as to what extent we have learnt from the crisis and whether we have made the appropriate policy responses. Towards this end, Bank Negara Malaysia has initiated efforts to map out a comprehensive Master Plan for the country's banking sector which, it is hoped, by the end of the day would propel the sector into world class status over the next decade. Nevertheless, it is still premature to reveal more details about the Master Plan, as work has only just begun. All I can say is that we are very committed and serious about making the appropriate changes in the banking sector for the benefit of current and future generations of Malaysians. Your understanding, co-operation and contribution in the course of the next few years would be critical to make our mission a success. On that note, I would like to end this session and declare open this Bankers National Conference 1999. I wish to congratulate the Faculty of Business and Management, University Teknologi MARA for successfully organizing this Conference. Enjoy the rest of the seminar and thank you for your attention. Bank Negara Malaysia 23 November 1999

Title: Keynote Address at the IBBM Chief Internal Auditors Networking Group's (CIANG) Third Annual Conference on "Risk Management and the Internal Auditor"
text: Governor's Opening Address at the Malaysian Insurance Institute Seminar on Human Resource and Management Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 07 Dec 1999 Venue: Shangri-La Hotel, Kuala Lumpur Language: English Terlebih dahulu izinkan saya mengucapkan terima kasih kepada MII kerana sudi menjemput saya untuk merasmikan Seminar bertajuk "Human Resource and Management" dan melancarkan tiga buah buku yang diterbitkan oleh MII. This Seminar is both timely and relevant. As we progress towards the next millennium, human capital will certainly be a key driver and critical determinant to the success of an organisation. I am reminded of a friend who told me his organisation was in a mess, because the Human Resource Department was neither humane nor resourceful! I am also told that people who work in the human resource department must have tact ? and tact is defined as the ability to tell a person to go to hell in such a way that the person will enjoy the journey! We are indeed fortunate to be approaching the turn of the century on a firm footing. The strong rebound of the Malaysian economy in the third quarter of 1999 confirms that the economy has recovered and is officially out of recession. The Malaysian economy grew by 8.1% in the third quarter of this year, the highest growth rate since the onset of the economic crisis in 1997. This remarkable growth reflects the Government's commitment to turn around the economy. It also proves that high and sustainable economic growth Malaysia enjoyed prior to the 1997 crisis is within reach if we Malaysians put on our thinking caps and pull our resources together. With the economy back on the recovery track, I believe that the prospect for long term growth is bright and I am positive that all sectors, including the insurance sector, are gearing towards better performance in the near future. This recovery was also evident in the insurance industry, whereby, total premium income of the industry had increased by 1.6% in the first nine months of 1999, compared with a decline of 8.4 % for the corresponding period in 1998. The economy has improved ? yes ? but we cannot afford to be complacent. There is much work yet to be done. It is crucial that we capitalise on the growth momentum achieved and use the opportunity provided to reinforce the basic foundation for future growth. The development of human capital will be critical in establishing that foundation. In a knowledge-based era, human capital will determine the prospect and extent of our future achievement. The importance of efficient and productive human capital alongside with other external drivers of change, namely globalisation, liberalisation and technological advancements, must not be underestimated. These change agents are, without doubt, the propellers and pace-setters of the economic growth in the next millennium. The degree of success in managing our economy and our ability to attain continued economic growth will hinge on effective management of human capital. As such, it needs no further emphasis that human resource development and management must be given top priority by top management. It is of utmost importance for business concerns to ensure that their human resources are managed effectively and optimised for future growth. I would like to stress here that investment in people must not take a back seat under the guise of being prudent in spending. Such investment is crucial and must continue to be at the forefront of management's attention. The difference between a successful organisation and those not so successful lies with the management's priority to develop its human resources. Those who continue to give top priority to the development of their human resources in good or bad times, are likely to be more successful in the long term than those who do not. An unwavering commitment to staff welfare and development will reap rewards in securing staff loyalty and their undivided commitment to corporate objectives. This will pave the way to higher levels of achievement for any organisation. To be successful, an organisation should be much more than a sum total of dedicated and committed individuals working together to achieve common goals for the benefit of all. In a rapidly evolving industry such as the insurance industry, responsiveness to customer needs is a crucial test of the insurance company's survival. With increasing sophistication of needs and higher expectations, there is an urgency for insurance companies to set competitive strategies leading to product innovation, organisational capability and creation of a pool of highly skilled and knowledgeable workforce. The lack of expertise currently hampering the development of the local insurance industry should be a thing of the past in the next millennium. Malaysian insurers should be self-reliant in terms of technical expertise, especially in underwriting large and complex risks. For the Malaysian insurance industry to thrive and stay ahead amidst an increasingly challenging environment, the Malaysian insurers need to be at the forefront, backed by a corps of experts or specialists in their own field who would stand as pillars supporting the organisation. To acquire the necessary skills, we must in the interim be open to acquiring knowledge and expertise even from outside the country. Bank Negara Malaysia has played its role by adopting a flexible policy on the employment of foreign experts by insurers in Malaysia. It is up to the personnel in the insurance industry to take advantage of this opportunity to learn as much as possible from their more knowledgeable foreign counterparts. While this approach is being pursued, parallel efforts must be made to identify and bridge gaps in the insurance sector's manpower requirements. On this aspect, the insurance industry together with MII, has an important role to play in building a pool of qualified local experts capable of leading the industry forward. I am glad to note that steps in this direction are being taken with the setting up of recognised courses and lectures as well as the publication of several books in collaboration with the industry and MII. Bank Negara Malaysia welcomes such initiatives from practitioners in the insurance industry. With the economic recession now behind us, insurers should refocus their attention on the other pressing issues confronting them. Top on their list should be to consolidate and position themselves for a more liberalised market, as pressure for us to open our market is expected to be increased. Towards this end, we hope to see more insurers engaging in the merger and acquisition exercise currently being promoted in the insurance industry. As to four insurers which have recently completed their M & A programme, I believe they are in the midst of integrating their operations. The post-merger integration exercise need to be managed well to avoid uncertainty and anxiety among employees owing to different corporate background, values, culture, vision and goals of the merging entities. Admittedly, the people issue in a post-integration exercise is a sticky one, but as with all other things, adversities can be minimised if it is well-managed. The fact that many entities have experienced a quantum leap in their turnover following their integration, proves that the human resource issue in a M & A can be successfully resolved. Although I am no expert in this field, I am inclined to think that the timely execution of a well-planned integration process and good communication of the plan to all levels of staff in the company, from an early stage, will go a long way in securing its success. Much therefore lies with the company and its human resource department in taking a more proactive and responsive approach in managing the people issue in a M & A.
