The role of the human resource department cannot be over emphasised in maintaining staff harmony and level of productivity in the merged entity, as it copes with what can be destabilising effects arising from a change in management. Work processes will need to be streamlined, duplication removed and approaches reconfigured, as the company strives to achieve a higher level of competitiveness, in line with its new or redefined mission and vision. Changes of such scale draw a range of reactions from acceptance to scepticism and resistance. However, most staff, with the proper approach taken by the management to handle the problem, will eventually accept changes and the stimulation and improvement they represent. On the other hand, changes are bound to fail when employees lose faith in those changes, sometimes due purely to miscommunication and misunderstanding. It is therefore imperative that the management manages the situation well, by providing the appropriate motivation and maintaining the morale of the employees, while at the same time, propelling them into accepting the changes implemented. Failure to do so will indeed prove costly, not only to the company and its management, but also to its shareholders, as business disruptions set in and profit margins get eroded. I am pleased to note that one session at this seminar has been dedicated to discussions on corporate governance. It is my firm belief that an effective human resource and management system must promote good corporate governance. From a company's perspective, corporate governance is simply the systems and processes by which a company achieves its objectives. That is just corporate strategy. But as many of you know, the significance of corporate governance extends far beyond that. Corporate governance is also about protecting the rights of investors, creditors, depositors and policyholders ? the right of those who do not have direct control or influence over how a company is managed and therefore, may not be in a position to secure the protection of their own rights. In this sense, corporate governance is about corporate responsibility. Effective human resource management is central to any corporate governance system. While processes and structures can, to some extent, mitigate conflicts and increase transparency, the human factor remains the most crucial component of good corporate governance. The ingenuity of man cannot be underestimated. As the old saying goes, where there is a will, there is a way. Given the right openings and opportunities, man will find a way to overcome even the best controls. Under these circumstances, the integrity of your personnel and management will determine the integrity of your operations. This is where human resource management comes into play. Your policies on recruitment, training, job allocation, and remuneration will all have a direct impact on corporate governance in your organisation. In line with the Government's efforts to nurture good governance practices in the corporate sector, Bank Negara is formulating a prudential framework of good corporate governance for the insurance industry. The framework will embody the principles and best practices dealing with the duties and responsibilities of directors as set out in the Malaysian Code of Corporate Governance. In addition to this, the framework will establish basic principles of good corporate governance in other key organisational aspects of insurance operations including management accountability, corporate independence, internal controls and operational risk management, public accountability, and financial and management reporting. In a service-based industry such as finance and insurance, your organisation will be known by its people. That is a reality which we cannot escape. It is therefore important that human resource strategies are developed towards achieving a professional, competent, honest and responsible work force -people who are able to uphold best practices of good corporate governance. Good corporate governance will not only uphold the image of our own organisations and the industry which we represent; more than that, every well-governed institution will add another brick in the wall to support a sound and stable economy. On this note, ladies and gentlemen, it is my great pleasure to declare open the MII Seminar on "Human Resource and Management". I am sure your participation in this Seminar will be both useful and rewarding. I also hope that your active deliberations with the distinguished speakers and fellow participants will provide fresh insights into the critical issues and challenges facing the financial services and its implications. I am also happy to launch three MII publications, namely: M & A in the Financial Services Industry Focusing on Insurance and Banking - Corporate Governance; and An Overview of the Insurance for Large Onshore Construction Projects. I wish this Seminar a great success and all of you a rewarding experience. Bank Negara Malaysia 7 December 1999

Title: Speech at the Launch of the Joint Report on Nature-Related Financial Risks in Malaysia
text: Deputy Governor Dato' Dr. Zeti's Speech at the Young Malay Professionals Congress 2000 - "Globalisation and Open Market - Challenges for Bumiputera Entrepreneurs" Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Putra World Trade Centre, Kuala Lumpur Speech/Interview Date: 26 Feb 2000 Language: English I. INTRODUCTION The world in which we live in is being subject to constant waves of change that is dramatically altering the economic and financial landscape in which we operate. As we go forward, this pace of change can be expected to intensify. To prosper in this ever changing environment, there needs to be an awareness and an understanding of the nature of these changes and its radical implications and consequences. Survival in this modern economy will require new approaches and strategies. In this new environment, previous approaches that have brought success have become no longer relevant. It will now take much more than incremental improvements to produce the desired results. It will require radically different ways of doing things. If the progress that has been achieved by the Bumiputra entrepreneurs so far is considered to be less than satisfactory, it can be expected that as we go forward in an increasingly more challenging economic and financial environment, it will become even more difficult to succeed. Staying ahead and surviving involves pursuing strategies that aims to secure durability and sustainability over the longer term. Entrepreneurs that have caught a wave and prospered on a short-term business trend without developing capabilities and competitive positions will risk the future of their business as the wave subsides. For the Bumiputra entrepreneurs to remain resilient and competitive over the long term, it is important to understand the effects of the powerful force of these waves of change that are constantly shifting and reshaping the economic and financial landscape. This needs to be supported by efforts directed at continuously building the capacity and capability not only to deal with the emerging risks but more importantly, to become well placed to take advantage of the opportunities presented by the new environment. The first part of this paper will discuss the fundamental changes that are shaping the new economic order. The following section will highlight the implications of these changes and the challenges it presents, in particular, to the bumiputra entrepreneurs. It is hoped that this will form a basis for discussion that could contribute towards the formulation of resolutions planned for adoption at the conclusion of this congress. Essentially, the task ahead is to develop a dynamic generation of bumiputra entrepreneurs that are equipped for long term performance, that are able to be matched against global standards and that are able to prosper in the modern economy. II. WAVES OF CHANGE SHAPING THE ENVIRONMENT This section attempts to bring into perspective three fundamental forces that are shaping the business world in which we operate. Virtually all business at some point will need to address the challenges brought about by the advancement in technology, the process of globalisation and the trend towards a more knowledge-based economy. Technological advancements have within a short period of time produced the most far reaching changes on the modern economy. The trend towards liberalisation has resulted in an increasingly highly integrated and globalised world. Against this trend, knowledge has become a vital element that is transforming businesses and becoming a major factor generating growth. These forces of change acting together are mutually reinforcing and are having a tremendous impact on the evolution of the modern economy. Rapid Advancement in Technology The technological revolution has provided faster ways to communicate and function in the new economy. The evolution of the global network has accelerated our ability to be connected and to do so at an incredible speed. This has resulted in an economy that is intensely inter-linked. While networks have always existed in every economy, its vast and rapidly expanding scale has transformed the dynamics of the new financial and economic order. The advances in technology has radically changed the way of doing business, the markets and the organisational structures. It has virtually redefined every business process, function and business relationship. The advances in technology has enabled the emergence of a new economy in which the digitisation of information has allowed for wide spread two way electronic communication that operates in real time. It has become a powerful tool that allows business to obtain information about almost anything at incredible speed. The decline in the interaction costs following this advancement is one of the important factors that is shaping businesses as we move forward. The rapid fall in communication cost brings opportunities in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. Traditional communication and delivery channels are now being replaced with more efficient alternatives. People no longer have to depend on a centre to be connected. Businesses can not only expand beyond national boundaries but is now taking place over cyberspace. Markets no longer need to be physical but instead can exist in computer networks. While physical infrastructure will continue to be important, business transactions are now increasingly being undertaken in the virtual world of cyberspace. In this process, the digital world is generating unexploited productivity gains beyond known dimensions. Integrated, Interlinked and Globalised The process of liberalisation together with the power of technology has resulted in highly integrated trade and financial markets in the global system. These combined forces have produced an economy that is intensely inter-linked and globalised. Trade liberalisation policies in the form of reduction in tariff and non-tariff protections by individual countries have led to the rapid opening of markets. Such tariff and non-tariff barriers are set to be further dismantled resulting in individual markets becoming less and less protected. At the same time, the advancement in technology has allowed businesses to deliver products faster, and gain wider access to information thus allowing business to access markets more easily and quickly. The integration of our domestic economy with the world economy is reflected by the high volume of exports and imports in our economy. In the more recent period, we have seen the intensification of liberalisation of financial and capital markets in the form of removals of restrictions of cross border capital transactions. Technological changes have accelerated the speed with these which payments are made and securities are transferred in the global financial system. This has resulted in a high degree of integration of individual domestic markets with the global financial markets. These developments have changed the structures of markets, and the institutions and their dynamics in the national and global economy. In this environment businesses and economies have now become more inter-dependent. It has been argued that the greater mobility of capital facilitates a more efficient global allocation of financial resources. It provides a channel through which the Government and private sector can borrow and lend at relatively more attractive rates. From an investors perspective, international flows have expanded the opportunities for portfolio diversification. These benefits of globalisation however, require the efficient functioning of the international financial markets. The recent decade has seen time and again the breakdown of the market system as demonstrated by the increased frequency of financial crisis in different parts of the world. The East Asian crisis illustrated the vulnerability of small emerging economies to such cross border flows. Countries have also become vulnerable to problems in one financial market that can easily spill over to affect other markets in other economies. This presents significant challenges to the authorities to ensure the safety and soundness of the financial system and a stable environment for economic growth. Although the globalisation process accords the private sector with increased opportunities anywhere in the world on a real time basis, businesses however, face greater risk of potential instability for their business in this environment. Towards a Knowledge Driven Economy While knowledge has always been important in enterprise and wealth creation, knowledge in the new economy has now become the main engine of growth and a fundamental driver of business performance. Driven by greater competitive pressures, by the advances in technology, by the increasingly differentiated consumer demands, by the rapidly falling structural barriers and dissolving business boundaries, businesses no longer have a choice but to become more knowledge-based. In this environment, performance will increasingly depend on how this knowledge is exploited. These developments have resulted in the transformation of the economy from one in which the traditional physical assets such as labour, land and capital are important towards an economy in which there is greater dependence on intangible intellectual assets. Recognition of the growing importance of this is evidenced by the increasing significance in corporate spending on knowledge associated activities. The importance of knowledge is not only in the new creative and innovative industries and high-tech businesses but in all businesses. This includes all corporate sectors, in particular, the manufacturing, construction, services and banking. Marshalling knowledge in the new economy is becoming an important strategy for businesses not only to improve their products and services but also to enhance productivity and efficiency. While the education and skills levels of the work force is an important element in the knowledge-based economy, of greater importance is the ability to translate the knowledge into enhancing the capability of the business. In this knowledge driven economy, new strategic approaches, are required. A new mind-set that relies on strategic thinking, increased flexibility and creativity and the ability to make fast decisions is important in the new economy. Businesses therefore need to identify the knowledge required for their business and develop a framework for it to be accumulated, shared and utilised. The life span of knowledge in the new economy is however short as information and knowledge becomes rapidly out-of-date. Unlike previously, learning has therefore to become a continuous life long process. Information and knowledge needs to be regularly updated and replenished. Very often, entrepreneurs tend to be absorbed with current developments and short-term pressures and due attention is not accorded to knowledge management. Unless a conscious effort is made and the motivation for knowledge becomes a part of the business culture, the desired results will not be achieved. III. THE CHALLENGES AHEAD These changes have dramatically altered the economic and financial terrain. Given that we can expect even greater changes ahead, the new emerging operating environment will continue to pose new challenges to the Bumiputra entrepreneurs. Staying at the forefront will require understanding the emerging features of the new economy and recognising that the requirements for success in this new economy is also changing. A More Competitive Environment The new environment will be characterised by increasing competitive pressures. The globalisation process has brought about a more competitive environment as markets become increasingly open with an increasing number of new entrants to the market. The rapid spread of technology is contributing to a more competitive environment. The two way channels have allowed business to reach more customers. Information and communication have made it easier for new entrants to compete in the market. Business therefore need to be on top of the situation and anticipate changing market needs and respond rapidly to the changing demand requirements. Technology is also dissolving the boundaries between industries, rendering some obsolete while creating new industries. New products and services have emerged at lower costs as product cycles become continuously shortened. In the new economy, it is not only the advancement in productivity that is important but also creativity and innovation. Surviving means recognising and grasping the changing opportunities in this more competitive environment. In this environment, the ability to compete is no longer just based on access to raw materials, land, capital and labour. It will demand much more. It will depend on how these resources are exploited. Competition is not just in terms of productivity but also quality and innovation. All too often, the focus of strategies has been to place emphasis on business reengineering. Such management programmes generally involve cost reduction measures. Although valuable, such programmes are not a substitute for strategies for the future. In this environment, it is the ability to amass skills and exploit knowledge that will give businesses the competitive edge. Bumiputra entrepreneurs need to recognise they can no longer compete as previously. Previous practices of doing business need to be adjusted and adopted. The new environment calls for greater focus on building capacities to survive in this competitive environment. In so doing, this greater competition while being a threat to survival, can also become a motivation to drive the advancement of businesses in the new economy. An Environment of Greater Uncertainty In this global environment of continuous change, it becomes increasingly difficult to predict the future. In the new economic environment, businesses can expect to be confronted with increased levels of uncertainty. Previously, under stable business environment, it was possible for businesses to identify distinct business trends. Assessment of previous business trends were relied on for developing business plans. While such forecast may not be precise, given that all business face some degree of uncertainty, the predictions did provide a basis for the corporate plan. Such business however, become highly unprepared when a sudden change occurs in the business environment. In the event of the emergence of new competitors, a new distribution channel, a new technology or a disruption in supply, such business would be significantly disadvantaged. Under an increasingly more uncertain environment, the traditional approach can no longer be applied. Making sound strategic decisions under uncertainty requires a different approach. In an environment of greater uncertainty, businesses are often caught unaware by such sudden changes. However, with the appropriate techniques, the uncertain environment can be managed. While no amount of analysis will enable an accurate prediction of the future, strategies can be developed to take into account this uncertainty. Businesses need to first identify the range of possibilities that could affect their business in the future. In these circumstances, it is important to understand the forces that could determine these possible changes. In this way, businesses can formulate strategies that will succeed in the alternative environments. Businesses can than be better prepared to respond quickly to the changing conditions. More aggressive businesses may in fact attempt to shape the future outcome of their business by creating a new product or service. The prospect of failure of such strategies however, cannot be ruled out. The uncertainties and risks associated with this strategy needs to be taken into account. Such businesses need to have strategic flexibility to be able to change the course of their business should this occur. In moving forward we need to look beyond the horizon, to have an ability to face an environment that is fundamentally different from the present one. What is needed in the new approach. There needs to be an understanding of the range of possibilities that could occur and a capacity to implement strategies that would succeed under different circumstances. The ability to recognise potential future developments and to be able to adapt and adjust to these developments will increase the potential to compete in the future. Greater Reliance on Knowledge Knowledge will become an increasing important component in the growth equation of any business in the new economic order. The competitive advantage will be gained from exploiting knowledge. Ideas and information have become an increasingly important part of products and services. Increasingly, companies will be judged by their knowledge assets and their ability to translate these assets to create shareholders value. Businesses in the new economy need to recognise the increasing power of knowledge and the need to accord priority to knowledge management. The previous emphasis given to management information systems and data processing now needs to evolve into knowledge systems that can be exploited throughout the entire value chain of the business. While physical assets will remain important in the new economy, it is not the equipment or the product itself but its knowledge content that will be important. In the future, what will count is the ability of the business to attract, retain and continuously enhance the capabilities of its knowledge worker. In such a world, a businesses need to learn faster than their competitors. Life long learning will become the only sustainable advantage. Any firm can have the same technology and any product can be copied. To succeed in the future, businesses need to build systems to use knowledge more quickly and effectively than their competitors. However, subjecting workers to an information overload can also be counter productive. An environment that combines speed and relevant knowledge requires structure and strategic focus. Systems and processes need to be established to guide the business towards more productive use of their intellectual resources. Speed becomes the Essence In the new economy, gains are accorded to those who are the fastest to recognise change and are the first to exploit the new opportunity. In a world in which almost all activity can be achieved at a faster pace, businesses that are rigid and too slow to respond to change can expect to face increasing difficulties in the new economy. Technology has facilitated processes that has built speed into everything that we do. Processes and systems that have become outmoded need to be replaced. Successful businesses in the new economy are those that have instituted a culture of speed and immediacy of execution. The new business in the new economy is essentially a "real time enterprise". Businesses need to respond in real time. To respond quickly to market developments, businesses need information immediacy. The speed of access to knowledge therefore needs to be continuously enhanced. Speed however needs to be generalised throughout the entire system to ensure an overall rapid response. Problems occur when parts of the value chain of the industry is slow resulting in inefficiencies for the industry as a whole. Obstacles also emerge when businesses have difficulty understanding how to change their business practices and business relationships in response to changes that have occurred. In particular, a greater understanding of the benefits facilitated by the new technology is important so that the advantage can be effectively drawn from the development. Greater Transparency and Disclosure In the new economy, business face a greater demand for better information, increased disclosure and for more transparent systems. Businesses will therefore, face the challenge of coping with the numerous new reporting requirements that are occurring to keep pace with the changing business environment. Global standards are also becoming increasingly rigorous and will continue to impose increased requirements on businesses. Traditional reporting that have tended to be based on current and previous financial statements will give way to greater emphasis on the future. Greater importance will also be accorded to non-financial as well as financial measures of performance. Non-financial information is becoming increasingly important in evaluating business performance. Investors have also become increasingly demanding, requiring reporting systems to demonstrate how shareholders value has been created. It is argued that this greater transparency enhances investor confidence. Going forward, it can be expected that management, regulators, private investors and financial markets will all continue to put increased pressure on management to comply with the increased standards of transparency on their business performance. In addition, there will be greater demands to align reporting frameworks to those that have international acceptance to achieve standardised reporting practices across borders. Greater Alliance and Collaboration Smart partnership becomes highly relevant in this new economic order. Businesses increasingly recognise they need to collaborate to compete more effectively. Businesses can improve their performance by drawing on ideas and techniques developed outside their business. In the new environment, few businesses have the skills and capability for research and development and for innovation. These alliances and collaboration can result in the transfer of technologies. In addition, links to research agencies and universities can become an important source for innovative ideas. Strategic alliances in the form of joint venture partners can also become mutually beneficial allowing the partners to co-prosper. It enables businesses to learn from others. In addition, partnerships with suppliers, customers and other complementary businesses can also promote knowledge sharing and the upgrading of skills. Very often businesses that are focussed on short-term gains do not see the tremendous benefit gained from collaboration and partnerships. The Domination of Consumers The decline in interaction costs following the advancements in technology and communications has allowed for increased information to be available to consumers. The tide of information flow to consumers have driven firms to relate directly with consumers, accessing their demands and anticipating their needs. This environment, in which customers are more well informed, places greater competitive pressures on the firm. Customers can infact, express their requirements to exaction and influence product creation. While previously, product and services were already differentiated for different target groups, it can now be expected to become even more differentiated and customised. Consumers are no longer passively accepting products and services as given. Increasingly, consumers have a say in indicating their requirements. Consumers are also able to search for those products or services at the prices they are prepared to pay. Having access to customer information allows businesses to make an assessment of current consumer behaviour and potential future behaviour. This particularly applies to financial services which has already become highly differentiated. Understanding the changing business requirements of firms have contributed to product innovation in the financial services industry. This is evidenced by the proliferation of products in the financial world. To be able to take advantage of the changing nature of demands, business however, need to have the ability to adjust and redefine their business in response to these changes. Of importance, is the ability to ensure that these changes can occur throughout the value chain of the product or service being provided. The New Entrepreneur Entrepreneurship has always been central to the growth process. The new economy, however, demands greater entrepreneurial savvy. The new entrepreneur is operating in an environment that is increasingly more ambiguous and competitive, an environment in which new technologies, new products and new markets are constantly emerging. In this more challenging environment, there is a need to continuously develop and enhance a culture of entrepreneurship that is based on innovation and risk taking. The focus is on creativity and wealth creation and not on the rearrangement of existing assets and corporations. The focus is on building the capacities and capabilities that is sustainable beyond the short term. Businesses that want to perform in the future need to begin to build their capacities today. There have been many who have ventured into businesses, yet only a few have actually achieved high growth. Very often this has been due to the lack of strategic focus, lack of competitive edge, lack of having the right people, the lack of access to the right finance, not having the information vital to the business, the lack of innovation and creativity, the lack of ability to take advantage of new technological capabilities, the lack of capability to manage the growth and the lack of ability to adjust to sudden changes that occur in the environment. Businesses that lack focus and the inherent capabilities and discipline will risk falling behind. In this new economic age, there is no authoritative source, no single prescription that can provide guidance to entrepreneurs to chart their development. Businesses in this new environment cannot be expected to evolve the same way. In the new environment, bumiputra entrepreneurs are challenged to determine their own business strategy, their own organisational structure and systems and to evolve their own culture. Access to financing is an important element to ensure funding for viable business. It is recognised that the availability of financing has at times been a constraint, particularly, for new investments in new industries -the early stage industries. Despite efforts to enhance access to financing, the gaps still remain. While this reflects to a certain extent the lack of capability of existing institutional arrangements to evaluate the viability of such businesses, efforts are underway the develop alternative forms of financing to meet these new requirements. While the Government can play an important role in developing the supporting infrastructure and providing a positive environment, however, ultimately it is the entrepreneurs themselves that will determine their performance. Government will continue to focus on providing the support infrastructure and creating a positive economic and financial environment to improve the chances for success. However, a highly interventionist approach in the modern economy will not provide the foundation for self-sustaining growth in the future. The Government is an important facilitator, but it is the efforts of the entrepreneurs themselves that can build self-sustaining businesses in this more challenging environment. IV. RISING TO THE CHALLENGE Distinct efforts need to be made to prepare for the new economic age. The strategy has to be developmental. High fliers who never developed capabilities will not be equipped for the long term. Enterprises have no choice but to invest in strategies that will support their future growth. Being Knowledge Driven In recognising that the future lies in a knowledge based economy, where knowledge is an important component in determining performance, it is important to put in place the building blocks for the management of knowledge in businesses. In addition, the aim is also for the economy to shift to a knowledge based economy and cultivate the development of new industries based on knowledge based industries. The main motivation for companies to implement knowledge information systems is the gains it generates from cost efficiencies. Such efficiency driven knowledge management systems focus on ways to use information more effectively. The first step involves identifying the knowledge needs of the firm. The task then is to structure and disseminate the information. Individuals in the organisation should not need to waste time searching for information required. Systems need to be established to share the information throughout the enterprise. While businesses need to have instant access to all the necessary information, it may not be possible for small enterprises to set up an information unit within their own establishment. Groups of enterprises could collaborate to develop an information centre for this purpose. A further motivation for knowledge management is that which focuses on learning and strategic innovation. In this situation, learning is integrated into the core business activity and drives the innovation and wealth creation in the business. Such knowledge management aims to enhance the competitive position of the firm by creating new products. The knowledge based system in this kind of enterprise requires different processes and supporting infrastructure. Such knowledge generates new insights that can be used to gain competitive advantage. Such information is analysed to generate new ideas and new approaches, products and services. The business culture in such an environment needs to change significantly to one in which there is sharing, mutual trust and respect. Information may be rejected because it is viewed as inconsistent as with earlier convictions. However, attitudes that lacks flexibility can contribute to business failures when such appropriate response is not taken because the information is ignored. In designing knowledge management systems, whether it be to enhance efficiency or for strategic innovation, the challenge is to develop a knowledge management system that would be most effective towards achieving a knowledge based enterprise. For the bumiputra enterprises, the challenge is to provide better information and to establish learning benchmarks. The traditional way of organising our businesses have left us unable to deal with all the information that has been accumulated. In many for the more advanced countries, the Government has played an important role as a direct investor in creating the knowledge base for businesses. The creation of information infrastructure for an industry, for example, can serve just like any other utility, that is, to provide information. Advisory services have also been have also been provided to assist businesses with information requirements. Collaboration between the private sector and the Government can also enhance the infrastructure for research and development to provide support to the knowledge based activities. Setting the Performance Standards In the process of modernisation, performance needs to be bench marked against the best. Such benchmarks need to be developed to monitor and review progress in performance. Key features in world class performers in industries can be identified. Standards and targets can be set in terms of all areas of business including productivity, quality and innovation. This would enable business to assess where they stand in the modernisation process. Goals on what is to be achieved can be set for all areas of business. Progress can then be continuously be reviewed against the benchmark. Performance gaps can be identified. Constraints to achieving the benchmarks can also be identified. In this way, short comings holding back the business can be addressed. In addition, delays and wastage can be detected. Such benchmarks will encourage improvements in all areas of the business and will drive commitment to deliver results. The challenge is for the business community to develop such benchmark indexes to serve this purpose. Promoting Strategic Alliances Various forms of strategic alliances can be forged to strengthen the ability to compete more effectively. Such alliances are particularly advantageous for smaller businesses that do not have the skills and resources to undertake research and development, or carry out customer surveys. Alliance can be forged with academia, universities and large business to exploit on their research potential. Competitive positions can also be enhanced through partnership and joint ventures with other businesses. This are particularly beneficial with businesses that have complementary skills and technologies. Collaborations with other business including those abroad would allow for learning new processes and best practices. Such global alliances can also enhance market possibilities. Bumiputra enterprises need to draw up programs that could identify and explore the various forms of potential collaborative alliances that could strengthen their businesses and the network that could be developed to facilitate the process. Successful bumiputra entrepreneurs can play an important role in nurturing and developing new bumiputra entrepreneurs. Industry groups can also be formed to consolidate information base and for sharing of knowledge. Various successful programmes have been adopted in a number of countries in which there are formal adoptions of small enterprises by successful firms which provide advisory services and a wide range of other assistance. Bumiputra entrepreneurs therefore need to explore the ways in which collaborative efforts can be undertaken. Enhancing Capacities To secure a self-sustaining business when the requirements for success is changing, there has to be continuous investment in capabilities. In order to effectively invest in the capabilities of the business there has to be clarity in the strategic focus of the business. In an environment in which market conditions are unstable and volatile and in which opportunities are abound, businesses need to have a strategic focus. Having a vision is a source of stability in this uncertain environment. The challenge is therefore to be vision driver despite operating in an environment of intense short term pressures. The lack of clarity in goals often results in poor business decisions. Vision provides an indication of the desired future for the business. It articulates the business definition and the business relationships and forms the basis for the formulation of strategies for the business. The investment in the future involves making investment in technology, the workforce and strategic alliances in all areas to develop faster and smarter businesses. Also important is building on organisational capabilities that is flexible and that is able to adapt to the changing environment. While the ability to raise capital will continue to be vital for any business, in the future, it will be the ability to amass skills. Recruiting the best and continued efforts to upgrade the skills within the business will be important. This should involve establishing learning targets and creating a culture of life long learning. Collaborative partnerships with other large firms, with institutions of higher learning and the Government can improve the quality of expertise in smaller firms. The advantage is gained from learning from the best and at an early stage in the business. Skills developed however, need to be retained. With the appropriate rewards and if employees stand to gain a share in the wealth of the company this can be achieved. Greater reliance on technology and maximising its use also better equips the firm for the future. Finally investing in the culture of the enterprise also contributes positively to the performance of the firm and increases the capacity and agility of the firm to adjust to changing condition. Benchmark targets can be established for all the areas to enhance capacity. It is key that capacity enhancement takes place across the board. Framework and strategy is to enhance capacity therefore needs to be constantly developed. The Government can play an important role in providing infrastructure for relevant education, information and knowledge base and improve further the access to financing and capital. Framework for rehabilitation is also important to provide assistance in the event of an adverse exogenous developments in the industry or in the over all economy. Government initiatives can also provide greater opportunities for increased participation in business. V. CONCLUSION There is no one formula to develop a generation of successful bumiputra entrepreneurs that can contribute not only for their own economic survival but for the overall wealth creation of this country. While immediate term solutions will provide some progress, the issue at hand requires a developmental solution. Such fundamental results cannot be achieved within a short period of time. We are therefore, presented with the challenges of instituting structural and developmental initiatives in response to the changes that have already altered the environment. The extent of our interconnectedness and the speed at which changes are occurring will present increasingly mounting challenges. This paper has identified four main areas that can contribute to increasing the potential for self-sustaining performance of bumiputra entrepreneurs. This includes generating bumiputra enterprises that are more knowledge driven, that are benchmarked against the best, that place greater reliance on strategic alliances, and that have strategic programmes for enhancing capacities. A framework can be developed to explore the initiative that can be undertaken to achieve these objectives. The bumiputra community can in collaboration with other communities and in partnership with the Government achieve a shared vision to effectively prosper in the future. Bank Negara Malaysia 26 February 2000

Title: Speech at the MyFintech Week 2022
text: Deputy Governor Dato' Dr. Zeti's Speech at the Venture Capital Europe-Asia 2000 Conference - "Accelerating Economic Growth through Venture Capital" Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Putra World Trade Centre, Kuala Lumpur Speech/Interview Date: 28 Mar 2000 Language: English Introduction The fundamental forces of change arising from globalisation, advances in technology and greater reliance on knowledge for value creation is shaping the new economy. The new economy is essentially a global economy, a digital economy and a knowledge economy. This new economy brings with it, the promise of the potential for higher growth. However, with it are risks and challenges that need to be carefully managed. To fully realise the potential gains of the new economy, distinct efforts need to be made to prepare for the shift to the new economy. These efforts which are developmental in nature, will take time to produce results. During the process of adjustment, it can be expected that the dynamic and mutually reinforcing forces of change will continue unabated. The preparation for the transition to the new economy will therefore require efforts on several fronts. This conference focuses on financing and capital for the new growth businesses, a vital element for the transition to the new economy. In this new economy, financiers need to be as innovative as the entrepreneurs. It is a pleasure for me to speak today before such a distinguished gathering of venture capitalists and entrepreneurs. This conference presents an excellent opportunity for venture capitalists and entrepreneurs to meet and hopefully begin on a journey in a venture that will be mutually rewarding. My presentation will begin by providing a perspective on the implications of the changing environment on the Malaysian economy. Against this background, I will discuss the potential role of venture capital in the transition towards the new economy. This will be followed by an overview of the status of the venture capital industry in Malaysia, and the role of Government in promoting the growth of the industry. Issues and challenges faced by the industry are discussed in the concluding section. Towards The New Economy Economic transformation is not new to Malaysia. Over the decades Malaysia has achieved economic transformation on several fronts. Malaysia has moved from a commodity-based economy to one in which the manufacturing sector dominates and more recently to one in which the services has gained greater significance. Malaysia has also shifted from the importance of the Government sector in the economy to one in which the private sector dominates. Malaysia has also moved from a regulated system to an increasingly more liberalised and deregulated system.Within the manufacturing sector Malaysia has also shifted from labour-intensive to more capital-intensive activities, from the production of assembly type products to higher value-added products and from simple production process to more integrated and technology-driven processes. More recently, the strategy has been to shift from an investment-driven growth towards a more productivity-driven growth in which the efficiency in the utilisation of resources as well as technology is a more important part of the growth process. The strategy is also for the services sector to feature more prominently in the shaping of the growth process and to facilitate Malaysia's progress into the next stage of development. The services sector is seen not only as providing the range of new services as income increases but also as an essential element in expanding the technological capacity and productivity of the economy as well as in enhancing international competitiveness. During each phase of the economic transformation over the decades, there was increased job and wealth creation that enabled Malaysia to achieve higher standards of living. The transformation seemed to be part of a natural process in which investors were responding to the changing opportunities that emerged that resulted in a shift of capital to new activities in which comparative advantage had emerged. The adjustment during each phase was however, gradual and without resulting in any major dislocation or destabilising consequences on the economy. The relatively young and trained workforce allowed for greater flexibility and mobility of labour. In essence, the transformation was a continuous evolutionary process with the vision of the end game clearly articulated in five year development plans. However, in the current environment, the scale and speed of change has increased dramatically. In this environment, the process of economic transformation has become discontinuous and unstable. We are also no longer accorded the time to fully understand the process and to develop the capabilities to deal with the emerging dislocations arising from the transformation. Structural Change in the Malaysian Economy: Gross Domestic Product by Type of Activity Agri-culture, forestry, logging and fishing Mining and quarry-ing Manufac-turing Construc-tion Services GDP 1970 30.8 Percent of GDP 6.3 13.4 3.9 41.9 100.0 1980 1988 1990 1998 1999 22.9 18.6 16.3 9.4 9.3 10.1 19.6 4.6 40.1 100.0 12.7 21.1 3.2 45.1 100.0 9.4 24.6 3.5 46.8 100.0 8.1 27.9 4.0 55.6 100.0 7.3 30.0 3.6 54.2 100.0 The transformation of the Malaysian economy since 1970 shows that the share of the agriculture sector declined from 30.8% in 1970 to 9.3% in 1999 while the share of output accounted for by the manufacturing sector steadily increased. By 1988 the manufacturing sector overtook the agriculture sector to account for a share of 21.1%, while the share of agriculture declined to 18.6%. Thereafter, the share of the manufacturing sector increased to 30% in 1999. The share of the services sector also increased from 41.9% in 1970 to reach 50.6% in 1993 and rising to 54.2% in 1999. Within the services sector, all sub-sectors except for government services gained importance. In particular, the share of the finance sector increased from 7.7% in 1987 to 12.1% in 1999. The share of distributive trade also increased from 10.8% to 15.2% during the same period. It is envisaged that going forward, new areas of growth in technology and knowledge based activities would gain significance. This trend towards the new economy has been driven by three fundamental forces of change, the rapid advances in technology, the liberalisation of trade and financial markets and the greater reliance on knowledge for value creation. Virtually all economies at some point in time will need to address the challenges brought about by these developments. Given the structure and stage of development of the Malaysian economy and given that it has been very much an integral part of the global economy in terms of trade, investments and financial flows, these developments can be expected to have significant implications on the domestic economy. The advances in technology has resulted in economies that are intensely inter-linked. While networks have always existed in every economy, its vast and rapidly expanding scale has now transformed the dynamics of the new financial and economic order. The advances in technology has radically changed the way of doing business, the markets and the organisational structures. It has redefined every business process, function and business relationship. In the new economy, the digitisation of information has allowed for widespread two way electronic communication that operates in real time. It has become a powerful tool that allows access to information about almost anything at incredible speed. The decline in the interaction costs following this advancement is one of the important factors that is shaping businesses in terms of bringing opportunities, increasing efficiency and effectiveness. Traditional communication and delivery channels are now being replaced with more efficient alternatives. Business activities have not only expanded beyond national boundaries but are now taking place over cyberspace. Markets no longer need to be physical but instead can exist in computer networks. While physical infrastructure will continue to be important, business transactions are now increasingly being undertaken in the virtual world of cyberspace. In this new, digital world, productivity gains beyond known dimensions are being generated. We have also seen the process of liberalisation together with the power of technology resulting in increasingly integrated trade and financial markets. These combined forces have produced an economy that is intensely inter-linked and globalised. Trade and financial liberalisation policies by individual countries have led to the rapid opening of markets. At the same time, the advancement in technology has allowed businesses to deliver products faster, and gain wider access to information thus allowing business to access markets more easily and quickly. The integration of our domestic economy with the world economy is reflected by the high volume of exports and imports in the Malaysian economy accounting for about 200% of GNP. In the more recent period, we have seen the increasing liberalisation of financial and capital markets in the form of removals of restrictions on cross border capital transactions. Advances in technology have accelerated the speed at which these payments are made and securities transferred in the global financial system. This has resulted in a high degree of integration of individual domestic markets with the global financial markets. These developments have changed the structures of markets, and the institutions and their dynamics in the national and global economy. In this environment businesses and economies have become more inter-dependent. Finally, knowledge in the new economy has become a fundamental driver of growth and business performance. Driven by greater competitive pressures, by the advances in technology, by the increasingly differentiated consumer demands, by the rapidly falling structural barriers and dissolving business boundaries, businesses no longer have a choice but to become more knowledge-based. In this environment, performance will increasingly depend on how this knowledge is exploited. These developments have resulted in a shift in relative significance of traditional physical assets such as labour, land and capital towards greater dependence on intangible intellectual assets. The importance of knowledge is not only in the new creative and innovative industries and high-tech businesses but in all businesses. This includes all corporate sectors, in particular, the manufacturing, construction, services and banking sectors. Marshalling knowledge in the new economy is important not only to improve products and services but also to enhance productivity and efficiency. In the knowledge-driven economy, new strategic approaches are required and learning has to become a continuous life long process. This new environment will be characterised by increasing competitive pressures. The globalisation process has brought about a more competitive environment as markets become increasingly open with an increasing number of new entrants to the market. While the two way channels have increased the reach to more markets, information and communication have also made it easier for new entrants to compete in the market. Technology is also dissolving the boundaries between industries, rendering some obsolete while creating new industries. New products and services have emerged at lower costs as product cycles become continuously shortened. In the new economy, it is not only the advancement in productivity that is important but also creativity and innovation. Surviving means recognising the changing opportunities in this more competitive environment. In this environment, the ability to compete is no longer just based on access to raw materials, land, capital and labour. Competition is also not just in terms of productivity but also quality and innovation. In such an environment, it is the ability to amass skills and exploit knowledge that will generate the competitive edge. The new environment calls for greater focus on building capacities to survive in this more competitive environment. This greater competition while being a threat to survival, can also provide the motivation to drive the advancement in the new economy. In Malaysia, the development strategy thus far has focused on investment and trade-led growth. The policy initiatives taken, as set out in the Industrial Master Plan, generated employment, increased exports and contributed significantly to the nation's well-being. During the period 1987 to 1997, real GDP expanded strongly at an annual rate of 9.3%, while the real gross fixed capital formation increased by 18.1%. The Government also invested heavily in infrastructure to provide world class physical infrastructure to support domestic and foreign private investments. Significant increases in investments including those by multinationals saw the expansion of capital-intensive plants and positioned Malaysia as one of the main exporter of electronics in the world. During this high growth period, the contribution of investments to GDP rose from 23% in 1987 to 49% in 1997. While growth in Malaysia depended largely on capital formation, the industrialisation of Malaysia also took place with low cost of labour. Educated and disciplined labour at competitive wage rates encouraged such investments. In the new environment, investment-driven growth is no longer sufficient to achieve the medium-and longer-term goals envisioned. The challenge to Malaysia is therefore to evolve new sources of competitiveness and build new capabilities to produce new sources of economic growth. Advancement in technology provides the new opportunities. However, the economy needs to structurally adjust to position itself to take advantage for productivity and efficiency gains as well as the development of new growth activities. In Budget 2000, the Government announced the formulation of the Knowledge Economy Master Plan. While the importance of knowledge is relevant to all businesses and industries, the new economy calls for enterprises that are innovative, technology-driven and knowledge-based. In this regard, ideas-based start-up small and medium-sized enterprises are likely be prominent, if not dominant features, in the new economy. Looking ahead, the key drivers of economic growth and job creation in a country are not natural resources or a significant labour force, but innovative ideas and knowledge, arising from significant investments in research and development which can be commercialised to form the basis for rapid growth of the economies. Financing Options For High-Growth Activities While ideas and talent are the principal requirements for economic growth in the new economy, the access to appropriate and adequate finance is necessary to foster the development of knowledge-and technology-intensive enterprises. Small enterprises with ideas, particularly at the start-up or the early stage of growth, generally have difficulty in obtaining appropriate financing. Access to financing is a vital element for the commercialisation of innovative ideas and for effective research and development (R& D). Financing is also needed to attract talent and expand markets to enable companies to grow rapidly to gain the "first mover" advantage. Such high-growth enterprises are characterised by the high usage of capital and the need for injection of funds at frequent intervals so as to sustain expansion in the early stages of their development. The traditional sources of funds to finance the so-called "old-economy bricks and mortar" businesses are the banking institutions. For the new generation of start-up enterprises which are expected to feature more prominently in the new economy, alternative forms of financing are required. Banks have generally been cautious in providing financing to such enterprises in the early stages of their development. Banks have tended to focus on the value of collateral in the form of fixed assets, and require a track record of cash flows to finance repayment. Since the collateral which could be offered by such enterprises are generally intangible (in the form of ideas and knowledge) and in the absence of a track record, such enterprises have encountered difficulty in securing loans from banks. In addition, banking institutions generally have not developed the expertise in assessing and measuring the value of the "intangible assets". Given that bank lending will continue to be an important source of finance in the economy, banking institutions need to be proactive and increase their capacity and ability to finance such-high technology and knowledge based activities. Banks not only need to enhance their ability to evaluate the risks associated with the innovative and technology businesses but to develop new products and services to meet the new requirements of enterprises whose assets are their talent rather than physical assets. However, to fully tap the opportunities arising from innovative ideas, alternative forms of financing also needs to be made available. To support the transformation towards the new economy, the financial sector needs to be innovative and dynamic, increasing its capacity to respond to the changing business requirements. Alternative financing mechanisms need to be developed. In this regard, venture capital (VC) financing has tremendous potential in Malaysia to contribute to the growth of these technology and knowledge based enterprises. Venture capital companies (VCCs), generally focus on the early stages of growth of such enterprises. In addition funding, in countries where venture capital has been successful, such VCCs provide added value to their investee companies through advice on strategic planning, business management and sourcing of knowledge workers. VCCs generally bring with them experience, expertise and network of contacts, which can be valuable towards forging strategic alliances. VCCs essentially become active partners in expanding the business. In addition, the business credibility of those enterprises that are backed by VC financing is often enhanced, given that they have passed the tough "acceptability" test of the VCCs. Through such "endorsement", VC-backed enterprises receive ancillary benefits in the form of the additional comfort provided to their suppliers and customers. The stringent and comprehensive due diligence performed by VCCs can also facilitate such enterprises to secure additional funding from banks at a later stage. Other than such "formal" venture capital financing through VCCs, which are often in the form of partnerships or limited companies, other potential "informal" venture capital financing sources include "business angels", corporate ventures and intrapreneurial ventures. "Business angels" are private high net-worth individuals who provide equity financing directly to the enterprises, especially in start-up and early-stage ventures. Although the amount of risk capital provided by "business angels" is usually small, the financing from "business angels" is an important source of financing that enables ideas to be translated into commercially viable concepts that are ready for formal venture capital financing. "Business angels" are also value-added investors that generally play an active role in the businesses in which they invest in. Such "informal" venture capital is the single largest source of risk capital for entrepreneurial firms in the United States and Britain, significantly larger than the "formal" venture capital industry. In Britain, the ratio of "informal" venture capital to "formal" venture capital in terms of amount of funds invested is two to one while in the United States, the ratio is even higher at five to one. Another potential source of venture capital funding for technology and knowledge-based enterprises are corporate venture funds. Corporate venture funds are funds set up by large corporations for investment in enterprises that fall within their strategic area. These funds are set up to supplement their own internal R& D efforts. Some large corporations have also set aside funds to assist their own employees to start up companies through what has been termed "intrapreneurial venture capital". These funds provide seed capital for employees to start up companies that use the research that the employees had undertaken in the corporation. The large corporations also take up equity in the companies started by their own employees. By providing "intrapreneurial venture capital", such corporations are able to capitalise on their employees' creativity while moving risky projects off their balance sheets in addition, to retaining the talent within the corporation. For a number of countries, the establishment of an exchange that accords priority to technology-based companies has provided an alternative source for raising funds. The establishment of the Malaysian Exchange of Securities Dealing and Automated Quotation Berhad (MESDAQ) was an important development towards providing an alternative source of raising capital for such technology-based enterprises. The exchange also serves as an exit mechanism for venture capital financing. In Malaysia, other developments include the setting up of Malaysian Enterprise Network (MENet) which essentially is an internet based community which offers alternative investment and financing options by linking private limited companies incorporated in Malaysia to target investors. The Malaysian Venture Capital Industry The financing pattern in Malaysia has also evolved over the years, in line with the transformation of the Malaysian economy. Growth in the earlier period was mainly financed by loans from the banking system and the issue of debt instruments by the Government. In 1970 for example, financing via bank loans and by the public sector (which was mainly through MGS) together accounted for 91% of total financing. With the shift in public policy in the 1980s to consolidate its activities and to promote the private sector as the main engine of growth, new financing patterns emerged. The share of financing by the public sector declined from 43.1% in 1970 to 20.9% in 1980 and 11.1% in 1990. Much of the financing of private sector activities during the 1980s and 1990s continued to be intermediated through the banking system. In recent years, as a result of the Government's efforts to develop the private capital markets, the equity and private debt securities (PDS) markets have expanded significantly to complement and to diversify the risks away from the banking system. The share of financing from the equity market has increased from 1.2% in 1980 to 22.8% in 1990, while the share of PDS has risen from 5.6% in 1990 to 24.8% in 1998 and 43.9% in 1999. While the share of venture capital, though relatively small, it has however, been rising from 0.1% in 1992 to 0.5% in 1998. The Government recognises the important role of venture capital in financing the new growth areas and efforts have been directed to develop the venture capital industry. 1970 1980 1990 1998 1999 Banking System 47.9 66.6 56.7 23.0 18.5 Sources of Financing for the Economy (% share) Public Sector PDS Equity Industrial Finance Institutions 43.1 0.0 9.0 0.0 20.9 0.2 1.2 0.0 11.1 5.6 22.8 0.5 37.2 24.8 4.7 4.1 15.4 43.9 9.3 2.4 Venture Capital 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.5 0.1 External 0.0 11.0 3.3 5.7 10.3 The "formal" venture capital industry in Malaysia began in 1984 with the establishment of Malaysian Ventures Berhad. As for the "informal" venture capital market, data is not available at the present time. Although the venture capital industry has existed in Malaysia for several years, the number of funds and venture capitalists are still relatively small and insufficient to provide the extent of capital and expertise that is necessary to fund and nurture knowledge-based and technology-intensive start-up enterprises. Based on the annual Bank Negara Malaysia survey of venture capital companies in Malaysia, the number of VCCs has risen from six in 1990 to 13 in 1992, and to 30 by the end of 1999. Similarly, the assets of the VCCs have grown from RM346 million in 1992 to RM1.7 billion at the end of 1999, or an average annual increase of 32%. Of the 30 VCCs, the Government has stakes in 19, reflecting the important role of the Government in promoting growth of the VCC industry. Among the balance of 11 VCCs without Government shareholding, nine are subsidiaries of financial institutions. In terms of participation from nonresidents, nine or 30% of the 30 VCCs have some form of foreign shareholding. Of the nine, only one VCC has a majority foreign stake. This suggests that Malaysia has not taken full advantage of the flow of institutional sources of finance into the venture capital industry on the international market. U. S. funds, for example, are increasingly investing in European venture capital funds, and U. S. venture capital funds actively seek out and invest in European start-up companies. In terms of the stages of financing, 28.4% of the investments during 1999 were in the bridge/ mezzanine/ pre-IPO stage. Meanwhile, investments in the crucial seed and start-up stage accounted for only 4.5% and 7.9% respectively. The share of seed stage financing had in fact declined from 7.8% in the previous year. This development is discouraging, as seed capital is vital to ensure that the development of an initial concept can reach the start-up stage. In addition, the survey also showed that the VCCs in Malaysia have tended to be relatively geared. Liabilities of VCCs amounted to RM1 billion while shareholders' funds totalled RM728.3 million. Recognising the important role that financing plays in supporting the development of home-grown enterprises in knowledge industries that provide high value added and high productivity, a number of initiatives have been taken by the Government. The aim is to further improve the enterprises access to financing, including venture capital financing. Among the recent Government programmes related to venture capital and financing for small-and medium-enterprises was the establishment of two venture capital funds totalling RM500 million that was announced in the Budget 2000. This included the RM200 million fund to finance high-technology projects to be channelled through Bank Industri dan Teknologi Malaysia Berhad and the RM300 million fund to finance investee companies. Bank Negara Malaysia and two commercial banks are providing the capital to this fund. Tax incentives are also being given to VCCs in the form of full tax exemption on all sources of income received during the VCC's life span or for a period of ten years, whichever was earlier. A venture capital fund, the MSC Venture One fund, was also established in June 1999 to provide venture capital financing to innovative and emerging information technology and multimedia companies at the start-up, growth and pre-IPO stages. To date, the RM120 million MSC Venture One fund has announced its first investment amounting to RM3 million, and made commitments in three more companies which are expected to be announced soon. Several Government grants have also been set up for small-and medium-scale enterprises that require financing particularly at the early stage. The available Government grants include, among others: the MSC Research and Development Grant Scheme; the Industry Research and Development Grant Scheme; the Demonstrator Application Grant Scheme; the Technology Acquisition Fund; the Commercialisation of R&D Fund. Enterprises can also approach the Credit Guarantee Corporation for financing as well as for financial guarantees to obtain loans from banking institutions. Although the provision of financing is necessary, capital is only one piece of the jigsaw. In essence, there are other drivers to develop a venture creation environment. A holistic solution, across the spectrum of capital, infrastructure, entrepreneurs, ideas and regulatory environment, is needed to promote a significant venture community in Malaysia. The Government recognises the important role it has in providing the supporting infrastructure and facilitating the development of technology and knowledge-based enterprises. Several building blocks have already been put in place: the Multimedia Super Corridor initiative, including Cyberjaya and smart schools; the setting up of Technology Park Malaysia and incubation centres; the acceleration of the university building programme, including technology universities such as the Multimedia University; the establishment of research institutes such as MIMOS and SIRIM; an effective legal framework to protect intellectual property rights, including the implementation of Cyberlaws; the establishment of MESDAQ to provide a viable exit mechanism; the establishment of the Human Resource Development Fund; the development of a National Master Plan for E-Commerce; the development of a National Information Technology agenda; and last but definitely not least, the development of the K-Economy Master Plan. Challenges Ahead One of the key success factors for knowledge-based SMEs to prosper is the development of a critical mass of entrepreneurial talent, including not only inventors and innovators, and venture capitalists, but also financiers, lawyers, accountants and other professionals. To achieve this, there is a need for the creation of a positive environment to nurture domestic entrepreneurs, technopreneurs, netpreneurs as well as to bring back Malaysian talent from overseas. With the rising number of Malaysian start-up enterprises, the setting up of more venture capital funds, including foreign funds, to finance viable entrepreneurial ventures in Malaysia will be necessary. The increased availability of funding sources would encourage the formation of new enterprises. Malaysia also needs to attract the flow of institutional sources of venture capital to build up the critical size of the venture capital industry. The availability of venture funding in Malaysia needs to be enhanced to retain winning ideas developed by Malaysian entrepreneurs in the country. In addition to capital, the mobilisation of talent, including foreign venture capitalists who have expertise and experience in assessing intangible ideas and intellectual property, as well as in nurturing start-up enterprises by providing them with advice on business management as well as providing a global network of contacts would support the process. The mobilisation of talent, creativity, knowledge, skill and other capabilities would generate a "brain gain" that will contribute to the development of Malaysian venture capitalists. At the same time, there is a need to encourage the growth of local venture capitalists who are capable of financing knowledge-based ventures. Local VCCs can also initiate joint ventures with foreign VCCs to take advantage of their respective comparative advantage. Local VCCs can position themselves by providing their foreign partners the local knowledge and monitoring that are necessary to nurture promising start-up enterprises into successful companies while benifitting from their more experienced foreign counterparts. Another area is to increase the number of Malaysian entrepreneurs in technology and knowledge industries. Successful ventures will also thrive in an environment in which there is the development of an entrepreneurial culture and community. Relative to successful entrepreneurial-driven countries like the U. S., Malaysia does not have the critical mass of entrepreneurs, technopreneurs and netpreneurs, that is needed to generate sufficient volume of "deals" to be financed by VCCs. In Silicon Valley for example, eleven new companies are formed every week and one is floated on the stock exchange every five days. This issue has also been the experience of European countries, according to a 1999 European Community report (1). The reasons for the relatively lower number of entrepreneurs include among others, the excessive punishment for failure as well as the cautious attitude towards risk-taking, which could well be due also to the punishment for failure. Business failures tend to be "blackmarked" by bankers and suppliers. In contrast, the "right to fail" is considered part of the learning process of business in the United States. Therefore, society, culture and laws need to change to accept that in the new economy, failure is part of the learning process. The burden of building a significant and vibrant venture community that will enable the Malaysian economy to shift rapidly from a capital-intensive economy to an advanced and globally competitive knowledge economy, should not depend solely on the efforts of the Government. The private sector too has an important part to play in Malaysia's efforts to develop a significant venture community. In this regard, I would like to highlight a number of initiatives that can contribute towards this process. As mentioned earlier, in many developed economies, the existence of "business angels" has played an important, role in closing the funding gap for enterprises, particularly those in the seed and start-up stages. In Malaysia, however, financing from "business angels" have not been significant. Given that "business angels" are an important intermediate financing channel for such enterprises, their development needs to be promoted. Indeed, several developed economies such as the U. S. and Britain, have established "business angel networks" to facilitate potential private investors and companies seeking financing. There is also an European Business Angels Network. These networks typically operate on the basis of publishing an investment bulletin containing descriptions of companies seeking capital, which is circulated to investors registered with the network. Some networks do this also through electronic matching and investor forums. The private sector should take the lead in forming such "business angel networks". In addition to the "business angel networks", the venture capital community in Malaysia could also organise regularly scheduled informal networking events. These informal events would serve not just to provide a forum for people to know each other, but also a forum for ideas to be exchanged and deals to be concluded. As efforts are directed towards building the nation's knowledge and technology base through capability development in our universities and research institutes, the private sector could work closely on the research innovations created by these institutions, and commercialise them into products with business potential. In this regard, the private sector, namely, entrepreneurs, financiers and academicians can improve their links through networking and clustering between universities, research centres, financial institutions and business associations. The private sector could organise business plan competitions to encourage a critical mass of entrepreneurial activities and enhance innovation. In the U. S. for example, students participate in business plan competitions, some of which are subsequently financed by venture capitalists who monitor the competitions. Finally, venture capital companies can promote strategic alliances among their portfolio of investee companies to take advantage of the synergies present. In addition, the talent bank from the VCCs' wide network of investee companies could also be tapped to solve the business problems or promote the business of the other investee companies in their portfolio. Over the next few days, many of you will be concluding your own "deals" here at the "Business Matching" sessions after the conference. Indeed, more of such forums should be encouraged. For Malaysia to succeed in evolving towards an advanced knowledge-based economy, we will need the involvement of the whole community, especially the venture capital and entrepreneurial community. The community is present here today, and there is no time like the present. In conclusion, I wish to take this opportunity to wish you a productive conference and success in the new economy. Bank Negara Malaysia 28 March 2000 1 The Competitiveness of European Enterprises in the Face of Globalisation - How it Can be Encouraged,European Commission, January 1999.

Title: Closing Speech at Sabah Financial Carnival
text: Assistant Governor Datuk Zamani's Opening Address at the Conference on Corporate Governance Speaker: Assistant Governors / Advisers Speech/Interview Date: 04 Apr 2000 Venue: Nikko Hotel, Kuala Lumpur Language: English This morning, you have heard the Keynote Address by Encik Ali Abdul Kadir, the Chairman of the Securities Commission. Therefore, it gives me great pleasure to be here this afternoon to deliver the Opening Address for this section of the Conference on Corporate Governance.
