This conference is indeed very timely, as corporate governance has become a buzzword in the light of the recent high profile corporate failures. These failures have forced governments, regulators and boards of directors to review and evaluate fundamental issues of corporate governance to protect the public and investors' interests as well as the interest of various other stakeholders within the economy. However, before I proceed, let me take this opportunity to congratulate the three organisations -The Malaysian Insurance Institute, the Malaysian Institute of Corporate Governance and the Malaysian Association of Certified Public Accountants for their commendable efforts in jointly organising this conference. The presence of a wide interest group here today, consisting of professionals from the insurance industry, accountants, directors and senior management, further confirms my belief that, honesty and responsibility rank high in your pursuit of creating value for your companies. The financial crisis that hit the East Asian economies has highlighted the significance of good corporate governance and best business practices to many countries in this part of the world. There is a growing recognition that good corporate governance is essential to protect the interests of investors, shareholders, bankers and insurers, and the public at large. Some of the forces at work are: The recent volatility and instability experienced in emerging markets which highlighted weak management practices and poor control and governance on the part of the board of directors, which in turn, contributed to the financial collapse of many large companies; Increasing demands from shareholders and investors for high standards of corporate governance from the companies they invest in; and Increasing focus from governments and regulators world-wide for good corporate governance on the part of the board and management of companies. As a side remark, the recent Asian financial crisis emanated, in part, from the private sector. This was so as the governments of the countries severely affected by the crisis had registered budget surpluses in the years prior to the crisis. As such, there has been much talk within the international circles, of bringing the private sector into the process of crisis resolution. I believe that this highlighting of good corporate governance is part and parcel of this move of involving the private sector in crisis prevention and resolution. Just what constitutes good corporate governance is still a topic of debate. However, according to the World Bank, from a corporation's perspective, the emerging consensus is that corporate governance is about maximising value subject to meeting the corporation's financial and other legal and contractual obligations. From a public policy perspective, corporate governance is about nurturing enterprise while ensuring accountability in the exercise of power and patronage by firms. I am tempted to go along with the definition provided in the Report on Corporate Governance that was released by the Government in March 1999. In the Report, corporate governance is defined as "the process and structure used to direct and manage the business and affairs of the company towards enhancing business prosperity and corporate accountability with the ultimate objective of realising long-term shareholder value while taking into account the interests of other stakeholders." The practice of good corporate governance demands a sense of conviction and commitment from the people who run the company  namely, the board members and senior management. Boards of directors are now expected to ensure that the interests of all parties are protected, and that, the company is run in a manner that is fair and equitable to the shareholders and the public. The challenge is for you, ladies and gentlemen, to work these values out in practice. Directorship is a heavy responsibility and one must take these challenges seriously, as society depends on directors to discharge their duties independently. The board of directors sets the culture in the company  and today, the culture to be nurtured is, to serve with honesty and integrity. From time to time, questions are raised as to what value does the board of a company add. What would be lost if it ceased to exist? What would be the effect of changing the nature, composition or operations of the board and how do you make it more useful or beneficial? Ideally, the board of directors should be the heart and soul of a company and its fountain of wisdom. In the longer term, whether or not a company grows or declines depends very much upon the sense of purpose and direction, the values, the will to generate customer satisfaction, and the drive to achieve, develop and learn, that emanate from the board. Without vision, sense of purpose and ambition, a corporation can wither and die. Whether or not managers display leadership qualities depends in turn, upon the extent to which they are motivated and empowered by the board. The management team is likely to take its cue from the "role model" behaviour of directors  behaviour that can inspire and motivate  or sap the management spirit. Boards vary greatly in the value they add. Some boards are positive instigators and enablers of change, whilst others are bystanders, or even obstacles to progress. I would venture to say here that Board meetings should be carried out in a more open, constructive atmosphere, in which directors have enough confidence to vigorously challenge each other's views and assumptions. This should vastly improve the chances of providing healthy oversight over the companies. Some of the characteristics that determine a good board are the experience and professionalism in their work, integrity and understanding of the roles expected of them. Board members should display a thirst for knowledge and the desire to lead their organisations to innovate and adapt to new challenges. They need to understand their role and work together as a team to guide their organisations forward. Directors should constantly evaluate the adequacy of information and also ensure that they have adequate time to digest such information. If boards are to be effective in evaluating management and approving corporate strategy, they need to develop knowledge not only about the company's financial results  which are an indication of past performance, but also need to evaluate the company's progress in accomplishing its strategy. Still on the subject of knowledge  directors and management will have to gear themselves for the dawn of the knowledge economy and play an active role in knowledge management. Currently, there are two major underlying forces shaping the emerging economy. Firstly, globalisation and liberalisation, which translates into the world becoming increasingly open to cross border activities. The second force is advances in information and communication technology which is leading to cost savings in business transactions and increasing efficiency in the value chain. These forces are shaping the way economic activities are undertaken and are fast changing consumer tastes and demands. Directors in the new "knowledge economy" must leverage on the "soft" factors, such as, ideas, information, skills, knowledge and relationships to re-think their strategy for success. They have to embrace knowledge management, which may be applied towards creating an organisational capability that combines culture, context and infrastructure to deliver high value information for better decision-making. Directors and management should therefore fully engage themselves in building and exploiting intellectual capital, which will be the sole source of competitive advantage. Their success or failure in managing knowledge to adapt to the changing marketplace and their responsiveness to society's demands for good principles of corporate governance will determine the company's survival or demise. Ladies and gentlemen From the perspective of the development of the local capital market, sound corporate governance is important not only to attract long-term foreign capital, but more especially, to broaden and deepen local capital markets by attracting local investors -both individual and institutional. Unlike international investors who can diversify their risk, domestic investors are often captive to the system. As a group, domestic investors frequently constitute a large potential pool of stable long-term resources that are critical to the nation's development. For Malaysia's local capital market to grow, corporate governance standards will need to be improved, to give investors the protection that they require in return for providing capital. The fact is that good corporate governance practices are now becoming a necessity for every country and business enterprise, and are no longer restricted to the activities of public-listed corporations in advanced industrial economies. In the midst of growing international pressure for adherence to good corporate governance standards, it is imperative that our businesses take a serious view of adopting good standards of corporate governance. Let me touch a little on the relationship between the board and management. While a basic responsibility of the board is to ensure that the company is managed in a way that serves the owners' interest in successfully perpetuating the business, it also has to act as an independent monitor of management. It should ask the tough questions that management might not ask itself. This needs to be done continually, not just in crisis situations but also when the company is doing well. The board is in an ideal situation to do this since it is somewhat removed from executive management and does not carry the bias of a company's past success and its culture. In this era where conglomerates and group structures are the norm, the importance of corporate independence to good corporate governance cannot be underestimated. Transactions conducted between related parties are inevitable but these should be at arm's length, at terms that are comparable to normal commercial terms. Companies should try as far as possible to ensure full disclosure of such transactions, and the group should also be structured in such a way as to provide for a reasonable degree of independence. Last but not least, corporate governance is best carried out in an environment that is open and transparent. Investors are increasingly looking for better information, increased disclosure and more transparent systems. Globally, standards on disclosure are becoming increasingly rigorous with increased requirements on businesses. Towards this end, it is important that there be comprehensive, timely and regular reporting of financial and non-financial information so that investors and the public are kept fully informed at all times. In addition, the management of companies and its external auditors should play a crucial role in ensuring the integrity and comprehensiveness of such information. I am pleased to inform you that in line with the Government's efforts to nurture good governance practices in the corporate sector, Bank Negara has formulated and will announce soonest possible, a prudential framework of good corporate governance for the insurance industry. The framework will embody several of the principles and best practices dealing with the duties and responsibilities of directors as spelt out in the Malaysian Code of Corporate Governance. In addition to this, the framework will establish basic principles of good corporate governance in other key organisational aspects of insurance operations including management accountability, corporate independence, internal controls, operational risk management, public accountability, and financial and management reporting. Good corporate governance is here to stay. All of you present here, whether as management, accountants or auditors of companies, can begin to make a real difference to the way your companies are run, by adopting good corporate governance principles. By doing so, you will be enhancing your business prosperity and in the long-term, that of all your stakeholders. On this note, Ladies and Gentlemen, I wish you a successful conference, and I am sure, with such a distinguished list of participants, the discussions would generate greater commitment towards good corporate governance. Lastly, I would like to thank you for your kind attention. Bank Negara Malaysia 4 April 2000

Title: Speech at the International Conference on Takaful
text: Governor's Keynote Address at the Fourteenth Conference with Financial Institutions - "Towards a More Efficient, Effective and Stable Financial System" Speaker: Tan Sri Dato' Seri Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman Speech/Interview Date: 12 Apr 2000 Venue: Bank Negara Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur Language: English Let me again welcome all participants to this Fourteenth Conference with Financial Institutions. I am sure we all feel a little more relieved this morning compared to this time last year given the more favourable economic environment and better financial performance for our institutions. When we met about this time last year, we were not very certain how strong the economic recovery would be. As it turned out, the turnaround has been faster and stronger than we had expected. The growth of 5.4% for 1999 is impressive by any standard. We are further encouraged that this growth process appears to be sustained in the coming year. We expect the real GDP growth to strengthen to 5.8% this year, while the market has forecasted a higher figure of around 6.5%. The stock market has regained its momentum while consumer confidence has been improving steadily, as indicated by the rise in consumer spending. Restructuring efforts have shown signs of success in arresting the problem of indebtedness experienced by the corporate sector. The non-performing loans (NPL) of the banking system have moderated to a much lower level of 6.6%, based on 6month classification, as at end-December 1999, from the peak of 9% as at end-November 1998. The capital strength of banking system has also improved, with the risk-weighted capital ratio (RWCR) improving from 11.8% as at end-1998 to 12.8% as at endFebruary 2000. Similarly, the performance of the banking institutions has improved significantly due to improvement in asset quality and improving market and economic conditions. For 1999, the banking institutions as a whole, registered preliminary unaudited pre-tax profits of RM5.3 billion as compared to a pre-tax loss of RM5.7 billion in 1998. It is now clear that we have succeeded in steering the economy out of the recent crisis, and more importantly, we did it our way. The effectiveness of the Government crisis management measures in mitigating the full impact of the financial crisis and preserving our economic fundamentals and the social fabric, is now receiving international accolade. Our consistency and determination in policy implementation have eventually paid off. However, we cannot afford to become complacent. Despite the positive economic outlook and improving market sentiments across the region at present, there is no guarantee that our future is secure from any threat of instability. In a world where global financial markets are highly integrated, the risk of contagion and the possibility of financial shocks happening again in the future cannot be discounted, and the best defence is to strengthen our economy to meet these challenges head on. It is imperative, therefore, that we understand the key forces affecting the financial industry while we strategise and position ourselves for the future. The globalisation and liberalisation of financial markets, the emergence of a global capital market, and declining costs due to advancements and improvements in technology, are the three main forces that will determine the future landscape of the financial sector. Financial products are converging across asset classes, and the rapid pace of innovation and change will see consumer demanding for more efficient and sophisticated products and services. The barriers to the various markets are breaking down, creating almost a borderless economy. All these developments create uncertainties, and demands caution and proper sequencing of liberalisation measures to maximise the net benefits to our economy. The direction of policy will be to ensure a well-managed process of deregulation and the strengthening of the banking institutions, so as to build greater domestic capacity and capability to compete in this new environment. Indeed, an important underlying element to improve the effectiveness of the domestic banking institutions is to encourage greater domestic competition. Inefficient players will be subject to market forces to improve their position or soon be pressured to exit the market. Today, we see that the need to remain relevant and competitive in a more liberal environment has created a big wave of mergers and acquisition among global players. The mega-merger involving three Japanese banks, The Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, The Fuji Bank and The Industrial Bank of Japan, announced in August last year, to create the world's largest banking group, with more than USD1.31 trillion in total assets is one of the examples. Cross industry merger which seeks to enhance synergy, such as that between Citigroup and Traveller's, is also becoming a global trend in the financial industry. Here, I must commend the local banking institutions for responding well to the major consolidation exercise which is intended to build a more competitive and strong financial sector, in order to remain relevant in the face of intense global competition in the future. Looking forward, it is extremely crucial that Malaysia develops a resilient, competitive and dynamic banking system to ensure that the banking sector plays an effective role in supporting the economic transformation process. The strategic move from a production-based economy towards a knowledge driven economy, where information is a key commodity, is high on our agenda. At the same time, the small and medium scale industries should be nurtured further to become an important fabric of a successful economy to support large multinationals, including our own which are expanding internationally. The main challenge for the banking sector is therefore to serve all sectors of the economy in the most efficient manner such that the use of capital is optimised. Failure to provide the right type and mix of financial services will result in our companies having to look for alternative sources abroad. This is already happening although on a small scale and we have to arrest this trend. The success in developing an efficient, effective and stable banking system depends very much on the combination of the right operational and institutional framework for the banking sector. On BNM's part, we would seek to ensure that the operating environment in the banking industry does not inhibit growth but encourages product innovation, skill building and operational synergy. The general orientation across the world today is towards a greater reliance on market discipline in order to allow competition to germinate. Under such an approach, the market will be entrusted to allocate risks and resources, while the main task of the supervisor will be to ensure that an over concentration of risk or abuse of power does not occur, and that the welfare of consumers remains protected. Market forces will provide the discipline required and shape the industry, where winners will be rewarded and laggards will eventually disappear. In this way, market discipline will encourage prudent and stabilising behaviours among players in the banking system. Market forces in this context will determine market conduct, while banking regulation preserves the sanctity of transactions and best practices. Although market forces will encourage greater competition, it would be too naive to assume that markets will work perfectly and are always able to provide the required discipline. Throughout history, there had been instances of excessive price volatility in financial markets and asset price bubbles due to excessive optimism of the banking institutions which had led to economic overheating and financial crises. This is too big a risk for small economies like Malaysia, where problems arising from such market imperfection will have adverse implications on the overall stability of the economy. Therefore, there is a need to balance between market discipline and traditional regulatory oversight. The optimal regime is, therefore, a well-supervised market-driven approach where market discipline acts as a complement to, rather than a substitute for, the traditional activities of bank regulators. In subscribing to a supervised market-driven approach, the traditional regulatory framework will continue to be strengthened to ensure that financial institutions continue to operate in a prudent manner. The instincts of banks that are driven by private enterprise will be tempered by the need to ensure that public interests are not compromised by excessive risk-taking. The externalities that arise with financial products and financial markets are considered too important, both socially and economically, for BNM to place individuals' savings and financial investment entirely under the vagaries of market instincts. In addition, in order for disclosure-based system to be fully effective, it has to rely on the ability of the market to analyse and respond correctly to financial information. Inability of market participants to do so could lead to market over-reaction that could further erode consumer confidence in the banking institutions and threaten the stability of the overall system. In this regard, essential elements of the regulatory framework under the supervised market-driven approach will rest on a disclosure-based system and greater consumer protection. The expected outcome of this comprehensive and complementary approach to bank regulation is a set of strong responsive banking institutions, capable of supporting Malaysia's financial needs efficiently. Under a disclosure-based system, bank directors and management would be made more accountable for their actions through greater transparency and public disclosure of banks' information. Such information, if made available on a timely and regular basis, will provide market participants with greater scope to react to developments affecting a bank's financial condition. Wellmanaged banking institutions will benefit in terms of lower cost of funding, while weaker banking institutions will face market pressure to improve their position. The potential negative response by market participants to excessive risk taking activities will impose discipline and promote prudent behaviour among bank management. Given the close market scrutiny, banks' directors and management are expected to be more vigilant in their actions and improve their skills so that they can apply close surveillance on the banks' risk exposures and internal weaknesses. The Board of Directors would be ultimately responsible for the operations and financial soundness of the bank. In this respect, there is a need to ensure that board members are well qualified for their positions and capable of exercising sound judgements, independent of the views of management or large shareholders. It is the responsibility of each and every banking institution to ensure that this criteria is fulfilled well before any application for new board appointments is forwarded to BNM for approval. BNM would also urge shareholders to nominate professionals as their nominees on the board of banking institutions to enhance the independence and objectivity of the board. The appointment of professionals as board members will enhance the corporate governance structure as they can bring new perspectives from other businesses, provide strategic directions to the banking institution especially during times of corporate stress. In the context of preparing a comprehensive action plan for the development of an efficient and effective banking sector, BNM will undertake a holistic approach of the financial system developments and a review of the present regulatory framework to ensure its consistency with the objectives I have already mentioned. Any policy changes will need to be sequenced in the most appropriate manner to ensure that it achieves the desired objectives. In this regard, I wish to inform you that BNM is currently in the final stages of developing a Masterplan for the Malaysian financial sector. The Masterplan for the Malaysian financial sector will amongst others, identify and recommend the best possible policy options to be taken by BNM, in shaping strategic directions of the banking industry. The objective of the Masterplan is to create an efficient, effective and stable financial system, which has a set of core domestic banking institutions, and capable of supporting the real sector, as well as meeting the nation's social objectives. One important priority of the Masterplan will be to improve the efficiency and effectiveness as well as to increase competition among domestic banking institutions. This is primarily to address the problem of widening performance gap between the domestic banking institutions and the incumbent foreign institutions in Malaysia, let alone international players. The next step towards introducing greater competition will be the levelling of the playing field with incumbent foreign players in the banking industry within a well-defined time frame. The protective environment in which the domestic banking institutions are operating in would no longer be sustainable in the longer term. Besides the need to formulate strategies to develop an effective, efficient and stable financial system, the Masterplan will also recommend measures to further improve the present infrastructure in meeting social-economic objectives and at the same time, minimises distortions to the efficient functioning of the banking system. All these will be announced in detail when we release the Masterplan by this year. Pending the Masterplan, I would like to announce a new policy package for the industry to work on immediately. Some of the measures will represent an affirmative action programme to assist domestic financial institutions, to enable them to upgrade themselves in order to compete with the incumbent foreign players in the market, as a more levelled playing field will be introduced. The financial crisis has indeed highlighted the areas in which prudential regulations would need to be tightened quickly. Indeed, a number of measures have already been implemented over the course of the last two years to strengthen the prudential framework with the ultimate objective of minimising sources of systemic risks and hence improving the overall resilience of the banking system. One of the areas that BNM is reviewing, is the implication of group structures on the financial soundness of the banking system. Although BNM is prepared to be flexible over the group structures, this flexibility will be accompanied with a set of prudential measures to ensure that the integrity and stability of the banking institution is not compromised. BNM also expects the holding companies to be a source of strength to their bank subsidiaries. In this regard, BNM will expand the scope of its supervision to cover bank holding companies and will impose a set of regulations to be complied with by the holding companies. The regulations will specify the scope of permissible activities of bank holding companies, minimum capital requirements and to require bank holding companies to obtain the approval from BNM prior to publishing their annual accounts, and for the payment of dividends to their shareholders. In addition to these specific measures, firewalls for companies within the group will also be properly defined to address potential of conflict of interest situations. The recent crisis has also highlighted the need to review the measures that were implemented to restore confidence in the banking systems. One example is the present explicit guarantee given by the Government for all deposits within the banking system. While this measure was effective in restoring confidence and curbing contagion risks under a crisis situation, it may bring undesirable long-term consequences for market efficiency, particularly with respect to moral hazard. Explicit guarantee may induce some banking institutions to engage in excessive risk taking activities that will place the depositors' money as well as the tax payers' money at risk, as public funds may have to be used to resolve the problems of banking institutions. Banking institutions should recognise that the responsibility to maintain overall banking system stability should not be the sole responsibility of BNM and that they too would have to shoulder part of this responsibility. BNM will therefore, put in place a mechanism whereby the moral hazard from such guarantee of deposits can be minimised if not totally eliminated. One such mechanism being considered is some form of deposit insurance fund to be managed by BNM. The details of this mechanism will be announced by BNM in due course. Consistent with global trends towards consolidation, the banking industry is currently undergoing massive structural improvement. Following rationalisation of the finance company industry in 1998, the domestic banking institutions are consolidating further via the current merger programme. By the end of the year, the domestic banking industry will be rationalised to 10 domestic banking groups. With each banking group having a minimum shareholders' fund, unimpaired by losses, of RM2 billion and a minimum total asset of RM25 billion, the domestic banking industry can look forward to having a more credible set of financial players that will spearhead future development of the banking sector. BNM will ensure that banking institutions gain the maximum benefit from the merger process. In addition to the internal synergies derived from the merger, some incentives will be accorded to these banking institutions to allow them to realise greater cost savings and increased efficiency. In this regard, I would like to announce that all domestic banking groups can now undertake cross-selling activities and internal rationalisation, that is, they are now allowed to sell products within the group and pool common functions and resources at a centrally chosen location. In terms of branches, the rationalisation of branches will be allowed to take its natural course with the ongoing merger exercise. In the areas where more than one bank has branches, banks will be allowed to close down or relocate the branches elsewhere, on condition that at least one bank branch remains to serve the area. I encourage all banking institutions to take advantage of these policies so as to enable them to provide the most efficient and effective banking products and services. The details of the policy will be communicated to the banking institutions shortly. On the issue of mergers, let me remind the affected banking institutions that the merger process must not in any way affect their lending activities. The sustainability of the economic recovery hinges very much upon the availability of and accessibility to financing for the private sector. While BNM has not prescribed any lending target for this year, I am happy to note that the banking industry as a whole has forecasted an encouraging loan growth of 10%, with some banking institutions forecasting even higher growth for this year. Indeed, the economy can only record stronger growth this year if the banking institutions display strong commitment in achieving this forecasted loan growth. In this regard, banking institutions must, therefore, ensure that the merger teams are separate from the operational staff who are involved in day-to-day lending operations. BNM will not tolerate poor lending performance in any banking institution and will certainly not accept mergers as an excuse to justify sluggish loan growth of banking institutions. I also see the ongoing merger process as bringing opportunity for domestic banking institutions to improve their efficiency by undertaking a thorough review of their workflow processes, particularly with respect to front-end services. There have been numerous complaints from customers about the long queue hours, lengthy and cumbersome loan approval processes, and inconsistency or inaccuracy of information provided on financial products. These have to be improved. Domestic banking institutions must continuously improve their quality of services to customers. Customer complaints represent a good measure of customers' level of satisfactions with banking services, and the banks must take customer complaints seriously. As financial intermediaries and trustees of public funds, it is most critical that banking institutions offer the highest quality services and maintain public confidence in their integrity. At this juncture, let me strongly remind the banking institutions of the importance of safeguarding the secrecy of customers' information. Public confidence is the key to intermediation. If confidence is undermined, the ability of the nation to collect and deploy its savings will be impaired, and the principal means to economic growth and rising living standards through the intermediation function of banks will not be achievable. The importance of maintaining confidentiality of customers' information cannot be over-emphasised. We expect the boards and senior management to promote high ethical standards within their respective institutions and should bear the responsibility for any breach of confidentiality of information. High ethical standards in banks are neither a luxury nor an abstract ideal. Rather, they are a vital aspect of protecting and enhancing the bank's image, and ensuring its long-term business survival. As our banking sector becomes increasingly competitive, there is an urgent need for each banking institution to optimise on its particular strength. Each banking institution must exploit its competitive advantage to the fullest and focus on its strength in order to build greater efficiency and expertise in specific areas. The strategy to be the jack of all trade, but masters of none, may not be the right strategy for the 21st century, particularly in service-oriented sectors like banking. Banking institutions should always seek to improve their operational structure so as to allow them to conduct the most efficient internal rationalisation that suits their business strategy. Some of the examples would be the Lloyds Bank in the UK which specialises in retail banking, the State Street Bank in the United States which is well-known for its custodial services, and the Credit Agricole in France for its agriculture financing. It is important that banking institutions see the merits of specialisation and sticking to their core expertise. One of the trends I observe among international players is to use outsourcing service providers for their non-core activities. The ability to use outsourcing service provider has allowed the international players to benefit from cost savings and greater efficiency. Outsourcing to third parties would relieve the banking institutions from having to develop the infrastructure and expertise in non-core activities on their own. In order to ensure that domestic banking groups are provided with a greater avenue to increase their efficiency through outsourcing, BNM will allow domestic banking institutions to outsource a wider range of its activities to third parties. Except for activities that are integral to the core activities of banking institutions and activities that would put the banks' reputations and integrity at risk, domestic banking institutions will be allowed to outsource their non-core activities without having to seek prior approval from BNM. The guidelines on this subject will be issued shortly. Information technology is one of the key forces affecting the financial industry. Advances in information technology (IT) have fundamental influence in shaping the dynamics of competition in banking. Headlines on cyberbanking or words like bankingonline are already becoming commonplace in the banking circles. Indeed, in the world of electronic commerce, IT brings both opportunities and threats. As for proactive and innovative banking institutions, IT will be an important enabler in improving internal efficiency as well as effectiveness in reaching out to the customers through alternative delivery channels, such as internet and mobile banking. On the other hand, for the banking institutions which are slow in responding, IT will further drag them behind the world best performer. BNM realises the importance of IT to create and develop an innovative and competitive banking sector and will ensure that banking institutions are well-positioned to reap the benefits of IT. In particular, internet banking services can facilitate banking institutions to undertake cross selling of financial products in a more effective manner and reach a bigger pool of potential customers. Towards this end, I am pleased to announce that with effect from June 2000, domestic banking institutions will be allowed to offer a full range of internet banking services. Domestic banking institutions should quickly set up their system and get the necessary approval from BNM. The consultative paper on the minimum guidelines on the provision of internet banking services will be issued to the industry for comments shortly. Domestic banking institutions will be given a one-and-half year grace period before the branching policy is reviewed to allow incumbent foreign banks to offer internet banking services. Advances in IT have improved the range of delivery channels available to the banking institutions. While this will help them in reaching to their customers, the associated risks will have to be managed adequately in order to ensure that the interests of consumers are protected and the credibility of the banking institutions are not affected. Like I have mentioned before, confidence is the key to banking. Banking institutions bear the responsibility to ensure that security of their IT systems are intact at all time and are abreast with the latest technological development. This was particularly evident with the high number of unauthorised ATM withdrawal lately. The recent fiasco caused by the cloned ATM cards teaches us to be vigilant and not sit on our laurels, while the crooks get more sophisticated and able to penetrate the ATM security system. In today's age where consumers are more demanding and conscious of security needs, failure by banking institutions to ensure high security standards is intolerable. This has now become a big issue and I urge banking institutions to give strong attention to ensure that ATM cards are fool proof to avoid such incidence from taking place in the future. Management of banking institutions should take steps to create awareness throughout their organisation that security is an important cultural value. Training should be provided to the relevant staff to keep them updated with new security risks and method of mitigating such risks. In this regard, I suggest that banking institutions implement the Guidelines on Minimum Standards for ATM Services issued by BNM well before the target date of end-June this year. All the factors I have mentioned are critical in developing an efficient and effective banking sector. But, let us not forget that the most important element to the banking institutions, above all, is the people. Of course bankers consider themselves to be nice people. I am told that when bankers die, they are buried at a much deeper level than others. This is because deep down bankers are nice people!. Leading institutions all over the world are those that are able to attract and retain the best talents. Talents and skills are crucial for banking institutions in order to develop expertise and hence enhance their competitive edge. The limited expertise in key areas at present appears to be contributing to the inefficiency and lack of innovation. To accord greater flexibility to the banking institutions in rewarding their staff, with immediate effect, the guidelines on wage moratorium will no longer apply to the banking institutions, for both the domestic and foreign banks. Nevertheless, the present rule on remuneration for the Chief Executive Officers and directors, which requires BNM's prior approval, will continue to apply. I am sorry about that. Board of directors of banking institutions will also need to ensure that remuneration given to the staff is not excessive and commensurate with productivity. With this flexibility, I expect significant improvement in the performance of domestic banking institutions in all key areas already mentioned. BNM will monitor closely the progress of the banking institutions and benchmark these institutions against world's best practices. Besides the urgency to develop an efficient banking system, we should not ever forget our socio-economic agenda. In the context of our economic transition, we need to ensure that priority sectors, especially the small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), financing the purchase of low cost housing and the Bumiputera community, continue to have access to bank financing at reasonable costs. In this regard, financing for these sectors should be viewed from a long-term perspective, as the benefits may not be immediate to the banking system. Availability of financing to SMEs, for instance, will allow the industry to thrive further and bring more business opportunities for the banks in the future. While bank financing is important for the survival of the SME industry, there are many other factors that are critical to improve their viability, including the availability of financial advice, financial management services and information management. In this regard, banking institutions need to ensure that these added-value services are made available beyond the mere provision of financing. It is timely for banking institutions to review their perception and strategy to support the SMEs industry and build necessary infrastructure to serve this sector. An important priority sector that requires special attention is the development of viable Bumiputera entrepreneurs, since the Bumiputera group is still lagging behind in economic development. The creation of a strong segment of Bumiputera entrepreneurs is crucial not only to improve wealth distribution but also to ensure the nation's political and economic stability. Given the general lack of financial expertise and business experience among many Bumiputera entrepreneurs, there is a need for banking institutions to help develop the culture and inculcate business discipline among Bumiputera entrepreneurs. In this regard, BNM has initiated discussions with the 10 anchor banks and a few foreign banks with large domestic networks on the setting up of Bumiputera Development Units, within each banking group, to ensure that greater attention is accorded to meeting the needs of the Bumiputera community. I would also like to take this opportunity to re-emphasise the need for banking institutions to promote greater use of Bahasa Melayu in the financial sector in order to cater to the needs of the largest group of the population in the country. The use of Bahasa Melayu in business correspondence will make banking institutions more friendly to and approachable by their customers. At the very minimum, simple contracts including housing and car loan contracts and application forms for banking products and services to the general public must include a Bahasa Melayu version. The government will also play its part to ensure that necessary infrastructure is put in place to enable the social objectives are met adequately, but in a manner that will not result in any distortions to the banking system. Hence, the existing framework to serve the priority sectors will be further improved and strengthened from time to time. As you all know, the Credit Guarantee Corporation (CGC) plays a crucial role in the context of lending to priority sectors, particularly to the SMEs. With the availability of guarantees from CGC, banking institutions are more willing to take the risks of financing the priority sectors. Recognising the importance of CGC in this context, BNM will inject an additional capital of RM1 billion into CGC this year, while the government has allocated a total of RM300 million for CGC to build up its guarantee reserve fund. The capital injection will allow CGC to expand its activities in supporting the development of SMEs. In order to increase the efficiency of the operation of CGC further, I am also pleased to announce that CGC will be opening 14 new branches nationwide to cater for the needs of the SMEs. This will ensure that CGC's guarantee facilities are easily accessible to SMEs at all time. We often receive complaints that SMEs were not able to get financing expeditiously from banking institutions. With the new branches to be set up, CGC will be able to perform its own credit analysis on the customers and hence grant the guarantee even prior to the SMEs approaching the banks. Given the significant variance in the quality of credit analysis among banking institutions at present, this will be the most suitable short-term measure. Eventually, of course I will expect banking institutions to undertake this function by improving their credit processes and having the necessary skills to assess and evaluate credit risks of SMEs. Given the improvement in the infrastructure, in particular the operations of CGC, I do not see why banking institutions should shy away from lending to the priority sectors in the future. Let me now turn to the insurance industry. The insurance industry also turned around in 1999 after experiencing two years of negative growth as a result of the financial crisis that seriously mauled the Asian markets. The crisis drove home one important point, that is, the importance for the industry to have a strong capital base, sound risk management techniques and operational efficiency for it to achieve sustainable growth and development. In the context of the forces of increasing globalisation and liberalisation, efforts must be taken immediately to address the weaknesses at a deeper level. Consolidation has been one of the core strategies pursued by BNM to build a stronger and more resilient insurance industry. We have called for industry consolidation on various occasions. Merger activities worldwide are taking place at a relentless pace, and virtually all these deals are market driven. BNM has also responded positively to the proposal by the insurance industry for a package of incentives to promote market-driven mergers. That being the case, I wonder what then is preventing merger activity from taking place in a significant way in our own insurance industry? While I am happy to note that three mergers have been completed and three are at various stages of implementing their merger plans, I certainly wish to see an increased merger activity among insurers, particularly from the financially weaker and smaller insurers. Let me take this opportunity to re-emphasise that BNM has not waned in its resolve to build a core of financially strong insurers through consolidation. If the current approach does not yield the expected result, we may consider other measures, including increasing the minimum capital requirements beyond the present level of RM50 million, setting specific deadlines for completion of merger exercises and finding merger partners for insurers which are unable to do so on their own. Insurers are advised to seriously consider consolidating their financial positions. Certainly, there is no room for those who wish to wait in the shadows, on the false hope that they will survive somehow. You have a choice: either you decide your future on your own through mergers or else you will be forced to disappear from the market through new capital requirements. The insurance industry has also made a headstart in the use of internet as delivery channels when a group of insurers and a takaful operator were given approval in mid 1999 to establish an interactive website that allows their policy-owners to renew motor policies online. Recognising the wide-ranging capabilities of the internet and its increasing prominence in business activities, we have taken a further step to revise the existing policy on internet insurance. In this respect, I am pleased to announce that eligible insurers and takaful operators are now allowed to offer online purchase and renewal of their insurance and takaful products, subject to the prior approval of BNM. As a regulator, be it for banking or insurance, our concern in respect of internet activities is the protection of depositors' and policyholders' interests. I would therefore, urge those establishing interactive websites to ensure that your systems are equipped with adequate security features to preserve the integrity of internet transactions. I have outlined some of the key forces that we need to understand in strategising our future direction. It is of critical importance that banking and insurance institutions have a good understanding of the vision already laid out by BNM. Without that understanding, the desired objectives and targeted milestones will not be achieved. We must put all our efforts together to make this vision a reality and we must act while we have the capability to do so. Our future is still very much in our hands and we must not wait until others come to dictate our destiny. I believe that the measures I just announced will lay the foundation for our future. I now leave it to you to take the full advantage of these new policy measures. Thank you very much for the attention. Bank Negara Malaysia 12 April 2000

Title: Remarks at the Green Swan 2021 Global Virtual Conference by Bank for International Settlements
text: Governor's Speech at the Launch of Maybank's Internet Banking Service Presenter: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz / Venue: Nikko Hotel, Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 09 June 2000 / Good morning and greetings, First of all, I would like to thank Maybank for inviting me to launch the Maybank internet banking service named Maybank2u.com this morning. The launch of this Maybank2u.com is a historic milestone as it marks a significant advance in the increasing use of technology by our banking system. In this regard Maybank has once again proven its superiority by emerging as the first bank in Malaysia to introduce banking services over the internet. The rapid development in the field of technology and communications has had a significant impact on the banking sector. Technological advances have enabled banking products and services to be offered more efficiently and effectively. At the same time, the higher level of IT awareness among the customers of banking institutions has led to the increasing demand for banking products and services through electronic channels. To ensure that banking institutions remain competitive in this more challenging environment, the competition strategy must continue to be improved and strengthened from time to time. This is important to ensure that the strategy is always relevant and appropriate to the environment we are facing. With the liberalisation and deregulation process becoming more pronounced, the banking industry should recognise that the existing business strategy must continue to be enriched. Banking institutions will be exposed to a new atmosphere that requires them to be always pro-active, innovative and competitive. Banking institutions will not only compete with each other, but also have to deal with the involvement of non-banks such as telcos to gain customers and business opportunities. In this setting, the existence of more efficient electronic transmission channels such as the Internet should be used as widely as possible. In an increasingly challenging era of globalization, banking institutions need to act quickly in diversifying their products and services. The offering of products and services through internet channels, for example, will not only help banking institutions maintain and expand their markets, but it is also expected to reduce operating costs in the long term. As you are aware, a "payment gateway" was launched on 22 March 1999 for the convenience of transactions via the Internet. To date, only four local banking institutions have used this facility. At the same time, the GIRO service between the banks was also launched on 21 April. To date only seven local banks have used the facility. I hope that the local banks will be able to make the most of all the opportunities and facilities that have been provided to the fullest. Banking institutions in Malaysia in particular should take advantage of the much lower cost of Internet access in Malaysia compared to other countries in the region in order to increase the faster and more effective participation in e-commerce. With the constantly improving infrastructure and encouragement programmes by the government as well as the increasing use of the Internet in the country, the chances of penetrating new markets are greater. There is no denying that Internet Banking opens up opportunities for banks to grow and increase shareholder value. Banking institutions should ensure that their involvement in banking over the internet should be consistent with their overall business strategy. Cost and interest analysis should be carried out first to ensure that the investments made will bring profit in the long term. At the same time, every banking institution must have a clear concept that can be translated into a profitable business plan, before engaging in banking over the internet. In addition, the provision of adequate resources in terms of manpower and technology is critical in achieving the success of their planning. Banking institutions in Malaysia should not ignore important issues such as the provision of structured business planning, branding, marketing strategies and sound risk management. One of the most important factors in determining the success of banking institutions in the supply of products and services over the internet is the ability to create a high level of security. In this regard, banking institutions should strive to raise awareness among their employees that the security aspect is an important culture in banking operations. Suspicion about the possibility of intrusion on the security system of the electronic channels of the banking institution will reduce the interest of customers to use the facilities. In order to avoid such a situation, banking institutions that offer products and services over the internet should always ensure that the level of security provided is the best and is constantly being improved in line with current technological developments. At the same time, banking institutions should also play a leading role in educating and providing accurate information as well as exposure to customers on security aspects as well as the advantages of internet usage. In addition to security challenges, banking institutions also need to be prepared to deal with issues involving their reputation. Banking institutions need to be aware that through the internet they will be faced with a different group of customers than the average customer. These customers often want a more efficient, safe and customer-friendly service. Therefore, banking institutions should give emphasis and priority on the time and accuracy factor in offering banking products and services over the internet. As we know, investing in information technology is an important factor in determining the future of a banking institution. In fact, as we know, financial institutions, especially internationally, have made significant investments in providing their IT infrastructure. In this regard, I understand that the Maybank Group has allocated a considerable amount for investments in this internet banking technology. I hope that all these hard work will be a catalyst for all the management and staff of the Maybank Group to continue to provide quality services. All technological innovations introduced will be more effective when equipped with a more efficient level of service. Before ending my speech, I take this opportunity to once again thank the Maybank Group for inviting me to launch the Maybank Group's Internet Banking services on this historic day. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Maybank Group and wish the Maybank Group all the best. With my BISMILLAHIRRAHMANIRRAHIM speech, I am pleased to officiate the launch of the Maybank2u.com  The first Online Financial Gateway  in Malaysia. Thank you. Central Bank of Malaysia 9 June 2000

Title: Keynote Address  at the World Bank's Aiming High Webinar Series
text: Governor Dato' Dr. Zeti's Welcoming Address at the Conference on "Central Banking and Sustainable Development in the 21st Century" Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Kuala Lumpur Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 28 Aug 2000 Introduction It is my great honour and pleasure to welcome you to the Conference on Central Banking and Sustainable Development in the 21st Century, organised in honour of the late Tun Ismail Mohamed Ali, the first Malaysian to assume the post of Governor of the Central Bank of Malaysia. This conference brings together Central Bankers, policy makers, academicians and members of the financial and business community to discuss aspects of Central Banking in the 21st Century. This conference takes place during a time of unprecedented change in the world economic and financial order. This conference takes place in an environment in which global financial markets have become increasingly vulnerable to instability and crisis. There has been significant debate on how to address the issues and challenges that have emerged from these developments. Central banks have been at the forefront of this debate. Today, we are gathered here to discuss and exchange views on issues faced by central banks and to pay tribute to a man whose life time contribution was instrumental in laying the foundation for the development of Bank Negara Malaysia and the financial system of Malaysia. A Tribute to Tun Ismail Ali Tun Ismail Ali was the longest serving Governor. His tenure spanned over 18 years, from 1962 to 1980. He saw the assets of Bank Negara Malaysia increase from RM125 million in January of 1959 now to exceed RM129.2 billion. The Bank which started with a staff of 100 now has 1,826 employees. He has seen the financial system facilitate the economic transformation from an economy. During his tenure, the economy which was dominated by primary commodities transform to one in which the manufacturing and services industries have become major components of the economy. His efforts in shaping the evolution of the Malaysian financial system and the Central Bank contributed to facilitate the economic transformation and progress that was achieved. Tun Ismail Ali was born in Port Klang on 16 September 1918, into a family of ten. He received his early education at the Victoria Institution in Kuala Lumpur. He won the prestigious Queens scholarship to study at Cambridge University in 1938. He returned to Malaysia nine years later with brilliant academic achievements, which included a Bachelors and a Masters Degree in Economics and a Barrister-at-law from Middle Temple, Inns of Court. His career in the public service started in 1946 when he was one of the two Malays recruited directly into the prestigious Malayan Civil Service. After independence in 1957, Tun Ismail Ali travelled to Washington to set up the Federation of Malaya Embassy in Washington and became its economic minister. In Washington, he served as Executive Director of the World Bank representing Malaysia and a number of South East Asian and African countries. In 1960, Tun Ismail began his Central Banking career as the chief architect for building a sound monetary and financial system for a young nation, his first two years as Deputy Governor and then as the Governor. During his 20 years in the Bank, Tun Ismail was dedicated to building the Central Bank into a premier institution and developing the Malaysian banking industry and its financial system. Tun Ismail Alis legacy is best summed up by his contribution and his role in the development of Bank Negara Malaysia. As the head of the Central Bank he saw his primary role and responsibility in the early years of its existence as building a body of traditions in the Bank, a tradition of absolute integrity, a tradition of competency at all levels in the organisation, a tradition of efficiency even to the point of ruthlessness, a tradition of dependable expertise in economic affairs and monetary matters, and above all, a tradition of being able to recognise and accept absolutely the dictates of the national interest as against the interests of the individual. He strongly believed that the respect and influence of the Bank depended on the virtues and standards that the Bank was able to develop and maintain. With a firm hand Tun Ismail Ali guided the Bank through its formative years making a lasting impact on the Bank. He cultivated the culture of integrity, competence and professionalism and imbued its people with the values and virtues of hard work and prudence. Tun Ismail Ali was not the easiest person to work with. Noted for his straightforwardness and sharpness of mind, Tun Ismail expected the highest standards of professionalism and excellence from himself, his staff and the people he dealt with. His reputation for meticulous attention to detail was well known. An alert thinker, he was held in high esteem by his contemporaries for the soundness of his judgment. While a few found it hard and at sometimes almost impossible to work with him, many who had worked with him found the experience most enriching. Tun Ismails views on both personal and public spending were based on prudence. His uncompromising stance on this principle was well known. Never would he compromise his principles, nor would he bow to request for favours. He owed his influence and prestige both to his competence and his unquestionable integrity. Within the Bank, Tun Ismail is well known for the remark that the central bank would be independent within the government rather than of the Government. While he recognised the formal responsibilities defined in the law, he rightly judged that the positive informal working relationship with the government was essential if the Bank was to be effective. He saw no substitute for a close and respectful relationship between the government and the Central Bank. A high degree of coordination and mutual respect was seen to be important. Maintaining a sound financial system depended very much on public confidence in the banking industry and on the integrity and competence of the financial institutions management. During the early days of the Malaysian banking industry, Tun Ismail Mohamed Ali placed emphasis on these traditions in institution building. He made it clear that he expected the senior management of the financial institutions to be professional and committed to providing quality banking service to the public. Those bankers who failed to pass this test, would come to know of it quickly and in not an unambiguous manner. Tun recognised the Central Banks relationship with the financial system was of immense importance. The relationship with the system formed the foundation on which public confidence in the banking system was built and maintained. It is incumbent upon banks and bankers to recognise their role in the smooth functioning and development of the economy and the public trust entrusted on them to manage their banks soundly and efficiently. He believed that bankers integrity should be beyond reproach. For the unscrupulous, dishonest and unprofessional, the full weight of the law would be brought to bear on them for abusing any public trust. Twenty years after his retirement, there is no alternative for prudent management in maintaining a sound financial system. Tun Ismail Alis success as a central banker was derived from his innate understanding of Central Banking. His beliefs were anchored on the objective of promoting monetary stability and to preserving a sound and resilient financial structure. While these objectives were explicit in law, he knew that how these roles was to be achieved was not always clear. He acknowledged that there was no set of rules to follow. However, he recognised that to be an effective central banker discretion had to be exercised within the confines of the broad objectives and mandate of the Central Bank. But central to this discretion was the need for the Bank to be an efficient organisation with the reputation for integrity and sound judgment. His single-minded pursuit of these principles would lay the cornerstones of the Malaysian financial system. Circumstances have changed over time, but these fundamental objectives continue to remain at the heart of central banking in the current environment. Tun Ismail understood well that unlike in developed countries where the central bank operates in a framework of well established and highly developed financial institutions, the central bank in developing countries has to assume far greater responsibilities. Central Banks in developing countries are often entrusted with multiple, sometimes even competing objectives. Depending on a stage of a countrys development, the Central Bank is responsible for :- initiating new mechanisms and institutions to fill the gaps in the financial system. This include developing the financial infrastructure to ensure the provision of adequate credit for specialised economic activities not met by the banking system; to provide adequate banking facilities throughout the country to ensure balance growth; developing the financial markets in particular money, foreign exchange and capital markets; according priority to the social agenda by influencing the direction of lending and accessibility of credit across purposes, regions and social groups; and Tun Ismail carried out the task of building financial infrastructure in a newly independent country with determination. The years that followed would see outstanding progress made in the creation of the pillars that still support the Malaysian banking infrastructure to this day. Under his stewardship :- the Central Bank actively encouraged the domestic owned banking institutions to expand their branch network to areas where banking facilities were either inadequate or non-existent. He gave attention to the needs of the less privileged and priority was given to ensure that the farmers, small traders and enterprises, had access to banking services. During his tenure, domestic commercial banks expanded their network from just eight banks with 12 branches to 21 banks with 398 branches nationwide, a large number of which were located in rural areas; the Bank actively promoted the growth of the inter-bank market by commencing to the issue of Treasury bills and other new money market instruments; the Bank also played a key role in encouraging the growth of the capital market by creating an extensive market for Malaysian Government securities. He was also instrumental in the establishment of the Malaysian Stock Exchange and an active foreign exchange market; and the Bank was directly involved in the establishment of a number of specialised financial institutions that now continue to provide important support to Malaysias economic development. An important milestone during Tun Ismails tenure was the assumption of power to issue currency. The new Malaysian ringgit was issued on June 12, 1967 to replace the Malayan dollar issued by the Currency Board. The assumption of currency issuing powers in addition to the management and supervision of the banking system in Malaysia marked the realisation of a fullfledged Central Bank, and paved the way for the next stage of evolution in Malaysias monetary system. In 1973, Tun Ismail followed up with the bold decision to allow the ringgit to float independently to maintain price stability following the breakdown of Bretton Woods. Under the Tun, the ringgit enjoyed a long period of stability. Legend has it that the ringgit was so petrified that it behaved While Tun Ismails devotion to his country was unwavering he was also a regionalist who held strong convictions on the need for a regional approach to the promotion of growth and financial stability in South East Asia. With foresight, he recognised very early on, before the word globalisation became fashionable that it was not possible to ignore the reality of the ever-growing interdependence of the world economy. The international nature of some of the financial problems faced by countries in the region even then, pointed to a need for closer cooperation among the central banks. With this in view, he worked towards laying the foundation in regional cooperation between Malaysia and its neighbours that has prevailed to this day. On the strength of his character and good intentions, he built relationships with his counterparts in the region that were sealed not with agreements and MOUs, but with a large measure of mutual trust, respect and dependability. Because of these relationships, we benefit immeasurably today from the formation of the South East Asian Central Banks (or better known as SEACEN) Grouping. It was the cooperation between SEACEN members that gave rise to the Annual SEACEN Conferences, the SEACEN Research Training Centre, the ASEAN Swap Arrangement and the South East Asian Voting Group at the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. These enduring relationships between SEACEN members continue to serve the region well to this day. The list of Tuns numerous contributions to central banking at both the national and international level goes on. In the span of 18 years as Governor of the Central Bank, Tun Ismail irreversibly changed the landscape of Malaysias financial system. Tun Ismail Chair at University Malaya The role of the Central Bank will continue to evolve with the changing times and circumstances. With an increasingly volatile and uncertain external environment and combined advances in technology and the communication fields, central banks with no doubt be faced with increasingly formidable challenges. Tun Ismails contributions have contributed to providing the foundation for the Bank to face these challenges with confidence and with purpose. For that, he has earned himself an important place in the economic history of Malaysia. In a tribute to honour Tun Ismail Mohamed Ali, the first Malaysian Central Bank Governor and in recognition of his considerable contribution to the country, I am pleased to announce the establishment of the Tun Ismail Chair in Monetary and Financial Economics at the University of Malaya, the oldest university in Malaysia. The establishment of the The Tun Ismail Ali Chair, is aimed at enhancing the academic excellence in the area of monetary and financial economics. Achieving excellence was strongly believed and practiced by Tun Ismail Mohamed Ali. The second and no less important objective of the Tun Ismail Chair is to achieve pragmatic scholarship: In this context, the aim is not to look for pure theory. That may be pursued by others further up the ivory tower. The intention here is to develop a generation of graduates that have their feet on the ground and hands on the keyboard, with an ability to deal with the reality and problems of today  and tomorrow. In this regard, it is envisaged that renowned academicians as well as reputable practicing economists whose areas of specialisation are on monetary and financial economics will be appointed to the Chair. We believe the Tun Ismail Chair will contribute towards building a strong foundation in the field of money and finance among the next generation of Malaysian economic graduates. Thus, the holder of the Chair will be expected to give lectures to students, to give at least one public lecture to the banking industry and to conduct workshops for faculties in Economics and Finance from other local universities. The holder is also expected to give guidance to a selected number of outstanding graduate students to prepare them for doctoral programme either with universities in Malaysia or abroad. The Tun Ismail Chair will be funded by an endowment fund of RM 12 million established and managed by Bank Negara Malaysia. It is expected that the fund will generate sufficient funds to cover the estimated annual costs of up to RM 1 million per year for maintaining the Chair. In so doing, we hope to attract top academicians from any part of the world to share their wisdom with us. The holder would be expected to be in Malaysia for a minimum of three months and a maximum of 12 months each year, the period to be entirely determined by the holder. We do not expect such top calibre persons to be able to come for longer than this period, as it would take them out of their mainstream. In addition, we aim to meet their high costs so as to ensure the best qualified person. in essence, the person appointed should be one who would have met Tun Ismail Mohamed Alis high standards. Bank Negara Malaysia hopes that the setting up of the Tun Ismail Chair will contribute towards efforts in enhancing the knowledge and expertise of local graduates in particular, and the academic and financial community in general, on issues relating to monetary and financial policies. Closing As we move into the 21st Century, we should not forget the legacy of Tun Ismail Ali - his person and his work and the eternal value of traditional virtues. Tun Ismail set impeccable standards of integrity and commitment to excellence. I am deeply honoured to be able to pay him this tribute, which can, at best, be inadequate for a man of Tun Ismails legendary stature. As a Governor, I am committed to uphold the traditions in the central bank, and to expand and strengthen the foundation for the development of an efficient and effective financial system that is able to withstand the economic cycle and thus contribute to overall macro economic stability and economic growth thereby securing sustainable prosperity as we enter the 21st Century. May his legacy continue to inspire us to excellence. Bank Negara Malaysia 28 August 2000

Title: Speech in conjunction with the Launching Ceremony of the National Strategy for Financial Literacy 2019-2023
text: Governor Dato' Dr. Zeti's Speech at the SEACEN Seminar "Impact of e-Banking and e-Commerce on Central Banking Funtions" Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Hotel Istana, Kuala Lumpur Speech/Interview Date: 09 Jan 2001 Language: English It is indeed my honour and pleasure to welcome Your Excellencies and delegates from the 12 SEACEN member countries to this 3-day SEACEN Seminar on the "Impact of E-Banking and E-Commerce on Central Banking Functions". I would like to also welcome you to Malaysia, and for those of you who are here in Malaysia for the first time, I hope you will have the opportunity to discover the country during your short visit here. Selamat Datang. The SEACEN seminar series have provided an excellent opportunity for member central banks to foster closer ties amongst central bankers, facilitating exchange of knowledge and experiences among the participants and enhancing the level of collaboration between central banks. I hope that you will walk away from this seminar with greater awareness on this important subject of the potential implications of new technology and emerging e-business models on the banking industry and central banking functions, and return home with new ideas and knowledge to deal with the issues and challenges posed in this rapidly changing business environment. The topic we have before us for this seminar is indeed very appropriate and timely for the new year. The remarkable technological advancements in the last decade has permeated several aspects of our economy and has offered boundless possibilities in the financial system. The introduction of Internet offers seamless opportunities, sweeping through the global system and challenging the existing business structures and systems. The rules today are being redefined, new players are emerging and new ways of doing things constantly challenge the way we think. For regulators, these changes pose a greater challenge in the promotion of financial stability and integrity. As such, this Seminar should serve as a forum for central bank supervisors in this region to deliberate the key issues on the supervisory and regulatory aspects and to maintain up to date knowledge on e-banking and e-commerce activities and to collaborate in these areas. These efforts are steps towards providing the foundation for a harmonised approach to the supervision of e-banking within the regulatory regional community, aimed at fulfilling the important supervisory responsibility of financial stability while at the same time developing an efficient market for the electronic delivery of banking services. Allow me to give our perspectives on some of the broad issues facing the financial system and central banking in this electronic age. In this electronic age, central banks continue to have the responsibility to manage the economy and the financial system to assure macro-economic and financial stability. In every country, however, the spread of e-money and e-commerce has raised questions about the role of the authorities in this more digitised market economy. As digital transactions become widespread, currency would essentially be issued by a variety of institutions. Some would even extend beyond the reach of our national boundaries. How then would monetary growth be managed? This would be compounded by whether control can be exercised over such institutions, in particular those new non-financial entrants into financial services. E-cash and e-commerce will make it increasingly difficult to define and measure both monetary aggregates, national income and wealth. How will the authorities monitor and track electronic transactions paid for with electronic cash. The commercial and financial institutions which record the transactions will be bypassed in this digital economy as direct e-cash transactions become the norm. For those transactions that take place in cyber space across borders, the issue of which authority has jurisdiction arises. In this new economy, the pace of financial innovation has intensified and has expanded the range of financial products requiring Central Banks to reaccess how we will meet our responsibilities. It has been argued that while the safety and soundness of the system necessitates greater government oversight, the changes brought about by the advances in technology has rendered the examination approach established earlier less relevant. It is argued that in this new environment, there should be greater reliance on market discipline. However, this requires markets to function efficiently and for consumers and markets to be well equipped with knowledge and understanding of the products and services and its implications and risks. In emerging markets, where the financial system is less developed, the task of the Central Bank is not only supervisory but developmental.
