Capacities and capability of institutions need to be enhanced, financial infrastructure needs to be put in place and consumers and markets educated accordingly. Among banks and bank regulators and supervisors, there seems to be agreement that e-banking activities should be supervised as with traditional banking activities, but with greater attention on risk management procedures, greater focus on processes and mechanisms and with greater co-ordination and co-operation among the banking supervisors as opposed to giving emphasis on actual portfolios and accounts. The supervisory processes for e-banking therefore needs to be sufficiently dynamic to supervise financial entities in the virtual community that operates across multiple localities, thus requiring more cooperation between bank supervisors, and also with the banking industry. With the development of the Internet and other cutting edge technology, this has become vital with the prospects that e-banking operations may emanate from a location outside the local jurisdiction, and introduced by non-licensed entities. In this connection, the role of the home and host country supervisors would need to be enhanced and clearly defined. In this regard, the formation of the Electronic Banking Group by the BIS (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision) in late 1999 is indeed an important step in the right direction to promote and enhance international co-operation and exchange of information among supervisors regarding e-banking risks and supervisory issues. The white papers of this group would also facilitate the adoption of a more similar approach by bank supervisors across countries, thus facilitating the need to address cross border issues. The trend for new entrants and existing banks to set up stand-alone banks or Internet-only banks requires our legal framework to be modernised to make them more realistic and consistent with the realities of the market. However, in moving forward, we need to proceed cautiously, facilitating innovation while ensuring prudent behaviour. While recognising e-banking transactions are more cost competitive compared to branch operations or even phone transactions, and that e-banks may be easy to set up, one needs to be mindful of the high start-up costs for an e-bank and the need to ensure security and safety of the system. Furthermore, these operations also require huge initial capital outlay as well as the need to provide adequate incentives to consumers in terms of attractive rates. This may result in negative or marginal returns in the short term. Recent reports in fact indicate that online banking has yet to live up to its expectations. Since their establishment, pure Internet banks only accounted for 0.02% of 9.6 billion in FDIC-insured deposits by year-end 1999. Nonetheless, customers have benefited as the new entrants have "forced" the existing players to be more competitive and efficient. To gain market share, the new entrants have resulted in keener competition by offering attractive deposit rates and new services, resulting in shifts in demand from the conventional providers of financial services to these new entrants. It is recognised that these developments also provide an increased range of products to a wider spectrum of consumers and businesses. While these activities may now be small in magnitude, if the trend persists in the financial market, it will require regulators to consider the implications on liquidity management, and the extent of coverage of the central bank's financial safety net for the deposits of Internet-only banks. Essentially, dealing with the implications of the rapid pace of development of e-banking requires supervisory agility, resources and changes to the existing rules and regulations. Central banks all over the world must therefore prepare themselves for the transition into this new business era. The new technology has essentially resulted in the convergence of products and services, blurring the lines between banks and non-financial institutions and bringing significant changes to the global financial markets. Businesses are increasingly using automated electronic networks to select, execute and process transactions. Technological progress has also made possible changes in market structure and business chains that have paved the way for further efficiency gains. During the transition period as conventional financial institutions adapt to this changing environment, we may see some disintermediation in the traditional banking functions and facilities, particularly in the retail payment area. Therefore, financial institutions need to innovate and build the necessary capacities and alliances to respond to these changes and to reintermediate and remain relevant. A further issue that needs to be addressed is the numerous issues and risks, which Internet presents. Appropriate monitoring system and policies needs to be put in place to deal with this. Essential in this process is the dissemination of accurate information to ensure the economic well-being of a financial system its stability. Security issues are another major source of concern in e-banking that needs to be addressed in an effective manner. Banks must examine their risks and the need for operating system security to maintain the integrity and reliability of their web servers, while allowing real-time, on-line electronic commerce, essential to Internet-based financial services. As security systems are continuously evolving with improving functionality, banks have to continuously progress and invest the new technology. Thus, in monitoring and managing the security threat, it is important for banks to have in place a strategic and proactive approach to information security and maintaining sufficient staff with information security expertise. Thus, it is extremely important for the regulators to address the broader issue of consumer protection and transparency framework, and the ability of the consumers to make informed decisions and take well-calculated actions. Finally, the Internet has enabled new forms of payment modes, such as digital money, person-to-person payments and barter trading through trade units instead of currencies. Some firms have already adopted the new e-commerce technologies, and others are increasingly realising the importance of making e-commerce an integral part of their businesses. However, it remains uncertain as to how quickly these technologies will change the business landscape. However, one thing is certain, ecommerce will speed up the process of globalisation and will expose the weaknesses in today' s marketing tools and commerce activities. These are a few of the major issues facing central bank today and I am sure the Seminar will explore further these and other important issues at greater length. To conclude, I must say how very pleased Bank Negara Malaysia is to be host to this Seminar. Today, we are in the period of learning and collaborating. It is recognised that e-banking is emerging as a powerful new force in the global economy. As corporations come to depend on e-commerce and extranets for their mission-critical business processes, the e-banking technology will become more and more important to our economic and ordinary life. Thus, we need to keep abreast with the new developments that affect the financial system and we need to co-operate to foster greater financial stability in our financial systems. Central banks must therefore continue to evolve, to remain effective in our central banking functions. While these developments have resulted in greater supervisory challenges, the advances in technology, have also enhanced the supervisory process. On our part we need to evaluate how we can modernise our approach to supervision and regulation, and improve our ability to assess the risks and to maintain an up to date information and knowledge base as well as to be in a position to recognise and deal with problems before they occur. The new technology should therefore also be used to develop new tools for supervisors to enhance the supervisory process. On this note, I am pleased to declare this seminar open and wish you a successful and beneficial seminar and a pleasant stay in Malaysia. Thank you. Bank Negara Malaysia 9 January 2001

Title: Speech at the Kijang Emas Scholarship Award Ceremony for Top Achievers in 2015 SPM Examination
text: Governor Dato' Dr. Zeti's Responses to Questions from BERNAMA Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 22 Feb 2001 Q.1: Several exchange rates of countries in this region have depreciated against the US dollar in recent months. Will it not be to Malaysia?s advantage to consider a depreciation of the exchange rate in order to preserve the competitiveness of its exports? Regional currencies experienced a depreciation in the range of 3.9% to 37.1% against the US dollar and the ringgit in 2000. However, since the beginning of this year, this trend has reversed and most have appreciated against the US dollar and the ringgit. In looking at the appropriateness of an exchange rate, countries do not just consider trade competitiveness. Countries facing depreciating currencies have in fact undertaken significant measures to resist the downward pressure on their currencies. A depreciating currency is not in the interest of a country and any competitive advantage derived from such a depreciation will only be temporary. Experience has shown that an exchange rate depreciation alone does not necessarily lead to a balance of payments surplus. This suggests that there are factors other than the exchange rate that are important in determining international competitiveness. There are also costs to using the exchange rate for competitive advantage. The recent financial crisis has also prominently highlighted the damage currency depreciations can do to the economy and financial system. The impact on private sector confidence is even more damaging. A depreciation of the exchange rate is likely to increase the cost of imports and result in higher inflationary pressures. Higher inflation will erode the competitive advantage derived from the currency depreciation. For countries that have high foreign debt, the currency depreciation will increase the cost of servicing the debt. The stability of the exchange rate is itself a competitive tool. For Malaysia, the peg against the US dollar has provided this stability and facilitated planning and pricing for manufacturers and traders. In our discussions with the private sector, particularly the manufacturers and traders, the feedback has been that the stability provided by the pegged exchange rate regime is beneficial and that it should be retained. Competitiveness in the international market place is only assured through increased productivity, product innovation, intense marketing and improvements in product quality. In the financial sector, Malaysia has also been able to undertake the financial sector restructuring at an accelerated pace and restore the health of the banking sector in this stable financial market environment. Malaysia has also been able to complete the consolidation of the banking sector. All this could not have been achieved in the time period that it has, if we had the kind of volatility and uncertainty that was experienced by several of the countries in the region. In determining a sustainable exchange rate, what is important is that the exchange rate be in line with the fundamentals of the economy. The current pegged rate of RM3.8 to the US dollar reflects our underlying fundamentals. Q.2: In recent months, foreign currency reserves of BNM have been on a declining trend. Is this an area of concern to the central bank? Under a pegged exchange rate regime, the stability of the exchange rate is obtained through higher volatility in the level of reserves. Adjustments in trade and capital flows will be reflected in temporary movements of reserves, rather than in volatility of the exchange rate. While there have been outflows, inflows will continue to emanate from trade and long-term capital inflows. These inflows and the existing high level of reserves provide the necessary capacity for Malaysia to finance outflows arising from the normal course of business transactions and the sentiment driven flows. Q.3: You mentioned FDI flows as contributing to the reserves in 2001. Can you give an indication of how large you expect these inflows to be? In spite of the uncertainty surrounding the growth prospects of the world economy in 2001, we expect the inflows of foreign direct investment into Malaysia to continue. This is based on the significant approvals given for foreign direct investment of US5.2 billion by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) in 2000 and US1.1 billion in investments in the multimedia super corridor approved by the Multimedia Development Corporation. Indications from the manufacturing sector are that, despite the slowdown in the US economy, the planned expansion of factory space will continue. FDI flows are also expected to increase following foreign acquisitions in selected industries in the services sector. Q.4: What would be BNM?s action in the event that inflows, especially from trade, are not coming in? The current account is expected to continue to register a surplus in 2001. Any moderation in export growth due to the slowdown of the US economy is expected to be offset by a similar reduction in imports and lower payments for services. Therefore, we expect the net inflow from the trade balance to remain in surplus and this will continue to serve as a buffer to finance outflows. Hence, we expect the reserves to be within comfortable levels. Q.5: At its current pegged level of RM3.8 to the US dollar, is the exchange rate undervalued or overvalued, or would you consider it as being fairly valued? Our assessment is that the ringgit is now close to its equilibrium value and is in line with the economic fundamentals. At the end of 1999, we assessed the ringgit to be undervalued by about 6-8%, based on its real effective exchange rate then. Over the span of last year, developments in the exchange rates of our trading partners and changes in inflation rates, have caused the real effective exchange rate of the ringgit to appreciate by 4.8% by end-2000. Therefore, the degree of undervaluation of the ringgit has diminished. In addition, the majority of the feedback we have received from the private sector is that the pegged regime continues to be beneficial and that it should be maintained at its current pegged level. In 2000, the regional currencies have depreciated due to specific developments in their respective countries. These countries recognise the negative implications of a depreciating currency and have responded with interventions and by raising interest rates. Right now, the assessment is there is no fundamental misalignment of the ringgit. In the current environment, there have been positive developments arising from the efforts by the major countries to avoid misalignment of their currencies and destablising global financial markets. Bank Negara Malaysia 22 February 2001

Title: Dinner Address at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Closing Dinner
text: Governor Dato' Dr. Zeti's Responses to Questions from The Edge Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 12 Mar 2001 Question 1: Why have reserves been falling steadily since May 2000 despite strong trade surpluses? Is this a cause for concern? Why? Why not? During the year 2000, we saw the international reserves increase in the early part of the year and then decline during the remaining part of the year. For the year as a whole the reserves declined by USD1 billion. Changes in the level of reserves essentially reflect underlying trade transactions and capital flows. Whether a country should be concerned as to the movements in its international reserve level depends on the underlying reasons for the changes in the reserve levels. The nature of the outflows that are occurring in the current period can certainly be distinguished from that which occurred during the period 1997-1998. While during the latter period, the outflows were dominated by short-term portfolio outflows, the outflows in the current period are in fact dominated by increases in transactions that reflect a stronger economy. More specifically, the outflows reflect the higher deficit on the services account, higher external debt repayments and significant increases in overseas investments abroad by Malaysian corporations in ventures that are viewed to be of strategic benefit to Malaysia. Following the increase in debt repayments, Malaysia has improved its external debt exposure. External debt to GNP has declined to 50.5% at end 2000 from 57.8% at end-1999. In addition, the maturity structure of the debt has been lengthened with the decline in short-term debt. The international reserves are now 6.3 times short-term debt compared with 5.1 times at the end of 1999. Even if we take into account the long-term debt due in the next 12 months, reserves are still three times larger. I would also like to emphasise that Malaysia?s reserves are unencumbered and usable. In addition, another factor that explain the decline in reserves in US dollar terms is the revaluation book loss due to the appreciation of the US dollar against the other major currencies. Given the reasons for which the outflows has taken place this does not raise concern. In addition, other considerations need to be taken into account. Firstly, that these outflows takes place when Malaysia had a high level of reserves. Our starting point was a high level of reserves. If reserve levels were low, there would be some vulnerability. Secondly, looking forward, it can be expected that our trade surplus will continue. While exports can be expected to moderate following slower US growth we can expect imports to also moderate given that the import of intermediate goods and certain imported services are related to export performance. Thirdly, external debt levels have strengthened thereby reducing Malaysia?s external vulnerability to international interest rate and exchange rate developments abroad. Question 2: In recent months, you have mentioned that the outflow in foreign reserves has been attributed to things like private and public foreign debt repayment, interest servicing, dividends and profits, reverse investments, and short term portfolio fund outflows. Can Bank Negara provide an actual breakdown on the exact amount of outflow in each of these components? If a monthly breakdown for the last year is not possible, could you provide a breakdown for the last year (2000) or for the last two quarters (Q3 & Q4 2000)? The net international reserves held by BNM declined by RM3.7 billion or US1 billion to RM113.5 billion (US29.9 billion) as at end-2000. As at end-February 2001, the reserves amounted to RM110.1 billion (US29 billion). The reserves level is adequate to finance 4.3 months of retained imports and is 6.3 times the short-term external debt. The breakdown can certainly be provided. As I mentioned these transactions reflect strong economic activity. Allow me to go into the details of outflows in 2000: The net outflows for the payment of services and transfers amounted to RM48.3 billion or US12.7 billion. These outflows include interest servicing and the payment of dividends and profits. The pattern of these outflows are not significantly different from previous years. Payments abroad from other services were higher in 2000 due to the buoyant trade-related activities and overall strong performance in the domestic economy. The higher interest rates abroad have also led to Malaysian exporters to keeping their export proceeds abroad for the maximum period allowed. It has also prompted an increase in trade credits extended to foreign importers. However, as the interest rate differential is rapidly narrowing, the incentive to maintain funds abroad will diminish. In addition, some export earnings are maintained in foreign currency accounts with banks in Malaysia. This represents some decentralisation of reserves. This is a positive development as holdings of foreign exchange by Malaysians will reduce the calls on Bank Negara?s reserves. Net overseas investments by the Malaysian corporate sector of RM7.7 billion (US2 billion), mainly in telecommunications, plantation and power projects. Net outflow of portfolio funds amounted to RM4 billion (US1.1 billion) from the External/Special External Accounts. In the first five months of 2000, there was a net inflow of funds (RM8.3 billion or US2.2 billion) with the impending reinstatement of Malaysia in the MSCI index at end-May 2000. During the period June and December there was an outflow of portfolio capital (RM12.3 billion or US3.2 billion). There was also the usual interest servicing of external debt in 2000. But during 2000, there was a much higher repayment of medium and long-term external debt by the Federal Government and the NFPEs. Together with the private sector, repayments amounted to RM15.8 billion (US4.2 billion). The loan repayments by the private sector reflected debt restructuring exercises by the corporate sector to refinance external loans through issuance of domestic private debt securities with lower interest costs. Prepayments also occurred because of higher interest rates abroad. Repayment of short-term debt by the non-bank private sector and the increase in net external assets of banking institutions amounted to RM8.8 billion (US2.3 billion). This reflected net inter-bank placements abroad for hedging of trade relatedactivities. Foreign exchange revaluation losses amounted to RM5.3 billion (US1.4 billion) with the appreciation of the US dollar against other major foreign currencies. Question 3: With outflow of portfolio funds presumably at a minimum (they've been fleeing for 2 years), that suggests that the highest outflows came from the other components. Is this true? Historically, do we usually have such high levels of debt repayment, interest servicing, reverse investments and dividends and profit payouts? If not, why the spike in recent months? As I have mentioned, the outflows have been due to other components other than portfolio capital. The outflows of portfolio capital has been less than previous years. In terms of debt repayment, this was high during the early to mid-1990s but slowed down during the crisis years of 1997-1998. But with the strong recovery that has been experienced in 1999-2000, the opportunity has been taken to repay and refinance external loans with lower cost domestic sources. Overseas investment has also started to increase again with the recovery of the Malaysian economy. Interest servicing on the external debt was higher in 2000, reflecting the higher interest rates abroad following monetary tightening by the major central banks in the industrial countries. Repayments of debt were also higher as corporates restructured and reduced external obligations. Overseas investment was also higher due mainly to timing factors of earlier commitments. The magnitude of outflows of dividends and profits has been in line with historical trends. Question 4: Some economists are concerned with the high levels of errors and omissions recorded in the latest balance of payment numbers. Is this a concern? Are the errors and omissions growing? In the first three quarters of 2000, the Errors and Omission amounted to RM8.1 billion (USD). After adjusting for exchange revaluation losses of RM5.4 billion, the unexplained amount reflect the normal errors and inconsistencies that occur in the course of compilation of the balance of payments statistics. The amount of E&O of RM2.7 billion amounts to 1.6% of the total merchandise trade and therefore is small. In the guidelines on balance of payments compilation issued by the IMF, the tolerable E&O level is below 5% of total merchandise trade. Question 5: Some economists suggest that the continued decline in reserves is mainly due to exporters keeping their earnings overseas to take advantage of higher interest rates, as they are allowed six months before they have to repatriate their earnings. When did this start happening and are the numbers growing? The guideline for exporters requires payments for exports to be received in the prescribed manner when contractually due, and not later than 6 months from the date of exports. It is not correct that many exporters have applied for permission to extend the period for bringing back their export proceeds. We have an efficient banking system to administer the inflow and outflow of funds. Based on the statistical returns submitted by banks, export receipts have certainly been brought back to the country, which are largely supported by Letters of Credit. Part of the decline in reserves reflects the normal leads and lags in the repatriation of export proceeds by the exporters. The factors that would determine the leads and lags include the interest rate differentials. The higher interest rates abroad in 19992000 has prompted the funds to be maintained abroad for the full six months from the date of exports. However, with the interest rate differentials likely to continue to narrow; the incentive to do this will diminish. Question 6: Speculation is rife that businesses and individuals are sneaking money out of the country, either legitimately by declaring (and repatriating) high dividends, overseas investments, through contra transactions, or via various "unofficial" means and channels. The unofficial means being talked about include under-invoicing exports and over-reporting imports. Can BNM confirm which of these you see or suspect to be happening? How rampant do you think these occurrences are and what is their impact on our reserves? Businesses and individuals can freely make payments abroad for trade and services transactions. Payments include payment for imports, interest payments and principal repayment of external loans and payment for education and other services. Only payments for investment abroad in excess of the equivalent of RM10,000 require approval by BNM. Approval is given under highly transparent criteria as reflected in the larger outflow of overseas investments by Malaysians. The foreign exchange administration rules are implemented transparently and efficiently by the banking system, and payments abroad can be effected through the banking channel. As previous trends show, it is normal for higher dividend pay-out in line with improved business performance. Residents are also freely allowed to offset their service receivables against payables except for export proceeds. Data compiled and published by BNM explains the purposes of payments abroad. While there may be instances of transfer of ringgit abroad in the form of cash carried by travellers that are beyond the permitted amount of RM1,000, this practice is not by any means widespread or rampant. Question 7: Do you expect reserves to continue falling in the coming months? Why? Why not? Where do you foresee the major drains on reserves to come from this year? Does the government plan to repay more foreign debt soon? For 2001, continued inflows of trade surplus and long-term capital are expected. This will cushion the outflows arising from the normal course of business transactions and sentiment-driven flows. Current estimates are that the current account of the balance of payments will continue to register a surplus. Following the slowdown of the US economy, a moderation in export growth is expected, particularly in the first half of the year. This moderation will, to some extent, be offset by a similar reduction in imports and lower payments for services given that these external payments are related to export activity. Therefore, we expect the net inflow from the trade balance to remain in surplus and this will continue to serve as a buffer to finance outflows. Other service payments are also expected to be lower in 2001. Hence, we expect the reserves to be maintained within comfortable levels. In 2001, there will again be the normal servicing of the external debt by the public and private sectors. However, Federal Government scheduled repayments will be lower. While scheduled repayment for NFPEs will remain high in 2001, the repayments will be financed by export proceeds and some new borrowings. Question 8: Is there a danger of Malaysia's foreign reserves falling to below the critical level (of being able to sustain 3 months of imports)? When do you think this will happen? What is the central bank doing to prevent this from happening? During the currency crisis in 1997-1998, the international reserves of our nation remained above USD20 billion. These reserves were unencumbered and Malaysia did not have forward positions. The reserves at that time was equivalent to 3.3 months of imports. In looking at the adequacy of reserves, it is important to look at the factors that would determine the future trend of reserves as well as the economic and financial background against which these developments take place. Given the strong fundamentals of the economy and the flexibility the authorities have to maintain pro-growth macro policies, it will contribute to ensuring a positive environment. Efforts to strengthen the banking system further have also yielded results. The banking sector, capitalisation levels are now much stronger (RWCR exceeding 12%) and banks have increased their resilience to face adverse external developments. Looking forward, other positive developments include the interest rate differential between Malaysia and the United States which was 3.15% at end-2000 is now narrowed in early 2001, the interest rate differential narrowed to 2.13% following the reduction in the Fed Funds Rate by 100 basis points. Market expectations are for further reduction in the US interest rates. Secondly, the significantly import growth have been mainly for export production, so that a slowdown in exports would prompt lower imports, thus allowing for a continued surplus in the trade balance. These factors will support reserve levels to be within comfortable levels. Bank Negara Malaysia 12 March 2001

Title: Remarks at the Centre of Excellence (ACE) Ground Breaking Ceremony
text: Governor's Statement at the 2000 Annual Report Press Conference Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Bank Negara Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur Speech/Interview Date: 28 Mar 2001 Language: English In the tradition of Bank Negara Malaysia, I have the pleasure to officially release the Bank Negara Malaysia Annual Report for the year 2000. The report releases the Bank's Annual Accounts for the year 2000, and provides an analysis of the economic and monetary developments in 2000, and gives the official forecast for the Malaysian economy for year 2001. The Malaysian economy recorded a stronger growth with significantly improved economic and financial fundamentals in the year 2000. This performance has placed Malaysia in a stronger position to respond to the more challenging economic environment in the year 2001. Real GDP recorded a high growth of 8.5%, in 2000, well above the 5.8% achieved in 1999. While growth was supported by strong external demand, it was rising private consumption and the strong revival in domestic investment that was the main contributor to economic growth. The strong private investment was seen in several industries where levels of production and capacity utilisation had expanded in response to rising demand. As a result, labour market conditions also improved significantly in 2000 with the unemployment rate estimated to have declined to 3.1%. Policy strategies to diversify the economic structure of Malaysia continued in the year 2000 to further deepen and widen the industrial base, to enhance the development of the services sector as a second engine of growth and to venture into new areas of growth. In 2000, the manufacturing sector, value added grew strongly by 21% with significant increases in production of both export and domestic-oriented industries, setting a new record for manufacturing production. Reflecting the overall growth of the economy, value added in the services sector also rose by 4.7%. Value added in the construction sector turned around to register a positive growth of 1.1%. Value added in the agriculture sector remained positive despite sharply lower growth in palm oil production and declines in rubber and cocoa production. The underlying strength of the economy is also reflected by the improved fundamentals. Despite higher oil prices, lower excess capacity, strong demand and employment conditions, inflation was contained below 2%. On the external front, the external balance remained strong as the large surplus in the current account and sustained long-term capital inflows provided a buffer to outflows for repayment of debt and overseas investment by Malaysia. The repayment of foreign debt by the private sector has led to a reduction in Malaysia's external exposure and a further improvement in the maturity structure of the external debt. The year also saw significant progress in the restructuring of the financial sector, which was achieved at a lower than expected cost of 7% of GDP. The positive and stable economic and financial environment also allowed for the successful completion of the banking sector consolidation exercise during the year. To-date, nine banking groups involving 51 banking institutions have completed the merger exercise resulting in the consolidation of 96% of the assets of the domestic banking institutions. In addition, the banking system has emerged stronger with a higher level of capitalisation and profitability and the improved portfolio quality. In the management of the economy, fiscal prudence was maintained in 2000 to ensure that the financial position of the Government remained strong. At the end of 2000, the total debt of the Federal Government was contained at 37% of GDP and external debt of the Government accounted for 5.5% of GDP. Debt servicing remained low, accounting for 16% of operating expenditure. In monetary management, low interest rates was maintained to support the growth process. During the year loan growth improved to record an increase of 5.4%. The issues of PDS also expanded, so that total financing comprising, loans plus PDS, rose by 9% in 2000. Growth of the Malaysian economy in the year 2001 will be affected by the less encouraging global economic conditions. In an environment of stronger than expected deceleration of growth in the U.S., a weak performance of the Japanese economy and uncertainty in the global financial markets, economic growth in the year 2001 is expected to moderate to 5%. The strong fundamentals prevailing and the previous prudent policies however, have accorded Malaysia sufficient policy flexibility to implement pro-growth measures to stimulate domestic demand and raise GDP growth in the year 2001 to closer to 6%. The new pre-emptive measures announced by YAB Perdana Menteri yesterday are measures to counter the effects of implications of the stronger than expected slowdown in the industrial economies. These measures directed at stimulating domestic demand can be expected to compensate for the slower external demand without creating new risks. The ample liquidity position, the stronger banking system and the more active private debt securities market will enable non-inflationary financing of this growth. The fiscal expenditure is directed at industries with strong domestic linkages and with minimum import content so as to maintain the favourable current account position in the balance of payments. In the immediate term the stimulus programme will in particular benefit the construction and services sectors. Increased allocations are also directed at projects and programmes that would lead to a strengthening of long-term productivity. The monetary policy stance will continue to remain accommodative to support economic growth. The current account position in the balance of payments in 2001 is expected to remain in surplus accounting for 6.8% of GNP in 2001. Inflows of long-term capital is also expected to be sustained, and together with the continued current account surplus, will be able to cushion outflows. With the prospect of low domestic inflation, strong financial position of the Government, low level of foreign indebtedness, the current pegged exchange rate at RM3.80 per US dollar remains sustainable and consistent with economic fundamentals. The growth momentum built over the last two years, the strength of the economic fundamentals and the implementation of the new measures are expected to generate sufficient impetus for output in the domestic economy to expand by 6% in real terms in 2001. The Government has been pre-emptive in ensuring that the Malaysian economy can sustain growth. It is therefore, important that the private sector contribute to this growth process by responding positively to these initiatives. Bank Negara Malaysia 28 March 2001

Title: Special Address at the Chartered Banker Conferment Ceremony
text: Transcript of Interview with Governor Dato' Dr. Zeti's on TV3's Money Matters Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 16 Apr 2001 Zalina (Host) : We have seen the depreciating of currencies in the region in recent months. However, Bank Negara had reiterated its stand that the ringgit should remain 3.80 to the US dollar. What are the risks of depreciating the ringgit as oppossed to maintaining it at its peg? Dato' Dr Zeti : To respond to that question, we need to recognise the importance of the exchange rate in our economy and our financial system. This is because we are open, the volume of trade is two times the size of our economy. The volume of foreign direct investments is one quarter to one third of total investment in a year. Therefore we want an exchange rate regime that facilitates trade and investment. Therefore we don't want an exchange rate regime that is prone to wide swings, we don't want an exchange rate regime that is prone to crisis. And we don't want an exchange rate that will respond to short term developments. If we look in the context of the current environment it would certainly not be to our benefit to depreciate the currency. We assess the currency now to be at fair value and if we were to depreciate or allow the currency to depreciate, we do not see any gains from competitiveness, in the sense that any form of depreciation for any country is usually accompanied by higher prices, higher inflation, higher import cost and higher cost of servicing our external exposure. All these would contribute to higher cost of doing business which would wipe out any gains derived from depreciating the currency. Furthermore, this generally precipitates competitive depreciation and as a result, in relative terms, it would wipe out the gains for an individual country. Thirdly, if you look at the current environment where there's an economic slowdown occuring in the industrial countries, particularly in the US, there will be a slowing down in external demand. Therefore, if you adjust your prices through the exchange rate by 5 to 10 % it is unlikely that you are going to get increases in demand in an environment where demand is slowing down. In effect, on balance, we assess that there would be no advantage and it would not be in our interest to precipitate greater uncertainty to allow either the exchange rate to float in this kind of environment or to adjust the peg. Zalina : Rumours of devaluation has badly hurt the local stock market, as foreign players chose to liquidate their positions now, rather than face the possibility of a shrinking ringgit. What is your reply to the market belief that the local currency is, in fact, overvalued? Dato' Dr Zeti : We assess that our ringgit is at fair value at this point in time. If you recall in early 2000 last year we experienced significant inflows when it was expected that Malaysia would be reinstated in the MSCI Index. We experienced significant inflows, and there was a rally in the stock market. At that time it was said that the ringgit be appreciated and that it should be appreciated to 3.20, and some even said 3.00. And now within such a short period of time, of less than 12 months, it is suggested that the ringgit should be depreciated to 4.00 or 4.20 when in fact our fundamentals have been strengthened compared to twelve months ago. If you look at Malaysia's report card, in particular, against all the reasons why it is sometimes suggested that a currency system is not sustainable. One, is the level of foreign indebtedness ? on this note, Malaysia has strengthened its position. We have repaid our debts, we have reduced our foreign indebtedness, we have improved the maturity structure of our debt in that we have reduced the short term portion of that debt, and Malaysia's external position is therefore strong in that respect. We have also strengthened our banking system. We certainly do not have a fragile banking system. During the last two years, the capitalization has improved, the quality of portfolio has improved, as reflected in the low level of non performing loans and the higher level of capitalization and the improved profitablity of the banking system. And we have in fact consolidated the banking system. We took the opprtunity last year to complete that exercise. We have also favourable fundamentals, that inflation is low and finally, we have a strong level of reserves, even at this point, USD27 billion. We do not have forward positions. These reserves are therefore unencumbered and usable. And that is why, we feel that suggestions that the currency is overvalued is based on sentiment and on short term factors. As I have highlighted earlier, if you have such wide swings in response to short term developments in your exchange rate, it will be impossible to conduct business. Zalina : 27 billion, unencumbered and usable. At what point would you consider putting out warning signals? Dato' Dr Zeti : Well this would not be as straightforward as that. It is very unfortunate that people pay attention to one figure rather than looking at why reserves adjusted or what accounted for the movement in the reserves level. It does not reflect capital flight taking place. Zalina : Is the continuing decline not a cause of concern for Bank Negara? Dato' Dr Zeti : You need to look at the reason for the decline. If the reason was due to capital flight - we would be concerned. But in the month that you're talking about, that is the month of March, we had a decline of almost one billion. This was due to an exchange revaluation loss, an unrealised revaluation loss, because we make a revaluation adjustment at the end of every quarter. We used to do it at the end of the year, but it was such a major adjustment that we now do it every quarter. The central bank reserves are diversified, the currency composition is diversified in terms of the major currencies, that is the US dollar, the euro and the yen. As a result of the appreciation of the US dollar and the depreciation of euro and the yen, we have a revaluation loss. But as currencies adjust over time, given that our management of our reserves is not based on short term movements, we take into account a more medium term outlook, these adjustments are therefore absorbed through our revaluation adjustment that take place. Zalina : You've mentioned that there is no capital flight, but foreign fund managers at the same time, are seen to be liquidating their positions on the stock market - is the situation serious enough to warrant a mechanism to mitigate the outflow of funds? Dato' Dr Zeti : Well, there's probably activity of foreign funds liquidating their positions in the stock market in response to developments in global stock markets where we have seen this to occur. But, we have not seen the kind of foreign portfolio outflow that corresponds to this liquidation. For example, in the year to second quarter of the year 2000, yes, we did see portfolio capital outflow take place. The funds that came in during the first quarter did flow out in the second and third quarters. But however, in the more recent months, in first quarter of this year, we have not seen significant portfolio outflows. Given that our ringgit is less vulnerable to speculative attacks since we already have in place the control of noninternationalisation of the ringgit and we have a pegged exchange rate regime; we do not feel any further mechanism is required on portfolio flows. There will continue to be a free inflow and outflow of portfolio funds. Zalina : There are rumours saying there's a run on US dollars in Malaysia. Allegedly, there is a shortage of the greenback among money changers. Is Bank Negara aware of this? Dato' Dr Zeti : We don't think that's correct at all. Certainly anyone can walk into any bank and get the foreign currency that they require. At the time even when we fixed the exchange rate and when there were suggestions that the black market could emerge, we imported significant amounts of foreign currency notes, to make sure that there was an adequate supply. So no, we don't think that this is the case. Zalina : If re-pegging the ringgit each time to suit market conditions seem like a short term solution, doesn't this strengthen the argument for a floating exchange rate? Dato' Dr Zeti : Well, if you look at the experience of currency adjustments, different industries obviously will be affected in different ways, but in all our discussions with the manufacturers and exporters. What they have said to us is if we ask them to choose between competitiveness and stability, their choice is stability and predictibility. And if we were in a floating exchange rate regime, we probably in the first quarter of last year have appreciated to RM3.00 in this situation, there would have been concerns of rising costs, of imports, and rising costs of their external exposure. On the other hand, if in the current environment we were to respond to short term movements and allow the currency to depreciate to 4, 4.20, 4.50 and so on, there would be concerns on why the currency is being allowed to depreciate. The memory is perhaps very short . We forget that when we moved from RM2.50 to RM2.80 and then to 3, in waves of adjustment that occurred over 18-month period, there were concerns and questions raised as to when this depreciation was going to stop, when was this currency depreciation going to stablise? In our view, Malaysia has the opportunity to make all the competitive gains through efficiency gains. The government on its part has made several initiatives to provide a positive economic environment and to keep the cost of doing business in Malaysia low. This is the only way competitiveness can be sustained. As I mentioned, any depreciation by one country would precipitate depreciation by other countries and this could even occur by contagion. It may not even occur by the choice of the country. It may be viewed by the market that the country would no longer be competitive and therefore precipitate further downward adjustments of a particular currency. Therefore it is really to no countries? advantage because in relative terms in the end, the competitive gain is not there. And in the meantine, the countries concerned would have experienced the uncertainty and instability. We already know from our experience in 1997 ? 1998 that it leads to economic contraction and higher prices and inflation. Zalina : What about the suggestion that we try a crawling peg, where the ringgit is allowed to move within a certain band? Dato' Dr Zeti : Well, the experience of those who moved within a band in an unstable period, the band is often tested and therefore destabilised. For a country, whatever exchange rate regime, it is operating, I think it is important to look at whether the underlying fundamentals can support the regime; whether it's a floating exchange rate regime, whether it is a band or whether it's a pegged exchange rate regime; policies needs to be directed to make sure that the underlying fundamentals will support that exchange rate regime. In other words, a low level of inflation and sound financial position of the government, sound banking system; all these would support the sustainability of the exchange rate regime. Bank Negara Malaysia 16 April 2001

Title: Opening Address at the INCEIF Endowment Fund (IEF) Launch Dinner
text: Governor Dato' Dr. Zeti's Interview with The Star Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 03 May 2001 Question 1: Banks are at various stages of taking off as merged entities. How do you view their progress so far? The merger programme of the banking institutions has resulted in the consolidation of 51 banking institutions into 10 banking groups. The mergers which involved the consolidation of 96% of the total assets of the banking institutions was achieved with minimum disruption and dislocation to the system. This has been a major accomplishment by the domestic banking industry. The domestic banking groups are now in a position to reap greater benefits from economies of scale, through greater investment in technology and the more substantive pool of skilled staff. This will allow the banking institutions to make further gains on efficiency and competitiveness with each banking institution having attained the minimum of shareholders funds of RM2 billion and total assets of RM25 billion. Of importance is that the valuation during the mergers has been market determined. Furthermore, the mergers were achieved without any disruption to the intermediation process. Lending activities have continued to improve and the financial restructuring has progressed to an advanced stage. In particular, the financial restructuring was achieved at minimum costs. Moreover, new developments, including the introduction of internet banking has remained on track. The period of consolidation also saw an improvement in asset quality, capitalisation and profitability of the banking institutions. With the legal mergers now completed, the focus is now on the operational integration process so that the banking groups can operate as a single entity. Amongst others, this involves the harmonisation of the computer systems, mapping of the different job grades and pay structures and the rationalisation of branches. To date, more than half that is, six banking groups have already completed their systems integration, while the remaining three groups are expected to complete the process in June of this year. Based on the rationalisation plans that have been submitted, staff dislocation is expected to be contained. To minimise the impact of this rationalisation, a comprehensive retraining and re-skilling programme has been developed with the co-operation of the major players and Institut Bank Bank Malaysia (IBBM) to facilitate a smooth transition of the affected staff into new areas in the financial industry and to other industries in the economy. The completion of the legal and operational mergers will place the Malaysian banking institutions in a better position to respond to the forces of change, in particular, to advances in technology and the greater demands for more customised and differentiated products and services by consumers and businesses. It will allow the banking institutions to be less vulnerable and more resilient to external developments and thus be in a better position to contribute to the economic growth process and the development of the nation. Question 2: By the end of this year, what are some of the achievements that you hope to see in the banking sector? The financial sector masterplan (FSMP) launched earlier this year outlines the medium and long-term strategies for the development of the financial sector. Under the first phase of the FSMP, the focus would be to enhance the capacity and capabilities of domestic banking institutions before proceeding to the second phase of the development towards a more competitive environment. Having achieved industry consolidation, domestic banking institutions would be expected to enhance the range of financial products and services as well as to engage actively in cross-selling their products in order to increase group efficiency and effectiveness. Banking institutions would also be expected to establish individual targets in terms of performance, efficiency and service quality that will be benchmarked against international standards. Of importance is for the banking institutions to be able to provide the range of products and services at a more competitive pricing. Banking institutions need to recognise that inefficient players can expect to be eventually displaced. To be competitive the complete range of financial services need to be provided at the lowest cost. From the technology front, greater adoption of technology should also be expected within the industry at all levels, from back office to the front desk. As the domestic banking institutions have been given one and half years head start vis-?-vis the incumbent foreign banks with regard to offering the full-range internet banking services, the expectation is for the banking institutions to take the opportunity, establish the learning curve and demonstrate a firm commitment to their electronic banking strategy. Improvements would also be expected in the area of risk management, which would continue to be one of the most important supervisory focuses. With large pool of resources after the merger process, banking institutions are expected to enhance further their risk management systems and capabilities. Specifically, all banking institutions would be expected to adopt best practices outlined in the Credit Risk Management Guidelines to be issued by BNM. This is an important element that would contribute towards ensuring financial stability. The greater amount of resources available through the merger should be managed well and fully utilized to allow the banks to cater for the demands of the larger pool of customers in a more effective and efficient manner. Greater involvement in financing the various sectors within the economy, in particular the small and medium sized industries, the services sector, the high technology sectors will become increasingly more important in our economy. It is important that activities of all levels in the country has access to these financial services. Banking institutions are therefore expected to improve their skills in financing the specialised sectors within the economy. Such skills would be important to ensure financing to these sectors. Banking institutions also need to be part of the process of meeting the social agenda in the most effective and efficient manner. Banking institutions' involvement would also be expected in initiating effective consumer education programmes which would serve towards putting the foundation for active consumerism that will become one of the key drivers of improvement in service quality and efficiency of banking institutions. Finally, in this more challenging year, in which the external environment is less favourable and in which growth will be driven by the domestic sector, access to bank credit will be of vital importance to support the growth process. Over reaction to external developments, having a short-term outlook and not looking beyond the immediate term will be among the factors that will contribute to destabilise the situation further. Bankers are therefore expected to take a long-term perspective in their business actions and decisions and not to over react to short-term developments that is driven by sentiment. What is surely important is for the banking institutions to ensure the sustainability of their profitability in the future. This certainly cannot be achieved without economic stability. While there are several important elements that will determine the country?s overall performance, banking institutions will need to recognise that they are an important player that is key to the country?s overall resilience and performance. Question 3: What are some of the areas that banks should do more to educate consumers especially in view of the changing financial sector landscape? Banking institutions are responsible for product transparency and to allow consumers access to better information. Active consumerism would need to be developed through the consumers having better understanding of financial products and services, their rights and responsibilities, as well as the available avenues for redress. With respect to increasing product transparency, banking institutions would be expected to develop clearly defined guidelines for comparable disclosure of all fees, interest rates, yields and other standard product features, in order to achieve more complete disclosure to consumers for all financial products. Banking institutions are also expected to develop a dictionary of common terms used to describe and compare products and standardise disclosure rules in formats consistent with internationally recognised best practices to allow clear and transparent analysis and comparison of product features. In providing avenue for redress, an effective mechanism to address consumer related issues such as through the availability of complaint desks should be established by all banking institutions. Consumers should be made aware of this mechanism and should be encouraged to pursue formal and legal redress if they suffer harm due to purchase of financial products and services. In a broader context, a well structured consumer education programme needs to be implemented on a widespread basis through various means such as publications, dissemination through mainstream media, roadshows and integrating into the curriculum in schools and institutes of higher learning. In particular, this needs to be targeted at retail customers who are generally less well informed compared to corporate customers. Banking institutions are expected to play their role actively in these initiatives. With respect to specific groups of borrowers such as the small- and medium-sized industries (SMIs), the education programme would go beyond understanding individual products and services, to include greater understanding of financial planning and management. Consumers should constantly be encouraged to take advantage of the availability of new and more innovative sources of information such as the internet, to increase their awareness of developments in the banking sector. In the long run, better- informed customers could increase competitive pressure in the financial sector for more efficient and effective delivery of banking services. Question 4: Are you satisfied with the level of innovation and quality of services offered by banks? Please elaborate. Certainly, banking institutions have made significant improvements in terms of the range of products that are offered over the years. However, there is room for greater product and process innovation by domestic banking institutions in the future. As the domestic market become increasingly more competitive, the pressure for the provision of quality services will increase. With regards to the level of quality of services, in particular among the domestic banking institutions, there are still significant gaps to be narrowed in order to be at par with international standards, especially with respect to front office or counter services. As society develops, customers will demand for greater convenience and efficiency. There is also a greater demand for more personalised services or products that are specifically tailored and customised to the individual customer and business requirements. Banking institutions therefore need to be more responsive to these changing demands and the expectations for more differentiated high quality services. As domestic banking institutions enhance their capabilities in terms of level of technology, skills as well as research and development, progress should take place in this front. Moving forward, banking institutions would be expected to embark on various strategic alliances in their pursuit to enhance their existing capabilities. Significant benefits exist from collaborating and co-operating with other banking institutions and non-banking institutions, to gain access for example to cutting-edge technology, skills and scale. Alliances with non-banking institutions such as telecommunication operators and information and communication technology (ICT) companies will also increase the level of innovation amongst banking institutions. Question 5: In view of the global situation, what would be some of the challenges facing the banking sector in Malaysia? As the domestic economy become the key driver of economic growth, one of the immediate challenges for the banking sector would be to support the growth of domestic industries by providing the required type of financing. With the changing domestic landscape, and as the domestic economy becomes increasingly diversified, the nature of financial requirements will become more diversified, ranging from the requirements of large corporates to small and medium-sized industries (SMIs), the traditional activities and new industries involving high technology and knowledge contents. To meet the specific needs and be able to assess risks related to these industries, banking institutions would need to equip themselves with new skills. Small and medium-sized enterprises, particularly those in the early stage of business, often face difficulty in obtaining bank credit as they lack the collateral and the track record usually required by banks. This would require enhanced ability to assess the viability of the business. The challenge for the banks, therefore, is to be able to assess the business viability of these enterprise in order to ensure appropriate, and reliable earning forecasts. It is critical for banks to be able to develop appropriate risk pricing models and tailor a suitable financing structure to fit the needs of these businesses, while continuing to operate profitably. The intensifying process of globalisation and liberalisation would certainly continue to pose challenges for domestic banking industry. With the impending liberalisation of domestic market and greater integration of global financial market, competition can be expected to intensify. Banking institutions will need to rapidly adapt to the new changing environment. Of importance is to strengthen efficiency and become more competitive. Rapid advances in information and communication technology (ICT) has also significantly revolutionised the banking business, transforming processes as well as the strategic focus of banking institutions. It has fully opened the doors for new business opportunities as well as offering new methods of delivery of banking products and services, such as through the internet. Under the new environment, competitiveness will not depend only on physical presence as in traditional markets, but rather on the ability to capitalise the technology strategies so as to deliver efficient and effective services. Successful banking institutions will be the ones that are able to leverage most from the ICT revolution as greater recognition is accorded to ICT as a driver of change. The 21st century will also see changes to the regulatory philosophies and framework following the development of an increasingly more complex and competitive market. The new regulatory philosophy allows for a greater role for market discipline. This approach emphasises on high standards of corporate governance, transparency and accountability. In adapting, banking institutions would need to reassess their internal practices as well as the overall corporate culture to be consistent with the new rules and regulation. Question 6: It is said that one of the challenges could be in loan growth especially with the development of the bond market. Please comment. The bond market in Malaysia has developed significantly in terms of market size, the wider range of instruments and products and a higher level of market efficiency. The development of the domestic bond market has become even more important with the increased diversification of the Malaysian economy and rapid economic transformation. For long-term activities and projects, it is important to have an alternative source of financing. A well functioning domestic bond market would not only provide borrowers with an alternative source of funding, but would also diversify some of the credit risks associated with debt financing from the banking sector to the investing public. As the economy expands in depth and breadth, the financing for economic growth should emanate from a variety of sources. While financing from the banking sector would remain the most dominant source of financing, the equity and bond market would be an increasingly important alternative to bank borrowings. The development of the bond market would not in anyway be hindrance to loan growth as it complements the banking sector in providing alternative types of financing required by the domestic economy. It is envisaged that bank borrowing will grow further, providing about 60-70% of total financing needs of the economy, with its special role in supporting specific industries. Question 7: Big things are happening on the IT and Internet banking front. How are these going to transform the local banking sector to be more competitive? Technology now plays a greater role in banking. The Internet, in particular is being actively used as another way in which banks can reach out to new and existing customers by providing an alternate distribution channel. Furthermore, there are tremendous opportunities to facilitate further communication channels for internal communication and for the integration of externally generated data with inter-organisational information. The importance of such technology has already been recognised. The investment in new technology platform can be expected to rise. This will be targeted at improving the key capabilities of banking institutions, such as marketing, customer services and delivery of products and services. Greater adoption of IT by our banks would also result in improvements in the banks? information systems as well as integration of internal IT platform. All this would, result in greater integration of the banking business with technology and that would eventually translate into greater operational efficiency in the banking sector and allow for the evolution of new business approaches and more competitive pricing. Moving forward, we expect banking institutions to be aggressive to explore new approaches and ideas including assessing the possibility or viability of establishing virtual banks or internet-only banks in this country. Question 8: Do you see a time when Malaysian banks will venture overseas to buy over banks there? The decision to venture abroad needs to be a business decision for the banking institutions. Banking institutions venture abroad in pursuit to enhance their presence within the international financial market and diversify their business operation. At present six of our domestic banks, namely Malayan Banking Berhad, Public Bank Berhad, Southern Bank Berhad, RHB Bank Berhad, Hong Leong Bank Berhad and Bumiputra ? Commerce Bank Berhad have operations overseas, mainly in the Asian region. While most of the these overseas presence are in the form of overseas branches or joint ventures with overseas banks, there were also those where the domestic bank acquired foreign banking institutions. As international trade and investment becomes even more significant, this trend can be expected to continue. This can even promote further international trade and investment. Question 9: What is the potential for asset securitisation in the banking sector?. What is Bank Negara's position on asset securitisation? Banking institutions undertake asset securitisation (which involve the selling of an institutions assets to a third party or special purpose vehicle which in turn issue securities to fund the purchase) for a number of reasons such as for liquidity purposes, enhancing capital adequacy as well as enhancing returns on assets. Additional liquidity generated from securitisation activities would allow banking institutions to originate more new loans, thus, contributing to the overall growth of the banking industry and the economy in general. In Malaysia, the National Mortgage Corporation, Cagamas Berhad, is currently the only financial intermediary involve in the securitisation, in particular, housing mortgage loans. However, with the introduction of Guidelines on the Offering of AssetBacked Debt Securities by the Securities Commission in April 2001, a number of banking institutions have shown interest in the securitisation of other assets. The various prudential aspects of securitisation are currently being revised to address a number of regulatory issues in particular those related to the secrecy of consumers information and the sale of assets in order to facilitate further the development of the securitisation market. Question 10: How do you see the development in Islamic banking and Takaful within the next one or two years? Islamic banking and finance has made steady progress since it was first introduced in the early 1980s. In the next one or two years, the expansion of Islamic finance can be expected to be more robust and to accelerate progressively. For this year it is expected to expand to meet the 8% target in terms of market share of assets, deposits and financing relative to the total banking industry. During the year, the Islamic banking institutions (comprising the Islamic banks and banking institutions participating in the Islamic Banking Scheme or IBS banks) will implement specific measures to strengthen their institutional and operational capabilities, improve efficiency and effectiveness and to increase research and development. Over the medium term, investments in training and manpower expertise in the field will also contribute to this process to strategically position themselves towards achieving this expansion. Furthermore, the IBS banks are expected to complete the rationalisation of their Islamic banking operations and emerge stronger and more efficient. All these positive developments will place the Islamic banking institutions in a better position to expand their market share and achieve critical mass. Malaysia will also develop Islamic banking and finance as a niche business in Labuan IOFC. This will in particular take a significant step forward with the establishment of the international Islamic money market later this year. Malaysia will also participate actively in the global arena to promote cooperation among Islamic countries in developing the Islamic financial services industry, in particular, to enhance and coordinate initiatives to develop instruments and procedures and to develop the standards to facilitate soundness and stability of the Islamic financial services industry. Bank Negara Malaysia 3 May 2001

Title: Speech at the 10th World Islamic Economic Forum (WIEF) - "Sukuk Development and Financial Stability"
text: Governor's Speech at CGC iGuarantee Portal Services Launching Ceremony Presenter: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz / Venue: Istana Hotel, Kuala Lumpur / Language: Bilingual (English/Malay) / Speech/Interview Date: 09 Jul 2001 / First of all, I would like to express my appreciation and gratitude to you, especially to Yang Berhormat Dato' Seri Mohamed Nazri Abdul Aziz, Minister of Entrepreneur Development for the opportunity to spend time together at the launch of CGC portal services this morning. The launch of this portal service is another success for CGC in its move to continue to play its role more effectively in assisting the growth of SMEs in the country. As informed under the Financial Sector Master Plan, Small and Medium Industries (SMEs) have been identified as a key sector that contributes significantly to the country's economic growth. As an important sub-sector of the economy, SMEs need funding support to grow the sector. As such, appropriate efforts should be continued to assist the SME sector including providing loan facilities through a more robust and efficient guarantee system. Since its inception, the CGC has experienced continued demand for its guarantee under its various guarantee schemes thus ensuring the much-needed access to credit for small and medium enterprises. This demonstrates that the guarantee mechanism has been accepted as an effective means in determining the direction of loan growth, especially in the development of Small and Medium Scale Industries (SMIs) in the Malaysian economy. In this respect, CGC remains committed in assisting small and medium scale enterprises (SMEs) to obtain institutional financing through its guarantee mechanism. The increase in the Corporation's paid-up capital to RM1.635 billion has better positioned the Corporation to fulfill its guarantee commitment and obligations. Moreover, with the increase in paid-up capital and the restructuring exercise undertaken by the Corporation, it has expanded its capacity to enhance the access to credit for SMEs. In an effort to expand the target group further, the Corporation recently revised the eligibility criteria to allow companies with shareholders' fund of up to RM10 million to borrow under the schemes, thereby allowing wider access to the guarantee. With this move, the Corporation has greater flexibility in assisting more SMEs in the future. The Corporation registered a commendable performance last year, guranteeing 8,595 loans amounting to RM2.05 billion compared with 8,277 loans valued at RM1.92 billion in the previous year. During the same period, the Corporation also recorded an operating revenue of RM123.3 million and net profit of RM153.3 million. Following the increase in paid-up capital by RM1 billion, the Corporation's total shareholder's fund now stands at RM2.45 billion. Recognising that SMEs may face difficulties in securing financing from financial institutions, especially those that lack collateral, the Corporation has formulated and introduced the Direct Access Guarantee Scheme (DAGS) which commenced in August 2000. This scheme provides an alternative delivery channel for SMEs to gain access to credit and allows SMEs to apply for the credit facilities that they require directly to the Corporation. With the introduction of this Direct Access Guarantee Scheme, SMEs involved in identified sectors are expected to benefit from the expanded role of the Corporation, which has also involved the opening of CGC branches nationwide. The Corporation is also aware of the growing need for the use of information technology in various business transactions. To assist the SMEs, the Corporation is launching its web service portal that allows for on-line loan applications via the Internet. The service portal also provides comprehensive information on loans for SMEs and the comparison of the various loan schemes that are available in the market. It is hoped that this new service will provide a conducive "market place" between potential borrowers that require financial assistance and the financiers that provide the financing, and the CGC as a guarantee service provider. In addition, the service portal will also provide information on SMEs to interested parties via its SMI Directory which the SMIs will be able to utilise at no cost. Through the iGuarantee, it is now possible for SMEs to make loan applications directly via the Internet. Loan applications may be submitted 24 hours a day throughout the year. Moreover, one single submission will simultaneously reach all financial institutions (FIs) in Malaysia, following which CGC will select the best loan offer available and present it to the SMIs. This system will help applicants to overcome the need of submitting multiple loan applications while maintaining the confidentiality of the information provided. As SMEs constitute the majority of business activities in Malaysia and their contribution towards growth of the national economy is important, the Corporation remains fully committed in assisting SMEs realise their financing needs. The SMIs are encouraged to increase the use of information technology to remain competitive in the global market. In today's environment, a business that lacks ITbased knowledge will lose out on the potential benefits that the Internet provides. Overall, I believe that the web portal would be beneficial to all businesses including the financial sector. I would therefore urge the participation of all financial institutions in this effort to assist this target group. As we embark into an era of e-banking, it is only appropriate and timely that the credit guarantee system, which supplements the banking system, becomes internet-based and with its added features. I believe financial institutions will view the introduction of iGuarantee as yet another effective and viable means to assist the SMEs gain ready access to institutional credit. Full use should therefore be made of the iGuarantee which has been designed for the benefit of both SMEs and financial institutions. For the SMEs, time will be saved when they no longer need to travel between different financial institutions and at the same time will be able to receive competitive offers on their loan request. For the financial institutions, there will be greater opportunity to reach out to a larger customer base provided by the portal. Viewed in totality, the portal aims to address the needs of both the SMIs as well as the financial institutions. CGC will continue to work closely with the Ministry of Entrepreneur Development to assist entrepreneurs in the country in selected sectors such as vendors and franchises to obtain the necessary financing, in order to grow resilient and competitive businesses and to ensure that the country's economic well-being can continue. Finally, on behalf of the Board of Directors, I once again express my gratitude and appreciation to the Honorable Minister and the Ministry of Entrepreneur Development, government agencies, commercial banks and financial companies as well as the Halls and Business Associations for their support and presence in this morning. I believe that such cooperation and support will continue to be given in order to achieve the common ambition to help entrepreneurs and SMEs, as well as to make a positive contribution towards the country's economic improvement efforts. Bank Negara Malaysia 9 July 2001

Title: Speech for the Launch of the Asian Banking School
text: Governor's Speech at the Launching Ceremony of the "Financial Services Industry Term Register Book" Presenter: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz / Venue: Bank Negara Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 21 Sep 2001 / First of all, I would like to thank the organisers for inviting me to deliver a few words at this glorious event and launch the book of the Financial Services Industry Term Register. In this regard, I would like to congratulate the parties involved, in particular Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka, who has spearheaded several programmes under the Private Sector National Language Movement, which has started since 1996, and extended to 2005, as well as its success in publishing the book Register of Terms of the Financial Services Industry. . Indeed, the goal of increasing the use of the Malay language in the financial services industry sector is complementary to the goal of developing this sector.
