This surpassed the total conventional bonds issued. Going forward, in meeting the changing requirements of the economy, there is a need to elevate the level of effectiveness and efficiency of the Islamic financial market. This requires further expansion of the breadth and depth of the Islamic financial market, and the development of a new breed of bankers who are able to exploit the untapped potential of this market. Until today, the universal nature of Islamic banking business, particularly in the field of investment banking, has yet to be fully exploited. Emphasis has been on expanding traditional banking activities. Although fee-based activities are becoming an increasingly important source of income that can enhance the returns to the shareholders and depositors, fee income constitutes only a small portion of the total income of the Islamic banking institutions. There is therefore a need to enhance capacity to tap the potential Islamic investment banking activities offers. The successful issuance of the first sovereign global Islamic Sukuk by the Government of Malaysia demonstrated the strong interest in Shariah-compliant financial instruments. This issue has acted as a catalyst for other countries and corporate players to tap the global Islamic financial market. Leading global investment banks are now according greater focus and resources to tap this potential and have become important players in this market. The skills and expertise to tap this market still resides with the global investment banks. Our domestic Islamic banking institutions must therefore embrace the challenge to enhance their capacity and capability to emerge as world-class bankers that are able to lead arrange these issues, rather than assume a participatory role. Domestic Islamic banking institutions face the impending challenge of not only having to engineer innovative financial structures that are able to meet sophisticated requirements of the diverse clientele base but also, to ensure that these structures are Shariah compliant. Islamic banking institutions are urged to allocate adequate resources for research and development. This is important if Malaysia is to realise its potential as a regional hub for Islamic banking and finance. The pace of the development of Islamic banking and finance in Malaysia has exceeded our earlier expectations. To further enhance the pace of development and progress, Bank Negara Malaysia will bring forward the financial liberalisation for the Islamic banking sector than was envisaged in the Financial Sector Master Plan. This will generate spill-over effects that will enhance the diversity and spur the overall development of the Islamic financial system, thus providing the enabling environment for Malaysia to become a regional Islamic financial hub. It will also promote greater competition and act as a bridge between Malaysia and other global Islamic financial markets. This will involve issuing new Islamic bank licences to qualified foreign players with presence in the global Islamic banking industry. As we embark on this journey, and as we pursue our own strategic course, it is essential to ensure that these efforts reinforce and complement each other and arrive at the same destination, towards Malaysia as a regional Islamic financial centre. I wish CIMB Islamic success in its endeavour and I look forward to their contribution to the development of the Islamic financial industry in Malaysia. Dengan lafaz Bismillahirrahmanirrahim, saya dengan sukacitanya merasmikan pelancaran CIMB Islamic. Terima kasih.

Title: Keynote Address at the Banca D'Italia: Seminar on Islamic Finance "Islamic Finance: A Central Bank's Perspective"
text: Governor's Opening Remarks at the ASEAN Anti-Money Laundering Workshop Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Speech/Interview Date: 28 Jul Venue: Renaissance Hotel Language: English 2003 Good morning and welcome to the ASEAN Anti-Money Laundering Workshop 2003. We are honoured today with the presence of Yang Berhormat Datuk Dr. Ng Yen Yen, Deputy Finance Minister to deliver the keynote address for this Workshop. Bank Negara Malaysia is indeed pleased to have the honour of hosting this Workshop, which is organised as part of our commitment to the ASEAN Plan of Action to Combat Transnational Organised Crime. In an increasingly globalised and interdependent environment, the impetus for closer financial co-operation in this region has assumed increased importance. In the recent years, co-operative initiatives have intensified to strengthen regional defences against external shocks. These include the enlargement of the ASEAN Swap Arrangement, the Chiang Mai Initiative and, more recently, the Asian Bond Market and the Asian Bond Fund Initiatives. The increase in regional financial co-operation emanates from the recognition that by working together we can strengthen our ability to safeguard the stability and integrity of our financial systems. In this connection, this ASEAN Anti-Money Laundering Workshop represents another important step towards regional financial co-operation to strengthen our regional defences against external shocks, including attempts by those who seek to abuse our financial systems for their illegal activities. The continued upgrading of skills among the regulatory and law enforcement agencies is vital to ensure our success in combating money laundering. It is important that those that are directly involved in implementing anti-money laundering measures are adequately equipped with the necessary expertise to undertake their tasks and responsibilities. This Workshop is therefore timely, as it brings together participants from various countries in this region to deliberate and learn the various aspects on establishing an effective national anti-money laundering programme. The Workshop will cover the important issues in the area of the legislative framework for this purpose, the establishment of a Financial Intelligence Unit, the required law enforcement efforts as well as other issues of current interest. Several experts have also been invited to share their knowledge and experience. Money laundering is not a new phenomena. At its most fundamental level, the fight against money laundering is based on the recognition of its serious adverse implications on the economy and society at large, if left unchecked. Money laundering has a negative effect on economic growth as it diverts resources to unproductive activities and as it facilitates corruption and crime. Money laundering activities perpetuate crimes as they encourage the underlying criminal activity from which illicit proceeds are generated. Given that financial institutions are important catalysts for economic growth and development, it is important to ensure that our financial system is protected from any potential abuse by money launderers. A sound and strong financial system is vital to a countrys economic growth process. An environment of financial strength and integrity is essential for businesses to flourish. It is within such an environment that investors will have the confidence in the system to invest, and create wealth, incomes and employment. In contrast, any abuse of the financial system by money launderers would undermine public confidence in the financial system, with all its negative consequences. The impact of money laundering on financial institutions is greatest during the placement and layering stages, when illicit funds are laundered but not yet fully integrated into the economy. Financial institutions exposed to such criminal intent would suffer reputational risk as money laundering tarnishes the good name of these institutions. At its extreme, criminal elements can have a hold on a financial institution, increasing the prospect of internal fraud and other criminal activities resulting in the risk of financial failure. Legitimate businesses would naturally avoid dealing with such institutions that are perceived to be associated with criminal elements for fear of being perceived to be connected to such criminals. Clearly, the integrity and credibility of financial institutions are important hallmarks that ensure the customer and investor confidence that their funds are in safe hands. The highest priority has therefore always been accorded to efforts to ensure good corporate governance in our financial institutions. In Malaysia we have put in place laws and regulations and guidelines to promote sound banking practices. These operating conditions have been and are being continually reviewed to take into consideration recent developments. These included the newly revised 40 Recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) and the requirements of the AntiMoney Laundering Act 2001 (AMLA). Malaysia adheres to the highest standards in our fight against money laundering. Our commitment to combat money laundering has been implemented in a comprehensive manner. All supervisory, regulatory and law enforcement agencies have been called upon to include the task of combating money laundering as part of their core functions. To co-ordinate the law enforcement efforts of the various agencies, the National Co-ordination Committee to Counter Money Laundering (NCC,) was formed. This has proved to be an effective body to co-ordinate activities across agencies. In the NCC, the member agencies work together, discuss the areas of concern, undertake research and are updated of the developments in the country as well as at the international level, on matters relating to money laundering. Money laundering activities, as we well know, are primarily driven by greed, and as such, appropriate legislation is necessary to ensure that such criminals will not be able to profit further from their ill-gotten gains. Since the AMLA was brought into force on 15 January 2002, the number of predicate offences increased from 119 to 150 at present. In implementing Part IV of the AMLA, an incremental approach has been taken to ensure that the reporting institutions, be it financial institutions or otherwise, are prepared and able to comply effectively with their obligations under AMLA. The Minister of Finance has invoked the mandatory reporting of suspicious transactions on such institutions which conduct substantial cash-based transactions. As part of our efforts to ensure the implementation of a comprehensive anti-money laundering system, the Financial Intelligence Unit was established in Bank Negara Malaysia. The Financial Intelligence Unit receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports and disseminates financial intelligence on such activities to the relevant law enforcement agency for investigation and subsequent prosecution. The Supervision Departments of the Bank have also developed an anti-money laundering supervisory framework. This arrangement assesses the effectiveness of the anti-money laundering compliance framework at the financial institutions. In our ongoing efforts to strengthen our anti-money laundering regime, the Financial Intelligence Unit has also commenced its consultative process with stock brokers, accountants and lawyers. This step is taken prior to having the Anti-Money Laundering Act 2001 invoked in the reporting obligations on these entities. While greater awareness of the anti-money laundering regime within ASEAN is important, co-operation among ASEAN member countries is also essential to facilitate cross-border investigations into money laundering activities. Programmes such as the one being held today needs to be conducted regularly and enhanced by drawing on new information, developments and techniques. This is an important part of the process, to evolve a high level of appreciation of the law enforcement issues in the fight against money laundering. I am confident that this Workshop will achieve its objective to promote awareness and strengthen further the anti-money laundering regime in this region. In this context, I encourage all participants to take advantage of the opportunity accorded by this programme. We look forward to your participation and support to develop new ideas and approaches to address the serious issue of money laundering in your deliberations at this Workshop. Thank you.

Title: Speech at the LOFSA's Luncheon Talk with Foreign Embassies in Malaysia
text: Governor's Welcoming Remarks at the 10th Session of the Islamic Summit Conference Dinner Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Sheraton Imperial Hotel, Kuala Lumpur Speech/Interview Date: 11 Oct 2003 Language: English Bank Negara Malaysia is indeed honoured to have the opportunity to host this dinner in honour of your Excellencies and distinguished guests from members of the Organisation of Islamic Countries. Let me take this opportunity to welcome you to Kuala Lumpur. We hope that this 10th Session of the Islamic Summit Conference would set new opportunities to strengthen and enhance co-operation among the Organisation of Islamic Countries (OIC). While the world economy has benefited from the tremendous opportunities accorded by the more globalised environment, trends indicate an increasingly more unbalanced global growth. This trend has also reinforced structural weakness and unbalances in the major economies. These trends, if left to continue would jeopardise the prospects for sustained world growth. Our quest for shared global prosperity requires concerted efforts on all fronts to promote a more balanced global growth. In these endeavours, there has to be more balanced patterns of global trade and financial flows. The opportunity therefore needs to be taken to explore the new opportunities to strengthen the economic and financial relations between our countries. In so doing, it would contribute towards increasing the prospects for a more balanced global growth. Malaysia has always been highly integrated to the global economy. We are one of the most open economies in the world. This is not only in terms of our high volume of trade, but also in terms of foreign direct investment and in terms of foreign presence in our financial sector. Our trade volume amounts to more than two times the size of our economy. In terms of foreign direct investment, we have been the recipients of such investments for more than one hundred years. It has accounted for one quarter to one third of our annual aggregate investment, in addition, foreign presence in our banking sector is about 25% while in the insurance sector, the foreign participation is even higher with two thirds of the assets being under foreign ownership. Malaysia is part of the Asian economies which represents one of the fastest growing regions in the world. Our history shows that in view of our geographical position, we became the centre of trade between the nations to the west and east of us. Indeed, Malaysias active participation in the global economic and financial system, and our relatively higher degree of openness enables Malaysia to be an important gateway to East Asia. Malaysia has for more than three decades had an average growth performance of about 7%. From time to time our economy has been setback by external developments, but we have been able to manage these challenges and recover within a short period of time. In this more challenging environment, our strategy has been to continuously strengthen our foundations and our capacity to manage these new risks and challenges. As the Central Bank, our specific role has been not only to promote an economic and financial environment that will provide an enabling environment for growth and development, but also to develop a financial system that not only supports this growth process but that is resilient in facing a more challenging and competitive environment. One area that we have focussed attention is the development of an Islamic financial system as a viable and vibrant component of our financial system. A comprehensive Islamic financial system is now in place with the core components of banking, takaful, and the money and capital markets. Attention has also been focussed on the financial infrastructure including the regulatory and supervisory framework as well as the best practices in standards of governance and transparency. Malaysia has also participated actively in the promotion of the Islamic financial infrastructure on the global front. We believe the integration of Islamic banking and finance into the global financial system will contribute toward achieving our shared aspirations for financial stability to ensure balanced growth in the global economy. The OIC has 57 member countries with a combined population of 1.25 billion, accounting for 20% of the worlds population. There are significant prospects for trade and investment among the OIC countries. The diverse economic structures of OIC members should be seen as an opportunity to expand trade and investment ties. Indeed, we look forward to the positive outcome of your deliberations during the 10th Session of the Islamic Summit Conference. We also hope that you will have the opportunity to enjoy Malaysia. On that note, I wish you a pleasant evening.

Title: Keynote Address at the Euromoney 8th Annual Islamic Finance Summit: "Islamic Finance and Global Financial Stability"
text: Governor's Opening remarks at the Seminar on Medical and Health Insurance for Insurers and Takaful Operators Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Auditorium, Bank Negara Malaysia Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 14 Oct 2003 Saya ingin mengalu-alukan kedatangan tuan-tuan dan puan-puan ke Seminar Insurans Perubatan dan Kesihatan pada pagi ini. Seminar ini adalah sebahagian daripada siri seminar yang dianjurkan oleh Bank Negara Malaysia dari masa ke semasa untuk ahli lembaga pengarah dan para pegawai kanan penanggung insurans dan pengendali takaful mengenai isu-isu dan cabarancabaran semasa yang dihadapi oleh sektor insurans dan takaful. Siri seminar in bertujuan meningkatkan pengetahuan dan kesedaran ahli lembaga pengarah dan pegawai kanan mengenai isu-isu penting ini bagi memastikan perkembangan teratur pasaran, serta memastikan kemajuan prestasi setiap institusi secara berterusan dengan perlaksanaan amalan kewangan dan perniagaan yang sihat dan berhemah. Seminar kali ini difokuskan pada insurans perubatan dan kesihatan. Private medical and health insurance has an important role in complementing and supplementing the national healthcare system. Indeed, more and more Malaysians are turning to the insurance and takaful industries for insurance protection to finance their healthcare requirements. This has led to the substantial expansion in medical and health insurance business in the last five years, with premiums increasing at an average annual rate of 16% to nearly RM1 billion in 2002. Medical and health insurance currently accounts for more than 5% of total premiums in the insurance industry. Going forward, we can expect more Malaysians to allocate an increasingly larger proportion of their income for healthcare provisions. Although Malaysia has a relatively young population, demographic changes point to an expanding aging population with the improvement in living standards and advances in medical science and healthcare facilities. At the same time, any changes in the extended family structure would increase pressures on individual responsibility for medical care. These developments pose significant social policy challenges for the national healthcare system to ensure access to fundamental medical facilities for all Malaysians in the most efficient and cost effective manner. In this regard, private healthcare financing will become increasingly important in complementing and supplementing the healthcare facilities in the public sector. Public sector healthcare financing has already been on an upward trend in recent years. The Government healthcare expenditure is expected to approach RM9 billion by 2004, from about RM2.8 billion in 1995. Healthcare expenditure as a proportion of the overall Government budget is projected to increase from 5% to 8% over the same period. With the ratio of retirees to the active population projected to double by the year 2020, the demand for healthcare is projected to increase further, creating additional pressures on financing for healthcare and in particular, private healthcare financing. Private sources of financing for healthcare currently account for almost 40% of Malaysias total healthcare expenditure. These are mainly in the form of direct medical expenses incurred by individuals as well as the payments made by employers towards the medical expenses of their staff. Over time, other private sources of financing, including private medical and health insurance schemes, can be expected to feature more prominently in the overall healthcare financing structure. In this evolution, private medical and health insurance will be an integral element in efforts to achieve a seamless and comprehensive national health care system. The increasing demand for private medical and health insurance has, however, brought to the forefront a number issues, including escalating costs, that require immediate attention. The industry has already taken some important initiatives in the development of coherent industry solutions to address escalating claims costs. These include dialogues with the private medical service providers and the establishment of a panel of accredited hospitals and incentive measures such as the cosharing of medical costs. Indeed these efforts by insurance industry are important steps in establishing common principles of sound business conduct in private health care financing. Given this line of business, it is important for the development of more comprehensive and sustainable solutions that will also take into account the broader socio-economic considerations. At the same time, however, ongoing reforms in the conduct of medical and health insurance business also need to address the specific information needs of the business. From the industrys perspective, the establishment of a comprehensive and credible database on various aspects of the Malaysian medical and health insurance sector will facilitate more scientific underwriting and rating systems employed by insurers, as well as more effective management of risks associated with moral hazard, fraud and abuses. The lack of sufficiently detailed data currently constitutes a significant impediment to the ability of insurers to effectively meet the demand of the community for medical and healthcare covers. A comprehensive database is essential not only for more accurate pricing of medical and health products, but also to enable insurers to better understand and monitor developments affecting their business. These include the profile of policyholders and their risk categorisations, consumer preferences, the types of illnesses and medical treatments that contribute substantially to claims expenses and clinical information affecting relationships with medical service providers. Equally important is the need to address the information needs of consumers in the sale of medical and health insurance products and services. Last year, medical and health insurance accounted for 25% of total complaints received by Bank Negara Malaysia. Besides premium rate increases and delays in claims settlement, the complaints mainly related to the lack of transparency at the point of marketing and sale of the medical and health insurance products. This underscores the importance of meeting the information needs of the potential policy owners. It is essential that the terms of medical and health insurance policies sold are clearly explained to policyholders, particularly the effects of policy exclusions and conditions imposed by insurers on the extent of coverage afforded to the policyholder. The issue of increased transparency and disclosure in the sale of medical and health products is important. In many cases, policyholders are not aware of or do not fully realise the implications of particular clauses in the policy contract that deal, for example, with pre-existing conditions, co-insurance and waiting and survival periods. Insurers cannot assume such knowledge on the part of the average consumer. It is incumbent on insurers and their intermediaries to ensure that the average consumer is given clear information about the product at the point of sale to enable the consumer to understand his rights and responsibilities and to determine if indeed, the product adequately meets his needs. There should also be greater awareness among consumers on the avenues available for them to seek redress in the event of dispute. To promote greater transparency in the business, Bank Negara has issued guidelines on minimum standards of product disclosure and transparency in the sale of medical and health insurance policies. These standards require insurers and their intermediaries to provide the details of the essential features of medical and health policies so that policyholders will understand the important provisions of the policies, in particular, with respect to the premiums, benefits, exclusions and limitations. Meeting these requirements must also be supported by the adoption of the highest ethical standards and practices by insurers and intermediaries in their dealings with customers. Insurers should therefore strive to continuously enhance the degree of disclosure and transparency demonstrated in their conduct of the business to prevent the erosion of public confidence in the industry as a whole. The challenges faced in the conduct of medical and health insurance are significant, particularly in the light of the social considerations that must also be brought to bear on business decisions and strategies. They are, however, not insurmountable. While the various approaches to deal with the challenges are encouraged to permit innovation and improvements, the future development of medical and health insurance in the country will require the industry to proceed on a common platform at some level with respect to what constitutes the basic fundamentals of commercially sound, and socially ethical, business conduct in this area. Todays seminar provides a platform on which insurers, individually and collectively, can build on to explore new ground, develop new ideas and options and formulate new strategies to effectively manage the issues confronting the business, and thereby achieve sustained and viable business growth. On that note, I wish you a productive and stimulating seminar.

Title: Welcoming Remarks at the 44th SEACEN s' Conference
text: Governor's Address at the OIC Business Forum Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Putrajaya Marriott Hotel Speech/Interview Date: 16 Oct 2003 Language: English Managing Diversity - Economic Progress, Racial Harmony and Religious Tolerance: The Malaysian Experience Diversity, far from being a potential source of conflict, can be a source of strength and opportunities. At the international level, the world we live in is characterized by pronounced diversity. Our ability to manage this diversity to the benefit of the global community can indeed increase our prospects for sustained shared global prosperity. At the national level, the Malaysian experience in managing our own diversity has been to accord priority to economic and financial policies that promote balanced growth. The thrust of our policies has been to achieve a greater balance between high quality growth and a more equitable distribution of the economic progress; a greater balance between domestic and external sources of growth; a greater balance between the role of the public and private sectors; between consumption and investment-led growth; between the different regions across the country; between the different economic sectors; and between the respective communities in our society. It is indeed my honour to speak at this OIC Business Forum and to be here at this session with the Honourable Minister Dato' Hishammudin on the topic of managing diversity. My remarks this afternoon will focus on the strategies that Malaysia has adopted in managing our economy and the financial system to achieve this more balanced growth, and in doing so, build the foundations on which the diversity can become a source of strength and opportunities. Economic Strategy In achieving the objective of balanced growth, economic policy in Malaysia has concentrated on the diversification of the economy. For almost five decades our economic structure has undergone waves of transformation. The Malaysian economy has shifted from a commodity based to a more industrialized economy, reinforced by the discovery of petroleum and, more recently to an economy where the services sector is becoming an increasingly important source of growth. The emphasis has always been to identify new areas of competitive advantage and develop new sources of growth to sustain the long-term development of the Malaysian economy. In the recent decade, the focus has been on the development of the ICT industries. In the development of the respective economic sectors, a balanced approach has been adopted to accord attention to the development of Small and Medium-scale Enterprises (SMEs) to complement the development of large corporations as well as the large MNCs operating in Malaysia. Each component is an integral element in the industrial structure with SMEs as suppliers of components and parts to the larger corporations, or as providers of support services or final products and services. As part of this process, greater attention has been focused on the development of SMEs as they not only represent important "incubators" of entrepreneurial talents but also have an important role in generating endogenous sources of growth and employment. Indeed, as a small, open economy where trade accounts for more than 200% of GNP, the Government is committed to promoting the role of the private sector as the main engine of growth. The role of the Government has been to set the broad direction to give clarity to the goals - the vision of our aspirations - and to provide the enabling environment for private enterprise, and smoothen the economic cycle to ensure steady growth and development. The long-term policy direction is set within the context of our 20-year Outline Perspective Plans (including "Vision 2020" on Malaysia's industrialisation strategy). Specific policy measures and strategies to achieve the long-term objectives are outlined in 5-year Development Plans, while shorter-term issues are addressed in the annual budget programme. The Government's role in providing an enabling environment includes the provision of the physical infrastructure, driving institutional development and capacity building, enhancing the Government delivery system to reduce the cost of doing business and providing a stable and sound macroeconomic environment. While the Government assumes an important role in providing the strategic direction and enabling environment, the development of the domestic economy rests largely with the private sector. Over the last five decades, the private sector accounted for nearly 70% of national output. In addition, more than 90% of the labour force works in the private sector. A significant proportion of the financing that supported Malaysia's economic transformation has emanated from private investment, including foreign direct investment inflows. The role of the private sector can be expected to become increasingly important in sustaining economic growth in the future. Their role will be to continually seek new areas of comparative advantage and new market niches to contribute to income and wealth creation in an increasingly more challenging and competitive environment. Financial Sector Strategy A key component of the Government's strategy is to develop a financial system that is effective, efficient and resilient; that will not only support the growth process but will also facilitate the economic transformation towards a diversified economic structure, and thereby achieve sustainable growth and development. The financial sector is seen as an important facilitator of growth. The development of the financial sector has taken into account the need to balance between the objectives of financial stability and efficiency and the social agenda. Specific strategies to facilitate a more balanced growth has been to develop a more diversified financial structure that is able to meet the different requirements of the economy and to ensure that there is increased access to financial services by all economic sectors, regions and communities. In this regard, efforts have emphasised the development of a comprehensive and diversified financial infrastructure, including mircocredit at one end of the spectrum to provide financial services to mirco-enterprises, and at the other end of the spectrum, venture capital to provide financing to ICT and knowledge driven activities. Important components of the financial structure include the banking sector, the insurance companies, the capital market and the specialised and development financial institutions, which provide alternative avenues for financing. The development of the corporate bond market, in particular, has enabled firms to improve their ability to better manage their funding risks while reducing the risks arising from over-dependence on any single form or source of financing. The development of the corporate bond market has also enhanced the efficiency of capital allocation by enabling firms to tap alternative sources of financing at competitive cost, thereby contributing to increased efficiency, higher investment and consequently contributing to overall growth. The banking sector will, however, for some time to come, remain the single most important source of financing in Malaysia. Attention has therefore been focused on institutional development and capacity building in the banking sector. This has been identified as an important objective to achieve in the first stage of our 10-year Financial Master Plan to develop the financial sector, that is to develop a core of strong and forward-looking Malaysian banks that are able to face the challenges of liberalisation and globalisation. A major milestone in financial sector development was the banking merger and consolidation programme. This has been reinforced by the promotion of greater operational efficiency, greater leveraging on technology, strengthening risk management and corporate governance practices, enhancing the supervisory and regulatory framework and the development of a framework for consumer education and protection. While electronic banking is expanding at a rapid pace, in the current environment, an area that has been given priority is to ensure that the banking system conducts its intermediation functions across the country in terms of physical presence in all regions. Over the decades, we have seen the establishment of a strong and extensive banking network in urban and rural areas across the country. In this regard, the number of bank branches throughout the country has increased from 131 in 1960 to 1,660 in 2003. The number of persons served per branch has correspondingly declined dramatically from 62,800 to 28,060 for the same period. The aim of this policy is to increase access to banking services for all the various sectors and regions in the economy. A further issue that has been taken into account is the need to balance the pursuit of greater efficiency in this increasingly more competitive environment against the need to provide basic fundamental financial services to the community at large at minimal costs. While pricing for financial products and services should, for the most part, reflect costs, it is also important to take into account the social agenda which is an integral part of balanced and sustainable growth. As was discussed in the previous session, an area that Malaysia has focused attention on is the development of an Islamic financial system as a viable component of our financial system. Indeed, the development of a comprehensive Islamic financial infrastructure with the core components, encompassing Islamic banking, takaful and the money and capital markets, will serve to further strengthen the financial system as well as diversify options to meet the varied requirements of Malaysian consumers and businesses. International Co-operation Malaysia's approach in managing diversity also applies to our relations in the international arena. Malaysia has actively sought to strengthen trade and investment linkages with other developing countries across the world. Such a policy is based on the premise that by working together, individual countries can maximise the synergies of each individual country's comparative advantage for the mutual benefit of all parties. Increasing specialization and complementarity drives the law of comparative advantage. As individual countries find niche areas within the globalised network of production based on comparative advantage, this will facilitate optimizing the potential for overall global growth. The stronger cooperation among diverse countries will indeed open such new opportunities. In this endeavor, OIC countries can drive this co-operation and integration. The OIC has 57 member countries with a combined population of 1.25 billion, accounting for 20% of the world's population. There are significant prospects for trade and investment among the OIC countries. The diverse economic structures of OIC members should be seen as an opportunity to expand trade and investment ties. Conclusion The Malaysian experience suggests that in managing diversity, there is a need to develop economies that have the agility to adjust to changing economic conditions, to emphasise on capacity enhancement and institutional development and to focus on the role of the Government in providing the enabling environment. It also requires economic and financial policies that balances between growth, efficiency, and equity considerations. A strategy of balanced and broad- based growth that gives due consideration to the social agenda offers the best chances of success. Indeed, diversity can be managed to become a potential source of strengths and opportunities in our pursuit of overall shared prosperity.

Title: Speech at the Sir Purshotamdas Thakurdas Memorial Lecture - "Managing Financial Liberalisation and its Challenges: Implications for Emerging Economies"
text: Governor's Speech at the IFSB Summit - Islamic Financial Services Industry and The Global Regulatory Environment Approaches to Regulation of Islamic Financial Services Industry Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: The Park Lane Hotel, London Speech/Interview Date: 18 May 2004 Language: English Preserving financial stability in the Islamic financial system extends beyond the regulatory framework to the building of an intermediation system that is robust and resilient, that is efficient and competitive and that is able to contribute to the growth process. Islamic finance has evolved to become a dynamic industry that has extended beyond domestic borders to become an integral component of the international financial system. Indeed, amidst the changing global financial landscape, the Islamic financial industry has demonstrated its ability to operate in an increasingly more challenging and competitive environment. The challenge before us is to maximise the potential and the seamless opportunities Islamic finance accords. Each component  the financial infrastructure, the institutions, the legal, regulatory and supervisory framework and the Shariah infrastructure all have an important role in the progressive development of the Islamic financial system. The strengthening of these respective components will provide the foundations on which future sustainable progress and expansion can be realised. It is my honour to be invited to speak before this distinguished audience at this conference organised by the Islamic Financial Services Board on approaches to regulations of the Islamic financial services industry. While the rapid expansion of Islamic finance has been achieved in an environment of financial stability, the regulatory and supervisory agenda continue to be an important priority. Todays increasingly challenging environment of heightened risks have prompted reassessments of existing prudential rules and supervisory approaches amongst regulators to develop a dynamic regulatory and supervisory framework to achieve financial stability in all areas of the financial services sector. No less attention has been given to these issues in Islamic finance. Indeed, the work that is being undertaken by the IFSB to develop prudential, regulatory and supervisory standards and core principles that are in compliance with Shariah rules and principles represents a breakthrough in the regulation and supervision of the Islamic financial services industry. My remarks today will focus on regulatory approaches adopted for Islamic banking institutions that take into consideration the context of the varying customer-banking institution relationship based on the contracts entered into that is inherent in the Islamic financial transactions. These considerations are essentially required to take into account the Shariah governance which reinforces the efforts to achieving the stability and soundness of the Islamic financial system. My presentation will also touch on areas of challenges in the formulation of the regulatory approach that arise from the multi-facet role performed by the Islamic banking institutions, and for systems in which Islamic finance operates side-by-side with the conventional financial system. Objective and Regulatory Philosophy In designing and implementing financial regulation for Islamic banking institutions, the challenge is to formulate a framework that not only takes into account the unique characteristics peculiar to Islamic banking business, but that does not put Islamic financial institutions at a comparative disadvantage and affect their competitiveness and growth potential in the overall financial system. Imperative is that the regulatory requirements need to be consistent with the injunctions of Shariah. Secondly, it needs to take into account the multi-faceted role performed by the Islamic banking institutions. Thirdly, in a dual financial system where Islamic financial institutions operate in a system side-by-side with conventional banks, including that where conventional banks may offer Islamic banking products and services through Islamic banking windows, the regulatory approach adopted needs to provide a level playing field. Islamic banking institutions in most jurisdictions have to a large extent been governed by the same regulatory framework that is applied to conventional banking operations reinforced by the compliance to the Shariah framework. However, as the conventional banking framework is premised on an interest-based debtor-creditor relationship, the regulatory framework for conventional banking is built to assess and mitigate risks arising from loan-based financial transactions. Islamic banking is different in term of its underlying philosophy on the prohibition of interest. This in turn shapes the nature of the financial transactions that has its own risk characteristics. The specific risks associated in Islamic banking activities therefore needs to be identified to ensure its prudential regulation is adequately addressed. It is within this context of diversity of systems and players that the regulatory approach adopted needs to ensure harmonisation and a level playing field for a competitive and robust financial system. Efforts towards achieving this objective will include the elements of greater transparencies and disclosure, a strong legal and judiciary system, reinforced by strong Shariah governance. It is in this aspect that the IFSB assumes a key role in developing prudential standards aimed at addressing issues peculiar to Islamic banking and identifying the gaps on existing regulatory and prudential standards. The IFSB represents an important catalyst that will contribute to enhancing the resilience of Islamic financial institutions in the global financial system and that will strengthen the foundation for the progress in the development of the global Islamic financial landscape. The multiple contractual relationship of Islamic banking institutions A strong regulatory framework must have the important elements of adequate capital standards, effective risk management practices and strong governance. In building a sound prudential framework for Islamic banking, aligning regulatory capital requirements to the underlying risks requires a dichotomisation of the risk intricacies in the Islamic banking asset portfolio. On the asset side, the Islamic banking institutions enter into different financing modes that have varying risk characteristics, ranging from the low risk sales and lease-based modes to the higher risk equity-based modes of finance. Each of these modes of finance have a distinct intrinsic characteristic dictated by its underlying Shariah principle, and thus entail different risk profiles. An equity-based finance, may for example involve higher risks and therefore attract higher capital requirement. In this regard, the challenge in formulating the risk management infrastructure in Islamic banking institutions lies in having an accurate assessment of the various risk variants underlying the alternative modes of finance to provide for their effective quantification and management. Similarly, the liability structure of Islamic banks is characterized by two distinct categories of deposits: demand deposits which is not subject to risks associated with banking business and for which the principal is guaranteed, and investment deposits which involves risks and hence, is eligible to share the profits earned from the banking business. Given this liability structure of Islamic banking institutions, the design of the regulatory framework for Islamic banking needs to give emphasis to full financial disclosure, prudent risk management and adherence to Shariah principles. This will serve as a firewall to prevent the transmission of risks from investment deposits to demand deposits thus enhancing transparency, depositors protection and systemic stability. Rate of return framework A further regulatory challenge arises from the liability structure of Islamic banking institution and the determination of a standard rate of return for account holders. Unlike conventional banking where returns are pre-determined, profit-sharing depositors of Islamic banking institutions know their returns at the maturity of the deposits. These returns are subject to the earnings of the assets that is shared between the Islamic banking institutions and the profit-sharing depositors. In the event of loss, the depositor as the capital provider will bear the losses. As the deposits in Islamic banking are for the most part are in the form of profit-sharing deposits, it places a higher degree of fiduciary risk on the management to ensure the funds are utilised in the most efficient manner. Hence, regulators need to establish an effective rate of return framework to provide standard methodology for deriving the rate of return for depositors. Of equal importance is the need to address the information asymmetry between the Islamic banking institutions and the depositors by enhancing the level of transparency and ensuring that depositors would receive fair returns on their investment. Within the regulatory context, the framework would provide a means of assessing the efficiency of Islamic banking institutions as well as their profitability, prudent management and fairness. In this regard, Malaysia has introduced the Profit Equalisation Reserve in the rate of return framework. To generate rates of return that are competitive and stable, the Profit Equalisation Reserve acts as a mechanism to mitigate the fluctuation of rates of return arising from the flow in income, provisioning and total deposits. This reserve is appropriated out of the total gross income and is shared by both the depositors and the banking institution. In a dual banking environment, the ability to maximise risk adjusted return on investment and sustain stable and competitive returns is an important element for the development of a competitive Islamic banking system. Regulatory approach in a dual banking system In a dual banking environment where Islamic banking institutions are operating side-by-side with conventional banking institutions, it is important to maintain harmonisation of the regulatory infrastructure, thus providing a level playing field for both the Islamic and conventional financial industry. The challenge lies in the development of a rigorous regulatory framework, legal and tax structure that will not position any of the financial players at a disadvantage. Of equal importance is the need to ensure that there is no opportunity for regulatory arbitrage in banking practices that makes one system more superior to the other in terms of product pricing. The Malaysian experience has a further variant of the dual banking model where conventional banking institutions are able to offer Islamic banking products and services. In Malaysia, the Islamic financial system operates in parallel with the conventional system. The system has remained competitive and resilient as demonstrated by its growing market share and its ability to withstand adverse development. Their resilience to market vulnerabilities was demonstrated during the 1997-1998 Asian currency crisis. While the Islamic banking institutions observe similar international standards prescribed in the banking regulatory and supervisory framework and are subject to the same supervision by the Central Bank, the Islamic banking institutions are required to observe additional requirements, including observing minimum Islamic banking fund for its Islamic banking operations and maintaining an internal separation of accounting books. Further steps have been taken to require the banking institutions to disclose the fair and true value of the Islamic banking operations in the form of Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Statements as part of the Notes to the Accounts in the principal financial statements of the banking institutions. This is to duly reflect the different risks and unique characteristics inherent in Islamic banking as compared to conventional banking. Where Islamic banking operates on a window basis, the existence of a firewall is to ensure the strict compliance to Shariah. Whilst the appropriate regulations and standards are vital to mitigate the risks involved, of equal importance is the oversight and monitoring of the Islamic banking institutions through effective supervision by the regulatory authority to ensure that the prudential requirements are observed. Lack of oversight, inadequate check and balances, and over exposure to risks are amongst the factors that may result in vulnerabilities to the system. The best of regulations and financial safety nets would not be able to avoid such vulnerabilities if early warning systems are not in place. To effectively perform the supervisory functions, there has to be an understanding and appreciation of Islamic banking business and operations. Supervisors therefore need to be fully equipped with the required knowledge and skills to be able to identify the risks involved in various Islamic banking transactions to effectively conduct supervisory oversight of Islamic financial industry. Enhancing Shariah framework and governance A distinct feature of Islamic banking vis-a-vis conventional banking is the requirement to set up a Shariah advisory committee within the Islamic banking institutions. The establishment of Shariah advisory committee is important to serve as a check and balance to ensure that the management and operations of the Islamic banking institutions does not deviate from the Islamic principles in the formulation of their policies. Integral to this process is to achieve unity in diversity of the interpretations of Shariah injunctions in the realm of finance. In this regard, the IFSB has an important role to strengthen the current initiative to achieve a greater degree of convergence and harmonisation. Strong adherence to the Shariah is also enforced through guidelines and procedures to ensure its compliance amongst the Islamic banking institutions. Procedures for decision-making by the Shariah advisory committee of the Islamic banking institutions therefore need to be clear and transparent. The role and responsibility of the committee therefore needs to reflect their responsibility and accountability to the management and the public. Their position is comparable to the auditors of the Islamic banking institutions. Hence, the financial reporting by an Islamic banking institution is required to provide the necessary disclosure to report on the conformity of its operations with the Shariah principles. These will promote the foundations for building public confidence and assurance that the Islamic financial products are Shariah compliant. To enhance the Shariah framework in Malaysia, the Shariah advisory council at the central bank acts as a sole authority on all Shariah matters pertaining to Islamic banking and finance. Being an apex body, the council standardises Shariah ruling on similar issues to provide greater certainty and confidence to the financial institutions and to the investors and consumers. To strengthen the Shariah and legal framework, the Malaysian Judiciary has set up a dedicated High Court to adjudicate cases involving Islamic banking and takaful in accordance with the existing Malaysian civil laws. Any dispute, within or outside the court system that calls into question issues concerning Shariah is referred to the Shariah advisory council for guidance and clarification. Alternatively, disputes may also be referred to the arbitration centre for resolution. In this connection, Malaysia will enhance the Regional Centre for Arbitration in Kuala Lumpur to serve as a platform to deal with dispute cases on Islamic banking and finance, and to extend these services beyond our borders. Conclusion The challenge to develop regulatory standards that remain true to Islamic core principles is an important element in the development and growth of the Islamic financial services industry. The development of an Islamic financial system that is able to contribute towards stability and balanced global growth needs for its development to be achieved in the context of a rigorous and robust legal, regulatory and supervisory regime. This is reinforced by effective supervision, strong Shariah framework and an efficient judiciary system that promotes confidence and soundness in the Islamic financial system. It is with the combined commitment and concerted efforts by regulators, the industry and market participants that these goals can be achieved.

Title: Speech at the Launch of Kuwait Finance House Research
text: Governor's Welcome Speech at the Launching Ceremony of the duitsaku.com Website Presenter: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz / Venue: Bank Negara Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 19 Oct 2004 / The Honourable Dato' Hishammuddin Tun Hussein, Minister of Education Malaysia. Ladies and gentlemen and respected students. "Financial education is a branch of knowledge that needs to be mastered by all groups, especially in this dynamic and challenging economic and financial environment. To ensure the effectiveness of knowledge in the long term, the younger generation of Malaysians now need to be exposed to this knowledge, as early as possible. With constant exposure, it is our hope that there will be a new generation of Malaysians who have the skills to administer their own financial affairs." First of all, I would like to thank Yang Berhormat Dato' Hishammuddin, for being present at the Website Launching Ceremony, duitsaku.com, this morning. The development of this website is a joint initiative by Bank Negara Malaysia and the Ministry of Education Malaysia, to provide a platform for students, to gain knowledge on financial education, through interactive learning methods. Malaysia is a country with a large number of young people and high domestic savings rates. In terms of economic management, this high savings rate is one of the important fundamentals to enhance the country's economic resilience. In a situation where economic performance continues to be challenged by global uncertainty, this source of savings is able to ensure that private consumption activities, continue to support domestic economic development. With the domestic savings rate still remaining at 36% of the Gross National Product, we still have the potential to lower the savings rate, without jeopardizing the future prospects of the country's economy. Higher consumption rates can be an important generator of economic growth. However, what should be emphasized is that these uses should be managed based on their respective capabilities. In order to maintain sound financial management, a conducive environment for the people to save and practice spending prudently should be provided. This is because a wise balance between spending and savings is essential to ensure financial security and living standards in the long term. The ability to balance this requires knowledge, commitment and the ability to plan and manage finances. We need to ensure that financial goals are set, financial resources are carefully managed, and expenses are monitored systematically and in detail. With this, the financial position, spending capacity, debt load handling as well as savings, each of them can be fully controlled. In establishing the foundation of this financial education platform, Bank Negara Malaysia has entered into a joint venture with the Ministry of Education Malaysia and financial institutions, to expose students to appropriate financial education. The joint venture, which is one of this national agenda, was started with the Adoption Schools Programme in 1996, which saw all schools adopted as adopted schools by financial institutions. To strengthen the foundation of financial education, the School Student Finance Club programme was implemented in 2001, as a co-curricular activity for students outside the classroom. The book was introduced in 1999 to help students record their daily financial transactions. Every year, the Money Book is distributed to all students through their respective school adoption banks. It is this practice of recording daily financial activities that will be the basis for the students, forming a responsible attitude towards their personal finances. In line with the development of information technology, Bank Negara Malaysia and the Ministry of Education Malaysia have focused on having the Wang Saku Booklektronic, and placed on an interactive website. The production of this website is complementary to the practice of financial planning by using the Saku Money Book. The goal of this joint venture is to make personal financial management a popular subject and continue to be of interest to the students. This duitsaku.com website is aimed at students at the primary and secondary school levels. The simple and user-friendly features, accompanied by the attractive mascot design called "Si-Mut" and "The Bee", will surely influence the students to continue browsing the site, to gain new information and knowledge. In addition, students have the opportunity to interact and discuss with cyber friends from all over the country. They also have the opportunity to take part in challenge tests themed on financial education, such as contests, games, quizzes, calculators and other activities. Given the importance of financial education and its impact on economic activities and growth, it is Bank Negara Malaysia's hope that financial education be accepted as a curriculum subject in the classroom. The achievement of financial education goals will also support the goals of the Consumer Education Program as set out in the Financial Sector Master Plan which is currently in the implementation stage. It underscores the importance of information and guidance on financial affairs to the public. It is hoped that Bank Negara Malaysia hopes that the website launched today will be fully utilized by the public, especially the younger generation to improve their skills in planning and managing prudent finances.

Title: Speech at the Dinner announcing the IFSB Annual Meetings & Events and Global Islamic Finance Forum 2007
text: Assistant Governor's Speech at the Launching of RM5 Polymer Banknote Speaker: Assistant Governors / Advisers Speech/Interview Date: 26 Oct 2004 Venue: Auditorium, Bank Negara Malaysia Language: English Bismillahirrahmanirahim Y.Bhg Dato' Halipah Esa Timbalan Ketua Setiausaha Perbendaharaan Kementerian Kewangan Tuan Haji Wan Mansoor bin Wan Omar Pengarah Bahagian Hal Ehwal Pengguna Kementerian Perdagangan dan Hal Ehwal Pengguna Honored Members of the Notes and Coins Advisory Committee (NCAC) Distinguished guests Members of the media Ladies and gentlemen Assalamualaikum, dan selamat sejahtera. Allow me to first welcome you on this occasion to mark the introduction of the RM5 polymer banknotes, the first of its kind to be issued as banknotes in circulation in Malaysia. Beginning today, a total of 80 million pieces of RM 5 polymer banknotes would be available for distribution and circulation nation wide. Bank Negara Malaysia through our office and branch network and all commercial banks have made the necessary logistic arrangements to ensure that members of the public will be able to obtain sufficient supply of the new polymer notes. With the introduction of the RM5 polymer banknote, Bank Negara Malaysia will also from today discontinue the issuance of RM5 paper banknote for circulation. As at today Bank Negara Malaysia has issued a total of 120 million pieces of RM5 paper banknotes, which will continue to be legal tender and continue in circulation until this particular denomination of paper banknotes is fully withdrawn over time. Bank Negara Malaysia has made sufficient procurement of RM5 polymer bank notes to ensure an orderly, gradual and ultimately complete replacement of RM5 paper banknotes from circulation. The RM5 polymer banknotes are similar to the existing RM5 paper banknotes in design, color and size. Some of the existing security features in the RM5 paper banknotes are also retained, but few critical changes were made to incorporate security features that are unique to polymer banknotes, to enhance the overall security level of the denomination. The unique feel of polymer substrate itself will make new RM5 distinguishable, and therefore serves as an important authentication feature for the public. I would like to mention here the two most easily recognizable new security features incorporated in the RM5 polymer banknote that members of the public should be aware of. These security features are only possible through the use of polymer substrate. They are: Firstly: A clear window with the shadow image of the Prime Minister's Office at Putrajaya; and Secondly: an opaque or non transparent window on the back of the banknote, with a Kijang logo. With today's introduction, Malaysia joins a group of 18 countries around the world that have adopted the polymer banknote technology, and issue polymer banknotes for both circulation and commemorative purposes in the past 15 years since this banknote technology was commercialized. In addition, there are 5 other countries that have issued commemoratives polymer banknotes. There are currently about 5.3 billion pieces of circulating polymer banknotes in the world which is roughly about 5% of total world's banknotes-in-circulation. Malaysia had in fact initially used this technology in 1998, when Bank Negara Malaysia issued a limited number of RM50 polymer banknotes to commemorate the Sixteenth Commonwealth Games hosted by our country in that year. Ladies and Gentlemen, The adoption of polymer banknote technology will increase our portfolio of technological options. Bank Negara Malaysia's decision to issue RM5 polymer banknotes is a significant strategic move to further diversify our sources of banknotes procurement, supplementing our existing policy and practice of procuring paper banknotes from multiple suppliers. We have benefited from the high degree of price competition among banknotes suppliers, driven mainly by the current consolidation taking place within the industry and production overcapacity among banknote printers worldwide. The adoption of polymer technology by Malaysia will certainly enhance the healthy competitive elements in our bank note procurement processes in particular, and currency supply chain management processes in general. Ladies and Gentlemen, The substrate on which RM5 polymer banknotes are printed, is made of an oil-based plastic film and produced using a proprietary process with specialized equipment which makes this product not commercially available. Some of the security features of RM5 polymer notes are incorporated during the process of substrate production, while others during the printing process. The process of printing RM5 polymer banknotes are similar to that of paper banknotes, after which the banknotes are treated with layers of protective varnish. We expect RM5 polymer banknotes to maintain high level of durability and retain their quality while in circulation. They should have a significantly extended lifetime as the RM5 polymer banknotes do not absorb dirt or liquids, stay clean and hygienic to handle. The over-coating varnish should also add to cleanliness, protect the printing, reduce ink rub-off or ink wear, and ink dust, under a normal condition of usage and handling. An effective "clean note policy" in this country could promote a high sense of pride among our people in our national currency, which could encourage the desired positive attitude and behavior in the handling of notes in day-to-day activities. High quality notes facilitate manual and machine-assisted notes processing. The unique feel of polymer notes which are stronger, more rigid, cleaner and with minimal damage could make manual counting, validating, sorting, and packing a lot easier, faster and with less errors. Polymer notes which are in good condition feed into machine better, keep machine sensors clean and functional without causing unnecessary machine breakdown, which could lead to more efficient and effective notes processing at banks, retail centers, Cash In Transit companies, and other cash handlers' ends. With enhanced machine processability of RM5 polymer banknotes, we hope to see some forms of process reengineering taking place within the industry, with significant productivity and efficiency gains. Ladies and Gentlemen, We expect the public at large will respond positively to the introduction of RM5 polymer banknotes. For the past several weeks preceding today's launching, substantial collaborative work has been undertaken by the officers of Bank Negara Malaysia, financial institutions, major retailers, consumer associations, Cash In Transit companies, and other commercial entities with significant cash processing activities. I would like to take this opportunity to thank all parties involved. More activities and collaboration will take place in the coming weeks and months, focusing on distribution and public education. I ask your continuous support and participation in this program. With the introduction of the RM5 polymer banknote at this juncture of time, we hope to bring a little bit of excitement to Malaysians, our children especially, during the coming Hari Raya, Deepavali, Christmas and Chinese new year festive seasons, when they find new, crisp RM5 polymer banknotes in their customary duit raya, ang pau or gift packets. On that note ladies and gentlemen, may I now invite you to join me in this simple celebration to mark the official launching of RM5 polymer banknotes.

Title: Keynote Address  at The Islamic Forum Dubai 2014
text: Deputy Governor's Speech at the 2nd Annual Asian Islamic Banking & Finance Summit : Accelerating Growth of The Islamic Financial System Through Effective Linkages And Integration Speaker: Dato' Zamani Abdul Ghani Venue: Mandarin Oriental Kuala Lumpur Speech/Interview Date: 20 Sep 2005 Language: English Bismillahirrahmanirrahim Assalamualaikum warahmatullah and Good Morning It is my honour to be invited to address this distinguished audience at the 2nd 'Asian Islamic Banking & Finance Summit', organised by the Euromoney Seminars. I understand that the organizer has gathered distinguished and prominent international speakers to share their views and knowledge on the current development and issues in the area of Islamic finance. At the outset, I hope that presentations and discussions during this Summit would highlight and deliberate on the important areas pertaining to Islamic finance that would contribute towards further development and growth of the global Islamic financial services industry. Alhamdulillah, we have witnessed a significant and profound global growth of Islamic finance. The advancement and progress that has been achieved in the development of Islamic finance thus far has demonstrated its potential in strengthening its role as an effective form of financial intermediation that support the needs of the economy. Nevertheless, the challenges before us are to sustain the performance and to further accelerate the growth of Islamic finance in order to meet the greater demand and expectation of the financial community as well as consumers and investors. My remarks today will focus on key areas in which greater attention should be given with the objective of building effective linkages and integration in the Islamic financial services industry to accelerate its growth. I strongly believe that better linkages and integration can be made by instituting the necessary infrastructure to facilitate efficient capital and trade flows and creating vibrant financial markets. The essential infrastructure should also include strengthening information sharing and human talent management, as well as promoting the adoption of standard regulations and market practices. These are the four key areas that l will focus on this morning. Building the necessary infrastructure to facilitate efficient capital and trade flows Let's begin with building the necessary infrastructure to facilitate efficient capital and trade flows. The Islamic financial services industry, without doubt, has achieved commendable growth during the past decade. To further accelerate its growth in the years to come, there is a need to build a system that would be able to facilitate efficient capital and trade flows. This requires the development of an Islamic financial system which has all the required infrastructure. This should include:(i) Islamic financial players from the banking, takaful, capital market, fund and wealth management, as well as other non-bank Islamic financial sectors; (ii) creating a conducive tax, legal and Shariah framework; and (iii) a comprehensive range of Islamic financial products and services. These are the main pre-requisites for an efficient functioning of an Islamic financial system. In this context, we observe that the Islamic financial industry today is undergoing different stages of development at national and regional levels. A few countries have made significant advancement and progress while others have yet to make more meaningful moves in this area. As such, we would like to urge and assist, wherever possible, for them to adopt the right strategy and focus in building the necessary infrastructure which would better integrate with existing ones. In the case of Malaysia, significant progress has been made over the last two decades in developing the Islamic financial system. We believe that we have a clear well-defined strategy, and we have dedicated our resources to develop a comprehensive Islamic financial system supported by a structured legal, tax and Shariah framework. Today, Islamic finance in Malaysia is growing at a double-digit growth rate. The Islamic banking and takaful sectors have achieved market shares of almost 11% and 6% in terms of assets, respectively. Having achieved this significant development, we are now making progress towards realizing our aspiration to position Malaysia as an international Islamic financial hub. It is also our commitment to continuously establish linkages in promoting the development of Islamic finance at the global front. In this case, Malaysia has been actively extending technical assistance to many countries and has been encouraging Malaysian financial institutions to venture abroad. In addition, we have liberalized our Islamic financial industry by allowing the establishment of three new foreign Islamic banking institutions. Malaysia has also allowed foreign investors to participate up to 49% in the equity of all the newly established Islamic banking subsidiaries of the Malaysian banking group and four new takaful operators. These four new takaful licenses would be issued to qualified parties and the closing date for the submission of application is 31 October 2005. In addition, I wish to highlight that Malaysia, in close coordination with the Islamic Development Bank, has established a taskforce to spearhead, among others, the development and promotion of trade, investment, Islamic banking as well as takaful and retakaful industries among OIC member countries. These are the main initiatives to be undertaken under a Memorandum of Understanding signed in 2004 between Malaysia and the Islamic Development Bank. Creating vibrant financial markets Having an active Islamic financial market is one of the contributing factors that will accelerate the growth of Islamic finance. A vibrant Islamic financial market will facilitate fund raising and investment activities and will also promotes the creation of primary and secondary markets for Islamic financial instruments. In this respect, some progress has been achieved. We have seen the primary issuance of globally accepted Islamic financial instruments such as the global sukuk. In turn this global issuance of sukuks has played its role in building the linkages between different parties in the financial markets, such as issuers, investors and traders. While the issuance of sukuks at the primary market level has paved the way for the creation of a supply of Islamic financial instruments, it has not led as yet, to the promotion of active secondary markets. A greater focus is needed, therefore, in this aspect. One of the reasons for the lack of trading could be attributed to the insufficient supply of sukuks. Given its limited supply, investors prefer to hold these instruments for investment rather than trade them in the secondary market. This reflects the huge potential for issuers to tap the large funds available through the issuance of sukuks at competitive pricing to meet investors' demand. At the same time, there is the assurance of some liquidity in the market. Malaysia's experience has shown that our first sukuk issue has successfully attracted new as well as a wide range of investors thus enhancing the establishment of linkages and the integration of our Islamic financial sector into the global system. In a similar context, the International Islamic Financial Market (or the IIFM) Board can also play an effective role in promoting a vibrant Islamic financial market. As entrusted, the IIFM endorsement can facilitate cross border listing of sukuks at various international exchanges. The development of standardized documents that conform with internationally accepted Shariah interpretations would also promote global acceptance of Islamic financial instruments. Malaysia has also liberalized the foreign exchange and administrative rules to further strengthen our international linkages. We have allowed multilateral financial institutions or multilateral development banks and multinational corporations to raise ringgit denominated instruments in the Malaysian capital market. This measure has thus far attracted two prominent financial institutions, namely the International Finance Corporation and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development to issue ringgit denominated instruments based on Islamic principles. We would like to see more of these issues in the future in order to create a larger supply of these type of instruments so as to promote the secondary market for these instruments. Another important aspect in developing the Islamic financial markets is to have timely and reliable financial market indicators to track the performance of each instrument. Malaysia has recently launched the Dow Jones-RHB Islamic Malaysia Index which tracks more than 80% of Shariah-compliant stocks on the Malaysia stock exchange. The move to include the Dow Jones-RHB Islamic Malaysia Index within the global Dow Jones Islamic World Index has increased the potential for further investments into Malaysian Islamic equities. This has also contributed to the continued progress and rapid growth of the Islamic financial markets. This integration between domestic Islamic indices with the global index, such as Dow Jones, would also achieve some form of economies of scale with reduced duplication of efforts in promoting both domestic and international recognition. This l believe, is a good example of how increased connectivity and rapid financial market transmission have widen the investment avenues to the investors, and thus contributed to the growth of Islamic finance. Strengthening information sharing and human talent management Another critical, or the third success factor that requires significant attention is the promotion of information sharing and talent management in Islamic finance. This is particularly important as Islamic finance is somewhat at the early stage of development, as compared with the conventional financial system. The sharing and the exchange of information and knowledge should include country's experience in developing an Islamic financial system, the application of Shariah principles in product creation as well as the availability of database and statistics for the purpose of conducting research. This would contribute towards promoting information symmetry amongst the global financial players and markets. As we are all aware, there has been much variation in the Islamic financial products offered today. This variation is not only in terms of definition and treatment, but also of the different underlying Shariah principles and interpretation. While the variety of products are welcomed in the market, the basis of Shariah interpretations has raised some concerns in terms of its permissibility and acceptability which may hinder the smooth progress and innovation in the creation of Islamic financial products. There is therefore, a greater need now for more disclosure and transparency on the bases of Shariah considerations, and that these be disseminated and made widely accessible to the financial communities. This would enhance understanding and appreciation of the different Shariah considerations, and therefore facilitate further cross border investment in the various Islamic financial instruments. A side, but still a very important aspect on the issue above is the initiative to promote intellectual discourse on Shariah matters. As part of this initiative, Bank Negara Malaysia had organized the first Shariah Scholars Dialogue in June this year in conjunction with the IDB Board of Governors Meeting.
