Such a dialogue should be organized periodically in order to provide more opportunities for the Shariah scholars to share and learn from each other's experience. In addition, Bank Negara Malaysia has established a dedicated endowment fund amounted to RM200 million to facilitate the activities of Shariah scholars. Other than financing the periodic dialogues among the Shariah scholars, the fund would also promote research, provide scholarships and establish better interaction among these Shariah scholars and industry practitioners. It is hoped that this effort would contribute effectively to further enhance interaction and understanding in the area of Shariah and Islamic finance. Having a sufficient pool of Islamic financial practitioners to effectively steer the industry is another critical prerequisite for the Islamic financial industry to sustain and accelerate its growth. In addition to knowledge in finance, these practitioners should also have sound understanding of the Shariah in order to create products, structure the market and manage the resultant risks. Promoting the adoption of standard regulation and market practices The last key area that l wish to highlight today is promoting the adoption of standard regulation and market practices. The launch of the Islamic Financial Services Board in 2002 marked a major milestone in the setting of the required internationally accepted regulatory and supervisory framework for the Islamic financial services industry. To date, the IFSB has made commendable progress, and this include the issuance of two exposure drafts on capital adequacy and on risk management for industry feedback. Three other standards are being worked on, and these relate to corporate governance, transparency and market discipline, and the supervisory review process. These standards have taken into account the unique features of Islamic finance and, therefore, Islamic financial institutions will be assessed by a uniform international regulatory and supervisory standards. This will position the Islamic financial institutions on a level playing field with their conventional counterparts in terms of capital strength, financial resilience and capabilities. We could add accounting standards and Islamic rating agencies in this key area, but I believe this would be touched and deliberated upon by the other speakers. We are about to enter into a more advanced stage of development of Islamic finance. This being the case, we must thereby rise to the occasion and face all the challenges. I am confident that if our generation rises to the challenges, Islamic finance would continue to play a prominent role in meeting the needs of the global economy and in ensuring the stability and effectiveness of the international financial system, Insya Allah. On this note, I wish you a successful Summit. Thank you.

Title: Keynote Address at the Regional Conference on Investment Climate and Competitiveness in East Asia - "Financial Reforms and Investment Climate"
text: Governor's Keynote Address at the Regional Conference on Investment Climate and Competitiveness in East Asia "Financial Reforms and Investment Climate" Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Hotel Renaissance, Kuala Lumpur Speech/Interview Date: 21 Nov 2005 Language: English It is my pleasure to be here today to speak at this Regional Conference on Investment Climate and Competitiveness, coorganised by the World Bank and , the Economic Planning Unit of , and Bank Negara Malaysia . This subject on investment and competitiveness is of particular significance to Asia in the current environment when the world economy is confronted with the problem of unsustainable global imbalances that ha v s e brought with it, risks to the global growth prospects. While the resolution to this problem is seen as a shared responsibility by the respective regions in the world economy, Asia is seen as having a particularly major role in the absorbing the burden of adjustment process. Among the issues that have been cited as constraints to the adjustment process are the relative lack of strength in domestic demand outside the United States; the large gap between savings and investment in major regions of the world; and the fragmented structure of global capital intermediation that hinders surplus regions from financing productive investments within their own region. An important role for Asia in the adjustment process is to contribute towards the rebalancing of global growth. This is not only in terms of strengthening regional consumption demand but also increasing the home bias for investments by channelling an increased part of the surplus savings into productive investment in the region. As the investment climate improves, opportunities will expand, there will be potential for sustained productivity improvements, incentives for cost reductions, incentives for increase entrepreneurship and productive behaviour. The investment climate and competitiveness in Asia will therefore indeed be important in determining the extent of the role that Asia might have in contributing towards the orderly adjustment process of the unwinding of the global imbalances. The investment climate and competitiveness of an economy is shaped by a wide range of factors. These include the economic stability, the monetary and financial stability and what is equally important is that it is supported by social and political stability. My remarks this morning will focus on financial reforms and the investment climate. The financial sector has a major role in facilitating the overall functioning of the economy. It represents the nerve centre of the economy. The financial sector represents the means by which allows for the intermediation of funds are intermediated through which the - mobilis ation and allocation of ing and channelling the funds to productive investment s are undertaken . The greater the financialisation of savings, the greater will be the potential for the channelling of savings to productive activities through the formal financial sector. The financial sector also facilitates the means o f or payments and the transmission of monetary policy. The effectiveness of the financial sector in performing its functions depends on its ability to meet the changing requirements of the economy and the , ability to withstand the economic cycle . The financial sector is also an important factor in facilitating and finally to allow for greater economic flexibility and thus be a major factor in driving the economic transformation process. In order to contribute to the low cost of doing business, i t he financial sector also needs to be efficient and competitive. This includes being able to meet the economy's financial customers' requirements at the best possible values. The Asian region has seen significant transformation of its financial landscape driven by the globalisation process, the shift towards greater market orientation and the advances in technology. Emerging market economies in particular need to focus on capacity building development and financial infrastructure development building . This includes strengthening the financial institutions, developing the domestic financial markets and putting in place the legal, regulatory and supervisory framework that will ensure the soundness and stability of the financial system. This decade has also seen wide-ranging financial reforms taking place, including reforms relating to greater market orientation to achieve and enhanced operational efficiency, productivity and innovation and , the strengthening of standards of risk management, corporate governance and degree of disclosure and transparency. Initiatives have also been undertaken to relate s to restructur in e g , rationalis ation e and consolidat i e on the industry to strengthen capacity and address areas of weakness, risks and vulnerability. These initiatives include the establishment of institutional arrangements for restructuring and rehabilitation to be undertaken. The liberalisation process in a number of countries has been intensified to include the liberalisation of foreign ownership limits in domestic institutions to the issuance of new licences and relaxation of rules for foreign transactions. This has been for the most part to enhance inter-regional and global linkages and to facilitate greater trade and investment across borders. These reforms have brought with them new risks that need to be managed to ensure the maximum benefits of more competitive pricing, higher quality of product offerings and greater innovation in the range of products and services offered. The argument has always been made that the deregulation, removal of controls and liberalisation would produce a more optimal allocation of resources which would lower the cost of capital and thus enhance the investment climate and the overall growth prospects of the economy. The experience has shown that the lack of preparedness has often resulted in marginalisation and destabilising consequences. Appropriate strategies therefore need to be adopted to manage this globalisation process. Of importance , is the need to understand the implications of the changes, build the capacity to deal with the implications of such changes, have the capacity and mechanisms to conduct surveillance to monitor developments and finally, to have at the disposal of the monetary authorities, the capacity for policy response to manage the financial developments in the new environment. In the final part of my presentation, let me share with you Malaysia's experience on the financial dimension in influenc ing of the investment climate, particularly on the Malaysia's financial reform s that Malaysia has implemented as part of our efforts and commitment to continuously enhance the investment climate. The objectives of these efforts are to enhance the flexibility of the economy, strengthen its competitiveness, soundness and investor confidence in the economy. The financial system in Malaysia has played an important role in providing a stable and positive environment while facilitating diversification of the economy - allowing for focus on the areas of comparative advantage, including new areas of growth that have higher value added potential. Most important is that it provides a supportive environment for private enterprise sector economic activity to flourish . Not only has it provided a supportive enabling environment for private sector activity and kept the cost of doing business low, but it has also increased been translated into greater resilience and enhanced stability. It has also been important in making Malaysia an attractive destination for investment. Between 1988 and 1997, Malaysia received foreign direct investment (FDI) averaging 7.7% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) annually, one of the higher ratios in the world. Even in during the period 1998-2004, notwithstanding the shift in global patterns of FDI in flows, Malaysia continued to receive FDI amounting to 6% of GDP. The financial system in Malaysia has had an instrumental and complementary role in creating providing a vital constituent in the creation of a sound investment climate. While the economic, political and regulatory elements provide the underlying investment - conducive -friendly environment, the financial system provides the link for financing and financial services and the infrastructure for investments to function be allocated efficiently in across the economy. Malaysia has undertaken a proactive approach in formulating the financial reforms and in the development of the domestic financial infrastructure , taking into account the initiatives to the specifications and stage of development of the financial sector and the context of the prevailing and prospective environment to ensure that the stability of the financial sector i n particular, and the economy in general is s not destabilised compromised . The objective is to build a resilient, efficient and effective financial sector that is able to meet the changing needs of the domestic environment and provide a catalytic role in the transformation of the economy. Careful considerations were also given to the trades-offs of the conflicting objectives to promote efficiency and innovation within the financial sector whilst maintaining financial system stability and ensuring that the system has the capacity to adapt to changes in an orderly manner. Another important consideration in designing and implementing financial reforms is to also take into account the socio-economic agenda of the nation. As central banks of emerging economies, consideration also needs to be given to develop a financial system that is inclusive, that allows for all segments, target groups and the different activities to have access to financial services so that balanced growth can be achieved. Malaysia has also adopted a gradual approach to liberalisation of the financial sector. The process is sequenced, taking into consideration a number of factors. The overriding objective is preserving financial stability. It is important that the domestic banking institutions are ready and have the ability to adapt and respond positively to the dynamics of liberalisation so that the as to be able to reap maximum benefits from this process can be realised . As part of this process, Hence, lead time has been given for domestic banking institutions to enhance their efficiency and capabilities to strengthen their capacity to operate in a more competitive environment and to sharpen their competitive edge and elevate themselves and to gravitate to benchmarks achieved by international players. Without T t his pre-condition , is important prior to any liberalisation so as to avoid any may have destabilising implications on financial stability, which may in turn adversely affect and thus weaken the investment climate of the country. Our The Financial Sector Masterplan that was launched in 2001 outlines depicts our strategy on financial sector development and the approach towards liberalisation. The Masterplan provides the blueprint for lays the foundation for the medium and long-term development of the financial sector and the integral steps that need to be taken to achieve the objective our endgame of creating a financial sector that is resilient , and competitive and efficient that is able to contribute more effectively and meaningfully to the economic growth and development process . In the first phase of the Masterplan, focus is accorded to nurture a core of strong and forward looking domestic financial institutions that are more efficient, competitive and technology - driven and that are able to face the challenges of liberalisation and globalisation. The focus of the first phase i wa s essentially on enhancing capacity of domestic institutions and building and enhancing the domestic financial infrastructure. Following the first phase, greater deregulation and liberalisation can be expected to through providing greater operational flexibility to incumbent foreign players will increase the level of competition. These measures will be are implemented gradually, taking into consideration depending on the ability of the financial system to absorb the changes. The final phase of the Plan will involve gradual assimilation into the international financial system global competition with possible introduction of new foreign competition. This phase will also be characterised by see greater participation of domestic banking institutions in the global financial system. markets. It has been close to five years since the introduction issuance of the Masterplan. Significant progress in building the capacity and capability of the our domestic financial institutions and the establishment setting up of the necessary financial infrastructure to provide the foundation for growth of the financial sector, has been achieved. The strengthening of the financial sector has also been driven by the restructuring, reengineering, rationalisation and consolidation efforts that have been undertaken during this period. This has also been reinforced by strengthened risk management practices and infrastructure and the adoption of , high governance standards and adoption of best practices. The banking sector, in particular, is now anchored by a core group of domestic banking institutions that are well-capitalised, benefiting from the industry-wide consolidation programme that was completed in 2002. The capitalisation of the banking system is strong, with a risk-weighted capital ratio sustained at high levels of more than 13%, whilst the asset quality has improved significantly. The banking system has also continued to record strong profits amidst greater diversification in their income sources and continuous improvement in their operational efficiency. The financial sector is also supported by a thriving and evolving Islamic financial system which provides a comprehensive range of products and services based on Syariah principles. Significant milestones have been achieved thus far in terms of the development of the financial infrastructure, and the regulatory framework for Islamic banking. Complementing the developments in the banking sector and Islamic financial sector, the insurance and takaful sectors have also made marked contributions in supporting the economic transformation process. Premiums and contributions of these sectors have continued to expand at double digit growth rates in the first half of 2005 . , with the general sector rebounding strongly after two consecutive years of slow growth. The underlying fundamentals for sustainable expansion growth have also strengthened, with stronger solvency positions, continued profitability and improved underwriting discipline. In tandem with the holistic development of the financial sector, focus has also been accorded to develop the capital market, in particular, the bond market and the venture capital industries towards achieving the objective of building a strong, vibrant and diversified financial sector. The corporate sector , , including foreign multinational corporation s and multilateral agencies are now able to have access to our domestic bond market. Financial institutions have now also embrace d higher levels of technology and improved business processes that enable them to capitalise on larger business opportunities and reap benefits from economies of scale and cross-selling of products and services. Significant milestones have also been achieved in the delivery of personalised and customised financial solutions to meet the increasingly complex needs of consumers. Utilisation of new delivery channels through innovative technology-based mechanisms has also increased, leading to more effective and efficient distribution of products and services to customers. The continuous ability of the financial sector to meet the increasingly diversified and discerning discerning needs and preferences of the various segments of customers with greater product differentiation and value added services are will strengthen ing their competitive advantage and contribut e ing towards enhancing the investment climate for investors. In tandem with these efforts, internal reorganisation and reengineering of processes to achieve higher levels of operational efficiency have also been emphasized. By December 2005, all Seven out of ten finance companies would have successfully merged with their respective commercial bank . and the remaining ones are expected to merge this year. Also, the framework on investment banks will pave d the way for to rationalis ation e of the merchant banking, stockbroking, discount house and universal broking industry. The creation of investment banks is envisaged to enhance the capacity and capabilities of domestic capital market players to be able to compete meaningfully in an increasingly challenging environment, hence contributing to the development of a dynamic and vibrant capital market that effectively supports the and support economic growth and transformation process of the economy . Efforts to develop the financial sector are not confined to capacity building of the domestic financial institutions. These initiatives have also been complemented by efforts to develop the financial and consumer protection infrastructure. An Efforts are being directed to evolve an efficient and effective payments system that has the agility to take advantage of the evolve with the advent of new technologies that ha s ve emerged. been established. We have also embarked on a ten - year comprehensive consumer education programme to elevate the financial literacy of consumers and promote consumer activism as a mean s to promote greater inclusion and also to drive performance of the financial sector. Continuous enhancements are also underway to strengthen the consumer protection framework. The establishment of a deposit insurance system in Malaysia recently represents one of the various initiatives that have has now been implemented. been put in place. In terms of the regulatory approach, we have evolved from a "rule-based" approach to a more one that is more flexible approach, th at is and "principle-based". This Such an approach aims to promote competition and innovation whilst maintaining sufficient regulations to ensure financial prudence and stability in the financial system. Emphasis is also given towards developing broad prudential guidelines and principles, with enhanced focus on identifying risks at the system level and ensuring that individual financial institutions have the necessary systems capacity to undertake and manage risks. Within this context, Flexibility is hence accorded to the financial players have the flexibility to design their own strategies and market niches. Th is e supervisory process has also been is also complemented by strengthened and more rigorous surveillance mechanisms at both individual institution and system levels ha ve been instituted . Given the now strengthened position of the financial sector, several liberalisation measures have been accelerated ahead of the schedule in advance of our commitment in the Masterplan. We have brought forward a A series of measures that were brought forward include such as the liberalisation of the provision of internet banking by foreign banks in January 2002, and the removal of the 50:50 quota on credit granted to non-resident controlled companies between foreign and domestic banks in April 2003. Three new full-fledged Islamic banking licen s c es to foreign financial institutions were also issued, ahead of the original plan to do so in the third phase of the Masterplan. Other measures that have been accelerated include the increase in the foreign equity participation limit in investment banks and Islamic subsidiaries to 49%, and the flexibility for commercial banks, including the foreign commercial banks to provide factoring services as part of commercial banking business or through a separate legal entity. Other initiatives include the We will also be according greater operational flexibility to the locallyincorporated foreign banks to increase the number of their in terms of establishment of branches. These liberalisation measures which will be done in stages , signi reflect fy Malaysia 's commitment to undertake liberalisation at a pace that provides a mutually beneficial situation in for the domestic economy. To conclude, the The strong and stable financial system, supported by a comprehensive legal and regulatory and supervisory framework, has been a positive factor supporting Malaysia 's growth potential . It has provided , providing investors with a safe and stable environment that is conducive for sustainable performance. Efforts will thus continue to focus on enhancing Malaysia's long-term growth potential especially in ensur ing ing that the financial sector continues to perform its role in the economy , responding to its be strong, dynamic and responsive to the needs of the real economy. and functioning efficiently. Skills and expertise in the financial sector will continuously be enhanced so as to create a pool of expertise that can contribute effectively to this process. financial sector and economic development. Areas that will receive special attention will be to develop Malaysia as an Islamic banking and financial hub and to enhance our competitive advantage as a business process outsourcing centre. Amidst all these efforts, Malaysia we will continue to strengthen existing and create new our global linkages through trade, investment, financial flows, strategic alliances, cross - border mergers and acquisitions, internationalisation of businesses, mobility of the workforce as well as regional and international cooperation. This will enable Malaysia to participate in the opportunities and enhance its inter-linkages particularly with regional economies to strengthen further the mutually reinforcing growth potential of the region.

Title: Welcoming Speech at the Launching of the duitsaku.com Website
text: Governor's Speech at the Dinner announcing the IFSB Annual Meetings & Events and Global Islamic Finance Forum 2007 Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 18 Mar 2007 It is my great pleasure to welcome you to this dinner which is being held in conjunction with the Annual Meetings of the Islamic Financial Services Board and the Global Islamic Finance Forum 2007 that will take place at the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre on 26-29 March. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Honourable Dato' Seri Syed Hamid bin Syed Jaafar Albar, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Malaysia, for accepting our invitation to be our guest of honour this evening. Islamic finance was first introduced in Malaysia almost 30 years ago. It was then considered a niche industry, created to meet the special requirements of the Muslim community. Today, Islamic finance has gained widespread acceptance among Muslims as well as non-Muslims as a viable form of financial intermediation in the global financial system. Indeed, Islamic finance has evolved to become an integral part of the international financial system. It is now being offered in more than 60 countries and with an asset size of over USD 1 trillion. Going forward, the prospects for Islamic finance are indeed promising, with the demand for Islamic financial products and services expanding at exponential rates. To support the orderly growth and development of Islamic finance, it is important that the necessary financial infrastructure and regulatory framework are in place. In this regard, the IFSB was established to have the important role of developing the international prudential standards for Islamic banking and finance in the global financial system. This is aimed at ensuring the soundness and stability of the Islamic financial system. The development of such prudential standards in Islamic finance is key to facilitating and supporting its development as a viable, competitive and sustainable mode of financial intermediation in the international financial system. This year, 2007, marks the 5th anniversary of the establishment of the IFSB. Malaysia is honoured to be the host country of the IFSB. The Government has been committed to providing the IFSB with the fullest support and cooperation so that the IFSB will be able to achieve its mandate as the international financial standardsetter for Islamic finance. I am pleased to mention that next year, IFSB will move to new premises that is in close proximity to Bank Negara Malaysia. The new building will also house our Bank's learning centre that will have cutting edge and the state of the art facilities which we will share with the IFSB. In addition to being focused on the prudential standards for Islamic finance, the IFSB also provides an important platform through its regular series of seminars and conferences - to highlight and deliberate issues concerning the various aspects of Islamic banking and finance. In particular, the IFSB fosters active engagement and collaboration with the financial industry from all parts of the world. In this connection, from the 26th until 29th March 2007, IFSB will be convening its 10th Meeting of the IFSB Council and its 5th General Assembly. In addition to these Annual Meetings, the IFSB will be hosting a series of public lectures and seminars. In conjunction with these IFSB events, Bank Negara Malaysia is pleased to host its first Global Islamic Finance Forum (GIFF) from 26 to 29 March 2007. The objective of these seminars and forums is to promote the sharing of experiences and dialogue among the international financial community on the leading issues in Islamic finance. Many of the sessions will be presented by renowned experts and practitioners in their respective fields. It is hoped that these seminars will serve as a catalyst to drive further innovations and developments in the area of Islamic banking and finance. In closing, I would like thank the Honourable Dato' Seri Syed Hamid bin Syed Jaafar Albar once again for being with us this evening. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the diplomatic community at large with your extensive international networks represents an important channel for the dissemination of information on the opportunities that Islamic finance offers to the business, financial communities and authorities from around the world. In so doing, it would contribute towards supporting the further progress of Islamic finance. Finally, I would also like to take this opportunity to thank the staff at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for their support and cooperation in facilitating the important work of the IFSB. We believe that our collaborative efforts in the development of Islamic finance will facilitate the further strengthening of the international economic and financial linkages in the global economy and thus increase the potential for more balanced global growth.

Title: Welcoming Address at the Official Launch of International Centre For Leadership In Finance (ICLIF)
text: Governor's speech at the Sir Purshotamdas Thakurdas Memorial Lecture - "Managing Financial Liberalisation and its Challenges: Implications for Emerging Economies" Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Mumbai, India Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 12 Nov 2007 Introduction Emerging economies have increasingly gained a more important role in the global economy and the international financial system. This trend has become more pronounced in the recent decade. This increased role is reflected in its greater contribution to global growth, international price adjustments and financial flows. As a consequence, this greater international economic and financial integration has increased the potential for emerging economies to contribute towards the rebalancing of global growth and towards achieving international financial stability. Among the fundamental factors that have contributed to this increased significance of the emerging economies has been increased economic and financial liberalisation. While increased liberalisation has progressed significantly in the area of international trade and investment, this more recent decade has witnessed the intensification of financial liberalisation. Financial liberalisation has occurred on several fronts, in the financial sector, the financial markets and the capital account of the balance of payments. This accelerated pace of financial liberalisation has resulted in the increased internationalisation of domestic financial systems in emerging economies. Previously, the financial sector was generally domestic oriented and the capital account had wide ranging restrictions. In the current environment, there is a greater presence of foreign interests in the financial sector, an increased foreign participation in the domestic financial markets and a growing volume of cross-border financial flows to emerging economies. My remarks this afternoon will focus on issues concerning financial liberalisation and their implications on emerging economies with special focus on Asia. It is my great honour to be here today at the Indian Institute of Banking and Finance to give this year's Sir Purshotamdas Thakurdas Memorial Lecture. Sir Purshotamdas Thakurdas had very much believed in the free market mechanism but he also believed in the need for the transition towards greater market orientation to be managed so as to ensure the growth and development process. My remarks today will extend these principles to the transition towards increased financial liberalisation in emerging economies. While increased foreign participation in the domestic financial system brings wide ranging benefits, it also has implications on our other national objectives. These include the goals of achieving financial inclusion, balanced growth and social stability, all of which are key pre-conditions for sustainable growth and development. Financial liberalisation, however, also involves tradeoffs that may increase the risks to achieving these goals. The subject of my paper today will be to highlight these challenges and the implications for its management both for the policy makers and for the financial services industry. For the policy makers, it involves deciding the nature of the policy intervention and the policy environment, while for the industry, it involves the steps that need to be taken to be adequately equipped and prepared for a more challenging environment. Financial Liberalisation: Its Benefits and Trade-offs Financial liberalisation involves increasing foreign interests and participation in the domestic financial system. This includes increased entry of foreign financial institutions in the domestic financial system and the removal of barriers to cross-border financial services offered by financial intermediaries that are located outside the domestic financial system. An area of liberalisation that has gained greater significance since the 1990s has been the balance of payments capital account liberalisation. This has involved the removal of restrictions on the convertibility of the currency and on international financial transactions and allowing for the freer inflow and outflow of funds. Such financial liberalisation needs to be distinguished from financial deregulation which involves the move towards greater market orientation, the withdrawal of state interests in the domestic financial system and the reduction of interventionist financial policies. The case for increased financial liberalisation maintains that it would facilitate the development of a more efficient and robust financial system. Such financial liberalisation, however, is also accompanied by increased risks. For emerging economies, the net economic payoffs arising from financial liberalisation is therefore less clear. To fully realise its benefits, the associated potential risks of such liberalisation needs to be effectively managed. The financial infrastructure and intermediaries need to be sufficiently developed and strengthened so as to ensure its efficient functioning in a significantly more competitive environment. It has also been maintained that financial liberalisation will increase efficiency in the financial intermediation process and that it will lead to a more efficient mobilisation and allocation of funds thus reducing the cost of financial intermediation. Other benefits are that it would also provide technology transfer, bringing in new expertise and encourage greater financial product innovation. A further argument for financial liberalisation is that the increased competition would bring about greater market discipline and thus enhance competitiveness. The increased foreign participation in the domestic financial markets would also contribute to increased market liquidity and more competitive pricing. It will contribute to creating market based mechanisms and encourage a more efficient allocation of capital in the economy. Finally, it is argued that it will contribute to the development and expansion of the financial markets, in particular, the debt related markets that is important to financing investment activity. Indeed, such liberalisation has the potential to contribute towards increasing the depth, breadth and liquidity of the domestic financial markets. With the more efficient functioning domestic financial markets, it would improve the transmission mechanism of monetary policy. Meanwhile, the argument for capital account liberalisation is that capital flows represents an important external source of financing and would contribute towards increased investment and growth. It would also contribute towards a more efficient allocation of funds across international borders. Liberalisation of the capital account in the form of removing restrictions to foreign exchange transactions would also increase flexibility of managing foreign exchange transactions and thus increase the potential to better manage risks while also reducing the cost of doing business. Finally, it is argued that such an environment would result in greater market discipline and thus promote financial stability of the domestic financial system. There are, however, downside risks to financial liberalisation. In particular, the focus on achieving a more competitive environment without taking into account its impact on the domestic economy could promote conditions that result in a widening of income disparities. Despite significant strides in developing the domestic financial system in most emerging economies, financial inclusion has generally not been commensurate with this progress. A World Bank report released this year estimated that only 30 percent of the adult population in Asia are participating in the financial system. Financial liberalisation without being accompanied by conscious measures to address this could worsen the pattern of development. Financial liberalisation is also expected to result in greater international economic and financial integration and thus increased vulnerability to developments and cycles in other parts of the world. This issue is highly relevant in this current environment. Will the current financial events in the United States and Europe have a material impact on the financial markets and economies of the emerging economies? This interdependence of the financial systems and economies and the contagion effects would be among the outcomes of financial liberalisation. In addition, foreign financial institutions are generally affected by conditions and developments in their home country rather than by local conditions. Financial liberalisation could for example, amplify further the implications of financial stress from other parts of the world on the domestic financial system. It could also accentuate and amplify asset bubbles and boom bust cycles. Finally, there is also the risks of marginalisation of domestic financial institutions. This would to a large extent depend on the health and competitiveness of the domestic financial institutions. An issue that continues to confront emerging economies is the highly volatile capital flows and its consequent effect on the domestic financial markets, the financial system and the economy. Such short term flows have resulted in financial pressures on the exchange rate. The resultant excess liquidity following excessive inflows could also potentially fuel asset and price inflation while sudden reversals of foreign funds from the domestic financial markets could also have adverse implications on the domestic corporate and household sector, thus affecting the overall economy. These potential risks and vulnerabilities continue to be a challenge even in the more developed financial systems. Financial Liberalisation in Asia Let me now turn to the financial liberalisation in Asia . While Asia has always been integrated with the global economy, arising from its significant international trade and investment activities, this high degree of openness has become even more pronounced since 1990. The trade volume in Asia has increased from 19 percent of the total world trade in 1990 to 26 percent in 2006. In addition, foreign direct investment into Asia has increased from USD80 billion in 1996 to USD200 billion in 2006. The average ratio of total trade to GDP in Asia is high at about 100 percent. At one end of the spectrum, Singapore , Hong Kong and Malaysia have ratios that exceed 200 percent, while the lowest ratio in the region exceeds 50 percent. While financial liberalisation is a more recent phenomenon, it has gained significant momentum in this recent decade in most emerging economies. Although this is very evident in Asia , the pace of financial liberalisation within the region has been uneven. The increased opportunities, the attractive prospects for the Asian emerging economies and the dismantling of various forms of barriers have been among the factors that attracted increased foreign interest and participation in the region. In the early 1990s, it was also the search for new areas of growth by major international banks beyond their domestic borders given that their own domestic markets had become saturated and intensely competitive. This provided the impetus for trade negotiations which led a number of countries to gradually remove restrictions on entry and foreign equity participation in domestic financial institutions. This trend was reinforced by the increased economic integration of the region. Further financial liberalisation was also prompted by the privatisation of state owned banks in a number of countries. Table 1 shows increased foreign participation in the largest banks in the selected Asian economies between 1997 and 2007, with the most pronounced increase observed in Korea and Indonesia. Foreign participation in the financial sector also rose further in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis following the involvement of foreign investors in the recapitalisation of domestic banking institutions. While for a number of the crisis affected countries several closures occurred, there were also subsequent sales of troubled financial institutions. Since the end of the 1990s, the increased pace of financial liberalisation for several of the emerging economies was largely independent of crisis related influences. Asia had entered into a new era in which there has been the gradual deregulation and reform of the financial sector. This included the move towards greater market orientation, removing portfolio restrictions and the introduction of market determined interest rates with monetary policy instruments also becoming more market based. As the domestic financial systems became strengthened, there was increased relaxation of foreign equity ownership restrictions and more liberal policies on foreign banks operating in the domestic financial system. During the period 1998 to 2003, the value of foreign direct investments in the financial sector in the emerging economies in Asia (through cross border mergers and acquisitions) is reported to have been eleven times larger than the annual average for the first half of the 1990s. Asia has continued to be among the fastest growing region for such cross border activity. Foreign participation as measured by the percentage of total banking assets owned by foreign-controlled banks during the 1990s was either non existent or less than 10 percent. It has now increased up to 18 percent in 2002 (Figure 1). Figure 1: Ownership structure in banking systems (as % share of total bank assets as at end-2002) Sources: National central banks; national supervisory authorities; Hawkins and Mihaljek (2001); Cardenal et al (2003); BIS calculations In the decade following the Asian crisis, the emerging economies in Asia have also extensively developed the capital markets, in particular, the bond and equity markets. The growing significance of such markets can be observed in Table 2. At about USD 9.6 trillion in 2005, the assets of East Asian financial markets is equivalent to about 20 percent of the US financial market and about half of that of Japan . However, measured in terms of market capitalisation, East Asia 's equity markets have more than trebled since 1997. The bond markets in the East Asian Region have also seen significant growth during this period (Table 3). Of significance, is the notable increase in the participation of foreigners in the financial markets in Asia , in both the bond and equity markets. Equity flows into emerging Asia increased twelve-fold over the 1990 levels to reach US638 billion in 2004 (Figure 2). This market openness reflects the gradual relaxation of controls on foreign participation in the capital markets. Figure 2: Portfolio Assets Held by Nonresidents in Emerging Markets (in percent of GDP) Figure 3: Equity Market Integration 1/ (Share of S&P/IFC Investable in percent of S&P/IFC Global) In the bond markets, debt security holdings by foreigners in value terms, increased more than 60 percent between 2001 and 2005 (Table 4). Foreign ownership of local bonds and the issuance of local bonds by foreigners is freely allowed in most emerging Asian economies. This has contributed to increasing the liquidity of the bond markets and has evolved a more diversified structure of the financial system. This progress achieved in the development of the domestic financial markets has however, become a further factor to attract increased capital inflows. Table 4: Bond Markets in East Asia : Foreign Participation Economy Debt Security Holdings by Non-residents (USD billion) 2001 2005 China 7.03 11.23* Indonesia 8.84 18.29 Korea 36.80 62.30 Malaysia 2.74 14.82 * China : 2004 figure Source: ADB Asian Bonds Online Liberalisation of the capital account in the emerging economies in Asia has resumed since the 1997-1998 financial crisis following the strengthening of the banking sector, the development of the domestic financial markets, the increased flexibility of the domestic financial system, and the enhancement of the regulatory and supervisory framework. In addition, most of the Asian emerging economies have during this period built up their international reserve levels. While the capital account liberalisation process has intensified, most countries have sequenced the process. In India , the Tarapore Committee Report of 2006 has proposed a three phase capital account convertibility between the period 2006 - 2011. Malaysia has since 2003 progressively dismantled foreign exchange rules to increase market flexibility, to lower transaction costs and to promote new areas of activity. In several of the Asian emerging economies, there however, remains a number of safeguards. Several lessons were learnt from premature capital account liberalisation during the 1997-1998 crisis. Among these safeguards is the non-internationalisation of the domestic currency which limits lending of the domestic currency to nonresidents. Other safeguards include limits to the volume of different forms of foreign exchange transactions. Against the backdrop of the ongoing capital account liberalisation in the region, net private capital flows into the region have reached a record high of USD255 billion in 2006, exceeding the net private flows to Asia that occurred in 1996, prior to the crisis. The search for higher returns, market expectations for exchange rate appreciation and risk diversification activities have added further to the pull factors that have drawn capital flows to emerging economies in Asia. Figure 4: Rising net private flows Implications for the Financial Sector Increased foreign presence brings with it a more competitive environment. It is argued, that such an environment would promote increased innovation, greater efficiency in pricing and improved quality of financial services. It is further maintained that increased foreign shareholding in domestic institutions would bring new expertise and best practices which would in turn contribute to enhancing financial stability. Furthermore, it can become an additional source of capital as well as open up new markets for the domestic institutions. Despite these potential benefits, most emerging economies have not yielded to the call for an accelerated pace of financial sector liberalisation. The experience has shown that certain pre-conditions need to be in place for financial liberalisation to produce mutual benefits. Moreover, the wide ranging trade-offs that may accompany financial liberalisation need to be managed to avoid its adverse repercussions on the domestic financial system and the overall economy. An important agenda for emerging economies is ensuring balanced growth. This presents the challenge of balancing the implications of promoting a more competitive financial system while also ensuring inclusive and balanced economic growth. Unmanaged, financial liberalisation can result in significant divergent patterns of growth which would widen further the income gap. This could in turn have implications on social stability and thus the sustainability of the growth and development process. While the presence of foreign banks can provide added stability from domestic-induced shocks, the high degree of financial openness could render the domestic economy to become more sensitive to external shocks. In particular, the growing presence of foreign banks could increase the vulnerability to the risk of contagion emanating from adverse market developments in the home countries of these financial institutions. The effect of contagion within regions, and across seemingly unrelated regions also have the potential to become pronounced. With only a few exceptions, commercial banks remain the main providers of credit in most emerging economies, accounting for an average of 90% of total credit. Korea , Thailand and Malaysia are notable exceptions where deposit-taking institutions other than commercial banks, also exists. The marginalisation of domestic institutions can thus result in disruptions to credit supply, damage confidence which in turn, would affect economic activity. In periods of uncertainty, the experience has been that foreign financial institutions are among the first to withdraw credit lines. This was evident during the 1997-1998 East Asian financial crisis. The penetration of financial services in many parts of Asia are currently at well below the desired levels. Data on the number of branches per 100,000 population in the emerging economies in Asia (Table 5) range from 1.3 in China to 13.4 in Korea compared to an average of 35.6 in the G-7 countries. The number for India is 6.3 while Malaysia is 9.8. The experience is for foreign banks to concentrate in urban centres which are viewed as the regions with the potential for the highest returns. Foreign banks have been found to focus on the larger corporations and the high-end SMEs. This risks creating credit gaps to important segments of the economy. The marginalisation of domestic banks thus raises the broader concern over the access to financing by certain economic sectors, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and the lower-income segments. Table 5: Financial Access: Branch Penetration Across Countries Country Number of branches per 100,000 population Bangladesh 4.47 China 1.33 India 6.30 Indonesia 8.44 Korea 13.40 Malaysia 9.80 Pakistan 4.73 Philippines 7.83 Singapore 9.13 Sri Lanka 6.87 Thailand 7.18 Developed (G-7) countries (avg.) 35.64 Source: Beck, T. et al (2005) A BIS study 1 has further shown that over the period 1994-2004, domestic banks in emerging market economies (including the regions of Asia, Latin America and Central Europe ) participated in total credit expansion to a greater degree than foreign banks. More specifically, for every 10 percentage point increase in the credit to GDP ratio, credit extended by domestic banks expanded on average by 8% of GDP, compared with only 1.5% of GDP reported for foreign banks. To promote broad-based growth across all sectors of the economy, many Asian economies have therefore maintained policies on lending to priority sectors as a measure to address such credit gaps as financial systems are progressively liberalised. The implementation of Basel 2 presents further challenges to domestic banks which may be disadvantaged compared to the larger and more sophisticated foreign banks due to the huge capital investments required to reap the capital efficiencies. Strengthened capabilities in the context of this development becomes vital. Addressing the talent scarcity in the financial services industry in Asia has also become more challenging. In India alone, close to 300 commercial banks (including cooperative and regional rural banks) with over 70,000 offices nationwide are now competing for talent alongside an increasing foreign presence in the industry. The approach to financial sector liberalisation in several of the economies in Asia has therefore been sequenced and managed so that it is also consistent with other policies in the economy. In Malaysia , Indonesia and Thailand , the sequencing of liberalisation measures are outlined in a financial sector masterplan. The plans essentially indicate the commitment to progressive liberalisation, and on the nature of the liberalisation measures, thus providing the advance time for the formulation of business strategies and preparations that are needed by the industry. On financial surveillance and financial stability, the strengthening of home-host supervisory cooperation has also become more important. To this end, more robust coordinating mechanisms between the host and the home countries have been developed. Particularly in the current environment, emerging economies need to be particularly vigilant in the surveillance of cross-border financial market developments and the potential vulnerabilities of the foreign banks. Ten years after the crisis, Asia 's financial sector is significantly stronger, better positioned to withstand foreign competition and to absorb the impact of any market disruptions that may result from international contagion transmitted to the domestic financial system. Banks in Asia have generally reported improved profitability, capital adequacy, efficiency and asset quality (Figure 5). Significant progress has also been achieved in developing the domestic financial infrastructure and the supporting legal system. In addition, effective safety nets have been established in most emerging economies and for consumers to cope with greater exposure to risk. There have also been the improvements in the rate of financial innovation and stronger governance and risk management capabilities which have strengthened the foundations for operating in a more competitive environment. Figure 5: Strengthened banking system * NPL for China in 1998 is estimated by JP Morgan * CAR is for year end-March 31. **NPL for India is for 2001 instead of 1998 *Figures for 2000-01 and 2003-04 are not available. *Figures are for 1995-96 and 2005-06 respectively Source: World Bank, IMF, national authorities Implications for financial markets and the economy The higher foreign participation in Asia 's financial markets also provides a further channel through which conditions in the international financial markets can rapidly spread to local financial markets. While the emerging market economies have demonstrated resilience in the face of the recent turbulence in global financial markets, continued large capital inflows may, however, increase the risks of excessive asset price appreciation, rising inflation and disorderly conditions in the foreign exchange markets. The 1997 Asian financial crisis and the recent US sub-prime crisis, provide an indication of the significantly higher risks that can arise from large capital inflows and outflows. After a prolonged and sustained period of net private inflows into Korea , Indonesia , Malaysia , the Philippines and Thailand in the 1990s, these flows were reversed in waves over several months following widespread speculative activity during 1997-1998 period. The more recent episodes of financial disturbances have also shown that even the more sophisticated investors over-reacted to uncertainties in financial markets. This is generally exacerbated by the complexity of the structured financial transactions which has in this more recent period masked the underlying risks through the effects of multiple layering, and the lack of understanding by investors of the markets, due to incomplete information. In most of Asia , the financial reforms pursued to strengthen the sector, to develop the domestic financial markets and to increase exchange rate flexibility have been factors that have made our markets even more attractive to the short-term investors, thus generating even greater capital inflows. At the national level, the Asian economies have adopted a combination of strategies in managing capital flows. This has involved increasing the flexibility in exchange rates, adopting marketdetermined interest rates and removing restrictions on foreign exchange transactions including allowing for hedging. The more diversified players in the market have also contributed to the more efficient functioning of the markets. An important lesson from the Asian financial crisis has, however, been in the area of financial market development and liberalisation. The deeper and more developed financial markets are better able to absorb the immediate liquidity arising from the large capital flows. The magnitude of these flows that have continued to increase significantly suggests that higher buffers are still needed while the financial system develops further. Importantly, large capital flows and the subsequent potential for increased volatility has been recognised as a challenge that cannot be sufficiently addressed by any individual country on its own. During the 1997 crisis, the region did not come together to contain the crisis and to collaboratively facilitate a resolution. Wide ranging and divergent strategies were adopted to restore stability and to manage the crisis. Ten years on from 1997, a regionally-integrated approach has now been put in place. National efforts are being reinforced by increased regional cooperation. Such cooperation has been in the areas of strengthening surveillance, liquidity support mechanisms, including the expansion of the ASEAN Swap Arrangement and enhancements of the bilateral swap arrangements under the Chiang Mai Initiative. Surveillance systems have also been enhanced to better identify the risk exposures arising from the increased financial flows. Other efforts underway include putting in place the financial and institutional infrastructures and the harmonization of standards and regulations to foster linkages in the regional financial markets among the ASEAN economies. The significant capital inflows have contributed to sharply increasing the levels of international reserves (Table 6) and the volatility in the capital markets and the foreign exchange markets. While reserves have reached record highs, for most of the emerging economies, only a part of this increase reflects the performance on the current account and that a significant part of the reserves have been built as a result of short-term flows. These inflows represent a claim on the reserves and thus there are risks that development in either the domestic or international financial markets may at any time trigger reversals. Table 6: Foreign Exchange Reserves of Selected Asian Economies Reserves (in US bn) Reserves as % of GDP 2000 2006 2000 2006 China 165.6 1,066.3 13.8 40.3 India 40.0 177.3 8.7 20.3 Indonesia 29.4 42.6 17.8 11.7 Korea 96.2 239.0 18.8 26.9 Malaysia 29.9 82.5 33.1 55.4 Philippines 11.3 23.0 14.9 19.5 Singapore 80.4 136.8 86.8 103.5 Thailand 32.7 67.0 26.6 32.5 Source: National authorities, IMF Exchange rates in emerging economies in Asia have also experienced a significant increase in volatility. During the Asian crisis, the exchange rates were depreciated in waves over a period that lasted one and a half years. The Indonesian rupiah depreciated by 85%, the Thai Baht by 58%, the Malaysian ringgit by 47%, the Korean won by 54%, the Philippine peso by 41% and the Singapore dollar by 22% (Table 7). After one and a half years, the currencies finally stabilised. During the intervening period there was a high degree of uncertainty bringing about an eventual economic contraction in most of the countries. Table 7: Exchange Rate Performance of Crisis Affected Countries and Selected Regional Currencies Against the US Dollar Maximum Depreciation* Broad Crisis Period End-Crisis to Present Currency Crisis Start to Through End-1996 to End-1998 End-2000 to 9 Nov. 2007 (%) Change Malaysian ringgit -46.8 -33.6 14.2 Singapore dollar -21.9 -15.2 20.3 Thai baht -58.3 -30.0 37.2 Indonesian rupiah -85.3 -70.5 6.0 Korean won -53.5 -30.2 39.0 Philippine peso -41.4 -32.2 17.0 Chinese yuan - 0.2 11.7 Japanese yen - 1.8 3.3 Indian rupee - -15.6 19.2 Note: * Approximation based on daily exchange rate data from Bloomberg In the current environment, strong inflows of short-term capital have been experienced in most of the emerging economies in Asia exerting upward pressures on the regional exchange rates. Most regional currencies have appreciated in the region of about 3% to 39% since 2000. For a number of countries there has been considerable discussion as to whether this has affected competitiveness. The exchange rate is only one of the factors that may affect the export performance. Other factors including demand conditions, prices and quality have been important. The experience, in fact, shows that exchange rates that were pegged to the US dollar over the period 1999 to 2001 appreciated significantly against most currencies when the US pursued a strong dollar policy. Yet, during this period, these countries continued to experience balance of payment current account surpluses. Malaysia 's own experience has been to enhance competitiveness and to move to new areas of comparative advantage. In the context of these developments, the pressure on the exchange rate is likely to continue regardless of the exchange rate regime. No regime will be insulated from the demands of the current global environment. The global experience has shown that when exchange rates have failed to perform their function, it was not due to the regime but due to other weaknesses that were prevailing in the economy or the financial system. What becomes vital is that the macroeconomic policies are consistent with the chosen regime. Such capital inflows also have important implications on asset prices. This will continue to be a challenge for policy. Raising interest rates to rein in exuberance in the capital markets will attract further capital inflows. Following significant inflows, the stock market indexes in most Asian markets have increased sharply (Table 8). Table 8: Stock Market Index of Selected Asian Economies End 2000 31 Oct 2007 % Change China 2,076.3 5,589.6 169.2 India 3,826.8 19,243.2 402.9 Indonesia 416.3 2,624.4 530.4 Korea 504.6 2,028.1 301.9 Malaysia 679.6 1,398.4 105.7 Philippines 1,467.8 3,784.9 157.9 Singapore 1,892.6 3,771.6 99.3 Thailand 264.9 894.6 237.8 Source: National authorities, IMF While most Asian markets are well supported by strong corporate earnings and sound economic fundamentals, events in other parts of the world including tightening liquidity conditions or corrections in the international financial markets will prompt profit taking in our markets. Such market behaviour has generally generated a protracted period of continued volatility. Economies that have large institutional investors, including pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and developed insurance industries will be able, in part, to mitigate this volatility. Strong growth conditions will also be a major underlying element that will reduce the contagion from the advanced economies on the Asian financial markets. Conclusion There is no one approach in managing financial liberalisation. Its success depends on the circumstances prevailing and stage of financial sector development in each respective economy. The approach to liberalisation needs to be pursued in a pragmatic manner that is sensitive to the different objectives to be achieved in each individual economy. More importantly, there also needs to be sufficient development of the financial infrastructure, the capability and state of preparedness of the financial services industry in order to ensure resilience and of the policy environment to ensure stability. Emerging economies would then be well positioned to share the benefits of financial liberalisation and thus achieve a mutually reinforcing shared prosperity. 12 November 2007 1See Mihaljek (2004)

Title: Welcome Speech of assistant  at SME Financing Seminar and Finance Clinic
text: Deputy Governor's Opening Address at the Opening Ceremony of the 10th ASEAN Insurance Regulators Meeting and 33rd ASEAN Insurance Council Meeting Speaker: Dato' Mohd Razif bin Abd. Kadir Speech/Interview Date: 15 Nov 2007 Venue: Prince Hotel and Residence, Kuala Lumpur Language: English - Unlocking Opportunities - It is my great pleasure to be here today at the 10 th ASEAN Insurance Regulators meeting and the 33 rd ASEAN Insurance Council Meeting in Kuala Lumpur . Let me first extend a warm welcome and "Selamat Datang" to all the delegates from abroad as well as to fellow Malaysians here today. During this Visit Malaysia Year', which is also the year of Malaysia 's 50th Anniversary celebrations of our independence, I do hope that our foreign delegates will make time to enjoy Malaysia 's diverse culture and the many unique sights, sounds and flavours. I am indeed honoured to be officiating the opening of the 10 th ASEAN Insurance Regulators Meeting and the 33 rd ASEAN Insurance Council Meeting. I understand that several fruitful meetings and exchange of ideas have already taken place yesterday, and several meetings have been outlined over the next two days to discuss various matters, revolving around the theme towards moving the ASEAN insurance industry forward. The ASEAN region has recorded significant growth with member countries growing at an average rate of 6% in 2006. ASEAN countries have grown stronger and our trade and cooperation have expanded further. Building on these existing strong linkages, ASEAN is expected to further progress in deepening and broadening its economic pie within ASEAN and in the region. The ASEAN region as a group accounted for approximately 8.3% of Asia's total GDP in recent years and generated around 22% of Asia' total export, placing the region second behind China, Asia's largest exporter. In 2006, ASEAN foreign direct investment rose by 27% to reach USD52 billion and total exports increased by 16.5% to reach USD758.04 billion. Trade among ASEAN countries has also increased tremendously. In fact for Malaysia , our trade with the ASEAN region comprised about 25% of our total trade. As we move towards AFTA and the removal of tariffs, the economic integration between countries in the region will deepen further. The encouraging economic growth prospects of ASEAN present tremendous growth potential and opportunities for the ASEAN insurance market. This increases the need to accelerate the development of insurance markets in the region to support the explosive growth in trade within ASEAN. Over time, the aim should be to achieve a better balance between reliance on foreign insurance markets and the domestic insurance markets within ASEAN to support economic activity. This will contribute towards achieving greater risk diversification, while at the same time, reaping more benefits for ASEAN economies from increasing economic integration. ASEAN currently has a total population of 568 million, and a large proportion comprising of a young workforce in the middle income group. The changing priorities and lifestyles of this new generation, growing wealth and increasing proportion of middle income population will also support continued and further growth in demand for investment-linked and wealth management products. As a result, the insurance industry has, and will continue to, expand its role beyond merely providing protection products. Against this backdrop, prospects for increasing the insurance penetration rate in our economies are clearly positive. However, this will hinge on the ability of the industry to respond to these changing demographics and dynamics in the financial system. In 2006, the insurance premiums averaged 2.95% of GDP in South East Asia as compared with 8.8% in the U.S. or 16.5% in the U.K. Compared to the banking sector, the insurance industry remains relatively less developed and commands a significantly smaller percentage of the total financial assets of the region's financial system. To tap these opportunities, appropriate strategies, new thinking and approaches will be required. In this regard, a significant development has been the evolution of alternative distribution m echanisms for insurance products and services in the region, notably through bancassurance. Indeed, bancassurance has developed in a number of ASEAN markets into a viable alternative distribution approach to the traditional agency force. Perhaps, in those markets where the insurance distribution channels through agency force have yet to be firmly established, bancassurance could provide a quantum leap to allow insurers to rapidly widen their outreach by tapping into an established banking network and client base. Worldwide, insurers have been successfully leveraging on bancassurance to gain a foothold in markets with low insurance penetration and a limited variety of distribution channels. B ancassurance can increase market penetration given the relatively higher level of public confidence in dealings with banks. For the banks and insurers, capitalising on synergies derived from tapping into the banks' extensive customer base to offer consumers comprehensive financial solutions while optimising on the branch network have proven to be highly successful strategies towards mutually improving productivity and profitability. In Malaysia , bancassurance constitutes a significant feature of Malaysia 's financial landscape, and continues to develop rapidly in terms of market reach and operational sophistication. These developments have contributed towards significantly raising the nation's insurance penetration level and enhancing the competitive structure of the insurance industry. In addition to bancassurance, the Internet is emerging as a promising medium for insurers to advertise products and service policyholders. With the rapid technological advancements and increasing consumer demands for more efficient delivery of products and services, it offers the potential for insurers to target a wider market, improve client service and conduct business seamlessly across borders. While planning for effective distribution channels may become the key differentiating factor in the growing region today, one must not overlook the implications of the changing demands of the general public. The ageing of the population is an issue of increasing importance in the developing world. All across Asia , the number of people aged 65 and above is expected to grow dramatically over the next 50 years. For the region as a whole, the population in this age group will increase by 314 % from 207 million in 2000 to 857 million in 2050. Many nations are finding it increasingly difficult to provide adequately for the needs of their aged through state-provided social security. Faced with such prospects, planning for retirement has become more important, both for individuals as well as public policy to ensure sustainable financing and management of retirement and healthcare needs in the long term. In this context, the development of deep financial markets among ASEAN countries is critical. One of the significant challenges currently facing the insurance industry in this region has been the shortage of long term assets that match the duration of insurance liabilities. While the bond markets in several ASEAN economies have been extensively developed over the last decade, longer-dated papers remain scarce in most countries. This has been a key impediment to the development of private pension products needed to meet the increasing demand for channels through which the population can save for retirement. While there are significant efforts being made to further develop the longer end of the bond market, the engagement between the industry, regulators and Government needs to be maintained and intensified further to take this agenda forward. This is critical both for the management of risks in the industry, and to support sustainable growth in the longer term. Another untapped segment of the market is the takaful sector in view of the fact that Muslims constitute more than 40% of the population in ASEAN, mainly in Malaysia , Indonesia and Brunei . Globally, the Muslim population accounts for about 24% of the total population. This has supported the growth of the takaful market in recent years as an alternative to conventional insurance. The global takaful market is expected to grow between 15 and 20 per cent per annum. Based on the market penetration level which is at 6.8% in Malaysia and less than 5% in many Muslim countries, this represents significant market potential for the future growth of takaful business. The expansion of insurance markets in ASEAN will need to be reinforced by further consumer education to increase awareness among the public on the importance of long-term financial planning as well as to equip them to evaluate product features and make informed decisions. The insurers must recognise that it is an important responsibility on their part not just to ensure that adequate information is provided to the consumers, but that consumers are suitably advised in the sales process. This includes ensuring that information about insurance products is presented in a manner that is meaningful and easily understood by consumers. This distinction between quantity and quality is important. In this respect, we should learn from the unsatisfactory outcomes that have emerged in some of the more developed markets where product disclosures can run into 60-page documents, which no one can reasonably expect an average consumer to read, let alone understand. Ultimately, the purpose of disclosures must be to help consumers understand the risks associated with different product options. In this context, more information is not necessarily better. The quality of information and financial capability of consumers must be enhanced in tandem with improved disclosures. Of course, increasing product innovations also need to be matched by strong risk and portfolio management capabilities critical to ensure the long-term sustainability and viability of the products offered in the market as well as the financial soundness of insurance companies. The operating landscape in which we operate has also changed significantly. Convergence in financial services has blurred the boundaries between insurance, banking and capital market activities. In this environment, financial sector regulation and supervision has become significantly more challenging. The increasing linkages between insurance and the banking systems as well as capital markets have increased the importance of achieving a harmonised regulatory approach and standard across sectors to minimise possibilities of regulatory arbitrage between different types of institutions. Under such environment, the approach towards regulatory and supervisory framework also has to evolve in tandem with the change in the environment. Recognising these dynamic changes, Bank Negara Malaysia took efforts to strengthen our regulatory and supervisory capabilities as well as sharpen our focus. The organisational structure for the regulatory and supervisory functions within the Bank were realigned in November 2006 to move from the previous institutional based approach, to one that integrates the Bank's regulatory functions for the different financial sectors under its purview along functional lines. The new functional based, cross-sector regulatory structure allows us to modernise the regulatory framework for both the insurance and banking sectors at a more equal pace. The increased synergies created will enable the Bank to apply the best regulatory practices in both the banking sector to the insurance sectors. Under the new structure, the Bank is able to leverage on the more advanced developments in either sector to enhance the regulatory framework for both sectors, simultaneously if possible. At the same time, it allows us to develop and train our personnel to be better equipped in the constantly changing operating environment. These efforts, will promote a more consistent regulatory regime for both the banking and insurance sectors. A positive side effect that can accrue from this move is the enhancement of public confidence on the insurance sector which augurs well towards increasing the level of insurance penetration. Achieving a more integrated approach to cross-sector regulation was relatively easy in Malaysia as Bank Negara is the single regulator for both the banking and insurance industries. In other countries, greater coordination and collaboration between separate regulatory agencies can similarly contribute towards a more consistent approach to regulation and supervision across sectors in dealing with similar risks. While consistency in regulatory and supervisory approaches will contribute towards overall financial stability and increased regulatory as well as business efficiency, it is important to appreciate the fundamental differences between different market players. As someone put it, notwithstanding current trends in financial conglomeration, banks will always be banks, and insurers will always be insurers. As such, the risks stemming from the liability side of an insurance company is far more significant than the asset side, while the reverse is generally true for banks. While some dimensions of this are changing, such differences must be properly catered for in the regulatory framework as well as in insurers' own internal risk management practices. Human intellectual capital plays a pivotal role in driving the industry's future and competitiveness. The environment of increasing complexity in financial services that is accompanied by increasingly sophisticated consumer expectation place new demands on the skill sets and competencies of regulators and industry professionals. Adoption of the highest standards of professionalism and integrity is essential in generating public confidence in the insurance industry. It is therefore critical for us to continuously invest in human capital as the pace of progression for the insurance industry would to a large extent depend upon the capability of those working in the industry - their skill set, expertise and competency. Unfortunately for all of us, similar to other emerging economies, there is a scarcity of qualified and well trained personnel to meet the growing and increasingly complex needs of the industry. Therefore human capital development should not be viewed as an expense but as an investment for the future. Without such investment, our insurance industries will not be able to quickly make the leap forward and we risk losing the opportunities to players from more sophisticated economies that are ready on the sides to take advantage of our inadequacies.
