Efforts to strengthen the resilience of the insurance industry need to work towards converging to a more consistent application of regulatory standards to reinsurers and more effective supervisory cooperation, in particular with respect to internationally active reinsurers. This is essential both to protect primary insurance systems and facilitate the more efficient geographic pooling of risks. Fourthly, as part of the financial system, a key imperative for insurers is re-building the confidence of retail investors and consumers in financial institutions. This crisis has resulted in a significant destruction of wealth and crisis of confidence in the financial sector. While this has been more profound in the most affected countries, none of us have been really spared with consumers and investors alike retreating from financial services to different degrees. While the global reform agenda to date has focused on the analysis of market failures and its remedy, less attention has been directed at investigating the irresponsible practices of financial institutions that have put unsuspecting financial consumers in extremely vulnerable positions in the first place. It is now widely acknowledged that the financial crisis had a lot to do with ethics or rather, the absence of it. One commentary puts it this way - a company's character is defined by how they do what they do, how they keep promises, how they make decisions, how they engender trust, and how they relate to their customers, to the environment and to the communities in which they operate. Unfortunately, the companies at the centre of this crisis neglected the how' and stopped asking how they were making money, as long as they continued to make more money. In the process, basic values of integrity and equity to key stakeholders were abandoned, leaving the reputation of the industry in tatters. Achieving more meaningful and consistent protection for consumers will also be critical to rebuild confidence. For life insurers, this means responsible marketing, with more attention to the assessment of consumers' needs, and a commitment to providing products that promote the greatest value for policyholders. With the fragile state of confidence in financial services providers, boards and the senior management of insurers need to accord the same attention and resources to prevent misleading and deceptive sales practices, as they would devote to managing their own risk exposures. In July 2009, all licensed insurers and takaful operators in Malaysia will be required to comply fully with the expectations of Bank Negara Malaysia under the Guidelines on Introduction of New Products. A large part of the Guidelines is devoted to addressing the responsibilities of insurance companies and takaful operators towards consumers in ensuring that the needs and rights of consumers are respected, and that consumers are clearly and fully informed of the nature and risks associated with the products. With increasing emphasis by insurers on product innovation, growth and market share, initiatives to strengthen consumer protection will gain traction. However, their effectiveness in delivering better consumer protection will depend significantly on the interpretation by industry of such initiatives in a fast changing and dynamic environment. Several considerations come into play. Firstly, the value chain of finance has and will continue to evolve with new roles and partnerships. This will require industry to carefully consider how they will ensure that expectations under new product regulations are met across the entire value chain given the differing and potentially conflicting incentive structures that exist. The issues and considerations may be different, for example, between direct marketing, agency, financial advisors and bancassurance channels. The expected prolonged low interest rate environment must also be taken into account in managing consumer expectations. This should be appropriately aligned with the promises made to policyholders regarding their policy benefits. Insurers also have substantial insights into consumer behaviours and decision-making patterns which should be used as inputs to design products that provide sustainable value propositions for both consumers and insurers, rather than in the reckless pursuit of top line revenues at the expense of considerable reputational risk. Insurers should consider how these insights can be used more effectively to develop appropriate disclosure and communication policies that will aid, rather than confuse, decision-making by consumers. This should be reinforced by stronger incentives for proper advice which in turn contributes to better portfolios in the long term, and customer service. I began by drawing on the increasing convergence between banking and insurance and to suggest several priorities for the insurance industry as part of efforts to promote financial stability in the wake of the current financial crisis. I am, however, reminded that while the lessons form the crisis have clear relevance for the insurance industry, one should not forget the fundamental distinctions between banking and insurance. In its published letter on the statement that was issued by the G20 leaders following their summit in London, the Geneva Association highlights three notable shortcomings:- Firstly, no difference was made between those financial activities that caused the financial crisis, and those, such as insurance operations, that played little or no role in the evolution of the current crisis; Secondly, the call for accounting standards setters to work urgently with supervisors and regulators lacks consideration of economic realities associated with the unique long-term nature of insurance business; and Thirdly, reforms to the senior leadership of international financial institutions do not go far enough to ensure that their background adequately reflects the diversity of the financial services sector. As a result, insurance-specific knowledge is under-represented to the detriment of a more balanced approach which leverages on the specialist knowledge that the insurance sector can offer. An appreciation of these differences is clearly important to ensure that reforms that are being considered or pursued do not result in less efficient insurance systems without a commensurate reduction in risk, or worse, increase overall financial system risk by diminishing the role of the insurance sector in facilitating the diversification of economic exposures into uncorrelated risks. For this reason, insurance reforms and strategies must carefully consider suitable applications to insurance business. In addressing the distinctions between banking and insurance, it is helpful for boards, senior management and regulators to remain focused on the specific risks involved. To the extent that insurance companies have been allowed to engage in financial market transactions that depart materially from traditional insurance activities, similar risk exposures that arise in connection with such activities should be addressed in a consistent manner across the financial sector. The Malaysian insurance industry is undergoing a transformation of its own to provide a strong foundation for a more resilient and competitive industry in support of Malaysia's economic development agenda. I have already mentioned the implementation of the risk-based capital framework this year and new product regulations. These developments are part of a broader move towards introducing a more principle-based regulatory regime that will allow greater flexibility for insurers to compete and improve performance, but under a rigorous internal oversight and supervisory framework. Later this year, the Bank will consult the industry on risk management standards that insurers are expected to observe as part of this evolution. The distribution channels for insurance products and services have also broadened significantly with the development of bancassurance and financial advisers. This will contribute towards enhancing revenue and reducing costs, while enhancing consumer protection and improving the insurance penetration rate in Malaysia. In April this year, the Bank announced a liberalisation package for the financial sector aimed at strengthening Malaysia's economic interlinkages with other economies and enhancing the role of the financial sector as a key enabler and catalyst of economic growth. In the insurance sector, the measures include the issuance of new family takaful licences; higher limits of up to 70% on foreign equity participation in insurance companies and takaful operators; incentives for the consolidation and rationalisation of the insurance industry; the removal of restrictions on the establishment of branches and bancassurance tieups; and greater flexibility to employ specialist expatriates. These developments will create opportunities for insurers to build financial solidity, restore consumer confidence and respond proactively to changing consumer needs in a more uncertain environment. In pursuing these opportunities, the insurance industry needs to remember that the world has changed dramatically, and with it, the role and expectations of the insurance industry will assume new dimensions. The priorities of the industry should be equally weighed between preserving the inherent strengths and original purpose of insurance, while committing to meaningful change that is needed to secure long-term viability and contribute to financial stability. On that note, I wish you an enlightening dialogue and discussions over the next few days.

Title: Welcoming Remarks at Malaysia Country Showcase - IFSB Summit 2017
text: Assistant Governor's Speech at the Bumiputera Life Insurance Agent Convention 2009 and Bumiputera Chief Agency Excellent Award Ceremony 2009 : "Creativity Drives Performance" Presenter: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB / Venue: Legend Hotel / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 01 August 2009 / First, let me express my gratitude to Allah Subhanahu Wataala because with His grace and permission, we can jointly attend the Bumiputera Life Insurance Agents Convention and the presentation of the Bumiputera Head of Agency Excellence Award 2009. I would also like to thank (MII) who paid my respects to officiate the Bumiputera Life Insurance Agents Convention for the year 2009 this morning. If last year the number of participants attending this same convention was 321, this time, I am informed that the number has increased to over 500 participants. This shows that more and more agents are having a lot of confidence and seriousness in this career. I believe the number of participants will continue to grow in the coming days. I would also like to take this opportunity to congratulate those who have been selected to receive the Bumiputera Agency Head Excellence Award 2009. I was told that this award ceremony was held for the first time and indeed it was a recognition to the brothers and sisters present. Such awards should be an inspiration and encouragement to all of us to continue to strive more actively to enhance the level of excellent and competent service, integrity and quality in order to gain full confidence among the community. Hopefully, the success of our friends will serve as an example to be exemplary. This year's Convention theme selection, "Creativity Generates Performance" is appropriate. The increasingly challenging economic environment and the transformation of the current financial landscape, do not give us much choice but to undertake a paradigm shift to remain relevant in the insurance industry. Only those who are versatile, creative, innovative and serious in developing their respective careers as insurance agents can survive to perform their duties more efficiently and effectively to meet the increasingly sophisticated and dynamic needs of consumers. I would like to start the discourse this morning by briefly touching on the environmental challenges we are facing a string of global financial turmoil stemming from the subprime crisis. This financial crisis has caused many countries in the world to fall into a heavy economic recession compared to a few decades ago. Although Malaysia does not belong to countries with bad recessions, our country still has a negative impact on economic growth. In order to restore public confidence in the integrity of the financial system in this urgent and uncertain situation, governments around the world have been forced to intervene by taking proactive measures in an effort to restore stability and public confidence in the financial system in their respective countries. And most of these measures were taken by many Asian countries in 1997 - 98, which received such heavy criticism at that time. In this challenging environment, the insurance industry in our country continues to exhibit a stable financial position with adequate capital requirements. Our insurance industry is robust. This is a breakthrough for our industry. The performance of the general and life insurance industry showed positive growth by recording a 5% increase in consolidated average premium income in the past three years. The takaful industry recorded an impressive growth in general and family takaful contribution income of 32% over the same period. Similarly, the insurance fund's assets registered a growth of 7% to reach RM131 billion at the end of 2008. The assets of the insurance fund last year accounted for 5.1% of the total assets in the Malaysian financial system, significantly higher than the 2.9% achieved 18 years ago. Challenges Faced by the Insurance Industry and Agents Against the backdrop of this positive development of the insurance industry, the growth prospects of the insurance industry are very bright with business opportunities extending widely to competent agents. The market penetration rate (measured in terms of life insurance and family takaful policies in force on the total population), is still low at 48.5% compared to countries such as Japan and Singapore, where the rates are above 80% respectively. The market penetration rate among Bumiputeras is the lowest, which is less than 10%. This gives us the impression that the untapped market is still vast and the business opportunities for those who want to become insurance agents are encouraging. Statistics show that the involvement of Bumiputeras as life insurance agents is still at a low level. As of March 2009, Bumiputera agents accounted for only 17.8% of the total number of life insurance agents, which is 13,400 people. One thing we are proud of is that almost half of the total number of Bumiputera agents are highly qualified, at least at the college or university level. This high level of knowledge should be harnessed by the best agents that can be used as a catalyst to propel performance to even greater heights. The recognition of successful agents will encourage more young graduates to venture into this field as their respective careers. Most countries around the world are facing rapid demographic changes with a significant increase in the elderly population. The Asian continent recorded the highest increase in the number of senior citizens. In 2025, an estimated 700 million people in Asia are over 60 years old. We are also no exception to this demographic change. In Malaysia, the life expectancy of the population is currently 71 years for males and 76 years for females. This figure is expected to increase to 75 years and 79 years respectively in 2020. These demographic changes have particularly important implications for retirement and healthcare funding. It is expected that in the future, more Malaysians will allocate a significant portion of their income into private retirement schemes and medical insurance. Insurance companies and their respective agent representatives should take advantage of the changes in this dynamic insurance landscape, while also adopting a strategic approach to reap the golden opportunities that come with them. However, some preparations need to be done in advance, especially for those of you who are in the hall this morning. In stepping up to become a more successful agent, certain characteristics need to be applied within us. A high level of professionalism, integrity and good ethics are among the noble values that every insurance agent should have. This should be imbued with other competencies such as, extensive knowledge of products, customer needs, creativity and innovation as a prerequisite to continuously improve performance and quality of service. As for mastering creativity, a person is not necessarily born a creative person. Rather, it is a competence that can be mastered through strong commitment. I want to emphasize here that knowledge is the main pillar of creativity. With extensive knowledge of financial products that are in the market including insurance, creative insurance agents can offer customers a comprehensive financial package. A smart agent will be able to be with his clients for more than a generation, providing the insurance services that the client needs in his life cycle. Agents as financial protection advisors to clients can advise what is best for themselves and their families in order to secure their future. It is the responsibility of every agent to maintain a positive consumer and societal impression of the agency's energy as well as the insurance industry as a whole so as not to be tainted by mistrust and mistrust. Creative agents also dare to use imagination to implement new ideas and strategies out of the ordinary to meet the challenges they face. Common practices that can lead to a quick-satisfied attitude with the surrounding situation need to be scraped off. By having a creative and innovative nature or culture in overcoming and overcoming challenges, insurance agents will be more competitive. The success of our insurance industry should no longer be judged on the basis of premium income growth alone. On the other hand, the measure of success should also be based on the ability to introduce new changes, ideas and products as well as improve the quality of services that are geared towards the well-being of the people. Among the efforts to be focused by the brothers and sisters in generating better quality and viable business performance are the following: i. Continue to explore new strategies in marketing insurance products and services to customers that are based on the needs, changes and development of the environment ii. Change over time and deliver information and advice accurately and in line with customer needs. As a measure to ensure that the level of knowledge and skills of the agents is always high, a continuous professional development program has been introduced; iii. Explore new business opportunities, for example as a financial advisor with broader business prospects. Please be informed that those who are interested in opening and expanding their agency business or upgrading their business as a financial advisor can apply for a loan under the Micro Financing Scheme offered by financial institutions in Malaysia. Details of the scheme and how to apply can be found on Bank Negara Malaysia's website; And iv. To increase career opportunities for more Bumiputeras as insurance agents in view of the low penetration of insurance among the Bumiputera community. Recently, Bank Negara Malaysia has given flexibility to allow insurance companies to offer higher interest-free financing to new agents. It is hoped that this move will help to revitalize the industry. In addition, the Bumiputera Training Fund which is fully funded by the insurance industry provides specialized training for Bumiputera agents to enhance their professionalism. In the past five years, a total of RM985,323 of the total funds have been used to train more than 2,500 Bumiputera life insurance agents. The ever-circulating time and increasingly sophisticated technologies have spawned a wide-informed consumer society in various fields. These users are more vocal and dare to express their opinions and feelings. Now their will is becoming more sophisticated and dynamic and desperately expecting a high level of transparency. In this regard, in order to help consumers gain access to adequate information about insurance products, while at the same time ensuring that agents are able to provide accurate information to customers, a disclosure framework has been developed and will be implemented on 1 January 2010. This is intended so that the consumer can make a wise decision in the purchase of an insurance product. Agents should be prepared to face the current trend of increasing transparency in marketing and sales of financial products by adapting to deal with more educated and sophisticated consumers. Dear brothers and sisters, the value of transparency should be emphasized and practiced in any context, including in the insurance and takaful industries. As explained in verses 282 and 283 of Surah al-Baqarah, transparency is essential in every transaction to ensure that all parties are treated fairly. The verses also explain that all actions taken in a transaction are the responsibility of all parties involved. Based on this principle, transparency has become the fundamental pillar of all takaful transactions based on Shariah principles. Takaful operators are required to make adequate disclosures and make transparency a basis to improve corporate governance and protect the interests of all parties concerned. Among the important disclosure requirements to be made in a takaful transaction is that all information on a takaful contract, including charges and wakala fees should be clearly stated in each takaful document. In this regard, insurance companies need to be prepared to shift to the same level of transparency as well. Indeed, insurance agents are critical mediators to build a bridge between those who need financial protection and those who provide such services. As a representative of an insurance company, consumer interaction with agents forms the consumer's perception of the insurance industry. If the consumer experience of dealing with agents is satisfactory, the consumer's impression of the insurance industry is also positive. So is the opposite. In short, the agent's horn action symbolizes the insurance industry itself. What you can take from this fact is that agents as a catalyst for the integrity of the insurance industry's image should always be professional, ethical and responsive to the needs of customers. A frequent issue associated with the behavior of life insurance agents is the practice of policy replacement (Replacement of policy) carried out by unscrupulous agents by persuading customers to switch existing policies to new policies in order to earn higher commissions in the early years of the policy in force. Such a practice is certainly unfavorable to the consumer and is carried out solely for the benefit of the agent. The users involved will certainly feel deceived and thus, will end the familiar agent-customer relationship. Another thing that affects the good relationship between the agent and the client is that the untrustworthy nature involving the premium received from the client is not sent to the insurance company and is even used by the agent for personal purposes. In the event of an accident/accident, the customer certainly does not have the proper protection. These practices are not only untrustworthy but also an offence on the religious side. Insurance Peeling from an Islamic Corner Let me briefly touch on the takaful system that exists in tandem with the insurance system in a unique setting in Malaysia. Takaful has been identified as a promoted sector to strengthen Malaysia's position as an International Islamic financial centre. The government has been responsible for providing the Islamic financial system as an alternative or preferred system, which is equipped with products and practices based on Shariah requirements. Use this opportunity to develop a business. A competent agent will strive to understand the concept of takaful to make it easier for him to interact intelligently with customers. Takaful products either family or general takaful can be seen as giving choice to consumers who are currently more sophisticated in terms of taste. Now the number of takaful operators is eight in total. This is a healthy development in terms of expanding product diversity in the market to meet the diverse needs of today's consumers. It should be viewed positively as complementing the existing system with a single purpose, which is to offer a product that is suitable for the diverse needs of consumers. The government's efforts to develop the takaful sector have shown great success. In 1990, the total assets and income of takaful contributions was only RM28.4 million and RM38.2 million respectively. In March 2009, the assets and contribution income increased enormously, reaching RM10.4 billion and RM762.2 million respectively. Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Malaysian Insurance Institute for organising such a convention. Congratulations also to all recipients of the "Excellent Award for Head of Bumiputera Agency 2009". I am confident that, with a high level of creativity and innovation, clear goals and a strong passion towards improving the agency's business, I believe that our brothers and sisters are able to continue to move on to the milestone. With the phrase 'Bismillahirahmannirrahim', I am pleased to officiate the Bumiputera Life Insurance Agents Convention 2009.

Title: Welcoming Remarks at the WB-BNM Seminar on World Development Report 2014 - "Risk and Opportunity: Managing Risk for Development"
text: Keynote address by the Assistant Governor at the 9th ILIM Muhadharah Council entitled "The Position of the Islamic Financial System in Malaysia - A Survey" Presenter: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB / Venue: Islamic Training Institute Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 13 Oct 2009 / Praise be to Allah Subhanahuwataala, salutation and greetings to Allah? The great Prophet Muhammad Sallallahualaihiwasallam, also to his family, his companions and all his followers. Alhamdulillah, I am grateful to Allah SWT because with His grace, we met here for the success of the 9th Muhadharah Council of the Islamic Training Institute of Malaysia (ILIM). First of all, I thank the organizers for giving me the opportunity to deliver the keynote address at the Muhadharah ceremony this time. My speech today will put emphasis on two parts. The first part, I will touch on the development of the Islamic financial system in Malaysia. The second part is on strategies towards further strengthening our country's position as a leader in international Islamic finance. The Islamic finance industry in Malaysia has undergone a rapid transformation in recent decades. The industry has grown into one of the competitive components of the financial system in Malaysia and has become one of the drivers of the country's economic growth and progress. With the Islamic and conventional financial systems operating in tandem, Malaysia continues to promote the expansion of this sector at home and abroad. Malaysia has emerged as the country with the most comprehensive Islamic financial sector in the world, supported by all the components required by a financial system, namely Islamic banking, takaful, as well as the Islamic money and equity markets, based on a distinctive and comprehensive legal system. Over the past five years, the Islamic banking sector in Malaysia has registered double-digit growth with an average annual growth rate of 20% in terms of assets. In the second quarter of 2009, the share of Islamic banking assets from the total assets of the total banking sector expanded to 18.9% compared to just 10.5% in 2004. The takaful industry also recorded an impressive performance with an average annual growth rate of 25.1% in terms of contribution over the same period. The total contribution of the takaful industry also recorded a greater share in the entire insurance sector to reach 9.25% in the second quarter of 2009. Malaysia also remains the world's largest sukuk market, accounting for over 45% of the global sukuk issue in the first seven months of 2009. The recent financial crisis has opened up wide opportunities for the Islamic financial sector as one of the key alternatives to this global financial crisis. This is clear, although the global financial crisis caused some financial institutions to collapse in the conventional financial system, the Islamic financial sector was still able to register positive growth. With global Islamic financial assets expected to grow to USD1.6 trillion in 2012, the sector is expected to become more developed in the international financial markets with its own characteristics compared to the conventional financial system. The increase in the development of the Islamic financial sector can also be seen through the interest and commitment highlighted by international financial centres dominated by non-Muslim communities such as London, Paris, Hong Kong, Singapore and Japan to develop the Islamic financial sector in their countries. Thus, this is the best time and opportunity for Muslim countries such as Malaysia to strengthen their Islamic financial structure and products and highlight it to the world as the preferred method of global economic recovery. The positive development of the Islamic finance industry in Malaysia over the years is a result of the Government's strategic measures, together with the support of various parties in developing Islamic finance. Since the establishment of Tabung Haji and the first Islamic bank, the country has continued to navigate various efforts such as introducing the first takaful company and enabling conventional banks to also open counters offering Islamic banking and financial services. This initiative is supported by continuous efforts in strengthening the legal, regulatory, supervisory and Shariah framework to ensure that the Islamic financial sector can develop in an orderly manner and, at the same time, financial stability is maintained. The government's commitment to ensure that the country becomes the International Islamic Financial Centre was also realised in the Budget 2007 presentation. Various incentives were introduced including tax and stamp duty exemption on various forms of Islamic banking and takaful business operations. This development has prompted the country to implement a liberalisation process in the Islamic financial services industry in 2002. This move has increased foreign presence and participation in the Malaysian Islamic financial system, thus creating a diverse industry participant. The Malaysian bond market has also seen foreign entities issue bonds in ringgit and foreign currency denominations in the domestic market. Following these developments, Malaysia is now entering a new phase in the development of the Islamic financial system, with initiatives to promote Malaysia as an International Islamic Financial Centre. This initiative aims to strengthen Malaysia's Islamic economic and financial connectivity and further promote more active cross-border trade and investment. Among the positive developments that can be seen as a result of this liberalisation exercise is the increase and expansion of the use of various Shariah concepts in Islamic financial products. If previously many Islamic banking products used limited Shariah concepts such as Wadiah, Murabahah, Bai' Bithaman Ajil, and Bai' al-Dayn, now more other Shariah concepts have been adopted such as Ijarah, Mudarabah, Musyarakah, and Tawarruq. The variety of applications of this Shariah concept enhances innovation and variation in the offering of Islamic financial products. This development shows that increased competition between industry participants has made them more innovative in exploring new products to meet the needs of customers. Strategy towards Empowering Malaysia's Position as the International Islamic Finance Leader The Malay proverb states, "The round one does not come rolling, the pipih does not come to drift". The outstanding achievement in Islamic finance that the country has achieved today requires continuous efforts to ensure that the sector continues to thrive and be competitive, thus ensuring that our country continues to be ahead in this field. Therefore, let me share my views with the audience and present all some of the strategies that are considered important and necessary to be implemented in ensuring the continuity of the progress we have made over the years. First, produce dynamic Shariah scholars (mastering various fields of science). In responding to the Government's call to make Malaysia a reference centre for global Islamic financial Shariah practices, dynamic Shariah scholars play a significant role. In line with current demands and requirements, the mastery of knowledge by Islamic scholars and scholars today should not be limited to one specific field of knowledge. In fact, in order to continue to drive innovation and enhance the performance of the Islamic finance industry to greater dignity, strong economic and financial knowledge needs to be blended with a comprehensive understanding of Shariah. This is because the combination of deep knowledge is a recipe for the setting of Shariah law that underlies every Islamic financial product and service. Clearly, rapid innovation demands a robust set of skills and expertise for both financial and Shariah branches. The need to master these various fields of knowledge can be seen in the process of identifying Shariah compliance issues, in particular financial products and instruments. This requires the ability of Islamic scholars and scholars to understand the instruments and structure of the product in terms of concept and implementation. This coincides with a fikah method which says "a ruling (decided) depending on the understanding (of the issue discussed)". Therefore, failure to master and understand the relevant fields of knowledge will not only result in this method of fikah not being properly implemented, but the published results may not be accurate. The importance of mastering these various fields of knowledge is not only limited to the practice of Islamic finance alone. In fact, it is also a reality in other sectors such as manufacturing, industrial, technology and so on. The claim of mastery of these various fields of knowledge is not impossible and impossible. In fact, history has been? prove to us the greatness of Islamic scholars. For example, Imam al-Ghazali is one of the Islamic thinkers who has a wide range of knowledge and thinking, without leading to a particular field of knowledge and thinking.? Imam al-Ghazali has argued and debated issues arising from the discussion of kalam knowledge, philosophy, tasawuf knowledge and fikah knowledge through his writing. In addition, the Islamic world also has Al Farabi who is one of the famous Islamic philosophers and scientists in the field of philosophy, sociology and logic. Not limited to three areas, Al Farabi also made writing contributions in medicine, science and mathematics.? The glory of knowledge was continued by his protege, Ibn Sina, who is famous in medicine through the writing of Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (Rules in Matters related to Doctoral Knowledge). Ibn Sina's mastery of knowledge is not limited in medicine, but he is a lecturer in astronomy and philosophy. These figures of Islamic scholars should be inspired by Islamic scholars and scholars today in expanding capacity and improving quality for the development and sustainability of today's knowledge. Berasaskan kepada keperluan untuk ahli Syariah mahir dalam bidang kewangan, pelbagai inisiatif telah dilaksanakan oleh Bank Negara Malaysia untuk merealisasikan misi tersebut. Ini termasuklah membangunkan infrastruktur utama dan? sokongan buat sektor kewangan Islam. Antara inisiatif yang telah diambil ialah penubuhan institusi penyelidikan yang bertujuan untuk merangsang kefahaman yang tepat serta pentafsiran yang konsisten mengenai prinsip Syariah dalam kewangan Islam, baik ?di peringkat domestik mahupun antarabangsa. Antaranya, Akademi Penyelidikan Syariah Antarabangsa dalam Kewangan Islam (International Shariah Research Academy for Islamic Finance, ISRA) yang ditubuhkan pada bulan Mac 2008 untuk meningkatkan interaksi dan dialog sesama cendekiawan dan peserta industri, serta menggalakkan penyelidikan dalam bidang Syariah dan kewangan Islam. Penyelidikan dan dialog intelektual yang aktif akan menggalakkan inovasi dan kedinamikan ke arah memacu pembangunan kewangan Islam ke tahap yang lebih tinggi. Selain itu, keperluan untuk melahirkan lebih banyak tenaga mahir dalam kewangan Islam turut cuba dipenuhi menerusi ?program peringkat doktor falsafah dan sarjana dalam kewangan Islam yang ditawarkan oleh Pusat Pendidikan Kewangan Islam Antarabangsa (International Centre for Education in Islamic Finance, INCEIF). Namun, penubuhan institusi-institusi berkenaan sahaja masih belum mencukupi untuk mencapai matlamat yang disasarkan. Langkah kolaborasi? antara institusi kewangan Islam, ISRA dan INCEIF dengan institusi pengajian tinggi sama ada di dalam atau di luar negara perlu dipertingkat dalam melahirkan pelapis ulama dan cendekiawan Islam yang dinamik dan berkualiti. Ini merangkumi penilaian semula programlatihan yang sedia ada bagi memastikan ia selaras dengan keperluan pasaran yang sentiasa berubah. Pengambilan tokoh-tokoh akademik Islam berprofil tinggi untuk berkhidmat dengan institusi pendidkan tempatan juga dilihat sebagai salah satu inisiatif untuk membantu melahirkan individuyang lebih berkualiti dan mempunyai pendedahan yang lebih meluas. Kepentingan kemahiran berbahasa, terutamanya bahasa Inggeris, yang merupakan lingua franca dan bahasa Arab yang menjadi bahasa utama bagi kebanyakan ?sumber ilmu Syariah perlu diberi perhatian serius dalam memastikan modal insan yang serba boleh. Menerusi kefahaman ilmu yang jitu dan penguasaan mantap pelbagaibahasa, kita mampu menguasai segala cabang ilmu lantas ?menjadikan Malaysia sebagai pusat rujukan dan inspirasi pemikiran dalam fiqh muamalat. In a nutshell, human resources and human capital are considered as the main strengths in generating the development of the Islamic financial sector, not only in Malaysia but also internationally. Particular attention to efforts to produce dynamic Shariah intellectuals is becoming increasingly important especially in the face of an increasingly challenging era of globalization. To meet these challenges, we need a more real, orderly, systematic and consistent plan and strategy in producing more quality, competitive scholars and intellectuals who are able to generate the development of the Islamic financial sector in the future. Second, ensuring that Islamic scholars and scholars play a more proactive role in enhancing the development of the Islamic financial sector. Scholars occupy an important position in the Muslim community. The behavior of scholars became exemplary, the speeches of scholars became the guidelines and the advice of scholars became an indication. The acceptance or rejection of society towards ?a concept or idea is greatly influenced by the views of scholars. The Central Bank Act 2009 which was passed by Parliament recently recognized the position of the Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia as the body mandated to determine Islamic law in relation to Islamic finance in Malaysia. This is based on awareness of the important role and position played by scholars in ensuring Shariah compliance in all aspects of Islamic finance. This Act expressly obliges, not only Islamic financial institutions but also the courts and arbitrators to refer to the Shariah Advisory Council on issues related to Islamic finance. Any collective ijtihad or resolution decided by the Shariah Advisory Council is binding and must be complied with by all parties concerned. This new act indirectly puts the dignity of Islamic scholars and scholars at the highest level. Although Malaysia's Islamic financial performance has shown impressive improvement, we should not be too comfortable with our performance today. Islamic finance is an evolution and it demands continuous reform from time to time. We need to do a paradigm shift. Today's institution of scholars is no longer a reference centre, but also has a greater responsibility as the driving force of the Muslim community towards sustainable development, especially in the field of Islamic finance. Scholars should be bolder to come forward to innovate their thinking. There is no doubt that there are often differences of opinions and opinions among scholars on the interpretation of Shariah. However, this should not be used as an excuse to ignore the development and development of the Islamic financial sector. Instead, it should be presented as a challenge and an opportunity. A challenge because differences of views will result? deeper analysis and evaluation, while an opportunity because it promotes healthy ijtihad practices among scholars in addition to flexibility ?to test new fields. Such challenges and opportunities should be exploited by channeling all views and opinions to scientific mediums such as discussion, debate, dialogue, writing and research. Through the organization of these programmes, we can see a more active involvement among Islamic scholars and scholars to speak out? and share views. It will be a platform to generate smart thoughts and ideas, unravel and unravel all controversial views, spark invention and innovation, as well as educate and nurture a new generation. Here, too, we can cultivate the spirit of wanting to explore the latest areas or innovations, which have never been explored before. The companions of the Prophet PBUH have set a good example for all of us, in fostering a proactive attitude towards the environment and daring to express our views. For example, during the war of Badr, a friend of the Messenger of Allah? The Prophet PBUH, Hubab bin Al-Munzir, boldly expressed an opinion that contradicts the suggestion of the Prophet PBUH regarding the position of the Islamic army in the Badr valley. Hubab bin Al-Munzir has proposed a more strategic position for the Islamic Army to take control of the water source, thus blocking the enemy's path to the water source. This event shows? The Companion is brave and proactive in presenting a solution even though it seems to contradict the suggestion of the Prophet PBUH himself. The non-proactive attitude of the scholars will result in the Malaysian Islamic finance industry continuing to be unfit and lifeless. In this regard, it is appropriate that we take lessons from the history of the development of Islamic jurisprudence itself. The historical sources of Islamic jurisprudence have clearly recorded the era of gloom of the development of Islamic jurisprudence known as the closed era of the ijtihad gate. This era of gloom began when scholars felt that the sources of Islamic jurisprudence that had been left behind by previous scholars were ?adequate for? solving the problems of Muslims. They continue to limit themselves in the axis and space of existing sources of Islamic jurisprudence without any will to be jihadi in contemporary issues. The scholars who fought for the survival of ijtihad in those days were viewed as oblique and did not receive support. Nevertheless,? throughout the era, the movement to restore the practice of ijtihad continued to grow and was led by scholars such as Sheikhul Islam Abu Al-Abbas Taqiyuddin bin Taymiyyah (Imam Ibn Taymiyyah). The production of the book Majalla al-Ahkam al-Adliyyah in 1286 Hijrah became a sign of the end of the era of Islamic jurisprudence and the closure of the ijtihad gate. Nearly 1000 years of the Islamic world has been plagued by gloom due to the unfit and unactive attitude of scholars. Therefore, this era of gloom should not be allowed to repeat itself if we are to move forward and develop. Although Islamic scholars and scholars are urged to be proactive and bold in expressing their opinions and ideas, the tide of globalization demands? uniformity in the solution of an issue. This is important to avoid public confusion and to preserve market stability. Thus, ijtihad collectively among scholars is important as it is able to build consensus and consensus to ensure uniformity of Shariah practices of Islamic finance. The collective disclosure of ijtihad can be done through the decisions and fatwas of scholars which are then enacted through laws and guidelines. The publication of the Shariah Parameter Reference is one of Bank Negara Malaysia's measures to ensure the consistent application of the fundamentals of Shariah principles in Islamic financial practices in Malaysia. This is the result of active interaction and collective ijtihad? among Islamic scholars and scholars in the field of Islamic finance. This initiative is expected to enhance the understanding of the practical application of Shariah principles for Islamic finance in order to contribute towards a more innovative development of Islamic financial products and services, while encouraging scholars to continue to have a more persistent jihad. However, as the leader of the Islamic financial system, we need to be prepared to face various criticisms and negative comments in relation to the practice of the Islamic financial system in the country. Therefore, we need to be confident that the practice of Islamic finance in Malaysia is a practice that adheres to the principles? Shariah as long as it does not contradict any clear and clear evidences. In addition, Islamic scholars and scholars need to be bolder to appear openly internationally in explaining the approach and application of Shariah in the country. Third, enhance strong cooperation among all government and private agencies in realising the Government's mission and vision to make Malaysia an international Islamic financial hub. To ensure that the mission and vision of this Government is fully accomplished, all parties need to understand and appreciate the goal so that all efforts can be planned and integrated towards achieving the targeted objectives. Through perfect appreciation and understanding, we can identify the strengths and create synergies in the development of Islamic finance to be maximally utilised in the development of the country's economy. The process of realising the mission and vision of this Government requires an efficient and effective coordination mechanism? among all agencies. Every government and private agency must work together to ensure that the proposed strategies and action plans can be implemented successfully and effectively. All parties need to be prepared and flexible in making any necessary policy changes efficiently to meet the current dynamic demands. In addition, an open-minded attitude in giving and receiving constructive comments and suggestions should be present in every individual and agency for? more robust development and progress of Islamic finance. In conclusion, a concerted effort with the support and commitment of all parties including government and private agencies, industry participants as well as Islamic scholars and scholars in developing Islamic finance will have a positive impact on the country's economy, image and position of Malaysia among the international business and financial community. All parties need to mobilise together in implementing the proposed strategies so that we can ensure the continuity of the development and achievement of Islamic finance in Malaysia and globally, especially as the world begins to focus on the Islamic services and financial sectors as an alternative in the financial system. Finally, I pray that the Muhadharah Council this time can achieve the targeted objectives. Thank you, Wabillahi Tawfiq Wal Hidayah, Wassalamualaikum w.r.t.

Title: Keynote Address at the Chief Learning Officers Forum 2021
text: UCAPAN & WAWANCARA Print Shares Welcome Speech by Deputy Governor In Conjunction with the Launch of Financial Awareness Week 2009 Presenter: Dato' Mohd Razif bin Abd. Kadir / Venue: Terengganu, Malaysia / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 22 Oct 2009 / We are grateful to Allah SWT because with His permission we can be present today at the Financial Awareness Week Exhibition or M2K. With a deep sense of takzim, I welcome the presence of Yang Amat Berhormat Dato' Ahmad bin Said, the Menteri Besar of Terengganu for being willing to spend time despite his busy schedule and subsequently inaugurating M2K 2009. Thank you and appreciation to Yang Berbahagia Dato' Haji Mokhtar Bin Nong, Terengganu State Secretary for his unwavering support in the success of the M2K 2009 programme. We understand that Dato' Haji Mokhtar himself has given his full attention to ensure that the programme runs smoothly. Bank Negara Malaysia and other co-organisers, the Financial Mediation Bureau (BPK), the Credit Counseling and Management Agency (AKPK) and Perbadanan Insurans Deposit Malaysia (PIDM) would also like to take this opportunity to express their gratitude for the cooperation of the Terengganu State Government in the success of the M2K 2009 programme. The M2K 2009 programme was the second annual programme after it was first held in Johor Bahru last year. Themed "Financial Savvy, Cheerful Life", M2K is an annual initiative of financial education programmes aimed at raising public awareness and knowledge of financial services and management. M2K activities began with a series of financial education visits and briefings to target groups in universities, colleges, schools (including special schools), armed forces and police from 18 to 21 October 2009. This was followed by an integrated and comprehensive exhibition from 22 to 24 October 2009, which was participated by 61 relevant institutions and agencies. The M2K financial exhibition provides a platform for consumers to seek financial advice through counselling sessions and financial clinics. Seminars were also held for consumers and small and medium entrepreneurs as well as representatives from all districts in the state of Terengganu. In line with developments in the financial sector, Bank Negara Malaysia introduced policies on consumers aimed at increasing market confidence and subsequently to create a stable and progressive financial system. Bank Negara Malaysia is constantly working towards ensuring fair market practices, and enhancing the financial capabilities of consumers. Bank Negara Malaysia has also sought to improve public access to basic banking services as well as financing. In this regard, the banking sector since 2005 has introduced the Basic Savings Account and Basic Current Account to all Malaysians including small and medium enterprises (SMEs). This is to enable people to enjoy a minimum level of banking services and transactions at no cost or at a reasonable cost. In this regard, Bank Negara Malaysia has undertaken various initiatives to empower the public in financial aspects. This includes enhancing their financial capabilities by implementing bankinginfo and insurance consumer education programmes in collaboration with smart partners where various consumer education programmes have been implemented for consumer groups including school students, rural residents, women, nongovernmental organizations.call (NGOs), small and medium-sized entrepreneurs, senior citizens and disabled users. Its activities include financial education in schools, briefings and talks, financial workshops as well as financial exhibitions. The public's access to funding was also enhanced and given attention. A total of nine financial institutions are currently participating in the microfinance scheme based on the framework of microfinance institutions launched by the National SME Council chaired by the Prime Minister. Under this framework, microfinance is provided easily, quickly and easily, without the need for collateral. To date, RM554 million of microfinance under the scheme has been channelled to 52,000 borrowers. Under this scheme, the loan size ranges from RM500 to RM50,000 with an average loan of RM10,000 per borrower. In this regard, the World Bank in its report, 'Doing Business Report' has placed Malaysia in first place among 181 countries in the category of access to financing for three consecutive years. The public is advised to avoid getting caught or relying on illegal ceti-ceti or "Ah Long" as a source of financing for micro-enterprises. Getting a loan from "Ah Long" is not a solution, it will even add to the misery of life for them and their families. For the first eight months of the year, due to the economic slowdown, the financial institutions proactively scheduled and restructured loans amounting to RM2.2 billion involving 3,304 SME loan accounts. I would like to suggest that SMEs also take pro-active action and discuss with financial institutions to restructure loans that are most likely to be in trouble. Since the establishment of the Small Loan Settlement Scheme (SPPK) in 2003, its Secretariat at Bank Negara Malaysia has received 875 applications of which a total of 659 applications or 75% have been rescheduled, involving problematic loans of RM402 million. The scheme was established specifically to facilitate the loan restructuring process involving several financial institutions. Bank Negara Malaysia has extended the scheme to all SMEs by abolishing the maximum accumulated loan limit of RM3 million previously imposed. In addition to the above initiatives, Bank Negara Malaysia has also provided a comprehensive consumer protection infrastructure by creating a mechanism for the public to gain defense. This mechanism includes a customer-friendly Integrated Contact Centre and includes the Customer Service Centre, namely BNMLINK (Information and Service Advice Site), BNMTELELINK and the Complaints Management and Advisory Unit for financial service users to make inquiries, complaints or appeals relating to matters relating to products and services by financial service providers. Bank Negara Malaysia had just opened its fifth BNMLINK branch in Kuala Terengganu on 19 October 2009, in addition to the four existing branches in Penang, Johor Bahru, Kota Kinabalu and Kuching. This will increase the reach of BNMLINK and make it easier for users in nTerengganu especially and the East Coast states generally to access the services provided. In addition, from today, Bank Negara Malaysia will introduce a new method of service via short messaging service (SMS), where the public can contact Bank Negara Malaysia via SMS to number 15888. This method is more efficient and cheap to ensure that users can easily access financial services. Bank Negara Malaysia will follow up as soon as possible. The Financial Mediation Bureau (FMB) has also been established for the public to lodge complaints and seek resolution of disputes with financial service providers in Malaysia about financial products and services without going through a lengthy court process that involves high costs. The Credit Counseling and Management Agency (AKPK) is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bank Negara Malaysia which was specially established to provide financial education, counselling and financial advice services and credit management programmes to individuals who are likely or who have been caught up in the problem of non-performing loans. This problem if not addressed at an early stage can create social problems in society. AKPK's services have been expanded in almost every state capital. For the state of Terengganu, AKPK services are available at Bank Negara Malaysia, Kuala Terengganu branch, since October 2006. Although the Government and Bank Negara Malaysia have made a lot of efforts to make the public aware of the symptoms of the get-rich-quick scheme, there are still many who are stuck with schemes that promise decent returns. It is our hope that M2K can raise public awareness to be more cautious and report to Bank Negara Malaysia or the police when offered suspicious schemes. The involvement of the lords with schemes run by illegal syndicates is a legal offence. Ladies are advised to keep only in financial institutions regulated by Bank Negara Malaysia and other institutions licensed by the Government of Malaysia. And now, all your savings in commercial banks, Islamic banks, investment banks and financial development institutions that accept deposits under the supervision of Bank Negara Malaysia are fully guaranteed by the Government through Perbadanan Insurans Deposit Malaysia. Finally, we believe that M2K can achieve the goal of the organisers to be friendly with the people to understand the problem as well as to increase consumer awareness and knowledge of the opportunities offered by the financial institutions and the Government. The local community should take the opportunity to visit the M2K exhibition halls and participate in informative events to enhance your knowledge in the aspects of finance and financial services provided by the participating financial institutions and agencies. Once again, on behalf of Bank Negara Malaysia and other organisers would like to express my appreciation to Yang Amat Berhormat Dato' Ahmad bin Said, Menteri Besar of Terengganu and the Terengganu State Government for their cooperation and support in the success of M2k 20.09 this.

Title: Opening Address at the Seminar on Understanding the Concept & Application of Al-Rahnu
text: Governor's speech at Foreign Bankers' Association of the Netherlands : "A More Integrated and Cohesive Asia in the Global Economy" Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Amsterdam Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 22 Jun 2010 Asia is one of the more diverse regions in the global economy. Yet over the decade following the Asian financial crisis in the late 1990s, Asia has become a more integrated and cohesive region. The accelerated economic transformation of Asia during this period has reinforced this trend to sustain Asia as a high growth centre in the global economy. Asia has also been distinctive in terms of the resilience of its financial system in withstanding the recent international financial turmoil. This has allowed Asia to emerge with an early recovery in its economic growth process. It is my honour and great pleasure to be here on the occasion of the Annual General Meeting of the Foreign Bankers' Association of the Netherlands to speak on the developments that are taking place in Asia and the potential role of Asia in the global economy and the international financial system. Greater interdependence in the world economy is particularly relevant to Asia, As highly open economies, Asia is highly connected to the rest of the world and therefore vulnerable to external developments. At the same time, with its growing significance in the world economy, developments in Asia will also have implications on other parts of the world. Accelerated Transformation of Asia For more than five decades Asia has sustained high economic growth. More important, however, is the significant economic transformation that has occurred during this recent decade, in response to the changing domestic and international environment. Asia now and Asia previously is therefore significantly different. Asia today contributes about one third of world output and 28% of world trade. Asia's progress and development has lifted millions out of poverty, creating extensive employment and improving living conditions with better education and healthcare opportunities. The economic transformation has essentially resulted in more diversified sources of growth for Asia. From being export-led, domestic demand has now become an increasingly important source of growth. This is also reinforced by the shift from the public sector to the private sector as the main driver of growth. While Asia is highly diverse, a common feature prevailing is the tremendous economic flexibility of the Asian economies. Institutional development, the large skilled workforce, the shift to greater market orientation and the general macroeconomic stability have allowed resources to continuously shift to new areas of comparative advantage and for the Asian economies to remain competitive. Being highly diverse, Asia has also been able to leverage on the complementarities that exist in the different economies. This has generated an expansion in intra-regional trade, intra-regional investment activities and an increase in financial linkages between the economies in Asia. The Asian financial crisis was a defining moment for Asia. While most economies were able to recover in just over a year, in the decade that followed, wide ranging financial reforms were implemented. In addition, the development of the financial markets and the financial infrastructure were aggressively pursued to strengthen the capacity of the financial system. The legal framework and the regulatory and supervisory framework of the financial sector were also strengthened. Several important lessons from the crisis were also addressed, in particular, avoiding the excessive accumulation of debt whether by the household, corporate, financial sector or the public sector. Measures were taken to avoid the build-up of such leverage and excesses largely through prudential regulation. In addition, buffers were built during the good times. These reforms have yielded tremendous payoffs for Asia. With more developed financial markets and with better capitalised banking institutions equipped with strengthened risk management and governance practices, Asia did not experience any disruptions in financial intermediation during the 2008 - 2009 global financial crisis. The continued access to financing has in fact been important in sustaining domestic demand and in supporting Asia's rebound from the recent global crisis. The International Monetary Fund estimates that the emerging economies in Asia will grow by an average annual rate of 8.6% in the next five years. Asia is therefore very much part of the global shift that is taking place in which the economic power in the world will become increasingly more dispersed with the emergence of several growth centres in the global economy. Should Asia continue to grow by an average annual rate of 7% over the next ten years, it is estimated that Asia's share of the global GDP will increase to 40%. Let me further elaborate on these two developments, namely the strengthening of domestic demand in Asia and the intensification of regional economic and financial integration, that are mutually reinforcing in sustaining Asia's economic growth prospects. A more recent phenomenon supporting this trend is the strengthening of regional financial cooperation not only to preserve regional financial stability but also to enhance the prospects of the region. Strengthening Domestic Demand The strengthening of domestic demand is part of the structural changes taking place in Asia to diversify its sources of growth. Growth in most of the Asian economies was previously export-led. While several measures have been taken to promote domestic demand, the favourable demographic structure, the low levels of unemployment, the relatively low level of household debt and the policy flexibility to implement supporting monetary and fiscal policies have contributed to higher consumption. Other measures initiated are the social safety nets in the form of schemes and programmes for unemployment benefits, healthcare, education and retirement that have been put in place to reduce the need for high savings. The consequent increase in consumption demand has not only resulted in a significant expansion of the retail trade sector but Asia is also increasingly becoming an important consumer in the global economy. Private investment activity is also beginning to pick up after a period of over capacity due to the excesses prior to the Asian financial crisis. There are also plans for massive investment in infrastructure development to sustain the economic competitiveness of the region. The Asian Development Bank estimates that Asia will require about USD8 trillion of infrastructure investment in the next decade. Most important is that Asia has the internal capacity from its high savings to finance these infrastructure requirements. The stronger domestic demand in Asia is also well supported by the strengthened financial systems following the restructuring of the banking sector, the development of the capital markets and the strengthening of the regulatory and supervisory systems in the post-Asian financial crisis period. The reforms implemented also included the progressive deregulation and the move to greater market orientation and increased liberalisation. Today, Asia's capital markets are significantly deeper and more liquid. The bond market in emerging East Asia has increased by more than seven-fold since 1996, with a current value of USD4.2 trillion dollars. Emerging East Asia accounts for 7.2% of the total worldwide bond market at end-2009 compared to 2.5% in 1996. Asian banks have stronger fundamentals with improved risk management and governance practices, with capitalisation well above the regulatory requirements and with non-performing loans maintained at historical lows. Risk-based approaches to supervision have also been widely adopted across Asia. In addition, efforts also continue to be directed towards building institutions to protect consumers, to promote financial inclusion, enhance market discipline and to augment management capabilities. These efforts have ensured continued financial intermediation process and that this access to finance remains an important factor that supports the growth of the economies in the region. Intensification of Regional Economic and Financial Integration in Asia The second major development that has been taking place in Asia is the intensification ofregional economic and financial integration. While the individual economies in Asia continue to implement policies and reforms at the national level, greater attention is being placed on strengthening economic and financial linkages in the region. Intra-regional trade which has been a major contributor to the recent recovery in Asia, has risen from an average of 32% of total exports in 1995 to exceed an average of 50% in 2008. Of importance is the rising share of intra-regional trade for final demand in Asia. This reflects an important change in the pattern of trade amongst the Asian economies. The pace of intra-regional investment flows has also gained momentum. Businesses in the region are increasingly leveraging on regional complementarities as well as taking advantage of the opportunities created by the growing markets throughout the region. A more recent development is the strengthening financial integration within the Asian region. While regional financial integration will further facilitate the already strong trade and investment linkages in the region, a more important aspect of the increased financial integration in Asia is the more efficient intermediation of funds in Asia. This includes the recycling of some part of the sizeable savings in Asia to productive investments in the region. The average savings rate in Asia is 35% of GDP and Asia as a group has a total of USD4.8 trillion in foreign reserves. With greater liberalisation of the financial sector and the capital account, and the increased linkage of the national payments systems in Asia, there are increased financial flows within the region. This trend is reinforced by the increased presence of regional institutions in the individual domestic financial systems and Asia's favourable economic prospects and more developed financial markets. This has already resulted in volatile capital flows to the Asian region. Going forward, papers issued out of Asia will also likely assume greater importance as an asset class. It will serve to facilitate the further diversification of risks and thus, contribute to stability of the international financial system. It will also expand the options for investors and borrowers and thus, contribute to more efficient allocation of financial resources across borders. Asia's economic and financial integration, however, extends beyond its own region to the traditional markets in the developed economies, and more recently to other emerging economies in other parts of the world. Today, the economic and financial linkages between the emerging economies have also gained significance. While world trade has, on average, expanded by 16% over the period 2004-2008, Asia's trade with the Middle East and Latin America has increased on average by about 30%. Asia's trade with other emerging economies now stands at 13% of Asia's total exports. A further recent development is the increasing international dimension of Islamic finance which is also influencing the global patterns of financial and trade flows. Islamic finance today has contributed to increasing the financial and economic ties between Asia and the Middle East. The emergence of new financial centres in Asia and the Middle East has seen stronger investment and financial flows between the two regions. With the greater internationalisation of this form of financial intermediation, it has also opened up the prospects for the developed economies to forge stronger financial linkages with these dynamic growth regions of Asia and the Middle East. The inherent features of Islamic finance require that financial transactions are supported by an underlying economic activity, thus ensuring that there is a close link between financial and productive flows. Islamic finance is also based on the principle of profit-sharing and therefore risk sharing. Islamic financial transactions clearly define the arrangements at the outset, and provides the incentive for the appropriate due diligence to be undertaken by the Islamic financial institutions to ensure that the profits are commensurate with the risks being assumed. Aspects of governance and risk management are therefore strongly emphasised in the arrangements. This arrangement also demands for higher standards of disclosure and transparency which in turn, acts to strengthen market discipline. Regional Monetary and Financial Cooperation The Asian financial crisis has also prompted greater regional monetary and financial cooperation. Earlier regional cooperation had focused mainly on trade, investment and development. This decade has seen the cooperation shift to efforts to address financial stability issues, namely surveillance, crisis management, liquidity support arrangements, financial supervision and financial market development. Other areas include the payments and settlement system and capacity building in the financial sector. The route that Asia is taking to forge greater financial integration will therefore be different from that of Europe. Unlike in the European Union, Asia does not have centralised institutions to coordinate financial integration but rather has leveraged on the existing intra-regional groupings and networks to forge greater cooperation and collaboration in areas of common interest. This is mainly through the ASEAN3 and EMEAP which comprise the East Asia Pacific central banks. Secondly, a common currency is not on Asia's medium term agenda. To minimise exchange rate risks and to facilitate intra-regional trade and investment, a number of countries have initiated bilateral arrangements to use domestic currencies for trade settlement. There is also now a pooling of reserves so as to have in place liquidity support facilities for the region. Conclusion Let me conclude my remarks. Asia is very much part of the changes that are taking place in the global economy and the international financial system. Going forward, the pace of Asian regional economic and financial integration will gain momentum, driven by structural factors, by the conscious policy to put in place the enabling environment and by the benefits derived that are mutually reinforcing. The evidence in this decade has demonstrated that a more integrated and cohesive Asia contributes towards more balanced global growth, while a more resilient Asia contributes to greater global financial stability. While a more connected world in this new phase of globalisation will bring new vulnerabilities, it also brings with it the promise of new opportunities, new relationships and partnerships in the world economy, and thus, new prospects for a greater shared prosperity.
