text: Opening Remarks by Assistant Governor at the Seminar on Crisis Preparedness for Insurance Supervisors organised by AITRI -Toronto Centre, hosted by Bank Negara Malaysia Speaker: Mr. Donald Joshua Jaganathan Speech/Interview Date: 18 Apr 2011 Venue: Lanai Kijang, Bank Negara Malaysia Language: English Thank you for giving me this opportunity to deliver the opening remarks for this AITRI seminar. Firstly, I would like to thank the Asean Insurance Training and Research Institute for organising another leadership development programme, in collaboration with the Toronto Centre. I also wish to extend a warm welcome to all participants, particularly those from abroad. I understand that ? there are delegates from Asean as well as non-Asean countries. I would also like to take this opportunity to provide a brief introduction of AITRI. As you know AITRI has been established by the Regulators of the 10 member countries of ASEAN. AITRI is a non-profit organization and has been set up primarily to serve the training and development needs of the ASEAN member countries. I am pleased however, to note that AITRI has matured within a short span of time and now provides courses that are regularly attended by regulators beyond the ASEAN countries with the support of international bodies like the IAIS, OSFI and the Toronto Centre. The theme of this Seminar - CRISIS PREPAREDNESS is central to the role and function of insurance supervisors who are responsible to ensure continued safety and soundness of the insurance companies, the protection of consumers, the orderly growth of the industry and ultimately, the stability of the financial sector. Crisis preparedness does not have to be about the management and resolution of a crisis: it involves active and pre-emptive steps taken to prevent a crisis from happening in the first instance. In this highly interconnected world, it is critical for both the financial institutions and the supervisors to put in place adequate and appropriate safeguards to protect the financial sector and the economy as a whole from risks which might arise from within an economy or transmitted across borders. Whilst the focus of most discussions on crisis preparedness have rightly been on systemically important financial institutions such as large banking groups and non-bank financial institutions such as investment houses, hedge funds and mutual funds companies; it is important that the insurance sector is an integral part of of the framework due to its role in facilitating economic risk transfers and mobilizing of funds between economies across the globe. Although the insurance industry is not generally seen as a source of systemic risk, it is nevertheless not insulated from the dynamics and uncertainties of the financial system. In some cases, such risks might even arise by just being a member of a financial conglomerate with other financial institutions that are exposed to systemic risks. I am sure you are familiar with the case of AIG where the failure of a non-insurance part of the group severely impacted the operations of the otherwise financially healthy insurance entities within the group. The failure of the largest insurance group in USA sent tremors to more than 130 countries around the world where it operates and was eventually rescued by the US Federal Government.? The recent crisis has been unusual in its global scale and reach. In the past, financial crises have been largely limited to specific regions or types of economies. For example, the Nordic countries in the early 1990s, Latin America in the mid-1990s, Asia in the late 1990s, and the emerging market economies in the early 2000s. The recent crisis has had most impact on the major advanced countries, with the collapse of many large and established financial institutions such as Lehman Brothers, AIG, Northern Rock, Bear Stearns, and others. And so this crisis has provided many important lessons that are relevant for regulators and supervisors everywhere. Whilst many factors have been attributed to the failure of financial institutions during the crisis, what was common in many instances was the financial institutions' aggressive business models, coupled with inadequate supervisory oversight. Supervisors in particular have received the brunt of public criticism. In what has now become a favourite quote of the politicians and leaders, supervisors have been accused of being slow to act despite the clear warning signals. Admittedly many of the problems that arose during the financial crisis could be traced to flawed implementation of regulatory standards and principles; and to behaviour prompted by misaligned incentives. Even though there are no mechanisms that can guarantee that financial crisis will not happen, having a well-designed supervisory framework and effective surveillance will go a long way to minimise the likelihood and impact of a crisis. On this note, I encourage you to take note of the on-going initiatives taken by the international community of supervisory authorities to better manage the financial sector moving forward. Firstly, supervisors are required to have in place macro prudential surveillance to monitor the inter-linkages of potential vulnerabilities in particular cross-border transmission of risks. Secondly, macro-surveillance should be integrated with micro-surveillance to ensure that the supervision of individual firms takes into account risks that are impacting the financial system as a whole. Thirdly, supervisors must strengthen their engagement with firms on their business strategies to monitor accumulation of risk exposures across the sector. Fourthly, regional and international cooperation needs to be intensified to promote more effective supervision and regulation of an increasingly internationalized insurance industry. Towards this end, progress is being made on the formulation of a Home-Host Supervisory framework that encapsulates group-wide supervision, supervisory colleges, and recovery and resolution plans for internationally active financial institutions In conclusion, financial institutions and supervisors must be pro-active and vigilant, to prevent the recurrence of financial crises. Given the dynamics of the financial markets today, all of us here must strengthen our supervisory capabilities to respond effectively to developments that might affect financial stability, and to actively promote greater collaboration between supervisors. Finally, I would like to thank the speakers for enriching this seminar with their presence and invaluable experience. I also wish to again thank the AITRI and Toronto Centre for giving Bank Negara Malaysia the opportunity to host this program. To all our participants and resource persons from abroad, I hope your stay in Kuala Lumpur will be both pleasant and memorable.

Title: Opening Speech at the 11th Muzakarah Of Syariah Nusantara
text: Keynote Address by Assistant Governor at the16th East Asian Actuarial Conference Theme: "Venture into Uncertainty, Capture Opportunities" Speaker: Mr. Donald Joshua Jaganathan Speech/Interview Date: 12 Oct 2011 Venue: Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia Language: English It gives me great pleasure today to deliver the keynote address for the 16th East Asian Actuarial Conference, with the theme "Venture into uncertainty, capture opportunities". I would like to thank the EAAC committee and the Actuarial Society of Malaysia for organising this event in Kuala Lumpur. I also wish to extend a warm welcome to all participants, particularly those from abroad. Risk, Uncertainty and Opportunity Risk and uncertainty are defining characteristics of the world we live in. Modern evolution in finance is largely distinguished by its successful efforts first to understand, and then to control risk. This began with the development of probability theory leading more recently to the theory of porfolio selection, financial economics and the renowned but later somewhat disparaged Black-Scholes formula, as well as the developments in behavioral economics. However, despite the long strides made and milestones achieved along the way, there are indeed many miles to go before we sleep, to quote Robert Frost in his meaningful poem. As the financial world continues to transform in meeting the evolving needs of developed and emerging economies, the nature of financial risk continues to evolve in nature, scale and complexity. Innovations in the design and distribution of products have increased the choice, accessibility and affordability of insurance and other financial products for all segments of society. However, such innovations bring with them additional risks to financial institutions, customers, and the financial system as a whole. As East Asia grows in importance as a global trade and investment partner, the greater degree of interlinkages, both within the region and internationally, will increase the likelihood of financial risk contagion. This will require greater regional and global cooperation in the areas of macroprudential regulation and microprudential supervision, especially on entities that have presence in multiple jurisdictions. Forces of change impacting Asia over the next decade and opportunities for the Actuarial Profession Over the recent decade, the Asian insurance industry has seen significant progress and expansion. This has been driven in large part by rapid economic transformation taking place throughout the region, resulting in a growing and more affluent middle-income population. Going forward, we expect the industry to be shaped primarily by the ageing demographic in the region, inspiring the introduction of new products such as pensions, long-term care and annuities. While these new products fill a very real need, they are not without risk and will require significant care and diligence from the actuarial profession in their development and management. We also expect to see significant growth coming from the takaful sector. Globally, takaful contributions are expected to record an annual growth of between 15 to 20%, with the global takaful market size estimated to reach 7 US billion dollars by 2015. New family takaful licenses issued by Bank Negara in Malaysia earlier this year will allow both established and strong life insurance players that already have a presence in the domestic market, as well as new entrants to expand in the takaful space. Indeed, the development of strong and dominant family takaful players in Malaysia represents an important strategy of Malaysia as an International Islamic Financial Centre to tap a wider demography and the enormous growth potential represented by the 1.5 billion global Muslim population. Among the key recent developments in this sphere is the issuance of the Risk Based Capital Framework for Takaful by Bank Negara as a concept paper to the industry with the goal of harmonising the capital requirements between insurance and takaful. Against this backdrop of growth and innovation, there has also been a significant change in the regulatory landscape that will most certainly impact the work of actuaries. Through Solvency II, European regulators are charting new ground in terms of expectations on risk management by insurers. In particular, the directive recommends the "three lines of defence" model for managing risks within insurance organisations. This has key implications to the way the actuarial function is currently structured as it requires a separation between the operational duties of the function from its risk management responsibilities. Consistent with global developments, Bank Negara Malaysia is in the midst of reviewing the roles and responsibilities of the Appointed Actuary with the aim of achieving a more independent and effective risk management function. Bank Negara Malaysia has also issued a Guideline on Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) where insurance companies are required to have sound capital management, which requires the setting of Individual Target Capital Levels based on stress testing, amongst other measures. Inevitably as a profession with deep knowledge of how insurance works, actuaries within insurance companies will be heavily involved in this capital management process. This is not inconsistent with global developments where the Solvency II directive, for example, explicitly requires the actuarial function to be more directly involved in the implementation of risk management systems of the company. Concurrent to developments in capital standards, accounting requirements have also been undergoing unprecedented pace of change with the finalisation of the International Financial Reporting Standards for Insurance Contracts on the horizon. In this region, actuaries will be asked to play an expanded role, in particular with the unbundling of investment elements from traditional insurance contracts and the explicit valuation of options and guarantees contained therein. The Opportunity for Actuaries Outside the Traditional Areas The actuarial profession brings a very special value proposition to our rapidly changing interdependent and interconnected world. The actuarial profession trains its members to take a hard look at reality and to objectively map the risks and opportunities that lie ahead in the medium and long term. All actuaries are taught to advise their clients to prepare in the present for uncertainties of future contingent events. Perhaps if the rigour of the actuarial profession was applied in the management of credit default swaps, this would have made a difference to the outcome of the global financial crisis. But of course it has also been argued that the crisis owed itself not to the lack of financial or technical competence but rather to an abundance of unbridled greed. Probability theory and mathematics which are key elements of modern financial risk management may sound complex to some but are clearly bread and butter issues to the actuarial profession. And as actuaries, you are undoubtedly well aware that most of the significant financial risks do not exhibit normal behaviour, hence the more developed thinking in actuarial circles on measures that explicitly capture tail risks such as Conditional Tail Expectation instead of adopting a pure Value at Risk approach. Actuaries are also taught to employ a control cycle approach to all your tasks which involves the development of a model or a solution followed by a continuous review of that model and the assumptions it employs. This problem solving framework is useful in many other fields of the financial sector and will ensure models and assumptions are frequently reviewed with clear accountability for variance of actual results from those expected. This in-depth knowledge of financial risk and its management combined with a professional code of conduct and the active monitoring of compliance with this code puts the actuarial profession at an advantage in the field of risk management. However, this will entail actuaries moving out of their comfort zones and going beyond the traditional boundaries of insurance. In this regard, I would like to congratulate the profession on the creation of the Chartered Enterprise Risk Analyst (CERA) designation as an important step in the right direction. Conclusion I conclude with a thought from a well known Actuary. Frank Reddington once said that "the actuary's danger may lie in too close a preoccupation with his particular techniques. His real strength lies elsewhere; in a broad training whose firm roots are in mathematics and statistics, but whose branches reach out into commerce, investments, administration and all the bustle of humanityathe actuary cannot foretell the future...what he can do and does is to sense the wide-ranging possibilities that the future may have in store and to make them a living part of the present where decisions are made".... Indeed it is in times like these where a profession such as yours, trained in the measurement and management of risk, must come to the fore and help to build a more resilient financial future. With that, I would like to wish the distinguished speakers and participants of this seminar a fruitful and lively seminar. I fully expect the exchange of views to be both stimulating and informative. To all speakers and participants from abroad, I hope your stay in Kuala Lumpur will be both pleasant and memorable. Thank you.

Title: Speech at Kedah Financial Carnival
text: Speech by Deputy Governor at the Bumiputera Life Insurance Agents Convention 2012 'Professionalism Pillars of Success' Presenter: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB / Venue: Putra World Trade Center, Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 22 Sep 2012 / Alhamdullilah, first let us all express our gratitude to Allah swt because with His permission and grace we can gather this morning in conjunction with the Bumiputera Life Insurance Agents Convention 2012 themed "Professionalism of Success". I would also like to express my deepest appreciation and gratitude to the Malaysian Insurance Institute (MII) as the organiser of this Convention for giving me the opportunity to attend and deliver a speech today. Well done to MII for organising this Convention with the noble aim of developing bumiputera life insurance agents to be more productive and successful people, while being able to provide excellent services to the community. Industrial and Economic Development Dear Brothers and Sisters, Let me start the speech by revealing some facts about the current economic developments and talking about the performance of the insurance and takaful sectors. In the past 5 years, despite the country's economy facing the challenges of the uncertain international economic environment, the insurance and takaful sectors have shown positive and encouraging growth. During this period, total insurance premiums and new takaful contributions registered a positive growth at an average annual rate of 4.9%. The highest growth of 13% was recorded in 2010. This growth also reflects the contribution towards a significant increase in the number of Malaysians who already have insurance and takaful coverage. In 2011, statistics show that for every 100 Malaysians, 67 people are covered by a life insurance or takaful policy compared to 59 in the last 5 years. Meanwhile, the agent channel still remains an important life insurance marketing platform. The contribution from the agency channel amounted to 65% of the gross premium for 2011. Along with this development, agent productivity has also increased from a new premium of RM29,950 per agent in 2006 to RM46,260 in 2011. More importantly, the average income for life insurance agents continues to rise, well above the national average income, although the number of agents has increased significantly from 75,340 in 2006 to 83,174 in 2011. This does not include relatively high-numbered life takaful agents. If it is taken into account the individuals involved in this sector it is significantly more than 150,000 people. In terms of income, full-time insurance agents recorded an income of RM92,000 in 2011. This amount is three times the country's average per capita income. Meanwhile, the income of agents who work part-time only records an average income of RM7,000 per year. This shows that the prospects of being a successful insurance agent who works full-time are bright and able to earn a decent income. This development also proves that agents are able to increase their income in today's existing commission structure environment. It also shows that today's commission structure is capable of providing satisfactory turnover to productive agents. Studies also show that the commission structure practiced in Malaysia is comparable to the practice in other countries. Under the Financial Sector Plan 2011, Bank Negara Malaysia in line with current developments is considering giving more flexibility to the industry and insurance companies to formulate a commission structure that is in line with their respective business philosophies. It is hoped that by giving the industry the ability to determine its own commission structure, it will be introduced in tandem with the transparency of the commission structure itself. The disclosure of the commission structure is not new, it has even been practiced by most countries of the region. It is therefore important that agents are prepared to operate under a more transparent and liberal environment. However, the interests of the public will always be protected so that consumers do not incur unaffordable costs and are adequately and accurately informed to make decisions. New Opportunity Challenges and Opportunities Ladies and sisters, Looking ahead, the Government's target to make Malaysia a high-income country will also increase the income of agents. This is due to the fact that the increase in people's income will increase their ability to get higher insurance coverage. Currently, the per-capita expenditure allocated for the purchase of insurance and life takaful is only RM927, or 3.2% of the country's per-capita income. I expect this number to increase as more and more Malaysians fall into the category of middle and high income earners. Another recent development that has an impact on the development of the insurance industry is the changing demographic structure of the Malaysian population towards making the country's society ageing. In 2010, 8% of the Malaysian population was aged 60 and over. It is estimated that by 2040, this group will increase to 17%. Such developments will certainly open up new opportunities for agents to take the opportunity to expand their business reach which includes insurance/takaful products that are in line with the needs and needs of the ageing community. For example, annuity products, health protection and wealth management [wealth management]. In the 2011 budget, the Government announced a tax relief of RM3,000 on the purchase of annuity products for a period of 10 years beginning 2012. This tax incentive is intended to encourage the community to save for retirement. Social Responsibility of Agents Among the agendas highlighted by the Government is in developing a balanced, sustainable [sustainable] and inclusive national economy. This is to ensure that every citizen will be able to benefit from the growth in the wealth of the country. In this regard, the lowincome and rural population should not be marginalized in the current of change and development of the country. Therefore, under the Financial Sector Plan 2011-2020, Bank Negara Malaysia will encourage the insurance and takaful industry to develop insurance and micro-takaful products to expand the reach to the underserved. The provision of this insurance service will be made in a cost-efficient manner, accessible, easy to understand and easy to compensate. I want to touch on a social responsibility that in my mind is relevant to a career as an agent. As a group that is always at the heart of society and has a personal contact with the public, agents are well positioned to assist efforts to expand financial education among the public. Agents can improve service to the community by playing the role of a source of information to the public on financial affairs. The agent may provide appropriate explanations on developments related to current financial issues. With this, the brothers and sisters can help to educate the community to become more financially literate as well as to prevent them from falling into unregulated or illegal financial activities and will eventually lead to financial losses. I raise this issue because there are in the market at the moment, illegal investment schemes and unlicensed lenders. I'd like to touch a little bit about illegal investment schemes like the Quick Rich Scheme that are often talked about. There are many victims who have lost money and property due to such a scheme. Despite the fact that the authorities often broadcast warnings to citizens not to be fooled by such schemes, there are still a few citizens who are hit by sweet and false promises. Bank Negara Malaysia has also published press releases to assist the public in identifying the characteristics of illegal investment schemes. Among them: Offer of granting gold and other valuables as part of the promised return. People are also bribed with claims that the deposit was received as a loan to the company. Promising high or unrealistic interest rates or returns in a very short time. Some even promise returns that exceed 40% per annum. [ 'if it is too good to be true than it cannot be true'; Fish upstream downstream, like a sweet-mouthed bird don't wear]. The 'modus operandi' of this scheme is simple. At the beginning, early investors will be paid a return on investment as promised. However, when the operator of this illegal scheme discovers that there is a lack of liquidity to meet the depositor's demands, the operator will eventually get away with the money collected . As a result of loss and crying. I hope that you will always warn your customers about the dangers and futility of investing hard work in such an investment scheme. The same applies to the activity of taking loans from unlicensed lenders. I would also like to ask that the brothers and sisters take the opportunity to meet with their respective customers to remind them to refrain from obtaining financing from any lender that is not licensed by the authorities. This is because there are many who have become caught up in this activity which will eventually lead to unwanted harm to themselves and their families. Even if this activity is not curbed, it will be a chronic social problem that will cause severe social symptoms to society. In this regard, I am confident that as a responsible agent and safeguarding the long-term interests of their respective clients, ladies and gentlemen can play an important role by providing advice and disseminating this critical information to the public. Incentives to Develop Agent Energy In addition to the developments discussed just now, agents should always be concerned about the developments taking place in our environment. The emergence of alternative marketing channels that are gaining ground is among the developments that will have a direct impact on the agency channel. The impact will be higher if these alternative channels are considered more cost efficient and give direct competition to the agent channels. In addition, there are alternative financial products in the market such as unit trusts that can be a direct rival to insurance and takaful protection products. In fact, the introduction of increasingly innovative and complex insurance and takaful products will add to the challenges for agents to further enhance and update their knowledge and skills. In order to always be in a 'relevant' position, agents should always equip themselves with the latest knowledge of the products available in the market and always be ready to gain knowledge and improve knowledge in marketing financial protection products. It can be done through continuous training and ensuring that the advisory services provided are always up-to-date, relevant and forward-looking. Adequate training can also increase the level of professionalism of agents. In this regard, the importance of training should be nurtured since a person begins to venture into this field. To assist new agents in the insurance industry, I would like to inform you that Bank Negara Malaysia will allow insurance companies to provide more flexible training and development financing to insurance agents. This step will be taken by Bank Negara Malaysia in collaboration with the insurance industry to strengthen the industry. This financing facility is expected to help insurance companies as well as agents chiefs to attract more potential potential agents and who are genuinely interested in becoming successful and productive agents. In addition, to encourage life insurance agents to upgrade their business as financial advisors, an incentive package is being considered for this purpose. This initiative is expected to provide an impetus for the brothers and sisters to enhance productivity, skills and professionalism as successful life insurance agents. I would like to congratulate the recipients of the Best Bumiputera Agency Head and Best Bumiputera Personal Producer of the Year Award. This is what we want to see every year, more and more Bumiputeras have succeeded and outperformed this field. I sincerely hope that their success will serve as an example and encourage other Bumiputera insurance agent partners to move forward and continue to succeed in their careers. Before I end my speech, I would once again like to thank and congratulate MII and LIAM for successfully organising this glorious convention. I am confident that the various knowledge and knowledge will be shared by the discerning and experienced speakers for the participants present today. Hopefully, the efforts of the brothers and sisters do not end here alone and will continue until they achieve success at the international level. In the face of daily life sometimes we forget about our responsibilities as members of the society, sometimes in the race to achieve a better stage of life, we forget about the noble values that we need to cultivate, sometimes in fierce competition in the business sphere, we are alpa about our contribution to the country. I would like to read an old Malay saying that I think is very relevant in this 21st century: Carrying out duties, holding the line of duty, carrying out the trust, holding the slack, holding the right, holding the trample, making good on the promise, being despicable, defending the people, defending the nation, perishing, defending the country, the dead, helping, not hoping to be flattered , virtuous, hopeless to praise, Sacrifice, hopeless of reward, Work, hopeless wages, give, do not spare, Teaching, don't expect to be alone. Finally, I am grateful to officiate the Bumiputera Life Insurance Agents Convention 2012 with the theme, "Professionalism pillars of Success". text: Speech by Mr. Abu Hassan Alshari Yahaya Assistant Governor, Bank Negara Malaysia at the Launching Ceremony of Financial Literacy Month, Bursa Malaysia Presenter: Mr. Abu Hassan Alshari Yahaya / Venue: / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 08 Oct 2012 / I am very pleased to be invited by the Confederation of Consumer Associations of Malaysia (FOMCA) to officiate the launch of Financial Literacy Month today. I would like to express my appreciation to all parties involved in this organization for their commitment in improving financial literacy among consumers. The theme of Financial Literacy Month this time, which is, 'financial responsibility starts with me' is accurate because there are now many factors that are stressful and influence us to spend beyond our means. No one can fully help but our own because we have the power and responsibility to manage and make financial decisions wisely. The per capita income of our country's population is growing (from RM28,169 in 2000 to almost RM31,000 in 2012) resulting in an everincreasing level of consumption and higher demand for goods and services. Therefore, consumers need to be prudent in spending and wise to distinguish between needs and wants. Consumers need a careful plan in making important decisions for daily expenses and big expenses in life such as, education, marriage, buying a house, children's schooling, insurance, investment etc. Financial consumers should also know to choose a wide range of financial products and services. Therefore, we, as consumers, should equip ourselves with the knowledge and skills to enable us to make good financial decisions. Concerned with the challenges faced by consumers, Bank Negara Malaysia has partnered with various parties such as financial institutions, consumer associations, government agencies and academics to increase financial literacy among consumers by providing various programmes to help consumers in that direction. Bank Negara Malaysia's commitment is further strengthened by the Financial Sector Plan 2011-2020, which emphasises on the protection agenda, consumer education and financial inclusion. Financial responsibility begins with me In each phase of life, consumers often have different interests, responsibilities and financial wants. As our age and life increase and change, then our wants and needs also change. Financial planning prepares ourselves to face these life's opportunities and challenges. If we plan our finances efficiently we will feel that we are able to control our finances and ensure that we will spend within our true means. In addition, we can manage our debts well and avoid the negative effects of going bankrupt. As a responsible individual... what do we have to do Spend according to plan We need to prepare a budget plan and spend according to that plan. In this matter, we can find out the details of expenses and avoid overspending. By constantly recording our monthly expenses we know where our income and salary are going every month. Recording expenses can control expenses. Spend according to your ability and not intuition. Saving We also need to cultivate the habit of saving for the future or anxiety. We can save automatically by using salary deduction schemes, auto-debit or other means like that. The rate to be tabbed may be around 5% - 10% of the total income. Even if it only saves RM50 per month, but with compounded interest, eventually the accumulated savings amount will be high. Challenge yourself to gradually increase the amount of savings in order to have more money for the future. Separate in advance the amount of money to be tabbed from waiting at the end of the month where it is likely that a sum of money has been spent. Use technology to save on banking costs We can also use technology to reduce the cost of banking. By using internet banking and e-payment, we can save in terms of transportation expenses, pakir, energy and time. Improve financial knowledge We also need to improve financial knowledge to enable good and wise financial decision-making. Financial knowledge can be obtained through financial education organised by consumer associations, the internet, Bank Negara Malaysia's website, financial institutions and other relevant agencies. Among the financial education websites are the following: Progam Education Internet users through bankinginfo.com.my, insuransinfo.com.my and Islamicfinance info.com.my provide information, knowledge, understanding and advice for banking, insurance and takaful products and services. It is also posted on the website bankinginfo.com.my for users to compare fees and charges imposed by the financial provider's institution. Bank Negara Malaysia's website advises caution when making decisions regarding financial services offered by unlicensed parties. bankinginfo.com.my, insuransinfo.com.my and Islamicfinance info.com.my As a responsible user of financial services... Understand the terms and conditions of the agreement document We need to be more aware and understand the terms and conditions of the agreement document before agreeing to purchase products and use the services offered by financial institutions. This is very important to ensure that we understand the financial services and products to be received, the fees that will be charged and the rights as consumers if the financial institution violates the terms and conditions agreed by both parties. Self-discipline for loan repayment However, we need to discipline ourselves to manage loan repayments well. If we encounter any issues with regard to financial products and services, immediately discuss with the financial provider to find an effective solution. To be more effective, the financial education needs to be applied continuously from young age to adulthood to foster a high level of discipline in managing money. In this context, initiatives have been undertaken by Bank Negara Malaysia involving financial education in schools and the provision of financial education websites. AKPK provides the POWER Programme! for the youth. Financial management education through school co-curriculum Our children were first exposed to the importance of prudent financial management in 1997 through the Adoption School Programme by financial institutions. In 1999, the School Student Finance Club was created and our children started using the Money Book to record daily expenses to apply a sense of responsibility towards personal finances. To date, 11 million copies of the Money Saku Book have been distributed. In line with the widespread use of the internet, the money book was electronically created on the website, duitsaku.com, starting in 2004 with 110,000 members. Applying the element of financial education into the school curriculum in collaboration with the Ministry of Education Malaysia Moving forward, our children will get a formal and comprehensive financial education through the school curriculum. This is aimed at promoting financial capacity as a life skill from a young age. Elements of financial literacy will be integrated into the core subjects of the new primary and secondary school curriculum. The programme will be implemented in stages from 2014 for primary schools and 2017 for secondary schools. Among the elements of financial literacy to be applied are money, financial management and planning, savings and investment, credit and debt management, and protection and insurance. Financial education through the POWER! program by AKPK The POWER! programme, Your Ringgit Money Management organized by AKPK, is aimed at youths and first-time borrowers between the ages of 18 and 30. This program will provide individuals with exposure to the skills and knowledge to manage finances effectively and provide useful financial information, tips and tools to promote money management and prudent financial discipline. The scenario of the financial position of young people in the country should be given serious attention. 47% of young workers aged 18 to 35 have such a heavy debt problem that they spend as much as 30% or more of their monthly income to pay off debts. (Source: Study by the Center for Consumer Research and Resources in collaboration with Citi Foundation). By attending the POWER program! I hope that those young people will be more prudent in making their financial management decisions. Protection for Financial Consumers Complaints advice and resolution channels  financial institutions We should not run away or remain silent when faced with financial providers but instead be proactive by using the advice and complaint channels provided. The best way to get advice and resolve the issue is to get in touch directly with the financial provider's own institutions as they understand the issues raised and provide the best solution proposals such as through loan restructuring. To ensure that financial users can resolve complaints directly, each financial provider institution has its own complaints advice and management unit. Complaints advice and resolution channel  Bank Negara Malaysia Ladies and gentlemen may also contact Bank Negara Malaysia's Advisory and Service Information Site (BNMLINK) either at the head office in Kuala Lumpur or at Bank Negara Malaysia branches. To save costs, it is not necessary to come if the complainant lives far away; adequate by mail only. Alternatively, please contact Bank Negara Malaysia's customer service contact centre (BNMTELELINK) by phone: 1-300-88-5465). For information, since 2008, Bank Negara Malaysia has received over 1 million inquiries and complaints from individuals and entrepreneurs with an average of 1,600 per day. Channels of banking services for rural communities  Bank Negara Malaysia Malaysians who live far inland and find it difficult to obtain financial information and basic banking services, can now do so through Mobile LINK or MobileLINK services. At MobileLINK, the public can also raise various issues related to the poor quality and satisfactory level of service of financial providers. In addition, on 15 August 2012, agent banking was launched to enable the underserved to access financial services more effectively in terms of cost, through the use of non-bank retail channels. Advice and complaint resolution channel  AKPK Usually the situation will be more complicated when the consumer cannot pay the debts obtained from many financial provider institutions. In this situation, users need to quickly ask AKPK for help. Through the credit management programme, AKPK will seek the cooperation of the debt-giving institutions to restructure the loan payments according to the ability of sipeminjam. Complaint advice and resolution channel  FMB Another advanced settlement channel is the Financial Mediation Bureau (FMB) which is an independent mediation body for resolving disputes between consumers and financial provider institutions for free. Direction forward Moving forward, consumers will continue to experience a more diverse and sophisticated range of financial products and services. In such a financial environment, consumers need to equip themselves with knowledge and practical skills in relation to prudent financial management, financial products and services information, investment, debt management and so on. This knowledge will allow the user to make responsible financial decisions based on sufficient information. In this regard, the integrated support and cooperation by all parties involved such as financial institutions, consumer associations, government agencies, academics, educational institutions and others in preparing and implementing financial education programmes will increase consumers' financial literacy and empower and provide protection to them. The parties involved in this responsibility sharing can further enhance the coordination of their activities to improve effectiveness and reduce duplication. This integrated collaboration will have a more comprehensive impact in improving the level of financial literacy of consumers. Last but not least, I would like to thank the FOMCA and all those involved in the Financial Literacy Month program. With the phrase Bismillahirahmanirrahim, I am pleased to officiate the launch of Financial Celtic Month. Thank you.

Title: Speech at the 2017 Annual Dinner of BNM Kota Kinabalu Office, Sabah
text: Deputy Governor's Keynote Address at the Oil and Gas Funding Forum 2013 Speaker: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB Speech/Interview Date: 11 Jun 2013 Venue: Sasana Kijang, Kuala Lumpur Language: Terlebih dahulu, saya ingin merakamkan penghargaan kepada Malaysian Petroleum Resource Corporation kerana telah menjemput saya untuk menyampaikan sepatah dua kata pada persidangan Oil and Gas Funding Forum 2013" ini. Saya juga ingin mengalu-alukan kedatangan tuan-tuan dan puan-puan pada hari ini. Penganjuran forum ini di Sasana Kijang adalah bertepatan dengan aspirasi dan komitmen Bank Negara Malaysia untuk menjadikan Sasana Kijang sebagai sebuah pusat pertemuan minda dan kolaborasi utama di kalangan pemain-pemain industri kewangan. Building on the progress achieved over the last decade, the Malaysian financial sector is well positioned to continue to play an important role in financial intermediation through effective channelling of funds into productive sectors. As Malaysia advances into the next phase of economic development towards becoming a high-income, high value-added economy, the ability of the financial sector to continuously innovate and provide comprehensive and effective financial solutions to support strategic sectors like the oil and gas industry in Malaysia is no longer an option, but more of a necessity. It is therefore my great pleasure to be here today to speak at the Oil and Gas Funding Forum 2013 organised by the Malaysian Petroleum Resource Corporation. This forum brings together key industry players from the oil and gas sector and provides an important opportunity for the leaders in this sector to interact and exchange ideas with the financial institutions on sustainable financing opportunities for the oil and gas industry. My remarks today will hence focus on the prospects for further growth for the oil and gas industry and the vibrant financing ecosystem that is currently available in Malaysia. I will also share some thoughts on the imperatives for the financial sector in order to be able to continuously support this sector moving forward. Strong growth potential of the oil and gas industry The global oil and gas production has grown by around 1.5% annually in the last decade, driven by rising demand from the rapidly developing countries, notably China, India and Southeast Asia. Oil demand from these emerging economies has in fact overtaken demand from industrialised countries given the growing affluence of the population in emerging economies. These developments which have tipped the global consumption of oil and gas geographically is expected to continue. Based on a report by the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), oil demand globally is expected to increase to 107 million barrels per day (mb/d) by 2035, from 87 mb/d in 2010. Of this amount, 87% of the growth in oil demand will come from emerging economies in Asia. Malaysia, given its close proximity and increasing economic interlinkages with global energy consumers in Asia such as China and India, is well positioned to reap benefits from the increased demand for oil and gas. In 2012, the export of oil and gas from Malaysia increased to 19.8% of total exports, from 9.3% in 2000. The significant growth reflects the immense contribution of the oil and gas industry to the Malaysian economy, where the oil and gas sector accounted for 20% of GDP in 2012. In terms of contribution to the Government revenue, the oil and gas sector accounts for 35% of the total Government revenue for the period of 2011-2012 through dividend and corporate income tax payments as well as sales tax and export duty collected. The contribution of the oil and gas sector to the economy is also evident from the spill-over benefits to the other services sectors, namely transportation, construction and financial services. Additionally, it is encouraging to note that the Malaysian oil and gas companies have been venturing abroad, with the net investments abroad by oil and gas companies totalling RM 20 billion as at end 2012. Given the importance of the oil and gas sector to the Malaysian economy, the Government has in the past provided various incentives and infrastructure to support this industry. Under the National Key Economic Areas (NKEA), the Government has identified the oil, gas and energy sector as one the main drivers of the economy and has implemented several initiatives under the Economic Transformation Programme (ETP) to further boost the development of this industry. The ETP estimates that oil and gas sector will raise the total gross national income contribution to RM241 billion by 2020 with greater participation by the private sector. This is more than a 100% increase in gross national income received from the oil and gas industry prior to 2009. Recently, as part of the broader effort to diversify the economy and accelerate new sources of growth, the Government has reduced the tax rate for companies involved in the development of marginal oil fields from 38% to 25%, and has also launched the Global Incentives for Trading (GIFT) programme to encourage global companies trading in petroleum and petroleum related products to locate their regional operations to Malaysia. Under the programme, LNG trading companies that sign up before end-2014 is granted 100% income tax exemption on statutory income for the first 3 years of operations while companies involved in other petroleum-related commodities will enjoy a flat rate of 3% income tax. These fiscal incentives are expected to further spur the development of the oil and gas industry in Malaysia. Vibrant financing ecosystem For the oil and gas industry to meet its intended role as a strong contributor to economic growth, it is crucial that the financial sector is able to continuously innovate to better intermediate funds to this industry effectively and efficiently. Although the current financing ecosystem remains supportive to meet the needs of this sector, there is still capacity within the financial system to boost financing to the oil and gas industry. Allow me to share some statistics on current financing granted to this industry, and three observations on how the Malaysian financial system can play a larger role in supporting the growth and development of this industry, particularly to achieve the deliverables envisaged under the ETP. As at end-2012, the total loans financed by the banking sector to the oil and gas industry amounted to RM5.4 billion, an increase of 65.5% from 2011. In fact, financing to this industry has been growing at an average annual rate of 67.7% since 2006. This include financing of activities incidental to extraction of crude oil and natural gas. The domestic bond market has also been mobilising funds for this sector, with outstanding ringgit-denominated bonds amounting to RM 2.1 billion as at end-2012. In terms of foreign currency-denominated bonds issued by the oil and gas sector, it is much larger. For example, the foreign currency-denominated bonds issued by four large oil and gas companies amounted to USD 9 billion as at end-2012. In 2012, the services sector contributed 3.5 % of GDP growth and has emerged as one of the key contributors to growth over the last few years. The prospect for growth for support services activities in the oil and gas sector value chain is expected to expand with the increase in private investment activity and capital spending. The potential for growth in the oilfield and engineering support services for instance, is immense as the need for more technologically-advanced capabilities is required in areas such as enhanced oil recovery and deepwater exploration. Towards this end, it is critical for the financial industry to channel adequate financing for these companies to support their continued growth and expansion. I certainly see room for the financial industry to enhance their capabilities to better anticipate and assess the financing needs of companies providing services in the oil and gas sector. For some of these activities, traditional bank lending may not be the best or even the appropriate solution. Moving forward, there are sizeable opportunities for the financial sector to support the needs of this industry. Firstly, Islamic financial products offer a valuable proposition for enterprises seeking end-to-end Shariah compliant business financing. While Islamic financing today is largely carried out through non-participatory contracts such as mark-up sale (murabahah) and leasebased (ijarah) structures, the wider use of risk-sharing and participatory Islamic finance contracts such as the mudharabah and musyarakah structures in the future will provide a natural financing option to support the growth and development of the oil and gas industry, particularly for the smaller downstream companies. These profit-sharing and loss-bearing contractual agreements between the financier and entrepreneur would provide stronger incentives for both parties to ensure the success of the investment. Experience has shown that Islamic financing has demonstrated that its agile, competitive and cost-effective in funding wide spectrum of complex projects, and I believe that Islamic finance has the capacity to finance the oil and gas sector. Besides financing alternatives mentioned earlier, there are also ample opportunities for the oil and gas industry to raise funds via the sukuk market. In fact, the first issuance of sukuk in the world was by Shell MDS to finance its oil and gas activities in Malaysia in 1990. Since then, many oil and gas companies have explored using sukuk as a mode of financing. One of the key milestones was the first Emas" sukuk amounting to USD1.5 billion that was issued by Petronas in 2009. Emas" is Malaysia's designation accorded to foreign currency denominated bonds and sukuk originating from Malaysia in the global capital market. Today, Malaysia continues to strengthen its position as an international Islamic finance marketplace and remains a key market place for sukuk issuances globally. As at end-2012, the total sukuk issued in Malaysia accounted for 74% of total global sukuk outstanding, with Malaysia having one of the largest US dollar denominated sukuk market worldwide. Secondly, private equity financing can also play an important role in meeting the funding needs of start-ups, small downstream and midstream companies with growth potential in the oil and gas industry. Many of these smaller companies, which are important components in the national oil and gas value chain, may face difficulties sourcing for funds from the banking sector due to their less established track record and experience in the industry. Given that the industry is capital intensive, require highly specialized skill sets and experience and with proportionately higher risk of loss, the financiers to this industry would naturally expect to be more guarded to safeguard their interests. This is where private equity financiers can step in to bridge the gap in funding for these companies. Typically, these private equity financiers would originate from the sector, with specialized skills, know-how and experience to understand the commercial and sustainability aspects of the projects and the risks and challenges of the industry. Thirdly, Malaysia's financial system that has become more regional and international can serve as an important conduit to facilitate business expansion abroad. Domestic businesses that venture abroad now have better access to financing and financial services provided by Malaysian banks with presence abroad. To date, six out of the eight banking groups have presence in 21 countries with substantial overseas operations centred in Southeast Asia. A few of these banking groups have successfully emerged as leading regional players, with an important role in contributing to the overall economic development of the region. With the larger network abroad, Malaysian banks are well positioned to facilitate intra-regional trade and investments, including in the oil and gas sector where the growth prospects of this sector are strong. I pose a challenge for all who are present today, from the oil and gas players, financial services providers as well as consultants to work together to collectively come up with new and innovative funding solutions, taking on board the financial infrastructure that has been built over the years, such as the bond and sukuk markets, project financing and Islamic financing frameworks to finance the further expansion of the industry. Imperatives for the financial institutions moving forward While it is recognised that financial institutions have an important enabler and catalytic role to support economic growth, lessons from the recent global financial crisis have reinforced the importance of managing risk effectively to ensure financial stability and the effective functioning of financial intermediation is continuously preserved. The disproportionate growth of the financial sectors beyond the growth of the real economies has led to severe and profound ramifications to the real economies that would take many years to unwind and recover. At the international level, regulatory reforms are being widely debated, it is expected the outcome would significantly strengthen the regulation and supervision of financial institutions. A clear policy challenge ahead for regulators globally is to construct policy objectives and strategies that not only enhance stability for the future, but also to continuously support economic growth and creation of jobs. In this respect, a few imperatives must be present; supply of credits should not be disrupted especially to trade financing, infrastructure projects, SMEs and small businesses, regulatory and compliance costs should not caused increased in price of credits and regulatory framework should reflect the risks of our banking system, and not of the developed markets. To my mind, there are two fundamental issues for financial institutions to consider when assessing financial relationships with businesses, in particular enterprises in the oil and gas industry. Firstly, something simple should not be turned into something complex or difficult to comprehend. Banking products should be easily understood. There should be increased transparency in financial institutions' business activities, with the growth of financial activities firmly anchored to real economic activities. The recent global financial crisis provides a distinct example of how excessive leverage and exponential growth in financial activities that are detached from the growth of the real economy can become a source of widespread instability. An example, in 2011, combined data from the US NYMEX and ICE EUROPE indicated that the total volume for oil futures traded was 288 billion barrels per year valued at USD28 trillion, in contrast, global oil consumption was only 32 billion barrels per year or USD 32 billion. That means oil futures volume was more than 9 times the total volume of consumption. The reckless use of financial derivatives with oil treated as an asset class in recent years have led to greater speculative activities in the financial markets which in turn have contributed to the increased volatility of oil prices. The excessive speculation has decoupled price movements from the real fundamentals, affecting the growth of the real economy and diverting scarce capital from more productive economic ventures. It is hence clear that such risky and highly leveraged undertakings are not productive and sustainable in the long run. At the core of its intermediary role, the primary purpose of financial institutions is to serve as an enabler and facilitate effective intermediation by matching savings and investments for the purpose of supporting real economic activities and contributing to economic growth. Financial institutions should therefore and ought to continue to focus on serving the real needs of the economy in an effective, efficient and responsible manner. It is my view that ensuring a close link between financial transactions and the real economy is fundamental in promoting economic and financial stability and it is in the interest of the financial institutions' long-term sustainability. Secondly, financial institutions need to continuously enhance their capacity and capability to assess and manage risk. This is particularly important as financial institutions become more exposed to lending to smaller downstream and mid-stream companies in the oil and gas value chain. Traditional methods of credit assessment may need to be reviewed to take into account the innovation and capital intensive aspects of these businesses. The failure of several large and traditionally sound financial institutions during the global financial crisis has provided important lessons on the perils of lack of understanding on the inherent risks of financial products and poor transparency in financial dealings and emphasizing short-term gains against long-term sustainability. Strong risks management standards and practices supported by sound governance structures are hence important pre-requisites for financial institutions to build a profitable yet sustainable business especially as they embark on new areas of growth to support economic activities. Central to this is the enhanced expectations on the Boards of financial institutions, where they have a critical role to play to ensure effective alignment and implementation of risk management policies and capital management strategies that commensurate with the business strategy of the financial institutions. This is even more critical in an environment where prescriptive-based regulations are gradually replaced with principle-based regulations to cater to the increasingly complex financial system. Over the last 35 years, the oil and gas industry has grown by leaps and bounds. This is especially true in the case of Petronas that was formed in 1974 and grown into a company with an assets size of more than RM500 billion with operations in more than 30 countries. The corporation now is also one of the most profitable company in the world. A well-known international business newspaper described Petronas as 'a new seven sisters' reflecting the groups' influence in the oil and gas industry outside the OECD. Petronas's 5-year capital expenditure programmes of RM300 billion [of which 60% would be invested domestically] would significantly transform the oil and gas landscape in the country. The RAPID project value alone is estimated at RM60 billion. There are other downstream projects such as the Fertiliser Plant in Sabah, the Regasssification terminal in Melaka, Lahad Datu and Southern Johore and the Floating LNG Project. With these projects, lies the opportunities, not only for the banks but also for the capital market players. The challenge is whether Malaysian financial services industry have the capacity, the skills and the experience to tap into the opportunities of the ever expanding oil and gas industry. Conclusion There are tremendous opportunities for the oil and gas industry to collaborate with the financial industry to create a vibrant and sustainable financing ecosystem that is conducive for its growth and development. The financial industry at this juncture is undergoing a new trajectory of transformation and growth that will enable it to support Malaysia's transition towards a high value added, high income economy. For the oil and gas players, I also understand that there are heavy priorities ahead in the area of efficient management of funds and resources and strengthened research and development capabilities. These are critical agendas to further sharpen the competitive edge of the industry and to enable it to thrive and flourish at the next stage of development. It is hence timely for continuous dialogue between the oil and gas industry and the financial industry to ensure that the financial needs of the oil and gas industry are adequately met. Deeper understanding of the operations, risks and challenges faced by the oil and gas industry can certainly pave the way for better support from the financial industry. On that note, I wish you an engaging and productive conference.

Title: Speech by  Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB at the Sarawak Financial Carnival
text: Opening Speech by Deputy Governor Muhammad bin Ibrahim at the 7th Muzakarah Cendekiawan Shariah Nusantara Presenter: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB / Venue: Fairmont Hotel, Singapore / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 29 May 2013 / Strong Growth Rate of Islamic Finance globally Lately, the dynamism of the Islamic financial sector globally has undergone transformation. Today, with positive growth in Islamic financial assets in the range of 15% to 20%, we can see a proliferation of more than 600 Islamic financial institutions operating in 75 countries offering a wide range of Islamic financial products. According to the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB), Islamic financial assets are expected to reach USD1.6 trillion in 2012. In addition, the sukuk market also remains the preferred channel for international fund-raising, exceeding USD290 billion with issues in various currencies including the US dollar (USD), Singapore dollar (SGD) and renminbi (RMB). The achievements of the Islamic financial sector today will grow further if driven by effective infrastructure such as legal framework, taxation, operations, especially Shariah governance. Thus, this continuous effort has shifted the Islamic finance sector from an alternative component to a mainstream and competitive component. Although the global Islamic financial sector has begun to reach a level to be proud of, there is still a lot of work to be done. Shariah scholars can help by enhancing regional cooperation in the field of Shariah that is able to enable the Islamic financial ecosystem to cross borders. In other words, the Islamic financial system needs to evolve from 'domestic-centric' to 'regional-centric' and subsequently globalize it as a whole. Muzakarah Cendekiawan Shariah Nusantara as an Interaction Discourse Among the original and main objectives of the muzakarah was to foster close understanding and cooperation among Shariah scholars among the archipelago on the issues of fiqh muamalat and Islamic finance. Through such a platform, new ideas and views among scholars can be generated in an atmosphere of tolerance and respect despite having different cultural, economic and social backgrounds. Every year, through this muzakarah channel, Shariah scholars throughout the archipelago have given high commitment in discussing current issues of Islamic finance. Active interaction among Shariah scholars has inculcated a deeper understanding of several Shariah concepts and contracts including bai' 'inah, tawarruq, mudarabah, musyarakah, ijarah, wa'd and so on. This discussion is not limited to the implementation of all the pillars and conditions only, but all operational, legal and risk management issues are also thoroughly addressed. Based on the sharing of methods and best practices from each country, the muzakarah committees from each country will agree to find a solution to each problem with the presentation of resolutions at the end of the muzakarah. Since the organization of the first Muzakarah Cendekiawan Shariah Nusantara in 2006, the understanding of the main features of Shariah contracts has been greatly coordinated, issues and challenges have been listed and the angles that require research have been focused. The next step is of course by realizing the muzakarah resolutions into the mould of the legal landscape and the local atmosphere of the respective countries. Of course, this important mission demands greater contributions from scholars in ensuring that the implementation is always in line with Shariah requirements. In this regard, Malaysia has taken the approach by leveraging the teaching from muzakarah of Shariah scholars in its new legal formulation, the Islamic Financial Services Law Act 2013 (IFSA). The IFSA brings a new perspective by providing a legal basis for the Islamic financial regulatory framework that reflects the specific characteristics of various types of Shariah financial contracts with their own risk and return profiles. The unique features of this contract are clearly and comprehensively defined, ranging from the process of signing a contract to the dissolution of an Islamic financial institution. This is in line with the idea of enhancing competitiveness and innovation through the diversity of Shariah contracts adopted by Islamic financial institutions. Shariah Compliance Based on Shariah Contract Standards Serial discussion sessions such as today provide a broader perspective on the diversity of the spectrum of Shariah contracts. In my opinion, more emphasis should be focused on the practical aspects and execution of operations. This is very important in minimising legal risks and further strengthening public confidence in Shariah contracts. Although the existing legal framework is already conducive and facilitative in ensuring the smooth running of the Islamic financial market, the fact is that the Islamic financial sector continues to grow rapidly and this requires a futuristic legal framework. The diverse and sophisticated needs of customers have driven innovation, demanding continuous reform over time. In line with the trend of internationalization of Islamic finance, I expect the global pattern of financial and economic integration to also grow rapidly. And this will have a huge impact on the role played by Shariah scholars. Bank Negara Malaysia, in collaboration with the International Shariah Research Academy in Islamic Finance (ISRA) is redoubling efforts towards setting Shariah standards for Shariah contracts adopted in the Islamic financial sector in Malaysia, among them murabahah, mudarabah, musyarakah, ijarah, wadi'ah, istisna', kafalah, wakalah, wa'd, tawarruq, hibah and 'inah. The implementation of this Shariah standard is supported by operational standards in ensuring compliance by Islamic financial institutions. The operating standards take into account the principles of best practices that are in line with Bank Negara Malaysia's aspirations in terms of risk management, governance, disclosure of information as well as legal and accounting processes. The adoption of these standards aims to ensure consistency and certainty in practice as well as to strengthen public confidence in Islamic financial transactions. Shariah Compliance Aspects The main thrust of the Islamic financial sector lies in the Shariah compliance aspect. Adherence to Shariah aspects must be simple, practical and cost-effective. Failure to maintain Shariah compliance will not only expose the Islamic financial sector to credit risk or legal risk alone, but may also result in a risk of confidence in the Islamic financial sector. Therefore, emphasis should be placed on an ongoing basis through the enforcement of legal provisions as well as a competent Shariah governance structure. This combination of legal sets and Shariah governance structures not only enables more effective and planned regulation of Islamic financial institutions, but also serves as an axe to continuous efforts in providing a facilitative legal environment for Islamic financial transactions. In addition to promoting financial stability, the aspect of Shariah compliance has been given significant emphasis and it is one of the main objectives in the regulation under the Islamic Financial Services Act 2013 which was recently passed by the Parliament of Malaysia. This Act further upholds the requirements of regulatory legislation to ensure that the goals, operations, transactions and activities of the Islamic financial system are always in line with Shariah compliance. This includes the establishment of a Shariah Committee at the financial institution level, oversight by the board of directors in ensuring Shariah compliance, internal policies and procedures of financial institutions consistent with Shariah requirements and Shariah audit functions. In addition, the new Act empowers Bank Negara to enforce matters pertaining to Shariah compliance. Harmonization of Shariah Interpretation Differences and various opinions on rulings among scholars are common in the field of fiqh. However, it should not hinder efforts to develop and expand the Islamic financial sector. Rather, it should be considered as an opportunity that should be used to meet the needs of a society operating in various economic systems that have its own characteristics. The difference in views will also result in deeper analysis and evaluation. This phenomenon will also promote healthy ijtihad practices among scholars in addition to the flexibility to test new fields. Therefore, these differences of views should be celebrated by fostering mutual understanding and respect for each other. In fact, the differences of views among Shariah scholars should be exploited by channeling all views and opinions to scientific mediums such as discussion, debate, dialogue, writing and research. Through these programmes, we can see a more active involvement among Shariah scholars to voice and share their views. In my view, in expressing opinions in the interpretation of Shariah, a gap in views that is too significant can have a negative impact from the point of view of enforcement and public confidence in general if not handled properly. Even the gap in differences if not managed properly will limit the real potential of Islamic finance especially in increasing transactions that extend beyond the borders of countries and continents. In this regard, as an effort to reduce the difference of views in the interpretation of Shariah in the field of Islamic finance, we need to examine these differences in several aspects. Let me talk 3 things in this. First: Interaction among Shariah Scholars To ensure that the process of exchange of opinions and opinions can be carried out properly, Shariah scholars need to have an effective channel of interaction. In this regard, this muzakarah should be used by interacting and exchanging opinions not only among Shariah scholars, but also involving other participants such as legal and accounting practitioners. This is to enable different views on an issue to be presented in a complete and comprehensive perspective variation. The development of the Islamic financial system is still in its infancy, many aspects of Shariah have not been resolved. Society in general relies on the views of Shariah members in determining the compliance of products based on Islamic principles. Therefore, individually, Shariah scholars need to know how important the responsibilities and views issued especially those given in general if they are mispronounced or misinterpreted, personal views can cause confusion and undecided polemics. Second: Increased transparency in resolution setting Differences of views are common in the context of the issuance of Sharia law and if the coordination and harmonization of Shariah law cannot be achieved, the spirit of mutual respect should be backed up. In this regard, based on comparative studies conducted by ISRA on differences in views between several countries on Shariah issues in Islamic banking, it was found that the average alignment of Shariah views is 58.3%, especially in the issue of ta'widh, musyarakah mutanaqisah, mudarabah, qard and wa'd mulzim. While the average difference in Shariah opinion is 33.3% including 'inah, kafalah bi al-ujrah and ibra notification in the documentation. Based on this analysis, the differences in Shariah views are still on a minority scale and should not be used as a constant barrier or polemic in our efforts to develop the Islamic financial sector. Therefore, the setting of comprehensive Shariah law should be clear, and based on effective, robust and practical Shariah arguments, and can be implemented in the current situation. The aspect of transparency in every Shariah law is also very important to enable Shariah scholars to fully appreciate and understand the rationale behind the Shariah laws. This method, if practiced with integrity, will reduce the gap in Shariah interpretation among Shariah scholars as well as foster a harmonious understanding. In addition, transparently made arguments can be used by researchers as a starting point to formulate a new point of view. Third: The role of scholars in the writing and translation of scientific books The fast-growing Islamic finance sector, demands constant reforms over time. The institution of scholars today no longer bears the responsibility of being a reference centre alone. In fact, the institutions of scholars have and will play an additional role as the heart of the students to increase their knowledge in the field of Islamic finance. The involvement and contribution of expertise by Shariah scholars in translating Arabic books and writing into the national and English languages can expand the public's understanding of Islamic finance. This effort should also be supported by modern writings and more active involvement in electronic media and print media from time to time. The publication of this research and translation will not only provide a continuous source of Shariah, but also promote a more comprehensive interpretation of Islamic law. History has taught us that 'democratizing knowledge' has brought the civilization of a nation. Cover The current rapid changes and the rapid development of technology will certainly shape the transformation of the Islamic financial sector more significantly and will directly affect the determination of Islamic law on a contemporary issue. Therefore, this change will require the willingness of Shariah scholars to open their minds to generate new ideas as well as mutual respect for each other's views or formulations. The responsibility of interpreting Islamic law will be increasingly challenging, especially in debating the latest matters that require a new perspective, but at the same time are in line with the maqasid Shariah. I am confident that innovation will be generated through an atmosphere of openness of mind and paradigm shift, which is based on a perfect and comprehensive understanding of Shariah. Although the requirements of the Islamic financial legislation of each country are different, our goal is the same, which is the sustainability of the development of the Islamic financial sector. It is hoped that through this muzakarah, Shariah scholars can come up with new ideas that can be put into practice.

Title: Speech at the Launching of the "Register Term Financial Services Industry" Book
text: Governor's Speech at the IFSB 10th Anniversary Dinner Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Grand Hyatt Hotel, Kuala Lumpur Speech/Interview Date: 16 May 2013 Language: English It is my great pleasure to welcome Your Excellencies and distinguished guests to this IFSB 10th Anniversary Dinner, organised in conjunction with the 10th IFSB Summit. Tonight is a landmark celebration of the 10th year anniversary of the establishment of the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB), as we commemorate a decade of milestones and achievements of the IFSB and pay tribute to its members and industry stakeholders that have provided undivided support to the Board. Bank Negara Malaysia is indeed honoured to have the opportunity to host this 10th IFSB Summit, which is exactly ten years since we hosted the IFSB inauguration in November 2002. We are also very pleased to welcome back the Founding Members and many of the industry leaders that witnessed the inauguration of the IFSB. We are very honoured to have your presence at this Anniversary Dinner. It was in the year 2000 that the discussion began on the merits of establishinga dedicated organisation to develop a separate and distinct regulatory framework for the global Islamic finance industry. The aspirations of ten Central Banks and the Islamic Development Bank  was to lay the foundation for the development of a sound and stable Islamic financial system that will pave the way for its successful integration as a viable and credible component of the global financial system. A decade later, the IFSB has build a solid international reputation as a credible standard-setting body for Islamic finance, with the IFSB charting its achievements in increasing regulatory cooperation, encouraging uniformity of regulatory frameworks and enhancing the monitoring of financial risks in the Islamic financial system. The current global landscape of the Islamic financial system, with enhanced stability and resilience that has contributed to the vibrant growth and internationalisation of Islamic finance is a realisation of the aspiration and vision of the IFSB Founding Members. The efforts are largely attributable to the unwavering commitment and dedication of the members of the IFSB that have relentlessly pursued the goals. The increasing support for the IFSB, signified by its continuous growth of membership over the decade would ensure a progressive continuity in the work of the Founding Members. There are now 187 members from 43 jurisdictions. Malaysia is honoured to host the IFSB here in Kuala Lumpur, and is committed to provide full support in the journey to achieve a sound and resilient Islamic financial services industry.
