Strong international cooperation and collective support from member Central Banks and regulatory authorities of the IFSB and global institutions, as well as the strong connectivity with other international standard setting bodies and relevant organisations would ensure continuous close engagements that would allow the attainment of balanced views. The IFSB has had a key role in shaping the global Islamic financial industry, with a decade of achievements that have provided a solid foundation for the progressive growth of Islamic finance that is underpinned with stability. Significant contributions have been made by the IFSB in realising the recommendations in the eight building blocks identified in the Islamic Finance and Global Financial Stability Report 2010, particularly in the areas of prudential standards and liquidity management. It is encouraging that the cross-sectoral prudential standards issued by the IFSB since 2005 have now been implemented in nine countries and more are expected to follow as we progress forward. These standards have taken into account the distinct characteristics and specificities of Islamic finance. The effective implementation of these standards contribute to promoting the soundness and stability of Islamic financial institutions. There has also been strong support by the IFSB for its members to effectively implement the standards through technical assistance that aims to enhance juridictional preparedness in adopting the standards. The initiative of the IFSB to establish the International Islamic Liquidity Management Corporation (IILM) in 2010 is also a major breakthrough in strengthening the liquidity arrangements for the international Islamic financial system, particularly in facilitating more efficient cross-border liquidity management by Islamic financial institutions. The Islamic Financial Stability Forum (IFSF), set up by the IFSB in 2010, is another milestone in strengthening collaborative efforts amongst IFSB members by providing a platform for constructive dialogues for regulators to deliberate on issues relating to financial stability. Seven meetings have been organised since the first IFSF held in Khartoum, Sudan in 2010. A wide range of common issues pertaining to risks to financial stability of the Islamic financial system have been deliberated, all of which have the potential to further solidify global efforts in the areas that will contribute towards safeguarding financial stability. A joint initiative between IFSB and the Islamic Research and Training Institute (IRTI) to develop the Ten-Year Framework and Strategies for the development of the Islamic financial services industry that was released in 2007 has also provided guidance to national authorities in their initiatives to develop Islamic finance within their jurisdictions. A review of the framework was conducted in the recent IFSB-IRTI Roundtable Discussion in Doha and in the Pre-Summit Event of the 10th IFSB Summit two days ago. It is hoped that the assessments would provide further synchronisation to the implementation of the strategies. The IFSB has also paved the way for greater awareness on issues relating to regulation and supervision of Islamic finance through its active organisation of international conferences such as the IFSB Summits, seminars, workshops, meetings and dialogues that have been staged in many countries in different parts of the world. The milestones and achievements of the IFSB in the modern history of Islamic finance is a culmination of various collective wisdoms that have charted the path of the IFSB. In a decade, the IFSB has had the opportunity to be under the stewardship of all nine Founding Members that have successfully held the Chairmanship of the Board. As a Founding Member, it is indeed an honour to witness the crystallisation of ideas that had been envisioned to build a robust and sound Islamic financial system. The journey of the IFSB in these ten years was however not without its challenges. As we continue our journey ahead, the forces of globalisation, financial liberalisation, technological advancements, intensified competition, financial innovation and internationalisation of Islamic finance would create new risks that are more complex and with more profound systemic implications. It has therefore become more demanding and challenging for prudential regulation and supervisory oversight to manage these risks. In cognisant of this increasingly challenging environment, the role of the IFSB remains instrumental and a more robust and forward looking IFSB would indeed contribute towards a more effective policy response. More strategic partnerships would also expand the IFSBs capabilities in research, training and provision of technical assistance, all of which are critical to the development of the industry. Continued and stronger support for the IFSB, including active feedback from members on its Consultative Papers and participation in IFSB related events, as well as greater collaboration and cooperation between the members would further support the work of the IFSB. Consistent implementation of the prudential standards issued by the IFSB also enhances regulatory harmonisation and promotes full adoption of the standards. Of importance is the need for the IFSB to ensure that regulatory standards remain not only adaptive and effective in the changing regulatory environment, but also in riding the evolutionary waves of financial innovation that is prevalent in Islamic finance. Our quest and shared aspirations for financial stability requires concerted efforts on all fronts to foster a resilient and sound global Islamic financial system. The IFSB is an important part of these endeavours and its work remains relevant as we face a time of increasing uncertainties. The strategies identified in the IFSBs Strategic Performance Plan for the year 2013 to 2015 provides the focus for the IFSB to achieve the key result areas charted in the roadmap. I am confident that the IFSB would effectively manage its journey ahead amidst the increasing challenges, with the collective support from its members. Indeed, we look forward to the constructive outcome of the deliberations during this 10th IFSB Summit. We also hope that you will also have the opportunity to experience Malaysia during your time here. On that note, I thank you for your attention.

Title: Welcome Speech at Sabah Financial Carnival - "Using Financial Inclusion to Achieve aspiration to Improve Socioeconomic Status in Sabah"
text: Deputy Governors Speech at the 34th MIBA Annual Dinner 2013 Speaker: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 09 Nov 2013 It is my pleasure to be here at the 34th Annual Dinner of the Malaysian Investment Banking Association (MIBA). As 2013 comes to an end, we can reminisce on the many achievements that we have witnessed. Many of our financial institutions have made significant strides either with the introduction of new products and services, innovation of new financial instruments or expanding their operations beyond our borders. All these are even more admirable, given the uncertain external environment, and a more volatile financial market. In my remarks this evening, I would like to share my thoughts on a number of issues and developments in the financial sector. The Malaysian economy has remained resilient despite the more volatile and uncertain external environment. The domestic financial sector has continued to perform well financially, supported by sound underwriting and risk management practices, strong financial buffers and the timely introduction of macro prudential policies such as responsible financing practices. On the part of the Government, measures announced in the recent budget will further promote conditions for financial stability. Measures to enforce stricter regulations on foreign purchases of property assets and higher Real Property Gains Tax rates will help curb speculative activity and support a stable property market. In the long-run, desired outcomes, such as the reduction in household debt, the wider availability of affordable housing, and the reorientation of the housing market to real demand would create a sustainable and financially stable environment for our banks to operate. The Government is also embarking on various measures to strengthen its fiscal position by adopting strategies to gradually rationalise subsidies, introducing a Goods and Services Tax that would expand the countrys revenue base, and a commitment to reign in on the fiscal deficit to around 3% by 2015. Achieving fiscal sustainability is an important pillar for achieving sustainable economic growth. This is important not only to buffer against period of challenging economic turbulence, but also to secure greater flexibility in re-allocating resources to support the ongoing economic transformation process. A clear commitment and strategies towards more efficient fiscal management will eventually help boost investor confidence in our economic fundamentals and improve the countrys overall business climate. Let me now turn to the developments in the financial and capital markets. The Malaysian capital market has grown significantly in recent decades with a total size of more than RM2 trillion and a debt securities market which has breached the RM1 trillion mark. In Southeast Asia, Malaysia is home to the largest debt securities market and remains among the only two countries with a private debt securities market almost as large as the public debt market. Having achieved this, the next phase of development for the financial and capital markets would be to further diversify our financial market products and services that would support Malaysias vision towards becoming a high income and high value added economy. As part of this endeavour, various public infrastructure projects, such as that for public transportation will need to be funded, while innovation-driven economic activities and start-up ventures in areas such as green technology also require financing. New growth areas such as green technology and start-up ventures promise not only a sustainable path to development, but would open up new opportunities for our entrepreneurs. It would also catapult the country further up the value chain. Funding these new initiatives will require specialised knowledge in various technological fields, such as in green technology. This development also highlights the recent emergence of intellectual property as an important source of competitive advantage. Capacity building in these high-value domains require continuous and intensive learning and knowledge sharing; an area where the banking industry should allocate more attention. With new competencies and specialised knowledge, more market-based innovative financing can be structured, more innovative solutions can be created and more sectors can be served especially those in the new areas of growth. Broad strategies have been outlined in the Financial Sector Blueprint and the Capital Market Masterplan 2 to further accelerate the transformation of the financial system and capital markets to meet the evolving demands of the economy. An important initiative is to increase the efficiency and reduce the cost of financial market transactions in Malaysia. The new Financial Services Act 2013 and the recent amendments to the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009, have incorporated provisions that clarify the contractual rights and obligations, of the counterparties under close-out netting and collateral arrangements, thereby removing uncertainties surrounding the enforceability of such contracts. To further affirm Malaysias status as a netting-friendly jurisdiction, the enactment of a Netting Act was proposed by the Government in the recent budget. This will serve as an important catalyst in the development of the domestic derivatives market. A strong legal framework for close-out netting will also allow for quicker resolutions and lowers the risk of contagion; thus contributing to financial stability and certainty in closing financial transactions. Another focus of ours is to broaden the investor base in the capital market. The ability to mobilise funds from wider sources allows for the creation of a vibrant risk capital ecosystem, allowing innovative and cutting edge technologies to be financed. Greater investor diversity also contributes to financial stability by helping to disperse risks in the capital market. In this respect, we shall continue to review the foreign exchange administration and other regulatory rules that might further reduce the cost of doing business and create a conducive environment for investments in our financial markets. The resilience of the Malaysian capital market and its ability to sustain the wave of sell-offs that have hit emerging economies in the recent past is a testament to our efforts in developing a deep and liquid market facilitated by an efficient pricing mechanism, with a strong and diverse investor base. Going forward, opportunities to further deepen and diversify the investor base of our capital markets will grow as retail participation in the sukuk and bond markets increases. The experience of DanaInfra with its first sukuk issuance earlier this year was most encouraging. Retail offerings such as this allow Malaysians to diversify their investments portfolios. In this way, ordinary Malaysians also have the opportunity to have a direct stake in the construction of an important public project which they will eventually enjoy. I hope that the investment banking fraternity will see this as another new source of funds. While retail investors may well be accustomed to investing in the equity market, many are not familiar with the risk profile and characteristics of fixed income products such as bonds and sukuk. Continuing efforts on the part of the industry to educate retail investors will help to realise the full potential of this market, supporting the eventual issuances of bonds and sukuk across a wider base of potential investors. Malaysia is also a leading international centre for sukuk issuance. We need to maintain this position. We need to continuously deepen and improve the liquidity of the Islamic financial market. In this respect, we have made significant progress. The sukuk market has not only grown in size and volume but also in terms of range of structures and maturities. Just last month, Cagamas Berhad raised RM4.2 billion from its commodity Murabahah sukuk issuance, the countrys largest to date. In the next phase of growth, we hope to see Malaysian investment banks advancing the potential of multicurrency sukuk by leveraging on their expanding investor network and the well-developed supporting market infrastructures. Our global leadership in Islamic finance is also the product of many years of effort in developing a strong operational, regulatory and legal framework. The importance of establishing a strong and comprehensive framework for Islamic finance cannot be stressed enough. In addition to bringing about greater legal and operational certainty, it enables Islamic contracts to be treated with finality and certainty, according to their distinctive features, while preserving the sanctity and validity of transactions consistent with the requirement of the Shariah. The Islamic Financial Services Act 2013 strengthens Shariah governance and compliance by Islamic banks. Issuances of detailed Shariah standards and operational guidelines will further strengthen Shariah governance. The Law Harmonisation Committee that was set up in 2010 has reviewed 17 laws in Malaysia, and identified nine issues to be addressed to enable Islamic financial transactions to be conducted with greater legal efficiency. One of these issues has been successfully resolved for implementation. The infrastructure to deal with potential disputes relating to Islamic finance has also been strengthened. Last year, the Kuala Lumpur Regional Centre for Arbitration (KLCRA) launched the KLCRA-i Arbitration Rules which serve as dispute resolution for Islamic transactions and incorporate the latest international best practices. Translated into six languages, the KLRCA-i Arbitration Rules, is the first set of global rules which embody Shariah principles that can cater to the arbitration needs of the international community. With these enhancements, KLRCA is uniquely positioned to be a preferred arbitration centre for both domestic and international jurisdictions. I hope the banking community will give their full support to this endeavour. Allow me to now turn to the subject of prudential regulations and supervision. Our work to strengthen the regulatory and supervisory framework is aimed at protecting the safety and soundness of financial institutions and the financial system. Our financial system now rests on much stronger foundations that enable an efficient intermediation role by the banks and support sustainable economic growth. We were in a much stronger position at the onset of the 2007/08 Global Financial Crisis and this allowed us to weather the crisis unscathed. That said, we will continue our efforts to further strengthen the regulatory and supervisory framework, ensuring that it remains fit for purpose as our country's financial system and economy develops. The implementation of Basel III and other regulatory reforms in Malaysia are aimed at ensuring that we do not repeat the mistakes made by others. Stronger capital buffers, sufficient liquidity and prudent levels of leverage will ensure that Malaysian banking groups grow in a safe and sound manner and enable them to pursue active domestic and regional expansion expansion. Many have, however, rightly pointed out that there are important implementation considerations that need to be addressed so that domestic bank competitiveness and growth potential are not undermined. We are conscious of this and seek to ensure that the implementation of the reforms and new regulatory framework will not disproportionately affect intermediation activities and increase regulatory and compliance costs. A pragmatic approach to the implementation of Basel III is adopted in Malaysia, with the provision for a gradual implementation of the new rules, taking into account the operational environment of our banking industry. Constructive and active engagements with the industry will enable us to anticipate, and where necessary pre-empt any unintended consequences to the banking industry and the economy. The importance of and demand for sound corporate governance and risk management will increase as Malaysian financial institutions become larger and more complex, operating in increasingly diverse markets. A sound and robust compliance framework should assume an increasingly important role in the governance structure of financial institutions. Within Bank Negara Malaysia, work has commenced to review and strengthen compliance practices in the financial industry. This work will entail proposals directed at, among others, raising the stature and strengthening the independence of compliance functions, while also giving them adequate resources to carry out these responsibilities effectively. We recently commenced industry engagements and expect to detail out specific proposals next year, and we look forward to receiving further feedback and input from the industry. The importance of a robust governance structure and process cannot be understated. The LIBOR fixing scandal and more recent news of exchange rate manipulation have clearly demonstrated the consequences of failure in the compliance framework in some financial institutions. While these events have imposed great costs on the financial industry through legal penalties, the repercussions run deeper as public confidence in the financial industry is eroded by these scandals and could prove more challenging and expensive to restore. Industry associations like MIBA can play an important role in furthering this objective, through its various activities aimed at promoting sound, professional and ethical business practices. In particular, we need to maintain the public trust and confidence, not only in the industry as a whole but in bankers as individuals. As the global economic recovery remains gradual and uneven, the importance of developing a sound strategy for navigating the challenges has never been more apparent. The future will be bright for those who are able to adapt, and agile enough to position themselves strategically. For those who defy change, the future would be bleak as the world would leave them behind. The future is exciting and full of opportunities. This is the future we look forward to, and we hope that MIBA, an industry-driven organisation, would contribute to the process of constantly developing and enhancing a sound, progressive and resilient financial industry.

Title: Speech at the Launching of CGC's i-Guarantee Service Portal
text: Governors Speech for the Launch of the Asian Banking School Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Sasana Kijang Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 18 Dec 2013 It is my pleasure to be here today for the launch of the Asian Banking School and concurrently the designation of IBBM as the Asian Institute of Chartered Bankers. While the Asian banking sector has remained resilient throughout the global financial crisis, Asia has not been immune to the volatility and uncertainty in the global economy and the international financial system. The ongoing international financial reforms also continue to influence our financial sector development. These developments and reforms which have largely focused on strengthening the prudential framework, have significant implications for the talent that is necessary to support these changes. Greater than before, there is now also increased expectations for higher standards of governance, ethics and professionalism in the financial sector. The emergence of a changing configuration of the global economy with a more significant contribution of emerging economies to global growth has also resulted in a change in the operating environment for businesses. In particular, there is now greater cross-border connectivity and interdependence. In our own environment, the demand for the right talent continues to intensify as our nation transitions towards a higher value-added economy amidst these global structural shifts. Business complexities in the years ahead warrant a serious consideration on the quality of the talent in the industry to ensure that the right talent is in place, at the right time with the right knowledge, skills and expertise. The establishment of the Asian Banking School demonstrates the important leadership that IBBM is providing in raising the calibre and dynamism of the talent in the industry. It is envisioned that the Asian Banking School will have a key role in raising the bar for professional certification and capability development that will meet the higher standards and demands of the banking industry. With the demand for talent expected to exceed supply over the next few years in many of the economies in our region, the case for talent development is a strong one. The education programme being offered under the Asian Banking School will therefore be important in the efforts to meet the increased demands for high quality talent for the financial industry. It is estimated that our demand for such talent will rise by 39% in the next ten years. Beyond numbers, it is vital that the financial industry workforce is equipped with the skills needed to support the high growth and niche areas including risk capital financing, wealth management, investment advisory services and foreign exchange management. Core competencies in the fundamental areas of sound financial and business practices will also need to be continuously strengthened. This will require the alignment of the curriculum to keep pace with and to anticipate the market developments and regulatory changes. This is to ensure that the professional qualifications meet the higher standards. As the Malaysian economy continues to transform, it is imperative that the banking industry continues to meet the ultimate objectives for its existence to provide effective financial intermediation and to serve the economy. Improving the efficiency of this intermediation process throughout the entire economic cycle needs to be an important part of this agenda. Key in this process is the role of the reference rate or the base lending rate (BLR). Given the highly dynamic environment, it is important to ensure that this reference rate continues to be relevant. In the recent period there have been indications that the BLR as a reference rate has become less relevant. The BLR has therefore become less meaningful as a basis for the pricing of loans, as the retail lending rates on new loans being offered by the industry are at a substantial discount to the BLR. In general, such a reference rate needs to serve three important roles. First, it needs to allow banks to vary the floating lending rates to reflect changes in funding costs. Second, the reference rate needs to also reflect changes in monetary policy. And third, the reference rate should be a basis for the pricing of retail loans. As part of the review of the interest rate framework, the Bank will issue a consultative paper outlining the new reference rate framework to the industry in early January 2014. This is part of the continued evolution of our financial system to which the industry needs to adjust and progress to ensure that it better serves the economy. Important in capacity building of talent for the industry is to recognise all the changes that are taking place in our environment including the structural changes that are occurring. Included in this is to progressively anticipate the changes in the talent demography. The new generation of knowledge workers will demand for greater empowerment in managing their career development. This will also entail the greater use of technology to deliver the education programmes that will need to be beyond the traditional classroom learning approaches. This will improve learning outcomes and promote outreach and scalability of the Asian Banking School. Concomitant with this strategic move is the transformation of the industry training institute to the Asian Institute of Chartered Bankers. It is envisaged that this repositioning of this institution as a professional body for professionals in the banking industry will enhance its status as a value-adding and more effective membership organisation. This initiative will be very much in line with the aspirations to promote higher standards of professional conduct in the financial services industry through an emphasis on quality and integrity in banking education and practices. Membership in the Asian Institute of Chartered Bankers should signify the observance of the highest code of conduct, a factor that should provide assurance of the professional integrity of the members in performing their role in a manner that engenders public trust and confidence. The launch of the Asian Banking School and designation of the Asian Institute of Chartered Bankers marks yet another milestone in the ongoing efforts to bring the financial services industry education and training landscape to a new level. Both entities are expected to drive and support the transformation of our talent landscape. Coordination by the industry and the other relevant agencies including from other parts of the financial system within the circle of our talent landscape will also be most essential in achieving this transformation. You cannot work in a silo in a highly connected financial system. It is the collective efforts that will contribute towards strengthening and raising the level of professional standards of our workforce in our financial system. The success of this endeavour will depend heavily on the strong support by the industry. With this, let me take this opportunity to commend the Council of IBBM for their commitment, together with that of the Steering Committee, in taking these initiatives forward to its successful fruition. Bank Negara Malaysia supports these endeavours and I have full confidence that these two institutions will rise up to our great expectations in the development of talent for the banking sector, and in raising the level of professionalism in the industry as we advance our financial services sector into its next level of performance in a significantly challenging and changing economic environment.

Title: Speech at the National Congress on Economic Recovery - "The Way Forward"
text: Welcome Speech by Assistant Governor, Encik Bakarudin bin Ishak at the Signing Ceremony of the 'Wholesale Guarantee' Agreement between CGC and OCBC Al-Amin Bank Berhad Presenter: Bakarudin bin Ishak / Venue: Lanai Kijang, Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 10 Apr 2014 / First of all, I would like to congratulate Credit Guarantee Corporation Malaysia Berhad (CGC) and OCBC Al-Amin Bank Berhad on the initiative to launch the 'Wholesale Guarantee' product to further enhance the access of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to financing. Indeed, CGC continues to be the market leader in providing innovative products, according to the needs of SMEs. I am also informed that OCBC has always been active in supporting CGC's schemes for a long time. In 2011, OCBC and CGC collaborated under a portfolio guarantee scheme, involving a total of RM100 million of financing to SMEs. As of February 2014, financing to SMEs by financial institutions has increased by 14% to RM217.4 billion, involving over 700,000 accounts. Financing through CGC's support accounted for 3.4% of the total number of financing accounts to these SMEs. In this regard, financial institutions and CGC should play a more active role in continuing to support SMEs by providing a range of more innovative solutions to meet their financial needs, thus helping these enterprises to grow their businesses. The SME industry is an important growth agent to the country's economy. The industry has great potential to support transformation efforts towards high-income countries. Accounting for 97.3% of the total registered businesses, SMEs are the mainstay of the country's workforce. Their contribution to gross domestic product (GDP) in 2013 was 33.7% and under the SME Master Plan 2012-2020 developed by the National SME Development Council, this contribution is targeted to increase to 41% by 2020. Collaboration between Institutions in the SME Financing Ecosystem Under the Master Plan, access to financing has been identified as one of the key elements to propel SME performance to a higher level. In this regard, the 'Wholesale Guarantee' agreement between CGC and OCBC Al-Amin opens up new opportunities for cooperation among the financial community to support this goal. The 'Wholesale Guarantee' allows financial institutions to share risks with CGC for existing financing, thus providing capital relief to financial institutions. This in turn can increase the ability of financial institutions to provide more financing to SMEs. Malaysia now has a comprehensive SME financing ecosystem, with a number of institutions and mechanisms with specific mandates and expertise and appropriate resources. These include development financial institutions, CGC, Credit Bureau Malaysia as well as infrastructure such as the Central Credit Reference Information System (CCRIS), as well as various loan fund allocations and guarantee schemes. To complement this ecosystem, comprehensive advisory channels are also provided for them. The distribution of assistance throughout the SME development value chain is provided to ensure that the assistance provided is appropriate, appropriate and comprehensive. The collaboration between CGC and OCBC Al-Amin is an example of how institutions in this ecosystem can play a more effective role based on the advantages of their respective capabilities and expertise, in pursuing a common goal of increasing access to financing to SMEs. It is hoped that more such strategic collaborations are established by other institutions to provide more benefits to SMEs. The existence of this comprehensive SME financing ecosystem would be even more meaningful if all parties could optimally leverage it for the common good. In addition to the need for funds for businesses, SMEs, especially those new to business, need certain financial guidance and advisory services. This can help them become more successful and further strengthen their ability to repay the financing taken. Proactive measures by financial institutions to identify SME problem accounts will enable appropriate assistance to be channelled more quickly and effectively. The financial institutions may provide financial advisory services directly or refer these clients to appropriate agencies such as SME Corporation Malaysia, CGC and the like. This will ensure that financial institutions have a stronger and more viable customer base. Prudent Innovation supported by Good Infrastructure and Risk Management Capabilities In the face of the challenges posed by this increasingly challenging business environment, all parties need to take a more innovative approach to confront it. The SME industry should improve processes and change the business management model more effectively. This can be implemented through automation processes, to reduce business costs, increase productivity and thus improve the financial performance of the company. Financial institutions also need to understand how SMEs operate in this challenging era. The ability to assess the viability of a business or project should be strengthened to new, more appropriate methods. This is important, especially if it involves SME applicants who are venturing into new fields and that involve activities that have an impact on value added. The introduction of a good product in accordance with the requirements of the market will allow this product to develop on its own. Financial institutions and SMEs can take lessons from agent banking initiatives as an example of innovation and close cooperation between stakeholders, which has led to the achievement of goals in a short time. The initiative, introduced in 2012, aims to enhance the level of financial inclusion in Malaysia. Initially only 46% of the total mukims in Malaysia had access to financial services. In less than 2 years, this percentage has increased to 93% by the end of 2013. To date, there is a network of more than 5,000 bank agents and has registered over 1.4 million transactions amounting to RM1.6 billion. The success of this agent banking initiative is due to the fact that it meets the needs of customers who were previously marginalised from financial services. Close cooperation between financial institutions and third-party agents such as retail outlets, oil stations and post offices, making it easier for users to access banking services. This initiative also benefits bank agents as their business sales also increase due to the increase in customers to their business premises. However, innovation should be accompanied by the improvement and strengthening of infrastructure as well as more prudent risk management capabilities. This will allow the goal to be achieved more effectively and the benefits continue. Finally, once again congratulations to CGC and OCBC Al-Amin on this initiative and hope that this programme will run smoothly and successfully attract more interest among financial institutions to participate.

Title: Remarks at the ASEAN Risk Conference 2017 - "Perspectives and Issues in Navigating the Development of the Malaysian Financial Market"
text: Speech by Deputy Governor at the 2014 Bank Negara Malaysia Governors Cup Financial Institutions Competition Presenter: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB / Venue: Bank Negara Malaysia / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 26 June 2014 / Alhamdulillah, I am grateful to the Divine Hadrat as we were able to gather together this evening to complete the 2014 Governors Cup Speech Final Prize Presentation Ceremony. For the first time, this year's competition was held at Bank Negara Malaysia. I would like to express my appreciation to Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka and the Secretariat of the Competition for their joint efforts in organising this competition which is now in its sixth year. This competition is a language initiative of Bank Negara Malaysia under the Secretariat of the National Language Movement of the Financial Sector. The annual competition was organised to uncover the talents and skills of the employees of financial institutions in the field of public speaking. The importance of language in the mastery of knowledge and the development of civilization This evening I would like to share my views on the importance of language in the mastery of knowledge and the construction of a civilized society. Indeed, language is an important introduction in the search and dissemination of knowledge. Therefore, there is no doubt that language activities such as public speaking, debate and translation are among the important activities that support the effort. Even since time immemorial, the development and progress of a civilization depends a lot on the democratization of knowledge derived from the sources of previous civilizations. The knowledge of these various civilizations, usually a foreign language, was later translated into a language understood by the local community. Indeed, a language will be 'lingua franca', a language of association or relationship if it is a language that is able to expand and expand knowledge. Language will only live and become important if it is the cause of knowledge that can develop and branch out the capabilities of the mind. For example, in Baghdad in the era of Islamic civilization, the movement for the translation of books from previous languages, especially Greek, was carried out on a large scale in the 9th and 10th centuries. As a result of this translation effort, civilization in the Middle East has acquired knowledge that in turn has sparked an era of progress. Even the advancement and sophistication of technology in medicine, astronomy and mathematics today is widely contributed by Islamic civilization1. In Uzbekistan, Al Farghani has booked a risalat on the main astronomical tool, strolable, which gained widespread reading in medieval Europe. This risalat is about the knowledge of calculating the degree of circumference of the earth. Among the readers of the risalat was Christopher Columbus, the first European said to have reached the American continent. Many more interesting examples. Omar Khayyam, among others, discovered the theory of Kubic equalization geometry, identifying and dividing 14 types of "third-degree equations" and parallel theory (parallel theory) that became popular after 700 years after its introduction. While the Roman empire dominated Europe, Latin had developed in Europe and became the language of knowledge. European universities use Latin as the medium of instruction of knowledge rather than a widely used language. As a result, knowledge and progress only hover among the few European elites who master Latin while the people are still ignoring knowledge and retreating. It is only when knowledge is conveyed in the indigenous language of its people that it can be understood, harnessed and widely disseminated. It was through the democratization of knowledge that the outbreak of the European industrial revolution in the 18th and 19th centuries2. Similarly, the process that takes place in Malaysia, if the Malay language is to be accepted and adopted and disseminated quickly and effectively, it must be a language of knowledge and have economic value. It is the language that drives the knowledgeable people that will build the country's economic prosperity and further entrench and build the Malaysian nation. From this perspective, efforts to translate books from foreign languages should be intensified with the objective of mastering and expanding the source of knowledge and thus producing a confident, visionary and competent society. Looking back on the days of the Malacca Malay civilisation, the Malay language ranks highest in the region as it is used in trade and economic activities with regional countries3. In those days, the Malay language had economic value as it was used as a 'lingua franca' for trading. As noted in the historical fold, the success and progress of civilization would not have been possible if the people at that time could not convey and develop their knowledge system through the use of the Malay language.4. In this context, I believe the wider use of the Malaysian language by financial institutions can help the client segment of financial institutions who are more comfortable communicating in this language. It will also enhance and expand the customer's understanding of the products and services offered by financial institutions. I believe in organising this competition as one of the noble efforts for the dissemination of knowledge related to finance and banking. Bank Negara Malaysia has also given great commitment in translation efforts to disseminate information and knowledge as well as to cooperate in organising seminars on Islamic finance especially. Several translation initiatives and seminars have been conducted, 1. Translation of Arabic books to enrich the collection of reference materials for the field of Islamic banking and finance: On the awareness of the importance of enriching the treasures of knowledge through translation efforts, Bank Negara Malaysia together with the Institute of Islamic Banking and Finance Malaysia have taken the initiative to translate the muktabar books from Arabic. Among the books that have been translated and published include the Book of Qawaid al-ahkam by Imam Izzaldin Abdul Salam, the Book of Radd al-Mukhtar written by Ibn Abidin and the Book of Madkhal fiqh al-am written by Sheikh Mustafa Ahmad Zarqa. 2. Publication of Shariah Resolutions in Islamic Finance: This publication is a compilation of all Shariah resolutions produced by the Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia to deepen the understanding of Shariah interpretation and the consideration of fiqah legislation for the Shariah decisions. It turns out that the response to this competition is getting more and more encouraging. Starting with only 17 participants in 2009, the number of participants increased every year. In fact, this year alone the number increased to over 80 participants (2013: 51 people). What is even more interesting is that the participants of this competition reflect the plural Malaysian race. Well done and congratulations to all the participants who will compete and show their oratorical talents with great enthusiasm as well as delivering thoughtful and thorough arguments. I hope that efforts to increase the use of the Malaysian language in financial institutions will continue and all financial institutions will support language activities at the national level. And once again thank the DBP for working together to make the event a success today. In closing, I would like to thank all those who have been directly and indirectly involved in the organization of this oratory competition. Thank you. 1 Al-Hassani (2012). 1001 Inventions: The Enduring Legacy of Muslim Civilisation. Washington D.C.: National Geographic. 2 Brown (1986). The Wisdom of Science. United Kingdom: Cambridge University Press. 3 Barnard. (2004). Contesting Malayness: Malay identity across boundaries, Singapore: Singapore University press. 4Andaya & Andaya. (1984), A History of Malaysia, London: Palgrave Macmillan.

Title: Remarks at the Kijang Emas Scholarship Award Ceremony for High Achievers - "Growing Our Nation's Best"
text: Deputy Governors Keynote Address at the Islamic Finance Education: Global Roundtable Discourse Speaker: Wan Mohd Nazri Wan Osman Speech/Interview Date: 21 Aug 2014 Venue: Sasana Kijang Language: English Firstly, I would like to extend the apologies of Deputy Governor, Dato' Muhammad bin Ibrahim, who could not make it to today's roundtable discussion. I am honoured to be here on behalf of the Deputy Governor and be given the opportunity to share my thoughts on the subject of talent enrichment. Our efforts today in developing high-quality and comprehensive academic curriculum standards for Islamic finance are very timely and extremely important. I wish that today's roundtable sessions draw valuable opinions and incite fruitful discussions on ways to enhance the study programme for Islamic finance. Let me start by giving two broad contexts. Painting the landscape that we have today, we can see a number of key trends shaping the banking sector that signals specific talent needs. This includes the evolving regulatory requirements, radical shift in technology, emphasis on risk management and demographic changes that prompt product innovation for new sets of customers. To ensure that the industry remains competitive and innovative, it needs individuals who are well-versed with regulatory treatments, technology-savvy and inventive as potential differentiators in the banking business. Hence, getting the right talent is not only critical in responding to these changes, it is an imperative especially for new developing industry like Islamic finance. This is the first broad context. Let me share some statistics. It is anticipated that the overall Malaysian financial sector requires about 200,000 workforces throughout the years until 2020. As at end 2013, the Islamic financial institutions employ approximately 17,621 employees, which constitute around 11% of the total workforce in the overall financial sector. These numbers reflect talent demand and this is only for Malaysia. However, in our effort to meet this demand, we must not forget to place utmost importance on quality. Only quality talent would drive the industry's advancement. This is the second broad context. These bring us to the essences of my remarks. To get to our desired outcomes, we must begin with an end in mind. What is the quality we aim to achieve? I would like to highlight three distinctive characteristics of high-quality talent that we want to secure for Islamic finance. Firstly, we need talent who can cater to the needs of the industry, whom will be sought after by the Islamic financial institutions. Secondly, we need talent that can contribute breakthrough ideas, ones whom will spark innovation and capable to envision and chart the future direction of the industry. And thirdly, we need talent who are solidly grounded on conceptual understanding and contemporary industry knowledge, ones who can carry the industry's transformations. Our ability to produce the right kind of talent will be the key determinant in charting the future path of Islamic finance. The question is how? Today, I would like to touch on five key actions that we can undertake to unlock the potential of high-quality talent. Get the best brains for the Islamic finance programmes First and foremost, to ensure we supply the right individuals responsible for transformations in the industry, we need to attract the brightest minds. With continuous evolution, the industry demands more product innovation and development in supporting new growth areas for Islamic finance. Thus, it is paramount for the Islamic financial institutions to secure talent with an innovative mindset. Therefore, the search has to begin as early as the admission of students into universities. Universities should seek not only the capable students, but the best students available out there as the first step to unlock the potential for high-quality talent. In order that we recognise one when we see one, we must do it right from the entry point. Academic entry requirements must be set high with the aim to gather a strong pool of brainpower that can be educated, suited to the needs of the market. I believe when we impose stronger controls at the entry points, we will enable the industry to get access to potent human capital that are able to produce revolutionary ideas to cater to the changing financial environment. When Islamic finance is equipped with striking intellectual capacity, it heightens the credibility of the industry and safeguards its prominence. Breeding versatile talent to enhance employability Onto my second point, as soon as we have secured the brightest students, we need to harness these abilities through providing a holistic curriculum. As job complexities intensify, we require talent with higher skill sets to navigate the financial world. We need to challenge their curious minds and sharpen their skills. On this note, it is necessary that the Islamic finance curriculum of the university must be embedded with skills that will enhance graduates' employability. Among the competencies that are highly sought after are integrated and analytical thinking skills, technical skills with digital capabilities and the ability to deal in crisis conditions. With these skills ingrained in the curriculum structure, we get to nurture the desired talent from the very start. It is also fundamental to inculcate strong values of ethics and integrity that underpin Islamic finance among the students. Teach mutual respect from the very beginning through educating the students with all Mazhab teachings. The differences of opinions should not be seen as a hindrance to the development of Islamic finance, but an opportunity to meet the needs of diverse communities. Open their minds, let them explore Islamic finance from all angles. In this way, students get to appreciate the intellectual differences and value the flexibility in rooms of differing opinions. We don't want to only produce talent that are equipped with the know-hows, but also build ethical characters that are able to make good moral judgements. This is how we breed versatile talent to cater to the high needs of the industry. Establishing a conscious learning environment Thirdly, in establishing a learning environment that is conscious of the emerging issues that exist in our world today, the faculty plays a focal role. While theory-based education is integral, I believe the connection between classroom learning with the real world is a strong stimulant to knowledge acquisition. Therefore, the academic staff must be conversant with contemporary issues to be able to highlight this meaningful link to the students. This includes more active participation by the faculty in providing feedback to consultation papers from the financial regulators, for example Bank Negara Malaysia, which promotes greater appreciation towards regulatory developments relating to the financial sector. This will elevate the quality of teaching that takes cognisance of the external business environments, including international developments and social, legal and political trends. Along these lines, students will be trained with the ability to contextualise circumstances in accordance with current events. By raising the level of awareness, we provide them with a foretaste of the reality that is necessary for the syllabus to remain practical. Building a strong linkage with the industry Fourthly, we need to build a strong linkage with the industry to minimise potential mismatch of human capital needs. Nurturing the best talent for Islamic finance is a shared responsibility between the academia and the industry as a whole. The supply of talented graduates must resolve the scarcity of talent that may impede the progress of Islamic finance. For this reason, close partnership between the two parties is key towards bridging the gap between talent upbringing in institutions of higher learning and the industry's requirements. In addition to joint working groups between the banks and the academia in tailoring the curriculum to the needs of the industry, greater engagement between them is also useful to maintain the close link. For example, a structured periodical interactive discussion with bankers provides students with insights and increased exposure of the real banking world. This is particularly beneficial in enhancing students' exposure and marketability. Joint research between the banks and the institutions of higher learning would be another avenue. I am certain the bankers would welcome to work together with the academia. Creating eminence of Islamic finance business school Finally, we need to raise the quality of Islamic finance business schools. To date, in Malaysia alone, we have over 30 domestic institutions of higher learning that offer academic courses relevant to Islamic finance. In raising the quality of these education providers and in promoting the highest standards for talent development in the Islamic financial sector, these institutions should consider seeking internationally-recognised and specialised accreditation, in addition to the mandatory accreditation. In the future, creating a single league table that ranks the Islamic finance business schools according to specified criteria and indicators will further create eminence of the Islamic finance education institutions. The league table will serve as the first benchmark to assess the performance of the business schools, based on the scoring of its wide-ranging qualities and educational offerings. In other respects, this ranking system will spur competition between universities and colleges in terms of promoting high-quality courses and programmes. What we strive for is excellence in our Islamic finance education offerings so much so that the quality of our graduates is selfevident. When we set to achieve this goal, our learning institutions will one day stand side by side with other prestigious universities in the global university league. Conclusion To conclude, let me emphasize that collaboration among all of us here is key. While we are addressing the talent shortage, we need to orchestrate our effort in producing high-quality talent for Islamic finance. As the industry is maturing and there is more interconnectivity between business functions, the call for expertise with well-rounded skills is even more demanding. That is why quality over quantity is key to ensure we hit the primary target set for human capital development. I believe when you are out of quality, you are out of business. But I also believe, if we are committed to drive this together, the talent in Islamic finance will be the centre of excellence. Thank you.

Title: Speech at the Opening of the 14th Muzakarah of Syariah Scholars of the Archipelago
text: Assistant Governor's Speech at the Launching Ceremony of the Prudent Financial Month "Financial Education For All" Presenter: Mr. Abu Hassan Alshari Yahaya / Venue: Sasana Kijang, Bank Negara Malaysia / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 13 Oct 2014 / I am very grateful and grateful to the Confederation of Consumer Associations of Malaysia (FOMCA) for this invitation for me to officiate the launch of the Prudent Financial Month 2014 today. This is the fourth year of the FOMCA's prudent financial month. I would like to express my appreciation to all parties who have been involved in this organization for their continued commitment and efforts in improving the financial prudence among consumers. In the past year, I have shared several important initiatives in benefiting consumers, namely financial education in general, consumer protection through supervisory and enforcement actions, enshrining existing laws and measures to address current issues such as lending practices by more responsible financial institutions. In line with the theme of this year's Wise Financial Month, "Financial Education For All", I would like to emphasize the importance of a person's in-depth financial education at every age. This year's theme coincides with the challenges facing consumers today. As you know, Malaysians are now facing the challenge of a rising cost of living, lacking enough savings for retirement and high household debt. According to statistics from the Employees Provident Fund (EPF), at the end of 2013, 69% of EPF contributors aged 54 had savings of less than RM50,000. Such savings can only last for five years, assuming a person spends RM800 a month. This is alarming given the ever-increasing cost of living. Meanwhile, household debt accounted for 86.7% of the gross domestic product. Although the increase in household debt has, in the near future, risen at a slower pace, at 11.5% in 2013 compared with 13.8% in 2012, household debt still needs to be given due attention to ensure that consumers do not have excessive debt that could be detrimental to them. 1. A highly skilled and knowledgeable workforce can increase income and guarantee well-being in life How to achieve a strong financial position? First, we need to have an adequate and stable source of income. In general, educated, skilled and highly knowledgeable individuals have advantages for better job opportunities and high incomes. One of the initiatives under the Economic Transformation Programme (ETP) is to produce a highly skilled workforce. This development is the latest development in Malaysia where a more skilled workforce needs to be emphasized with the need to increase income based on higher levels of productivity and competitiveness. The high level of income depends on the ability of employers and employees to continuously improve performance and productivity, reduce costs and always achieve better value-added levels over time. In this context, the need for employers to be more competitive, efficient and have highly trained and high-tech employees is very important. As for the employees, they need to have high talents and skills, which must be improved from time to time. Therefore the use of technology needs to be applied and the emphasis on productivity and value added is a key aspect. All the workers are also consumers. Productive and advanced workers also form visionary, disciplined, progressive and resilient consumers. The main pillar that can help all employees and consumers to be at a better and more sustainable level is education. The level of education must be more comprehensive, accurate and appropriate to the needs of the current society. This is so that the education can benefit the community to deal with daily life with more confidence and orderly. My speech this morning will focus on continuing financial education for all walks of life. To ensure that our society is equipped with comprehensive financial education, various initiatives through the application of continuous financial education at all ages, as early as children who have not attended school to retirees, have been introduced by various parties. The goal of stimulating financial literacy and empowering consumers is the same for various parties including the Government, statutory bodies, non-governmental bodies (NGOs), consumer associations and the private sector. The parties have implemented various initiatives to equip consumers with the knowledge to adopt a prudent financial culture. Here, I would like to share in more detail the various financial education initiatives that are being implemented by these parties. Financial education as an important life skill begins at an early age (children and adolescents) As outlined in the Financial Sector Plan 2011-2020, emphasis is placed on implementing elements of financial education in the school ecosystem. To achieve this, Bank Negara Malaysia in collaboration with the Ministry of Education Malaysia is integrating the financial education elements in the primary and secondary school curriculum in stages. Among the elements of prudent finance are the role of money, sources of income and career, financial management and planning, savings and investment, credit and debt management and insurance coverage. An element of financial education was introduced for third-year pupils in 2013, which is one year ahead of the date of targeted implementation. The element of financial education has been included in the Malay Language and Mathematics subjects. Furthermore, during the year, the elements of financial education were applied to the subjects of Mathematics, Bahasa Malaysia, English and Moral Education Year Four. The adoption of financial education for another school year is being implemented in stages. As for secondary schools, it will be introduced in 2017. In addition, financial education was also introduced as a compulsory module for students of the fifth semester of the Vocational College under the Diploma vocational Malaysia program. A trainee training programme (Train the Trainers) was implemented to enhance the skills and confidence of 100 main trainees at the Institute of Teacher Education in preparation for training trainee teachers at their respective Institutes of Teacher Education. The lecturers of the Vocational College also undergo financial education courses to be presented to the students involved. To complement and support financial education initiatives in schools, Bank Negara Malaysia has reviewed and enhanced the role of financial institutions under the Adoption Schools Programme. The financial institution will serve as a subject matter expert to provide advice to teachers on the technical aspects of financial management, including on financial products and services. This will enhance the effectiveness of the delivery of financial education delivered within the school. For the future, Bank Negara Malaysia will continue to work with the Ministry of Education Malaysia in ensuring the smooth application of the financial education element in the school curriculum. Among the areas of cooperation that will be carried out include applying the element of financial education in the training curriculum for teachers to further enhance the ability and confidence of the teachers in delivering financial education knowledge in schools. Empowering prudent finances for adults at all stages of life As you are aware, the Credit Counseling and Management Agency (AKPK) plays an important role as the leading agency to drive financial education initiatives specifically for adult financial users. With the aim of creating a financially literate society, the financial education initiatives under AKPK are designed based on four stages of adult life, namely at the level: higher education - where financial education is applied as a learning module in public and private Institutions of Higher Learning (IPT) (18 - 25 years); admission of the realm of employment - financial education is held at the place of work (20 - 30 years); starting and building a family life (25 - 45 years); And retirement ( 40 years). In formulating modules for adults, AKPK has done a thorough study and modified the programme taking into account the needs and level of financial awareness for each group level. The content of each module includes cash flow management, loan base, debt management, investment base, credit card usage and retirement. The financial education programmes under AKPK are as follows: 1. Personal Financial Management; POWER! - Management of Your Ringgit Money (through workshops and online education portals); Public Talk; And Finance Clinic for the target group To ensure the continuity of financial education, AKPK also organised a Trainee Training (Train the Trainers) programme at IPT as well as government and private organizations. For your information, any group or organization that is interested in obtaining AKPK's services through these programmes, please apply directly through its website (online booking). AKPK is ready to organize the programme applied according to the needs of the group or organization that applied. To address the issue where most Malaysians do not have enough savings for their old age, Bank Negara Malaysia will work with AKPK and EPF to develop a financial education module for retirement. From 2011 to August 2014, a total of 531,890 financial users have benefited from AKPK's financial education programmes: 268,385 (50.4%) participants attended personal financial management programmes, Public Talks and Financial Clinics; 194,520 (36.6%) participants attended the POWER!. The majority of the participants were government and private employees. Financial Education Long-Term Plan Over the next three years (2015 - 2017), AKPK will focus more on the "Entering the Realm of Work" as well as "Starting and Building a Family Life" segment. Both segments will involve adults between the ages of 20 to 45. This group represents 52% of the entire adult population in Malaysia, while the "Higher Education" and "Retirement" segments represent 10% and 20% respectively. While it will continue to be challenging, the implementation of future financial education initiatives is seen as more strategic and structured. AKPK will further enhance cooperation with government agencies, the private sector and non-profit organizations in its implementation. The financial education delivery mechanism for the "Higher Education" segment will be expanded through technology applications such as smartphone applications and online learning (online education portals). In addition, AKPK will also evaluate the effectiveness of the learning module and the entire program as well as an assessment of the changes in the behavior of the participants of the program. For this purpose, some target groups will be selected voluntarily to oversee their expenses within three to six months. 2. Financial education for the target group Financial education of rural communities continues to be the focus of Bank Negara Malaysia Sensitive to the problems faced by rural communities who are struggling to obtain information, knowledge and advisory services on banking and insurance, Bank Negara Malaysia has expanded its financial education initiatives for these target groups throughout the country through the LINK mobile service or known as Mobile LINK in collaboration with AKPK and financial institutions. In addition, Bank Negara Malaysia has also been working with FOMCA and the Penang Consumer Association (CAP) to provide financial education to rural communities in Sabah and Sarawak. Through this programme, participants were also briefed on financial services, financial crime and financial management. This programme aims to raise public awareness on prudent finance so that they are more careful in making decisions and managing their finances. In addition, the programme also informs the latest developments on financial crimes such as get-rich-quick schemes so that consumers understand the modus operandi of financial fraud and not get caught up in such schemes. More than 45,000 participants from 250 mukims nationwide have benefited from this programme. Financial education for groups exposed to household debt risk In an increasingly challenging situation with the rising cost of living and in desperation, there are some communities who borrow money without considering their ability to pay off their debts. They will be stuck with the debt burden when they are unable to pay off the loan repayment. When a person is no longer able to carry their debt burden, this situation will cause problems not only for the individual but the immediate people. In this regard, Bank Negara Malaysia in collaboration with AKPK has taken the step of developing a financial education programme specifically for those who are most likely to be exposed to this problem. Currently, government employees are the main target group for the program. Participants will be briefed on financial management (including debt management), financial consumer rights and various channels of advice and complaint resolution are provided. Since its implementation in 2012 to date, more than 22,000 government employees from various agencies have benefited from this programme. Participation of the private sector through strategic cooperation in financial education Apart from organising the Prudent Financial Month, FOMCA also collaborated with several financial institutions in Malaysia and the Malaysian Deposit Insurance Corporation (PIDM) to formulate several financial education initiatives specific to the target group. This strategic partnership is part of the "Corporate Social Responsibility" of the financial institutions and PIDM. Among the programmes in question are: My First Ringgit or My First Ringgit which was introduced in 2011 by ERA Consumer Malaysia with the support of FOMCA and Citi Foundation under Citibank Berhad. This program is a financial education program targeted at kindergarten children aged 4 to 6 years. It aims to educate them on the importance of money as well as to foster good financial habits among the younger generation. My Financial Coach or My Financial Coach with the support of Allianz Malaysia Berhad insurance company. This programme focuses on primary school year 6 students under the Bank Negara Malaysia Adoption School Programme with the aim of ensuring the continuity of prudent financial practices among youths. The program is run by volunteers appointed by Allianz Insurance. Through this programme, students are given exposure on the differences between needs and needs as well as increasing their financial decision-making capabilities. Since the beginning of the programme in 2012 to date, a total of 3,515 students from 35 schools have been trained and benefited from the programme. FOMCA is working with PIDM briefing on Financial Consumer Protection focusing on target groups. During its four years, a total of 59 programmes were carried out with the participation of 4,087 participants from all over the country. Through this programme, the public will be briefed on two important matters, namely the Deposit Insurance System and the Takaful and Insurance Benefit Protection System. FOMCA has been appointed by PIDM to provide this explanation. Being financially literate is one of the key keys to achieving life success and recognising its importance and impact on society, the Securities Commission also took the initiative to inculcate money management skills among young Malaysians. Among the financial education programmes implemented by the Securities Commission are: Kids & Cash - aimed at children aged 10 to 12 years, with the goal of inculcating a culture of financial management among them. The program educates children on the importance of saving money, wise spending habits and how to plan finances at an early age. Teens & Cash  targeted at teens aged 13 to 17. The main objective of this programme is to educate them on the fundamentals of financial management and wise investments. The content of the program covers the topics of budgeting and savings, identifying needs and wishes and basic knowledge of investments. Smart Managing Money - aims to create awareness and improve the skills of the adult community on financial planning, smart investment and avoid being deceived by illegal investment schemes. Participants of this programme will be exposed to the importance of planning finances and investments wisely, proper financial planning techniques, the basics of smart investments and the characteristics of illegal investment schemes. I am sure that there are more and more programs implemented by various parties that I have not had the opportunity to express one by one. I am sure that these other programmes are also very useful and enable more members of the community to be exposed to knowledge and financial management. Here, I would like to express my appreciation to all parties involved in providing the financial education. 3. Strengthening support infrastructure As I shared earlier, there are various financial education programs in the country and it covers all walks of life. This is the result of a multi-party collaboration over the past five years in giving priority to financial education for all financial users. However, how effective are these programmes in improving the financial capabilities of consumers and influencing their financial management practices? Effective implementation of financial education supported by the Financial Education Assessment Framework To ensure the implementation of sustainable and effective financial education initiatives and to produce results as expected, Bank Negara Malaysia has drafted a Financial Education Assessment Framework in 2013. There are three components outlined under this Framework which are: In detail, this Framework enables Bank Negara Malaysia to assess the impact of financial education programmes on the overall level of financial capabilities and literacy of the Malaysian population. The results of this assessment are also used to continuously improve existing financial education programmes. To realise this plan, a review of Financial Capabilities and Inclusions will be conducted in the month to November 2014 nationwide. The purpose of this survey is to obtain data and information on the level of financial capability and inclusion of the Malaysian community. A random sample of 3,000 respondents will be interviewed from house to house. The respondents covered all walks of life in Malaysia. 1. Benchmarking the level of money literacy and capabilities of Malaysian financial users; Evaluate the effectiveness of financial education initiatives carried out; And The study of behavior and aspects of financial consumer risk. Comprehensive access of reliable and up-to-date financial education information With the increasing momentum of financial education in schools and for adults, steps are also being taken to improve the infrastructure needed to support financial education initiatives. This is done by further improving users' access to interactive financial information and management tools. As social media becomes more accepted in the community, Bank Negara Malaysia has implemented communication initiatives to interact with financial users through this medium. As a result, Bank Negara Malaysia's Facebook fans as of October 2014 have increased to 39,320 (2013: 28,965) and Twitter followers have increased to 44,500 (2013: 34,936). To interact with the younger community, Bank Negara Malaysia is now actively using videos to educate them on financial matters. In collaboration with the Royal Malaysian Police, Bank Negara Malaysia leverages the YouTube channel to disseminate information about financial crimes. Bank Negara Malaysia will also introduce a new information channel through a smartphone app known as "BNM Mobile Apps" to further enhance users' access to information and interactive financial management tools. This initiative is in line with the development of communication technology where most users currently use their smartphone applications as a medium for information. BNM Mobile Apps will be developed to expand the reach of accurate and up-to-date communication and information delivery to financial users, while also helping users understand financial matters. This application is complementary to Bank Negara Malaysia's existing information delivery channels through Bank Negara Malaysia's corporate website and social media. 4. Coordination and implementation of integrated financial education initiatives at the national level under the Financial Education Network With the awareness of the importance of expanding the reach of financial education to all segments of society, stakeholders have conducted various financial education programmes or through strategic collaboration between stakeholders as previously shared. In this regard, Bank Negara Malaysia looks forward to working with stakeholders to produce a coordinated national strategy to improve the financial literacy of all levels of society. Bank Negara Malaysia also hopes that from this strategy, the initiatives that will be formed can be better aligned and overalled among stakeholders in a more comprehensive, strategic and high-impact manner. To achieve more sustainable goals in implementing financial education programmes by various parties, Bank Negara Malaysia will form a national Financial Education Network to facilitate more systematic and integrated cooperation. 5. Direction forward - Bank Negara remains committed to Bank Negara Malaysia's financial education agenda committed to continue to give priority to enhancing the financial capabilities of consumers through continuous financial education at all levels of society. However, this effort would not have been successful without the support and cooperation of all parties involved. Therefore, the responsibility for these financial education initiatives should be shared by all stakeholders. With a comprehensive education to produce a skilled and knowledgeable workforce and financial education initiatives, Bank Negara Malaysia believes financial users will be more knowledgeable and more responsible in their financial affairs and thus will be able to manage their finances better. We all hope that consumers will always foster a culture and prudent financial management practices for their future as well as better and more secure future generations. Finally I would once again like to thank FOMCA for inviting me to launch this Prudent Financial Month program. Hopefully, the program can be run smoothly and successfully. With the phrase Bismillahirahmanirrahim, I am pleased to officiate the launch of Prudent Financial Month 2014.

Title: Closing Speech at the 2017 Financial Carnival
text: Deputy Governors Speech at the Launch of "Ombak: Breath of Life" Exhibition Speaker: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB Venue: Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery, Sasana Kijang Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 13 Nov 2014 Terlebih dahulu saya ingin mengalu-alukan kehadiran tuan-tuan dan puan-puan ke majlis perasmian pameran lukisan oleh seorang artis yang terkenal di rantau ini. Hasil karya beliau adalah dikenali ramai peminat-peminat seni di Negara ini. Lukisan yang berada di belakang saya ini merupakan salah-satu daripada hasil karya beliau dari siri terbaru iaitu siri ombak yang saya yakin akan mendapat pengiktirafan yang sama seperti siri-siri lukisan beliau yang lalu. Bagi pihak Bank pada hari ini kami merasa amat berbangga kerana dapat menganjurkan pameran lukisan artis yang dimaksudkan iaitu Yusof Ghani, yang merupakan pameran solo beliau yang terbesar yang pernah diadakan. Yusof Ghani is an artist with a reputation only matched by his large-scale paintings. He keeps producing in sizes so substantial that the best place to view them is undoubtedly at our spacious Museum and Art Gallery. Like the staff of Bank Negara Malaysia, he is a tireless traveller. His journeys around the world have been a source of inspiration rather than exhaustion; and like a wave he keeps moving relentlessly from shore to shore. It is no coincidence that his latest series is called 'Ombak', which was also his choice of title for the exhibition itself. The 57 works assembled here show the ebb and flow of his creative impulses. It is the first complete survey of the paintings that he has been creating for three decades. We are proud to have these works in our gallery as many of them are like old friends. The Bank's first acquisition of a Pak Yusof painting was almost thirty years ago. What a reputation that Yusof Ghani has built, he has gone from being routinely described as most promising young artist to being promoted in one auction house's sales pitch as the most published artist in Malaysia. So far, however, his exhibitions and publications have been seemingly unrelated parts of the puzzle that make up this enigmatic artist.
