Greater interoperability will significantly increase the benefits associated with the rapidly growing remittance market. Smaller players in the industry would be better supported to increase their share of remittance flows. It will also promote a more competitive remittance market in which remittance service providers shift away from competing on captive corridors, to competing on the strength of their superior products and services. This in turn will allow for critical mass to be reached more quickly, thus encouraging investments in the supporting infrastructure and lowering remittance costs over time. Supporting business remittances The growth in cross border economic activities will also increase demand for business remittances to facilitate traderelated payments and settlements. World trade amounted to more than USD19 trillion in 2014 with about 27% contributed by the developing Asian region. A significant part of this is increasingly contributed by small and medium businesses. Remittance service providers can complement banks in supporting such businesses by increasing access to remittance services, including in more remote locations and outside normal banking hours. In Malaysia, the regulatory framework provides for remittance service providers to offer business remittances as part of the strategies to enable the provision of complete remittance business solutions to the market. Thus far, demand for business remittances has been encouraging with transaction values reaching in excess of RM430 million in the first nine months of 2015, compared with RM325 million in 2014. Nevertheless, given the larger transaction values and more complex activities involved in providing such service, which may potentially expose the service providers to higher ML/TF risks, the provision of business remittances has been implemented under a managed approach. This approach requires players to demonstrate the capability to manage risks associated with providing business remittance. In tandem with this, the amount of business remittance transactions to be conducted by a service provider shall commensurate with its operational readiness and robustness of controls to minimise risks. Expanding cross-border industry networks The remittance industry is one of striking diversity. Regulatory frameworks vary widely across the world, and to a large extent, have had an important role in shaping the structure of the industry and the institutions that operate within it. They also have an important influence on the development path of the industry. These conditions present opportunities for the industry to achieve much more collectively than it might through the sum of its individual parts. By further expanding and strengthening existing cross-border networks, the industry can enhance business linkages, establish and promote professional standards that can help to lift industries in less developed regimes, and tap into broader experiences and expertise to solve common problems. This will become more important as expectations of the industry increase - from the regulators to improve compliance; from the political leadership to support growth and development; and from its own customers to provide a reliable and efficient service. Helping remittance service providers deal with de-risking moves by the banking institutions, ensuring adequate standards of competence for compliance officers, and developing practical guidance for the implementation of risk-based approaches in managing more complex money laundering and terrorism financing risks are just some of the issues which the industry is currently challenged with. The industry would greatly benefit from well-organised domestic and cross-border platforms which have an action-oriented focus on addressing such issues. More can also be done by the industry to sponsor research in areas of mutual interest, many areas can be explored such as in evaluating risks associated with the adoption and applications of new technologies in operating remittance business, and assessing the impact of remittance developments on economic growth and social well-being as input to public policy. Additionally an industry best practice and expected standard and quality of operations should be formulated as a benchmark. These are some of the contributions that the industry can lead. Conclusion The long-term prospects and sustainability of the industry will ultimately be shaped by the priorities it chooses to focus on today. I am confident that the conference will offer valuable insights on what some of these priorities might be, and in the process, bring us closer towards further enhancing the role of remittances in improving lives and transforming nations. This is the prize that we must continue to keep our sights on. On that note, it gives me great pleasure to officiate the opening of the Money Transfer Asia Pacific Conference 2015. I wish all of you productive and fruitful discussions ahead. Thank you.

Title: Speech at the Maybank Myanmar Grand Opening
text: Deputy Governors Opening Remarks at the FOMCA Financial Education Conference: "Strengthening Financial Resilience of Malaysian Consumers" Speaker: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB Venue: Sasana Kijang Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 26 Nov 2015 It is my pleasure to speak at the Conference on Strengthening Financial Resilience of Malaysian Consumers this morning. It is important for all consumers to be equipped with financial knowledge and skills, in order to reap the benefits of economic growth and be resilient against changes in financial circumstances. Bank Negara Malaysia (the Bank) is pleased to have been collaborating with the Federation of Malaysian Consumers Association (FOMCA) and its associates for many years to elevate the financial capability of Malaysian consumers. This Conference by FOMCA and Education and Research Association for Consumers, Malaysia (ERA) represents another opportunity for the public and private sectors in Malaysia tocome together to further advance the financial literacy agenda. I would also like to record our appreciation to CITI Foundation for their support. Collaborative effort is important to promote the financial wellbeing of our society and the soundness and stability of the financial system. Being financially literate is a critical first step to help Malaysians better cope with changing demographics, rising costs of living, lifestyle pressures and evolving norms. Consumers with financial literacy are able to achieve key financial goals throughout their life stages, such as: - to accumulate assets and wealth, to start or expand business ventures, to raise a family or to invest for the future; and - able to create opportunities to improve standards of living across the board, despite individual circumstances. We are living in challenging times. A key concern in the current environment is to enhance the skills and capability of financial consumers, in particular households and small businesses, to manage competing demands on their limited resources. We must equip our public with the ability to manage their debt and expenditures wisely, and making saving and investment decisions in an increasingly complex financial environment. Efforts to enhance the financial competence of consumers have evolved over a span of two decades in this country. Consumers are becoming more knowledgeable and have greater confidence to make informed decisions on an expanding range of financial products, services and delivery channels. Despite this, financial capability among Malaysian consumers still remains relatively behind in comparison to other advanced economies. This has constrained the benefits that can be gained by consumers from participating in the financial system. Many consumers also continue to fall prey to unscrupulous market practices, in some cases, with severe financial consequences for the victims. Financial capability therefore is an important life skill. Just like any other life skill, it puts practical knowledge and tools in the hands of individuals that can be used to manage their financial affairs effectively and responsibly. The aim is to create generations of financial consumers who have a realistic grasp of their financial circumstances and can make sound financial choices that will enable them to enjoy a comfortable life. This is possible by nurturing prudent financial management traits such as: The ability to live within ones means; Understanding the benefits, risks and costs before purchasing a financial product; Able to differentiate and deal only with licensed and legitimate financial institutions; Knowing how and where to seek help early when experiencing financial distress; and Taking concrete steps to save and invest for the future. These traits continue to represent the central themes in the Banks financial education strategies. To be effective, financial education policies and strategies should ideally be supported by concrete evidence to ensure better use of resources and ensure that the financial education strategies are designed to address the specific needs of consumers. The use of strong evidence ensures that the nature and the extent of the problems are well understood, and the choice and design of the policy intervention to deal with the problem is optimal. This is particularly important for financial education programmes given that the programmes are very resource and time intensive, thus requiring such significant investments are properly accounted and justified. The recent nationwide Financial Capability and Inclusion Demand Side Survey 2015 conducted by the Bank has provided some useful insights on the key vulnerabilities and gaps faced by Malaysian households. This will be shared in more detail during the morning panel session today. In summary, the study reveals that while the financial infrastructure to promote access and utilisation of financial products and services are well developed in Malaysia but consumers generally lack the capability to make good financial decisions and do not have sufficient means to effectively participate in the financial system. This has important implications for financial education policies and strategies. One implication is that for the vulnerable segments of the population, the financial capability strategies need to be accompanied by concrete measures for income generation. The study highlights the inability of the lower income group to effectively participate in the financial system due to limited financial resources. Whatever resources they possess are predominantly utilised to meet essential needs with no financial buffers for the future. Another important implication is the need to better understand behaviour in financial decision making as a stronger basis for developing more effective financial education strategies. The application of such behavioural insights has substantial potential for improving financial decisions by consumers. It can provide insights on the way information ought to be presented to make it more intuitive to consumers, and focus our thinking on the appropriate design of financial education programmes so that they become more relevant and create a more lasting impact on financial behaviour. It is therefore important that greater collaboration to understand behavioural finance among key stakeholders and identify the levers that contribute to better financial decisions by consumers in different circumstances. It is also important to ensure that financial education initiatives are sustainable in promoting positive financial behaviours over time. Since 2011,financial education programmes in Malaysia have been designed and delivered to equip Malaysians of all ages with knowledge on financial management which are relevant to their stage in life. Among young Malaysian, focus is directed at inculcating good financial management habits that will positively shape their attitude towards financial matters. We are collaborating with the Ministry of Education (MOE) in designing a systematic integration of key elements of financial education curriculum for primary and secondary schools beginning 2014 and2017 respectively. We envisage that this will be extended to all school levels by 2021. This is a major breakthrough. We are laying the foundation for developing a financially capable society. In parallel, financial education programmes that target adults are being driven by Agensi Kaunseling Dan Pengurusan Kredit (or AKPK), alongside its debt management programmes. It is a comprehensive approach in providing support for Malaysians in managing their personal finances. In our work on financial education, the Bank has constantly strived to ensure that we are connecting with consumers in ways that are relevant to the times. In 2003, we published information booklets that educated the public on financial products and services. As internet usage increased, we also developed the bankinginfo and insuranceinfo websites, alongside online financial tools. BNM Telelink was introduced in 2007 to facilitate prompt and efficient response to issues or queries received from the public via telephone, fax, letter or email on matters related to the financial sector. BNM MobileLINK, introduced in 2011, provides an innovative channel for consumers in semi-urban and non-urban areas to interface with the Bank. Today, we continue to convey important messages to financial consumers through diverse channels including print media, radio, news portals and social media. The use of technology, in particular, to empower consumers with the appropriate information to aid in decision-making has been a central part of the innovation that we have been able to achieve in the area of financial education.In this context, mobile devices have become important tools that can also be leveraged on to support effective financial decision-making. In carrying this work forward, we are pleased to introduce today three new mobile applications that will help consumers make better financial decisions. These applications build on smart phone technology. Research has found that smart phones can have a significant impact in helping consumers make smarter choices. Study revealed that 70% of users who browse product reviews or get product information while shopping actually change their purchase decision. We shall use this insight. We are introducing three mobile applications: MyBNM, whichallowsconsumers to keep abreast with the latest financial news including announcements, financial fraud alerts and foreign exchange rates at their fingertips. The apps would assists consumers who seek information on the latest developments on the financial industry as well as updates on monetary and financial policies and regulations by the Bank. BNM MyLINK- is a one-stop mobile application which provides a direct interface between consumers and financial service providers in Malaysia. It provides a directory of conventional and Islamic banking, insurance and takaful companies as well as SME institutions which allow consumers to connect directly with financial service providers to make enquiries, obtain advice and address their complaints. MyTabung -is a tool for individuals to create a personal or household budget. Users can capture incomes, savings and recurring expenses with an on-the-spot display of the users financial standing and spending patterns. Individuals can also obtain financial advice and budgeting tips to guide them in practicing prudent financial management as a way of life. These mobile applications are available in both Bahasa Malaysia and English, and can be downloaded for free from Apple App Store and Google Play Store. We would like to invite all of you to visit our booth outside this Conference Hall to learn more about the mobile applications. The Bank had also earlier in May 2015 launched a mobile application named MyRinggit which helps consumers identify the security features of the Malaysian currency. Greater public and private sector collaboration toaddress the needs of consumers for reliable and professional financial advice must also be encouraged. Given the multiple facets of financial education content and programmes, there is an opportunity for the various key stakeholders to come together to align strategies, reduce duplication and identify gaps in order to maximise our collective impact while using resources in the most efficient way. It has been the Banks observation that coordinated financial education strategies tend to be sustained longer as there is greater focus, more optimal resource allocation and a more visible impact. In Malaysia, the Bank coordinates closely with various organisations including AKPK, the Securities Commission, Perbadanan Insurans Deposit Malaysia, Kumpulan Wang Simpanan Pekerja and consumer associations on financial education initiatives. Existing informal arrangements have the potential to be further expanded and developed to provide a national platform for articulating and driving a clear national financial education agenda and strategy for Malaysia. Strengthening the financial resilience of Malaysian is not just about educating them to make better financial choices, but is also about providing our consumers with the means to manage the effects of those choices, especially where consumers are disadvantaged in terms of relative power compared to the financial institutions that they deal with. Therefore, it has always been a priority of the Bank to develop a robust and effective advisory and redress mechanisms. This mechanism is an important part of the consumer protection and empowerment framework in Malaysia. The Bank, through BNMLINK and BNMTELELINK has advised close to 3 million financial consumers on financial matters or disputes with financial service providers. The establishment of a Financial Ombudsman Scheme (FOS) in early 2016 will further strengthen the financial dispute resolution arrangements available for consumers. The scheme will provide financial consumers with an effective and independent redress mechanism with minimum formality to resolve disputes between consumers and financial services providers. The service offered will be an alternative to the courts. In addition, AKPK will continue to provide financial education, credit counselling and debt management services at no cost to consumers. Conclusion The role of financial education has become even more important as a means to strengthen the financial resilience of consumers in a dynamic and constantly changing environment. More importantly, it needs to be approached holistically together with the consumer protection and financial inclusion agenda to achieve a lasting impact on improving the financial well-being of society. We have a pressing need for better research to enable us to design an effective financial education intervention policy and to prioritise where resources can be best allocated. From the national perspective, we need to better coordinate our efforts to leverage on available resources and generate innovative ideas to improve the effectiveness in delivering financial education to diverse audiences with multiple needs. It is my hope that deliberations at this Conference will lead to pragmatic and concrete steps that we can take collectively to elevate the level of financial capability and resilience for all Malaysians. On this note, I now declare open this conference, wish all of you an engaging and productive Conference.

Title: Keynote Address at the Money Transfer Asia Pacific Conference 2015
text: Deputy Governor's Speech at the Launch of "Art of ASEAN: Our Exhibition" Speaker: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB Speech/Interview Date: 26 Nov 2015 Venue: Bank Negara Museum and Art Gallery, Sasana Kijang Language: Welcome to "Art of ASEAN: Our Exhibition". I would like to specifically welcome Tan Sri Dato' Ajit Singh, the former Secretary of ASEAN as our guest of honour. The exhibition embodies the very purpose of the existence of ASEAN. This exhibition was envisioned, to bring us together for the cause of collaboration. Similarly with this building, it was designed to be a nexus for thought leadership, to hosts a learning centre with an advanced training facilities for developmental programmes and high level seminars for local and foreign participants, as well as providing an avenue for the exchange of views and experiences amongst central banking and financial community. Sasana Kijang is also now the proud home to five notable organisations; The SEACEN Centre, a regional learning and research Centre for Central Banks in the region and The International Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB), an international organisation for the setting of prudential standards for Islamic Finance, the Alliance for Financial Inclusion Permanent Headquarters, a global network of developing countries to advance financial inclusion globally. The World Bank Office and Asian School of Business have also become part of the Sasana Kijang community. This is a reflection of our efforts and commitment in promoting greater understanding and collaboration, in particular, amongst the central bank fraternity. In four years since the opening of the Art Galleries, a total of 19 exhibitions were held in this very building. Common threads are something more often heard about than actually seen. Within ASEAN, there are some threads that are common and also visible. Just as this exhibition weaves together a diversity of cultures, there is in the region, a heritage textile that does this at a practical level. This is not a textile exhibition, of course. A glance at the walls will confirm this. What we are looking at are the works of contemporary descendants of those cloths that are perhaps the region's richest heritage, and certainly the artifacts most sought-after by collectors around the world. Heirloom fabrics were, in their day, the most revered expression of Southeast Asian societies. They were a canvas on which creativity could be applied, beautifying the surroundings and proclaiming identity. There is another type of textile in particular that illustrates different routes to the same end, as well as putting this region of ours on the international art map. 'Ikat' cloths exist in many parts of ASEAN and very few other places. Their individually dyed threads, along with the imagination required to create an image that emerges from those threads, mark them out as something requiring commitment and extreme patience. The 'Ikat' cloths are universally admired. The word 'ikat' is a rare example of a Malay/Javanese word that has travelled the globe and been accepted in the English lexicon. It is derived from the word 'mengikat', meaning to tie together, and this provides a useful metaphor for our exhibition. It is in this context that when I mentioned 'our' exhibition, it does not refer to Bank Negara Malaysia but the word 'our' is a reference to the ASEAN's motto. "Our People, Our Community, Our Vision". It is about bringing people together, as "Ikat" is about bringing threads together, to create a complete picture out of a seemingly incoherent jumble. The process of "Ikat" weaving means almost-invisible threads of weft holding everything together while the swerved threads are proudly displayed. An apt description of ASEAN, an organization that binds disparate nations without always being visible to the 600-plus million population. An exhibition such as this provides a physical expression of the generally unseen collaborative power. 'Art of ASEAN: Our Exhibition' shows how societies have developed amidst the rapid globalization process over the last few decades. They are more attuned to global developments while still retaining their own communities' characteristics. These new canvases come in various shapes and sizes that are not so different from the traditional fabrics of the past. They may not be wearable but they still serve the purpose of making a visual statement. The sculptures and installations at our exhibition are also a continuation of a different regional heritage; one that places emphasis on three dimensions rather than two. Every part of ASEAN has this heritage, whether it is the architectural woodcarvings of Islamic societies or the allout imagery of deities in Hindu, Buddhist, Christian and tribal communities. With contemporary art, showcasing the works of individual nations is relatively straightforward. But combining them to provide a forum for all of ASEAN is not. There have been very few attempts made at showing the full range of regional creative output. This is not caused by a lack of enthusiasm; it is more about logistics and language barriers. Just as financial and economic integration is unfolding within ASEAN, there are signs of art becoming a cohesive force. Artists and galleries are moving more freely across borders, bringing ideas and friendships with them. It's a paradox that the auction capital of Southeast Asia moved from Singapore to Hong Kong some years ago, but maybe a neutral territory is required. In Malaysia, we are always glad to be host to regional artists in a building that was built for the task. In addition to the "Sasana" part of the Sasana Kijang name, meaning a meeting place of inquiring minds, we must not forget the "Kijang", an animal believed to be intelligent and agile. Despite folklore attributing the barking deer's arrival in the Malay Peninsula to Arab traders, it is indigenous throughout most of Southeast Asia and not many other places. So 'Kijang' fittingly symbolizes the intelligence and the agility of this Region in managing the many challenges that we face as a community. Although some ASEAN artists have migrated to other parts of the world, most continue to work in their homelands with occasional exchanges within the region. We are very privileged to host the collaborative efforts to assemble the work of artists from every corner of ASEAN. Many have joined us for this occasion today. They are rising stars, with a bright future in their countries and gaining growing reputations within the region. A community of artists is emerging, with few opportunities to display their works alongside those of their regional counterparts. Our exhibition will, we hope, provides that opportunity and fosters that cross-border cooperation that is integral to the development of art in a dynamic community. Even though this process might be organic, there are increasing initiatives within ASEAN to cement these artistic relationships. Many ASEAN initiatives have expanded the tourism industry significantly over the last few years. This should prove useful as tourists cum roving art lovers can stimulate the art market as history had shown in locations such as Renaissance Italy or in modern Bali. I envisage innovation such as the GOASEAN travel channel would further promote the region as a tourist destination and would further propel understandings on the heritage and culture among the ASEAN member countries. Common understanding and closeness cannot be forced by decree. It needs the ambassadorial skills of the artist, an individual who can usually see that one person's gain is not another's loss. What they really want is an audience, preferably with customers included. As the economies of ASEAN countries strengthen and societies become wealthier so does a common sense of purpose and an expanded interest in aesthetic expression. All ten nations have varied creative aptitudes, just as they have different economic strengths. In both cases, these are greater than the sum of their parts. The challenge is getting to see examples of this diversity side by side. With Our Exhibition, we not only have 'Our People, Our Community, Our Vision' but also Our Art Space. We are doing our small bit, to support the declared ASEAN commitment to community building by dedicating a space to showcase ASEAN works. At all times we have a display of ASEAN paintings in our South Gallery to promote fraternity among the ten nations. This has now been extended to the North Gallery for three months and we look forward to a continuous collaboration stretching into the future. I would like to thank the artists, galleries and institutions that helped bring these components together. The first of the eight priorities listed at the ASEAN summit is "to formally establish an ASEAN community". With greater cooperation and by leveraging on our different strengths, we can be part of a community that is not only better in terms of prosperity and stability but looks better as well. Thank you very much and I wish everyone an enjoyable experience of the exhibition.

Title: Keynote Address at the Insurance Information & Ratemaking Forum of Asia 2015 (IIRFA)
text: Deputy Governors Opening Speech at the Launch of the Directors' Remuneration Report 2015 Speaker: Datuk Nor Shamsiah Mohd Yunus Speech/Interview Date: 07 Dec 2015 Venue: Lanai Kijang, Kuala Lumpur Language: English Since its inception, the FIDE Forum has played an important role in bringing corporate governance issues to the centre-stage, with the continuing active participation of directors of financial institutions. In 2010, the FIDE Forum commissioned a study titled Performance Pays which advocated performance-driven remuneration for non-executive directors in Malaysia. The report to be launched today is another important initiative and valuable resource for boards. It will shed light on board practices on remuneration and contain specific recommendations to further advance efforts to strengthen corporate governance within the financial sector. The success or failure of any organisation is often attributed to the quality of its corporate governance. In heavily regulated sectors like banking and insurance, the collapse of financial institutions especially major global players invariably invites greater public scrutiny and the tightening of rules and regulations. This is what we saw in the aftermath of the global financial crisis in 2008. While it is important that the relevant corporate governance standards are further strengthened, this must be reinforced by an honest reflection on gaps that exist in practice and a strong response by those at the very top of the organisation to elevate an institutions governance practices and arrangements. It is in our collective interests to ensure that corporate governance practices in the financial sector remain sound over time. Regulation alone will not achieve this. As key public interest entities, financial institutions are expected to lead by example and remain at the forefront in regard to corporate governance practices. At the same time, greater expectations being placed on board members and the growing complexity of the business has increased the challenge of attracting the highly capable talents to join the board of a financial institution. Indeed, some may view that the weight of regulatory expectations and potential personal liability associated with being on the board of a financial institution has outstripped the professional satisfaction gained from such appointments. So, how can we move forward in resolving these tensions? In answering that question, I thought I would share some perspectives with you on our observations of board practices, drawing largely from our supervisory work. Rethinking the boards oversight approach The first concerns re-thinking the boards oversight approach. In recent years, regulatory concerns are increasingly dominating the agendas of many boards, both globally and in Malaysia. Regulatory frameworks must of course evolve to reflect not only the changing environment, but also maturing financial institutions and supervisory systems. But directors of financial institutions today would be forgiven, particularly in the more recent period following the financial crisis, for feeling overwhelmed by the continuous onslaught of new rules and regulations. A common reaction by boards has been to view each new obligation imposed on boards in isolation, adding incrementally to an already long and daunting list of things to do for the board. This can detract boards from maintaining a strong focus on their primary roles in strategy and monitoring the performance of senior management. For sure, stronger regulation has resulted in an increased emphasis on the boards oversight role. This is embedded in the Financial Services Act 2013 which expands and elaborates the duties of the board of a financial institution. The aim of regulation, however, is to ensure that boards implement a strong accountability framework for their institutions, and are actively engaged in the strategic business direction and oversight of risks of the institution. In other words, the board is expected to keep management honest, and be able to hold management to account for ensuring that the institution operates in a responsible manner in creating value for its stakeholders. In the case of financial institutions, the stakeholders are clearly not just the shareholders, employees and direct customers, but a much wider community of regulators, market participants and taxpayers that may be on the hook if an institution fails. Responding to each new regulatory development or emerging issue with a corresponding new or extended compliance and reporting process would achieve little more than longer board meetings and more voluminous board papers. It is therefore incumbent on boards to develop and maintain a cohesive approach to oversight. New and changing demands on the board should lead the board to keep under constant review how it will optimally function and the board dynamics. They should not merely increase board activity. In the area of risk, the Bank expects boards to devote time and rigour to deliberate and articulate a clear risk appetite framework which acts as a strong anchor for risk-taking across the organisation. But the board should direct and hold management to account for the operational aspects of the framework, including its effective implementation and promoting a sound risk culture. Only then can the board focus, as it should, on enterprise risks; sustain an active dialogue on emerging issues; and spend time understanding the impact of external conditions on the institutions strategy and internal capacity to adapt and evolve. This is especially critical in uncertain and difficult times. But more fundamentally, it is needed to energise and keep boards engaged and able to discharge their roles effectively. Done well, boards are likely to identify opportunities to further enhance board performance, including through improvements to board processes. Ensuring succession preparedness Effective oversight by the board invariably builds on strong management. This brings me to my second point which relates to the boards role in ensuring that a strong senior management team is in place and maintained with well-executed succession plans. Ensuring succession preparedness may well be the single most important role of the board. At a time when performance will depend on successfully delivering carefully crafted business strategies to address the effects of regulatory reform, technology change and market movements, financial institutions can ill afford disruptive transitions, or worse, leadership vacuums. In reality however, leadership changes in the domestic financial industry have often been less than ideal and the Bank has lately further intensified its engagements with financial institutions to change this. But there is another reason for boards to focus on succession. It is to reduce risks to boards themselves and increase the confidence of boards in performing their role as effective stewards of the institution. A strong management team can significantly alter the risk-reward balance for new talent joining the board. This in turn will strengthen the boards own succession and substantially improve prospects for the board itself to be rejuvenated. Promoting a healthy board culture My final point relates to board culture. It is widely acknowledged that a healthy board culture can be a key driver of board effectiveness. The emphasis on culture in the period since the global financial crisis stems from a recognition that behaviour is shaped by influences that run much deeper than policies, systems and processes which aim to regulate behaviour. This is also true for boards. A boardroom environment that values individual contributions, and that encourages spirited discussions and dissent allows directors to meaningfully shape the outcomes for the organisation. Boards should reflect a wide range of skills and experiences that can be drawn upon to expand perspectives and build collective knowledge, both of which are important ingredients for better decisions. At the same time, boards will need to make greater progress in areas that tend to be more sensitive, but which can significantly lift board performance. This includes improving the rigour and effectiveness of board evaluations, development and compensation. Keeping boards of financial institutions at the top of their game is not only good for the institution and the broader financial system; it is a valuable opportunity for individuals who are serving on boards to grow professionally. With more wide-ranging demands, how a financial institution rewards its board and taps into the talent pipeline for directors will be essential. There is no one-size-fits-all solution. But at its most basic level, any incentive system for boards must enable a financial institution to attract the specific skill sets and experience it requires on the board. This must also reflect the business and particular challenges that may be faced by an institution, for which the board will be expected to provide leadership. In FIDE Forums 2010 report, expanded further in its latest report, the case is made for fair and equitable remuneration, with practical guidance on how to best approach the design of board compensation. Broad-brushed approaches comparing absolute levels of compensation across financial institutions, which are still common in the industry, are shown to be woefully inadequate to reflect the level of time commitment and responsibilities, as well as the opportunity cost for individuals with specialised skills taking up directorships in financial institutions. Importantly, interactions between board compensation, board evaluations and succession plans need to be carefully approached as part of a cohesive system which works together to elevate board performance. In all of this, the independent judgment of the board in setting overall strategy and risk appetite and overseeing senior management performance must always be preserved. Conclusion The subject of corporate governance covers a broad canvas. I have chosen this morning to speak briefly on re-thinking the boards oversight approach, ensuring succession preparedness and promoting a healthy board culture because I believe these are particularly relevant to the challenge of ensuring sustainable high performing boards going forward. The Bank is greatly encouraged by the work of FIDE Forum and Iclif which has had, and continues to have, an important impact in building stronger boards in our financial institutions, and leading the way in board education and development. I would encourage financial institutions to participate in and support the activities of FIDE Forum which provide unparalleled opportunities for directors of financial institutions in Malaysia to interact on common issues with one another and the worlds leading experts in the field of governance. I am confident that the recommendations set out in the Directors Remuneration Report 2015 will further deepen our collective body of knowledge on how we can build highly effective boards. Drawing upon these insights, I hope to see financial institutions coming together and proactively prioritising initiatives and resources to better manage the talent pool for directors. With that, it is my great pleasure to launch FIDE Forums Directors Remuneration Report 2015.

Title: Speech at the Muzakarah Cendekiawan Syariah Nusantara 9th
text: Deputy Governor's Keynote Address at the 10th Anniversary Dinner of IIUM Institute Islamic Banking and Finance -"Islamic Finance and Education, Thinking Beyond" Speaker: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB Speech/Interview Date: 04 Dec 2015 Venue: IIUM Gombak Campus Language: English The 10th Anniversary Dinner of IIUM Institute of Islamic Banking and Finance (IiBF) is a significant milestone. As an alumni, I am proud that the institute has made great strides in developing and producing the required talent for the Islamic finance industry. Over the years, the IiBF has produced increasing number of Islamic finance graduates and we should take pride that a total of 14 PhD students have graduated this year, the highest number of graduates so far. We should aspire for our alumni and IiBF graduates to become captains and leaders of the industry. It is only this outcome that the institute should benchmark itself in measuring its success. While the celebration of success is well deserved for our Institute, as it in itself an important element to motivate and inspire continuous achievements, I believe at the same time, it would be meaningful if we reflect on our achievements and assess the extent of our success in upholding the true values of Islamic finance. While we acknowledge the steady growth and commendable milestones achieved in the industry over the last three decades, I thought we should ask ourselves, where does Islamic finance really stand today? Have we truly embraced the Islamic values embedded in Shariah and become a role model of ethics? Has Islamic finance been really innovative? Or simply adaptive? How successful are we in bringing about the required changes in the society that could contribute towards the betterment of the lives of the general public? Let us go back to the thirteenth century where Islamic civilisation was the epitome of social, economic and learning progress. The Muslim empire during the golden age of Islam has given birth to prominent Islamic scholars whom have pioneered many innovations and breakthroughs. These outstanding inventions in the Muslim world have paved the way for global civilisations, so much so, that Islam became torch bearers of various disciplines including science, mathematics and philosophy. The flourish of Islam was attributable to the Muslims endless pursuit of knowledge, their openness to learn from earlier civilisations and their stance against any forms of inequality or prejudices. Now, the state of the Muslims throughout the world is in disarray. Poverty, illiteracy and suppression of civil society are a few of the many challenges faced by the ummah. While the world environment and civilisation has changed and many people and countries have transformed and progress through the centuries, the Muslims conditions are worse than before. We are embroiled in polemics, endless disagreements, civil wars and strifes. We forgot about past success that could inspire us to take new leads to improve the conditions of the ummah. We are, it seems, to be forever in a state of quagmire. Many Muslims like to speak about the past but we should not speak of the old glory days of Islam and do nothing about it and continue to fall back and rely on the great inventions of the past. We ought not hold on to practices and views of yesteryears that were suitable for a foregone era but instead make brave and bold ijtihad that can position our religion at the cutting edge of technology, science and philosophy. It is most unfortunate to observe that most Muslim countries today are experiencing poor social and economic growth and are being left far behind compared to other nations. Why is this happening? Is it the religion? Is it the way it is being taught or practised? I believe that the sad reality of the current Muslim world is a reflection of the state of individuals in our society today. Our Ummah now is weak and at a low ebb. We lack the tolerance to opinions that contradict ours and we are too reckless in rejecting differing views. We are too quick to criticise and too hurried in passing judgement. We amplify pettiness and trivialise substantive matters. Our tendency to remain simplistic makes us lax in thinking and prevent deep thinking in coming up with solutions. These negative traits are ingrained characteristics that have been holding back the Muslim community from making progress. If we want to reawaken the Ummah, we need to embark upon a paradigm shift in our thinking, in our philosophy, in our technology, in our behaviour. Stop dwelling in issues of no significance and giving frivolous opinions on irrelevant matters. Start opening our minds by taking advantage of lessons derived from other great civilisations. As advocated by the Quran, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves (Surah Ar-rad, verse 11). The same holds true for Islamic finance. What has brought us this far would not guarantee success over the future. History is rife with many examples of ideas, concepts and industries that were conceived or invented in one place but were perfected elsewhere and hence found a new thriving home far from those who had originally invented it. If we are not alert and maintain the disposition to preserve or conserve what has been established and traditional; these tendencies to limit change would become the norm. This is dangerous as parochial thinking and dogmatism would be developed and bring development of Islamic finance to a standstill, preventing the industry to progress to a new level of excellence. Islamic finance has grabbed the attention of many, including multinational financial institutions in London, Paris, New York and Hong Kong. The IMF and the World Bank have allocated resources in the understanding and conducting of surveillance in the growth and application of Islamic finance. If we do not innovate and expand the lead we have now, we may see a shift of activities and dynamism of Islamic finance to somewhere else. And the centre of gravity for what has always been our claim to fame will drift away from us. History has shown that the Islamic civilisation has only grown when conventional and mainstream thinking were challenged and the propositions of fresh ideas that were built upon research, science and logic were propounded. To ensure dynamism and progress, we should begin by throwing away disruptive habits of amplifying differences and staying away from being too rigid and too narrow mindedness. Instead, more focus should be directed to the commonalities and the need for our minds to remain open and expansive. We ought to stop our damaging behavior on amplifying differences that leads to disunity and instead focus on common good that bring us together. In the context of Malaysia, Islamic finance presents vast opportunity for greater innovation to take place. Given our three decades of journey in developing Islamic finance, we should be confident enough to show leadership as our tireless efforts have brought the industry to the fore, increasingly making Islamic finance mainstream. But the skills and conceptual thinking that have pioneered our progress since the 1980s have most likely served its purpose. In forging ahead, we require a new way of thinking that is totally divorced from the mainstream views of today. Allow me to quote a hadith that may motivate us to undertake this calling; He who introduced some good practice in Islamic which was followed after him (by people), he would be assured of reward like one who followed it. (Narrated by Sahih Muslim) From that perspective, the future will greatly reward people of courage whom are bold enough to envision outcomes that are exclusive from the contemporary thinking. Tonight, I would like to raise some viewpoints relating to a design thinking in nurturing talent in the Islamic finance industry which I hope would spark reassessment in talent development. I will start with the first verse that was sent down to the Prophet Muhammad s.a.w, that is Iqra (read). Are Muslims nowadays among the great readers? As the first revelation, this verse marks the importance of reading in the pursuit of knowledge. In Islam, people of knowledge are held in high esteem. But without useful knowledge, making progress is impossible. Students of Islamic finance are therefore expected to have the thirst and hunger for knowledge and strive to be great readers. Equally important is the mastery of knowledge in diverse fields of disciplines to ensure comprehensive understanding of relevant subjects to make Islamic finance complete. In the Lost Enlightenment by Frederick Starr, the glory of Central Asia as a leading Islamic civilisation during the years between 800 to 1200 was manifested by its leadership in the development of trade and economy; its cities that were renowned for their sheer size and sophistication; the refinement of its art and more importantly its pioneering knowledge in various fields. The Muslims in Central Asians made significant breakthroughs in mathematics, astronomy, geology, medicine, chemistry, social sciences, philosophy, theology and music, just to name a few. They were ahead of their time and could use unprecedented precision in calculating the earths diameter, and authored many books that became important references on European medicine later during the century. Their creativity also shone through their poetic works which are known to be some of the worlds greatest poetries. They even named algebra. It is astonishing that a scholar working in Afghanistan could even prophesize that North and South America would exist, ahead of Columbus by five centuries. It is impressive that such an elite league of polymaths had appeared within a similar era of history. It is of no surprise that their masterpieces could greatly influence the European culture, beginning from the period of St. Thomas Aquinas until the scientific revolution, with similar tremendous impact in India and majority of Asia. It is in this spirit that our Islamic finance industry therefore needs a new cadre of Islamic finance developers whom are conversant not only in Shariah, but also in other related areas such as legal, economics, mathematics and finance. We need a group of scholars with multidisciplinary backgrounds whom have freed themselves from parochial thinking and straitjacketing. With diversity in knowledge, our talent in Islamic finance will possess an innate ability to mobilise the conceptual thinking propagated by various sects or Mazhabs in different Islamic schools of thought. Let us take an example from Imam Al Nawawi, one of the distinguished Islamic scholars whose work has benefitted thousands of people. His great desire for learning has driven him to author more than 40 books ranging from hadith, theology and jurisprudence, in his mere 45 years of living. If Imam Al Nawawi could write that many books of everlasting value in such a short period of lifetime, we should be capable of contributing more to the wealth of Islamic finance knowledge especially with greater access to information and technology at the present time. Unfortunately, it is sad to note that in the Islamic finance education today, we are short of basic textbooks that can be used as reference materials. Similarly, great works of yesteryears are not being translated. Books by Al Tabari, the great historian were only translated into English in 2000, more than 1000 years after they were first authored. Most Muslims, not conversant in Arabic, were not able to learn the lessons of history from a direct source. Instead, they have to rely on subsequent scholars for interpretations, views and opinions. This is in stark contrast where books authored by scholars and philosophies of great Muslims thinkers were translated into many languages and formed the basis for the advancement of other civilisations. Secondly, from great readers, great thinkers are born. Scholars of Islamic finance must not be passive, but active and courageous intellectuals that continuously strive for new breakthrough ideas. For example, the calibre and prestige of the great scholar, Ibn Taymiyyah, was distinctive not only by the level of knowledge that far excelled from other scholars of his time, but also by his bravery, boldness and nobleness in his teaching, through the issuance of legal verdicts and writing that expanded the boundaries of opinions. Together with his student Ibn Qayyim, they were known to be great thinkers and innovators, with vast knowledge and strong acquaintance with the differences in various mazhabs. During a time of strife and internal chaos, both great scholars were however regarded as heretics and I am sure were isolated and ostracised due to their unorthodox method of thinking and views. It was only many centuries later that their opinions were accepted and became mainstream and formed the basis of many modern Islamic finance contacts. We need scholars and thinkers of such stature. Ones who possess the courage and the boldness to traverse beyond contemporary issues and accepted norms. For instance, the Malaysian Founding Fathers would not be able to position the country to where it is now without their bold and outrageous vision. They have boldly laid the building blocks for future generation and place the country at the forefront of developments. Similarly, we need to be bold and courageous in building the required foundation to lead Islamic finance into the future. The future favors the bold. This adage is true and proven, and reflective of what we had embarked on to chart the growth of Islamic finance in the 1980s. Thirdly, the talents that will serve the industry must also maintain strong values of ethics and integrity that portray the principled values of Islam. This includes practising mutual respect to differing schools of thought. The differences in the opinions of the various Mazhabs is a blessing to the people as the diverse opinions enable the needs of society to be met. It should not be a cause for division. It should be a course of celebration in the pursuit of intellectual diversity. Hence, the students of Islamic finance must appreciate the intellectual differences and value the flexibility within the variation of views. Nevertheless, it is important to note that acquiring profound understanding on the diversity of opinions is not the endpoint. The criticality is in the application of the diversity. As important is the determination to search for practical and universal solutions and take advantage of common grounds in dealing with these differences. The ethical characters built through the Islamic value system must be translated and complemented with technical competency and supported by scientific practices. In adapting to the fast-paced developments in the world today, we need to supplement good moral judgement with practical and systematic approach that makes use of various theories and modelling. This is to prepare our talent in making inclusive decisions that are also based on quantitative valuation, on top of qualitative assessment. Embedding modern tools and techniques into the teaching of Islamic finance should help towards meeting this objective. In imparting these desired traits among the students of Islamic finance, the academia has a big role in setting the right intellectual climate to nurture visionary scholars. Ahead of admitting students, the universities that teach Islamic finance should first shift their mindset when measuring their key success indicators. The measure of effectiveness in an academia should not end at the point of students graduation but should extend beyond that mark to include students employability, their ability to contribute to practical and innovative solutions to the industry, and their impact to society at large. Therefore, members of the academia should measure their success using indicators beyond the day their students graduated. As an institution that is among the first to come into contact with our potential talent, universities have the privilege to mould future generations. To attract the brightest minds into the industry, universities should seek for quality talent as early as during student admission. Place high entry requirements for Islamic finance programmes to acquire the best brains for the industry. It is important to impose stronger quality controls at the entry points to capture outstanding talents with the right characteristics who have the potential to produce revolutionary ideas and philosophies. As Islamic finance is a relatively young sector, we need people who possess formidable intellectual capacity as change agents and leaders to move the industry into the millennium. Rethinking the fundamentals underlining the contemporary curriculum would be the catalyst for development of future Islamic finance education. With the aim to produce outstanding and multi-skilled graduates, the curriculum must strike a balance between academic learning and acquisition of important sets of expertise such as soft skills, agility, and the ability to articulate and sell ideas and strong problem solving ability. There is also a need to upgrade and revamp existing curriculum to equip students with knowledge from diverse disciplines. This will train the students to develop the ability to loop all knowledge and wisdom of previous civilisations and contextualise issues in accordance with the needs of modern times. The comprehension of multiple languages is also useful to understand intimately the success of previous Islamic dominions in different lingos. We want to mould and breed talents in Islamic finance that will become the great thinkers, great philosophers and great pioneers of the future. With these desired qualities ingrained in the curriculum structure, we will get to produce versatile and thinking talents that are highly sought after not only by the Islamic finance industry but by other fields as well. When it comes to quality, we need the IIUM graduates to be self-evident. As we aspire to be the global leaders, universities of Islamic finance should also continuously improve their learning pedagogy that is cutting-edge and innovative. Take the example from Harvard Business School that adopts case study methods of learning to produce effective decision makers recognised by the market. MIT, on the other hand, embraces action learning to provide empirical understanding through real life business experiences. In shaping the best talent for Islamic finance, we must develop teaching methodology and strategies that are able to groom our students holistically. Our teaching methodologies must be diverse and current. We must design an approach that transforms the education experiences of our students into the springboard for lifelong learning. Lastly, we need to professionalise the industry to raise the calibre of Islamic finance talent. Through increased professionalism and ethics, we can promote talents that will preserve the integrity and sanctity of the Islamic finance profession. IIUM can start this journey by adopting the professional standards advocated by the Chartered Institute of Islamic Finance Professionals when developing the curriculum of its Islamic finance programmes in the future. With the necessary accreditation by the Finance Accreditation Agency (FAA), the faculty can elevate the stature of its courses to form part of the students professional developments. Ultimately, the adoption of such standards will add to the prestige of this university as it reflects contemporary standards of the industries and in time attract more talented students to take Islamic finance as a vocation. It is our responsibility as a collective to have the vision and courage to step our game to another level in our endeavor to build talent for the Islamic finance industry. We have a call to answer, and we must not be afraid to fully liberate our thinking and silos and break new grounds. The exceptional Islamic scholars in the past have shown us the way and they have wellexemplified the path we should embark on. It is only with guts, the heart and the burning desire and passion that we can create original ideas and undertake radical changes that would bring about greater transformation in our industry. Islamic finance should be the leader, not a mere follower, not an adapter. Islamic finance should be at the cutting edge, not conventional, not mainstream. Islamic finance should be the trailblazer, not a laggard or a straggler. It is time for us to mould Islamic finance in a totally different light.

Title: SEACEN Seminar - "Impact of e-Banking and e-Commerce on Central Banking Funtions"
text: Governor's Speech at the Kijang Emas Scholarship Award Ceremony for Top Achievers in 2015 SPM Examination Speaker: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz Venue: Bank Negara Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur Language: Bilingual (English/Bahasa Malaysia) Speech/Interview Date: 31 Mar 2016 I am very pleased to welcome the audience to the 12th Golden Kijang Scholarship Award ceremony (twelve). This award is a special scholarship award and is in line with the Bank's commitment to produce continuous skilled manpower for the country. This Kijang Emas Scholarship differs from other scholarships offered by the Bank in that the recipients of this scholarship are free to choose the field of study of interest at a leading university in any country. Recipients of this scholarship are also not subject to the requirements to serve in the Bank. However, they are obliged to return to their homeland to work and contribute to the development of the country. This year, the Bank is pleased to announce the three recipients of the Kijang Emas Scholarship. They are Courtney Tang, Noor Adeebah Binti Mohamed Razif and Navineish Nair Rajan. I would like to congratulate them for their outstanding academic achievements and for their participation in co-curricular and sports activities. Let me also take this opportunity to recognise their parents and teachers. Their success is a culmination of your collective efforts, steadfast support and encouragement. To date, 48 high potential talents have been awarded the Kijang Emas Scholarship. The recipients have graduated or are currently pursuing their studies in diverse fields of study including Medicine, Engineering, Law, Economics, Dietetics, Actuarial Science, Accounting, Dentistry, Biochemistry, Genetics, Architecture, Psychology and Geophysics in top universities around the world such as MIT, the University of Chicago, University of Pennsylvania and University of Cambridge. Thus far, 21 recipients of the Kijang Emas Scholarship have completed their undergraduate studies, of whom 12 have returned while nine are still pursuing further specialisation before returning to serve our country. For the 2016 Kijang Emas Scholarship, we received a total of 146 applications from top SPM students scoring straight A for their 2015 SPM examination. From these applications, 22 students were shortlisted based on their SPM results and their involvement in co-curricular and sports activities. The students then underwent a rigorous evaluation process under the Banks "Kijang Academy" which assessed their technical and leadership competencies, as well as their values. We are pleased to award three outstanding students the Kijang Emas Scholarship this year. Having just completed their SPM examination, they will be enrolled into their respective pre-university programmes. Adeebah aspires to be a Biomedical Engineer while both Courtney and Navineish aspire to be Doctors. I am confident that all three of you will do your best and will contribute to the future of our country. The scholarships awarded annually are aimed at appreciating young Malaysians who are not only academically excellent and talented, but also have a good personality. Once again I would like to congratulate all the recipients of this scholarship. I hope that all of you will achieve success throughout the entire period of study. As a recipient of the Kijang Emas scholarship, in addition to striving to be excellent, you should also use the opportunities available to gain as much knowledge but still be flexible in using the knowledge. You should open your mind to new ideas and continue to adhere to pure values and morals. You are all role models for future young students. Finally, I wish you all the best and good luck to return to my homeland after graduation. Malaysia needs you to contribute to the future development and success of the country. That's it. Thanks.

Title: Opening Speech at the Launching of "From Sea to Summit" Exhibition
text: Deputy Governor's Opening Speech at the Launching of 'Chang Fee Ming - Terengganu: Selaut Kasih Sepantai Sayang' Exhibition Speaker: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB Venue: Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery, Sasana Kijang Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 27 Apr 2016 Welcome to the exhibition Terengganu: Selaut Kasih Sepantai Sayang. We are pleased to have the works of a highly regarded artists working in watercolour being displayed at this exhibition. The Bank has been fortunate to be able to bring together paintings done by watercolourist extraordinaire, Chang Fee Ming, from more than 30 different sources including private individuals. I have no doubt that this exhibition is one of biggest displays of his work ever assembled. I would like to thank the contributors and loyal collectors, on behalf of the Bank, for sharing their personal collection to be displayed here at our Museum and Art Gallery. Fee Ming, a self-taught artist has come a long way from his humble beginnings as a sign painter in the early 1980s. Since then, he has developed an impressive body of artworks that are acclaimed, exhibited and collected throughout the world. He has been bestowed international and local awards for his art and several publications that document his work have been launched since early 1990s. Regular auctions of his works at the premier auction houses Christies and Sothebys have also taken place since 1995. This is certainly a recognition of Fee Mings works as an artisan of unparalleled talent. A son of Terengganu, Fee Ming spent many years growing up in a Malay village by the sea of the East Coast. It is of no surprise that water, be it the Mekong River or the South China Sea is more often sensed than seen in his works. Being an acute observer of subjects that surround him, his earlier works focused more on landscape, which is also apparent in his recent works. Travel is and has always been the greatest source of inspiration for Fee Ming. Recognised as a contemporary painter-traveller par excellence, he has travelled to various parts of the world with greater attentiveness given to the South-East Asian region. He has drawn much inspiration from his tireless journeys and as evident in his works, his depth of understanding of Asian cultures and way of life is unrivalled. Defying expectations and stereotypes has always been part of his passion to understand people of all backgrounds. He is one that is driven by the curiosity to learn, to understand, and to capture the diverse ways of life in Asia through art. Fee Mings works bring to the fore the familiar cultures that we understand to exist but rarely encounter personally. For two decades, his richly detailed and vibrantly coloured paintings depict the stories of the rural people, culture and landscape of various places in Asia. In the beauty of his works there is also pathos. With this, he is known as a sensitive observer of culture as his works reinforces the importance of cultural understanding. Fee Ming has done Malaysia the service of capturing the setting that is intrinsic to the nations history, from the idyllic rustic scenes of paddy fields and kampong houses to the lives of communities by the sea. One of Fee Mings most featured masterpieces in this exhibition, the Orang ke Laut portrays the richness of the lives of fishing communities on the East Coast. Water, the element that helped the East Coast acquire the status of cradle of Malay civilisation is very much seen in this series. Viewers at this exhibition have the opportunity to observe up close Fee Mings mastery of technique. His first rate renderings of vibrant batiks that are the essence of aesthetics on the East Coast indicates his unwavering eye for fabric detail. In Terengganu, the cloths are more vibrant that in many places and it is this richness of palette that initially captivates Chang Fee Ming enthusiasts. His acute observations of the East Coast and views of weathered jetties and wrinkled hands captured using his chosen medium of watercolours truly acclaim that watercolours are highly appropriate to Malaysia and above all to the East Coast. We are proud to have decades of Fee Mings works that focus on Terengganu to be displayed at this exhibition. It offers us profound glimpses into the insights of Fee Mings portrayal of a part of Malaysia that inadvertently express how inter- communal harmony can be achieved. It is with greater understanding and acceptance of our different cultures that we can form a community that harmoniously interact to prosper beyond any expected boundaries. Through this exhibition, the Bank is giving its contribution to raise awareness and appreciation of the diversity that exists in our community by showcasing the nations arts that bring values and benefit to our society. To those whom are visitors and expatriates in Malaysia, this exhibition offers new perspectives on our cultures and its diversity. It draws viewers into a world that is unfamiliar even to most of its fellow citizens. At the same time, Fee Ming has given status to his subjects. He has made their unheard voices audible of which we hope would contribute towards certain aspects of nation building in a way that only an artist can. Above all, as the exhibition title suggests, he has done it with a lifetime of devotion. Thank you very much and I wish everyone an enjoyable and meaningful experience at the exhibition.

Title: Welcoming Remarks at the 22nd Asia/Pacific Group (APG) on Money Laundering Typologies Workshop
text: Encik Mohd Zabidi Md Nors Media Interview on Islamic Finance Speaker: Mohd Zabidi bin Md Noor Venue: Language: Speech/Interview Date: 29 Jun 2016 A. BIG PICTURE 1. What are the major wins for Islamic finance since its first introduction to the nation? The Islamic finance in Malaysia has made significant achievements over the past three decades. I would like to highlight three milestones which clearly encapsulate the phases of developments that the industry has gone through since its inception: The first is the transformation of Islamic finance in Malaysia from a niche market into the mainstream that has enabled Islamic finance to offer competitive financial solutions. This transformation is supported by strong foundations resulting from synergistic infrastructural developments, continuous institutional building, and robust regulatory and supervisory framework that have been put in place for over three decades. The market has grown by leaps and bounds. Prior to 2000, there were only two Islamic banks and two takaful operators in the country with total market share and takaful penetration rate of less than 5%. Now, Islamic banking assets have grown to capture more than a quarter (27%) of the total banking system while the takaful sector has increased its penetration rate to 14.8% of the populations. BNM has published our comprehensive statistical database that captures the growth of Islamic banking and takaful, alongside their conventional counterparts to allow continuous progress of the industrys growth and achievements. The key statistics have been published for many years in our Financial Stability and Payment Systems Report, while extensive data can be found in the Banks Monthly Statistical Bulletin that is available in the Banks portal. In terms of market players, there are now 16 Islamic banks and 11 takaful operators that offer competitive financial solutions with more than 100 financial products that are beyond the basic financial services to also include wealth management products, corporate financial solutions and investment banking services. Financial inclusion has also been strengthened over the years with Islamic financing to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) showing an encouraging upward trend of 29% average annual growth rate for the period 2010-2015. Financing opportunities for entrepreneurs are expected to be further enhanced with the recently launched Investment Account Platform (IAP) that serves as an online marketplace that matches investors with viable ventures. These market developments have further built resilience in the domestic market that enables Islamic finance to continuously contribute towards economic developments. Secondly, the development of strong foundations for Islamic finance has enabled Malaysia to further integrate with the global market. This is an important milestone in establishing connectivity between financial centres to facilitate greater cross-border Islamic financial transactions. Malaysia is currently the market leader for the sukuk segment with market share of more than 50% in sukuk outstanding since year 2000. Its vibrant marketplace has led to the issuances of multicurrency sukuk in US Dollar, Singapore Dollar, Chinese Renminbi and Japanese Yen as well as attracted foreign issuers to tap the domestic sukuk market including from Singapore, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kazakhstan and China. In terms of financial linkages, Malaysia has also strengthened cooperation with various countries such as the United Kingdom, Hong Kong, Turkey, Indonesia and Japan. These bilateral relations have paved the way for stronger Islamic finances offerings globally as well as resulted in the appointment of our local players as lead arrangers for some of the global sukuk issuances. These developments also have positive effects to our ancillary service providers where they gained prominence through greater engagement with the international market. It is also interesting that from another perspective, the internationalisation of Islamic finance provides a testimony to the inclusivity and versatility of Islamic finance that has extended beyond religious considerations. Now, customers of Islamic finance has expanded beyond the Muslim community to include customers of diverse backgrounds and origins. Growing presence of Islamic finance can also be observed in non-traditional markets such as in the European countries (e.g. Luxembourg and France), signalling greater acceptance of Islamic finance worldwide. I believe this phenomenon stems from the values and principles embedded in Islamic finance that are universal and cut across boundaries. In this respect, Islamic finance is indeed for all. The third milestone is Malaysias pioneering initiatives and thought leadership in Islamic finance that has enabled Malaysia to advance its innovation in the Islamic finance industry. Given the commitment to develop Islamic finance into a sustainable financial system, Malaysia has initiatied multiple developments that contributed towards further expansion of Islamic finance both locally and internationally. Key outcomes are reflected in major developments in the global sukuk market, for example in the issuance of the first sovereign and corporate sukuk. The Malaysian capital market has raised the bar for product innovation in the capital market through various innovative structures. The recent innovation is the issuance of the first Socially Responsible Investment sukuk in 2015 that links returns to the performance of the selected schools which are supported by proceeds from the sukuk investments. On the regulatory front, our modernisation of the regulatory framework (i.e. IFSA 2013) paves the way for the development of Shariah standards by the Bank. This regulatory initiative presents a monumental step, given its potential to reshape the Islamic financial landscape through enhanced clarity and certainty of Shariah contractual features in both Shariah and operational aspects. We aspire for these standards to be the international benchmark, given their distinct features that include operational guidances to support implementation of Shariah requirements at the institutional level. In our ambition to position these standards as a global reference point, translation work of these standards into Malay and Arabic language, in addition to English, has also been undertaken recently to further expand its outreach. At the back of such thought leadership lie in-depth research, thorough assessment and knowledge enrichment to provide continuous enhancements in the industry. In this regard, ISRA has played an instrumental role as a dedicated Shariah research arm as well as a knowledge repository for Islamic finance. It is recognised as one of the key players in Islamic finance research globally and has emerged as the top contributor in Islamic finance research between 2011-2013. This is complemented by our effort in capacity building and talent development that allows us to not only produce high-quality human capital but also enable us to export such talent abroad. INCEIF, for example, has enrolled more than 2,000 students from 80 countries and produced over 1,000 graduates to date. With talent enrichment and enhanced thought leadership, Malaysia will ensure continuous innovation in Islamic finance in tandem with the advancements of the market both locally and internationally. 2. What is the, next major milestone for the development of Islamic finance, moving forward? We have moved from domestic centric to being an international marketplace. Parallel efforts have been taken to develop a comprehensive financial system, while continuing to establish international linkages. All these initiatives have produced the desired outcomes as envisioned by the Bank. However, the rapid changes and dynamism of the industry require Islamic finance to strive even harder now. True to its name, Islamic finance needs to continuously carve its own branding and distinctiveness to provide wholesome value propositions. On this premise, the next frontier and the major milestone would be positioning Islamic finance to become more prominent and leading agent of positive change for the financial system, and operates within a network economy that is built upon shared values of integrity, inclusivity and sustainability. Greater attention will be devoted to value creation and value-based businesses that reflect the true essence of Islamic finance. What l meant is that Islamic finance moving forward should function as a value-based intermediation by emphasising on value-generating activities that could expand the spectrum of outcomes, which include both monetary gains and social impacts. As you are aware, the global movement towards responsible finance has become more apparent and stronger by the day, and with the increasing inclination towards value-based financial systems in the current atmosphere, Islamic finance is well-positioned to accentuate its innate features and become increasingly relevant in a world that is reorienting towards a greater sense of purpose. Islamic finance stands a great chance to take leadership in this evolution and further activate the market with a new business culture that emanates from its core underlying principles. In my view, there are two enablers that will set Islamic finance in motion in order for it to actualise this higher objective: Islamic finance to be at the forefront of technology-based finance.
