The technological disruption that brings about the advent of fintech opens doors of opportunities for the industry to take Islamic finance to the next level. Technology represents a powerful channel for Islamic finance to further deepen its value propositions and effectively deliver them in a more interconnected information society. Given these prospects, I believe the industry will rise to the occasion through a change in their thinking paradigm. This involves a transformation from a wait-and-see mentality to a more proactive mindset that aggressively capitalises on technology to innovate and challenge the existing norms. Instead of assuming the role of a mere adherent, the Islamic finance industry should emerge as a leader in technology-based finance that encompasses diverse aspects in financial businesses such as in product development, operational conditions, and even in strategic alliances. The fusion of state-of-the-art features in their future business models will enable the growth of Islamic finance to ride on technology on many fronts to sustain and elevate its positive trajectory. In fact, technological endowments may also advance the current small-scale segments in the industry, in particular enhanced penetration in the takaful sector and greater presence of Islamic finance in financing international trade. The recent establishment of the Investment Account Platform (IAP) as the first banking-intermediated internet-based platform in Islamic finance has already set the momentum for digitisation strategies to be the new normal in the banking business operational model. This development is set as catalyst for further emergence of other innovative delivery channels in Islamic finance that will improve efficiencies, reduce wastage and enhance customers overall experiences towards effective delivery of its value offerings. Islamic finance to inject a culture of innovation into the industry . The objective to transcend Islamic finance to a leadership position requires reinvention of the existing model that is preconditioned by holistic innovation and modification. At the heart of this requisite is the capacity of our talent to bring in innovative solutions and new approaches to the current system. Efforts to create conducive environment has to be accelerated and accustomed to a culture of innovation that energises talent to introduce new contexts and ideas. From my perspective, one way to encourage the creation of innovative ideas is through stronger industry-academia partnership where outcomes of breakthrough researches could be translated into practical business ideas and industrys practices. More effective collaboration between these two entities will foster effective information flow between the industries and the universities that ensure consistent understanding in visioning the future of Islamic finance and promoting practical and solution-driven researches. To further invigorate the market environment towards innovation, INCEIF will be organising a symposium to gather both industry players and academicians in a shared platform to develop and test breakthrough ideas in Islamic finance. This medium is envisioned to stimulate continuous generation of inspiring ideas to support innovations in the industry. B. REGULATION 3. Islamic finance and banking has now been incorporated into the key legislation. We are talking about the Central Banking Act 2009 and the IFSA. Are they sufficient for the moment? Yes, both the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009 (CBA) and IFSA 2013 are sufficient in terms of providing comprehensive legislations for the Islamic finance industry. The CBA 2009 in particular, has codified the recognition to the Islamic financial system alongside the conventional financial system. It is a very important provision as it reaffirms our commitment to continually develop Islamic finance in a dual financial setting. The Act also elevated the position of the Shariah Advisory Council (SAC) as the highest point of reference in any Islamic financial matters, thus strengthening its authority on Shariah matters as far as banking and takaful is concerned. I believe we are the only Central Bank that has embedded this highest recognition for the SAC in our Act. The IFSA on the other hand, further modernised the legislative framework for the Islamic finance sector in Malaysia. The Act not only provides for achievement of greater stability and growth of the industry, it also acts as a catalyst for greater legal and operational certainty for stronger end-to-end Shariah compliance. The Act also introduced an important foundation for the evolution of a contract-based regulatory framework for the Islamic financial sector. Furthermore, it has permitted the role of Islamic financial institutions to be expanded to include investment intermediation in addition to its existing credit intermediation. This is expected to further broaden and deepen the avenue for a more diversified Islamic banking business that can attract a wider customer base. I wish to bring your attention to the distinct provisions under Part IV of the IFSA on Shariah governance requirements. This provision provides greater clarity on the Shariah governance requirements, primarily on the role of the Board and management of the Shariah Committees and in particular the enforcement expectations. An important focus under this provision is the development of Shariah and operational standards for key Shariah contracts which l believe, would foster greater transparency and consistency of Shariah contract applications, thereby leading to greater certainty and strengthened Shariah compliance. Recent amendments to the Development Financial Institutions Act 2002 (DFIA) on Shariah requirements further ensure that the Islamic business activities of our development financial institutions (DFIs) comply with the same Shariah requirements as imposed on Islamic banks under IFSA. With such legal foundations in place, it is the onus of the industry to capitalise and take full advantage of the opportunities presented by CBA and IFSA in advancing the industry forward. Greater product innovations by Islamic financial institutions are expected to be encouraged through issuance of the various Shariah standards by the Bank. In particular, innovation in the area of investment intermediation would give them the additional competitive edge and at the same time, developing the appropriate expertise and internal system capabilities to identify and monitor the appropriate investment opportunities to support this new line of business. 4. What are the key building blocks still required for Islamic finance on the regulation front? Before l proceed to answer your question on the key building blocks, let me bring you back to the formation of the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB) in 2002, that serves as the global standard setting body to develop prudential standards for Islamic financial institutions. Over the last 14 years, the IFSB has been instrumental in issuing several prudential standards in Islamic banking, takaful and the capital market as part of its efforts to contribute towards the orderly stability of the financial system. In this regards, l wish to share with you an important document issued by the IFSB in 2010 i.e. "The Islamic Finance and Global Financial Stability Report" prepared by the Task Force on Islamic Finance and Global Financial Stability headed by the then Governor Zeti. This document encapsulates 8 key building blocks that are fundamental for policymakers worldwide in their efforts to strengthen the resilience and to ensure sustainability of the global Islamic finance industry. In the Malaysian context, l wish to note that we have implemented all the eight building blocks. For example, in the effective implementation and enforcement of prudential and supervisory standards issued by the IFSB, we have made great strides in this area, in particular by taking these standards into account in the formulation of our policies. Our Shariah Governance Framework for example is derived from the Standards on Islamic Governance Systems. Similarly, our Capital Adequacy Framework for Islamic Banks took several elements of the Capital Adequacy Standard issued by IFSB. In terms of disclosure requirements, the work undertaken by the Malaysian Accounting Standards Board and Malaysian Institute of Accountants to issue the Financial Reporting Standards for Islamic financial institutions (IFIs) further solidifies our commitment to strengthen the accounting, auditing and disclosure standards of IFIs as to facilitate effective monitoring and assessment of these institutions. An important building block which is a perennial issue to every IFI in most parts of the world is having in place an effective liquidity management for the industry. The Bank, with several other central banks have established the International Islamic Liquidity Management Corporation (IILM) in 2010, of which Malaysia is a founding member and its host country. The corporation has successfully introduced and facilitated effective cross-border Shariah-compliant liquidity management solutions through the issuance of a series of IILM sukuk issuance to meet the global liquidity demand of the industry. As at 1Q 2016, 23 series of IILM sukuk was issued with a cumulative amount of USD15.38 billion, making the current outstanding amount stand at USD2.2 billion. IILM has also remained as the largest and sole regular short-term sukuk issuer in USD, accounting for 48.9% of global short-term sukuk. The Bank has also strengthened our financial safety nets for the industry by providing adequate lender of last resort (LOLR) facilities and emergency financing mechanisms, as well as placing a Shariah compliant deposit insurance alongside the conventional deposit insurance. The Report also highlights the importance of enhancing capacity building and human capital development, in which the Bank shares similar aspirations through our pro-active, holistic and comprehensive approach by setting up the required ecosystem with the establishment of various talent institutions to address talent gaps in the industry. Other building blocks, such as developing an effective crisis management and resolution framework; as well as the macroprudential surveillance framework and financial stability analysis which are integral to strengthen the resilience of the industry have been captured in our various policies and guidelines. The rating agencies in Malaysia[1] are also actively involved in strengthening the rating processes as to be appreciative of the unique features and risk profiles of Islamic institutions and its instruments. C. INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT 5. From the central bank perspective, what are the key developments in the industry that has strengthened the industry? Why? Vision-setting for Islamic finance industry in the country has enabled coordinated infrastructural developments that solidify domestic market for subsequent international expansion. The BNMs Financial Sector Masterplan 2001-2010 (FSMP) and The Financial Sector Blueprint 2011-2020 (Blueprint) have outlined strategic reforms and envisioned future Islamic finance landscape to set the motion for the next phase of development in Islamic finance. These comprehensive roadmaps highlight key developments in these three broad areas namely on legislation, institutional building and talent ecosystem. The formulation of these strategic plans sets the overall direction of Islamic finance industry and ensures orderly development of Islamic finance in Malaysia. In Malaysia, continuous efforts in ensuring an enabling and accommodative legal infrastructure are undertaken either through dedicated legislations or amendments to the existing laws. Malaysias commitment to institute a dedicated Act for Islamic financial business has begun as early as the enactment of the Islamic Banking Act 1983 (IBA) and the Takaful Act 1984 that paved the way for the establishment of the first Islamic bank and takaful operator. In 2010, the Law Harmonisation Committee (LHC) was then established with a mandate to undertake objective reviews of other relevant laws that may pose legal uncertainty in Islamic finance and recommend appropriate changes to relevant stakeholders in providing legal recognition to Shariah contractual features. This has been important to support the consistency in application of Shariah contracts in Islamic financial transactions. After three decades, the diversity and maturity of the Islamic financial system has led to the development of IFSA 2013 as a significant milestone. It serves as a forward-looking Act that lays down the foundation for future Islamic finance developments as well as strengthens end-to-end Shariah governance and compliance primarily through the Shariah contract-based regulatory framework. As part of the dispute resolution mechanism, regulation on Financial Ombudsman Scheme introduced by the Bank in 2015 is aimed to enhance financial dispute resolution arrangements for consumers and to strengthen consumer protection. The Kuala Lumpur Regional Centre for Arbitration (KLRAC) has also published arbitration rules for Islamic banking and financial services Legal to facilitate legal redress for disputes relating to Islamic financial transactions. Progressive institutional building of Islamic banking players has increased market vibrancy in the Islamic finance industry. From a single player, the Islamic banking sector has grown in numbers following the involvement of conventional players through the Islamic windows set-up. The conducive environment provided by the Bank has facilitated the transformation of these windows into full-fledged Islamic banks licensed under the Islamic Banking Act 1983 and IFSA 2013. At the same time, we also brought forward the liberalisation of the Islamic banking sector by issuing three new licenses to foreign Islamic banks as per our international linkages agenda. The establishment of talent ecosystem comprising talent institutions such as INCEIF, CIIF, IBFIM, ISRA, ICLIF and ASAS enables sustainable development of professional and expertise that is required for Islamic financial services sector in Malaysia. The development of these specialised institutions, aims to develop financial services professional across the various levels, from the entry level for graduate to the leadership level for senior management and board of directors. While we are addressing the talent shortage, we need to orchestrate our effort in producing high-quality talent for Islamic finance covering specific areas like investment, risk management, governance and leadership, IT, capital as well as financial market. 6. What are some of the challenges facing the industry as a whole? Based on the major milestones that l have deliberated earlier on, Islamic finance industry would be challenged to meet the greater expectations to ensure sustainable growth momentum. Indeed, challenges are inevitable, and l am a strong believer that challenges, and to a certain extent positive disruptions are necessary to stimulate new thinking and approach if we wish to shape Islamic finance to new frontiers. Based on my preliminary observations after taking over the Islamic Banking and Takaful Department, the main issues facing the Islamic finance industry revolve around three broad areas, namely; i) leadership; ii) talent deployment and enrichment; and iii) awareness on Islamic finance. The latest innovative disruptions in the financial sector and the dynamic and fast-paced nature of the current environment leaves no option but for the industry to develop high-calibre talent and leaders in the industry whom are able to measure and assess their business directions, without solely depending on lagging indicators, but infusing leading metrics that align with the latest market trends and developments. Technological advancements through fintech and other solutions are already the megatrend, and the shortfall of effective and visionary leadership that is not able to recognise the vast opportunities in this development and to take actions upon them may prevent the market from making further strides in sustaining its growth. Those who fail to view technology as a stimulus for change may fall into complacency, and the thought that incremental innovation is adequate would find that one day they become irrelevant. As a relatively young industry, Islamic finance should be more nimble in embracing these trends, and hence the greater need of capable leaders with strategic visioning and the ability to implement bold ideas through unconventional ways in executing changes for the industry Another deeper issue that begs our attention is talent deployment. Despite the proliferation of Islamic finance education and training, we are still grappling with shortage of the right talent to lead and energise innovation and breakthroughs for the industry. Effective talent deployment and enrichment, in my mind, is the way forward in order to ensure existing capabilities are optimised while creating supportive environment that welcomes new ideas and perspectives. This calls for a balanced approach that acknowledges talent and potential strengths across all groups from the senior practitioners to the millennials and deploying them in the most synergistic way. The wealth of experiences among the senior practitioners can be benefitted through coaching and mentoring the young professionals to impart the wisdom and maturity of understanding the intricacies of finance and lessons to be learnt. On the other hand, the millennials whom are exposed to various technological advancements, such as real-time and speedy information gathering and global proliferation of information through social networking, should be seen as the young blood with new frames of mind that can offer fresh outlook and new insights. It is this group of millennials that should be empowered and encouraged to share their thoughts and visions to elevate Islamic finance to be a technology-based and technology driven industry. I believe that with the right talent deployment strategy, the industry will be able to maximise their capacity and unlock the potential strength that already lies within. On the third challenge, namely low awareness and understanding on Islamic finance, let me share with you some results from a national survey conducted by a leading consulting firm on Islamic finance awareness. We are startled that 53% of customers do not choose Islamic financial products because they are not aware of such products, while 24% of customers opt for conventional products over Islamic financial products as they perceive that there is no difference between these two categories. The survey also finds that 16% of customers still view Islamic financial products as solely for Muslims. These findings glaringly reveal that some misconceptions of Islamic finance still prevail to this day despite the more than three decades of its development in Malaysia. This includes misconceptions on the types of Shariah contracts employed in financial transactions, such as murabahah and bai inah where some quarters view that these contracts carry certain inherent risks, particularly for home financing and in the case of abandoned housing projects. This misconception is indeed untrue as the Shariah Advisory Council has thoroughly deliberated the details of the Shariah contracts used to ensure strong adherence to Shariah requirements. The development of Shariah and operational standards for key Shariah contracts fosters greater certainty and strengthened Shariah compliance, while encouraging a wider range of contracts to be used. The industry also plays a role in providing greater and continuous efforts to raise awareness on Islamic finance, and to address the prevalent misunderstanding on its product in order to promote further appreciation towards the value propositions of Islamic finance. For the takaful segment, raising awareness on takaful offerings is even more crucial in view of the low takaful penetration rate of 14.8% of the total population as compared to 40.5% of that in the insurance sector. Given Malaysias protection gap which is estimated to be worth RM2.5 trillion[2], there are immense opportunities for takaful to further penetrate the market. Alongside intensified consumer awareness on takaful, there must also be strengthened market conduct practices of takaful companies to create strong brand reputation that will reinforce the public trust in the ethical product propositions of takaful. D. SHARIAH ADVISORY COUNCIL (SAC) 7. How does the council function? 8. What are some of the key contribution of the Council? As a start, let me give you a brief overview of its background. The Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia (SAC) was established in 1997 and it takes on the role as the ultimate authority for the ascertainment of Islamic law for Islamic financial business. Since its establishment, the SAC plays a dynamic role in advising the Bank on Shariah issues relating to Islamic financial business carried out by the Bank. It is also a source of reference for Islamic financial institutions, the courts or arbitrators in respect of Islamic finance business. Furthermore, the SAC is also empowered to provide advice to any other persons as may be provided under any written law. These functions, as provided under section 52 of the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009 are supported by the autonomy that the SAC has which allows it to determine its own procedures. Their rulings are transparent and supported by written justifications. Over the years, these rulings are hardwired into the Shariah Standards. It is also important to note that, to reflect the critical role of the SAC, its members are appointed by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong from amongst persons who are qualified in Shariah, or who have knowledge or experience in Shariah, banking, finance, law or other related disciplines.[3] The SAC, as the final arbiter in the interpretation of Shariah principles on Islamic banking and takaful matters and practices has contributed immensely to the development of the Islamic financial industry in Malaysia. Of particular importance is its role in harmonising and standardising the Shariah rulings relating to Islamic financial business which have led to greater consistency and minimal disputes in the industry. For the industry, the publication of Shariah Resolutions in Islamic finance that contains the decisions of the SAC has been an important source of reference. This compilation includes the Shariah basis in the underlying issues and the SAC rulings on various contracts, products and other operational matters. The Shariah Resolutions are important documents which have been used extensively by the industry in developing their product offering. Now, as part of the strategy to strengthen the time-to-market for Shariah pronouncements, the Bank issues press release of SAC statements immediately after the SAC meetings. This release has enabled the industry to be informed of the latest decisions and its impact on their operations. The most recent and significant initiative relates to the Shariah Standards where the SAC has been instrumental in providing the Shariah pronouncements for 14 Shariah contracts, among others Murabahah, Mudarabah, Musyarakah, Tawarruq, and Istisna. These Standards aim to ensure end-to-end compliance with the Shariah rulings in the structuring of Islamic financial products and services, and is further complemented with the operational requirements to allow realistic implementation of the standards. The Standards also contain optional practices as guidance for the industry, particularly in relation to best practices. Moving forward, I also envision the SAC to be more dynamically involved in the industry. Firstly, the SACs members can leverage the stature by establishing themselves as global thought leaders and Islamic finance spokespersons. This would strengthen their positioning as the focal point of leadership and reference for the industry. Secondly, the SAC has strong potential to influence and shape the Shariah Committees of Islamic financial institutions to consistently be on the ground to ensure that they are able to champion customers needs by offering effectual references and solutions accordingly. Thirdly, in the area of research and human capital development, the SAC can also become the medium between the academia and the industry by facilitating the linkage between Shariah research and industry application. This initiative allows the SAC to help the industry in shaping their business models based on the research conducted and to drive innovation. Fourthly, I also believe that the SAC can contribute to the development of new talent in the Islamic financial industry by encouraging the industry to provide and foster more learning avenues and opportunities for Shariah graduates in order to generate qualified individuals whom are better able to contribute towards the development of the industry. 9. Reference to the SAC for court cases has been mandatory? How does this work? In regards to this question, I must make it clear that as stated under Section 56 of the CBA 2009, when Shariah issues are raised in court proceedings, reference to the SAC can be made by the court. To facilitate this process, the Bank has issued the Manual for Reference by the Court and Arbitrators to the Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia that provides guidance on what constitute Shariah matters; the expected time frame to respond; and the rights to be heard by the parties which could be in writing and/or orally. Essentially, it is also important to know that there are a few procedures and processes that need to be carried out prior to making reference to the SAC by the court. Firstly, before submitting a reference regarding Shariah issues to the SAC, the court and the arbitrator should refer to the published SAC decisions. If the court or arbitrator wishes to obtain more clarity on the Shariah issues, they may contact the SAC Secretariat to obtain information regarding the decisions. In the event that the issue is not available in the published documents or after clarifying with the SAC Secretariat, the court or arbitrator may refer the issue to the SAC. The manual has explicitly provided the types of Shariah issues that can be referred to the SAC and it must relate to matters that have been or have not been decided by the SAC. These questions include and are not limited to aspects of Islamic financial business such as business structures, products or services, implementations or operations, terms and conditions or documentation. I wish to clarify that in responding to Shariah issues posed by the court or the arbitrator, the SACs role is only to ascertain matters relating to the Islamic law. The SAC does not have the jurisdiction to make findings of fact, to apply law or to make a decision on an issue or case. It is because only the court or the arbitrator has the jurisdiction to do so. Once the SAC receives the issues from the court or the arbitrator, the SAC will identify and analyse the Shariah issues to ascertain the relevant applicable Islamic law. The court or the arbitrator will then make the decision by applying the Islamic law ascertained by the SAC on the case. After the SAC has made the decision on the Shariah issues raised by the court and arbitrators, it is mandatory on the court and arbitrators to be guided by the decision made. 10. Some quarters have suggested that it was unprecedented that another body outside of the courts - i.e. the SAC - makes a decision that is binding on the courts. Some have questioned the constitutionality of such SAC decisions? What is the current thinking on this matter at the central bank? I believe that it is very important for the public to comprehend that the role of SAC is limited and confined exclusively to the ascertainment of the Islamic law on Islamic financial business. Even though Section 57 of the CBA 2009 states that the court is bound by the ruling of the SAC, it does not detract the court from its judicial functions to resolve the disputes brought and submitted by the parties. This statement can be further supported by the Tan Sri Khalid Ibrahim vs. Bank Islam court case which highlights the importance of the SAC in resolving Islamic banking disputes without usurping the judicial power of the court. I would like to again emphasise that both civil and Islamic laws are required in resolving any Islamic banking disputes raised by the parties. However, given the defined role of the SAC, it is not legally empowered to perform any judicial function in determining the ultimate outcome of litigation. The judicial function to decide on the issues pleaded by parties remains with the court with the SAC as a reference point because the courts are well equipped only to adjudicate civil law issues whereas they are not trained to determine issues of Shariah compliance or non-compliance. As emphasised by Tun Hamid the former Chief Justice, the SAC would only state the principle as required by Shariah instead of saying whether the agreement is valid or otherwise. It is the court that will make a finding of facts and will apply the principles to the facts in order to arrive at a decision. Hence, the SACs involvement will in turn ensure a speedy and efficient ruling on an issue. ___________________________________________ [1] Malaysian Rating Corporation Berhad (MARC) provides ratings on a wide range of Shariah-compliant issuances by both domestic and foreign companies in the Ringgit-denominated Sukuk market. MARCs Islamic Financial Institution Governance Ratings introduced in 2010 provides a structured assessment of the quality of institutional governance in an IFI. MARC is also a technical partner to Islamic Development Bank (IDB)-initiated Bahrain-based Islamic International Rating Agency as part of efforts to create a sustainable and dedicated Islamic credit rating institution. RAM Rating Services Berhad (RAM) also provides ratings on a number of Islamic securities. [2] Based on a comparative study by the Malaysian Takaful Association and Actuarial Partners [3] The New Shariah Governance Framework 2009

Title: Speech at the Exhibition "For the Sake of the Motherland: 60 Years As a Central Bank"
text: Print Speech by Assistant Governor at Launch of Children's Day 2016 Presenter: Mr. Abu Hassan Alshari Yahaya / Venue: Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery, Sasana Kijang, Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: Oct 14, 2016 / Welcome to all those who attended the launch of Children's Day at the Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery this morning. This year, the theme "Art of currency" was chosen to support Bank Negara Malaysia's financial education initiatives as well as to provide exposure to the public, especially children, on the beauty of the works found in the currency we use today. This theme was taken in conjunction with the exhibition "Paperwork: Currency Art" which is taking place at the temporary exhibition space at Level 2, Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery. For the information of the attendees, financial education is an important element for Bank Negara Malaysia to form a financially literate society. Various initiatives have been made to support the Financial Sector Plan 2011 - 2020. Bank Negara Malaysia in collaboration with the Ministry of Education Malaysia has made every effort to integrate the financial education elements in the primary and secondary school curriculum in stages. Among the elements of prudent finance are the role of money, management and financial planning; savings and investments, sources of income and career; credit and debt management, as well as insurance coverage. At the Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery level, one of the ways to support financial education initiatives is through exhibitions and programmes such as the LATerasi Kewangan Exhibition, a financial literacy exhibition featuring a compilation of over 150 selected caricatures from 14 series of Buku Wang Saku by Datuk Lat; Exhibition "Know the Archipelago: The Money That Shapes the Region"; Malaysia's Numismatic Development History Talk Programme; as well as the celebration of Children's Day at the Museum. The Children's Day celebration began on 4 October and will continue until 30 November 2016. Various interesting activities have also been scheduled with the aim of improving the financial literacy level of children as well as giving children the opportunity to learn the history of currency. The programme included talks on "What is Money?", "Know Your Money" and "e-Payment Service". In addition, based on the concept of "Saving, Spending and Sharing", we also apply thrifty practices among children. "Let's Make Tabung Si Kijang" activities and visits to the Children's Gallery also educate children to make a choice between the needs and wants while spending the money they have as well as the importance of saving habits in order to be used in the future. Just now, we have witnessed how talented and brave the children from Tunas Kijang and Tadika Smart Reader are in performing in front of a large audience. It's a fun experience to see children show off their talents and show their creativity. We appreciate the cooperation provided by these two institutions. Every child needs their own "Hero", we as adults never despair of understanding and shaping children in order to be the best. In the eyes of underprivileged children, the "Feeding the Needy" Society is their "Wira" who has provided many aids such as basic necessities to survive as well as providing access to quality education to help change their fortunes in the future. These children may not have the opportunity to be here, but the Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery will approach them through the "School Bag Donation Campaign" initiative. It is jointly organised by the Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery with the "Feeding the Needy" Association with the objective of assisting underprivileged children in providing stationery and other educational materials for the school session next year. Thank you to Touch 'n Go Sdn Bhd, Royal Malaysian Police (PDRM), Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF), Fire and Rescue Department of Malaysia and other departments involved for their cooperation and support. Hopefully, this initiative will continue and be applied at all levels of society especially to children who participate in the programmes and activities provided. Thank you also to the attendees for being with us at the launch of Children's Day at the Museum 2016. I believe that this celebration will provide a meaningful experience for the children and parents who participate in the programme provided, as well as to learn the various knowledge available only at the Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery. Title: Welcoming Speech at the Life Insurance Association of Malaysia's 40th Anniversary Dinner
text: Governor's Remarks at the Opening of the Global Banking Leaders programme Speaker: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 28 Nov 2016 Thank you for the opportunity to speak at this opening of the Global Banking Leaders programme. Let me commend the efforts of all who have put together this flagship programme, particularly the Asian Banking School and Cass Business School. We have committed much resources and efforts in developing talent in the banking industry. Today, as part of a collaborative effort, we are charting a significant milestone for the banking sectors investment in human capital. This programme brings together some of the best resources and leaders in your respective fields. The structured content, courtesy of the Asian Banking School and Cass Business School, is comprehensive. But the unstructured content  the discussions among peers in the halls of this building, or the streets of Londons financial district  will be as invaluable. It is indeed befitting that a programme for global banking leaders should draw on broad and diverse global perspectives. As we face complex challenges in the financial industry, our most important strength must be the ability to harness different viewpoints, and to critique, challenge and improve them to deliver solutions that far exceed the sum of all its parts. Leadership in banking marches in lockstep with an unwavering commitment to professionalism. Until the Global Financial Crisis of 2007-09, the global economy was adding an estimated 150 million new consumers to the financial services industry each year. According to the World Bank, the rate of increase subsequently diminished in the immediate aftermath of the crisis. This is a sobering lesson on the consequences of lapses in professionalism, which ultimately led to a loss of trust in financial institutions. Episodes of widely publicised financial scandals in recent years are likely to have compounded matters. Public confidence and trust will ultimately be defined by the professional standards that our industry upholds. And the cost of professional lapses, both economic and social, will be far greater than experienced in the past as financial services become more inclusive and integrated globally. Therefore, it is important for us to start the first steps towards professionalising the banking sector. With these objectives in mind, there are two recent developments that would raise the standards of professionalism in Malaysias banking industry: 1. First, is the signing of the industry declaration in support of the Chartered Banking Programme, a flagship professional qualification for present and future banking leaders; 2. Second, is the expectation for all graduates who are employed by the banking industry to become members of the Asian Institute of Chartered Bankers, and complete a mandatory program on ethics and professional standards. Let me elaborate on these developments, BNM is a strong proponent of the Chartered Banker programme. It is our belief that such a programme can be a catalyst for change in the industry. The declaration by the industry today signals a clear commitment to the professionalisation of banking across all levels of the workforce. The introduction of professional banking credentials through the Chartered Banker program fills a conspicuous gap in ensuring that professional standards are observed and enforced in the banking industry. To unlock the full potential of the chartered banker qualification, the industry should recognise that this professional qualification contributes towards one's career advancement in the banking industry. Over time, the aspiration is to create a cadre of well-respected Chartered Banker holders that will serve as flag bearers for the banking profession. This qualification is a recognition that a banker should wear with great pride. Over the longer term, the industry should position the Chartered Banker professional qualification as a masters-level equivalent qualification. Continuous refinements and expansion of curriculum on a regular basis are imperative to ensure relevancy with contemporary and future demands for new skill sets. For this to happen, the input of the industry is essential. In this respect, the industry must take an active role in managing the changes that it wants to see to secure a deep talent pool for its future. This would entail working closely with AICB and the Asian Banking School. The industry must be the driver and support the changes needed to achieve a highly competent and professional workforce. It is us collectively, that will shape the future landscape of the industry. We can start the journey by taking a few meaningful steps. The drive for professionalism must begin at the entry level. Membership of AICB should be made mandatory. Graduates who are employed by the banking industry must become members of the Asian Institute of Chartered Bankers, and complete a mandatory program on ethics and professional standards. It is worth emphasising how important this seemingly small step is. Today, financial services is a complex business. Regulatory requirements, governance systems and decision-making frameworks are becoming more sophisticated. Making judgment calls have become an increasingly important part of dayto-day policy and decision making. In making these judgment calls, the ability to identify and resolve professional and ethical issues cannot be under-estimated. It is from this perspective that we need to educate and equip new entrants into the industry with good values, norms and ethics. As an industry we should not simply set our sights on incremental changes to address existing perceptions. We should aspire much more and higher - to rebuild a banking brand that is trusted and respected. To achieve this, as an industry we must continuously demonstrate our ability to deliver value to society. This is a higher call than just observing industry codes of conduct and ethics. It is about fulfilling a purpose expected of the profession. Because of the public trust entrusted to the banking profession, it should be expected that bankers are held to higher expectations that exceed requirements narrowly dictated by law or commercial interests. This should be driven by a strong sense of purpose. Not unlike the medical profession whose call is to save lives, the banking profession should fundamentally exist to contribute to the betterment of society. Today, banks rarely appear in the top 10 employers of choice, both globally and within Malaysia. Technology companies and others are becoming increasingly attractive employers of choice. One of the main reasons for this is the strong alignment of organisational direction and organisational purpose in many of these companies. Its employees feel a deep and emotive connection to the companys goals and purpose. This is hardly surprising. A Harvard study in 2014 found that a collective sense of purpose is an overwhelming differentiator in attracting top talent. The banking sector must similarly create a strong sense of purpose that reflects the needs and concerns of society  such as promoting sustainable finance, improving financial literacy and assuring inclusive access to financial services. Only then can we realise the full potential of positive finance in advancing social and economic development. Before I end, it will not be complete if I do not touch on recent developments in our ringgit exchange market and Bank Negaras announcements to reinforce and strengthen our market from being adversely impacted by speculative activities. When it comes to the development of the financial markets and our thinking behind ringgit policy, our philosophy has always been the same. Our market activity and exchange rate should reflect the economic realities of Malaysia. As such, when it comes to the pricing of the ringgit exchange rate, it should never be disconnected from real economic activities in the onshore market. This brings me to our view on the offshore ringgit non-deliverable forward (NDF) market. In recent weeks, speculative position taking in the offshore ringgit NDF market has had adverse impact on the domestic foreign exchange market. While the ringgit faced the same external shocks as many neighbouring countries, activities in this opaque market had exacerbated the depreciation pressure by disrupting the price discovery process. This, for me, should not be tolerated. For a small but highly open economy like ours, we face unique challenges. The volatile and erratic movements in the financial markets render the opening up of financial markets and continuous liberalisation more challenging. Nevertheless, as an economy that operates on free market principles, it is still a path we need to take. But we need to open up responsibly  we have to ensure the markets, players and products in our economy are transparent, fair and serve their intended purposes. Paradoxically, while there has been tremendous demand globally for transparency on governments and policymakers, the same level of intensity is not necessarily reflected for financial market players. Perhaps it is time to change the rules of the game. Financial market players, especially those in the NDF market, need to be as transparent as the demands they expect of others. Similarly, jurisdictions that govern them ought to make this opaque market more transparent and accountable. On the Banks part, our actions, including recent measures, are not new. The Bank has been taking measures to reduce the speculative and damaging influence of NDF since the early 2010s. It is our responsibility to ensure orderly functioning of the foreign exchange market and maintain public confidence in the financial system. The recent actions by the Bank are merely to reinforce our existing policy on offshore trading of the ringgit. Besides reducing the detrimental effects of financial market speculation on our markets, these policy reinforcements are aimed at instilling greater transparency, integrity and fairness in our financial markets. This is our responsibility as regulators and policymakers, of financial market development that aspires to see a more open and transparent market. On that note, it gives me great pleasure to join the score of executives here this morning who have been chosen as participants of the Global Leadership Programme. I have great confidence that you will find encouragement, reinforcement and inspiration throughout the program to become better and more enlightened leaders in your own organisations.

Title: Speech at the Launch of "Ombak: Breath of Life" Exhibition
text: Governor Muhammad Ibrahim's Closing Speech at the 2017 Financial Carnival Presenter: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB / Venue: Putra World Trade Centre (PWTC), Kuala Lumpur / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: Jan 15, 2017 / I would like to express my appreciation to the Honourable Brigadier General Khairy Jamaluddin, Minister of Youth and Sports, for taking the time to be with us and deliver the closing speech of the Financial Carnival. The support and cooperation of the Ministry of Youth and Sports for efforts to raise awareness among the youth on financial services, knowledge of financial management and consumer protection, we appreciate it. Indeed, the youths are a generation that will play an important role in realising the country's aspirations and aspirations towards National Transformation 2050. On behalf of Bank Negara Malaysia, I reaffirm our desire to continue to develop an inclusive financial ecosystem, ensuring that all walks of life benefit from a wide range of quality and affordable financial products, services and advice. Bank Negara will also continue to enhance financial literacy initiatives to enhance consumers' financial skills. Various initiatives are being and will be implemented to expand the learning of financial knowledge at the school and university level as well as high-impact financial education programmes for youths and adults. I have just been informed that as of 12 noon today, the edutainment Financial Carnival has attracted more than 20,000 visitors. From the feedback received, many visitors can learn for the first time the existence of various financial services channels provided by the relevant institutions and agencies. Visitors are from all walks of life including low-income groups, housewives, disabled people, students and school children, including from outside the Klang Valley. Early information, more than 8,000 visitors took this opportunity to receive individual advice from Bank Negara Malaysia, the Credit Counseling and Management Agency (AKPK) and the Financial Services Ombudsman (OFS). In addition, more than 500 savings accounts were opened and more than 500 financing applications amounting to RM94 million were made, including from small and medium enterprises. I am sure all visitors can make the most of the knowledge gained, especially on the importance of wise financial management. I am also excited about the level of financial awareness of the youths, as highlighted in the inter-university oratory competition, where a total of 38 participants from 16 universities competed. Various thoughtful opinions were voiced by these students on the issue of financial management and financial literacy from the perspective of the youths. I would also like to take the opportunity here to express my gratitude and appreciation to all the ministries, government agencies and financial institutions who have also worked together to mobilize as well as various contributions and sponsorships to realize the Financial Carnival. Without strong cooperation and support from all parties, this initiative would not have been possible successfully.

Title: Speech at the Briefing to Chief Executive Officers of Banking Institutions on the Corporate Debt Restructuring Committee
text: Financial Technology Enabler Group (FTEG) Chairman's Opening Remarks at Finnovasia KL Speaker: Aznan bin Abdul Aziz Venue: Pullman City Centre Hotel, Kuala Lumpur Speech/Interview Date: 20 Mar 2017 Language: English It is my great pleasure to deliver the final opening remarks at the inaugural Finnovasia KL, gathering fintech executives, entrepreneurs and investors from all over the world. Our motivation to promote innovation Few would dare to dispute the impact of technological change in reshaping the delivery and consumption of financial services. We have reached the tipping point. Where consumers and investors alike, now demand not only ease of use, but personalised digital interaction with their finances. Fintech has opened up new opportunities, in a way not seen before. It gives: 1. The potential to provide value added and customer focus services through the delivery of customised solutions using biometric technologies, big data and predictive analytics; 2. The potential to serve untapped markets as it opens up opportunity to reach out to market segments which would not otherwise be cost-effective. This is made possible by how agile and able for fintech in monetising data; 3. The potential to improve market and system efficiency for back-end operations. This includes the use of predictive analytics to undertake real time risk simulation and management; and 4. The potential to enhance compliance and regulatory productivity by automating mundane compliance tasks and reduce operational risks associated with meeting compliance and reporting obligations. Our motivation in supporting the development of fintech is in-line with our mandates and functions in the development of sound, progressive and inclusive financial sector while preserving financial stability. Innovation brought about by many exponential technology and advances can be disruptive to many of us  markets and consumers alike. But the power of innovation, if harnessed effectively could contribute to efficiency gains, creation and better access to new innovative fintech solutions. For Malaysia, we are exploring several critical enablers to provide the enabling infrastructure and the framework to maximise opportunities whilst minimising risks to financial stability and consumers. These are: 1. Facilitate the creation of Centralised Digital Identity to allow for effective and efficient management of customer due diligence and know your customer process; 2. Enabling Open API to allow for technology developers to tap into shared data for development of new and innovative solutions without compromising data security; 3. Facilitate the establishment of Community-based Cybersecurity Centre to allow for sharing of threat intelligence, apply best practices and enhance collective capabilities to deal with cyber-threats; 4. Enabling the use of Cloud Computing to allow for efficient and secure storage of data without compromising data security; and 5. Facilitate the adoption of Distributed Ledger Technology to allow for secure and efficient offering of financial services, particularly in addressing counterparty risks. We will work very closely with the industry and other competent authorities in those areas and we welcome your support in moving forward, including views and feedback. We also aspire to take our effort to another level. We want to solve real issues that matters to the people. And we want to create impact. This is precisely why we want to engage the public in getting ideas or wish list on what aspects of the financial services that can be improved using technology. We are initiating a call for participation known as Fintech Hacks. This initiative is for the public to submit their innovative ideas through our various electronic channels for the improvement of the financial services sector. There are several other related activities in the pipeline that we expect to launch this year. Check out our website, for latest updates. Myths and misconceptions Today, I would also like to take an opportunity to dispel some myths and misconceptions on our stance and regulations on fintech. First, the Bank is not open to new innovation As regulator, we have to walk the fine line between safeguarding financial stability and promoting innovation and growth. However, let me make clear that the Bank is open to new innovation. The Regulatory Sandbox that was issued in October 2016 clearly reflects our openness in facilitating value-added and meaningful innovation. With the Sandbox, we are willing to flex rules and regulations to enable testing where we deem that the solution contains strong value proposition and the risks can be appropriately contained. This will also allow us to reduce time to market for new innovative products, which under normal process might get stifled by regulatory hurdles. It enables us to ensure that our regulatory framework is relevant and responsive to innovations that can bring game changing outcomes to our financial services sector. Second, there will be regulatory status quo after the Sandbox For us, one of the underlying principles of the Sandbox is also to allow us to monitor and assess whether measures and safeguards in place are adequate to address the risks posed by the innovative solution. We are open to create new regulation or amend existing regulation to allow for such solution to be offered in the market under licensed regimes. The Sandbox allows us to learn from innovators and adapt to new and emerging risks emanating from the offering of new solutions. Thirdly, fintech company must collaborate with financial institution to participate in Sandbox Our Sandbox allows for standalone fintech company to test their innovative solution as long as it is able to prove that it meets the eligibility criteria and that it has appropriate measures and safeguards in place. In fact, most of the innovative applications received for the Sandbox are indeed from the fintech companies. Having said that, fintech company that collaborate with financial institution could gain added advantage from guidance and support provided. Additionally, it is also a given that only products or services that come under our purview of regulated businesses under our laws and regulations should come to test under the Sandbox. If you are peer-to-peer lending or equity crowdfunding provider you may wish to contact Securities Commission Malaysia. With the Sandbox, we hope to see game-changing results that unlock the value of technological developments. This is in line with our aspiration to deliver more efficient, innovative, accessible and safe financial services for consumers. With this in mind, we wish to welcome more innovative companies to submit their applications to participate in the Sandbox. We hope to see more innovative ideas that would contribute to Malaysias financial services industry, which will ultimately benefit Malaysians and the Malaysian economy, while rewarding risk-taking and creative innovators. Malaysia is fintech ready! Before I end my speech, let me put in perspective what Malaysia has to offer in the broader context of fintech growth and development. We believe Malaysia is uniquely positioned to be the test bed for innovative fintech solutions for emerging markets. A few factors give Malaysia the comparative advantage: First, is Malaysias leadership in strategic areas such as Islamic finance and financial inclusion. We are ranked highly among the top countries for the development of Islamic finance and we have also been recognised for our passion and commitment to advance financial inclusion agenda. This would naturally translate into our focus and support to fintech innovations that are tailored to serve these agendas. Second, Malaysias consumers profile and challenges are similar to those in other emerging markets. We are a middle income country with respectable Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growths of 4-5% and sizeable population of approximately 30 million people with high mobile and internet penetration. As such, Malaysia provides an ideal fintech consumer base. In addition, Malaysia ranks highly among other emerging markets in World Banks Ease of Doing Business. We are ranked rd 23rd overall in 2016 World Banks Ease of Doing Business, one of the highest among the emerging markets. Malaysia is recognised for pro-business policies and wide range of incentives to investors.This includes Multimedia Super Corridors (MSC) attractive incentives provided by the Malaysian Government. Finally, there is strong and holistic support from key stakeholders in driving not only the fintech ecosystem, but also ecommerce and SME entrepreneurship. The Bank collaborates closely with other competent authorities including Securities Commission (SC) and Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation (MDEC) to provide enabling infrastructure and conducive regulatory framework for a vibrant fintech landscape. All these factors put together make Malaysia an ideal ground for fintech companies to test and validate their solution before moving on to a bigger market. Naturally, we want to see more Malaysian-based companies coming up and expanding not just in Malaysia but also in other emerging markets, particularly within the ASEAN region. It has been almost a year since we established the Financial Technology Enabler Group (FTEG). In that short period of time we are starting to observe attitudes shift. However, much is still desired and that there is genuine need for paradigm shift. We must embrace technology and at the same time be mindful of the challenges that come with it. I call upon all of us to have a change in attitude in adapting to the rapidly changing fintech industry. Thank you.

Title: Keynote Address at the LOMA/LIMRA 17th Annual Strategic Issues Conference for CEOs and Senior Executives
text: Assistant Governor's Speech at the Malaysian Association of Money Services Business Annual Dinner 2017 Speaker: Puan Jessica Chew Cheng Lian Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 29 Apr 2017 It is my great pleasure to be here with you this evening at the annual dinner of the Malaysian Association of Money Services Business. I remember a time six or seven years ago when the Bank gathered the industry together at the auditorium in the headquarters of Bank Negara Malaysia to explain the new legislation that was being introduced for the industry. The industry then, and the industry today, is almost unrecognisable. You would have heard this said a few times now, and I think it keeps getting mentioned because the change has been so striking. Tonight, the industry will recognise companies that are leading the way in terms of exemplary customer service to the public, as judged independently by a global consulting firm. This is yet another reminder of how far the industry has come. In the last six years, the industry has almost doubled the value of money services transactions conducted through licensed MSB companies. We estimate that this included about 43% of worker remittances previously conducted through informal or illegal channels, that are now captured within the formal system. On average, MSB companies have increased their turnovers by more than 16%. More than half of the industry today is made up of MSB companies with annual turnovers of at least RM50 million, compared to only a third of the industry operating at this level 6 years ago. The public can conduct money changing and remittance transactions at over 2,500 locations nationwide, more than double the number of access points in 2011. An increasing number of companies are also offering online options for customers to conduct remittance and money changing transactions. The Bank is also happy to note that the industry received a positive assessment under the most recent mutual evaluation exercise conducted on Malaysia by the Asia Pacific Group (APG) on Money Laundering. As you know, the APG is an international organisation committed to the implementation and enforcement of international standards against money laundering and the financing of terrorism, working closely with organisations like the Financial Action Task Force, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The assessment is a rigorous process, so a positive assessment is something that the industry can take great pride in. In its most recent 2015 report, the APG specifically noted that mitigation of money laundering and terrorist financing risks in the MSB sector has improved significantly in recent years, while acknowledging that there are challenges among smaller companies that we are collaborating together with the industry to address. One of the key steps that we are taking is to provide compliance officers with appropriate training, and then supporting them to be professionally accredited. The MSB industry in Malaysia is also highly competitive, with among the lowest remittance costs in comparison with other markets. I know that this has been an issue of some concern among some players in the industry as margins have continued to narrow. As in any other industry, an environment of healthy competition that delivers more choice, provides better service and encourages innovation, generally benefits society. Tonights awards are a good example of MSB companies that have stepped up to deliver an outstanding customer experience in order to attract and retain customers. Many strategic partnerships between companies in the industry have also been formed over the years in response to greater competition. This has unlocked value for the companies by opening up new business opportunities and increasing cost efficiencies. Throughout history, whether in an organisation, an industry or a nation, progress and development have always been achieved through a process of creative destruction, adjustment and evolution. The industry will continue to transform and evolve, and in the process, it become more efficient and advanced in delivering superior products and services to the public. Bank Negara Malaysia remains committed to ensuring that the market for money services continues to function efficiently and sustainably in the best interests of consumers, and a competitive market is an important part of this process. The industrys remarkable development has not gone unnoticed. More than a few countries have been interested to study and learn from Malaysias experience. This prompted Bank Negara Malaysia to document the industrys transformation in a box article that we published in our latest edition of the Financial Stability and Payment Systems Report. Today, the industry stands among the more developed money services markets in the world and our MSB companies have a good reputation that will open doors for growth opportunities both within and outside Malaysia. The industrys credibility has also avoided the negative impact from de-risking strategies by banks that have been experienced in other countries. We should not forget however that good reputations are hard to earn, and easily lost. So while we have come a long way, a number of priorities must continue to stay in clear focus for the industry to progress further. Let me just mention three of these priorities. First, we must continue to work at reducing transactions that are conducted through informal channels  in particular, through education and enforcement activities. Since 2012, the Bank has taken enforcement actions against 140 illegal MSB operators. This included criminal and civil actions pursued against over 70 companies. We will continue to intensify our efforts on this front. Second, we must continue to raise compliance and professional standards across the industry, regardless of size. Every company that holds a licence must be able to meet the expectations that have been set to protect the integrity of the financial system and provide a high standard of service to the public. Over the years, more companies have been given licences for longer periods. This means that we have seen good improvements in the quality of compliance and operations. Companies that continue to receive shorter-term licences need to take stronger measures to address the issues that we have raised. Third, we should expect that financial markets will continue to remain volatile in the period ahead. It is therefore important for the industry to improve market arrangements to ensure that MSB companies will be able to respond efficiently to changes in demand for currencies by consumers and businesses. Such arrangements have to include better planning and management of currency stocks as well as sourcing strategies to ensure the ready supply of currencies at efficient market rates. Tonights MSB customer experience awards reflects an industry that aspires to place the customer first. A price advantage can be lost easily to your competitors, but a strong customer service culture is much harder to copy. Those of you that voluntarily took part in this process are sending a clear signal that your company and this industry takes customer service excellence seriously. The idea of customer service excellence is not only about the quality of service; it is also about the industry conducting itself in a way that builds trust in the industry. The Association therefore is to be commended for undertaking this initiative, as should all MSB companies that have supported it. I am also very happy to note the Associations launch of the MSB App this evening --- which will provide consumers with convenient access to price comparisons, locations of MSB companies, customer reviews, and avenues to lodge complaints and report illegal MSB activities. This App reflects an increasingly digitalised society and business environment where demands for greater transparency, convenience and consumer engagement have become the norm. The MSB App is a great example of how financial technology, or fintech, is changing how customers experience financial services. The possibilities are almost boundless as we are discovering through Bank Negara Malaysias recently launched fintech hacks. This is a project where we are inviting the public to submit ideas to improve financial services. Let me mention some of the suggestions we have received in the area of money services. Allow tourists to exchange their unused foreign currencies for e-money that can be used to make purchases at any airport merchant worldwide. Develop a peer-to-peer currency exchange app that will allow travellers to meet up and exchange currencies. Provide an app that will allow individuals to book and pay for foreign currencies using their mobile phones, and have the currencies delivered directly to them. And enable e-KYC for remittances. These represent opportunities for MSB companies to innovate and continuously improve on products and services that are meeting the needs of todays consumer. Companies can also come forward and test their ideas in Bank Negaras Regulatory Sandbox, and we will facilitate a safe environment for companies to develop viable solutions to identified problems. This is the time for MSB companies to be forward-looking, not hold on to the past; to be agile and responsive to change, not slow to evolve; to be bold and ambitious, not reactive; and to be secure in strong professional and ethical standards for conducting business, and not exposed to practices that can harm the industrys image and reputation. The Bank has every confidence in the industrys ability to grow and develop further from strength to strength, well supported by a dynamic Association that has had a key role in driving many of the accomplishments that have brought the industry to this point. On that note, thank you for having me here this evening. Congratulations to all the recipients of the customer service excellence awards, and all MSB companies that are present here for supporting the important work of the Association. On the part of the Bank, we look forward to the implementation of the industrys five-year strategic blueprint up to 2020. Bank Negara Malaysia will continue to engage constructively with the Association and industry on these initiatives to develop a modern, dynamic and progressive industry.
