text: Governor's Speech at the Exhibition "For the Sake of the Motherland: 60 Years as a Central Bank" Presenter: Datuk Nor Shamsiah Mohd Yunus / Venue: Sasana Kijang / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 12 Dec 2019 / Indeed, the Royal Institution has a special position in the historical fold of Bank Negara Malaysia. Despite the changes and challenges of succession, what remains is the portrait of the first Duli Yang Maha Mulia Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Almarhum Tuanku Abdul Rahman ibni Almarhum Tuanku Muhammad which adorns the right side of each denomination of our banknotes, from the first series to the present series. This portrait is not only the main identity of Malaysian banknotes known worldwide, but it also contains security features to prevent counterfeiting and ensure the integrity of Malaysian banknotes. 60 years ago, on 24 January 1959, the country witnessed an important event, the opening of Bank Negara Malaya which was officiated by His Royal Highness Almarhum Tuanku Abdul Rahman. The official opening of Bank Negara Malaya sets the foundation or foundation for the economic and financial development of Malaysia as an independent nation. At the event, he said: "Indeed, the establishment of Bank Negara will no doubt be recorded in the history of this state as one of the largest events since Merdeka. The Central Bank will have a heavy responsibility and an important role in the economic and financial affairs of the state". To date, what His Majesty has said has been an important thrust for us to carry out our duties for the well-being and development of the country. Bank Negara Malaysia always faces dynamic and complex challenges. It has a huge responsibility, and every decision has an impact on millions of Malaysians. This is the trust of Malaysians and this should not be taken lightly. In conjunction with this year's 60th anniversary, Bank Negara Malaysia, for the first time, presented the Exhibition "By Homeland: 60 Years as a Central Bank" which is a retrospective narrative in the context of the development and development of Bank Negara Malaysia as an institution. This exhibition: First, it will shed light on bank Negara Malaysia's broad mandate and role; Second, celebrate meaningful achievements as well as important events, and; Third, expose the challenges and difficult and complex actions faced by Bank Negara Malaysia. Not just a story of history, the aspiration of this exhibition is for each individual to dive into the role of Bank Negara Malaysia and its effects, as well as how they can play a collective role towards sustainable economic development. This is aimed at invigorating the spirit of identity and nationalism among the community. Translating the transformation of the economic landscape as well as its impact on the public, is not an easy one. Often seen as a horizontal topic, complex technical terms such as monetary policy, inflation, Overnight Policy Rate or Overnight Policy Rate, foreign exchange rate and financial stability should be clarified accurately and concisely in order to be easily understood. To achieve this, this exhibition has been injected with interactive, emotive and inclusive concepts through a combination of artefacts, old documents as well as interesting nostalgic films and photos that we have rarely seen before. The exhibition brings together behind-the-scenes stories from Bank Negara Malaysia's internal perspective through exciting partnership interviews from over 60 staff and former staff loaded with teaching and inspiration. The storytelling begins with the shouting story of the development of Bank Negara Malaya by a small group of 67 early workforces and limited space, further to the moment when Bank Negara Malaysia replaced the Currency Board as Malaysia's sole currency issuer in 1967, the empowerment of the local banking sector's supervision until the era of fintech innovation and subsequently to the discussion on the future of virtual banking as well as, advisory initiatives and services of financial issues. Nevertheless, the sky is not always sunny. Therefore, the exhibition also recalls the critical moments of the country's storm during the 1985 Deposit Takeaway Crisis and the 1998 Asian Financial Crisis and how Malaysia planned its own recovery efforts that were considered radical. 'If a picture's worth a thousand words, an object holds priceless memories'. The exhibition also showcases more than 100 exhibits as early as 80 years old until the latest. These include, the printing machine and the famous 'Banana Money' printing plate in the Japanese occupation, the unfit notes that were minted, the earliest ledger book that recorded the amount of currency stock in circulation, the phone used in the Operating Room during the 1998 Asian Financial Crisis, the old annual reports, the vintage tube collection and the evolution of the Bank's staff clothing ethics during the 60 years of service. The research and collection of this exhibition material would certainly not have been realized without the support of many parties. I am very grateful that this exhibition also looks at the collaborative efforts between Bank Negara Malaysia and the institutions/organizations that patronize the history and heritage of the country, government agencies, statutory bodies and financial institutions. Congratulations to these institutions on the continuous preservation and conservation of national treasures. As a complement to this exhibition, we also brought the '60 Bank Negara Malaysia Collection' Art Exhibition at the Art Gallery. The Bank's support for the local art industry is a testament to our confidence in the art treasures as a manifestation of the socio-economic development of the country, both physically and intellectually. The exhibition features 60 local artworks, acquired since the 1960s from various genres and materials, the work of pioneering, modern and current art artists. The Central Bank of Malaysia Act gives a clear mandate to Bank Negara Malaysia to maintain monetary and financial stability conducive to the sustainable growth of the Malaysian economy. In order to carry out this trust well, the role of Bank Negara Malaysia as an independent and professional central bank as provided by the Act is essential to ensure that the mandate given can be fulfilled effectively and enable Bank Negara Malaysia to focus on the economic and financial system perspective for the long term. Despite the increasingly challenging global environment and volatility in the international market. Bank Negara Malaysia as the protector and trustee of the country's financial system, will continue to hold that mandate and make it a priority. Nationally rooted, global-minded  Bank Negara Malaysia will ensure the steps taken in tandem with the passage of time to provide high-quality, integrity and professional services for the benefit of the country. Lastly, on behalf of Bank Negara Malaysia once again, I am grateful for the approval of Tuanku to launch the Exhibition "For the Sake of the Motherland: 60 Years as a Central Bank".

Title: Assistant  Datuk Zamani Abdul Ghani's Speech at the Launch of the "Premium-Link" Website for the Insurance Industry
text: Print Assistant Governor's Welcome Speech at SME Financing Seminar and Finance Clinic Presenter: Mr Adnan Zaylani Mohamad Zahid / Venue: Geno Hotel Shah Alam / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 12 Dec 2019 / On behalf of Bank Negara Malaysia, I welcome the attendees to the SME Financing Seminar and Finance Clinic today. We are pleased to have the honorable Deputy Minister of Finance to take the time to complete the launch of this SME capability strengthening initiative. We would also like to thank you for the support and cooperation of the Ministry of Finance, Government agencies, financial institutions and all stakeholders involved in the success of this initiative. For your information, this session is a continuation of BNM's efforts to enhance SMEs' knowledge and understanding of financing issues. During 2019, a total of 21 programmes at 7 locations were held including Miri, Kuala Terengganu, Melaka, Kangar, Sandakan, Langkawi and Selangor which were attended by more than 10,000 local entrepreneurs. 85% of the participants of the SME Financing Seminar and Finance Clinic stated that their knowledge and understanding has improved by attending this program. In addition, various issues are discussed interactively with this business community. Among the key issues raised include borrowing eligibility, lack of awareness and understanding of the financing schemes available to SMEs as well as loan scheduling and restructuring. As the global economy moves towards a more moderate growth situation, the Malaysian economy remains resilient, supported by strong fundamentals. Our funding ecosystem is strong and works well. As at end-October 2019, the total accumulated financing was RM314 billion or 813,000 SME accounts, of which financing approvals for the first ten months of the year amounted to RM59 billion to 98,000 SME accounts. Various holistic measures and initiatives have been taken to continuously improve the financing ecosystem and support the growth of SMEs. This includes encouraging more innovation from financial institutions, enhancing the efficiency of financing processes, strengthening SME finances and enhancing credit guarantee products. However, the fact is that there may be a handful of SMEs who have difficulty accessing financing. Ongoing initiatives to address financing constraints by some SMEs are one of the priorities of Bank Negara Malaysia and banking institutions. Among them are improvements in document requirements, support for SMEs in the field of financial management as well as new approaches in credit assessment through the use of alternative technologies and data. The implementation of the online financing application platform ("imSME"), operated by Credit Guarantee Corporation (CGC), has helped to reduce search costs and expand funding sources to meet SME financing needs. I am pleased to share that imSME has approved RM144 million in funding through this portal since its launch in February 2018. In addition, more than 7,500 entrepreneurs who were unable to match the financing at the portal were assisted by imSME Financial Advisors. These accredited advisors provide business or financial guidance and advice so that applicants can fix existing deficiencies in obtaining business financing. The SME financing ecosystem is also complemented by existing initiatives introduced by Bank Negara Malaysia including the Micro Financing Scheme, Credit Guarantee Scheme by CGC, BNM Fund for SMEs amounting to RM9.1 billion and the Small Loan Settlement Scheme to assist SMEs who have problems repaying loans. Bank Negara Malaysia is also concerned about the difficulties faced by SMEs in this regard. Therefore, financial institutions have been given two years of flexibility on the restructuring and rescheduling of SME financing so that they continue to be proactive in assisting SMEs with cash flow problems in the business. In the first 9 months of the year, more than 1400 SMEs were assisted through the restructuring and rescheduling of financing. To ensure that business and housing financing applicants continue to receive continuous advice and assistance, Bank Negara Malaysia, in collaboration with CGC, AKPK and financial institutions also offers one-stop advisory services to financing applicants who are unsuccessful in obtaining loans, by setting up a "Financing Advisory Service" or MyKNP. This one-stop centre offers advice on why applications are rejected, tips and steps that can be taken to improve eligibility for financing applications, as well as alerts on other or appropriate sources of funding, including alternative financing. In addition to financing, one topic I would like to bring to SME entrepreneurs to increase productivity and competitiveness is the use of electronic payment services or e-payments. Compared to conventional payment methods such as cash and cheques, e-payment has the potential to increase the efficiency and competitiveness of SMEs by offering more efficient, fast and secure services. The Bank Negara Malaysia study estimates that the costs incurred by traders to handle cash are high. We find that on average, for every cash payment made by the merchant and also for every cash payment the merchant receives from the customer, more than RM2 will come out as a handling cost. These costs include the cost of issuing and depositing cash in the bank, the cost of calculating, coordinating and storing cash in the business premises and losses incurred in the event of any theft or loss of cash. In this regard, Bank Negara Malaysia and the banking industry have taken continuous steps to facilitate access and convenience of epayment. For example, SMEs can use services such as Instant Transfer or DuitNow to make payments through various channels such as Internet banking, mobile banking and even ATMs. In addition, SMEs can receive payments from customers electronically by using payment card terminals or QR codes. In this regard, the DuitNow QR service has been introduced where the merchant only needs to display one integrated QR code to receive payments from bank account holders and non-bank electronic money account holders. I am pleased to share that DuitNow QR is now offered by 2 local banks while more banks and non-bank electronic money issuers will offer this service in stages next year. Finally, on behalf of Bank Negara Malaysia, I would like to express my deepest appreciation to Yang Berhormat Dato' Wira Haji Amiruddin bin Haji Hamzah, Deputy Minister of Finance, Ministry of Finance, Government agencies, financial institutions and all stakeholders for their support in launching and making a success of the SME Financing Seminar and Finance Clinic today. To the attendees, thank you for being willing to attend this event and hopefully this initiative can be implemented well and successfully and can be benefited by SMEs at the best. You are also welcome to participate in all scheduled programmes including pocket talk, financing seminar sessions and SME clinics as well as visiting the advice counters provided.

Title: Closing Speech at Kedah Financial Carnival 2018
text: Speech by the Deputy Governor at the Opening of muzakarah Cendekiawan Shariah Nusantara 14th Presenter: / Venue: / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 13 Oct 2020 / Alhamdulillah, my highest gratitude goes to Allah Subhanahu Wa Ta'ala, for with His grace, we are met virtually in the Fourteenth Muzakarah Cendekiawan Shariah Nusantara (14th) this year. The Impact of the COVID-19 Outbreak on the World We are stepping into 2020 with determination and aspiration. However, this year brings bitter challenges that go beyond our imagination. For example, mega-scale fires in Australia, major floods in Indonesia as well as the million locusts (deadly locusts) attacks of the worst magnitude in East Africa that occurred throughout January expose us to various challenges. [1] We are further shocked by the coronavirus Disease 2019 pandemic or COVID-19 which is spreading rapidly around the world, including the Southeast Asian region. The spread of the COVID-19 pandemic has infected over 37 million people and resulted in the loss of over one million lives so far. [2] In fact, COVID-19 has also hampered cross-border trade and business activities, as well as affecting the income sources of the community. The International Monetary Fund projected the world economy would contract 4.9% for 2020, far worse than the 0.7% contraction during the global financial crisis in 2008 and 2009. [3] If the spread of the pandemic is not handled appropriately, the world will face a tumultuous and protracted economic downturn. Although the COVID-19 pandemic is still on the rise and widespread, most of the country has begun to move towards recovery while continuing to deal with and control the spread of the pandemic. Islamic finance, especially Islamic financial institutions and Shariah scholars have a leading role in contributing meaningfully to this recovery process. Islamic finance needs to ensure that financial services add value and produce a positive impact on the economy and the well-being of society in general in meeting the demands of maqasid Shariah. Therefore, in line with the theme of muzakarah this time "Contemporary Islamic Finance: Reflection and Innovation", let me share two important points in dealing with the current crisis situation. First, Shariah principles are a key consideration in the face of the crisis and secondly, the digital platform as an important component of the recovery and regeneration of the new economy. First: Shariah principles are the main consideration in the face of the crisis In curbing the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic, various radical measures have been implemented such as the closure or restriction of the country's borders, control of movement within the country, as well as the closure of the economy as a whole or even on a targeted basis. These measures have a negative impact on the economic and social position. Business income for almost all sectors of the economy, especially tourism and hospitality, services, including small and medium enterprises were affected. As a result, the well-being of individuals who depend on living in these sectors has also been affected when their income is affected or lost altogether. This situation threatens the well-being of family institutions as well as social stability. The unemployment rate for the Southeast Asian region has also increased, while all economies in the Southeast Asian region are expected to contract for the year. [4] Despite the annoyance, the threat of COVID-19 has its own wisdom. The values in line with Islamic demands including courtesy, fairness and fairness and ta'awun are the basis of important considerations applied in the formulation of measures by the authorities to achieve the maqasid Shariah which emphasizes the well-being of religion, life, intellect, ancestry and property. In addressing the impact of COVID-19, various economic stimulus packages have been implemented by the rest of the world and the countries of the Southeast Asian region. Although the approaches may be different, the goal is to continue the business, especially SMEs, thus curbing the incidence of unemployment and reducing the burden of the people, especially the low-income group. This is in line with the principle of courtesy which targets the reduction of the burden incurred by customers. For example, the implementation of deferment of financing payments or moratoriums in several countries including Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, and Brunei Darussalam has provided temporary relief to debtors. Meanwhile, the government's funding assistance to micro-entrepreneurs and SMEs such as those implemented in Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia, as well as low interest rate financing facilities in Cambodia and Myanmar are aimed at making small entrepreneurs able to survive and revitalize their businesses. In addition, assistance in the form of salary subsidies such as in Brunei and Thailand as well as food assistance in Indonesia continues to ensure the welfare of the affected workers. [5] In Malaysia, the principle of courtesy is the basis for consideration of several decisions of the Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia. For example, Islamic banking institutions are not allowed to take into account the accrued profits for existing financing in determining the new principal amount for the restructured or rescheduled financing. Islamic banking institutions are also reminded to be fair and attentive in dealing with customers and in terms of determining profit rates. All this is aimed at easing the burden faced by customers and communities affected by COVID-19. Social finance in the form of zakat, waqaf and alms offers great potential to facilitate a more balanced and inclusive distribution of funds. Therefore, in order to address the impact of COVID-19 on the ummah, the use of financial social instruments has been intensified including by integrating such instruments into Islamic financial products. For example, the Fatwa Committee, the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore and the Indonesian Council of Scholars have expanded the interpretation of 'asnaf' by deciding that zakat assistance can be distributed to segments of society affected by COVID-19 including those who have lost their jobs or suffered from affected income. This enables any individual who has difficulty to meet the basic needs of obtaining zakat assistance to survive. [6] To date, the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore has channelled approximately USD 3.53 million in waqf asset income for the purpose of community development affected by COVID-19[7]. In the Philippines, Islamic Bank Trust officials have channeled sadaqah donations to Mindanao State University students who were stranded on campus due to the curfew. This contribution has ensured that the welfare of the affected students is maintained through food aid and other basic necessities. [8] In addition, the Indonesian National Zakat Amil Agency (BAZNAS) has entered into a collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme which uses zakat instruments to support the post-COVID-19 economic recovery process in Indonesia.[9] In an effort to help the low-income group generate income continuously through entrepreneurship to improve their financial position, Malaysia has introduced the i-TEKAD pilot programme[10]. This program involves the joint venture of banking institutions with state religious authorities and implementing partners who combine zakat instruments as start-up capital with microfinance for working capital. It also comes with structured skills development training including mentoring. Efforts to deal with the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic involved large sums of funds which also put pressure on the government's financial position. To date, an estimated USD9 trillion of fiscal funds have been channeled globally especially in various forms of financial assistance to the people and enterprises. [11] To enable the ummah's involvement in assisting the country's economic recovery and redevelopment, several countries have already issued retail-based social impact sukuk (retail-based social impact sukuk). For example, the 3-year sukuk ijarah amounting to USD300 million by the Indonesian government[12] as well as Sukuk Prihatin by the Malaysian government amounted to USD161 million with a maturity period of 2 years which provided an opportunity for the people to contribute towards rebuilding the country after the COVID-19 pandemic. Such initiatives are in line with the Siyasah Shariah principle 13 which opens up spaces and opportunities for the community to help each other on the basis of ta'awun. Second: digital platforms as an important component of the recovery and regeneration of the new economy The spread of COVID-19 and the practice of new norms have accelerated digitalisation in the economy as well as fostered new work culture and collaboration trends. Online businesses are becoming more and more vibrant, while digital payments are increasing so sharply. Digitalisation also affects the pace of economic recovery and the new structure of the economy as well as business practices and arrangements. For example, the Bank of Thailand has explored the potential of blockchain technology through a government savings bond issuance platform implemented in October 2020 recently. The use of this blockchain technology will not only ensure greater transparency and efficiency through cost reduction and operational difficulties, but also shorten the time of bond issuance process from 15 days to 2 days only. Such initiatives are in line with the expectations of investors who emphasize efficient and fast service. [14] In an increasingly sensitive society and business environment for technological developments, and in meeting customers' expectations of efficient, innovative, fast and customer-friendly services, the financial industry and enterprise owners need to review and restructure their business strategies and business models and products and services to remain relevant. Scholars also play a role in this process to clarify the Shariah requirements that need to be complied with in the affairs and certain components of the operations of financial institutions including the implementation of appropriate Shariah principles and contracts as well as practices in line with Shariah requirements. Islamic financial institutions also need to take advantage of the latest technology more intensively through collaboration with the Fintech community. Technologies such as "artificial intelligence" or AI, the internet for everything (internet of things, IoT), blockchain and so on can reduce operating costs and enable financial institutions to offer innovative and secure solutions to all walks of life and different types of businesses. For example, the digitisation of operations in the takaful business such as claims processing and customer service can preserve customer safety by reducing physical interaction during the movement control period. It can also speed up the claims process. Various digitalisation initiatives have been implemented to improve efficiency and access. For example, GlobalSadaqah has come up with a zakat and waqf payment platform through various electronic wallet applications such as GrabPay, Boost and Touch 'n Go. Through this platform, zakat, waqaf and alms can be channeled to charitable bodies more efficiently and transparently. [15] DBS Bank in Singapore has facilitated interaction with customers at this time through Singpass Face Verification technology which launches the digital banking registration process using a mobile phone. In the pursuit of exploring the potential of technology to deliver good services, basic matters need to be reassessed and empowered. The International Institute for Management Development (IMD) report on World Digital Competitiveness 2019 has outlined three key indicators adopted and measures the digital competitiveness of a country, namely technology, knowledge and availability in the future. [16] Therefore, apart from upgrading physical infrastructure such as broadband capacity - policy makers, individuals who are involved in the financial ecosystem including Shariah scholars are no exception to the demands to empower knowledge on the latest technological developments. This is important to ensure that Shariah scholars are able to make appropriate Shariah decisions based on an adequate understanding of the development of technology. Conclusion The fast tide of change will reach our imagination. Therefore, we need Shariah scholars to equip ourselves with agility in action, close cooperation between us, as well as flexibility in formulating appropriate solutions. In this regard, Shariah scholars have an important role to play in ensuring that financial institutions, with the cooperation of various parties, can support socio-economic development through appropriate and effective Islamic financial instruments. In this regard, I pray that this muzakarah will run smoothly and can be a platform as a catalyst to achieve the objectives targeted. __________________________ [1] "Blood-red skies loom over southeast Australia after deadly bushfires bring 'one of worst days ever', CNN, January 6, 2020. Title: Speech at the Business Continuity Management Conference - "Integrated Risk Management Approach for Maintaining Resilience & Sustainability"
Authorname: Tan Sri Nor Shamsiah Mohd Yunus
text: Keynote Address by Governor at the World Bank's Aiming High Webinar Series Speaker: Tan Sri Nor Shamsiah Mohd Yunus Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 27 May 2021 The Economist magazine recently published an article comparing the welfare of citizens across countries, based on a survey of various aspects of well-being. The title of the article was Money really can buy happiness and recessions can take it away. It maintained that citizens in high-income countries felt better off about their current life situation, have money for food, and access to good and affordable housing nearby. Quality of life is also better due to less tangible factors such as corruption not being widespread, feeling safe when walking alone at night, feeling well rested and having helped a stranger in the past month. Implicit in these findings is the idea that economic growth should go hand in hand with greater welfare. More than the dollars and cents of becoming wealthier, it is the improvements in the quality of life that countries aspire to achieve. And so, I was heartened to read in the World Banks Aiming High report that Malaysia is likely to transition to a high-income economy between 2024 and 2028. This panel discussion is thus very relevant to our situation, now more than ever. For Malaysia, the journey to become a high-income economy will not be easy. In the past three decades, only a handful of countries have managed to achieve that status, and importantly, to sustain their position. In fact, the road to becoming a high-income economy is more difficult today, as countries are confronted with challenges and uncertainties like never before. According to the OECD1 , the present landscape has new rules, new environmental constraints, new technologies and more competition. We will need to adapt to these changes, while managing other shocks that may come our way. What we dont want is for the economy to take one step forward, only to be pulled two steps back. Along these lines, allow me to share four points on how Malaysia can more confidently transition towards a high-income economy. An economy centred on innovation My first point is on putting innovation at the centre of our economic development. Malaysia has come a long way. From being a commodities-based economy, we have diversified into high-end manufacturing and modern services. This helped us advance into a middle income economy in the early 70s. Yet, since then, we have struggled to achieve productivity- and innovation-driven growth needed to become a high-income economy. Even today, the deficit in the innovation capability of our economy remains. For instance: Malaysia does not spend enough on R&D. In fact we spend less than half of other frontier economies like Korea, Taiwan and Singapore. Our R&D efforts have focused on generating scientific knowledge, but less on applying that knowledge. This has resulted in low commercialisation of R&D. A World Bank survey2 also indicated that most businesses do not innovate, and even among those that do, the focus is mainly on process or incremental innovation. If innovation is so important, why has Malaysia not innovated enough? I believe the answer lies partly in the innovation paradox  innovation is a complex process that requires a whole-of-economy approach. A study by Harvard 3 found that as much as 80% of national innovation capacity can be explained by the number of scientists and engineers, the stock of knowledge that the society has accrued, the public policy environment and the maturity of business clusters. Importantly, it requires strong interaction between these individual parts; the innovation system is only as strong as its weakest link. Indeed, Malaysia has been persistent in strengthening its foundations for innovation, but we must do more. We must do more to attract quality investments to promote a more innovative economy, including to do so more deliberately and thoughtfully. That is why the Governments commitment to adopt the National Investment Aspirations as a framework for determining the quality investments which Malaysia must attract is key. Industry and academia must also work together so that research can be better oriented toward serving the needs of the economy, and so that policy support and funding can be directed at areas with the greatest commercial and social potential. Finally, our spending on education, while it is high relative to peers, the returns have not commensurate with the investments made. The education and training system must be more forward-looking and cater to shifts we anticipate over the next 20  50 years. The key is to prepare the next generation with 21st century skills to meet these demands. Malaysia must secure innovation-driven growth in all parts of our economy. But we must set our minds to areas where the payoffs are the greatest. Three areas of opportunity come to mind: First, we must make best use of the resources which we are endowed with, such as to process commodities into chemicals and other derivatives to increase economic complexity. Agriculture productivity can also increase by adopting modern farming. Second, addressing climate change offers opportunities to attract investments and create high-quality jobs. The global economy needs USD23 trillion in green assets to meet the climate goals under the Paris Accord. 4 Third, Malaysia is among the best positioned within Southeast Asia to embrace the fourth industrial revolution 5. Malaysia already has one foot through the door in each of these opportunities; we are major producers of petro- and oleochemicals, solar panels, as well as E&E components that will power future mobility. We must engage in serious conversations on moonshot strategies to build innovative industries and companies. Only then can we set the foundation for a sustainable, dynamic and competitive Malaysian economy. A society that is more inclusive Economic growth does not necessarily go hand in hand with social progress, particularly if growth only enriches the few. Thus, my second point is on improving social inclusivity. Malaysia has made great strides in eradicating poverty. This is the result of numerous efforts to meet the needs of societys most vulnerable, and to provide them with opportunities for upward social mobility. Nevertheless, the COVID-19 crisis reminds us that shocks affect different segments unevenly, and this has clearly exposed gaps in our social protection system. It is therefore critical to accompany the transition to high income with efforts to close these gaps. The growing economic pie will provide the state with more capacity to deepen its social protection. We must use this space to future-proof the system to impending structural changes: Malaysia will transition to an aged nation status, with the old-age dependency ratio expected to increase to 16.6% by 2040. However, in a 2018 Employees Provident Fund study, two out of three active contributors are projected to have insufficient retirement savings to meet a minimum pension of RM1,000 per month. The nature of work will evolve, as we transition to a more knowledge-based, service-based and gig-based economy. Work arrangements are expected to become more flexible, and provisions must be made to ensure that workers remain adequately protected. Notably, provisions for shorter and more flexible working hours may entice women to participate in the labour force. The third change is the displacement of certain jobs, as we enter the dawn of the next industrial revolution. The trend towards automation and AI requires a smooth transition of the workforce into new skills and occupation areas. This is to ensure that existing and future talent is fully utilised, and skill-related underemployment is kept at bay. The question is then how can Malaysia mould its social protection system to better protect and empower its workers and citizens? We can consider this through the lens of the 4Cs: Coverage, Consolidation, Conditionalities, and Comprehensiveness. On coverage, social protection must be deepened and extended towards the growing segments of informal and selfemployed workers. Meanwhile, currently fragmented and overlapping programmes should be consolidated and rationalised, so as to channel funds to meet new needs of society, for instance better retirement aid. We can also impose conditionalities for various programmes to boost incentives and improve targeting capacity. Finally, there is a need for comprehensive active labour market policies to cater to the looming possibility of labour redeployment under the fourth industrial revolution. Maintaining planetary health for sustainable economic growth This brings me to our third point. In our quest to transition to a high-income economy, we must do so without losing sight of the goal of prospering, thriving and living sustainably. Since last year, we have had to deal with a negative global shock in the form of Covid-19. The pandemic has taken a heavy health and economic toll, with profound effects on poverty. At the same time, displacement and disruptions due to climaterelated events such as storms, flooding and droughts have persisted and intensified. Pandemics and climate-related risks produce similarly devastating effects on the real and financial sectors, causing recessions, unemployment and a large depreciation of value across all asset classes. There are many valuable lessons that we can learn from the current pandemic  including of the urgent need to pay more attention to planetary health. Of importance is how we can move closer towards realising Sustainable Development Goals or SDGs. We have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reset and reprioritise resources to reconstruct our economies and financial systems to be more sustainable and inclusive. This includes tackling climate change, given that climaterelated risks pose a growing threat to our very way of life. If left unmanaged, we would be faced with irreversible effects of climate change that would impact us far greater than the pandemic. With so much at stake, the whole country has a part to play in this mission. Even the Bank, where weve put the management of climate risk, as a top priority. Government that is agile and forward-looking My final point is on changes to the states capacity. In the time of change and modernisation, how we approach the governments role in innovation must also evolve. Let me be clear. It is not that the government should play no role in the economy, but rather, it might be timely for some new thinking about the role of government in the economy, and how it works with the private sector. After all, as moving forward requires the economy to consider not just cutting edge, but also bleeding edge ideas and technologies, we need to start thinking about novel and unconventional approaches. Several questions spring to mind. First, how should the government take calculated policy risks, while managing policy failures ? In building pathways to high income, ambitious industrial policies, or moonshot strategies, will play a key role. With any policy however, there would be uncertainty and possibility of failure. Development economist, Dani Rodrick, called for effective industrial policy to be less on the ability to pick winners, but on knowing when to cut losses. Too low a failure rate could also mean that we are playing it too safe. The objective, hence, should not be to avoid mistakes, but to minimise the cost of mistakes. This will require the Government to build its capacity to account for and quantify the associated risk within the decision framework. Only then can we make smarter, more intelligent bets to get the most bang for the buck. Second, how can the Government learn and execute better ? Focus should be as much on process and governance, as it is on the outcomes. While we have achieved leaps and bounds in economic development since our Independence, past reforms also provide important lessons in areas where we must strive to do better. We have had roughly 60-70 blueprints and masterplans over the years; not all have been executed to their maximum potential. Let us identify the gaps and shortfalls and move forward from there. We must also hone the public sectors ability to make incremental improvements and course corrections, as much as sweeping reforms. After all, correction mechanisms are what make governments smarter. Third, a strong and sustained focus on protecting and promoting the qualities of efficient and effective public institutions must define our path to becoming a high-income economy. Ultimately, attaining high income status must be commensurate with the governments ability to intervene less, but to intervene more smartly. As I bring my remarks to a close, let me be clear that although Malaysias journey to transition to a high-income economy will be challenging, it is not out of reach. The key is to have the right mindset and values so that we attain, not just the highincome target, but also the qualities of a developed nation and society. I look forward to an insightful discussion ahead about what it will take for us to cross the finish line. Thank you. 1 Perspectives on Global Development 2019: Rethinking Development Strategies , OECD. 2 Source: World Bank Enterprise Survey Data 3 3 Porter, M.E. and S. Stern (2002). National Innovative Capacity, The Global Competitiveness Report 2001-2002. 4 Stoiljkovic, N. (2017). The Paris Agreement is a 23 trillion investment opportunity. How can we unlock it? , World Economic Forum. 5 Accelerating 4IR in ASEAN: An Action Plan for Manufacturers , ATKearney (2019).

Title: Opening Remarks at the OECD-Asia Regional Seminar: Enhancing transparency and monitoring of insurance markets
Authorname: Tan Sri Nor Shamsiah Mohd Yunus
text: Governor's Remarks at the Green Swan 2021 Global Virtual Conference by Bank for International Settlements Speaker: Tan Sri Nor Shamsiah Mohd Yunus Venue: Language: English Speech/Interview Date: 04 Jun 2021 I am pleased to be in this panel. If there is anything history, or more recently the pandemic has taught us, it is that, in the face of existential threats, a collective and well-coordinated response is crucial. Central banks and regulators are uniquely placed to mobilise and coordinate climate action with other actors. Given the central role of the financial system in any economy, central banks and regulators have significant influence and a direct interest in actions by financial institutions to manage climate-related risks. The policy and supervisory steer that central banks and financial regulators provide have important consequences for progress by economic agents in strengthening climate risk mitigation and adaptation. Furthermore, as advisors to the Government on economic and financial policies, central banks and regulators often play a key role in helping Governments navigate an orderly transition to a low-carbon economy. Id like to focus my remarks today on how we are working with the industry and other financial regulators to respond to the climate challenge. JC3 and its evolution In Malaysia, Bank Negara Malaysia and the Securities Commission have established the Joint Committee on Climate Change (or JC3) with the financial industry to promote alignment on climate actions across multiple stakeholders. Through the JC3, financial regulators are working together with the stock exchange, financial institutions, institutional investors, NGOs and the Government. We started the JC3 with a narrow focus  acting as a network for sharing of experiences and coordinating actions. But within two years of its establishment, the JC3 has evolved to become a focal point for collective climate actions within the financial sector. Correspondingly, it has expanded beyond networking and coordination, to providing content, stewardship and advocacy. With financial regulators working alongside each other, the outreach of actions extends throughout the key components within the financial sector. The increasing breadth and depth of the work undertaken by its four sub-committees have supported a number of key initiatives to advance climate risk management and climate-related disclosures. This includes the issuance of the Climate Change and Principle-based Taxonomy that was piloted by selected JC3 members and phased adoption of the Taskforce on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). The JC3 is also taking on an increasingly important role in developing practical tools and solutions for financial institutions and to address barriers to green financing and investments. For example, the Bank is working with the industry via the JC3 platform to develop Guidance Documents on Climate Risk Management and Scenario Analysis. The guides underscore the need to manage climate-related risks as a financial risk within the broader enterprise risk management frameworks, while addressing the unique characteristics of climate risk such as its long-term horizon and non-linear features. Since 2017, Islamic financial institutions have also taken a leadership role in spearheading sustainable finance through the development of sectoral and activity impact-based risk management frameworks. Sectoral Guides focusing on palm oil, renewable energy and energy efficiency activities have already been issued, and will be followed by Guides for the manufacturing, construction and infrastructure, as well as oil and gas sectors by the end of this year. Through JC3, these complementary developments are being coordinated and integrated to build a credible foundation for the financial industry to support the transition efforts. Beyond the financial sector, the JC3 also actively engages with various stakeholders on climate and transition initiatives. The formation of a new sub-committee this year, to address data gaps for climate risk analysis is another major collaboration as part of JC3s efforts to strengthen climate risk management and scale up green finance. The JC3 is also pursuing broader engagements with key businesses to better understand transitioning issues and opportunities along the supply value chain. This will help inform the structuring of customised financial solutions for the different types of players within the entire value chain. Objectives and motivations for collaboration As a financial regulator and supervisor, it is important to be clear on the objectives and motivations for our collaborative efforts with the industry and other stakeholders. The primary goal for us is to support the appropriate consideration of climate risks in promoting resilient financial institutions. With this goal in sight, first we need to recognise that climate risk is a cross-cutting risk, for which risk management approaches and methodologies are largely still under-developed. Given this, there is much more to be discovered in terms of how it can be managed in an integrated manner with other financial risks. This suggests a need for an iterative process that will enable financial regulators and the industry to converge on supervisory expectations and a common framework for assessing physical and transition risks. As part of this process, we are examining the scope and specific approaches to incorporate climate-related financial risks within the Pillar 2 requirements. Secondly, the nature of climate-related risks calls for central banks and regulators to collaborate at the national level to support alignment of financial industry responses with national climate strategies and priorities. As I mentioned at the start of my remarks, central banks and financial regulators provide an important bridge between the financial sector and the Government to inform national policies, targets and strategies on the one hand, and financial sector responses to climate risk on the other hand. In Malaysia, JC3 serves as a focal point for engagements with the Malaysian Climate Change Action Council (MyCAC) [1] on national climate policies. Third, effective coordination with the industry serves to maximise transition benefits and minimise downside risks. For developing and emerging economies in particular, an inclusive strategy is key to avoid macroeconomic and social dislocations as we transition to a low-carbon economy. As financial and economic advisors to the Government, we are working with the Government to develop sustainable finance roadmaps that will mitigate risks of stranded assets if disorderly transition occurs. The Banks principles-based taxonomy was developed with this in mind. The taxonomy aims to facilitate the direction of financial flows to activities that support the transition to a low-carbon and climate resilient economy. It supports businesses in transition by recognising climate risk mitigation and adaptation efforts over time, while preserving the rigour of assessments by avoiding greenwashing. The taxonomy also encourages financial institutions to nurture and nudge businesses to transition to greener practices. It helps improve development outcomes, and builds capacity within businesses themselves to better manage climate-related risks. To further support transition activities, the Bank has also established funds to assist SMEs in pivoting their businesses to be more sustainable in the post-pandemic world. This includes transitioning to greener activities. The Bank is looking to further expand these facilities with a greater focus on green activities that are aligned with the taxonomy going forward. The Bank also sees great value in pursuing a coordinated and regionally coherent financial sector response to the climate challenge. Within ASEAN, the Bank is working closely with central banks in the region through the ASEAN Taxonomy Board in the construction of a regional taxonomy that can provide a common language for sustainable finance in ASEAN and promote efficiency. This will encourage the alignment of national taxonomies, building on common principles and a tiering system to cater to differences in financial systems, economic and social structures, and transition paths. Global coordination to improve climate equity Let me close with a final point on global coordination. As countries embark on different national transition paths at varying paces, a global challenge is the disproportionate impact on emerging economies. This makes it more difficult for them to control their own transition path due to economic and financial linkages [2]. This reality calls for a more coherent global coordination to galvanise collective actions, with stronger link to the NDCs [3] under the Paris Agreement, that would help improve climate equity and mitigate risks of disorderly transitions. This would compel countries that generate transition spillovers to provide financing, technology and capacity building support to assist smaller and developing countries to adapt to climate change and take mitigating actions. This, in our view, is a step towards a more equitable and effective global mechanism to respond climate risk at a faster pace. Thank you. [1] A platform to set the direction, to discuss climate change policies and actions, to drive green economic growth, to catalyse green technology and low-carbon growth at all levels, particularly in the federal and state Governments. [2] For example, measures to cut global GHG emissions (e.g. removing fossil fuel subsidies, emission caps and carbon taxes) could lead to higher risk of stranded assets in emerging and developing countries given their heavy reliance on fossil fuels. [3] Nationally Determined Contributions.

Title: Keynote Address at the16th East Asian Actuarial Conference Theme: "Venture into Uncertainty, Capture Opportunities"
text: 34 Shares Speech by Assistant Governor at Muzakarah Cendekiawan Shariah 15th Archipelago Presenter: / Venue: - / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 08 Jul 2021 / Alhamdulillah, with His permission, we are met virtually in the 15th Muzakarah of Shariah Scholars (15th) of the year. The Impact of COVID-19 Transmission on the World and Economic Recovery Measures After a year of the world grappling with the challenges and impacts of COVID-19 on the global economy and public health, we are moving into 2021 more prepared. However, the emergence of new variants of the actively mutated virus has added to the challenges in dealing with the spread of the pandemic and undermined the recovery efforts of economic activity. Economic recovery efforts require the support of various parties. In addition to the machinery of government and the basic sectors, all walks of life should agree on this effort. Not least the scholars who can play an important role based on their expertise. The formulation of a good policy requires observations that can balance the welfare of life and the economy so that the long-term impacts can also be better overcome. The crisis has had a significant impact on the economic growth of regional countries. Various stimulus packages have been introduced by the authorities to reduce the pressures faced by individuals and businesses1. In supporting this effort, financial institutions and Shariah scholars have an important role to play in applying compassionate and fair principles in the offering of assistance programmes that are responsive to the current situation and challenges faced by customers. Therefore, in line with the theme of this muzakarah "Post Pandemic Islamic Financial Industry: Impact, Challenges and Direction", let me share three aspects of the involvement of Relevant Shariah scholars in this economic recovery process. The first aspect is the active involvement of Shariah scholars in the formulation of economic recovery measures In the face of uncertainty due to the spread of COVID-19, the formulation of agile, elastic (flexible) and inclusive policies is needed. A robust policy accompanied by efficient implementation measures will help the economy towards recovery, while paying special attention to vulnerable groups. Based on the goal of achieving a comprehensive and inclusive recovery, the needs of each economic group and stakeholders in various sectors should be taken into account. For example, the financing payment assistance programme by banking institutions in Malaysia focuses on the cash flow needs of households and businesses at the scale and speed required during the downturn in economic activities. This is to reduce the financial burden for income-affected customers. The initial approach is to allow help to be offered more focusedly. Recently, with challenges increasing dramatically, this approach has been extended to almost all walks of life and businesses, as well as simplified the process. At the same time, the impact on banking institutions continues to be given consideration so that the resilience of the financial industry remains preserved. An important aspect of this approach is also to ensure that the choice to receive this assistance, including the form of assistance, remains in the hands of the user and that they have the opportunity to make the right decisions, appropriate to their situation. In this regard, the guidance of Shariah law in the face of crisis situations according to the perspective of hajah and darurah is important to balance the economic and financial industry's well-being, as well as the welfare of the individual. The clarity of this ruling can guide the formulation of a policy that is in accordance with the requirements of the Maqasid Shariah. The Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia has also decided that for financing to be restructured or rescheduled during the pandemic period, the principle of courtesy and fairness should be a fundamental consideration in the determination of new financing that should take into account the client's current financial position. Banking institutions are also reminded to always adhere to the guidelines on responsible financing practices.2 in dealing with customers. Thus, the explanation of Shariah regarding the definition of the affected from the dimensions of mu'sir and musir as stated in surah AlBaqarah, verse 280 is important. This interpretation can provide guidance in implementing a focused assistance program as well as applying the principle of courtesy as a basis for consideration in helping those who are experiencing difficulties. In addition, the expansion of interpretation in the determination of asnaf has also enabled the mobilization of zakat funds more broadly. For example, an initiative introduced in Malaysia by the Federal Territory Islamic Religious Council (MAIWP) through the #MusaadahCOVID19 program has provided emergency zakat assistance amounting to RM25.11 million.3 to the public, including those affected by the movement control order and the homeless, in addition to providing assistance to the health sector. The dynamism in Shariah interpretation that fits this pandemic environment can also guide banking institutions in identifying the customers who need the most assistance by providing appropriate payment flexibility. While in economic recovery efforts, effective strategies need to be in line with epidemic control measures, especially the achievement of group immunity. However, this effort involves large sums of funds. In this regard, the decision of the International Fiqh Academy on the permissibility of the use of part of the zakat fund has expanded the source of funding for the purpose of purchasing and distributing COVID-19 vaccines4. This is decided on the basis of siyasah syar'iyyah5 For the sake of life on the global stage. The clarity of the fatwa from such a maslahah framework can support epidemic containment efforts, especially as an alternative solution to limited funding sources and expand the scale of aid that can be extended. The second aspect is that about adaptation towards a new norm Today's situation brings a variety of new norms. One that is expected to be sustainable is digital transformation, which also provides opportunities towards achieving better financial inclusion. This is mainly to meet the financial needs of certain groups that cannot be met through traditional methods of supply. In the face of the impact of COVID-19 on the economy, such aspirations have become more meaningful and important to realise for the sake of an inclusive economic recovery. In this regard, the role of Shariah advisors is especially important in the application of a good Shariah compliance culture and clarifying Shariah requirements, such as the operation of digital financial transactions that are free from the elements of Islamic prohibition. Such situations also require Shariah scholars to look at a practical, relevant, and fair approach in addressing current needs and problems. Thus, the application of fiqh al-waqi' (i.e. the ruling of fiqh based on reality) is important to strengthen the fatwa decided in the development of appropriate policies. The third aspect of collaborationin enhancing synergies and success towards economic regeneration In an increasingly challenging economic environment, a systematic and comprehensive strategy can ease the burden of the affected groups, as well as improve the standard and quality of life of the community to a better level in order to achieve maqasid Shariah. Collaboration in empowering the use of Islamic social financial instruments is an initiative that will be explored in more depth. I want to bring an example of the iTEKAD pilot program6 introduced in Malaysia. This program involves close collaboration between banking institutions and the state Islamic religious council and other implementing partners with the aim of catalyzing the independence of the community, especially the income-affected. Through a combination of Islamic social financial instruments such as zakat, alms and cash waqf together with microfinance products, iTEKAD offers working capital resources as well as entrepreneurship training and continuous guidance to enhance skills and viability in the fields that participants are involved in. Through such joint ventures, access can be targeted to a larger scale so that socio-economic development goals can be achieved more inclusively. In a similar initiative niche, strategic collaboration between regulatory bodies such as Bank Negara Malaysia and the Securities Commission Malaysia aims to build capacity towards achieving the transition to a low-carbon economy for more sustainable economic practices. Such synergies are critical in the move towards a sustainable economic recovery, while continuing to address the impacts of climate change and worsening natural disasters. Through such a platform including cooperation and partnerships with countries, the brainchild of fresh and new ideas is expected to produce a clear and practical framework of Islamic law to support the regeneration of a sustainable and sustainable regional economy, as well as empowering Islamic finance for mutual benefit. Conclusion We are faced with a dynamic and challenging financial industry environment. The Islamic financial offering strategy should also be more creative and appropriate, without neglecting the basic Shariah compliance principles. We need to be vigilant and ready to adapt and innovate to remain beneficial and have a positive impact on the economy and society. Title: Opening Remarks at the Seminar on Crisis Preparedness for Insurance Supervisors organised by AITRI -Toronto Centre, hosted by Bank Negara Malaysia
text: 25 Shares Speech by Assistant Governor in conjunction with Sarawak Financial Awareness Campaign (Virtually) Presenter: Mr. Abu Hassan Alshari Yahaya / Venue: - / Language: English / Speech/Interview Date: 03 August 2021 / Sarawakians are handsome, when the smile of sweet pliers is on the stairs, Good morning everyone Sarawakians, meet us in the virtual realm. On behalf of Bank Negara Malaysia, I would like to welcome the attendees to the inaugural Sarawak Financial Awareness Campaign (ViSFA) which starts today and will run until the end of October 2021. We are pleased that the Chief Minister of Sarawak, Yang Amat Berhormat Datuk Patinggi Dr. Abang Haji Abdul Rahman Zohari bin Tun Datuk Abang Haji Openg took the time to launch the Sarawak Financial Awareness Campaign to improve financial literacy among the people of Sarawak. I would also like to thank the Minister of the Ministry of Domestic Trade and Consumer Affairs (KPDNHEP), Yang Berhormat Dato Sri Alexander Nanta Linggi, Minister of Entrepreneur Development and Cooperatives (MEDAC), Yang Berhormat Dato' Sri Dr. Haji Wan Junaidi Bin Tuanku Jaafar and Assistant Minister of Entrepreneur Development and Small and Medium Enterprises (MINTRED), Yang Berhormat Datuk Haji Mohd Naroden Haji Majais, for the support and cooperation given in the success of this Campaign. Not forgetting the ViSFA collaboration partners comprising the Financial Education Network (FEN), Ministries, Departments, Government and private agencies, associations, business entrepreneurs and all parties involved in the success of this initiative. My heartfelt congratulations and congratulations to Bank Negara Malaysia Kuching Office as the programme coordinator for the success of this ViSFA. The current Covid-19 pandemic not only affected the country's economy, but also affected individuals and businesses in various aspects. Concerned with the challenges faced by Malaysians, the Government and the financial industry have introduced various aid and economic stimulus packages to address the impact of the Covid-19 crisis. First, BNM in collaboration with the banking industry has improved the Loan Repayment Assistance, as announced by the Prime Minister under the PEMULIH package. Individual borrowers and micro-enterprises as well as Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) affected by the pandemic can start applying for a six-month moratorium since 7 July 2021. In addition, alternative assistance that is better suited to the needs and financial position of borrowers is also provided by banking institutions as well as the Credit Counseling and Services Agency (AKPK) under the Credit Management Programme or "Debt Management Programme, DMP". Second, BNM also has a settlement mechanism or "redress mechanism" to help people who have difficulty dealing with the bank. For example, if a borrower encounters any difficulties with their banks, or if the installment payments increase unreasonably when seeking moratorium assistance, the borrower may contact BNMTELELINK via bnm.my/RAsurvey to submit their complaint. Every day BNM LINK will deliver this feedback to the bank and ask for immediate action to be taken. BNM will continue to monitor every case of complaint submitted. Third, BNM has provided additional or improved financing facilities to provide assistance and support the recovery of SMEs. During the pandemic, more than 37 thousand SMEs have received financing in excess of RM15 billion under the 'BNM Fund for SMEs'. Recently, BNM has increased the allocation under the BNM Fund for SMEs by RM2 billion. This increase in the amount of funds available at the end of June to RM8.6 billion. The aid package and initiatives announced by the government are aimed at providing an injection to the country's economy for the purpose of the well-being of its people. However, it should be emphasized that we as individuals also have a role to play in making sustainable financial planning for the well-being of life. In this regard, the inaugural virtual Campaign is a continuation of the efforts of BNM and its collaborators in raising financial awareness as a whole, especially to the people in Sarawak by emphasising on the agenda of protection, consumer education and financial inclusion. The 3-month campaign has its own theme, where in August 2021 themed 'Financial Consumer Rights and Responsibilities', in September 2021 themed 'Manage Your Finances Wisely' and in October themed 'Financial Crime'. Surely we as individuals want to live a meaningful, comfortable and stable life and be free from financial difficulties and be able to cope with unexpected financial difficulties without experiencing financial burdens. In this regard, let me share some of the types of assistance/support provided by BNM, financial institutions and AKPK as well as financial management guidance that can be done in everyday life. First, the importance of setting long-term financial planning. Each individual is recommended to set future financial targets, for example for retirement time. This financial target is important as it will affect the day-to-day financial habits both in terms of generating income and spending patterns. These financial targets can also help us to make a choice of suitable financial products such as deposit/savings products, investments, protections and loans. If you do not know where you should refer to financial targets and financial management, I would like to recommend that you contact AKPK for further assistance. In addition to the Credit Management Programme (DMP) and Small Loan Settlement Scheme (SDRS), AKPK also provides two other essential services: - (i) financial education that offers information on basic money management skills as well as tips on how to handle debt responsibly and (ii) financial advice that provides personal advice on financial management including on debt-related issues. Both services are provided free of charge. For retirement purposes, the Employees Provident Fund (EPF) also has trained staff to advise on retirement plans so that you can enjoy a more comfortable retirement. In addition to the agencies I mentioned above, various digital financial applications have been provided either by financial institutions or related institutions to help people manage their finances better. Among them are the application of comparison of financial products or "financial comparison aggregators" such as ringgitplus.com and imoney.my which allows users to compare financial products in a single portal without having to physically visit a branch of a financial institution. Second, as financial consumers we should be aware of the rights and responsibilities of being a financial consumer including knowing the channels of complaints and settlements or "complaint and redress procedures". BNM also strives to foster fair, responsible and professional business conduct among financial institutions and protect the rights and interests of consumers of financial services and products. In 2019, BNM intensified efforts to advance high standards of professional conduct among financial service providers by introducing key principles on fair treatment of financial consumers. The standards are aimed at ensuring that financial users are treated fairly by financial institutions. Among other things, the standards stipulate that a financial institution must act in good faith and professionally by ensuring reasonableness in the terms of the contract, providing clear product information, providing advice or recommendations that are appropriate to the needs and financial situation of an individual. Complaints and claims of financial consumers should also be addressed promptly, fairly and effectively. Third, protect our lives and financial assets. According to the National Health and Morbidity Survey (NHMS) 2019 conducted by the Ministry of Health Malaysia, only 22 percent of Malaysians have personal health insurance or takaful coverage. While we may feel that insurance and takaful coverage is not something that needs to be prioritised, we also cannot deny that this insurance and takaful coverage can help provide coverage in times of contingency such as accidents, fires, accidents and loss of life. Recognising the importance of insurance and takaful protection schemes to the public, the government has provided various incentives to encourage public participation in the scheme. In the last Budget 2021 presentation, the government has expanded the social protection scheme to the B40 group through the Perlindungan Tenang Voucher Programme (RM50) and stamp duty exemption for the purchase of Perlindungan Tenang products for 5 years until 2025. Through Perlindungan Tenang, we can now purchase or participate in an affordable and easy-to-understand protection plan, with a simple and simple claims process. Also, avoid getting caught up in any get-rich-quick scheme. In this difficult situation, many are still affected and burdened with commitments and debts and this encourages individuals to take simple steps in the hope of getting multiple money, but will eventually become entangled with the trappings of criminal syndicates and fraud. Therefore, the public is reminded to always be cautious and not easily influenced by the offers of get-rich-quick investment schemes available on social media sites, whatsapp apps and other social media networks. On behalf of BNM and all involved, I hope that the people of Sarawak can make the most of this Campaign by participating in the webinar sessions provided and also following the various infotainment, trivia/quiz through ViSFA's official social media accounts. I also have high hopes that this Campaign will successfully educate and enhance the financial management knowledge to the people of Sarawak which in turn will be the starting point in building a financially literate society and transforming life towards a more prosperous direction. As the final storyteller, let me present a snippet of pantun: Sarawakians idup in consensus, Sik about race and religion, May ViSFA times to benefit, Let's not know for mutual benefit Thank you.

Title: Deputy Governor's Opening Remarks at the Launch of Financial Literacy Month 2022
text: Deputy Governor's Opening Remarks at the Launch of Financial Literacy Month 2022 Speaker: Datuk Jessica Chew Cheng Lian Venue: Sasana Kijang, Kuala Lumpur Delivery Date : 01 Oct. 2022 1. It is my great pleasure to welcome you to Sasana Kijang for the launch of the Financial Literacy Month 2022. On behalf of the Financial Education Network, I thank you for your presence here to join us in flagging off a month-long roadshow to help people across the country build greater confidence in financial matters. It is especially gratifying for our teams to be able to go on the road again, to meet and talk to people in person after what has been a difficult period for many. 2. This is the third year that the Financial Education Network is holding a financial literacy month. And while we have lined up many activities and programmes over the coming month, I know that no one here believes financial education starts and stops within a month. I was reminded again of this as we are about to share the results of the most recent Financial Capability and Inclusion Demand Side Survey, or the FCI Survey, in short, that was conducted in 2021. This is a survey that we carry out once in every three years to track how the level of financial capability in our society  measured in terms of financial knowledge, behaviour and attitudes  is changing over time. 3. The good news is that Malaysias Financial Capability and Literacy Index score has improved since the last survey. But behind that index score are much more layered observations of our societys financial attitudes and behaviours. And they reveal that putting financial knowledge into the hands of individuals is just the start. Helping people use that knowledge wisely and effectively in order to bring about lasting changes in behaviour is the race that all of us here are running together - to help as many people as possible reach the finish line of their financial goals. More details on the results of the 2021 FCI Survey will be available in the upcoming publication of Bank Negara Malaysias Financial Stability Review which will happen in the coming week. 4. For those of you who may not be familiar with the Financial Education Network, or FEN, we are an inter-agency platform of eight partner institutions that are committed to raising the level of financial literacy in Malaysia. In 2019, FEN developed a five-year National Strategy for Financial Literacy which is currently in its fourth year. 5. Let me take the opportunity to recap the aims of the National Strategy. They are to empower Malaysians to: first, save, manage and protect their money; second, plan ahead to secure a sustainable future; and third, protect against fraud and financial scams. 6. Fast forward four years, and these goals are as, if not more, relevant today. To deliver these outcomes, FEN is focused on shaping healthy financial attitudes from a young age; increasing access to tools and resources to help individuals manage their finances; and working across the spectrum of society to help individuals attain financial security, through sound financial planning and by cultivating sensible financial habits. 7. Since its launch, FEN members and partners have been working with the government, business community, education sectors, and NGOs to achieve the desired outcomes in the National Strategy. A significant milestone has been the collaboration with the Ministry of Education to incorporate financial education modules into all levels of the formal education system. FEN has also developed the Financial Literacy Core Competency Framework for Malaysian Adults which serves to guide the design and delivery of financial education programmes that can effect lasting behavioural change. To date, FEN has undertaken about 700 financial education programmes and initiatives, with more than 60 million interactions through its various outreach programmes. 8. FEN aims to put financial knowledge, tools and resources in the hands of as many people as we can across the country. And technology has been a powerful enabler for us to achieve this. At the same time, we continue to undertake more targeted efforts to support individuals and groups facing particular challenges, or who are experiencing circumstances that could make them more financially vulnerable. This includes rural communities, the youth, gig workers and lower-income households. For example, our collaboration with social enterprises has been focused on supporting the youth segment who are not in Employment, Education, and Training (also coined the NEET Youth). 9. COVID-19 has been a defining period for the world in many ways. While it has exacted a huge toll on society, it has also become a point of inflection for the adoption of digital financial services. The World Bank, in its Global Findex 2021 report released in June earlier this year, revealed that 79% of Malaysian adults use digital payments, of which 42% did so for the first time after the pandemic. This trend is evident in the strong adoption of e-payments recently, where e-payment usage in 2021 increased by 30% from 2020, a doubling of the long-term average growth rate prior to the pandemic. 10. To sustain this momentum, we will continue to work with the industry and key stakeholders to further promote e-payment adoption through a coordinated nationwide e-payment initiative under the banner of e-Duit, with the tagline Selamat, Senang dan Segera. 11. The evolution of digital financial services opens up enormous opportunities to deepen financial inclusion and expand access to previously excluded and underserved populations. But these opportunities can only be fully realised if our society is equipped to use digital financial services effectively, responsibly and confidently. Low awareness and trust, and limited digital and financial literacy, can become barriers to the adoption and effective use of digital financial products and services. 12. Individuals, therefore, need to be supported to understand the risks associated with using financial products and services that are accessed through digital means so that they can better protect themselves against these risks. Given the rate at which technology evolves, this can be daunting for the average consumer to keep up with - which is also precisely why financial education is so critical. 13. One of the more striking results from the 2021 FCI Survey is the low level of digital financial literacy observed, which is deeply concerning. One in three individuals surveyed stated that they would be willing to share their bank account passwords or PIN numbers with close friends. This increases the risk of online fraud, including being used knowingly or unknowingly as 'mule accounts to perpetrate fraud. Almost two-thirds of individuals surveyed do not pay attention to the security features of a website before they perform online transactions (such as to check if the page for making payment is legitimate and can be trusted). As a result, individuals are far more likely to be deceived into providing their banking credentials through a fake website that enables scammers to use their information to commit fraud. Using mobile devices and apps inappropriately has also led individuals to fall victim to fraud such as phishing, hacking, and data theft. 14. Combatting fraud is a high priority for the Bank, and we will continue to work with the financial industry, Government agencies and law enforcement authorities to further improve banking and payment fraud incident response and recovery actions. Alongside these efforts, increasing digital and financial literacy will be extremely important to build and preserve confidence in the use of digital financial services. Learning how to use digital financial services safely is just one dimension. An important goal of improving digital financial literacy is also to help individuals make better use of digital financial services to improve their financial well-being. With an explosion of digital tools that can help individuals plan and manage their finances better, a much wider range of financial solutions, and easier access to financial advice - financial literacy, including digital financial literacy, is critical to help individuals navigate the complexity that comes with more choice.
